question.p: 5. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Taoiseach the total anticipated costs associated with his foreign travel for St Patricks Day; the delegation size; and if a breakdown can be provided on these costs including on accommodation and flights. [18900/26]

speech.from: Taoiseach (Deputy Micheál Martin)
speech.p: The delegation accompanying the Taoiseach and his spouse on official travel for St Patrick's Day is comprised of eight people (six officials and two Close Protection Officers).
Invoices totalling €2,621 have been paid to date by the Department of the Taoiseach in respect of St Patrick's Day official travel.

Monthly Foreign Travel Reports for the Department of the Taoiseach are published on the Department's website. Further costs incurred by the Department in respect of St Patrick's Day official travel will be published in the relevant monthly Foreign Travel Report as invoices are paid.

All official travel is undertaken in line with the Department's Travel Policy which is based on guidelines laid down by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. The Department seeks at all times to ensure value for money is sought in respect of each official trip undertaken, consistent with the requirements of official business.

Deputy John Brady asked the Taoiseach if his Department or any body under its aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue. [19505/26]

speech.from: Taoiseach (Deputy Micheál Martin)
speech.p: Neither the Department of the Taoiseach nor the National Economic and Social Development Office - the only body under the aegis of the Department - made a disclosure to Revenue under the recent opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment.

question.p: 7. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Taoiseach for an update on the planned publication of the 2025 National Risk Assessment. [20431/26]

speech.from: Taoiseach (Deputy Micheál Martin)
speech.p: The National Risk Assessment provides an opportunity to identify and discuss significant strategic risks which may arise for Ireland. The most recent National Risk Assessment was published in September 2024 and remains valid today.
My Department is currently reflecting on the National Risk Assessment process with a view to producing the next iteration later this year.

However, it is important to note that the National Risk Assessment is just one element of the overall system of preparedness and resilience planning for Ireland and is not intended to replicate or displace the detailed risk management and preparedness carried out across Departments and Agencies. It is however an important opportunity to reflect on strategic risks facing the country in the years ahead.

question.p: 8. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Taoiseach if his Department uses a service (details supplied). [20569/26]

speech.from: Taoiseach (Deputy Micheál Martin)
speech.p: All Department of the Taoiseach official devices and the software applications that run on them comply with guidance provided by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). This guidance is based on risk assessments appropriate to the circumstances and is kept under continuous review by the Department and the NCSC.

The Department requires all users of official devices to exercise appropriate discretion in their use and to use these devices in compliance with the Department's ICT Policy, relevant legislation and the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour.

The Department's ICT Policy states that staff should not download, install or execute software applications for connecting to external Instant Messaging on computers provided by the Department without the prior approval of the Department's IT Unit.

[20671/26]

speech.from: Taoiseach (Deputy Micheál Martin)
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 9, 10, 11 and 12 together.
Circular 01/2020 requires all Government Departments, Offices and Agencies to record, monitor and value the carbon emissions associated with official air travel.

In line with Circular 01/2020, the Department of the Taoiseach is required to make annual payments to the statutory Climate Action Fund in the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment to offset carbon emissions that result from official air travel.

This annual payment is normally processed within the first quarter of each year in respect of the previous year which means that the Department's 2027 payment will cover air travel related to St Patrick’s Day 2026.
Payments relating to air travel undertaken by the Minister of State for European Affairs for St Patrick's Day are managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

question.p: 13. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade in light of the significant escalation in hostilities involving Iran and adjoining states between 28 February and 1 March 2026, during which her Department’s travel advice and consular outreach capacities were placed under heightened demand; the number of staff that were rostered, on duty, and actively responding to calls on her Department’s designated consular/emergency telephone lines (details supplied) over that weekend; the minimum and maximum number of personnel assigned per shift on those lines during that period; whether additional staff were seconded or diverted to support crisis consular operations; the average call handling time, call abandonment rate, and volume of incoming calls received on each consular/emergency line over that period; the criteria, rota system and escalation protocols used by her Department to ensure 24/7 consular hotline operation during periods of elevated demand; and the lessons identified or planned changes to resourcing and surge capacity for her Department’s consular contact centre arising from the experience of 28 February to1 March 2026. [18400/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade (Deputy Helen McEntee)
speech.p: A very significant consular support operation is ongoing for citizens across the Gulf and the Middle East impacted by the current conflict. This is being led by my Department’s Consular Crisis Team in Dublin, working closely with our missions across the region.

My Department has provided direct consular assistance to more than 2,450 citizens, as well as broader guidance to thousands more, including by providing accurate and timely travel advice, and through proactive messaging.

Since the start of the crisis, my Department has worked closely with EU Member States, the European External Action Service, the European Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre, authorities in host countries, and others, with a view to identifying all possible options to support Irish citizens. This intensive engagement will continue.

In what remains a complex and evolving situation, since 27 February last, 19017 Irish citizens registered on our citizen registration system, bringing the total number of citizens registered to 20842 in the UAE, 3797 in Qatar, 1749 in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, 717 in Bahrain, and 295 in Kuwait. Proportionally, the number of citizens who have sought specific guidance or assistance reflects these figures. Currently, my Department is providing assistance on 839 cases in the UAE, 356 in Qatar, 18 in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, 15 in Bahrain, and 14 in Kuwait.

Throughout the first week of the conflict, as demand for consular assistance increased, the core consular team expanded from 15 to 48. This included the addition of several senior staff members who helped to coordinate my Department’s response and the deployment of surge team members whose tasks ranged from call handling to e-mail responses, and consular outreach. Since then, in addition to the augmented core consular team, my Department has had a minimum of 20 surge team members on duty in any given 24 hour period, whose primary role has been to staff our crisis call centre, which currently operates on a 24/7 basis. More than 100 officers have contributed to the response efforts at various times.

On the initial weekend of the crisis (28/02-01/03), my Department handled 171 inbound calls through its Consular Crisis Centre, with an average queue time of 2 mins 27 secs. In addition, the Consular Duty Officer received 48 calls over that weekend.
To date, my Department has handled more than 2,450 inbound calls to the Crisis Centre, with an average queue time of just over 4 minutes.

My Department’s advice to citizens wishing to leave the region is that they avail of commercial options, which, are increasing. There are now 3 direct fights daily from the United Arab Emirates and Qatar Airways will resumes four direct Doha to Dublin flights per week from Friday,

I encourage all Irish citizens in the Gulf or surrounding region seeking assistance to contact my Department’s Consular Crisis Team in Dublin directly on 01-4082000 or their nearest Irish Embassy. Further information on my Department's travel advice is available at: www.ireland.ie/en/dfa/overseas-travel/ .

Officials from across my Department will continue to closely monitor the wider political and security context in the days and weeks ahead. I can assure you that they stand ready to provide all possible consular assistance to Irish citizens that request it.

question.p: 14. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will consider opening a permanent consulate in Taiwan; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18418/26]

26. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if consideration to opening an office in Taipei (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18775/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 14 and 26 together.

Ireland, along with our EU partners, adheres to the One China Policy. This means that we recognise the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China, and we do not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

However, this absence of diplomatic relations does not preclude the development of economic, cultural, and people-to-people connections with Taiwan; nor the meaningful participation of Taiwan in relevant multilateral fora.

Ireland’s working holiday authorisation programme with Taiwan is one example of our cultural and people-to-people links. This allows up to 400 Taiwanese passport holders to travel to Ireland annually to live and work for a 12-month period, and for a similar number of Irish passport holders to travel to Taiwan on a reciprocal basis.

There are also important economic links between Ireland and Taiwan. The latest available data from the Central Statistics Office for 2025 showed that Ireland exported goods worth approximately €458 million to Taiwan and imported goods to the value of approximately €4.31 billion. Ireland's trade in services with Taiwan in 2024 – the latest year for which statistics are available – showed €2.08 billion in exports and €872 million in imports.

In line with the EU’s One China Policy, the European Economic and Trade Office was established in 2003. This office represents all EU Member States, including Ireland, and seeks to strengthen economic and trade relations with Taiwan. Consistent with this approach, a number of EU Member States also maintain similar representative offices – rather than consulates – in Taipei. There are a also number of Taipei representative offices throughout Europe, including one in Dublin since 1988.

There are no plans for Ireland to open an office in Taipei. The opening of any new office is a resource intensive process, and as such decisions are evaluated on the basis of a number of factors, including cost-benefit considerations and whether existing offices already adequately cover the work involved. In this case, IDA Ireland manages the Taiwanese market from its Singapore office, and Enterprise Ireland from its office in Hong Kong.

On a general note, the establishment of new offices are always kept under review, with a range policy considerations taken into account before such decisions are taken, including alignment with Government policy.

question.p: 15. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views on the United States ending the International Fund for Ireland (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18436/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Over 40 years, the International Fund for Ireland has delivered transformative peace-building outcomes and strengthened community resilience. The Fund’s work remains relevant and impactful, in particular with communities that feel that the benefits of the peace process have not fully reached them. Its independence enables it to operate in sensitive environments, ensuring engagement with and support to marginalised communities.
The Government and my Department continue to engage with international partners, including the U.S., in respect of support for the Fund, and to advocate for sustained support.

[18721/26]

45. Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of Irish citizens currently registered her Department, or travelling in Qatar that have requested consular assistance; the engagement her Department has had with them in relation to evacuation; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19624/26]

Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she accepts that Ireland has not done enough to date to bring people home from Dubai (details supplied); and if she will now do everything possible to bring people home safely and as soon as possible; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20939/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 16, 25, 45, 46, 47 and 67 together.
A very significant consular support operation is ongoing for citizens across the Gulf and the Middle East impacted by the current conflict.

Since the start of the crisis, my Department has worked closely with EU Member States, the European External Action Service, the European Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre, authorities in host countries, and others, with a view to identifying all possible options to support Irish citizens.

My Department's approach to the provision of consular assistance to those who wished to leave the region throughout this period has centred on two primary axes. First, to pursue all possible options to facilitate Irish citizens on the limited number of flights still in operation and to request that direct routes to Dublin from the Gulf would resume, as soon as it was safe to do so. And second, in parallel, there was a clear focus on identifying and delivering repatriation options for Irish citizens, both through Government charters and those of our EU partners.

My Department has organised two repatriation flights, which departed from Muscat on 7 March and from Abu Dhabi on 11 March. These flights assisted the return of 380 Irish citizens and their families to Ireland, with a focus on those most vulnerable or stranded in transit. My Department reached out to hundreds of citizens in both categories.

Currently, there are three daily flights from the United Arab Emirates to Dublin. My Department’s advice to citizens that wish to leave the region remains that they avail of commercial options. While such options were initially limited in Qatar, officials from my Department, including the Embassy team in Abu Dhabi, have supported over 420 citizens to depart the country. We also continued to work closely with Qatar Airways to facilitate additional travel options and this has resulted in Qatar Airways scheduling four direct Doha to Dublin flights per week from Friday.

In light of the ongoing security situation, my Department continues to advise Irish citizens against all travel to Israel, Iraq, Iran, and Lebanon. Citizens are also strongly advised against non-essential travel to Kuwait, Bahrain, UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

Irish citizens remaining in the region are advised to remain vigilant, closely monitor developments and local media, and follow the advice of local authorities, including when this is to shelter in place.
Further information on my Department's travel advice is available at: www.ireland.ie/en/dfa/overseas-travel/
I encourage all Irish citizens in the Gulf or surrounding region seeking assistance to contact my Department’s Consular Crisis Team in Dublin directly on 01-4082000 or their nearest Irish Embassy.

My Department will continue to closely monitor the wider political and security context in the days and weeks ahead. I can assure you that my officials stand ready to provide all possible consular assistance to Irish citizens that request it.

question.p: 17. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will provide a schedule by consulate and embassy with the number of requests from Irish citizens for assistance in 2025 and to date in 2026. [18535/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has a long and proud track record of providing high quality consular services to Irish citizens abroad. This is a vital public service and a key priority of my Department.

As of 10 March 2026, consular assistance has been provided in over 5,100 cases by our Embassies and Consulates since 1 January 2025. This support includes cases involving missing persons, serious injuries, arrests, victims of crime, mental health issues and the deaths of Irish citizens abroad. This figure also includes assistance provided to Irish citizens throughout a number of crises over the past 15 months. The Department responded to consular crises across the world in 2025 and so far in 2026. The escalation between Iran and Israel in June 2025 led to a crisis response with citizens assisted to depart from both countries. We also provided assistance to 20 Irish citizens who were detained following their participation in the flotilla sailings to Gaza which took place in 2025. This assistance made sure that these citizens returned home safely.

Our largest consular response since COVID19 is ongoing, which has seen us provide direct consular assistance to more than 2,300 citizens (in the gulf region and beyond), as well as broader guidance to thousands more, including by providing accurate and timely travel advice, and through proactive messaging. This intensive effort will continue until such time as the conflict is over.
The numbers of cases recorded, arranged by year and the Embassy or Consulate which provided the assistance, is outlined below.

question.p: 18. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether she has engaged with her French counterparts regarding reports that France will expand its nuclear arsenal; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18578/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I have taken note of the President of France’s speech on France’s nuclear arrangements, including the proposed expansion of its nuclear arsenal, and my Department continues to study the detail closely.
Ireland continues to engage with France and all nuclear weapon states through the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and will do so at the Treaty’s Review Conference this year.

Upholding the NPT is a key pillar of international peace and security, and a priority for Ireland. Ireland will continue to advocate for the full implementation of the NPT, including the commitments and obligations of the nuclear weapons states on nuclear disarmament.
Ireland welcomes the stated continued commitment of France to the NPT.

question.p: 19. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions the Government have taken at EU level over the past 12 months to advance nuclear non-proliferation; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18579/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Ireland works closely with our EU partners to advance nuclear non-proliferation measures, including through upholding the international non-proliferation architecture.

In December 2025, the EU agreed Council Conclusions 15851/25 for the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) Review Conference in 2026, which include the EU’s priorities for advancing nuclear non-proliferation. These Council Conclusions set out the EU's support for the fundamental, independent and objective role played by the International Atomic Energy Agency. They state the EU’s commitment to ensuring that Iran must never be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons, and the EU’s commitment to diplomacy and negotiations as the only way to achieve a lasting solution to the Iranian nuclear issue. They call for DPRK’s abandonment of its nuclear programme in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner. The Council Conclusions also make clear the importance the EU attaches to nuclear weapon free zones, and its support for the establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction.
Ireland also works closely with EU partners at the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna, including on pressing regional non-proliferation challenges.

In the past 12 months, the EU has provided support for the following projects on nuclear non-proliferation: the UN Institute for Disarmament Affairs project on a Middle East Weapons of Mass Destruction Project; facilitating the 2026 NPT Review Conference; the Preparatory Commission for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation; and the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1540 (2004) on the non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery.

question.p: 23. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade following the closure of borders around Gaza her plans to assist with provision of aid to the region; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18709/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Government remains seriously concerned at the humanitarian situation in Gaza. We are committed to working with key partners to end the suffering across Gaza and the West Bank and to make progress towards a sustainable peace between Israel and Palestine through the implementation of the two-State solution. Ending the conflict and addressing the huge challenges facing Palestinians in Gaza is critical for regional security and stability.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire. On 28 February, Israeli authorities closed all borders into Gaza. They cited security concerns and stated that food stocks in Gaza would suffice for an extended period, despite UN reports that food supplies into Gaza fell by fifty percent in recent weeks. On 3 March, Israeli authorities partially reopened one entry point. This move is far from adequate.

Since the outbreak of the current regional conflict on 28 February, Minister McEntee has attended two informal Foreign Affairs Councils with EU counterparts and Ireland will be represented at another meeting of the Council on 16 March. We remain deeply concerned about the impact of checkpoint closures in the West Bank in the context of events in the region and we continue to raise this at EU level.

Minister McEntee has engaged extensively with Foreign Ministers across the Middle East, including on 5 March with the Palestinian Minister, Dr Varsen Aghabekian Shahin. On her visit to the Rafah Crossing in January, Minister McEntee announced a €42 million package of support for the people of Palestine for 2026. Despite restrictions, Ireland's partners are delivering on the ground in Gaza but we continue to call for unimpeded access for humanitarian aid into Gaza at scale.

We also continue to monitor the humanitarian situation across the wider Middle East with a view to providing additional humanitarian assistance where it is most needed. On 10 March, we announced an additional €3 million in humanitarian funding in response to the escalating humanitarian crisis in Lebanon.

question.p: 24. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her plans to review the Occupied Territories Bill. [18710/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: In June 2025, the Government approved the General Scheme of the Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill.

The main purpose of the Bill is to prohibit the importation of goods into the State from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, in line with the Programme for Government commitment.

Legally, the regulation of external trade in services is considerably more complex than is the case with goods at EU level. There would also be greater complexity when it comes to implementation than is the case with regard to trade in goods.

The Government has received the Attorney General’s advice on the question of whether the inclusion of services in the Bill is permissible under EU law. The advice, which is detailed and extensive, identifies a number of significant legal and practical issues with the regulation by a Member State of trade in services with a country or territory outside the EU. Following detailed consideration by officials in my Department, clarification has been sought from the Attorney General on a number of legal issues.
Any legislation must be legally robust, able to withstand challenge and progress the Government's broader policy agenda.
Work is advancing across a number of strands at official level as well as engagement at EU level.
It remains the Government’s preference that collective action would be taken at EU level and we continue to pursue this.

question.p: 27. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a list of companies providing sponsorship to Government for Ireland’s hosting of the Presidency of the Council of the European Union from 1 July to 31 December 2026; the monetary value of the sponsorship; and the nature of what the sponsorship is providing for and what it entails, in tabular form. [18795/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2026 will be an important opportunity for Ireland to shape Europe’s policy direction, lead important aspects of the EU’s work, and showcase Ireland’s engagement, expertise and values at the heart of the European Union.

It has been decided by Government that commercial sponsorship will not be sought for delivering the central operational and logistical requirements of Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union in 2026.

For other scenarios where the question of sponsorship may arise in the context of the EU Presidency, guidelines have been developed to facilitate clarity around the assessment and handling of potential sponsorship proposals. The guidelines have been developed in conjunction with the Chief State Solicitor’s Office and in line with guidance on EU Presidency-related sponsorship issued by the General Secretariat of the Council of the European Union, including in particular, in relation to avoiding conflicts of interest and ensuring that sponsorship cannot affect, or be seen to affect, the decision-making of the Council.

The EU Presidency sponsorship guidelines set out guiding principles in relation to any possible commercial sponsorship of aspects of EU Presidency events taking place in Ireland. They also confirm the process through which potential sponsorship arrangements should be assessed by Government Departments and Agencies and notified to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
In summary, they stipulate that Government Departments and Agencies:
• shall not enter into any sponsorship agreement without complying with the guidelines;
• shall notify the relevant Unit in Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade of any sponsorship proposals at an early stage;
• should put a formal agreement in place, if deciding to proceed with a sponsorship arrangement, clearly setting out the terms and conditions and the specific scope of the sponsorship.
Sponsorship agreements entered into will be recorded for transparency purposes on Ireland's EU Presidency website, in line with appropriate precedent.
To date, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has not been notified by Government Departments and Agencies of any such sponsorship agreements.

question.p: 28. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the total anticipated costs associated with her foreign travel for St Patrick's Day; the delegation size; and if a breakdown can be provided on these costs including on accommodation and flights. [18892/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: St Patrick’s Day offers a unique opportunity to connect with the global Irish diaspora, including over 30 million people of Irish descent in the United States of America. It is also an opportunity to promote Ireland’s economic and political interests overseas, with levels of publicity and media attention unmatched by other national days.

This year, I am very pleased to represent the State in Boston for a programme of St. Patrick’s Day engagements. In addition to participating in the annual South Boston St. Patrick’s Day Parade, I will engage with Massachusetts’ political leadership, support EI, IDA and Bord Bia client companies, and participate in a series of cultural and community engagements.
The total delegation size for the visit is four persons (Minister plus three). The visit is ongoing. The costs of the visit will not be available until after its completion.

question.p: 30. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her department has received any communication from the OSCE-ODIHR for Short-Term Observers for the Election Observation Mission to Hungary; the number of observers that Ireland plans to nominate; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18986/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Government is strongly committed to the promotion of democratisation, the protection of human rights, and the advancement of the rule of law, as core pillars of Ireland’s foreign policy. Support for international election observation represents an important element of this commitment. Ireland has contributed observers to such missions since the 1990s.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade maintains and administers a dedicated roster to facilitate participation in election observation missions organised by the OSCE and the European Union. The current five year Roster, which commenced on 1 January 2024, has 169 members.
One Irish Long-Term Observer is currently participating in the OSCE-ODIHR Election Observation Mission to Hungary, for Parliamentary Elections scheduled for 12 April.

In response to the OSCE-ODIHR call for Short-Term Observers, Ireland will nominate two individuals from the Electoral Commission, a member and an official. A further call for Locally Recruited Short Term Observers has been received, in response to which the Embassy of Ireland in Budapest is nominating one diplomatic officer.
It is therefore anticipated that Ireland's contribution to the OSCE-ODIHR Mission in Hungary will be one Long-Term Observer, two Short-Term Observers and one locally recruited Short-Term Observer.

question.p: 31. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether Ireland was represented at the Hague Group meeting in Amsterdam this week; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19026/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Both I and my officials interact with a wide variety of international partners on the Middle East which remains a major priority for this Government.

Ireland’s engagement is guided by our long-standing and principled position, notably respect for international law, respect for the equal right to self-determination, peace, security and dignity for Israelis and Palestinians alike, and unwavering support for the two-State solution.

While Ireland is not a member of the group referred to by the Deputy, this Government is committed to working with partners around the world in service of these objectives. Ireland did not attend the Emergency Meeting convened by the Hague Group in The Hague on 4 March. Ireland attended the Ministerial Meeting of the Hague Group that took place in New York on 26 September 2025 in an observer capacity at official level. Ireland also attended an Emergency Conference on Palestine convened by the Hague Group in Bogotá on 15-16 July 2025, also in an observer capacity at official level.

Ireland is using its voice at the UN, at the EU and at other international bodies to pursue a sustainable, long-lasting peace for Israel and Palestine. Ireland remains committed to working with key partners to end the conflict in Gaza, and to advancing a sustainable peace plan. Ending the conflict and addressing the huge challenges facing Palestinians in Gaza has implications for regional security and stability. Ireland is an active participant of the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two-State Solution. On 28 January, I hosted the eighth meeting of the Global Alliance at Croke Park in Dublin. The meeting brought together senior officials and diplomats from more than 50 countries and international organisations. The meeting shared Ireland’s experience of a successful peace process in Northern Ireland as part of ongoing efforts in support of the two-State solution.

Ireland stands ready to play our part in working towards a sustainable peace between Israel and Palestine through the implementation of the two-State solution, where two democratic States, Israel and Palestine, live side-by-side in peace within secure and recognised borders, consistent with international law and relevant UN resolutions.

question.p: 33. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a comprehensive update on the work undertaken as part of Ireland's role in chairing the Nordic+ group; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19153/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Nordic Plus is a group of eight traditionally like-minded States which provide Official Development Assistance (ODA): Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Iceland, Norway, the Netherlands, UK and Ireland. The group meets to foster political dialogue and coordination around key development issues. This provides a forum for informal, open dialogue with key development partners to enhance our joint international influence; gain insight into the development priorities and activities of other donors; and maintain strong links with key international partners at various levels. Such a broadly like-minded grouping is particularly valuable at a time of huge change and competing visions for international development.
Ireland took over the chairing of this informal group for the year from 1 May 2025, and has hosted three meetings at senior official level: in June 2025, October 2025, and March 2026.

The meetings have focused on sharing information around UN reform, the impact of changes in ODA, the pushback against gender and rights, climate negotiations, and ongoing humanitarian and development support to Ukraine and to Gaza, among other issues.

question.p: 34. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on meetings and other engagements between Ireland and the Nordic Baltic 8 group; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19154/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Nordic Baltic 8 group or NB8, is a regional cooperation format which, since 1992, has brought together five Nordic and three Baltic states (Finland, Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania) to discuss current issues of regional and international importance in an informal setting. It has no permanent separate structure or organisation. NB8's day-to-day work is coordinated each year by one of the eight partner countries, which sets the priorities and draws up the work programme for its year in the chair. As of 1 January 2026, Estonia took over the chair of NB8 from Denmark.

Ireland's relations with the Nordic-Baltic Region are informed by the Global Ireland Nordic-Baltic Strategy which sets out an ambitious plan for cross-Government engagement with this important group. Ireland, as a close partner and like-minded partner of all the members of NB8, participates by invitation in official level meetings regularly.

The Nordic-Baltic Six (NB6) is the same as the NB8 excluding Iceland and Norway which are not members of the European Union. Ahead of meetings of the European Council, Ireland joins the leaders of the NB6 plus Poland to discuss issues.

My officials keep in very close contact with the embassies of Nordic-Baltic countries here in Dublin and engage with the NB8 EU member states through the Permanent Representation in Brussels. Additionally our Ambassadors in the Nordic-Baltic region engage with the NB8 members in their countries of accreditation.

question.p: 35. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a breakdown of the cost of the €800 fee for charter flights to evacuate Irish citizens from the Middle East; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19195/26]

36. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the reason the Irish charter flights from Dubai cost €800 per person and the reason that figure is double the €400 per person cost of the UK Government flights; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19196/26]

48. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the total cost of the recent repatriation flight from Oman to Dublin; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19665/26]

49. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which the charge incurred by passengers on the recent repatriation flight was calculated; the reason for the charge; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19666/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 35, 36, 48 and 49 together.

A very significant consular support operation is ongoing for citizens across the Gulf and the Middle East impacted by the current conflict. This is being led by my Department’s Consular Crisis Team in Dublin, working closely with our missions across the region.

My Department has provided direct consular assistance to more than 2,450 citizens, as well as broader guidance to thousands more, including by providing accurate and timely travel advice, and through proactive messaging.

Since the start of the crisis, my Department has worked closely with EU Member States, the European External Action Service, the European Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre, authorities in host nations, and airlines, with a view to identifying all possible options to support Irish citizens.

My Department's approach to the provision of consular assistance to those who wished to leave the region throughout this period centred on two primary axes. First, to pursue all possible options to facilitate Irish citizens on the limited number of flights still in operation and to request that direct routes to Dublin from the Gulf would resume, as soon as it was safe to do so. And second, in parallel, there was a clear focus on identifying and delivering repatriation options for Irish citizens, both through Government charters and those of our EU partners. I would like to recognise the excellent cooperation we have had with all relevant partners in these efforts.

The Department has organised two repatriation flights, which departed from Muscat on 7 March and from Abu Dhabi on 11 March. These flights assisted the return of 380 Irish citizens and their families to Ireland, with a focus on those must vulnerable or stranded in transit. The Department reached out to hundreds of citizens in both categories, making travel arrangements with enough passengers to fill both planes.

While not all those citizens availed of the repatriation flights, we recognised this as an indicator of gradually increasing availability of commercial flight options. Currently, there are three daily flights from the United Arab Emirates to Dublin and as of Friday 4 flights weekly from Doha. My Department’s advice to citizens that wish to leave the region is that they avail of commercial options.

For both flights, the Department activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism (EUCPM), which made seats available to a number of EU citizens. The EUCPM has proven a valuable addition to our efforts to get our citizens home. Through the mechanism, Ireland continues to facilitate the departure of small groups of Irish citizens on flights organised by EU partners.

As was the case during the COVID crisis, citizens were asked to make a contribution towards the cost of the charter flights, which was initially calculated at half the seat cost, on the basis that all seats were filled by a paying passenger. This contribution was €800 for the flight from Oman, and €500 for the flight from the United Arab Emirates, with no charge for children under 16. In both cases, my Department met more than 50% of the cost of these flights, and, in the case of the flight from Oman, both arranged and paid for transportation, security, medical support and hotel accommodation. My officials also assisted citizens in financial difficulty to make alternative payment arrangements.

Ireland activated the EUCPM for both charter flights, and in line with the framework of the mechanism, Ireland will be eligible to recoup a significant portion of the total cost of each charter. The total cost for each repatriation flight will be made available in due course, including once any contribution from the EU Civil Protection Mechanism is taken into account.

My Department will continue to closely monitor the wider political and security context in the days and weeks ahead. I can assure you that my officials stand ready to provide consular assistance to Irish citizens that request it.

summary.i: Question No. 36 answered with Question No. 35.

question.p: 37. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views on the situation in Cuba; if she has raised the calls of an organisation (details supplied) for de-escalation and constructive dialogue in respect of same; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19227/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I note that the current situation in Cuba was discussed at the recent Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) Summit, where Ireland was represented by our Ambassador to Caricom.

At the Summit, all parties were in agreement that efforts should be made to address the growing crisis in Cuba. Ireland shares these concerns. Our position on the US embargo of Cuba is long-standing; we consider that it serves no constructive purpose and has resulted in significant negative impacts for the Cuban people over many years. Ireland, and the EU, has consistently called for the embargo to be lifted and have voted in favour of UN resolutions calling for the ending of the embargo, most recently last October at the UN General Assembly.

We have also long called for democratisation and political transition in Cuba. The Cuban government imposes severe restrictions on the fundamental rights of Cuban citizens, including freedom of expression and freedom of assembly. However, the only way to achieve this is through dialogue and engagement.

We share the recently expressed deep concern of the UN Secretary General in relation to the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Cuba. Ireland consistently provides humanitarian support to Cuba through our funding of global humanitarian funds, such as the United Nation’s Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies’ Disaster Relief Emergency Fund (IFRC DREF). Ireland contributed to the Hurricane Melissa relief fund in 2025 and further prioritises food security through a commitment to the FAO fund for Cuba.

question.p: 38. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding the average processing time for first time passports for infants; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19273/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: First-time applications are the most complex to process as they are, in essence, a verification of Irish citizenship. As such, a rigorous process is in place to validate the identity of applicants and to confirm their citizenship status.

The processing time for an online first time passport application is 20 working days. This turnaround time applies to fully complete and correct applications, and begins from the date that supporting documents are received by the Passport Service, not the date the online application is made. Applications that are incorrect or incomplete will take longer to process.

Since 2022, the Passport Service has operated a document management system whereby incomplete applications that require further supporting documents are prioritised once the additional documents are received by the Passport Service. These applications are then processed within 15 working days.

[19389/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Argentina is one of ten countries worldwide that Ireland has a bilateral working holiday agreement with. The Working Holiday Agreement between Ireland and Argentina allows young Irish and Argentinians, aged 18-35, to live, work, study and travel in each other’s countries for up to a year. The agreement promotes cultural exchange and closer ties between both countries, with Argentina home to the largest Irish diaspora in Latin America, with an estimated 500,000 Argentines of Irish descent.

Each year, 200 working holiday visas are granted under the scheme. In 2025, there were 4,498 applications received from Argentina. 4,970 applications were received in 2024. Applications for 2026 are due to open in June 2026.

question.p: 43. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if inspections of US military planes and planes under the command of the US military have taken place in Shannon Airport this year; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19604/26]

44. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will consider not granting authorisation for future stopovers of US military planes and planes under the command of the US military in Shannon Airport; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19606/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 43 and 44 together.

Responsibility for the regulation of foreign aircraft landing or overflying the State is shared between Departments. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has primary responsibility for the regulation of foreign military and state aircraft, while the Department of Transport leads on the regulation of civil aircraft. The Government is clear with all our international partners, including the United States, on the systems in place for both military and civil aircraft.

Under the terms of the Air Navigation (Foreign Military Aircraft) Order, 1952, all foreign military aircraft wishing to overfly, or land in, the State require diplomatic clearance from the Minister for Foreign Affairs.

Diplomatic clearance is subject to strict conditions including that the aircraft is unarmed; that it carries no arms, ammunition or explosives; that it does not engage in intelligence gathering; and that the flight in question does not form part of a military exercise or operation.

Successive governments have made landing facilities available at a number of Irish airports to the United States and other foreign military and state aircraft. This permission is subject to the strict conditions of the diplomatic clearance procedures which are set out above. This policy is well known and fully understood by the United States and other international partners.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade publishes statistics in relation to overflights and landings of foreign military and state aircraft on the Department’s website on a regular basis.
There is a separate system in place for the regulation of civil aircraft and flights, which is managed by the Department of Transport.

Since the start of the crisis, my Department has worked closely with EU partners, authorities in host countries, and others, with a view to identifying all possible options to support Irish citizens. This intensive engagement will continue.

question.p: 51. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will address concerns regarding the humanitarian crisis in Cuba, raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19897/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The deteriorating humanitarian situation in Cuba is of serious concern.

Ireland has consistently provided humanitarian support to Cuba through our funding of global humanitarian funds, such as the United Nation’s Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies’ Disaster Relief Emergency Fund (IFRC DREF). Most recently, following Hurricane Melissa in 2025, the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated €3.3 million for an urgent response. Likewise, the Disaster Relief Emergency Fund (IFRC DREF) fund allocated €1 million euro.

Ireland also supports Cuba through funding to the World Food Programme. Ireland has also specifically committed €100,000 through the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation to assist Cuba in managing food security.

question.p: 52. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of occasions in 2025 and to-date in 2026 where the Irish Ambassador based in Madrid has met formally with the Mayor of Madrid, in tabular form. [20032/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Ireland's Ambassador to Spain maintains regular contact with key interlocutors in Madrid, including the Mayor's Office, in line with standard diplomatic practice.

In March 2025, the Ambassador accompanied the Mayor of Madrid at a meeting with the then Minister of State with responsibility for Overseas Development Aid and Diaspora, Deputy Colm Brophy, during the Minister's visit to Madrid for St. Patrick's Day celebrations.

On 6 February 2026, the Ambassador paid a courtesy call on the Mayor of Madrid. At that meeting, the Ambassador discussed Irish-Spanish bilateral relations, Ireland's forthcoming Presidency of the Council of the European Union, and expressed appreciation for the valuable support provided by the Mayor's Office for the annual Ireland Week programme and the Madrid St. Patrick's Day parade.

The Government greatly values Ireland's bilateral relationship with Spain, and our Embassy in Madrid continues to engage actively with national, regional, and municipal authorities to advance Irish interests and strengthen the deep ties between our two countries.

question.p: 53. Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her plans in relation to passing the Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill 2025; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20160/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: In June 2025, the Government approved the General Scheme of the Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill.

The main purpose of the Bill is to prohibit the importation of goods into the State from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, in line with the Programme for Government commitment.

Legally, the regulation of external trade in services is considerably more complex than is the case with goods at EU level. There would also be greater complexity when it comes to implementation than is the case with regard to trade in goods.

The Government has received the Attorney General’s advice on the question of whether the inclusion of services in the Bill is permissible under EU law. The advice, which is detailed and extensive, identifies a number of significant legal and practical issues with the regulation by a Member State of trade in services with a country or territory outside the EU. Following detailed consideration by officials in my Department, clarification has been sought from the Attorney General on a number of legal issues.
Any legislation must be legally robust, able to withstand challenge and progress the Government's broader policy agenda.
Work is advancing across a number of strands at official level as well as engagement at EU level.
It remains the Government’s preference that collective action would be taken at EU level and we continue to pursue this.

question.p: 54. Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her attention has been drawn to many Irish people who were upset at her Department's recent social media video regarding Saint Brigid; the person or body responsible for the editorial of the video; and the cost of producing the video. [20243/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: My Department has managed international programming and messaging related to St. Brigid’s Day on an annual basis since 2017, with a special focus on celebrating the achievements of Irish women internationally. This year, 65 Irish Embassies and Consulates marked St Brigid’s Day, representing the broadest diplomatic support to date for this uniquely Irish celebration. Events organised by DFAT Missions globally for St. Brigid’s Day are often held in partnership with local cultural institutions, artists, academics, civil society organisations and Irish diaspora communities.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade uses social media and online platforms to communicate public awareness campaigns, to promote essential services to citizens and to highlight Irish positions and values internationally. Our social media and online platforms are also utilised, in conjunction with Team Ireland partners, to promote Ireland as a place to trade, invest, visit and study. This approach towards content on social media aligns to the approach of other Foreign Ministries in communicating key messages to international audiences. Over the last number of years, multimedia digital content campaigns have included multilingual content in up to 23 languages and have amassed tens of millions of views, resulting also in traffic to key Government of Ireland platforms, including Ireland.ie.

The video for the 2026 St. Brigid’s Day social media campaign, highlighting the achievements of Irish women internationally, was produced under a live contract held by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade for the Provision of Digital Content Production Services. This contract commenced in March 2025 following a public procurement competition advertised on eTenders (Ireland’s National Tendering Website) and in the Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU) in late 2024, and conducted in accordance with the open procedure under the European Union (Award of Public Authority Contracts) Regulations 2016 (Statutory Instrument 284 of 2016). Three tenderers submitted a bid to supply the service and these were evaluated in line with the guidance provided by the Office of Government Procurement. The cost of producing the 2026 St. Brigid’s Day video, under this contract, was €8,957, inclusive of VAT. The video received almost 2.4 million views, issued in nearly 20 languages and featured as part of numerous in-person events around the globe.

The development of the video in question was finalised at the end of January. It subsequently produced a range of feedback on different platforms online and in correspondence. The Department's digital campaign also included material which issued on the social media channels of my Department which highlighted the role of St Brigid of Kildare as a key figure in the history of Christianity in Ireland. As in all such instances, feedback received on the campaign, including constructively critical feedback, will help to inform future digital campaigns and opportunities to deliver key messages about Ireland to international audiences.

My Department has been pleased to profile the outstanding contributions of Irish religious internationally in its communications more generally. As part of the Department's St Patrick's Day social media campaigns, the vital humanitarian work of Fr. Shay Cullen in the Philippines was highlighted in both video and associated communications. In addition, my Department has profiled the work of Irish religious sisters on Ireland.ie, the international platform for the Government of Ireland, which has included articles detailing the work of Sr. Teresa McKeon in Sierra Leone, Sr. Louise Horgan in Thailand and Sr. Orla Tracey in South Sudan, among others. Our Departmental communications will continue to feature the very significant international contributions of Irish religious in its global communications over the years ahead.

My Department is also proud to support the work of Irish missionaries though Misean Cara, which we helped establish in 2004 as the link between Irish missionary organisations and Ireland's Official Development Assistance programme. In 2023, my Department renewed a four year partnership with Misean Cara, and committed to providing annual funding of €15.5 million in support of its members' vital work globally on education, health, climate resilient agriculture and human rights.

question.p: 55. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the amount of funding received by organisations (details supplied) from Government funding in the past ten years. [20253/26]

Trócaire and GOAL are long-standing and valued partners of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, delivering long-term development and humanitarian programming at scale, and reaching many millions of vulnerable people through Irish Aid funding support.

The table below sets out Departmental funding to Trócaire and GOAL through the ten-year period, 2016–2025. It should be noted that these organisations, as principal development NGO partners, may also access funding through multilateral channels, including United Nations agencies, European Union funding instruments, and other pooled funding mechanisms to which Ireland contributes.

58. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the amount of carbon that will be emitted on all transport and related actions undertaken by all Junior Ministers in her Department and their members of staff during their St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026. [20626/26]
59. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted due to St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026; and the amount paid. [20645/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 57, 58 and 59 together.

My Department is actively planning for St Patrick’s Day 2026. Flight bookings may not yet be billed to the Department via our travel provider, who is contracted via an Office of Government Procurement (OGP) Framework.

The Department fully complies with Circular 01/2020 regarding offsetting emissions associated with official air travel. The Department records flights taken at headquarters and at missions. This information is used to calculate the attributed carbon dioxide CO2 in kilograms. The total emissions calculated in tonnes are then valued at the prevailing rate of Ireland’s domestic carbon multiplier in the year the travel took place.

The Department will be compiling the 2026 return to the Climate Action Fund in early 2027 in advance of the prescribed return date ,per the Circular, of 28th February 2027. The information requested by the Deputy is unavailable at this time.

question.p: 61. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the procedure for changing a name on a passport, specifically if someone is looking to use their Irish language name; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20702/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: All passport applications are subject to the terms of the Passports Act, 2008 (“the Act”). The Act provides a legal basis for the various policies and practices that are applied by the Passport Service in the issuing of passports.

Section 10 of the Act provides that a passport will issue in the name of a citizen as it appears on his/her birth certificate or naturalisation certificate. However, a name change for a passport from that which appears on a person’s birth certificate is permitted under the Act in situations such as marriage, civil partnership etc. where civil, or legal documents are available to verify this change.

In cases where name change arises, other than by marriage or civil partnership etc, the Act requires evidence of the use of this new name over a two year period. If a person requests issuance of a passport with a name change consisting of the use of the Irish version of his/her name, the Passport Service may adopt some flexibility in this policy and may facilitate the request if the applicant provides proof of a minimum period of six months usage of the Irish version of their name. In such cases, the Passport Service will include an observation on the passport recording the person’s birth certificate or previous name. This observation must remain on the passport until the condition of two years proof of usage can be satisfied. After the required two years and if the person wishes to do so, he/she may reapply (full fee will be required), submitting the required two years proof, and a new passport may issue without the observation.

These rules seek to protect the integrity and security of the Irish passports against passport and identity fraud while allowing for genuine cases where name changes have occurred. The Irish passport has a strong international reputation due to the strength of security features within the book and the robust processes involved in its issuance.

speech.p: All passport applications are subject to the terms of the Passports Act, 2008 (“the Act”). The Act provides a legal basis for the various policies and practices that are applied by the Passport Service in the issuing of passports.
Applications to renew a passport before the expiry date, for the purpose of a name change, are allowed.

Section 10 of the Act provides that a passport will issue in the name of a citizen as it appears on his/her birth certificate or naturalisation certificate. In cases where name change arises, other than by marriage or civil partnership etc, the Act requires evidence of the use of this new name over a two year period. If a person requests issuance of a passport with a name change consisting of the use of the Irish version of his/her name, the Passport Service may adopt some flexibility in this policy and may facilitate the request if the applicant provides proof of a minimum period of six months usage of the Irish version of their name. In such cases, the Passport Service will include an observation on the passport recording the person’s birth certificate or previous name. This observation must remain on the passport until the condition of two years proof of usage can be satisfied. After the required two years and if the person wishes to do so, he/she may reapply (full fee will be required), submitting the required two years proof, and a new passport may issue without the observation.

These rules seek to protect the integrity and security of the Irish passports against passport and identity fraud while allowing for genuine cases where name changes have occurred. The Irish passport has a strong international reputation due to the strength of security features within the book and the robust processes involved in its issuance.

question.p: 63. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her plans to raise a matter (details supplied). [20770/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for providing details of the specific individual whose case you have raised.

The prevention and eradication of torture and other forms of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment has been a cornerstone of Ireland’s approach to human rights for decades. The absolute prohibition of torture is one of the cornerstones of the international human rights framework.

Ireland has consistently condemned the mistreatment and torture of prisoners by the Russian Federation. The horrific treatment of such prisoners detained by Russia in Ukraine is highlighted by Ireland across international fora, including at the EU.

As part of the EU’s response to the accelerating and systematic repression in Russia and the continuing deterioration of the human rights situation in Russia, on 27 May 2024, the EU adopted a specific sanctions regime relating to the human rights situation in Russia. This regime allows for restrictive measures to be imposed on those responsible for serious human rights violations or abuses, repression of civil society and democratic opposition, and undermining democracy and the rule of law in Russia.

More broadly, Ireland cosponsored the 2022 resolution of the UN Human Rights Council establishing an Independent International Commission of Inquiry to investigate all alleged violations and abuses of human rights and violations of international humanitarian law and related crimes in the context of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. At the Human Rights Council in March 2026 Ireland condemned the use of violence, including sexual violence, against civilians and prisoners of war held in Russian captivity in Ukraine.

During this month there has been a prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine of 500 prisoners each. I welcome this development. The conduct of negotiations and the implementation of such prisoner exchanges are matters for the Ukrainian and Russian governments.

question.p: 64. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she can address a proposal (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20797/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Government’s Diaspora Strategy, including through the Emigrant Support Programme commits to supporting vibrant networks among our communities abroad, recognising the role and expertise of our diaspora across the globe.

On my first visit abroad as Minister for Diaspora, I was pleased to have an opportunity to see at first hand the work undertaken in support of the Irish community in the West Midlands, particularly by the Birmingham Irish Association and the Coventry Irish Society, in areas such as community care, culture, sport and to hear about the plans for strengthening community networks, including through business and other sectoral networks.

The next Emigrant Support Programme (ESP) grant funding round covers the period July 2026 to June 2027 and I understand an application for 2026/2027 ESP funding has been submitted to the Department in respect of this initiative. The grant round closed on 4 February and officials are currently assessing the almost 600 applications received. Applicants will be notified of the outcome in July.

question.p: 65. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the extent to which the protection and promotion of democracy underpins Ireland's approach to overseas development aid. [20810/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Democracy, through effective and accountable institutions underpinned by strong governance and adherence to the rule of law, is central for the realisation of human rights and for enabling inclusive economic growth. Strengthening governance is one of the four key priorities of Ireland’s policy for international development, A Better World. It is essential for delivering on our overarching ambition to reach those furthest behind first. It underpins all our work to reduce humanitarian need, achieve gender equality and our climate action.

Institutions that track democracy globally, have noted that,, as of 2025, the number of autocracies in the world has surpassed the number of democracies. It is estimated that some 72% of the global population, approximately 5.8 billion people, is now living under some form of rule that can be considered autocratic. This has led to reversals in the rights to free speech, association and assembly in many countries. Weak democracy and governance can result in political instability and conflict, with devastating humanitarian impact, as demonstrated by the situation in Sudan.

Ireland’s Official Development Assistance (ODA) supports initiatives to strengthen governance and democracy. These include providing technical support for electoral processes and international election observation, protecting civic space and enhancing citizen participation, particularly the participation and representation of women. We also promote access to justice and upholding the rule of law, as well as promoting transparency and exposing corruption.

Democracy and governance initiatives are implemented through collaboration with a wide range of partners, including multilateral organisations and government institutions in our partner countries. These include Human Rights Commissions, Electoral Management Bodies and Ministries of Justice, civil society networks in partner countries as well as Irish and international non-governmental organisations.

New challenges to democracy have also emerged, including the growing role of deliberate disinformation, accelerated by advances in artificial intelligence, which poses significant risks to democratic processes and citizen trust. Ireland’s development programme continues to adapt and focus on addressing these evolving challenges to safeguard and strengthen democratic governance worldwide.

question.p: 66. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to outline the full extent of Ireland's diplomatic representation in India; and any plans to increase that representation. [20811/26]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Ireland's diplomatic representation in India comprises the Embassy of Ireland in New Delhi, the Consulate General of Ireland in Mumbai which opened in 2019, and three Honorary Consulates in Bangalore, Chennai and Kolkata.

The Embassy team comprises a total of 50 staff, consisting of four posted officers from Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, six posted officers from Department of Justice dealing with visa issues and forty locally engaged staff, most of whom are also engaged on visa issues. The Consulate General in Mumbai comprises three posted officers from my Department plus three locally engaged staff. An additional diplomatic officer will be assigned to the Embassy team in New Delhi later this year, as Ireland continues to work to deepen its engagement with India in line with the Government Action Plan adopted last March and also seeks to exploit the economic opportunities which will arise for Irish companies from the EU-India Free Trade Agreement concluded in January.

The issue of Ireland's diplomatic network is kept under regular review by my Department in close collaboration with other Government Departments and this will continue as we seek to build on the progress achieved under the Global Ireland 2025 Strategy and in the development of the Global Ireland 2040 strategy.
