question.p: 68. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will address the concerns raised by charter boat operators regarding the proposed three fish bag limit for recreational pollock fishing; the assessment his Department has carried out on the economic impact of this measure on small, tourism dependent charter operators and coastal communities who catch an annual 120 tonnes of pollock per year, as identified by the IFI recreational angling survey, out of a new total allowable of over 3000 tonnes; if he will confirm the financial assistance, mitigation supports or transition measures that are being considered for charter businesses whose viability may be threatened by the proposed restrictions; if his Department has examined the feasibility of allocating a defined 120 tonne allowance for the charter sector within Ireland's overall pollock management obligations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20516/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I am aware of the concerns raised by charter boat operators regarding the measures for recreational pollack fishing contained in Council Regulation (EU) 2026/249 on fishing opportunities. As these measures arise from an EU Regulation, which is directly binding on all Member States, a national economic assessment was not completed. The Regulation sets out a broad package of fisheries management measures and was agreed following scientific advice from the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES), international negotiations between the European Commission and the UK and agreement by EU Fisheries Ministers.

The ICES advice indicates that levels of pollack stock in ICES areas 6-7 (the Celtic Seas area including waters around Ireland) remain low and that catches should be restricted in line with a precautionary approach. As recreational catch accounts for a significant portion of mortalities, management measures for the recreational fishing of pollack were also proposed.

Ireland’s negotiations on this Regulation were led by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM). My Department, together with Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI), provided technical input to Ireland’s position, including highlighting the potential impact this would have on the Irish recreational angling sector, especially the charter boat sector. Initially the proposals under consideration for pollack were significantly more restrictive, including a one bag limit per fisher per day (with no releases permitted), a minimum conservation reference size of 42cm and seasonal closure from 1 January to 30 April. The final position adopted is more favourable, notwithstanding the impact these measures may have on the charter angling sector, and provides for a maximum of three pollack to be caught and retained per fisher per day, with catch and release permitted once that limit is reached.

Total allowable catch (TAC) for pollack applies to commercial fisheries only and is allocated between the EU and the UK. Under current EU fisheries management arrangements, recreational fisheries are not managed through the TAC system and are instead managed through measures such as bag limits.

At present there are no specific support schemes linked to these measures. However, I recognise that the Regulations present challenges for the sector and for businesses that depend on healthy fish stocks. In recognition of the wider pressures facing this sector, DAFM have established a Food Vision Seafood Sector Group to examine the challenges across the sector and to develop a framework of supports and actions to respond to these issues. This Group has been tasked with identifying both immediate supports and longer-term measures that will assist the sector in adapting to the current pressures and ensuring its sustainability in the future. I have asked my officials to engage with DAFM to ensure the perspectives of the recreational angling and chart boat sectors are brought to the attention of this Group.

question.p: 69. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to outline plans to ensure that 3% of publicly owned buildings with a total useful floor area of more than 250m2 are retrofitted each year in line with the revised Energy Efficiency Directive; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [17643/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Under Article 6(6) of the Energy Efficiency Directive Ireland has chosen an alternative approach to the 3% renovation rate. This alternative approach provides that at least the equivalent of the projected energy savings of this measure are achieved in the buildings owned by public bodies by 31 December 2030. The alternative approach involves the introduction of a renovation passport whereby retrofit measures can be counted towards the target as part of a longer pathway to ultimately reach zero- energy buildings or nearly zero-energy buildings.

The retrofit of the public sector building stock is essential to reaching our national and international decarbonisation targets and demonstrating leadership. My Department supports this through the Public Sector Energy Efficiency Programme and the Pathfinder Programme, in partnership with the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI).

The Pathfinder Programme supports a range of projects including the scale-up of major retrofitting projects across the health and education sectors and Local Authorities. I am bringing forward ambitious plans to develop the Pathfinder Programme between now and 2030 to support public bodies in their energy transition by offering up to 50% funding for projects, ranging from shallow retrofit to deep decarbonisation. The Programme for Government has recommitted to Ireland’s ambition to substantially reduce emissions by 2030 and to become climate neutral by no later than 2050.

The Public Sector Energy Efficiency Programme is an energy management and advisory programme which provides comprehensive supports and engagement, including training and the sharing of best practice, to help guide public sector bodies and schools in delivering energy efficiency improvements.

There is a concerted effort across the public sector to continue this leadership role. All public sector bodies must continue to lead by example in lowering energy consumption and costs by implementing the SEAI and the OPW 'Reduce Your Use' energy efficiency initiative for public bodies. The initiative provides a programme of energy saving activities during the winter months and offers energy saving advice for the public sector.

question.p: 70. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether the EU-wide digital recreational fisheries reporting system, RecFishing, which was launched on 9 January 2026, pursuant to the revised EU Fisheries Control Regulation, will be rolled out in Ireland; and whether it will be compulsory for all recreational anglers in Ireland to register and record their catches using the associated mobile application once the system becomes operational; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18325/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: New rules for recreational sea angling came into effect across the EU in January under a new EU Regulation 2023/2842, which amended Article 55 of the EU Fisheries Control Regulation 1224/2009. While the Regulation itself applies from January 2026, the practical application in Ireland will commence in line with national legislation, which is currently being drafted by the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and the Marine.

A mobile app (RecFishing) has been developed by the EU Commission and recreational sea anglers will be required to download the app so they can register and report relevant catches on the system. Reporting obligations, insofar as recreational sea angling in Irish waters is concerned, are limited to fish species that are subject to existing EU conservation measures such as catch and release, bag limits, seasonal controls etc. Currently these requirements apply to:
• blue fin tuna, which is subject to strict catch and release measures,
• seabass, which is subject to a daily bag limit and
• pollack, to which the EU has recently provided for a 3 fish bag limit for recreational anglers in Irish waters.

The app went live in January and is being made available to Member States on a phased basis, according to operational readiness and national timelines. It is expected that the app will be rolled out in Ireland later this year.

Inland Fisheries Ireland will be the competent authority responsible for implementing Article 55 measures. The initial phase of implementation will focus on education, guidance and awareness-building to support sea anglers in understanding and complying with the new measures.

question.p: 71. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason that the replacement heat pump grant was announced by the SEAI as allowable from 3 February 2026, only for a later announcement to say that this was not the case. [18338/26]

102. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if the newly announced SEAI grants for heat pumps will include costs to replace a heat pump; if there are other grants for replacements being designed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19617/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 71 and 102 together.

Between 2019 and the end of 2025, the Government has invested almost €1.7 billion through the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) retrofit schemes to support upgrades in over 244,000 homes including over 18,500 heat pump installations (with 4,347 of these installations in 2025, up 21% on 2024). It should be noted that, in addition to the SEAI schemes, 9,600 heat pumps have been installed under the Local Authority Retrofit Programme over the same period which also contributes towards our evolving national and EU decarbonisation commitments.

In 2026, a budget allocation of €640 million has been provided for the SEAI residential and community schemes, targeting over 73,000 home energy upgrades. This is up on the 58,000 home energy upgrades delivered in 2025.

The National Residential Retrofit Plan, which was announced in January 2026 and includes new and enhanced measures, has made retrofitting supports more accessible to households. It facilitates homeowners undertaking works to their home on a staggered basis, such as allowing homeowners to access windows and doors grants as part of individual measures, as well as increasing grant rates for insulation and heat pumps.
Specifically, in terms of heat pumps:

(i) the heat pump system grant has been expanded for a maximum total grant value of up to €12,500, and includes a €4,000 Renewable Heat Bonus grant for homeowners swapping out their existing system with a heat pump;
(ii) a new grant of €6,500 is available for replacement of an existing heat pump that has reached end of its life and is out of warranty, subject to compliance with the eligibility requirements;
(iii) the VAT rate for heat pumps was reduced to 9% in January 2025; and
(iv) three SEAI heat pump pilot schemes are underway, aimed at informing an appropriate process and approach to increase the number of heat pumps installations.
More information on the heat pump grant can be found on the SEAI website at: Air Source Heat Pump System Grants | Home Energy Grants | SEAI

The SEAI has advised that the temporary withdrawal of the replacement heat pump grant was initially necessary due to technical issues with its IT system, which prevented the processing of applications. Once the issue was resolved, the grant was reopened for applications on 5 March 2026.

My Department and the SEAI continue to ensure that grant schemes' terms and conditions, eligibility criteria and rates are kept under review taking account of demand, research, innovation, evolving technology and other relevant factors, making appropriate changes as necessary.

question.p: 73. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether applicants must complete BER assessments pre and post works following applications for SEAI warmer home grant; the change that is required in the BER rating to ensure that the grant application is successful; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18468/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Warmer Homes Scheme aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through the carbon tax receipts and the European Regional Development Fund.

The Warmer Homes Scheme is available to owner-occupied properties, based on the householder being in receipt of certain Department of Social Protection (DSP) income supports. The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty.
The eligible DSP payments are:
• Fuel Allowance;
• Job Seeker’s Allowance for more than 6 months with a child under 7;
• Working Family Payment (previously the Family Income Supplement);
• One Parent Family Payment;
• Domiciliary Care Allowance;
• Carer’s Allowance (where you live with the person you are caring for); and
• Disability Allowance for more than 6 months with a child under 7.

All homes participating in the Warmer Homes Scheme must have a BER in place. If an applicant does not have a valid BER in place, the SEAI will arrange for a BER assessment in advance of works taking place at no cost to the applicant. This may impact waiting times for applicants.
A post works BER is also required as part of the Warmer Homes Scheme process and, as with the pre-works BER, this is carried out at no cost to the applicant.
There is no requirement for a specific energy improvement between the pre- and post-works BER as part of the Warmer Homes Scheme process.[]

The upgrades that will be recommended for a property will depend on many factors, including age, size, type and condition of the property. For each eligible home, the SEAI’s technical surveyor will determine which upgrades can be installed and funded. These can include:
• attic insulation and appropriate ventilation;
• wall insulation and appropriate ventilation – cavity wall, external wall or dry lining depending on the property;
• secondary measures – lagging jackets, draughtproofing, energy efficient lighting; and
• in certain circumstances, heating system replacements, and window replacements.

As of February 2022, following a Government decision to improve targeting of the scheme towards the worst performing properties, homes that were built and occupied before January 1993 and have a pre-works BER of E, F or G are prioritised for works.
Homes built up to 2006, with BERs of D and above, can still apply under the scheme, though wait times for these better-performing homes may be longer as the worse performing homes are prioritised.

question.p: 74. Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his attention has been drawn to the new construction waste levy which is leading to significantly increased costs for construction projects at a time of housing shortage and house price inflation; his plans to review this levy or assist the sector in relation to this issue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18530/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Under the Waste Action Plan for A Circular Economy, the waste recovery levy of €10/tonne was introduced on the 1st September 2023 with an initial exemption provided for Construction and Demolition (C&D) waste. The intention of the waste recovery levy is to encourage higher value waste management practices by moving material management up the waste hierarchy from waste recovery to more recycling and re-use and to encourage greater efforts to segregate waste at source. Designing out waste in the first instance should be a priority in any project in order to maximise resource use.

However, according to the national waste statistics prepared by the Environmental Protection Agency, Construction and Demolition waste accounts for over half of the total waste currently being generated in Ireland, yet only 11% is currently being recycled or reused.

Following extensive consultation with key stakeholders in the construction and waste sectors, the Waste Recovery Levy Regulations and Landfill Levy Regulations were amended in 2024 to phase out the levy exemptions over an 18 month period. Removing the levy exemptions for C&D waste complements the introduction of a national by-product decision for greenfield soil and stone. This decision allows a substantial portion of C&D material conventionally disposed of, or inefficiently backfilled, to be reused as a by-product. As the levy only applies to waste and does not apply to by-products, this presents a significant opportunity for our construction industry thereby leading to savings in waste disposal, transportation and material costs.

It should be noted that in view of the ambitions outlined in the National Planning Framework for urban development, an exemption was retained for the levy of brownfield soil and stone from previously developed land.

The Circular Economy Strategy recently published by the Department recognises that the delivery of housing and essential infrastructure remains a national priority. Circular construction measures under this Strategy will be implemented in a proportionate and phased manner, aligned with housing supply targets and existing capital programmes. Measures in the Strategy will support, and not impede, timely housing delivery.

These measures include developing a Circularity Roadmap for the Construction Sector that will promote a long service life, flexibility of use, modular construction, separability, reuse of components, ability to recycle the construction materials used and the use of the highest possible share of sustainable construction materials. The Strategy also provides measures such as assisting local authorities to establish material storage facilities and facilitating secondary raw materials depots and marketplaces. These depots and marketplaces will incentivise reuse and recycling, operations to which the Waste Recovery Levy does not apply.

question.p: 75. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his plans to protect consumers from immediate increases in the price of oil by companies using current world events as an excuse to increase their prices; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18551/26]

129. Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the steps his Department are taking to alleviate household fears of ongoing price hikes in fuel prices; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20258/26]
137. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will review correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20531/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 75, 129 and 137 together.

Oil markets are responding to developments arising from the conflict in the Middle East and the Government is extremely conscious of the impact that the global spike in oil prices is having on people and businesses across the country.

My Department is working with the International Energy Agency (IEA), the European Commission and Member States as part of a co-ordinated response to these developments, including the recently announced IEA release of international strategic oil reserves.

In June last year, my Department established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewables commitments, and protecting security of supply and economic stability. The Taskforce membership includes representatives of various Government Departments and key energy sector stakeholders. A number of meetings of the Taskforce have taken place/are planned to focus on the current situation. Furthermore, an appropriate intervention aimed at the most acute areas of pressure will be considered by government at its next meeting.

The focus of the Taskforce is the preparation of an Energy Affordability Action Plan to be completed in Q3. The Action Plan will include a review of cost drivers within the energy sector and consideration of how the EU Action Plan for Affordable Energy and associated guidance can be implemented in an Irish context.

To ensure that the domestic fuel market operates in the interest of consumers, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, under the aegis of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, has responsibility for ensuring that the market is functioning correctly and that consumers are not being unfairly disadvantaged.

question.p: 79. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if a notifying authority has been designated for Ireland as required under the EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542; if a body will be designated in the near future; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18715/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The 2023 EU Batteries Regulation requires that batteries placed on the EU market are certified to conform with various sustainability, safety, labelling, information and due diligence requirements.
This 'conformity assessment procedure' involves calibration, testing, certification and inspection of batteries, and must be carried out by an approved conformity assessment body.
To operate as a conformity assessment body, an organisation must be first approved by the Notifying Authority of a Member State.
The Department is currently considering the appropriate designation of a Notifying Authority in Ireland.

question.p: 80. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the steps he will take to reduce the current environmental management cost (vEMC) levy on tyres from its current rate to a rate of €48 per tyre; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18845/26]

138. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the up-to-date position in relation to the extended producer scheme dealing with waste management (tyres and waste tyres regulation) 2017; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20576/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 80 and 138 together.

The environmentally sound management of waste passenger car, 4x4, van, and motorcycle tyres is funded by a visible environmental management cost (vEMC) applied to those tyres at point of sale. CircolELT, as the producer responsibility organisation, ensures the appropriate management of these tyres when they become waste. Agricultural, truck/bus, construction and industrial tyres do not currently incur a vEMC. Current charges are set out in the Eighth Schedule of the Waste Management (Tyres and Waste Tyres) Regulations 2017 (S.I. No. 400 of 2017) ('the Tyres Regulations').
The Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy 2020 commits to applying a charge to all categories of tyres provided for in the Eighth Schedule of the Tyres Regulations.

The vEMC is calculated to reflect sustainable environmental management of waste tyres. The cost is primarily driven by waste tyre weight, size and material composition. Each category must make a contribution to overheads and direct costs, with no cross-subsidisation between categories, ensuring cost allocation is fair and transparent.

The Department is considering the implications of an extension of the scheme on stakeholders and is working to ensure that any such extension is underpinned by fairness and appropriate cost allocation.

question.p: 81. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 151 of 24 February 2026, the reason a person (details supplied) has been denied supports made available to others in similar circumstances; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18858/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: My Department funds a number of grant schemes, administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), to support homeowners improve the energy efficiency of their dwellings. These include SEAI part-funded schemes which offer grants for individuals who can afford to contribute to the cost of upgrades, as well as fully-funded energy upgrades for people at risk of energy poverty through the fully-funded Warmer Homes Scheme.

As Minister I have no function in relation to individual grant applications. The SEAI handle operational matters for the scheme, and they will have all the information regarding the application. Applicants can contact the SEAI directly to get an update on the status of their applications by phone on 01808 2100 or by email to info@seai.ie. Oireachtas members can make queries on behalf of applicants by contacting the dedicated email address oireachtas@seai.ie.

question.p: 82. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the total anticipated costs associated with his foreign travel for St Patricks Day; the delegation size; and if a breakdown can be provided on these costs including on accommodation and flights. [18886/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: As part of St. Patrick's Day travel arrangements, I travelled to Brazil in my capacity as Minister for Transport. Any associated travel arrangements were made by the Department of Transport.

question.p: 83. Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the rationale for maintaining the special local draft net licence fee at €545 for Loughros Mór estuary when an ordinary draft net licence costs €398; the legal or policy basis preventing a reduction of the special local draft net licence fee; if consideration will be given to aligning the special local draft net licence fee with the ordinary draft net licence rate for the 2026 season; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18933/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The current duty of €545 for special local licences came into effect from 1 January 2022 through the Special Tidal Waters (Special Local Licences) (Alteration of Duties) Order 2021 (S.I. No. 733 of 2021). The fisheries listed as special local tidal waters in this Regulation are the River Erne, the River Owenea & Owentocker (Loughros), the River Lackagh, and the Rivers Owenmore and Owenduff.

Where a special local licence scheme operates, ordinary commercial licence holders cannot fish in those waters. The number of special local licences is therefore limited and the duty payable is reflective of the exclusive rights and economic benefits attached to those licences.

Section 74(6) of the Fisheries (Consolidation) Act 1959 allows me to amend orders relating to licence duties. I can assure the Deputy that Inland Fisheries Ireland, the Department and I are keeping this position under review but no changes will be made ahead of the 2026 season. Any amendment to that duty will require a legislative change and is subject to the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Sector Reform and Digitisation.

question.p: 84. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he would support the continuation of the reverse vending machine grants under the Re-Turn scheme for retailers who set up business after the end of 2025 deadline. [18996/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Re-turn is a producer-led and owned, not-for-profit company established by beverage producers to meet their obligations under the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations.
Re-turn is responsible for all operational and funding matters relating to the Deposit Return Scheme, including grants for Reverse Vending Machines (RVM).

Re-turn has advised that the RVM Grant Scheme was established as a targeted measure to assist eligible small and medium sized retailers with the upfront cost of purchasing an RVM, offering grant support of up to €12,000 paid over 3 years. The scheme was open for applications until 31 December 2025 and was designed to accelerate the early national rollout of return infrastructure under the Deposit Return Scheme. Uptake on the grants was significant, and almost 700 retailers have been approved or have already received their initial payment under the scheme.

The grant scheme was not intended to operate on an open-ended basis, but rather to support rapid infrastructure rollout during the early phase of the Deposit Return Scheme. At present, I understand that Re-turn has no plans to reopen the RVM grant scheme for new applicants. New businesses can participate in the scheme by installing an RVM on a commercial basis or using manual take-back.

Re-turn continues to support retailers in meeting their statutory obligations and in expanding access to convenient return points nationwide. The need for grant support will be kept under review as the scheme progresses towards its 2029 collection targets.

question.p: 85. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the oversight of works done by SEAI recommended contractors when the works are 100% funded by Government grants and who ensures the work is completed to standard. [19091/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Warmer Homes Scheme aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through the carbon tax receipts and the European Regional Development Fund. The SEAI continuously monitor the performance of all contractors operating on the Warmer Homes Scheme, including in relation to quality, level of complaints, timelines, and general administration.

Contractors operating under the Better Energy Warmer Homes Scheme, where some grants are offered at up to 100% of the median cost for those who are eligible, are subject to the SEAI's Domestic Technical Standards and Specifications, the Better Energy Homes Contractors' Code of Practice, and the Better Energy Homes Quality Assurance and Disciplinary Procedures for Contractors. Requirements in relation to performance, inspections, remediation and addressing non-compliance are set out in these documents.

question.p: 86. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the supports available to people who are unable to afford the upfront costs of retrofitting their homes prior to receiving grant monies from the SEAI; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19094/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Following Government approval in January, the National Residential Retrofit Plan 2026 continues to make home energy upgrades more accessible and affordable making it easier for homeowners to undertake deep retrofits on a phased basis in a way that suits their respective budgets. The measures announced include new and enhanced attic and cavity wall insulation grants, an enhanced heat pump system grant, and grants for windows and doors. The grants are administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI).

Homeowners can take a step-by-step approach to retrofitting their home by accessing a range of individual measure grants which were previously only available through a One Stop Shop. Recognising that costs have risen since 2022, grant levels for cavity wall insulation and attic insulation have been increased.

For the first time, homeowners can access a windows and doors grant as an individual measure for the installation of energy-efficient windows and doors (to replace poorly performing windows and doors), for homes where the building fabric will meet, or already meets, a specified minimum performance standard. Many homes will already meet this standard.

To help first time buyers of existing homes to get on the energy upgrade journey quickly and at minimal cost, a specific grant for attic insulation has been introduced. This will support first time buyers who might not be in a financial position to undertake a complete energy upgrade (i.e. a deep retrofit).
When applying for individual measures, homeowners have the option of:
• applying themselves and having the grant refunded once works are complete;
• applying themselves and having the grant paid to their contractor's bank account, who can choose to offer them a discount upfront; or
• applying through a participating One Stop Shop or Energy Partner which will carry out works for the homeowner and pass on the grant savings as a discount on works.
Homeowners can check eligibility for the new grants on the SEAI website at: https://www.seai.ie/grants/home-energy-grants/individual-grants

In addition, he Home Energy Upgrade Loan Scheme is helping homeowners invest in energy upgrades. The scheme is available nationwide and homeowners can borrow from €5,000 to €75,000 on an unsecured basis for a term of up to 10 years at significantly lower interest rates than those currently available in the market.

question.p: 87. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the date on which data centres operating in the State will first be required to report on their carbon emissions pursuant to Article 12 of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 (the Energy Efficiency Directive) establishing the European database on data centres; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19155/26]

88. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether the reporting deadline of 15 May under the Energy Efficiency Directive applies notwithstanding the current status of transposition of the Directive into Irish law; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19156/26]

89. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 135 of 18 December 2025, to set out whether the Q1 2026 deadline for the first reporting cycle of the energy efficiency directive is still expected to be met; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19157/26]

90. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 135 of 18 December 2025, to set out whether, in the event that the directive is not fully transposed into domestic legislation by the relevant reporting deadline; if he expects that the reporting obligations for Irish data centre operators will be deferred by a further year; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19158/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 87, 88, 89 and 90 together.

Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive 2023/1791 (‘EED’) provides for an obligation for Member States to require that owners and operators of certain sized data centres monitor and make publicly available, subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality, information on key metrics on their energy and sustainability performance. The required indicators do not include carbon emissions but relate to energy consumption, cooling, waste heat utilisation, water usage and renewable energy use, among others.

Article 12 of the EED is supplemented by the directly effective delegated regulation 2024/1364 which requires the same in-scope data centres, as under Article 12, to report these key performance indicators on their energy performance to a confidential EU database on data centres established and operated by the European Commission.

Reporting of this information by data centres in Ireland to this database is ongoing and the Commission is responsible for making it publicly available in an aggregated manner. This information is being used to establish an EU wide rating scheme to measure the energy performance and sustainability of data centres. I am advised that work on this initiative is being advanced by the Commission.

The two reporting requirements apply every year by 15 May. With respect to the transposition of Article 12, my Department has progressed drafting to an advanced stage. This includes the assignment of compliance oversight which my Department is seeking to implement as soon as possible. My Department continues to keep stakeholders and the Commission updated in relation to this matter.

The, Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) contains many new measures aimed at further enhancing energy efficiency across society. The Government has a very ambitious programme in place to enhance energy efficiency across all sectors of society, as a key part of the drive to decarbonise and achieve our climate targets. The Government is fully committed to implementing the EED and recognises the significant benefits involved.

summary.i: Question No. 88 answered with Question No. 87.
Question No. 89 answered with Question No. 87.
Question No. 90 answered with Question No. 87.

question.p: 91. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the National Building Renovation Plan; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19282/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: My Department is developing Ireland’s National Building Renovation Plan which will outline the approach to ensuring the renovation of the national stock of residential and non-residential buildings, both public and private, into a highly energy-efficient and decarbonised building stock by 2050, with the objective of transforming existing buildings into zero-emission buildings.

As part of our role in the coordination and development of this plan, my Department is currently in the final stages of collating the most up to date information by working alongside other Departments and bodies in the consideration of policies and measures, including those required under the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive, to be included in the plan.

It is anticipated that a draft version of the National Building Renovation Plan will be submitted to the European Commission in the coming months. Once that has been completed, a public consultation on a draft version of the plan will take place later this year, before submission of a finalised plan.

The public consultation will allow all stakeholders to share their views on the draft version of the plan, including individuals and groups most impacted by energy poverty. The public consultation will be well publicised to ensure all stakeholders are aware of the time window to provide their views. Once the public consultation is completed, all views will be considered and incorporated as appropriate into a final version of the National Building Renovation Plan.

question.p: 92. Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures his Department is taking to support the SEAI in reducing delays in the SEAI grant process; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19421/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Programme for Government commits to providing warmer, more comfortable and energy-efficient homes while reducing energy bills, cutting emissions and lowering reliance on fossil fuels. The Government’s National Residential Retrofit Plan, published at end January 2026, supports this commitment by setting out key retrofit policies and measures across four key pillars: driving demand and activity; financing and funding; supply chain, skills and standards; and governance.

Increased annual financial allocations set out in the National Residential Retrofit Plan underlines the Government’s commitment to progressing our evolving national and EU commitments, and has enabled capacity within the retrofit sector to grow substantially in recent years.

Between 2019 and the end of 2025, the Government has invested almost €1.7 billion through the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) retrofit schemes to support upgrades in over 244,000 homes, including over 33,500 fully funded upgrades under the Warmer Homes Scheme. In this period, output has increased from a base of 24,776 retrofits in 2019 to 58,000 home energy upgrades delivered in 2025, including 8,000 free full home upgrades under the Warmer Homes Scheme for households at risk of energy poverty.
In 2026, a budget allocation of €640 million has been provided for the SEAI's residential and community schemes, targeting over 73,000 home energy upgrades, further building momentum.

The new and increased grant rates I announced in January 2026 include: the heat pump grant rising to €12,500; increased attic and cavity insulation grants; new grants for windows and doors; and higher wall insulation grants for first time buyers. All of these will help put homeowners on the pathway to decarbonising their homes.

The increase in number of homes upgraded follows a range of measures introduced by my Department and the SEAI. These include the allocation of additional staff and active contractor engagement by the SEAI to significantly increase the number, capacity, and quality of contractors to meet the increasing appetite of homeowners who want to upgrade their homes. To this end, the SEAI is actively seeking and accepting registrations from manufacturers, distributors, and installers of windows and doors to join their approved contractor list, with some 300 having registered to date. This initiative is part of the new 2026 Windows and Doors Grant Scheme, aimed at enhancing home energy efficiency through registered contractors.

In addition to increasing and expanding grant supports for homeowners, the Government has taken tangible steps to expand the retrofit workforce, including the establishment of six Retrofit Centres of Excellence.

The budget of up to €3.7 billion to the end of the decade, supplemented by allocations from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), will enable the supply chains and contractor capacity continue to strengthen, gain in confidence, grow, take on staff, and further invest and innovate.

As Minister, I have no function in relation to individual grant applications. The SEAI handle operational matters for schemes, and they will have all the information regarding any application. Applicants can contact the SEAI directly to get an update on the status of their applications by phone on 01808 2100 or by email to info@seai.ie. Oireachtas members can make queries on behalf of applicants by contacting the dedicated email address oireachtas@seai.ie.

With respect to the agencies and bodies under my Department's aegis, the information sought in the Question is an operational matter for each of the State Agencies concerned and as such it is not information held by my Department. question.p: 95. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 249 of 3 March 2026, if his attention has been drawn to the longest extended period of below average rainfall on the Boyne system since 1975 which took place across 2024/2025 and has displayed a system weakness in the fry counting system; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19524/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The scientific advice informing measures for 2026 is provided by the Technical Group on Salmon (TEGOS), in its Status of Irish Salmon Stocks in 2026 with Catch Advice for 2026.

Stocks are assessed by TEGOS over the most recent five-year period, using an established, science-based methodology that is applied consistently across all salmon rivers. This methodology draws on best available information from a range of sources, including fish counter data, catch data and catchment wide electrofishing (CWEF) surveys. No single dataset determines the stock status of a river.

It is acknowledged that, in any given year, operational or environmental factors can influence data input and, for example, periods of low rainfall may affect river conditions and monitoring activities. However, this does not represent a weakness in the assessment system. The TEGOS framework is designed to take such variability into account, by using multiple indicators and by applying standardised assumptions that ensure consistency and comparability across river systems and years. The indicators and assumptions used in the assessment are set out in the general methodology sections of the TEGOS Report, which describe the data sources, modelling approach and assumptions that are applied.

question.p: 96. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his attention has been drawn to the fact that no public consultation took place in relation to the proposed closure of salmon angling on the river Boyne in 2026; his views on whether this is fair to anglers in Meath; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19525/26]

97. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures that will be taken to ensure anglers who have already purchased their licence will be compensated for the closure if the proposed closure of salmon angling on the river Boyne is implemented. [19526/26]

98. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the length of time he would expect a closure of the river Boyne for salmon anglers to take place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19528/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 96, 97 and 98 together.

The closure the River Boyne to salmon angling is proposed in the draft Wild Salmon and Sea Trout Tagging Scheme (Amendment) Regulations 2026 which have been the subject of two public consultations. The first public consultation was completed in late 2025, and the second consultation recently ended on 5 March 2026. Both consultations ran for a 30-day period as is required under the Inland Fisheries Act 2010 and the Department received a significant volume of submissions.

Overall, the status of rivers as open, catch-and-release only, or closed is based on a river-by-river scientific stock assessments carried out by the Technical Expert Group of Salmon (TEGOS). The TEGOS report for 2026 indicates that the Boyne salmon stock is meeting only 10% of its conservation limit and the scientific advice is that the river is closed to fishing. The status of the river will be reviewed annually by TEGOS, and the river may reopen once stocks improve and are assessed as meeting their conservation limit.

The proposed closure of the Boyne was first notified to anglers, through public consultation in November 2025, thereby providing adequate notice for anglers in their consideration of purchasing a licence for the 2026 season. I have been advised by IFI that angling licence sales for the 2026 season opened in December in response to angler demand. IFI’s Online Salmon Shop webpage (https://store.fishinginireland.info/) contains a ‘banner notice’ informing anglers that the 2025 status for open, closed and catch-and-release rivers and bye-laws remain in place while the 2026 measures are under consideration.

There is also a long-established principle that anglers must comply with the legal requirements applicable at the relevant time and the advance purchase of a licence does not confer any entitlement to fish otherwise than in accordance with the regulations and bye-laws in force at the time of fishing.

Notwithstanding the above, I recognise the disappointment of the local angling community who fish the River Boyne but I would emphasise that this proposed measure is necessary to ensuring sustainability of the species in this fishery.

summary.i: Question No. 97 answered with Question No. 96.
Question No. 98 answered with Question No. 96.

question.p: 99. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he has given consideration to releasing NORA fuel reserves to ease price and supply pressures; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19538/26]

131. Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide details of the fuel reserves held by Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20442/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 99 and 131 together.

The National Oil Reserves Agency (NORA) has operational responsibility for the day-to-day management of the State’s Strategic Oil Reserve. NORA currently holds 90 days of oil stocks. NORA stores petrol, diesel and kerosene, and does not maintain physical stocks of biofuels, fuel oil or crude oil. NORA’s oil is stored in various port locations throughout the island of Ireland, with the balance held in a small number of EU Member States. The locations at which NORA’s oil is stored are monitored under tight security in accordance with normal industry standards.

As the Deputy may be aware, member countries of the IEA have agreed to initiate an action to release Strategic Oil Reserves to address the supply issues that are emerging on foot of the conflict in the Middle East. Ireland's contribution to an IEA 400-million-barrel release is approximately 1.6 million barrels. That level of contribution equates to approximately 10.5 days of supply. On behalf of Government, I have written to NORA on operationalising this release.

question.p: 100. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on a matter (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19556/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Oil markets are responding to developments arising from the conflict in the Middle East and the Government is extremely conscious of the impact that the global spike in oil prices is having on people and businesses across the country.

My Department is working with the International Energy Agency (IEA), the European Commission and Member States as part of a co-ordinated response to these developments, including the recently announced IEA release of international strategic oil reserves.

In June last year, my Department established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses while delivering key renewables commitments, and protecting security of supply and economic stability. The Taskforce membership includes representatives of various Government Departments and key energy sector stakeholders.

The focus of the Taskforce is the preparation of an Energy Affordability Action Plan to be completed in Q3. The Action Plan will include a review of cost drivers within the energy sector and consideration of how the EU Action Plan for Affordable Energy and associated guidance can be implemented in an Irish context.

To ensure that the domestic fuel market operates in the interest of consumers, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, under the aegis of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, has responsibility for ensuring that the market is functioning correctly and that consumers are not being unfairly disadvantaged.
The course of action referred to in the Question is not being considered due to the impacts it would have on human health and the environment.

question.p: 101. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if the impact on the cost of electricity, with growing demand for electricity from data centres has been brought to his attention or that of his officials. [19575/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment (Deputy Darragh O'Brien)
speech.p: The Programme for Government outlines the Government's policy position in relation energy policy, housing policy, climate policy, FDI growth and the many other goals and objectives. It reflects the balance between the many opportunities and challenges facing the country and the actions that will be taken over the lifetime of this Government. It recognises that increased and unprecedented investment and delivery in our grid and expanding our energy generation capacity is a priority.

Notwithstanding this, the Programme for Government acknowledges the increased energy cost pressures on households and businesses. Government has introduced a suite of measures over recent years to help households and businesses deal with the cost of energy, including taxation and energy incentives, and accelerating the rollout of more renewable energy infrastructure to support a decarbonised electricity system. My Department has also established the National Energy Affordability Taskforce to identify, assess and implement further measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses.

Data centres are critical infrastructure for our modern economy, economic growth, and the delivery of public services. They provide the foundation for almost all online aspects of our lives. The Government is committed to delivering a balanced approach to facilitate additional demand for energy by data centres while also ensuring the competitiveness of our energy system to enhance security and affordability for consumers and businesses. To this end, the Large Energy User Action Plan published in January will guide the sustainable development of strategically significant energy intensive industries, including data centres, in alignment with Ireland’s broader Government objectives. In addition, the Commission for Regulation of Utilities' (CRU) 2025 Large Energy Users Connection Policy provides increased transparency in respect of new data centre connection obligations establishing a pathway for connection that addresses security of supply and network constraint considerations, while promoting Ireland’s renewable energy ambitions.

Responsibility for the regulation of the electricity and gas retail markets is assigned to the CRU. Prices are set by all suppliers based on commercial and operational considerations. Electricity network tariffs recover the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the network from users connected to the electricity system. The CRU have commenced an electricity network tariff review which will consider the potential structural reviews to ensure continued equitable balance across different user groups.

summary.i: Question No. 102 answered with Question No. 71.

question.p: 103. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the funding opportunities available for projects relating to citizen science; if his Department have engaged with groups promoting citizen science projects; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19618/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The key role of citizens and communities in achieving environmental and climate goals is valued and understood by Government. My Department engages with several groups involved in promoting citizen science. The work of these groups contribute to our understanding of our natural environment and the responses necessary for its protection.
In 2025, €3.127 million was provided through the Circular Economy Fund to the Irish Environmental Network (IEN), an umbrella organisation whose 41 members are nationally active environmental NGOs.
Examples of IEN member organisations that ran successful citizen science projects include:
• Birdwatch Ireland where citizen science is a key input into the annual Irish Garden Bird Survey;
• Irish Wildlife Trust where volunteers contribute citizen science data identifying species including plants and insects;
• Native Woodland Trust where citizen science has contributed to the search for potentially disease-resistant Wych Elm trees; and
• Sonairte, an organisation which mobilises citizen science in the recording of outdoor air quality.

Other IEN members using citizen science and who benefit from this funding include An Taisce, Green Economy Foundation, Green Sod Ireland, Irish Whale and Dolphin Group, Vincent Wildlife Trust and Leave No Trace.

Furthermore, strand 2 of the Community Climate Action Programme, funded by my Department’s Climate Action Fund, supports projects that enable local climate action. One of these, Beaches & Dunes for Climate Adaptation, delivers training for community groups on how to protect and enhance beach and dune ecosystems as a nature-based solution to coastal flooding and erosion. One output is an online citizen science map to collect data on dune ecosystems.

The EPA, which operates independently under my Department, is active in several important projects which use citizen science to collect data on projects in areas such as clean air and water, sustainable living, and biodiversity monitoring and mapping.

question.p: 104. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the membership of the Accelerating Renewable Energy taskforce; the dates on which the taskforce has met since its inception, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19642/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce (“ARE Taskforce”), comprising some 12 Government Departments and State Agencies, has met regularly since its inception in 2023 to monitor and progress actions.

The Pillars and working groups of the ARE Taskforce meet on a regular basis to deliver on the annual taskforce work programme. In addition, the ARE Taskforce PMO meets with industry representative bodies regularly to allow for engagement to deliver on objectives and associated timelines and address barriers affecting achievement of onshore renewable electricity targets.
The dates of each ARE Taskforce meeting and a breakdown of its membership are included in the attached document.

question.p: 105. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the dates on which he exercised his power to request additional information from the distribution system operator as outlined in 2 (3) (d) on the Electricity Costs (Emergency Measures) Domestic Accounts act 2024; to provide a breakdown of each of these figures in each of the categories identified; the dates on which these figures were received since the schemes inception (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19692/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: As part of Budget 2025, the Government approved a new tranche of Electricity Credits, the Electricity Costs Emergency Benefit Scheme IV through which over 2.2 million households received two payments of €125 (inclusive of VAT) in the November/December 2024 and January/February 2025 billing cycles, at a total estimated cost of €570 million (excluding VAT).
The scheme was operated by the Distribution System Operator (ESB Networks) and electricity suppliers, and overseen by the Commission for Regulation of Utilities.

The Electricity Costs Emergency Benefit Scheme IV came into effect on the commencement of the Electricity Costs (Emergency Measures) Domestic Accounts Act 2024 on 17 October 2024. Under Section 4(1)(a) of the Act and in line with the Electricity Costs Emergency Benefit Scheme Regulations 2024, ESB Networks in its role as the Distribution System Operator was required to determine the number of domestic electricity accounts on the scheme's "relevant date" on the 22 October 2024.

Following this determination, ESB Networks issued notification that there were 2,237,381 Meter Point Reference Numbers (MPRNs) registered on the Central Market System with a classification of domestic customer at that time.

ESB Networks further notified the Minister on 20 December 2024 (Effective Date) that the number of registered MPRNs on the Central Market System with a classification of urban domestic customers (DG1) or rural domestic customers (DG2) had increased to 2,243,950.

Across the two payment periods of the Act, a total of 4,255,753 credits were granted to eligible domestic electricity accounts, worth a combined value of €488,049,754.04. A total of 226,269 credits, worth a combined €25,948,528.92, remained unallocated and were returned by suppliers to ESBN for onward transfer to my Department.

Aside from the 191,611 credits across the two payment periods that were designated for low-usage customers and remained unallocated, 34,646 credits remained unallocated due to the supplier allocated with the credits being unable to identify an account holder for the respective MPRNs.

question.p: 106. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the actions taken to date to fulfil the Programme for Government commitment to use surplus renewable energy to assist households in fuel poverty; the specific milestones achieved; and the timeline for full implementation. [19707/26]

[19709/26]

Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department has undertaken a cost benefit analysis of capturing a portion of the reported €1.369 million per day in value currently being lost; and if so, to publish that analysis and the assumptions used. [19710/26]

110. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT) will not report until at least July 2026; and the reason interim actions have not been taken to utilise wasted renewable energy for energy poverty alleviation ahead of Budget 2027. [19711/26]

111. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to direct the CRU and EirGrid to develop a Social Use of Surplus Energy (SUSE) pathway that prioritises dispatch down energy for pre programmed immersion controllers or other socially targeted loads, and to outline the necessary market rules (e.g., settlement, metering, curtailment signals). [19712/26]

112. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his Department's position on curtailment compensation where generators facilitate no cost social redirection of otherwise wasted electricity; and whether State aid clearance is envisaged. [19713/26]

113. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to approve a national pilot to convert a portion of curtailed energy into hot water heating for households in energy poverty, noting EnergyCloud's estimate of 3 kWh per tank (equating to 512 million tanks potentially heated from the waste volume cited); and to provide targets, geographic spread, and monitoring metrics. [19714/26]

114. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to allocate a ring fenced fund to cover enabling hardware (smart switches/controllers), installation, communications, and programme administration for households identified as being in energy poverty. [19715/26]

116. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the way in which households on low incomes will be identified, enrolled, and prioritised for any surplus-energy-to-hot-water scheme; and the way data protection and consent will be managed when interfacing with energy suppliers and network operators. [19717/26]

117. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to model the bill-saving impact per household from receiving automated hot-water boosts during curtailment periods over a full year; and to publish the distributional impact across household types. [19718/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 106 to 114, inclusive, and 116 and 117 together.

My Department is acutely aware that with the scale of distributed renewable electricity generation sources coming forward, the grid needs to be more flexible to account for the intermittent nature of renewables. Moreover, for the decarbonisation pathway to be efficient, our energy system must be smart. A smart and flexible energy system will reduce consumer energy bills by reducing the amount of generation and network assets that need to be built to meet peak demand. Consequently, the deployment and integration of energy smart appliances, such as electric vehicle charge points, domestic battery energy storage systems, heat pumps, and hot water heating solutions, is a crucial step for empowering households and businesses to play a central role in Ireland’s energy transition.

EnergyCloud is a privately-organised and funded social enterprise, and my Department is not in a position to assess savings associated with the programme, or the characteristics of beneficiaries of the programme to date. Officials from my Department have met with EnergyCloud on a number of occasions, and will continue to engage with EnergyCloud and other relevant stakeholders to identify areas for cooperation in relation to tackling energy poverty and renewable energy waste

A new Demonstration and Innovation Delivery Programme is under development by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland with the intention of identifying solutions to smart energy challenges, testing applications and assessing impacts. This will be crucial for the successful integration of flexible energy assets in homes, businesses and communities and will ensure that these assets can optimise energy use for consumers, as well as allow consumers to participate in flexible demand management services as these become available.

The National Energy Affordability Taskforce has also been established by my Department to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses, while delivering key renewable commitments and protecting security of supply and economic stability. It will consider the use of smart technologies to benefit energy poor households and other vulnerable citizens.

The First Report of the Taskforce set out measures for consideration in the Budget 2026 process. The focus of the Taskforce has now turned to the preparation of an Energy Affordability Action Plan to be completed in Q3. The Action Plan will include a review of cost drivers within the energy sector and consideration of how the EU Action Plan for Affordable Energy and associated guidance can be implemented in an Irish context.
