question.p: 115. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of households currently assessed as being in energy poverty (reported as c. 550,000); the number in electricity bill arrears (over 320,000); and whether the Department will integrate a 'surplus energy credit' into the Household Benefits Package or Additional Needs Payments. [19716/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment (Deputy Darragh O'Brien)
speech.p: Households spending above 10% of total income on their energy needs (excluding energy for transport) are counted in the current measurement of energy poverty. In 2022, based on this measure, the ESRI estimated that the number of households at risk of energy poverty was. ?It should be noted that targeted measures to support households at risk of energy poverty are paid to a significant share of households. For example, Fuel Allowance has been expanded to benefit 470,000 households.

The most recent Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) figures on household consumers in arrears are for December 2025. This data shows that approximately 192,000 or 8% of electricity customers are in arrears greater than 90 days. 320,000 or 14% electricity customers are in arrears of any length. This level of arrears is obviously a concern.

The National Energy Affordability Taskforce was established last June to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses. The first report of the taskforce set out measures for consideration as part of the Budget 2026 process. Many of these options were reflected in budget decisions. Examples of targeted budget measures aimed at improving energy affordability include:
• the Fuel Allowance being increased by €5 per week to €38, supporting over 470,000 households who most require Government assistance to meet their energy costs;
• to directly support working families, the Fuel Allowance was extended to recipients of the Working Family Payment. This will benefit approximately 50,000 families;
• from September 2026, those who move from Disability Allowance or Blind Pension to employment will be able to retain the Fuel Allowance for 5 years; and

• record funding of €640 million has been allocated for Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland's residential and community energy upgrade schemes (including the Solar PV Scheme). This allocation will support the highest ever budget for the Warmer Homes Scheme which is targeted at households in energy poverty.
In addition, the VAT reduction (from 13.5% to 9%) on electricity and gas bills has been extended to the end of 2030, saving households up to €100 per year.

It is important to note that the Department of Social Protection can also provide support through the Additional Needs Payment to help households meet expenses, including those who face difficulties with fuel bills. A Heating Supplement may also be paid to assist people that have exceptional heating costs due to ill health, infirmity or a medical condition and are unable to meet those costs out of household income. The Heating Supplement can be paid throughout the full year.
There are also a range of CRU customer protections in place.
Changes to the Household Benefits Package and Additional Needs Payments are a matter for the Department of Social Protection.

summary.i: Question No. 116 answered with Question No. 106.
Question No. 117 answered with Question No. 106.

question.p: 118. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his plans to expand eligibility criteria for the SEAI warmer homes scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19732/26]

119. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if consideration can be given to including the invalidity pension as a qualifying welfare payment for the SEAI warmer homes scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19733/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 118 and 119 together.

The Warmer Homes Scheme aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax receipts and the European Regional Development Fund.
The Warmer Homes Scheme is available to owner-occupied properties, based on the householder being in receipt of certain Department of Social Protection (DSP) income supports.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty.
The eligible DSP payments are the:
• Fuel Allowance;
• Job Seeker’s Allowance for more than 6 months with a child under 7;
• Working Family Payment (previously the Family Income Supplement);
• One Parent Family Payment;
• Domiciliary Care Allowance;
• Carer’s Allowance (where you live with the person you are caring for); and
• Disability Allowance for more than 6 months with a child under 7.

The Invalidity Pension is not a qualifying payment for the Warmer Homes Scheme. However, households where someone is in receipt of the Invalidity Pension may also qualify for one of the DSP payments that are eligible payments for the Warmer Homes Scheme, such as the Fuel Allowance. This would be subject to the household meeting the relevant DSP operational guidelines and means test where required for the respective payment.
The scheme eligibility criteria are kept under ongoing review by my Department, together with the DSP, to ensure they are consistent with, and complementary to, the income support schemes offered.
The Government also has other schemes and supports in place which may be of assistance where there is an urgent need:

• the DSP's Additional Needs Payment is a payment available to people who have essential expenses that they cannot pay from their weekly income. Additional Needs Payments are paid under Supplementary Welfare Allowance which is administered by the Community Welfare Service or the DSP. Details are available here: www.gov.ie/en/service/4eb45-additional-needs-payment/; and

• the Housing Aid for Older People Scheme is available to assist older people living in poor housing conditions to have necessary repairs or improvements carried out. The scheme is administered by Local Authorities. Details are available here: www.gov.ie/en/service/1ca60-housing-aid-for-older-people-grant/.

summary.i: Question No. 119 answered with Question No. 118.

question.p: 120. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment given the statutory requirement under the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 to publish an annual update to the Climate Action Plan, can he clarify the precise legal and scientific basis for the delay in publishing the updated Plan for 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19827/26]

121. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment in light of correspondence from five senior climate and legal academics disputing his justification for the delay of the updated Climate Action Plan, the specific evidence or advice that underpins his position. [19828/26]

122. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the revised timeline for publication of the updated Climate Action Plan; and the way in which he assesses the impact of this delay on Ireland’s ability to meet its legally binding 2030 emissions reduction targets. [19829/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 120, 121 and 122 together.

This Government is committed to delivering on Ireland’s responsibility to address the climate crisis and work remains ongoing across Government Departments to carry out climate mitigation efforts every day. The rollout of retrofitting, renewable energy deployment, and more affordable electric vehicles continues at pace. Government focus is on implementation particularly of high impact actions.

Ireland now has the lowest level of GHG emissions in 35 years which is notable given concurrent demographic and economic growth including an increase of approximately 1.5 million people, more than one million new homes and over one million extra vehicles on our roads.

We are making significant strides toward our target of 80% renewable energy by 2030, having now reached the major milestone of 8GW onshore renewable electricity generation. We are now prioritising the development of our offshore wind capacity. We have doubled our wind energy capacity over the past 10 years, just last month wind energy provided a record 50% of our electricity.

This Government has also approved an unprecedented investment of €18.9 billion in Grid for the period 2026 – 2030 which is fundamental to the electrification of homes, businesses and transport. The 2025 ZEVI target for electrical vehicle sales of 195,000 was surpassed in October 2025, with sales now at 212,000. I have also recently announced an unprecedented package of new and enhanced grants for homeowners across the country who are looking to benefit from home energy upgrades under the National Residential Retrofit Plan.

These ongoing efforts are supported by Climate Action Plan 2025, in tandem with its predecessor, Climate Action Plan 2024, both of which remain in place and provide a strong framework for continued delivery of climate action across all sectors, as many of the measures and actions in these plans are multi-annual in nature and effect. Work remains ongoing across Government Departments to deliver on these commitments and carry out climate mitigation efforts supported by enhanced governance and delivery arrangements.

In line with our Programme for Government commitment, enhanced implementation governance structures to support accelerated climate action delivery have been put in place in 2025 to streamline structures and ensure that key strategic projects are supported.

Looking forward and in parallel with an implementation focus, work is currently underway on the next Climate Action Plan. Following the extensive recommendations delivered by the Joint Committee on Climate, Environment and Energy late last year, the Government is taking the necessary time to carefully finalise the Carbon Budget process and the next Climate Action Plan should reflect the outcome of that process. In that regard, we are working toward bringing a draft of the new Climate Action Plan to Government later this year.

The ongoing transition to a climate-neutral economy has profound implications for our economy and society. In formulating the next phases of our plans, the Government must carefully consider a wide range of factors to ensure the approach is ambitious, feasible, fair and sustainable. It is vital that our climate policies and emissions reduction pathways deliver the best possible value for money while maximising the net benefits to society. We must protect the long-term competitiveness of the economy, maintain the State’s attractiveness for investment, and maximise employment opportunities while ensuring a just transition that supports communities right across the country.

summary.i: Question No. 121 answered with Question No. 120.
Question No. 122 answered with Question No. 120.

question.p: 123. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment given the Environmental Protection Agency’s assessment that current and planned measures will result in Ireland missing its 2030 targets by a significant margin, the additional measures being prepared to close this gap. [19830/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: This Government is committed to delivering on Ireland’s responsibility to address the climate crisis and work remains ongoing across Government Departments to carry out climate mitigation efforts every day. My priority is accelerating implementation of high impact actions with the rollout of retrofitting, renewable energy deployment, and more affordable electric vehicles continuing at pace.

Ireland now has the lowest level of greenhouse gas emissions in 35 years, which is notable given concurrent demographic and economic growth including an increase of approximately 1.5 million people, more than one million new homes and over one million extra vehicles on our roads. The Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) most recent emissions reporting confirms that Ireland has recorded overall greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions for a third consecutive year, with a decrease of 6.8% in 2023 followed by a further 2% reduction in 2024.

This progress is further underlined by recent international comparisons from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) in June 2025 which confirms that Ireland's emissions intensity per unit of Gross National Income (GNI) is significantly lower than other developed economies, and indicates that we are successfully decoupling our continued economic growth from emissions.

The latest EPA projections report highlights that meeting Ireland's 2030 target will be challenging. According to this report, which is based on the latest available data, a 23% reduction is projected against the target of 51%. It worth noting, however, that the EPA's projections are updated annually in light of delivery progress and emerging data, and their definitive assessment of Ireland's performance against the 2030 target will be made after that date.

In the meantime, we are focusing on significantly accelerating our delivery. This means doing more and doing it faster and, in this regard, it is worth noting the unprecedented progress currently being made including:
• We are making significant strides toward our target of 80% renewable energy by 2030, having now reached the major milestone of 8GW onshore renewable electricity generation.

• Just last month wind energy provided a record 50% of our electricity. We have doubled our onshore wind energy capacity over the past 10 years and we are now prioritising the development of offshore wind capacity.
• This Government has approved an unprecedented investment of €18.9 billion in Grid for the period 2026 – 2030 which is fundamental to the electrification of homes, businesses and transport.
• The 2025 ZEVI target for electrical vehicle sales of 195,000 was surpassed in October 2025, with sales now at 212,000.

• I have recently announced an unprecedented package of new and enhanced grants for homeowners across the country who are looking to benefit from home energy upgrades under the National Residential Retrofit Plan.

In line with our Programme for Government commitment, enhanced implementation governance structures to support accelerated climate action delivery, have been put in place in 2025 to streamline structures and ensure that key strategic projects are supported. The Climate Action Delivery Board (CADB), which I now chair, and the Climate Action Programme Board (CAPPB) provide co-ordinated oversight and strategic direction on the delivery of the Climate Action Plan measures and actions and provide oversight and support to delivery taskforces in delivering their work programmes. Through these structures we will continue to focus on closing the gap to reach our 2030 targets.

question.p: 124. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the long promised €75 annual support payment to support waste collection costs for persons with lifelong or long-term medical incontinence; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19865/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The waste collection market is serviced by competing private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable legislation, including contract, consumer and competition legislation. As Minister, I have no power to set prices in a private competitive market.
My Department has engaged with relevant public bodies and representative organisations with respect to the waste disposal costs for incontinence wear.

The National Waste Collection Permit Office (NWCPO) has conducted a study on incentivised charging structures in the waste collection market. This study also considers mechanisms for supports in relation to households disposing of medical incontinence products based on international practice. Recommendations from the study will be considered together with the ongoing study to explore the feasibility of transitioning our national waste collection from its current competitive licensing system to a franchise tendering system.

The recommendations from both studies including any future policy decisions in relation to waste collection and regulatory arrangements will help to inform the next iteration of the Waste Action Plan for a Circular Economy. Any future decisions will be taken in line with the relevant framework and following appropriate consideration of the studies findings.

question.p: 125. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of oil boilers and gas boilers installed in the warmer homes scheme and warmth and wellbeing scheme for 2025 and to-date in 2026, in tabular form. [19911/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Warmer Homes Scheme aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through the carbon tax receipts and the European Regional Development Fund.

The Warmer Homes Scheme is available to owner-occupied properties, based on the householder being in receipt of certain Department of Social Protection income supports. The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty.

The Warmth and Wellbeing Pilot Scheme was a joint energy, social and health policy initiative led by my Department with the Department of Health, the SEAI and the Health Service Executive. The scheme opened to applicants in 2016 and closed in February 2022. The aim of the initiative was to improve the living conditions of vulnerable people at risk of energy poverty and living with chronic respiratory conditions. The scheme provided free, extensive energy upgrades to eligible homes making the homes warmer and healthier to live in. The health and wellbeing benefits of energy efficiency are internationally recognised, but this scheme aimed to validate those benefits in an Irish context.
The results of the Warmth and Wellbeing Pilot Scheme are being used to inform policy development and scheme improvements.

The information sought is an operational matter for the SEAI, an agency under the aegis of the Department. It is suggested that the Deputy contact the SEAI directly in relation to this matter. The SEAI has established a specific email address for queries from Oireachtas members so that such queries can be addressed promptly and in line with the SEAI’s objective to deliver services to the highest standards. The email address is oireachtas@seai.ie.

question.p: 127. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether Ireland remains committed to UN Sustainable Development Goal 7, namely ensuring access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all, considering both energy price hikes and Ireland's persistently high emissions. [20097/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Programme for Government commits to accelerating Ireland’s progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030 and to adopting a coordinated approach to drive impactful action globally, both at home and abroad, addressing critical areas such as poverty eradication, climate action, access to affordable and clean energy and improved living standards for all. The 2030 Agenda aims to achieve the SDGs for all people and for all groups of society. A key commitment under the 2030 Agenda is that no one should be left behind. SDG 7 is to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all.

Energy affordability is a priority for this Government. The interim report of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce was published last November and set out measures for consideration in the Budget 2026 process. The Government acted in the Budget and provided significant supports to enhance energy affordability. This included increased rates of payment and widened eligibility for Social Protection payments, a reduced rate of VAT on electricity and gas, as well as the biggest ever retrofit budget.
The Department of Social Protection also provides support through the Additional Needs Payment to help households meet expenses, including those who face difficulties with fuel bills.

Regarding price-setting, ultimately, this is a matter for energy companies. To address supply issues, Ireland shall participate in the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) 400-million-barrel release of strategic oil reserves through the National Oil Reserves Agency (NORA).

Furthermore, I continue to engage with energy retailers to ensure that hardship funds and focused measures are in place for any customers who find themselves in difficulty. A range of protections are also in place for customers experiencing difficulties in paying their bills.

Finally, Ireland reached a major milestone in its clean energy transition last week, achieving 8GW of installed renewable electricity capacity. This marks a significant step in our transition to securing our energy future and achieving SDG 7 at home.

question.p: 128. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the action his Department is taking to legislatively protect invasive/non-native bream (Abramis brama) stocks in Lough Mask under the Conservation of and Prohibition on Sale of Coarse Fish Bye-law (No. 806) 2006, considering the expansion of bream culling operations on the lake by Inland Fisheries Ireland this calendar year; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20229/26]

148. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his departmental officials continue to legislatively conserve invasive/non-native roach (Rutilus rutilus) under the Conservation of and Prohibition on Sale of Coarse Fish Bye-law (No. 806) 2006 in Lough Melvin SAC considering their continued population growth as referenced in an Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) fish survey report published on 12 February 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20716/26]

149. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his departmental officials will continue to legislatively conserve invasive/non-native pike (Esox lucius) under the Conservation of Pike Bye-Law (No. 809) 2006 in Aughrusbeg Lough SAC, Connemara, County Galway considering their recent anthropogenic introduction as referenced in an Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) fish survey report published on 12 February 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20717/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 128, 148 and 149 together.

The Conservation of and Prohibition on Sale of Coarse fish Bye-Law No. 806 of 2006 and the Conservation of Pike Bye-Law No. 809 of 2006 are currently under review. A public consultation process, to inform the review, was completed by Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) in late 2025, the results of which will be presented to the Department in due course. I will consider recommendations brought forward by IFI before deciding whether any legislative or policy changes are required.

question.p: 130. Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will consider amending section 61 of the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992 to require that all licensed discharge points, under both section 4 authorisations and EPA industrial and emissions licences, be equipped with standard 24/7 remote water-quality monitoring devices, installed above, at and below each discharge point; and that all data from these devices be transmitted in real time to a central open Government database, noting the EPA’s limited routine deployment of such technology, the need for independent continuous monitoring rather than intermittent self-reporting, and the potential for a nationwide real-time monitoring network to be delivered at minimal cost to the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20440/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Section 61 of the EPA Act 1992 pertains to water quality policy and legislation with regard to monitoring sanitary authorities. As Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, I have no function in these matters. This is a matter for my colleague the Minister of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

summary.i: Question No. 131 answered with Question No. 99.

question.p: 132. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of households that have availed of the solar PV for the medically vulnerable scheme for each of the years it has been in operation; the amount of funding that has been used to deliver solar panel installations as part of the solar PV for the medically vulnerable scheme for each of the years it has been in operation, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20494/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Solar PV Scheme for Medically Vulnerable Customers is a targeted initiative designed to support the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels in households registered under the life support category of the Priority Services Register.

Initially launched as a pilot in 2022 as a response to energy sector challenges arising from the war in Ukraine, the scheme was agreed for households on the life support category of the Priority Services Register maintained by ESB Networks at that time.

Some 470 homes have benefitted from the scheme to date and my Department expects that figure to grow significantly, now that the scheme is in the process of being extended (to include all eligible homeowners registered under the life support category of the Priority Services Register with their energy supplier, regardless of when they were registered).

Most energy suppliers have agreed to provide the scheme for their customers, with some suppliers more advanced in their programme than others. The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) report that 137 systems were installed in 2024 with expenditure of €1.78 million. 473 systems were installed last year with expenditure of €2.4 million. This year will see a major expansion of delivery with an allocation of €11.7 million to support over 1,900 homes.

The information sought is an operational matter for the SEAI, an agency under the aegis of my Department. It is suggested that the Deputy contact the SEAI directly in relation to this matter. The SEAI has established a specific email address for queries from Oireachtas members so that such queries can be addressed promptly and in line with the SEAI’s objective to deliver services to the highest standards. The email address is oireachtas@seai.ie

question.p: 133. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether households are still required to have been registered on the life support category of the priority services register maintained by ESB Networks as of the 22 November 2022, to qualify for the solar PV for the medically vulnerable scheme (details supplied); if yes, whether his Department has considered changing this criterion to allow households who have since been registered to avail of the grant; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20495/26]

134. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if assistance will be provided under the SEAI solar PV for the medically vulnerable scheme to a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20496/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 133 and 134 together.

The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for customers/households who are registered on the life support category of the Priority Services Register. These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment, including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines or respirators. As a result, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.

The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers, with each energy supplier contacting their own eligible customers directly in line with the work plans for their solar PV installers. Eligible households can avail of a fully funded 2kWp solar PV system including survey/design, supply, installation, and the post works BER. It is important to note that suppliers, who manage the administrative aspects of the scheme under the SEAI, issue offers to eligible homeowners in batches.
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme was designed in 2022 using the Households/MPRNs on the Life Support Category of the Priority Services Register as maintained by ESBN at that time.

Due to the strong uptake and the positive impact already observed in over 470 homes, in November 2025 the scheme was extended to include as eligible all homeowners who are registered under the life support category of the Priority Services Register with their energy supplier, regardless of when they were registered, as long the house is built and occupied on or before 31 December 2020.

Each of the energy suppliers is responsible for contacting their own eligible customers directly, in line with the work plans for their solar PV installers. Contractors are sending letters of interest in batches, based on their operational capacity and business plans.
A homeowner can participate on the pilot scheme through the following operational energy suppliers:
• Flogas
• Bord Gáis
• SSE Airtricity
• Electric Ireland

speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 136 and 135 together.
My Department is continuing to prepare Ireland's Social Climate Plan in close consultation with the European Commission and relevant Departmental stakeholders.

In line with the requirements of the regulation, a public event on the draft Plan, co-hosted by my Department and the European Commission, will be held in the coming months. At this event, information will be shared on the contents of the draft Plan as well as detail on how the consultation process completed last year fed into the design of the draft. Following the event, a final draft Plan will be submitted to Government for approval. It will then be submitted to the European Commission for final approval.
To facilitate this level of engagement, the Plan will be submitted to the Commission, for approval, later this year.

question.p: 143. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he would consider expanding the membership of the Biomethane Implementation Group, which has been established to oversee implementation of the National Biomethane Strategy and delivery of the 25 key strategic actions to ensure the necessary infrastructure and supports are in place to aid development of an indigenous biomethane sector of scale, to include the National Biogas Concern Group (NBCG) to ensure communities are represented within the decision making process; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20692/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Delivery of the Government's indigenous biomethane ambition by 2030 will have multiple cross-sectoral benefits for Ireland’s economy, energy security and emissions profile.

The Biomethane Implementation Group has been established to oversee implementation of the National Biomethane Strategy. The group is made up of entities that have specific responsibility for implementation of individual actions from the strategy. Its role is to monitor the delivery of the overall 25 key strategic actions set out in the strategy and support overall target achievement. In addition to members of the group having specific actions from the strategy to deliver themselves, the Biomethane Implementation Group has been assigned lead responsibility and ownership for delivery of 4 actions, and is identified as a key stakeholder in the delivery of a further 2 actions. Due to the groups specific responsibilities, it is not envisaged that the National Biogas Concern group would be included in the Biomethane Implementation Group at this time.

The group continues to engage with action owners to monitor implementation and a full progress report on delivery of actions within the National Biomethane Strategy is now published on the biomethane policy information page on the Gov.ie website.

My Department is committed to offering information and support to address concerns, foster the sharing of information and promote transparency around AD developments and the role they will play in decarbonisation in Ireland. The online information website is now live and will be gradually updated with additional relevant information. It is available at the following link on Gov.ie: Biomethane policy information.

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: In late 2023, the Department signed a Funding Agreement with the Angling Council of Ireland (ACI), the national governing body for angling in Ireland, to provide funding for disbursement to ACI affiliated organisations to support their participation in the AAG.

I understand that the Federation of Irish Salmon and Sea Trout Anglers (FISSTA) was not and is not currently affiliated with the national governing body (ACI) so therefore it was not possible to include them for the purposes of this Agreement.

question.p: 146. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason a probability threshold of 85% was initially chosen as a datum governing Lough Corrib SAC for the draft Wild Salmon and Sea Trout Tagging Scheme (Amendment) Regulations 2025 & Conservation Measures for the 2026 Season given that a baseline of 75% has been a core scientific standard since 2007; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20713/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment

The 85% did not represent a datum governing Lough Corrib SAC specifically. It was a proposed probability threshold that would apply nationally if adopted.

question.p: 151. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the proposals to issue exploration licences in respect of potential energy reserves in Irish territorial waters; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20952/26]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: As outlined in the 2022 Policy Statement on Petroleum Exploration and Production, my Department no longer accepts new applications for exploration licences for natural gas or oil. This commitment was made effective immediately upon the previous Government taking office in June 2020, and the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 placed this commitment on a statutory basis.

question.p: 152. Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Defence the number of workers who retired from the public service in each of the last three years who have a fast accrual element to their public service pension; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18967/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: There are a number of different cohorts within the public service who have entitlement to what is known as ‘fast accrual’ in their pensions.
I do not have responsibility or information in relation to all of the public service, but I can provide information regarding personnel who retire from the Permanent Defence Force (PDF).
The number of personnel who retired from the PDF in the last 3 years is as follows:

The occupational pension entitlements for PDF personnel are governed by the Defence Forces Superannuation Scheme, and with the exception of a very small number of specific personnel, provide for fast accrual pension entitlements.

The specific pension entitlements of individual members of the PDF depend on various factors such as the date a person first joins the public service, as well as retiring rank and pensionable service and remuneration.

question.p: 153. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Defence the proposals she is implementing in relation to recruitment in the Defence Forces; the number which have been recruited for each of the years 2021 to 2025; the number that have retired in the same period, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18421/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: Increasing recruitment and retention of personnel in the Defence Forces is a key priority for me as Minister for Defence. As a government, we are committed to putting the resources in place to achieve Level of Ambition 2 and a crucial element of this is personnel expansion. A range of measures have been undertaken to tackle recruitment and retention challenges in the Defence Forces over the last number of years. As a result, we have seen a stabilisation in the strength of the Permanent Defence Force in 2024 and an increase of almost 200 personnel in 2025.

In addition, it is very positive to see that interest in a career in the Defence Forces continues to grow, with a total of 16,510 applications received in 2025. Increases in application numbers and in the overall strength of the PDF demonstrate that the key enabling measures which the Government has introduced to support and drive Defence Forces recruitment and retention are yielding results. I want to build on the progress achieved in 2025 and have set a target of 850 inductions for 2026.
Additional information pertaining to the number of inductions and discharges from 2021 to 2025, as requested by the Deputy, has been provided by the military authorities in the following table:
The term 'discharges' encompasses the number of personnel who left for a variety of reasons including on age grounds, at end of contract and voluntary discharges.

Turnover rates in the Defence Forces are carefully monitored, and I am pleased to say that an encouraging indicator of the stabilisation in the strength achieved in recent years, has been a reduction in the turnover rate from an average of 10 percent per annum between 2021 and 2024, to under 8 percent last year.

A range of measures have been undertaken to support the retention of personnel in the Defence Forces in recent years. These include increases in the maximum ages of recruitment and retirement respectively, the extension of private secondary healthcare to all personnel, and the application of the provisions of the Working Time Directive across the Defence Forces subject to certain exemptions. In addition, the Patrol Duty allowance payable to Naval Service personnel at sea has been doubled after ten days at sea in a calendar year while the Naval Service tax credit has been extended for a further five years.
There continues to be significant progress on pay with all personnel benefiting from a pay award delivered in February with a further increase due in June.

Underpinning these and other measures, I ensured that Budget 2026 provided a record allocation of €1.49 billion for the Defence Sector, an increase of €145 million on 2025. These funds include provision for the recruitment of a net 400 additional PDF members per annum

Significant strides continue to be made on a number of recruitment and retention fronts and the allocation of record levels of expenditure is illustrative of my commitment to enhancing the recruitment and retention rates in the Permanent Defence Force in order to meet the targets set in Level of Ambition 2.

question.p: 154. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Defence to outline Ireland’s Naval Defence capabilities and assets; to compare it with five years ago; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18446/26]

summary.i: The following deferred reply was received under Standing Orders.

debateSection.summary: This question was due for answer on the 24th of March this year however the information was not to hand at that time.
The attached table sets out the Permanent Defence Force capabilities and assets in 2026

A key priority for me as Minister for Defence is to ensure that the current operational capability of the Defence Forces is maintained and further developed. In the context of an evolving geopolitical and security environment, it is essential that Ireland continues to enhance the capabilities of its Defence Forces.

One of the key recommendations from the Commission on the Defence Forces was to implement a top down capability development planning process (CDPP) to bring planning for Defence Forces capabilities in line with best practice. In early 2023, a Capability Development Unit was established in the Department within the Strategic Change and Capability Development Division. It is civil/military in terms of staffing, with military staff from across the three services of the Defence Forces, providing an overarching joint perspective to capability planning.

The Unit is now well established and in the final stages of the upstream phase, the key output of which is a 12 year Capability Development Programme, that will identify, at a high level, the capability requirements for the Defence Forces out to 2040. This programme will inform future decisions on the prioritisation and development of capabilities in support of the strategic Level of Ambition 2 set out in the Defence Policy Review, the Maritime Security Strategy and the objectives outlined in the Strategic Framework and the updated Detailed Implementation Plan for the Commission on the Defence Forces. I expect this Programme to be finalised later in 2026.

Once finalised, the Programme will be implemented through rolling four-year Capability Development Plans, the first of which will cover the period 2028 to 2032. Capabilities will then be developed and acquired in line with available capital allocations under the National Development Plan. This structured and phased approach will guide future investment decisions as part of the overall development of Defence Forces capability.

question.p: 160. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Defence the position regarding the implementation of the Regeneration and Development Plan of the Reserve Defence Forces; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18641/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: My key priority is the modernisation of our Defence Forces, and revitalising our Reserve Defence Forces is a vital part of that transformation process.

The Reserve Defence Force (RDF) Regeneration Plan, published in July 2024, coordinates 27 actions across four objectives [(i) Recruitment & Retention, (ii) Resourcing, (iii) Training & Education, and (iv) Integration & Deployment], to modernise the RDF and ensure it can seamlessly train, operate, and deploy with the Permanent Defence Force.

The Military Authorities have provided the table below which outlines the status of each of the actions in the Regeneration and Development Plan. 12 actions are complete and have moved to implementation and / or integrated into business as usual. 3 actions are on schedule. 12 actions are continuing to progress. 0 actions have significant barriers to completion.

td.p: Strategy to implement multiple induction streams for continuous recruitment into the RDF.

p.b: Enabling of RDF Multi Induction Streams.

td.p: Regulatory provision be made for the induction of personnel via several mechanisms in addition to general service recruitment.
- Continuing to progress. - Regulatory underpinning is required for the direct entry of personnel at non-commissioned ranks. Evaluation currently under consideration.

p.b: RDF Master Messaging and Communication Strategy.

td.p: A strategy to coordinate an ongoing public awareness campaign highlighting the RDF.
- Complete - Implementation ongoing through the Reserve Strategic Engagement Team (ReSET).
A communication strategy to increase the awareness and understanding of the RDF amongst key industries. Strategy will promote the mutual benefits of service in the RDF.

- Continuing to progress - An Employer Protection Review is due to commence in Q2 2026. The Defence Forces intend to hold workshops with employer representative bodies in order to develop an employer engagement strategy.
A communication strategy to increase the awareness and understanding of the RDF amongst third level students. Strategy will promote the benefits of service in the RDF.
- Complete - Implementation ongoing through the Reserve Strategic Engagement Team (ReSET).

p.b: RDF Local Engagement Teams to promote the RDF.

td.p: A mechanism for the training, resourcing and deployment of RDF Local Engagement Teams (LETs) to complement public awareness campaigns.
- Complete - Implementation ongoing through the Reserve Strategic Engagement Team (ReSET).
A strategy to ensure the RDF is a positive working environment that reflects contemporary Irish society.
- Complete - Initiatives being implemented via recruiting strategy and Defence Inclusion Office work streams.

p.b: Review of RDF Personal Kit Issue Requirements.

td.p: - Complete - Implementation via DF Clothing Committee.

p.b: Review Logistics Regulations to Equip RDF.

td.p: The equipping of Reservists has robust regulatory underpinning.
- Complete - Implementation via DF Clothing Committee.
An assessment of RDF Unit capabilities to ensure RDF Units are resourced appropriately.
- On schedule. - Assessments commenced in Q1 2025 and scheduled for completion in Q3 2026.
An assessment of RDF Unit facilities to ensure RDF Units are resourced appropriately.
- On schedule. - Assessments likely to be completed in Q3 2026 to inform DF building plan (2027).

p.b: Assessment of all resource requirements underpinning operationalisation of Single Force Concept.

td.p: A continuous assessment of resources required to underpin the Single Force Concept.
- Complete - Resource planning and management process in place.
A whole of career training and education strategy for Reservists.
Modularisation and utilisation of blended learning to increase accessibility to training and professional military education.
- Complete - Project team with oversight established.

p.b: Recognition and utilisation of Reservists Qualifications and Skills.

td.p: A mechanism for the assessment and recognition of civilian qualifications be established.
Civilian to military bridging be introduced to facilitate the utilisation of Reservists qualifications, skills, and experience. This initiative to be complemented by introducing a skills database.

- Continuing to progress. A project team has been established within the SPARX programme to examine how Reservists civilian skills can be better utilised. Potential solutions scheduled for April 2026.
RDF activity is recorded and reported monthly. Data used to assess performance and determine operational readiness levels.

p.b: Establish RDF Management Offices in Brigades and Formations.

td.p: Develop COA for the provision of a staff function that will oversee the implementation of the RDFRDP within the Brigades and Formations. These staff will support the day-to-day functioning of RDF Units.
- Continuing to progress- Development in line with future force design work streams.
A standing mechanism comprising of key stakeholders established to facilitate the provision of appropriate regulations to enable the regeneration and development of the RDF.
- Ongoing - Amendments to regulations carried out on a needs basis.
Review of the application of the Single Force Concept. Initiatives developed to enable operational deployment on a routine basis.
- Continuing to progress- RDF Deployment Framework has been developed will enable Unit Commanders to deploy Reservists as required.
Protocols for the deployment of Reservists overseas developed.
- Continuing to progress- Protocols for overseas deployment of Reservists under development.
The Army Reserve force structure to be reviewed and transformed to support the wider transformation of the Army.
- Continuing to progress- Development in line with future force design work streams.
The establishment of the NSR to be increased to a minimum establishment of 400 personnel. Disposition and organisation to be considered.
- Continuing to progress- Development in line with future force design work streams.

p.b: Reserve Transformation - Air Corps Reserve Establishment.

td.p: An Air Corps Reserve with an establishment for a minimum of 200 personnel be developed.
- Continuing to progress- Development in line with future force design work streams.
Former and retiring members of the PDF be invited to apply to the FLR. Mechanism for the assignment of personnel of the FLR to parent units.
- Continuing to progress- Regulatory underpinning required to enable the voluntary transfer of enlisted personnel to the FLR is scheduled for Q2/Q3 2026.
Develop enhanced military capabilities across all domains utilising Reservist skillsets. Explore appropriate conditions of service for such specialists.
- Continuing to progress- Awaiting outcome of Action 15 (SPARX programme).

- Exploring options for the establishment of a Third Line Specialist Reserve for personnel with specific skillsets. Personnel may serve under a modified induction and effectivity criteria that is not constrained by physical or cognitive ability - Project in discovery phase.

p.b: Reserve A/CHOD, Service A/Chiefs and Senior Enlisted Leaders.

td.p: Reserve A/CHOD, Service A/ Chiefs and Senior Enlisted Leaders Appointed.
- Continuing to progress- This action cannot be progressed until there is a CHOD in place.

p.b: Application of the Working Time Directive.

td.p: RDF deployment and activities conducted in accordance with the provisions of the WTD as it applies to the DF.
- On schedule - RDF training activity is out of scope. RDF support activity is in scope when on Supplemental Military Service (SMS). Reservist hours recorded for SMS.

speech.p: Furthermore other areas of work underway in the Reserve Defence Force sphere include:
• A new RDF Recruitment system, which will result in a more streamlined and user-friendly process for applicants;

• A significant RDF advertising awareness campaign will be coordinated across all media modes including television and radio adverts, to raise the public’s awareness of the opportunities available in the RDF;

• A substantial expansion of the RDF budget which continues to increase in pace with the enhanced role of the RDF. To illustrate this, the budget allocation in 2025 was €3.542m and I have further increased it to €4.535m for 2026.

• To ensure the framework for the Reserve is fit for purpose a review of the current legal and policy framework governing the RDF is underway. The second part of this review will focus on options for employment protection legislation.

question.p: 161. Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Defence the number of Defence Forces personnel, by rank, that would be needed to fully train a new army cadetship class of 65 personnel. [18681/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: The Army Cadet Course Syllabus of training is a specialised and intensive training programme of 17 months’ duration.
The military authorities have provided the requested information on the number of instructors required to train an Army Cadet class of 65 persons and this is set out in the following table:
The 2026 Cadetship competition recently closed for applications. Last years competition attracted in excess of 1,800 applications and resulted in 79 inductions.
In 2024 the number of Cadets inducted increased to 80 and I have instructed that this continue in 2026. Currently there are 145 Cadets in training across the Defence Forces of which 106 are Army.

question.p: 162. Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Defence if the maximum age limit to join the Defence Forces is 39 years of age, can an individual join right up to their 40th birthday; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18867/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: I am advised that the age limits for personnel wishing to enter the Defence Forces are as set out in Regulations made pursuant to the Defence Act 1954, as amended.

The nature of military service requires that the age profile of personnel in the Defence Forces be appropriately managed to ensure that capability requirements are met. In that context, the maximum recruitment age was increased in 2024 to 39 years of age for General Service Recruits, Cadets, and certain specialists. Candidates must be under 39 on the closing date for applications for each competition, or in the case of General Service Recruitment, be under 39 on the date of application. Additionally, the maximum recruitment age for Direct Entry Officer specialists was increased to 50, and candidates for Direct Entry competitions should accordingly be under 50 on the closing date(s) for applications.

I am also advised by Defence Forces management that conditions and eligibility criteria for entry to and for service in the Defence Forces, including the methodology used for assessments, are subject to continuous review and modification, having regard to the needs of the organisation, health and safety and the development of best practices.

Increases in the maximum recruitment ages is one of a number of key enabling measures introduced by Government to drive and support Defence Forces Recruitment. Other measures we have undertaken include the extension of private secondary healthcare to all personnel, the application of the provisions of the Working Time Directive across the Defence Forces subject to certain exemptions, increases to Patrol Duty allowance payable to Naval Service personnel at sea, and extension of the Naval Service tax credit to 2029.
In addition, there continues to be significant progress on pay with all personnel benefiting from a pay award delivered last month with a further increase due in June.

I am pleased to say that these enabling measures are beginning to yield results. A total of 790 inductions were achieved in 2025, while the overall strength of the Permanent Defence Force grew by almost 200 personnel. Interest in a career in the Defence Forces continues to grow with overall application numbers increasing from a total of 9,479 in 2023 to a total of 16,510 applications last year. Opportunities for careers in the Defence Forces remain open via a diverse range of ongoing competitions including those for general service and for Direct Entry specialist roles, while the 2026 Cadetship competition has recently closed for applications.
The Irish Defence Forces value diversity and inclusion and foster a culture of respect, dignity, and equality for all members.

question.p: 163. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Defence the position regarding the super medium helicopter programme; when a model will be selected given that the programme is now two years old; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18939/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: My priority as Minister for Defence is to ensure that the operational capability of the Air Corps, Army, and Naval Service is maintained and developed. This is to enable the Defence Forces to carry out the roles assigned by Government. Equipment priorities for the Air Corps, Army, and Naval Service are considered in the context of the established capability development and Equipment Development Planning (EDP) processes.
Capital investment in aircraft continues with the placing of the following contracts in recent years:
• Two new Airbus C-295 in Maritime Patrol Aircraft delivered in 2023.
• One new Airbus C-295 in a Military Transport configuration. This aircraft was delivered in October 2025.
• One new Dassault Falcon 6X Strategic Reach Aircraft. This aircraft was delivered in December 2025.
• Four Airbus H145M Light Utility Multi-Role Helicopters. These aircraft are in production with phased delivery planned in 2027 and 2028.

Future procurements are progressed in the context of the rolling Equipment Development Plan (EDP), which encompasses a programme of sustained equipment procurement/acquisition across the Air Corps, Army, and Naval Service as identified and prioritised in the Strategic Framework, the recently updated Detailed Implementation Plan for the Report of the Commission on the Defence Forces.

This is part of the ambitious programme of work to move to Level of Ambition 2 ( LOA2) and will ensure that the Air Corps and the wider Defence Forces have the major equipment platforms, ancillary equipment and force protection equipment required to carry out their important roles both at home and overseas.

Capital funding of €1.7 billion has been allocated to Defence under the National Development Plan for the period 2026-2030. The funding represents an increase of €600 million or 55% on the previous baseline figure of €1.1 billion.

Future Air Corps projects identified within these planning processes include the acquisition of a fleet of super-medium helicopters to replace the current fleet of AW-139 medium helicopters. This projects is underway and is in the assessment phase in accordance with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines. No fixed timeline has yet been set for the selection of a specific helicopter type.

I am satisfied that the ongoing programme of prioritised sustained investment in upgrading and enhancing Air Corps capabilities will ensure that the Defence Forces continue to be suitably equipped to fulfil all roles assigned by Government.

question.p: 164. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Defence if her Department will provide assurances and a commitment that funds are available for all the programmes on the detailed implementation plan; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18940/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: Thank you to the Deputy for this question.
The Detailed Implementation Plan was published on 10 February 2026. This document sets out the updated timelines for the implementation of the recommendations of the Commission on the Defence Forces.
The Defence Group budget for 2026 is €1.492 billion an increase of €142 million (11%) in the Defence group allocation compared to 2025.

The 2026 allocation includes the highest ever level of capital funding, at €300 million in 2026. This level of capital investment ensures that significant progress can be made on key projects under the Detailed Implementation Plan, including Counter-UAS technology, the priority Military Radar Programme and other vitally important Defence projects. Emphasis is also being placed on targeting investment in accommodation and gyms to incentivise and retain new entrants to the Forces.

The revised NDP Capital allocation for the Defence Vote Group for the period 2026-2030 is €1.7 billion. This represents an increase of €600 million (55%) on the previous baseline of €1.1 billion. For 2026, the Defence capital allocation increased by €66 million to €300 million, with a further rise to €360million in 2029-2030.

The Government approved the move to ‘Level of Ambition 2’ (LOA2), as set out in the capability framework devised by the Commission on the Defence Forces (CoDF) in July, 2022. This provided for a rise in the Defence budget to €1.5 billion, in 2022 prices, by 2028, as part of the annual Estimates process.

The delivery of the Updated Detailed Implementation Plan will be progressed from within the existing Defence Vote Group allocation, with the appropriate budgetary provision for 2027 to 2028 to be determined within annual estimate processes, as well as the relevant elements of the Defence Sectoral Plan under the National Development Plan 2025-2030. All timelines for implementation under the Updated Detailed Implementation Plan are consistent with the NDP profile and the Defence Sectoral Plan.

question.p: 167. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Defence if the security duty allowance will be paid to Irish reservists for all activities undertaken during the Irish presidency of the EU.; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19671/26]

A proposal to bring the RDF in line with their PDF counterparts has been approved in principle by the Department. Consideration of the criteria to be applied, the mechanism for applying for and payment of SDA to members of the RDF is being advanced by the Defence Forces.

question.p: 168. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the date on which Government approval was granted for the procurement of the Falcon 6X aircraft; whether a formal memorandum was submitted to Government; and whether a cost-benefit or options appraisal accompanied that submission. [20283/26]

169. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether alternative aircraft types were assessed during the procurement process for the Falcon 6X strategic reach aircraft; the number of aircraft types evaluated; and whether a formal options appraisal document exists. [20284/26]

170. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the estimated total lifecycle cost of the Falcon 6X aircraft over a twenty-year operational period including maintenance, fuel, crew, insurance and infrastructure. [20285/26]

171. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether a formal operational requirement document was prepared prior to the procurement of the Falcon 6X aircraft; and whether that document specified passenger capacity, range, medical evacuation capability or other operational criteria. [20286/26]

172. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether the procurement of the Falcon 6X aircraft was ranked as a priority capability requirement relative to maritime surveillance, naval fleet staffing, radar capability or subsea monitoring capability. [20287/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence (Deputy Helen McEntee)
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 168 to 172, inclusive, together.

My priority as Minister for Defence is to ensure that the operational capability of the Army, Air Corps and Naval Service is maintained and developed. This is to enable the Defence Forces to carry out the roles assigned by Government.

The capital funding of €1.7 billion allocated in the latest National Development Plan 2026 to 2030 to Defence represents an increase of €600 million on the previous baseline of €1.1 billion. The revised capital allocations will enable targeted progression on key elements of Government commitments within Level of Ambition 2 objectives.

Ongoing planning for the acquisition of military equipment is conducted through the utilisation of the Defence Equipment Development Plan, which is a rolling plan, considered through joint civil-military co-operation, and provides a consolidated, structured basis for ongoing investment in military equipment to develop and maintain necessary capabilities. This work is progressed under the guidance of the Strategic Framework for the Transformation of the Defence Forces, which was published in February 2026, the Report of the Commission on the Defence Forces (CODF) and the updated Detailed Implementation Plan for the Report of the Commission on the Defence Forces.

Governance for Defence acquisitions include the High Level Planning and Procurement Group (HLPPG), a monthly working group comprising of senior civil and military management of the Department of Defence and the Defence Forces. The HLPPG provides a joint civil and military forum for oversight and approval of expenditure in accordance with Public Spending Code requirements which included a cost benefit analysis options appraisal. As the value of this acquisition was within the threshold for approval at Ministerial level there was no requirement for a formal memorandum to be submitted to Government for approval.
Concerning the other matters raised, the Deputy may wish to refer to my previous response dated 4th March 2026 under PQ 17554/26.
As set out in that response, the CoDF recommended the “Enhancement of the Air Corps’ fleet with the addition of a fixed wing aircraft with strategic reach capability”.

The Dassault Falcon 6X is a next generation strategic reach aircraft which will enhance the State’s transport, airlift and medical evacuation capabilities, with a range of over 5000 nautical miles meaning it can reach the west coast of the United States without the need to refuel. The aircraft replaces the Learjet 45 operated by the Air Corps for over 20 years, which seated 7 passengers. The acquired Falcon 6X can carry up to 14 passengers.

It provides the State with an independent and flexible air transport service, which is an increasingly essential requirement to assist the Government in meeting Ireland’s national and international obligations.

In addition, the aircraft will be used for a broad range of other taskings, including the evacuation of Irish citizens from critical situations, air-ambulance patient transfers, medical evacuation or repatriation of Irish Defence Forces personnel deployed on overseas missions, and logistics support for the transport of supplies to Irish Defence Forces overseas missions.

In 2023/ 2024 an open competition with multiple bidders was conducted under the procedures as set out in the Defence and Security Directive 81/2009/EC, and in accordance with the requirements of the Public Spending Code. The suitability of the aircraft submitted by aircraft manufacturers in response to the competition, in terms of range, passenger capacity and other parameters, was extensively considered and assessed under strict criteria set out within the documentation published openly within the course of the competition, which can be viewed at www.etenders.gov.ie.
Following this a contract was awarded to Dassault Aviation S.A., a French company, for the provision of the Falcon 6X strategic reach aircraft.
A Civil Military Project Team comprising Officials from my Department and the Air Corps delivered this project, with legal support being provided by the Office of the Chief State Solicitor.

The award of the contract followed a robust analysis of the options that met the identified capability requirement, as specified by the Public Spending Code. This analysis considered operational requirements, including seating. The new aircraft will provide the independent and flexible strategic reach air transport service which is an increasingly essential requirement to assist the Government in meeting its national and international obligations.
The commercial information of unsuccessful tenderers is protected both by public procurement law and the Freedom of Information Act, and I am not in a position to disclose such information.

The total cost of the Falcon 6X aircraft procurement was just below €53 million excluding VAT. The delivery of the Dassault Falcon 6X strategic reach aircraft represents a significant enhancement of the State’s transport, airlift and medical capabilities, and is further evidence of the Government’s ongoing commitment to enhance the capabilities of the Defence Forces.

In addition to the acquisition of the Falcon 6X strategic reach aircraft, capital investment in aircraft has included in recent years; two new Airbus C-295W Maritime Patrol Aircraft delivered in 2023; one new Airbus C-295M in Military Transport configuration delivered in October 2025; and four Airbus H145M Light Utility Multi-Role Helicopters, with these aircraft in production for phased delivery in 2027 and 2028.

The strategic reach aircraft will enter full operational service in March 2026, and operational costs will be published monthly on the Department's website, accessible at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/organisation-information/e8132-routinely-published-information/#ministerial-air-transport-service-mats.

I am satisfied that the Defence Forces, including the Air Corps have the necessary modern and effective range of equipment available to them which is in line with best international standards in order to fulfil all roles assigned to them by Government.

question.p: 173. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the annual number of applicants to the Reserve Defence Forces in each year from 2018 to date in 2026; the number accepted for training in each year; the number who commenced the joint induction training syllabus; the number who successfully completed that training; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20333/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: The Military Authorities have provided the table below, which sets out the number of applications and attestations to the RDF from 2018 - Feb 2026.
*As at 28th February 2026

The RDF Joint Induction Training Syllabus was introduced in 2024. Its purpose it to create a common standard of foundation training for all new reserve recruits. This joint approach reflects that adopted for new recruits into the Permanent Defence Forces whereby Recruits undergo training as a collective and are then assigned their Units on completion of training. For Reservists they commence their recruit training with their parent Units. The syllabus is delivered across midweek training evenings, weekend training days and a two-week full-time training period. The two-week training camp is delivered in a joint setting with Recruits from across the Defence Forces undertaking training in a collective setting.

The syllabus generally takes 9-12 months to deliver. On completion of which the Reservist is qualified as an Army Private or an Ordinary Rating in the Naval Service. Reservists then progress to their professional training appropriate to their Service or Corps. The conduct of joint training enables the pooling of resources and thus achieves greater efficiencies in the delivery of training. Joint training also ensures there is a standardisation of the desired training outcomes. These standards are vital at the induction stage as they provide a solid foundation upon which a Reservists can commence their career and their professional development. As with any military course there is an inherent level of attrition.
The Military Authorities have also provided the table below, which sets out the number of Recruits (Grade 1) Who were discharged from 2018 - 2025.

It should be noted that these figures do not directly correspond to the attestations above. The reasons for withdrawal from training are numerous. Reservists are encouraged to complete an online exit interview that is monitored by the DF organisational psychologist. Reservists will also, where possible, be interviewed by an appropriate member of the Unit staff. Units report that approximately 70% of those who withdrew from training did so to undertake a career in the Permanent Defence Forces or An Garda Siochana. In the remainder of instances, the Reservists personal circumstances may have changed and they were not in a position to make the time commitment necessary for the completion of the training.

It should be noted that approximately 20% of the annual discharges across the RDF are for the purpose of joining the PDF. Some Recruits join the RDF with the goal of progressing to a career in the PDF while others are attracted to a career in the PDF because of their experience in the RDF.

question.p: 174. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the current policy targets set by her Department for the strength of the Reserve Defence Forces under the Reserve Defence Force Regeneration Plan published in July 2024; the projected strength targets for each year to 2028; and the measures being implemented to achieve the stated objective of reaching an effective strength of 80 percent. [20334/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: The strength of the Reserve Defence Force, as of the 31 January 2026, was: -
• 204 First line Reserve personnel and
• 1,607 Second Line Reserve personnel which is comprised of 1,473 Army Reserve personnel and 134 Naval Service personnel.
My key priority is the modernisation of our Defence Forces, and revitalising our Reserve Defence Forces is a vital part of that transformation process.

In that context, the Reserve Defence Force (RDF) Regeneration Plan published in July 2024, contains 27 actions across four objectives, namely: Recruit & Retain; Resource; Train & Educate and Integrate & Deploy.

One of the 4 operational objectives of this Plan is to improve the induction process with the aim of achieving an effective strength of 80% by 2028. To this end a baseline target of 300 inductions has been set for 2026. This target is based upon the resourcing of the induction process and the capacity of the units tasked to deliver the induction training. As the RDF regenerates the Defence Forces will set further annual recruitment targets. The baseline target for 2027 will be set in Q4 2026 based upon a review of 2026 figures and an examination of the resourcing capacity projected for 2027.

Implementation of the regeneration plan is being monitored by the Defence Forces Office of Reserve Affairs to address any blockages arising and to ensure progress across the 27 actions. The recruitment measures include the development of: a Reserve Defence Force Recruitment Strategy; Multi Induction Streams; a Master Messaging and Communication Strategy; an Employer Engagement Strategy and; a Third Level Engagement Strategy.
Other areas of work underway in the Reserve Defence Force sphere include:
• A new RDF Recruitment system, which will result in a more streamlined and user-friendly process for applicants;

• A significant RDF advertising awareness campaign. This will be coordinated across all media modes including television and radio adverts, to raise the public’s awareness of the opportunities available in the RDF;

• A substantial expansion of the RDF budget which continues to increase in pace with the enhanced role of the RDF. To illustrate this, the budget allocation in 2025 was €3.542m and I have further increased it to €4.535m for 2026.

• To ensure the framework for the Reserve is fit for purpose a review of the current legal and policy framework governing the RDF is underway. The second part of this review will focus on options for employment protection legislation.

question.p: 176. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the level of annual funding allocated specifically for the development, training and equipment of the Reserve Defence Forces in each year since 2020; whether the Government intends to introduce a dedicated capital funding stream for Reserve Defence Forces capability development; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20336/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: My key priority is the modernisation of our Defence Forces, and revitalising our Reserve Defence Force is a vital part of that transformation process. This is reflected in the substantial expansion of the RDF budget which continues to increase in pace with the enhanced role of the RDF. To illustrate this, the budget allocation in 2025 was €3.542m and I have further increased it to €4.535m for 2026.

Reserve Defence Force (RDF) funding is provided for by Subhead A.5 of the Defence Vote. This allocation provides current expenditure funding for the Army Reserve (AR) and the Naval Service Reserve (NSR). It also provides for the payment of gratuities to members of the First Line Reserve (FLR).

There is no ring-fenced or dedicated capital budget allocation for the RDF. As such, the relevant Subheads across respective functional areas are resourced to provide for both PDF and RDF requirements. The RDF also benefits from the increasing levels of capital investment now evident in Defence Equipment, Infrastructural, Transport & IT capabilities.

question.p: 177. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence whether her Department maintains structured data on the reasons for resignation or discharge from the Reserve Defence Forces, including exit interviews or retention surveys; if not, whether she intends to introduce a formal retention monitoring system to support the objectives of the Reserve Defence Force Regeneration Plan; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20337/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: The Military Authorities have advised that they don’t maintain consolidated data with regard to reasons for resignation or discharge from the RDF.
Trends and anomalies are investigated though regular engagement between the Office of Reserve Affairs and the Reserve Defence Force Senior Staff Officers in the Brigades and Formations.

The reasons for resignation or discharge are numerous. Reservists are encouraged to complete an online exit interview that is monitored by the DF organisational psychologist. Reservists will also, where possible, be interviewed by an appropriate member of the Unit staff. Approximately 70% of those who withdrew from initial training did so to undertake a career in the Permanent Defence Forces or An Garda Siochana. In the remainder of instances, the Reservists personal circumstances may have changed and they were not in a position to make the time commitment necessary for the completion of the training.

It should be noted that approximately 20% of the annual discharges across the RDF are for the purpose of joining the PDF. Some Recruits join the RDF with the goal of progressing to a career in the PDF while others are attracted to a career in the PDF because of their experience in the RDF.
