question.p: 179. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Defence the number of procurement projects currently underway within the Defence Forces; the stage each project has reached within the capability development lifecycle; and the estimated value of each project. [20412/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: The revised National Development Plan capital allocation for the Defence Vote Group for the period 2026-2030 is €1.7bn. This represents an increase of €600 million (55%) on the previous baseline of €1.1 billion. For 2026, the Defence capital allocation has increased by €66 million to €300 million.

The Updated Detailed Implementation Plan for the Report of the Commission on the Defence Forces was published last month alongside the Strategic Framework 2026. These documents outline my Department's key priorities in the transformation of the Defence Forces, and support the actions, that will be taken in the months and years ahead, to implement the recommendations of the Commission on the Defence Forces, including crucial equipment and infrastructure projects.

Capital investment in Defence primarily supports the renewal, retention, and acquisition of major defence equipment as well as the development of defence infrastructure. This expenditure strengthens military capabilities and contributes to a more secure and resilient society.

Given the critical importance of robust radar capabilities in safeguarding national security and ensuring comprehensive awareness of activity across Ireland’s air and maritime domains, the progression of the Military Radar Programme is an absolute priority for me in 2026. The Military Radar Programme includes three elements - Land Based Long Range Primary Radar; Ground Based Air Defence systems, to include a Counter Unmanned Aerial Systems capability; and Maritime (ship-borne) Radar.

Following Oireachtas approval of a Supplementary Estimate for the accelerated procurement of Counter Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) capabilities for the Defence Forces, the required capabilities are now being procured with planned delivery, and training, being carried out during 2026. Other vitally important Defence projects set to advance in 2026 include Subsea Awareness, Software Defined Radio, and Light Utility Helicopters along with a wide range of essential Force Protection equipment.

As Minister for Defence, I am committed to ensuring that this increased capital funding allocation also enables further progress on a range of Defence Forces Built Infrastructure projects encompassing accommodation, offices and gyms, together with critical investment in aircraft hangars and naval berthage. It will also complement a number of important ongoing infrastructural projects, including the development of the Cadet School HQ, at DFTC and a new Medical Facility at Casement Aerodrome.
Additional capital investment will also be directed at improving Defence Forces IT, Transport, Engineering and Ordnance capabilities.

The geopolitical landscape is changing rapidly, and security challenges are emerging, however, I believe the capital funding envelope now provided to 2030 will enable further targeted delivery of measurable capability enhancements to the Defence Forces.

A key priority for me as Minister for Defence is to ensure that the current operational capability of the Defence Forces is maintained, and further developed upon. I believe it is essential in this evolving geopolitical and security environment, that Ireland enhances the capabilities of our Defence Forces and this objective will be aided by the implementation of a Capability Development Planning Process.

One of the key recommendations from the Commission on the Defence Forces was to implement a top down capability development planning process (CDPP) to bring planning for Defence Forces capabilities in line with best practice.

In early 2023 a Capability Development Unit was established in the Department. It is civil/military in terms of staffing, with military staff from across the three services of the Defence Forces, providing an overarching joint perspective to capability planning. The Unit is now well established and in the final stages producing a 12 year Capability Development Programme, that will identify, at a high level, the capability requirements for the Defence Forces out to 2040. This ongoing piece of work, once complete, will inform the prioritisation of capabilities the Defence Forces will progress in moving towards the strategic level of ambition set out in the Defence Policy Review, and the objectives as set out in the recently published Strategic Framework and Update to the Detailed Implementation Plan for the Commission on the Defence Forces. I expect the Capability Development Programme will be finalised in the first half of this 2026.

The Programme will then be implemented through rolling 4 year Capability Development Plans, the first of which will cover the period 2028 to 2032. Capabilities will then be developed and acquired in line with capital allocations under the National Development Plan. My immediate priority is progressing as quickly as we can to Level of Ambition 2, as committed to the Detailed Implementation Plan and the Programme for Government.

Full details of the Defence NDP 2026-2030 Sectoral Plan are available on the Government website www.gov.ie. The updated Detailed Implementation Plan and Strategic Framework are published on my Department’s website www.gov.ie/defence

question.p: 180. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Defence the statutory basis, if any, under which troops may be deployed as aid to the civil power following the expiry of the Emergency Powers Act 1976 in 1995; who and in what circumstances may such deployment be authorised; and to provide details on any instances since 1995 where this has been authorised and implemented. [20565/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: My colleague the Minister for Justice Home Affairs and Migration and An Garda Síochána have primary responsibility for the internal security of the State. Among the roles assigned to the Defence Forces in the White Paper on Defence is the provision of Aid to the Civil Power which, in practice, means providing assistance to An Garda Síochána when requested to do so. Any such assistance is provided by the Defence Forces on the general approval of the Minister for Defence following a request for assistance from An Garda Síochána to the military authorities.

In addition, there are a number of enactments under which members of the Defence Forces (specifically members of the Naval Service) are authorised to undertake duties in support of An Garda Siochána or other State bodies (e.g. the Customs Service of the Revenue Commissioner). The functions in questions are generally concerned with the enforcement of the provisions of the enactments in question. During 2025, in excess of 3,100 Aid to the Civil Power operations were completed by the Defence Forces including 24/7/365 armed guard at Government Buildings, Explosive Production Facilities etc along with other intermittent activities such as Explosive Ordnance Disposal Callouts, Explosive Escorts, Naval Service Diving Operations, VIP Visits, Search Operations etc.

Due to the voluminous number of requests, it is not possible to provide full details of requests from 1995 in this response, however, details are published in the Department of Defence and Defence Forces Annual Report on a yearly basis and are publicly available:

question.p: 183. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Defence if she has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted due to St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026; and the amount paid. [20641/26]

speech.from: Minister for Defence
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 183, 181 and 182 together.

In line with Circular 01/2020, Government Departments, Offices and agencies are required to record, monitor, and value the greenhouse gas emissions associated with official air travel usage and, no later than 28 February each year, make a payment to the Fund Manager of the statutory Climate Action Fund related to these emissions for the preceding year.

Travel for St. Patrick's Day 2026 for myself and the Minister of State, Thomas Byrne TD, was arranged by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, therefore that Department is responsible for the administration of carbon emissions associated with official air travel in accordance with Circular 01/2020 as set out above.

question.p: 185. Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide an update on the progress of the first National Safety Camera Strategy, when he expects it to be published; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20522/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras.
There are currently 5 average speed cameras in operation across the road network. These are located in the following locations -
• Dublin Port Tunnel
• N3 Cavan
• N5 Mayo
• N2 Meath
In addition there are nine static safety cameras in operation. These are located at the following locations -
• N17 Mayo
• N59 Galway
• N13 Donegal
• N69 Limerick
• R772 Wexford
• N22 Cork
• N80 Carlow
• N25 Kilkenny
• Dolphin's Barn Dublin 12

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

question.p: 186. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport the actions his Department has planned to reform the Road Safety Authority; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18248/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: In 2024, my Department commissioned Indecon Economic Consultants to carry out an independent, external review of the Road Safety Authority (RSA). This review was presented to Government and published in November 2024.

In total, the report made 34 recommendations. At the core of the recommendations was that the operational services run by the RSA should be separated from its research, media campaigns, partnerships and education programmes to improve road safety. A related recommendation was that the RSA’s public interest work should receive Exchequer subvention.

Since the publication of the review, RSA reform activities have been taken forward on a number of fronts. For the first time since 2012, the fees for certain RSA services increased on 1 January 2025 to raise additional revenue and improve the RSA’s financial position; €18m has been specifically ringfenced for annual investment in public interest work in both 2025 and 2026; the Road Safety Communications Steering Group was established in December 2024; the Department of Transport took over central responsibility for the coordination of the Government’s Road Safety Strategy commencing with the July 2025 publication of the Phase 2 Action Plan; and, a new Chair and three new ordinary members were appointed to the RSA board during 2025 with a stronger focus on the RSA’s operational mandate.

In terms of the recommendation to separate out the RSA’s operational and public interest functions, I have decided not to pursue this recommendation as I believe that reform can be delivered more efficiently and effectively within the existing RSA organisational structure. I have directed my officials to prepare revised reform proposals in line with this decision and will present these to Government in the coming weeks.

question.p: 187. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport the plans his Department has to reform wider road safety governance given that many different road safety responsibilities are spread across many different agencies; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18249/26]

308. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding any reforms being considered to the coordination structures for road safety governance to further strengthen implementation of the Road Safety Strategy 2021–2030; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19641/26]

366. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport the steps his Department is taking to review and strengthen governance structures in relation to road safety; the way in which responsibility for meeting national road safety targets is coordinated across the Road Safety Authority, An Garda Síochána, Transport Infrastructure Ireland and local authorities; and whether consideration has been given to establishing a single oversight mechanism or dedicated office to improve accountability and delivery of safety outcomes. [20076/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 187, 308 and 366 together.

The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030. The Strategy has the target of reducing road deaths and serious injuries by 50% this decade, and to achieving Vision Zero—as close as possible to no deaths or serious injuries on Irish roads—by 2050.

The Phase 2 Action Plan 2025–2027 under the Strategy was published in July 2025. In total, the Phase 2 Plan contains 12 primary and 77 support actions, with the potential to deliver truly transformative change. Actions are being delivered through partnership and collaborative working by road safety stakeholders.

My Department is responsible for the central co-ordination of the Road Safety Strategy and implementation of the Phase 2 Action Plan is overseen at Ministerial level by the Road Safety Leadership Group (RSLG). This Group is chaired by me and is attended by the Minister for Justice and Home Affairs. This Group also comprises senior officials from all key road safety partners including An Garda Síochána, the Road Safety Authority, Transport Infrastructure Ireland, National Transport Authority, the Courts Service, MBRS, HSA and the Local Authorities.

The Group oversees implementation of the Strategy. Action owners are required to report quarterly on actions in their areas and the RSLG meets quarterly to review these updates and to discuss progress on the delivery of the 12 Primary Actions. Additional updates as required are provided on the 77 support actions.
A Road User Safety Forum is also in place and gives a range of road user and road safety advocates an opportunity to contribute to the Phase 2 Action Plan.

question.p: 188. Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 352 of 4 February 2026, the funding allocated to and drawn down by Waterford City and County Council in each year 2010 to 2025 for roads, by funding scheme, in tabular form. [18253/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals.
National roads allocations for years 2020 -2026 are available at: https://www.tii.ie/en/tii-library/reports-accounts/.

I have referred the question to TII for a direct reply regarding 2010 - 2019 funding allocated to Waterford City and County Council. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on these roads are funded from councils’ own resources and supplemented by State Road grants. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million in our regional and local roads across the State. This will facilitate an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works. Waterford City and County Council have been allocated €23,253,950 for 2026.

As regards the total funding allocated to and drawn down by Waterford City and County Council by grant type for the years 2010 to 2025, details of the regional and local road allocations and payments to local authorities are outlined in the regional and local road allocations and payments booklets which are available on the Oireachtas Digital Library.

Full details of the 2026 regional and local grant allocations are available at https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/press-releases/ministers-for-transport-announce-over-15-billion-for-national-regional-and-local-roads/.

question.p: 189. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the reason for the significant reduction in allocation for the Shannon Crossing project from €13.39 million in 2025 to €5 million in 2026; if this reduction indicates a delay or rescoping of the project; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18269/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources supplemented by State road grants.
The Shannon Crossing, Killaloe Bypass and R494 Upgrade scheme is one of a limited number of strategic regional and local road improvement schemes being undertaken under the National Development Plan.
Construction of the Shannon Crossing, Killaloe Bypass and R494 Upgrade scheme was completed in May 2025, and therefore received a lower allocation this year.

question.p: 190. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport his views on the efficiency of funding allocations for bridge rehabilitation in County Clare, given that several structures including Shragh Bridge, Derryfadda Bridge, and Bunratty Lower Bridge have received repeated allocations in both 2025 and 2026, the total projected completion cost for these projects; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18270/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport (Deputy Darragh O'Brien)
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from Councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

My Department provides grant assistance to local authorities under the Regional and Local Road Grant Programme for a number of targeted programmes, including the Bridge Rehabilitation Grant Programme. Applications are sought each year from local authorities under this programme for consideration for funding in the subsequent year.

In 2025, Clare County Council received an allocation of €689,500 under the Bridge Rehabilitation Grant Programme for 22 schemes. The planning and implementation of these schemes is the responsibility of Clare County Council. The total amount of funding drawn down under this grant by Clare County Council in 2025 was €215,557.

question.p: 191. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the reason for the significant cost increase for the Lough Alewnaghta road protection scheme (CL/CCAR/26/002) from €45,000 in 2025 to €160,000 in 2026; the factors that led to this more than threefold increase; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18271/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

My Department provides grant assistance to local authorities under the Regional and Local Road Grant Programme for a number of targeted programmes, including the Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience Grant Programme. Applications are sought each year from local authorities under this programme for consideration for funding in the subsequent year.

Clare County Council's application for funding in 2025 for the Lough Alewnaghta road protection scheme was to undertake site investigation work and the design of a permanent solution. The Council's application for funding for the scheme in 2026 is for works to raise the level of the road.
The planning and implementation of the scheme is the responsibility of Clare County Council.

question.p: 192. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport if he is satisfied that the expenditure of over €126,000 on bridge inventory and maintenance inspections in County Clare over the 2025-2026 period represents value for money; the proportion of this funding that was allocated to external consultants versus internal council resources; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18272/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from Councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

In 2025, the Department introduced funding for Bridge Inventory and Maintenance Inspections which is subject to a maximum of 10% of a local authority's previous year’s Bridge Rehabilitation grant allocation. The purpose of the allocation is to assist local authorities to focus on preventative maintenance to prolong the lifespan and ensure continued functionality of the bridges. This allocation is being made available to assist local authorities with the collection and recording of bridge inventory data and with salaries of local authority technical grade staff performing inspections on structures.
In 2026, Clare County Council received an allocation under the Bridge Rehabilitation Grant programme of €740,000, which included €65,000 for Bridge Inventory and Maintenance Inspections.

question.p: 193. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the reason Clare County Council received one of the lowest per-kilometre capital allocations for national roads in the State in 2025, necessitating a threefold increase in 2026 to address the deficit, if he will consider multi-annual funding arrangements to avoid such volatility in future allocations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18273/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals.

The National Development Plan review (Sectoral Investment Plan) published by Government on 26 November 2025 sets out capital ceilings for transport to 2030. This has provided indicative funding under Programme Area C- Road Networks & Road Safety of €9.7 billion, subject to the annual estimates process. This represents a significant increase in funding over the 2021 to 2025 period. As a result, this year an increased number of new national road projects have been allocated funding. I can confirm that Clare County Council received approximately €6.5m as part of the 2026 National Road allocations announced in February. Future funding will be kept under review and considered in terms of the overall envelope available to TII.

question.p: 194. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the justification for allocating €100,000 to a new scheme at R478 Liscannor Village in 2026, given that recurring structural issues at locations such as Annaghneal (R-468) and Westbury (L-3183) remain unresolved and have required consecutive years of funding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18274/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: In accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, each local authority has statutory responsibility for the improvement and maintenance of their regional and local roads. Works on those roads are funded from local authorities' own resources and are supplemented by State road grants. Of these grants, the vast majority (approximately 90%) are targeted at the maintenance and renewal of the network with c. 10% of the remaining funding invested in new roads/bridges or for road realignments.

My Department provides grant assistance to local authorities under the Regional and Local Road Grant Programme for a number of targeted programmes, including the Safety Improvement Works Programme. Applications are sought each year from local authorities under this programme for consideration for funding in the subsequent year. Councils are made aware of this and are asked to submit applications in order of priority. Proposals for individual Safety Improvement Works projects costing in excess of €250,000 are outside of the scope of this scheme and are to be considered under the Specific Improvement Grant Programme.

Any road improvement projects proposed by local authorities for consideration for funding under the Specific Improvement Grant Programme are assessed by the Department on a case-by-case basis. All projects put forward by local authorities for consideration must comply with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines and the Department's Transport Appraisal Framework. Given the limited funding available for regional and local road improvement works it is important for local authorities to prioritise projects within their overall area of responsibility with these requirements in mind.
In 2026, Clare County Council received an allocation of €100,000 under the Specific Improvement Grant Programme for the R478 Liscannor Village scheme.
Furthermore, Clare County Council is responsible for deciding its annual programme for road maintenance and the Department has no role in that process.

question.p: 195. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the specific works planned under the €500,000 allocation for former national roads (CL/FN/25/001) on the R-458 in 2025; if these works have been completed within the allocated budget; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18275/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources supplemented by State road grants. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

My Department provides grant assistance to local authorities under the Regional and Local Road Grant Programme for a number of targeted programmes, and up to 2025 this included the Former National Roads Programme. Applications were sought each year from local authorities under this programme for consideration for funding in the subsequent year. The purpose of this grant was to provide assistance to local authorities specifically for the maintenance of former national roads.
In 2025, the funding drawn down by Clare County Council under the Former National Roads Programme was €233,926.
Planning and implementation of the scheme is the responsibility of Clare County Council.

question.p: 196. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the basis for the calculation of the Discretionary Grant for Clare County Council, which increased from €3,614,500 in 2025 to €3,687,500 in 2026; the criteria used to determine this annual adjustment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18276/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million in our regional and local roads across the State. This will facilitate an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works.
The three most significant grant programmes for local authorities in terms of monies and maintaining the road network to a serviceable condition are:

1) Restoration Maintenance Grant:This mainly supports the road surface dressing programme. This is important in terms of sealing the road surface (preventing the ingress of water) and in maintaining adequate skid resistance;?

2) Restoration Improvement Grant:This grant funds the road pavement strengthening programme and is fundamental to maintaining the road network. It caters for pavement overlay works and for complete road rehabilitation works as well as related drainage works, where required; and
3) Discretionary Grant:This grant can be used for a variety of maintenance and repair works on roads and can also be used for winter maintenance purposes.

The funding that each local authority receives under these grant programmes is based predominately on the road length with some allowance for traffic factors. Based on an overall budget of €86.19 million for the Discretionary Grant, Clare County Council's allocation in 2026 has increased. Department grants are intended to be supplemented by a realistic level of funding from local authorities’ own resources.

question.p: 197. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport the reason regional and local roads in North Clare (specifically L5248, L1098, R476) remain in poor condition despite overall funding increases; if he is satisfied with the value-for-money of repeated patching versus full resurfacing on high-traffic local roads; the contingency funding which exists for roads where residents are undertaking basic maintenance themselves; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18277/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million in our regional and local roads across the State. This will facilitate an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works. In 2026, Clare County Council has received an allocation of €31,788,700. Of this €26,628,700 has been allocated for the protection and renewal of Clare's regional and local roads.

Within the budget available for the regional and local road grant programme, the Department's grant funding for the maintenance of regional and local roads is allocated on as fair and equitable a basis as possible to eligible local authorities. In this context, grants in the main grant categories are allocated based on the length of the road network within a local authority's area of responsibility with some account taken of traffic. It is envisaged that grants will continue to be made available on that basis.

Clare County Council is responsible for deciding its annual programme for road maintenance and the Department has no role in that process. It is also open to each local authority to allocate its own resources to priority areas. It should be noted that decisions regarding allocations to individual Municipal Districts are a matter for each local authority, taking into account the funding available to it from local and State sources as well as its particular priorities.

In 2018, the Department introduced ring-fenced funding for Community Involvement Schemes (CIS). The purpose of the CIS is to facilitate local community participation in the repair of local roads. The focus of the programme is on the repair of more lightly trafficked public roads which might not be high on the list of a local authority's annual roadwork programme. Under the scheme a local community can contribute in money or in kind, for example by making labour or machinery available.

While community contributions in the range 15% to 30% had been required up to 2021, depending on the mix between works and monies, the contribution rates were reduced to a minimum of 10% for monetary contributions and 20% for works contribution. This is more in line with Local Improvement Scheme contribution rates.
From 2026 the contribution rate for monetary contributions has been reduced to a minimum of 8%, with the contribution rate remaining at 20% for works contribution.

In order to allow for sufficient planning and applications for this scheme, local authorities are invited to apply for funding for CIS projects for a two-year programme, with the latest round of applications received in late 2025 for the 2026/2027 period.
In 2026, Clare County Council received an allocation of €786,600 under the Community Involvement Scheme.

It should be noted that Exchequer funding for regional and local roads is intended to supplement realistic contributions from local authorities’ own resources. As the statutory road authorities for their areas, it is open to local authorities to prioritise investment on regional and local roads.

question.p: 198. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Transport if he will re-evaluate the role, structure, and accountability of the Road Safety Authority in light of recent figures showing that 12,500 learner drivers in Wexford are now facing a 17-week waiting time for a driving test; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18327/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: The Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, including testing and scheduling matters. The latest information provided to me by the RSA indicates that as of 7 March, the average waiting time for a driving test in Wexford was approximately 10 weeks. This marks a significant improvement on the 29 week average wait time in April 2025 and is in line with the national average service level agreement target of 10 weeks.

The Deputy may wish to note that the RSA publish detailed monthly information on the driver testing service on the CSO website, including the breakdown of waiting times and distribution of testing capacity by test centre. This information is available at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/product/RSADTS.
In 2024, my Department commissioned Indecon Economic Consultants to carry out an independent, external review of the RSA. This review was presented to Government and published in November 2024.

In total, the report made 34 recommendations. At the core of the recommendations was that the operational services run by the RSA should be separated from its research, media campaigns, partnerships and education programmes to improve road safety. A related recommendation was that the RSA’s public interest work should receive Exchequer subvention.

Since the publication of the review, RSA reform activities have been taken forward on several fronts. For the first time since 2012, the fees for certain RSA services increased on 1 January 2025 to raise additional revenue and improve the RSA’s financial position; €18m has been specifically ringfenced for annual investment in public interest work in both 2025 and 2026; the Road Safety Communications Steering Group was established in December 2024; the Department of Transport took over central responsibility for the coordination of the Government’s Road Safety Strategy commencing with the July 2025 publication of the Phase 2 Action Plan; and, a new Chair and three new ordinary members were appointed to the RSA board during 2025 with a stronger focus on the RSA’s operational mandate.

In terms of the recommendation to separate out the RSA’s operational and public interest functions, I have decided not to pursue this recommendation as I believe that reform can be delivered more efficiently and effectively within the existing RSA organisational structure. I have directed my officials to prepare revised reform proposals in line with this decision and I will present these to Government in the coming weeks.

question.p: 200. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Transport whether he can provide the waiting list timeline in respect of each test centre in County Galway, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18337/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service. This includes all testing and scheduling matters. Therefore, the information requested by the Deputy is held by the Authority. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's questions to the RSA for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.

Pending this response, the latest information provided to me by the RSA indicates that as of 7 March, the average waiting time for a driving test in the Galway test centres at Clybaun Hotel, Carnmore and Loughrea were 11, 13 and 8 weeks respectively. This marks a significant improvement on the waiting times in April of last year, when those figures were 26, 42, and 22 weeks. I expect the RSA to continue to work to bring the wait time in the Galway test centres in line with the 10-week target as soon as possible.

Additionally, the Deputy may wish to note that the statistics for waiting times for individual test centres are made available on the CSO website on a monthly basis and can be accessed via the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/ROA36

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The Luas Contract is awarded jointly by the NTA and Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII). The day-to-day operation of the Luas is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII).
Noting the above position, I have referred your question to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question.p: 204. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport the supports currently available to persons with ADHD, dyspraxia, dyslexia and other neurodivergent conditions to assist them in preparing for the driver theory test; whether any structured learning supports, tutoring programmes or accessible preparatory courses are funded or approved by the State; the number of such supports available nationally and by county; to outline any plans to introduce dedicated learning supports to ensure equitable access to driver licensing for neurodivergent learners; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18403/26]

205. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department has conducted any assessment of barriers faced by neurodivergent individuals in accessing driver education and licensing, particularly in relation to preparation for the driver theory test; if not, whether such a review will be undertaken; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18404/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 204 and 205 together.

Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for all aspects of the National Driving Test Service. Neither I nor my officials are involved in the service at an operational level. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's questions to the RSA for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.

Pending this more detailed response, I am informed that the Driver Theory Test provider offers various options to accommodate candidates who may require special assistance to take their test. Additional supports include a voiceover option whereby the questions and answers are read out to the candidate over headphones. Additional time may also be allowed for a candidate to take the test. In addition, there is also a reader recorder service available whereby a staff member will read the questions and answer options to the candidate and record their answers on screen. Other services offered include dyslexia support, professional and Irish Sign Language (ISL) video clips, or ISL interpreters.

Test Day Assistance and Support Services must be booked in advance by calling 0818 606 106 or via the postal application form available for download at https://theorytest.ie/general-information/test-day-assistance-support/
The RSA assures my Department that they continuously seek to review its services to ensure customers are supported and welcomes the feedback of customers and their advocates.

question.p: 206. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Transport the current average waiting time for a driving test at the Carlow test centres; the steps being taken to reduce delays for applicants in County Carlow; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18422/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service. This includes all testing and scheduling matters. Therefore, the information requested by the Deputy is held by the Authority. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's questions to the RSA for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.

Pending this response, the latest information provided to me by the RSA indicates that as of 7 March, the average waiting time across the two centres in Carlow was 10 weeks. The average wait time at the Carlow centre as at 7 March was 8 weeks and 12 weeks at the Carlow Talbot Hotel centre.

The Deputy will be aware that reducing driver test waiting times has been one of my key priorities since taking office. To that end, in May 2025, I directed the RSA to produce and publish a service recovery plan to meet the 10-week average national waiting time target by September 2025, which was achieved.

In September 2024, my Department conveyed sanction for 70 additional driver testing posts on a permanent basis, bringing the permanent sanction to 200, which represents a doubling of permanent posts since June 2022. As of 7 March, 194 testers were in place, which marks a significant increase on the 151 available at the beginning of 2025. The RSA is working to reach its full complement of 200 testers this year subject to the next successful training and onboarding of new recruits.

I would also highlight that, to manage demand effectively at national level, testers, although formally assigned to specific centres, are routinely deployed to other locations as required. The RSA has also indicated that overtime and bank holiday testing will continue in 2026.

The driver testing booking system now makes available cancelled test slots for candidates to take up at short notice. I would encourage learner drivers awaiting a test to monitor this channel, which may provide an opportunity to book an earlier testing date.

Additionally, the Deputy may wish to note that the statistics for waiting times for individual test centres are made available on the CSO website on a monthly basis and can be accessed via the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/ROA36

debateSection.summary: A referred reply was forwarded to the Deputy under Standing Orders

question.p: 209. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Transport the plans to expand electric vehicle charging infrastructure along major routes in Kilkenny; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18425/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The Programme for Government commits to substantially increasing the number of publicly available EV charging points and to develop a new National EV Infrastructure Strategy.
In delivering on this commitment, a new National EV Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028 has been developed by my Department, and was published for public consultation on 26th February.
My Department has also launched a number of schemes to provide for increased high quality charging on the national network.

The EV Recharging Infrastructure LDV En-Route Grant Schemes, which include sites in Kilkenny and are administered by Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), will significantly expand high power charging availability across the national, regional and local road network, creating a more convenient and reliable system for drivers nationwide. Each recharging pool will provide fast and ultra-fast recharging points, so that people can charge their EVs quickly.

There is also a Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan. This plan, which focuses on destination and neighbourhood charging, was published in 2025. The plan will be led by Local Authorities in partnership with both public and private sectors. Kilkenny has been identified under Region 5 with counties Waterford, Wexford, Carlow, and Regional Lead Tipperary.

A third initiative, the Shared Island Sports Club EV Charging Scheme provides funding to install a network of publicly accessible chargers in communities nationwide through their local sports clubs. Included in the scope of the Scheme are 227 clubs of which 179 are in Ireland and 48 in Northern Ireland. There are 2 eligible clubs in Kilkenny: Erin's Own GAA and St. Patrick's Ballyragget GAA Club.

Government will continue to facilitate the rollout of further high powered chargers as having an effective and reliable charging network is an essential part of enabling drivers to make the switch to electric vehicles.

question.p: 213. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department or the National Transport Authority has examined the option of developing an overground shuttle rail link between Clongriffin DART station and Dublin Airport; whether a feasibility study, cost benefit analysis or route assessment has been carried out; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18470/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Following the publication of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in July 2024, my Department, with the support of the European Investment Bank and in conjunction with the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland, oversaw the preparation of the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy. The Prioritisation Strategy was published in December 2025 and outlines the approach to sequencing and optimising the recommendations of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in the coming years.

In the short-term to 2030, the Prioritisation Strategy specifies a number of 'Early Interventions' to be delivered in the coming years, including passing loops at Mosney and Skerries to boost the rail network’s resilience and capacity. These investments are funded to be fully delivered by 2030 under the NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for Transport, published in November 2025.

The Prioritisation Strategy also identifies 'Major Projects' with longer lead-in and development timelines. These projects are generally targeted to secure the necessary approvals within the next five years such that construction works could commence thereafter, and include line speed improvements, capacity enhancements and electrification of the Dublin-Belfast line.

The Prioritisation Strategy has a 20-year time horizon, which does not cover the entire period to 2050 envisaged by the All-Island Strategic Rail Review. Projects not included in the Prioritisation Strategy, including a rail spur from Clongriffin to Dublin Airport, are intended to be progressed in the longer-run.

It should be noted that individual programmes and projects referred to within the All-Island Strategic Rail Review and the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy will be advanced subject to funding and relevant approvals, as required under the Infrastructure Guidelines.

In advance of the rail spur, MetroLink will connect Dublin Airport to the heavy rail network at Glasnevin and Tara Street stations. The project will therefore help deliver strategic connectivity for Dublin Airport across the island of Ireland.

The Glasnevin MetroLink station will also enable direct interchange with Iarnród Éireann services to Sligo and Kildare and the planned DART+ West service to Maynooth. Meanwhile, the MetroLink Tara Street station will facilitate interchange with rail services towards Wexford, and DART services along the Dublin and north Wicklow coastline.

Furthermore, the MetroLink stops at O'Connell Street, St Stephen's Green and Charlemont will allow for easy access to nearby Green Line and Red Line Luas stops. Several MetroLink stops will also be within close proximity to BusConnects services, including Swords Central, Northwood, Collins Avenue, Griffith Park, Glasnevin, O'Connell Street, Tara Street and Stephen's Green.

[18471/26]

In advance of the rail spur, MetroLinkwill connect Dublin Airport to the heavy rail network at Glasnevin and Tara Street stations. The project will therefore help deliver strategic connectivity for Dublin Airport across the island of Ireland.

question.p: 215. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport the way in which the proposed MetroLink will improve airport access for communities along the northern DART line including Howth, Clontarf, Raheny and Artane; whether passengers from these areas will be required to travel into the city centre to interchange; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18472/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As the Deputy may be aware, as Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the planning and development of public transport infrastructure, including MetroLink.

MetroLink will be a fully segregated and mostly underground new railway line between Swords and Dublin City Centre, the first of its kind in Ireland. It is a key project under the National Development Plan 2021-30. MetroLink will be able to carry a peak capacity of 20,000 passengers per hour per direction in the future.

The stations on MetroLink's route will connect with Iarnród Éireann and DART/DART+ services at Glasnevin and Tara Street stations. The project will therefore help deliver strategic connectivity for Dublin Airport across the island of Ireland.
The MetroLink Tara Street station will facilitate interchange with DART services along the Dublin and north Wicklow coastline.

As part of the DART+ programme, DART+ Coastal North will provide an extension of DART services from Malahide to Drogheda, serving stations on the Northern line. The Railway Order for DART+ Coastal North was approved by An Coimisiún Pleanála in August 2025.

Three fleet orders have been placed comprising 285 battery-electric and electric DART carriages. The first order for the purchase of 95 DART carriages, have started to arrive in Ireland and are currently undergoing certification and safety testing. It is intended that the new battery-electric sets will be initially deployed on the Northern Commuter Line serving Dublin to/from Drogheda from 2027, which will provide additional capacity on the line.

The NDP Sectoral Investment Plan published by my Department in November 2025 notes that there is also the potential to commence works on elements of DART+ Coastal North, including supporting infrastructure such as track passing loops and a new platform at Drogheda station, prior to 2030, in advance of works on Overhead Line Equipment (OHLE).

Noting the NTA's responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question.p: 218. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport the way in which road collision data is compiled; the agency or body that is responsible for compiling these statistics; if his Department have access to this data including the location of collisions; whether his Department is undergoing work to identify the most dangerous roads in the State based on this data; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18511/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Road collision data in the State are primarily compiled through a long-standing, multi-agency process involving An Garda Síochána, the Road Safety Authority (RSA), and the Department of Transport.

An Garda Síochána is responsible for collecting and recording road traffic collision information at the scene of each incident. These data are then transmitted to the RSA, which undertakes validation, analysis and publication of national road safety statistics. This includes details such as collision type, severity, and location. Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) also has full access to this data as part of its requirement to comply with the European Directive for Road Improvement Safety Management.

The RSA has a statutory remit to report on fatal, serious and minor injury collisions on public roads. The RSA receives both collision data from An Garda Síochána and coronial data for this purpose and produces official statistics to help develop evidence-based road safety interventions.

TII operates a dedicated Reactive Road Safety Programme for the national road network. Under this system collision data are used to identify high-collision locations across the network. Where such sites are detected, TII formally notifies the relevant Local Authority and requires the Local Authority to propose a scheme, as the road authority, to address the issues identified. TII subsequently provides funding for targeted safety improvement schemes to address the issues identified.

The Department of Transport provides funding to Local Authorities each year under the Low-Cost Safety Improvement Scheme to support small-scale engineering measures that address identified road safety issues for regional and local roads. Through the Department of Transport Support Office, the Department issues Location of Interest (LOI) reports annually to each road authority. These reports identify high risk locations based on collision data analysis and assist Local Authorities in reviewing potential safety issues on their networks and preparing applications for the following year’s funding programme. Since 2022, more than 400 locations of interest have been funded under low-cost safety schemes and local authorities continue to review and apply for funding to complete additional schemes each year. This year €14 million has been allocated, representing an increase of €1 million (approximately 8%) on 2025 allocations.
The Department also funds larger Road Safety Interventions through the Specific Grants and Strategic Regional and Local Roads Grant programmes.

Separately, TII has recently published the Network-Wide Road Safety Assessment (NWA). This safety rating system evaluates approximately 2500km of the national primary road network by combining both historical collision data and data from current proactive infrastructure inspections.

question.p: 219. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Transport the status of the National Safety Camera Strategy; when it will be published; the number of average-speed camera zones planned for deployment; on which road classifications they will be located; the projected timeline for full operational deployment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18526/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras.
There are currently 5 average speed cameras in operation across the road network. These are located in the following locations -
• Dublin Port Tunnel
• N3 Cavan
• N5 Mayo
• N2 Meath
In addition there are nine static safety cameras in operation. These are located at the following locations -
• N17 Mayo
• N59 Galway
• N13 Donegal
• N69 Limerick
• R772 Wexford
• N22 Cork
• N80 Carlow
• N25 Kilkenny
• Dolphin's Barn Dublin 12

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

Noting the above position, I have referred your question, on this occasion, to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question.p: 222. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Transport whether he is considering opening a new round of applications for the Safe Routes to School Programme for schools that did not apply in the original round but have identified a subsequent need; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18533/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The Safe Routes to School (SRTS) Programme was launched in March 2021 with the aim of supporting walking, scooting, and cycling to primary and post-primary schools, and creating safer walking and cycling routes within communities, through the provision of infrastructure interventions including, in some cases, School Zones.

These projects should help alleviate congestion at school gates and increase the number of students who walk or cycle to school. The Safe Routes to School Programme is funded by my Department through the National Transport Authority (NTA) and An Taisce's Green Schools is co-ordinating the programme.

Invitations to express interest were sent to all primary and secondary schools in the country, and 932 applications were received from schools across every county in Ireland. Schools are processed in tranches, with four rounds having been announced to date. Over 500 schools are either active in the programme or have had projects completed. It should be noted that all schools that applied to the original call for applications were accepted into the programme, and if not selected in the rounds to date will be selected in forthcoming rounds.

Given the pipeline of projects due for completion and the number of remaining schools waiting to enter the programme, there are currently no plans for an additional call for schools to join the SRTS programme. It should however be noted that funding for Active Travel infrastructure for schools is not confined to the Safe Routes to Schools Programme alone. In some cases, schools outside the SRTS Programme are included in wider Active Travel projects if they are in the vicinity of these works.

question.p: 223. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport his views on the merits of creating delineated regulations within the existing road traffic act that would differentiate between someone who broke the speed limit by 20% or less and someone who went over that threshold; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18537/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Motorists who speed currently face three penalty points and a fixed charge notice (FCN) of €160, rising to €240 if not paid within 28 days. If after 56 days the motorist has not paid the FCN, the offence is referred to the courts, where the motorist may choose to accept the penalty points and pay a €320 FCN up to seven days before the court date. If the motorist chooses to go to court and is convicted of a speeding offence, they could be fined up to €1000 and receive five penalty points.

The Programme for Government commits to reviewing a graduated penalty points system and this commitment is reaffirmed in the Phase 2 Action Plan 2025-2027 of the Government’s Road Safety Strategy. Primary action 7 of the action plan commits to develop the legislation for graduated speeding sanctions to ensure a structured and proportionate approach to penalising speed violations based on severity and risk.
My Department is progressing a new Road Traffic Bill this year which will include provisions to support the introduction of a graduated penalty points system for speeding.

question.p: 224. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport his views on the merits of requiring the provision of a specific location where a fixed charged notice for speeding was incurred as part of the issuance of the fine by An Garda Síochána; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18538/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that both the English and Irish language versions of the fixed charge notice form, as set out in the Road Traffic Act 2010 (Section 36(1) (Prescribed Notice) Regulations 2017 (SI 243 of 2017), require that the Guard completing the form specifies the location of the alleged offence in question. In the case of speeding, the form also requires specific detail of the speed zone at that location and the speed at which the driver was detected.

question.p: 225. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the last time a review was carried out of the appeal mechanism for the penalty points system for road traffic offences; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18539/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that, as addressed in my Department's response to Parliamentary Question 11653/26 of 17 February, there is no specific statutory penalty points appeals procedure provided for in the Road Traffic Acts. On that basis, I cannot point the Deputy to any previous review as there is no appeals mechanism to review.

A driver may, in very limited and exceptional circumstances, such as the theft of a vehicle, a verified detection error or a genuine medical emergency, apply to An Garda Síochána for the cancellation of a fixed charge and, by extension, any penalty points associated with that charge. A driver who cannot provide sufficient grounds for such a cancellation has the option of refusing to pay the fixed charge and arguing their case in the District Court.

My Department is of the view that the cancellation procedure and the option of going to court provide adequate recourse to drivers who feel they have been unfairly issued with penalty points, and does not consider the introduction of a statutory appeals mechanism to be necessary at this time.

question.p: 226. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the Public Service Obligation Programme, in particular the introduction of the new route 33 service to Whitechurch; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18563/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Investment in public transport nationwide is an all time high. The 2026-2030 National Development Plan outlines a €24.3 billion investment in Ireland's transport sector, with a focus on enhancing public transport and active travel. This marks a transformative moment for Ireland’s transport system, delivering sustainable and accessible travel options to connect us all. Additionally, as secured in Budget 2026, the PSO programme and associated services are being supported by an unprecedented increase in funding of €940 million - a 43% increase compared to last year.

The focus for 2026 is on stabilising and strengthening the PSO position, ensuring services already in place can operate reliably and sustainably, and progressing improvements that are already in train. We are therefore focused on consolidating and strengthening the current network, while progressing improvements already underway, including Phase 7 BusConnects route adjustments and the new Mullingar town service. The NTA will continue to prioritise improvements, within its €940 million allocation.

With over 363.5 million journeys undertaken in 2025, supported by the PSO programme, Ireland’s public transport system is at a pivotal point. Growing passenger demand, urban congestion, and increasing reliance on public transport for commuting and essential travel highlight the need for reliable and sustainable services.

At the same time, the public transport sector is currently experiencing workforce shortages, particularly among drivers, mechanics, and craftworkers. This challenge is affecting some service performance across the network. However, operators are actively engaging with the NTA and the Department to identify and implement solutions to address these resource constraints.

In this context, maintaining and strengthening the existing network is essential to safeguard the delivery of high-demand services to ensure they can operate effectively, while supporting longer-term reforms to enhance capacity, accessibility, and efficiency across the system. The PSO funding allows the NTA to operate the network on a sustainable basis and to prioritise any necessary changes in line with operational capacity and passenger needs. Subsequently decisions on service changes or enhancements are a matter for the NTA, taking account of available funding, operational readiness, and driver availability.
I can assure you the Government remains fully committed to expanding and improving our transport network, ensuring that public transport is an affordable, reliable and attractive option for all.

[18567/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.

Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). Moreover, the contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
Noting the above position, I have referred the question regarding tolls to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.
