question.p: 229. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport the steps his Department has taken to ensure that Ireland has properly enforced Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 in relation to aviation occurrence reporting and whistleblower protection; whether his Department is satisfied with the performance of the Irish Aviation Authority and the Health and Safety Authority in this regard; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18573/26]

230. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department has engaged with the Office of the Ombudsman regarding jurisdictional refusals in aviation safety oversight complaints involving alleged regulatory failure; whether he is satisfied that current oversight mechanisms comply with Ireland's obligations under EU aviation safety law; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18574/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 229 and 230 together.
Regulation (EU) 376/2014 on the reporting, analysis and follow-up of occurrences in civil aviation has been fully implemented and applied in the State.

Ireland has provided for statutory protections for employees and contracted personnel who report or are mentioned in occurrence reports collected in accordance with Articles 4 and 5 of Regulations (EU) 376/2014 to ensure that they are not subject to any prejudice by their employer or by the organisation for which the services are provided based on the information supplied by the reporter.

S.I. No. 195/2020, European Union (Reporting, Analysis and Follow-up of Occurrences in Civil Aviation) Regulations 2020, designated the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) as the competent authority in the State for the purposes of Regulation (EU) No. 376/2014.

In addition to designating the IAA as the competent authority for Regulation (EU) 376/2014, S.I. No. 195/2020 also designated the IAA as the “just culture body” responsible for the implementation of paragraphs 6, 9 and 11 of Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 376/2014.
The IAA’s role under those articles is to ensure:

• there is refrain from instituting proceedings in respect of unpremeditated or inadvertent infringements of the law (Article 16.6) which come to it attention only because they have been reported pursuant to Articles 4 and 5;
• that an employer or an organisation for which the services are provided do not subject any personnel to any prejudice based on the information supplied by the reporter (Article 16.9); and

• that each organisation, after consulting its staff representatives, adopt internal rules describing how ‘just culture’ principles, in particular the principle of non-prejudice, are guaranteed and implemented within that organisation (Article 16.11).

S.I. No. 195/2014 also provides for the redress for contravention of Article 16(9) through the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC). This provides a forum for any person to seek redress if they believe they have been prejudiced, by allowing them to lodge a complaint with the WRC. The S.I. also sets out the application of the Unfair Dismissals Acts 1977 to 2015.

The IAA is also a prescribed body under the Protected Disclosure Act 2014, regarding all matters relating to the management of Irish controlled airspace and the safety regulation of Irish civil aviation and the oversight of civil aviation security in the State. The prescribed person to receive such disclosures is the Company Secretary of the Irish Aviation Authority.

Directive (EU) 2019/1937 on the protection of persons who report breaches of Union law (Whistleblower Directive) outlines the importance of whistleblower protection in terms of preventing and deterring breaches of EU rules on transport safety. Article 3 of the Directive provides that where specific rules on the reporting of breaches are provided for in sector-specific Union acts, those rules apply. The Directive clearly states that the specific rules on the reporting of breaches provided for in Regulation (EU) 376/2014 shall apply.
The IAA has separate and distinct processes for managing protected disclosures and for dealing with complaints as the just culture body.
I am satisfied that the IAA, in respect of its role as the just culture body is enforcing Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 in relation to aviation occurrence reporting and whistleblower protection.
I have no responsibility for the Health and Safety Authority and cannot comment on its arrangements.

summary.i: Question No. 230 answered with Question No. 229.

question.p: 231. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Transport following the decision in December 2025 to abandon the planned restructuring of the Road Safety Authority, to state which body or individual is now responsible for delivering the Government's target of halving road deaths by 2030; whether the Government has examined the Road Safety Commissioner model or equivalent statutory accountability mechanisms used in Sweden, Norway, and Finland; and if not, the reasons for same; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18575/26]

250. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Transport the governance reforms that are being considered to ensure delivery of the national target to halve road deaths by 2030; whether consideration has been given to establishing a statutory Road Safety Commissioner with independent oversight of delivery across agencies; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18969/26]

263. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport if he will examine the potential establishment of a statutory road safety commissioner with clear responsibility for overseeing and coordinating national road safety policy and for monitoring progress towards Ireland’s 2030 road safety targets, in view of the increase in road fatalities in 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19104/26]

279. Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Transport to support the establishment of a position of Road Safety Commissioner to oversee the implementation of the Road Safety Strategy, in particular, the aim of achieving a 50% reduction in road deaths in Ireland by 2030; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19287/26]

343. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if he has any plans to appoint a statutory road safety commissioner with the power to deliver safety targets set for 2030, in light of the increasing death rate on our roads; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19881/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 231, 250, 263, 279 and 343 together.

Road safety is a core priority for me and the Government and the current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030. The Strategy has the target of reducing road deaths and serious injuries by 50% this decade, and to achieving Vision Zero—as close as possible to no deaths or serious injuries on Irish roads—by 2050.

The Phase 2 Action Plan 2025–2027 under the Strategy was published in July 2025. In total, the Phase 2 Plan contains 12 primary and 77 support actions, with the potential to deliver truly transformative change. Actions are being delivered through partnership and collaborative working by road safety stakeholders.

My Department is responsible for the central co-ordination of the Road Safety Strategy and implementation of the Phase 2 Action Plan is overseen at Ministerial level by the Road Safety Leadership Group (RSLG). I chair this Group which is attended by the Minister for Justice and Home Affairs. This Group also comprises senior officials from all key road safety partners including An Garda Síochána, the Road Safety Authority (RSA), Transport Infrastructure Ireland, National Transport Authority, the Courts Service, Medical Bureau of Road Safety, Health and Safety Authority and the Local Authorities

The Group oversees implementation of the Strategy. Action owners are required to report quarterly on actions in their areas and the RSLG meets quarterly to review these updates and to discuss progress on the delivery of the 12 Primary Actions. Additional updates as required are provided on the 77 support actions.
A Road User Safety Forum is also in place and gives a range of road user and road safety advocates an opportunity to contribute to the Phase 2 Action Plan.

The RSA has the statutory remit for the promotion of public awareness of road safety and of measures, including the advancement of education, relating to the promotion of the safe use of roads. The Deputies may be aware that the Department is developing revised proposals for reform of the RSA while retaining the current overall structure of the Authority. Having considered the recommendations of the 2024 Indecon review of the RSA, Minister O’Brien and I have decided not to replace the RSA by the creation of two new entities. However, we are strongly of the view that change is still needed and that reform of the RSA remains necessary. Updated reform proposals, including consideration of using high-profile road safety ambassadors, will be informed by the findings of the Indecon review and experience over the last year. I will present these proposals to Government in the coming weeks.

question.p: 236. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding his plans to improve road safety and decrease road deaths; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18667/26]

375. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Transport his plans to improve road safety and significantly reduce the number of fatalities on Irish roads; and to consider reviewing the role of the RSA. [20191/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 236 and 375 together.

The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030 , which was launched in December 2021 and follows international best practice, aligns with EU and UN targets, and is based on the Safe Systems approach. The Strategy has the target of reducing road deaths and serious injuries by 50% this decade, and to achieving Vision Zero—as close as possible to no deaths or serious injuries on Irish roads—by 2050. A great deal of work is currently underway to deliver on the targets set out in this Strategy.

In July 2025, I published the Phase 2 Action Plan under the Road Safety Strategy , which will run from 2025 to 2027. This phase of the Road Safety Strategy identifies 12 primary actions that are transformative in nature, and which are themed across the overarching, internationally recognised safe systems approach. These 12 actions are supported by a suite of a further 77 support actions which are also being implemented in partnership with road safety stakeholders.
Some of the key actions in the Phase 2 Action Plan include:
• Expanding network safety analysis of the road network to identify high-risk locations, guide investment decisions and prioritise safety interventions including for the local road network.
• Expanding the use of Safety Cameras
• Continued implementation of the 2023 Speed limit review.
• Reviewing and overhauling our learning to drive curriculum

We are progressing a significant legislative programme. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill is targeted for enactment by the summer and will, among other measures, restore direct collision data sharing with local authorities. The next Road Traffic Bill is also under development to advance Programme for Government commitments around graduated speeding penalties and the camera enforcement of mobile phone and seatbelt offences.

We have implemented in full Phase 1 of the Speed Limit Review reducing the default speed limit on rural local roads from 80km/h to 60km/h. Phase 2 in relation to reducing speed limits from 50km/h to 30km/h in urban/built up areas is now underway. In October, local authorities were directed to review existing speed limits on roads in built-up and urban areas. Local authorities will, where appropriate, implement lower speed limits of 30km/h in cities and towns and have been directed to conclude this process by 31 March 2027.

The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan. A first National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed and I expect to publish it shortly. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future.

In the coming weeks, we will also be introducing regulations to fully ban scramblers from use in public places and enhance Garda powers of seizure. These regulations are being made in memory of Grace Lynch and the scrambler ban will be known as Grace’s Law.

Protecting vulnerable road users is a key priority. Safe and Healthy Modes of Travel is one of the seven Safe Systems pillars that underpin the Strategy, and Primary Action 1 of the current Action Plan will see the National Transport Authority invest significantly in improved infrastructure for pedestrians and other active travellers in the coming years. Supporting this action, Budget 2026 has made €360m available for such investment over the next year.

This year we are investing over €1.5billion in our roads. In addition through schemes like the Low-Cost Safety Improvement Scheme under which €14m in funding is available to local authorities for 2026 and the Reactive Road Safety Programme my Department and TII are supporting local authorities to address identified road safety issues across the roads network.

There has been a significant increase in spending on public awareness, communications and education campaigns by the RSA. In 2026 the RSA has again ringfenced funding of €18 million for awareness, education and promotional campaigns. This will ensure a continued focus on campaigns that make our roads safer for all road users, including and especially vulnerable road users.

In 2024, my Department commissioned Indecon Economic Consultants to carry out an independent, external review of the Road Safety Authority (RSA). This review was presented to Government and published in November 2024.

In total, the report made 34 recommendations. At the core of the recommendations was that the operational services run by the RSA should be separated from its research, media campaigns, partnerships and education programmes to improve road safety. A related recommendation was that the RSA’s public interest work should receive Exchequer subvention.

Since the publication of the review, RSA reform activities have been taken forward on a number of fronts. For the first time since 2012, the fees for certain RSA services increased on 1 January 2025 to raise additional revenue and improve the RSA’s financial position; €18m has been specifically ringfenced for annual investment in public interest work in both 2025 and 2026; the Road Safety Communications Steering Group was established in December 2024; the Department of Transport took over central responsibility for the coordination of the Government’s Road Safety Strategy commencing with the July 2025 publication of the Phase 2 Action Plan; and, a new Chair and three new ordinary members were appointed to the RSA board during 2025 with a stronger focus on the RSA’s operational mandate.

In terms of the recommendation to separate out the RSA’s operational and public interest functions, I have decided not to pursue this recommendation as I believe that reform can be delivered more efficiently and effectively within the existing RSA organisational structure. I have directed my officials to prepare revised reform proposals in line with this decision and will present these to Government in the coming weeks.

question.p: 237. Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Transport if Irish Rail will cover the costs in the interim to shorten the gap between platform five and train carriages at Connolly Station, as the gap between some train carriages and this platform at this station is quite big. [18678/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008, the National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for the provision of public transport infrastructure and services within the Greater Dublin Area. In the case of the DART network, the NTA fulfils this statutory remit in collaboration with Iarnród Éireann.

Noting the NTA's responsibility in this matter and the specific queries raised by the Deputy, I have referred the Deputy's questions to the NTA for a direct, detailed reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 days.

Pending this more detailed response, the DART+ Fleet project within the wider DART+ programme is underpinned by a ten-year procurement framework for new electric and battery-electric fleet. One of the primary objectives of the design of the DART+ Fleet is to provide improved accessibility for train users. Low level flooring and entrance doors will reduce the stepping height for passengers and improve access for persons with reduced mobility.

The new carriages will prioritise independent access, with each of the low-height doorway thresholds being equipped with an automatic retractable step and offering the potential for unassisted level access from suitable platforms, aligned with platform enhancements.
Three fleet orders have been placed comprising both battery-electric and electric carriages, bringing the total number of DART carriages ordered to 285, made up of 57 five-carriage trains.

The first order for the purchase of 95 additional DART carriages, (65 battery-electric and 30 electric) have started arriving in Ireland and are currently undergoing certification and safety testing. It is intended that the new battery-electric sets will be initially deployed on the Northern Commuter Line serving Dublin to/from Drogheda from 2027.

question.p: 242. Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Transport the inspection or monitoring which is undertaken by his Department to ensure that approved driving lessons are in compliance and accurately recording the completion of lessons in the drivers log book; if he is concerned whether some instructors may be filling in log books without the lessons having been completed in full; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18737/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service, including regulation of Approved Driver Instructors (ADIs). In that regard I have referred the Deputy's question to the RSA for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.

I am informed by the RSA that its voluntary code of practice for Approved Driving Instructors (ADIs) sets standards for professional, ethical, and safe instruction. ADIs are assessed or check tested bi- annually as part of the ADI re- registration process. During this check test, copies of training records from the Essential Driver Training Logbook (EDT) are inspected to ensure that all entries and information is accurate and properly maintained.

Additionally, ADIs who upload EDT sessions are monitored to ensure compliance and to detect any irregular or potentially illegal activity. The RSA Data Analysis team oversees this process and can review training volumes and ADI activity levels.
I am informed that this oversight allows the RSA to identify unusual patterns or volumes of training sessions that may indicate non-compliant or unlawful activity.
lf a learner or anybody has any concerns in relation to the behaviour of an ADI I would recommend that they contact the RSA directly.

question.p: 243. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if he considers it appropriate for Transport Infrastructure Ireland to refuse to meet with a Municipal Committee of Kildare County Council (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18742/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Cycle Network (NCN); Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) manage the delivery and oversight of NCN projects.

The NCN identified core cycling corridors around the country which, when delivered, will help increase cycling rates amongst residents, leisure users, and tourists alike. The ambition of the NCN is significant; it will provide an excellent level of connectivity nationally.

For road safety reasons and cyclist comfort and confidence, the NCN plan emphasises the importance of physical segregation between cyclists and motorists on busier roads. Pilots are being conducted to assess various segregation techniques in situ to inform future infrastructure projects. The Moone to Timolin scheme is such a pilot, offering an opportunity to trial different road separation treatments along the R448.

This pilot has been delivered by Kildare County Council as the road authority and is funded by TII. I understand that the scheme underwent a formal consenting process which involved public consultation, and that in September representatives from TII, Kildare County Council and Aecom met with local stakeholders to hear their concerns regarding the scheme.

The Deputy’s query relates to a further meeting request from the Athy Municipal Committee to TII. I understand that TII have invited Kildare County Council to include the Moone to Timolin Pilot as an agenda item at their next delegation meeting. These delegation meetings represent an optimum and efficient use of available resources for both parties. They provide local authorities with the opportunity to set the meeting agenda and for TII to ensure that the relevant staff are in attendance to respond to the respective agenda items.

Noting this long-standing practice, and to maximise resource use, I suggest that the Athy Municipal Committee engage with their colleagues to request that the Timolin to Moone Pilot Scheme is included as an agenda item on the next TII/Kildare County Council delegation meeting.

question.p: 244. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Transport to provide an up-to-date status on the CIÉ superannuation scheme for those who have not received an increase in their pension for the past 18 years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18829/26]

248. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport if he will confirm that the pension increases for retired Córas Iompair Éireann workers will be progressed imminently by his Department, as confirmed by the Taoiseach during a meeting of the Committee on Finance, Public Expenditure and Reform, and Taoiseach on the 26 February 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18873/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 244 and 248 together.

As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. As a commercial semi-state body, Córas Iompair Éireann (CIÉ) are responsible for the provision of pension schemes for their employees.

Following on from the constructive and collaborative approach of the Trade Union Group and CIÉ management in reaching agreement on a pathway forward as of May 2025, my Department, alongside our financial and commercial advisors NewERA, are currently engaging with all relevant stakeholders. This includes CIÉ, the Pensions Authority and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Services, Reform and Digitalisation on the next steps in progressing the agreement and bringing CIÉ pensions onto a more stable footing for the benefit of active, and retired scheme members, including review of the relevant statutory instruments and the matter of increases to pension payments.

My Department and all relevant stakeholders are endeavouring to achieve the same at the earliest, keeping in line with the appropriate procedures, compliance with all applicable requirements, and necessary approvals as part of the formal process, which is now well underway.

question.p: 251. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Transport the number of average-speed camera systems currently operational on the national road network;the plans to expand their deployment to high-risk routes; the timeline for any expansion programme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18970/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras.
There are currently 5 average speed cameras in operation across the road network. These are located in the following locations -
• Dublin Port Tunnel
• N3 Cavan
• N5 Mayo
• N2 Meath

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

question.p: 252. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has identified the highest-risk road sections for fatal and serious collisions on the national and regional network; whether a targeted safety redesign programme is planned for these locations; the funding allocated for such works; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18971/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the planning, design and construction of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals.

I understand from TII that TII does not rank roads against each other, but instead operates a dedicated Reactive Road Safety Programme for the national road network. Under this system—set out in TII standard GE-STY-01022 (“Network Safety Ranking and Prioritisation – Reactive Approach”) collision data is used to identify high-collision locations (1km sections) across the network.

Where such sites are detected, TII formally notifies the relevant Local Authority and requires the Local Authority to propose a scheme, as the road authority, to address the issues identified. TII subsequently provides funding for targeted safety improvement schemes to address the issues identified. This process is detailed in GE-STY-01036 (“Road Safety Improvement Schemes”). On average €26 million is allocated to this programme each year.

For more information on the Reactive Road Safety System please see this website: https://cdn.tii.ie/publications/GE-STY-01022-03.pdf and for more information on the Improvement Scheme process, please see this website: https://cdn.tii.ie/publications/GE-STY-01036-01.pdf

Separately, TII has recently published the Network-Wide Road Safety Assessment (NWA). This safety rating system evaluates approximately 2500km of the national primary road network by combining both historical collision data and data from current proactive infrastructure inspections. The website can be viewed here: tii-nwa-2024-map-national-primary-roads.pdf (https://linkscan.io/scan/ux/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cudGlpLmllL21lZGlhL2xqMG40NTQ1L3RpaS1ud2EtMjAyNC1tYXAtbmF0aW9uYWwtcHJpbWFyeS1yb2Fkcy5wZGY=/CB2FE3C87BBF40CEC6E3D2B6BC20973C4D105DAE6536891815B13DDEE9F441A0?c=5&i=1&docs=1)

In respect of the regional and local road network, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, each local authority has statutory responsibility for the improvement and maintenance of their regional and local roads. Works on those roads are funded from local authorities' own resources and are supplemented by State grants.

Where a fatal road traffic collision occurs, the relevant local authority engineer and investigating member of An Garda Síochána meet at the site of the collision and jointly complete a collision report form named LA16. This is an action of the Road Safety Strategy 2021 - 2030.

The completed LA16 form, outlines the details of the collision, weather conditions and road conditions including signage, road markings, speed limit, roadside environment and classification of the road etc. These forms are submitted to the Roads Management Office who maintain the dataset.

My Department also funds a Network Safety Analysis of the Regional and Local Road Network across the entire country. Using available collision datasets high collision locations are identified and Locations of Interest (LoIs) reports are produced.

These LoI reports are then issued to the relevant local authority and form the basis for application for funding under the Safety Improvement Schemes Grant. In 2026 my Department allocated €14 million in Safety Improvement Schemes Grant to the sector which is funding over 330 safety schemes nationally which is an 8% increase over the 2025 allocation.

question.p: 253. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Transport the accountability mechanisms are in place to ensure delivery of the Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030 across relevant agencies; whether performance reporting against the 2030 fatality reduction target will be published regularly; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18973/26]

280. Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Transport the body is responsible for overseeing the implementation of the Road Safety Strategy; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19288/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 253 and 280 together.

The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030. The Strategy has the target of reducing road deaths and serious injuries by 50% this decade, and to achieving Vision Zero—as close as possible to no deaths or serious injuries on Irish roads—by 2050.

The Phase 2 Action Plan 2025–2027 under the Strategy was published in July 2025. In total, the Phase 2 Plan contains 12 primary and 77 support actions, with the potential to deliver truly transformative change. Actions are being delivered through partnership and collaborative working by road safety stakeholders.

My Department is responsible for the central co-ordination of the Road Safety Strategy and implementation of the Phase 2 Action Plan is overseen at Ministerial level by the new Road Safety Leadership Group (RSLG). This Group is chaired by Minister Canney who is responsible for Road Safety and is attended by the Minister for Justice and Home Affairs. This Group also comprises senior officials from all key road safety partners including An Garda Síochána, the Road Safety Authority, Transport Infrastructure Ireland, National Transport Authority, the Courts Service, MBRS, HSA and the Local Authorities

The Group oversees implementation of the Strategy. Action owners are required to report quarterly on actions in their areas and the RSLG meets quarterly to review these updates and to discuss progress on the delivery of the 12 Primary Actions. Additional updates as required are provided on the 77 support actions.
A Road User Safety Forum is also in place and gives a range of road user and road safety advocates an opportunity to contribute to the Phase 2 Action Plan.

question.p: 254. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport if he will pursue a formal exception for short-term car rental operators in EU negotiations in relation to the zero-emission vehicle sales target; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18979/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I am aware of the concerns from this sector in relation to the proposal. We have met with representatives in various occasions. For context, many Member States, including Ireland, are relying heavily on a rapid transition to deliver on their decarbonisation plans. Ireland’s Climate Action Plan target is to have 30% of the national vehicle fleet be electric by 2030. This is Ireland’s single biggest transport mitigation action up to 2030.

The proposal on Clean Corporate Vehicles forms part of the European Commission’s Automotive Package, published on 16 December 2025. It is designed to accelerate the transition to zero and low emission corporate fleets, reduce fossil fuel expenditure in road transport and accelerate the availability of zero emission vehicles on the second-hand market.

Member States retain flexibility for the implementation pathway of the national targets. The corporate fleet sector is diverse, consisting large and small companies, ranging from traditional company car executive fleets to large shipping and freight companies, last-mile delivery fleets, leasing companies and short-term rental companies. Each of these sub-sectors have unique conditions that would make a one-size-fits-all approach ineffective.

We are considering the proposal in detail in terms of how it aligns with the overall objective of incentivising demand for EVs and any wider impacts. This includes an analysis of the number and profile of companies in scope, fleet characteristics and market conditions.

It should be noted that the measure remains at proposal stage, with negotiations underway at EU level. The Regulation will not be finalised until agreement is reached between the Council and the European Parliament, a process that is expected to run through 2026. As Ireland prepares to assume the EU Presidency in July 2026, it is committed to playing a neutral and constructive role in facilitating dialogue among member states.

question.p: 255. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Transport the steps being taken to ensure that app-based taxi platforms provide accurate information and prevent misleading practices that inflate fares (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18980/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.

As the Deputy may be aware, SPSV operators are self-employed and may decide to sign-up, or not, with a licensed dispatch operator, such as Uber, FreeNow by Lyft and Bolt. They are not obliged by my Department or the NTA to be affiliated with any dispatch operator but where they choose to do so, they are free to contract with a dispatch operator of their choice. They also decide on their own hours of work within the SPSV regulatory framework.

The NTA has published a Call for Inputs consultation on the dispatch operator licensing framework. A sustainable taxi sector is an important element of Ireland’s transport system, and I encourage all stakeholders to take the opportunity to feed into this important piece of work, as this input will inform the NTA's process and decision-making in revising the current dispatch operator framework. The closing date for the receipt of submissions is 17th April next. The public consultation can be viewed here: https://consult.nationaltransport.ie/en/content/call-inputs-dispatch-operators

Given the NTA's responsibility in regulating dispatch operators, I have referred your question to the NTA for further information. Please advise my private office if you have not received a reply within 10 working days.

question.p: 256. Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport if he will engage with Transport Infrastructure Ireland, or the National Transport Authority, to engage consultants to further explore route options for light rail transit in the Galway metropolitan area with a view to identifying an "emerging preferred route"; if such a plan for a preferred route exists; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19010/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for the planning and development of public transport infrastructure including light rail.
The Programme for Government commits to examine further investment in light rail for our cities.

The NTA is currently developing the Galway Metropolitan Area Transport Strategy (GMATS), in conjunction with Galway City Council and Galway County Council. This strategy will replace the existing Galway Transport Strategy adopted in 2016 and will provide a long-term strategic planning framework for the delivery of transport and the integrated development of transport infrastructure and services in the Galway Metropolitan Area.

Part of the development of the new GMATS necessitates mode specific analysis and this is being undertaken in the form of a Light Rail Feasibility Study and a Strategic Roads Feasibility Study. Both studies will form part of the analysis used to inform the development of the multi-modal GMATS, alongside recommendations for active travel, bus, rail, roads and demand management measures.

In Galway, the Light Rail Feasibility Study was published by the NTA in October 2024 for information and has shown that there could, under the right conditions, be a case for developing a light rail system in Galway. The feasibility study will form part of the evidence base used as an input into the development of the Galway Metropolitan Area Transport Strategy, which will be subject to a full environmental analysis and public consultation process in due course. It should be noted that any future light rail project in Galway will only be advanced subject to funding and securing relevant Government approval under the Infrastructure Guidelines.

The NTA considers that it is appropriate to await An Coimisiún Pleanála’s determination on the re-submitted N6 Galway City Ring Road application in order to fully develop the draft GMATS. Of course, once sufficiently developed the draft GMATS will be opened to full public consultation.

In the meantime, implementation will continue on the current Galway Transport Strategy. A significant amount of planning and design has already taken place which will enable construction activity in the coming years across active travel, bus and rail related projects including BusConnects.
Noting the NTA's responsibility, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 days.

summary.i: A referred reply was forwarded to the Deputy under Standing Orders.

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport.

Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 and the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009, the Oireachtas assigned statutory responsibility to the National Transport Authority (NTA) for promoting the development of an integrated, accessible public transport network and public transport infrastructure. question.p: 259. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Transport for an update in relation to the proposed second platform in Clara train station, County Offaly; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19065/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Following the publication of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in July 2024, my Department, with the support of the European Investment Bank and in conjunction with the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland, oversaw the preparation of the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy. This Strategy was published in December 2025 and outlines the approach to sequencing and optimising the recommendations of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in the coming years.

In the short-term to 2030, the Prioritisation Strategy specifies a number of 'Early Interventions' to be delivered in the coming years, including new track passing loops and platforms to boost the rail network’s resilience and capacity. These investments are funded to be fully delivered by 2030 under the NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for Transport, published in November 2025. A second platform at Clara train station is included in these Early Interventions.

It should be noted that individual programmes and projects referred to within the All-Island Strategic Rail Review and the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy will be advanced subject to funding and relevant approvals, as required under the Infrastructure Guidelines.

Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Transport if he will provide an update on the status of the proposed reopening of the Mullingar–Athlone railway line; the extent to which the project is being examined following its inclusion in the All-Island Strategic Rail Review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19121/26]

269. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department, the National Transport Authority or Iarnród Éireann plans to undertake a detailed feasibility study or cost-benefit analysis on the reopening of the Mullingar–Athlone rail line; the timeline for any such study; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19122/26]

270. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Transport the steps being taken to ensure the former Mullingar–Athlone rail corridor and associated railway lands are preserved for potential future rail use; and if there are any proposals to repurpose or alter sections of the alignment. [19123/26]

271. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department has examined the potential impact of reopening the Mullingar–Athlone rail line on commuting patterns to Technological University of the Shannon in Athlone from towns along the Dublin–Sligo line including Mullingar, Longford, Edgeworthstown, Enfield, Kilcock and Maynooth. [19125/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 268 to 271, inclusive, together.

Following the publication of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in July 2024, my Department, with the support of the European Investment Bank and in conjunction with the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland, oversaw the preparation of the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy. This Strategy was published in December 2025 and outlines the approach to sequencing and optimising the recommendations of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in the coming years.

In the short-term to 2030, the Prioritisation Strategy specifies a number of 'Early Interventions' to be delivered in the coming years, including new track passing loops and platforms to boost the rail network’s resilience and capacity. These investments are funded to be fully delivered by 2030 under the NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for Transport, published in November 2025.

Examples of Early Interventions include the recommissioning of Platform 2 at MacDiarmada station in Sligo, a passing loop between Sligo and Boyle, a second platform at Enfield, and a passing loop west of Claremorris. These interventions will support rail frequency and reliability improvements for residents of Athlone and Mullingar and their surrounding areas.

The Prioritisation Strategy also identifies 'Major Projects' with longer lead-in and development timelines. These projects are generally targeted to secure the necessary approvals within the next five years such that construction works could commence thereafter.

The Prioritisation Strategy has a 20-year time horizon, which does not cover the entire period to 2050 envisaged by the All-Island Strategic Rail Review. Projects not included in the Prioritisation Strategy, including the reinstatement of the line between Mullingar and Athlone, are intended to be progressed in the longer-run.

It should be noted that individual programmes and projects referred to within the All-Island Strategic Rail Review and the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy will be advanced subject to funding and relevant approvals, as required under the Infrastructure Guidelines.

question.p: 272. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport if his attention has been drawn to the long standing issues with getting a bus service to a location (details supplied); his views on the possible solutions at this location; and if he will make a statement on the matter. speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As the Deputy may be aware, BusConnects is a transformative programme of investment in the bus system, providing better bus services across our cities, including Galway. BusConnects is the largest investment in the bus system in the history of the State and is managed by the National Transport Authority (NTA).

In 2023, the NTA carried out an extensive review of the bus network in Galway, in collaboration with Galway City Council, Galway County Council, local bus operators, and with the specialised expertise of transport designers Jarrett Walker and Associates. In April 2023, a draft new network was published, and the feedback and submissions received have informed the final new bus network published in December 2023.

The new bus network will enable more people to avail of public transport, resulting in increased access to a greater number of schools and workplaces across Galway City, Bearna, and Oranmore. Once this network is implemented, approximately 67% of residents will live within 400 metres of a high frequency bus route running every 15 minutes or better.
Noting the NTA's responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 days.

question.p: 273. Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Transport the total annual expenditure on road safety by the RSA and Transport Infrastructure Ireland respectively, in each of the past five years; the way in which this compares with equivalent expenditure in Finland, Norway, and Sweden on a per-capita basis; and whether the Government has assessed the cost-effectiveness of deploying a national network of automated speed cameras, given international evidence that such networks are net revenue-positive within two years of deployment. [19189/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport (Deputy Seán Canney)
speech.p: Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, RSA has statutory responsibility for the promotion of public awareness campaigns and for the advancement of education specific to the safe use of roads. Given that the RSA does not receive Exchequer funding for this work, which is elaborated upon below, I have referred the Deputy's question to the RSA for direct response. I have also referred the Deputy's question to TII for a direct reply. I would ask the Deputy to contact my office if a response has not been received within ten days.

Pending this response, the Deputy may be aware that the Road Safety Authority has been largely self-funded in respect of its operations since 2014. The RSA ordinarily receives annual Exchequer funding of approximately €1m to fund historic pension liabilities and its activities as Ireland's Automotive Market Surveillance Authority, which is an EU obligation that the RSA fulfils on behalf of Ireland.

The RSA has again ringfenced €18m for investment in road safety public interest activities. This includes awareness, educational, and promotion campaigns. This is in line with investment in 2025 and is part of a wider shift to bring a renewed focus on campaigns that make our roads safer for all road users.

In addition, on 9 March Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) published its Road Safety Improvement Scheme Programme Activity Report 2025, setting out how road safety risks are identified, prioritised and addressed across Ireland’s National Roads network. TII indicated that it invests an average of €26 million each year through the Road Safety Improvement Scheme programme. In 2025, more than 210 safety improvement schemes were advanced nationwide, with over 80 schemes at construction and close-out stages. These schemes address a wide range of risks on the network, including junction safety, roadside hazards, speed management and facilities for vulnerable road users.

Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras. There are currently five average speed cameras in operation across the road network. In addition there are nine static safety cameras in operation.

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

summary.i: A referred reply was forwarded to the Deputy under Standing Orders.

question.p: 274. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the way in which his Department will ensure that the recent European Commission ruling concerning night-flight limits at Dublin Airport is to be addressed by the planning system and planning authorities; the oversight mechanisms that are in place to ensure compliance with EU aviation noise regulations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19205/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Ireland’s National Aviation Policy (NAP) supports the sustainable development of Dublin Airport. I firmly believe that development at the airport needs to balance the legitimate views of those who live and work in the surrounds of the airport with the objectives of the NAP and needs of business and tourism.

On the 10th of February 2026, following completion of its assessment of An Coimisiún Pleanála’s July 2025 decision, the European Commission issued a notification advising that the process used by An Coimisiún Pleanála for the proposed introduction of operating restrictions at Dublin Airport did not fully follow the Balanced Approach process, as set out in Regulation (EU) 598/2014.

In line with the provisions of EU Regulation 598/2014 (the EU Aircraft Noise Regulation) and the Aircraft Noise (Dublin Airport) Act 2019, as the independent competent authority for this matter, An Coimisiún Pleanála will now have to examine this Decision and consider appropriate next steps.

With regard to aircraft noise regulation, the competent authority for the purposes of aircraft noise regulation in Ireland is the Aircraft Noise Competent Authority (ANCA), a separate and independent Directorate within Fingal County Council. However, oversight and enforcement of compliance with any relevant planning conditions are matters for the relevant independent planning authorities.

In its role as aircraft noise regulator, ANCA carries out an annual assessment of the effectiveness of the noise management measures at Dublin Airport and publishes a report on the findings on its website. This is in addition to publishing annual reports by the airport authority on the compliance by airport users with the noise management measures.

If through regular review or an assessment of the potential impact of development at the airport it is indicated that new or amended measures are required to manage aircraft noise at the airport, ANCA will facilitate a period of public consultation on draft proposals to address any noise problem or potential noise problem.

I understand that ANCA is currently carrying out an assessment of the noise situation at Dublin Airport, including examining the effects of noise on local communities and the potential noise impact of planning applications at Dublin Airport that seek permission for infrastructure and increases to the permitted passenger capacity of the airport.

Finally, the Aircraft Noise (Dublin Airport) Act 2019 includes a requirement that I appoint a person to carry out a review of the performance by the aircraft noise competent authority, ANCA, within seven years of enactment. In line with the legislation, the first such statutory review of ANCA is due to commence this year.

question.p: 275. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the legal advice received by his Department regarding the implications of the European Commission's finding that the night-flight restriction decision by An Coimisiún Pleanála breached EU regulations; his views on whether appropriate procedures will be followed in any reconsideration of the matter; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19206/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I firmly believe that it is important that in ensuring the sustainable development of Dublin Airport, to balance the legitimate views of stakeholders who are concerned about the environmental and aircraft noise impacts at the airport, with the objectives of the National Aviation Policy, and the needs of business and tourism.

As you will be aware, on the 17th of July 2025, An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) published its final decision in relation to night-time air traffic operations at Dublin Airport, which included, amongst other conditions, a restriction on flights on the new north runway between midnight and 6am except in exceptional specified circumstances.

On the 8th of August 2025, ACP notified the EU Commission of the operating restrictions set out in its July 2025 decision, as required under Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 598/2014, and the Commission subsequently undertook an assessment of the process followed by ACP in its decision.

On the 10th of February 2026, following completion of its assessment, the EU Commission issued a notification advising that the process used by ACP for the proposed introduction of operating restrictions at Dublin Airport did not fully follow the Balanced Approach process, as set out in Regulation (EU) 598/2014.

The Balanced Approach involves consideration of a range of measures, such as reduction of noise at source, effective land-use planning and management, and noise abatement operational procedures, before implementing any noise-related operating restrictions at an airport.

In line with the provisions of Regulation (EU) 598/2014 and the 2019 Aircraft Noise Act, as the independent competent authority for this matter, An Coimisiún Pleanála will now have to examine this Decision and to determine the most appropriate next steps.

question.p: 277. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the progress to commence and update relevant regulations and codes of practice in respect of the seizure of scramblers and use of drones in respect of same. [19225/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: The Government approved the preparation of regulations to fully ban the use of scramblers in any public place on 4 February. It is my intention that these regulations will close any cases where scrambler use may previously have been legal outside of appropriate off-road settings and bring additional legal clarity to the existing position that scramblers are banned for use on the road in almost all cases. My Department is working with the Office of the Attorney General and the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel with a view to making these regulations in the coming weeks. I also propose to impose greater financial penalties on seized vehicles to reduce the number that re-enter circulation.

Under powers introduced by section 41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994, An Garda Síochána has the power to seize mechanically propelled vehicles, such as scramblers, being driven on public roads without tax or insurance. Once seized, An Garda Síochána has the power to dispose of a seized vehicle three weeks after the date of detention, provided two weeks' notice of the intention to dispose is given. Separate seizure powers, introduced by the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023, exist with respect to dangerous driving.

The current fees in respect of a vehicle seized under section 41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994 are set out in Statutory Instrument 460/2011. I intend to introduce regulations to increase the fees associated with release of mechanically propelled vehicles, such as scramblers, which have been seized under this section. The precise value of this increase is yet to be determined and will be made in consultation with the Minister for Justice.

Enforcement of seizure powers, including the development of a Code of Practice on the use of drones, is a matter for An Garda Síochána and the Minister for Justice is better placed to answer questions on this issue.

question.p: 278. Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Transport if Dublin City Council and the other Dublin local authorities currently have access to collision location data from 2019 onwards; the reason the Road Safety Authority ceased sharing this data with local authorities in 2020, given that the Data Protection Commission stated in April 2024 that GDPR should not prevent the proportionate publication of anonymised crash-location details; to explain the way in which local authority road engineers are expected to identify and redesign dangerous junctions for cyclists and pedestrians without access to this data; and to provide a specific date by which the National Vehicle and Driver File Bill 2025 will be enacted to restore this access. [19234/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Collision data are collected by members of An Garda Síochána at the scene of road traffic accidents. These data were previously shared with local authorities, via the Road Safety Authority, to enable them to identify locations of interest (accident blackspots) that would benefit from safety improvements. Due to the presence of personal information in the data, legal advice related to GDPR has meant that local authorities stopped receipt of collision data since November 2023. As well as sharing of the data, the local authorities have identified an issue with the legal basis to process the data, once received. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill 2025 will, once enacted, provide a legal basis for local authorities to receive and process the collision data.

As an interim measure, the Department of Transport has been undertaking detailed collision analysis on the regional and local road network to identify locations of interest. When locations of interest are identified, the Department notifies the affected local authority. In turn, local authorities can apply for funding of low-cost safety schemes for these locations of interest.

The General Scheme of the National Vehicle and Driver File Bill 2025 has been approved by Government and is with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel for drafting. The passage of this Bill is a Programme for Government commitment and will amend the Roads Act 1993 to provide a basis for the resumption of direct sharing of road traffic collision data with local authorities. The Bill will be published in the coming weeks with enactment targeted for the first half of 2026.

Question No. 280 answered with Question No. 253.

question.p: 281. Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Transport the measures his Department is taking to address road safety; whether her Department will support the creation of a statutory road safety commissioner; deploy average-speed cameras on high risk routes; review and high risk road sections for redesign; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19298/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030 and a great deal of work is currently underway to deliver on the targets set out in this Strategy.

The Phase 2 Action Plan published in July 2025 contains 12 primary and 77 supporting actions, with the potential to deliver real transformative change. These actions are grounded in the internationally recognised Safe Systems approach and will be delivered through partnership and collaborative working by road safety stakeholders. Some of the key actions include –
• investing significantly into new and improved active travel and public transport;
• expanding the use of safety cameras;
• expanding network safety analysis of the road network to identify high-risk locations, guide investment decisions and prioritise safety interventions including for the local road network;
• implementing in full all actions in the Phase 2 Action Plan based on the 2023 Speed limit review;
• reviewing and overhauling our learning to drive curriculum.

Delivery of the Phase 2 Action Plan is being co-ordinated by my Department and is being led by the Road Safety Leadership Group which brings together senior leaders from across road safety stakeholders including – AGS, DOJ, RSA, TII,NTA, HSA, MBRS and Local Authorities. This group is chaired at Ministerial level by Minister Canney and is attended by the Minister for Justice and Home Affairs.

Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras. There are currently five average speed cameras in operation across the road network. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan of the Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

TII operates a dedicated Reactive Road Safety Programme for the national road network. Under this system collision data are used to identify high-collision locations across the network. Where such sites are detected, TII formally notifies the relevant Local Authority and requires the Local Authority to propose a scheme, as the road authority, to address the issues identified. TII subsequently provides funding for targeted safety improvement schemes to address the issues identified. Separately, TII has recently published the Network-Wide Road Safety Assessment (NWA). This safety rating system evaluates approximately 2500km of the national primary road network by combining both historical collision data and data from current proactive infrastructure inspections.

In addition my Department provides funding to Local Authorities each year under the Low-Cost Safety Improvement Scheme to support small-scale engineering measures that address identified road safety issues for regional and local roads. Since 2022, more than 400 locations of interest have been funded under low-cost safety schemes and local authorities continue to review and apply for funding to complete additional schemes each year. This year €14 million has been allocated, representing an increase of €1 million (approximately 8%) on 2025 allocations.

The RSA has the statutory remit for the promotion of public awareness of road safety and of measures, including the advancement of education, relating to the promotion of the safe use of roads. The Deputies may be aware that the Department is developing revised proposals for reform of the RSA while retaining the current overall structure of the Authority. Having considered the recommendations of the 2024 Indecon review of the RSA, Minister Canney and I have decided not to replace the RSA by the creation of two new entities. However, we are strongly of the view that change is still needed and that reform of the RSA remains necessary. Updated reform proposals, including consideration of using high-profile road safety ambassadors, will be informed by the findings of the Indecon review and experience over the last year. I will present these proposals to Government in the coming weeks.

question.p: 282. Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Transport the total amount spent on road infrastructure in each region under the current National Development Plan, in each of the past five years, in tabular form. [19324/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on these roads are funded from councils’ own resources and supplemented by State road grants. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million in our regional and local roads across the State. This will facilitate an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works.

The primary focus for capital investment under the National Development Plan continues to be the protection and renewal of the regional and local road network, together with some targeted investment in road improvement projects.

As regards the total amount spent on regional and local road infrastructure in each region under the current National Development Plan for each of the years 2020-2025, details of the regional and local road allocations and payments to local authorities are outlined in the regional and local road allocations and payments booklets which are available on the Oireachtas Digital Library.

Full details of the 2026 regional and local grant allocations are available at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/press-releases/ministers-for-transport-announce-over-15-billion-for-national-regional-and-local-roads/.

As Minister for Transport I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals.

National roads allocations for years 2021 -2025 are available at: www.tii.ie/en/tii-library/reports-accounts/. Full details of national roads allocations for 2026 are available on the TII website: 2026-tii-la-national-roads-allocations-booklet.pdf

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport.

Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 and the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009, the Oireachtas assigned statutory responsibility to the National Transport Authority (NTA) for promoting the development of an integrated, accessible public transport network and public transport infrastructure. The NTA in turn works with the relevant public transport operators, for example Irish Rail, who have responsibility for day-to-day operational issues, to progressively make public transport accessible.
