Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Transport the preparation the Government has regarding the Clean Corporate Vehicles legislation; the supports that will be provided for impacted tourism and transport industry; if any exemptions will be sought; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19374/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Thank you for your correspondence.

Many Member States, including Ireland, are relying heavily on a rapid transition to deliver on their decarbonisation plans. Ireland’s Climate Action Plan target is to have 30% of the national vehicle fleet be electric by 2030. This is Ireland’s single biggest transport mitigation action up to 2030

The proposal on Clean Corporate Vehicles forms part of the European Commission’s Automotive Package, published on 16 December 2025. It is designed to accelerate the transition to zero and low emission corporate fleets, reduce fossil fuel expenditure in road transport and accelerate the availability of zero emission vehicles on the second-hand market.

Member States retain flexibility for the implementation pathway of the national targets. The corporate fleet sector is diverse, consisting large and small companies, ranging from traditional company car executive fleets to large shipping and freight companies, last-mile delivery fleets, leasing companies and short-term rental companies. Each of these sub-sectors have unique conditions that would make a one-size-fits-all approach ineffective.

We are considering the proposal in detail in terms of how it aligns with the overall objective of incentivising demand for EVs and any wider impacts. This includes an analysis of the number and profile of companies in scope, fleet characteristics and market conditions.

It should be noted that the measure remains at proposal stage, with negotiations underway at EU level. The Regulation will not be finalised until agreement is reached between the Council and the European Parliament, a process that is expected to run through 2026. As Ireland prepares to assume the EU Presidency in July 2026, it is committed to playing a neutral and constructive role in facilitating dialogue among member states.

question.p: 294. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport to provide funding for the M50 Liffey Crossing Active Travel Project; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19390/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to active travel. Under the Roads Act 1993, the planning, design, and construction of individual Greenways or active travel on national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Noting the above position, I have referred your question, on this occasion, to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question.p: 295. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has calculated the estimated cost of a €5,000 per vehicle scrappage scheme for private diesel cars registered before 2015; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19395/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The Government is fully committed to supporting the transition to zero-emission and the delivery of the ambitious target to have 30% of private car fleet switched to electric by 2030.

Funding and incentives for Electric Vehicles are under regular review by Departmental officials with a view to targeting exchequer funding which can deliver most effectively against Government priorities. The relative cost of EVs versus their ICE equivalents is improving year on year. My Department has in the past year reviewed a number of options for EV incentives, as set out in the Programme for Government.

Based on available data, there are around 1.1m ICE cars registered before 2015, including 650,000 diesel vehicles. As such, a global scrappage scheme of €5k for such vehicles as suggested by the Deputy would be extremely costly to the State. While targeted scrappage schemes can be effective in certain instances, any scheme of this nature would need careful consideration in terms of wider policy, operational and budgetary implications.

question.p: 296. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the number of private diesel cars registered before 2015 that are currently licensed and taxed in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19396/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: As Minister of State with responsibility for International and Road Transport, Logistics, Rail and Ports, I wish to advise that, as of 28 February 2026, a total of current 518,104 taxed vehicles were registered on the National Vehicle and Driver File (NVDF) database prior to 2015.

question.p: 297. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding his efforts to accelerate the transition to electric and sustainable transport; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19397/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: My Department remains firmly committed to accelerating Ireland’s transition to electric and sustainable transport, in line with our emissions reduction obligations and the Programme for Government.

The Sustainable Mobility Policy (SMP) provides the overarching framework to 2030 for increasing active travel, shared mobility and public transport, reducing reliance on the private car, and delivering a more efficient, low-carbon transport system.

On 4 March, my Department published the SMP Action Plan 2026–2030, the second Action Plan to have been developed under the SMP. This new Plan strengthens the Government’s commitment to delivering high-quality alternatives to the private car. It supports major public transport infrastructure projects such as MetroLink, BusConnects, DART+ and the reinstatement of Athenry-Claremorris section of the Western Rail Corridor, as well as expanded active travel infrastructure, the Safe Routes to School programme, Park and Ride delivery, bus and rail fleet electrification, and improved accessibility across the transport network.

In addition, last year my Department published the ‘National Policy Statement on Shared Mobility and the Provision of Hubs’. This Statement aims to bring greater coherence to the development of shared mobility services and hubs, providing new and more sustainable alternatives to the private car. The NTA is working on two key initiatives –

• a Mobility Hubs Pilot Programme, which will deliver a dense network of hubs to be rolled out across five locations - Cork City, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown, Carlow, Dundalk and Sligo – encompassing shared escooters, ebikes and shared EVs; and
• the expansion of public bikes schemes in the regional cities to provide more options over a wider area including a greater proliferation of ebikes.

To further strengthen this Government’s commitment to decarbonising transport, a new strategy Moving Together: A Collaborative Approach to Systems Change in Transport 2026–2030 was also published on 4 March. The aim of this strategy is to encourage collaboration and to find innovative ways for better managing transport demand and congestion, while supporting and reinforcing the objectives of the SMP. It focuses on the generation of demand from private traffic and freight movements and consists of broad-ranging recommendations for achieving greater efficiency across all sectors including actions in support of a transition to EVs.

The new draft National EV Charging Infrastructure Strategy 2026-2028, published on the 26th February, aims to accelerate the delivery of EV infrastructure across Ireland. It includes a comprehensive plan to expand and future-proof the national EV charging network, ensuring that charging infrastructure continues to keep pace with the growing demand for electric vehicles.

The strategy focuses on delivering accessible, reliable, and comprehensive charging infrastructure through to 2028, supporting Ireland's transition to cleaner transport and aligning with national and EU climate goals.
Last year, the Government met the 2025 target of 195000 EVs on Irish roads in September, and there are currently over 219,000 EVs on Irish roads.

Over €120m has been allocated in 2026 to support the transition to zero-emission and the delivery of the ambitious target to have 30% of private car fleet switched to electric by 2030, which includes funding for EV grants and EV charging infrastructure. This underpins the Government's commitment to making electric vehicles accessible to all.

Having an effective and reliable charging network is an essential part of enabling drivers to make the switch to electric vehicles. The public charging network has grown in recent years, and the continuing expansion and modernisation of the EV charging network will ensure drivers can use their EVs with confidence and certainty.

TII are leading on the delivery of charging infrastructure along our motorways and national primary and secondary routes and we have launched grant aid programmes for the delivery of significant high powered charging infrastructure on these roads over the next year, to provide all EV drivers with reliable access to charging points across the country.
In addition, the Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan describes how Local Authorities will facilitate the provision of local charging networks that will meet user needs.

Ireland also maintains a generous range of incentives to support drivers’ transition to electric, including a purchase grant for battery electric vehicles; a home charger purchase grant; VRT relief of up to €5,000; and a low rate of annual motor tax.

question.p: 298. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the number of publicly available EV charging points in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19398/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion and modernisation of the electric vehicle (EV) charging network over the coming years.

To date, almost all EV charging infrastructure delivered in Ireland delivered has been done so on a commercial basis, with little government subvention. This is anticipated to change in 2026, with a significant step up in delivery of government-procured EV infrastructure, with national road EV infrastructure, sports club EV infrastructure and a number of Local Authority pilots all to be delivered this year.

It is estimated that there are approximately 1,500 publicly available charging pools (locations with more than one charging station), with approximately 130Kw of power available. The Department of Transport does not currently track exact numbers of publicly accessible EV charging stations. A number of commercial apps are available to provide this data to the public. However, ZEVI, an office of the Department of Transport, is developing a Data Strategy and associated data platforms that will, once in place, enhance the Department’s ability to monitor this infrastructure and facilitate the provision of comprehensive and accurate information on EV charging infrastructure to the public. This Strategy is being finalised following consultation and will be published shortly.

The system will enable the collection of data from charge-points in near real time and provide it on an Open Data basis. The obligation on charge-point operators and owners to share this data is legislated for in the EU Alternative Fuel Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR).

In order to achieve Ireland’s EU targets under AFIR, it is expected that there will be 3,200 – 6,210 public chargers required nationally by 2030, depending on the level of power supplied at each. AFIR requirements state that there should be 1.3kW of capacity on the national network per BEV and 0.8kW capacity per PHEV.

ZEVI published for consultation a refreshed National EV Infrastructure Strategy in February that sets out the next phase of Ireland’s EV charging infrastructure rollout. This updated strategy will build on the progress of recent years under the 2022-25 National EV Infrastructure Charging Strategy and ensure charging infrastructure keeps pace with the rapidly growing level of EV adoption in Ireland.

Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Transport the details of assessments carried out on current Irish Rail accessibility policies, including advance notice requirements and mandatory staff assistance; whether these policies comply with Ireland’s obligations under disability equality and public transport access standards and legislation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19450/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport.

Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 and the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009, the Oireachtas assigned statutory responsibility to the National Transport Authority (NTA) for promoting the development of an integrated, accessible public transport network and public transport infrastructure. The NTA in turn works with the relevant public transport operators, for example Irish Rail, who have responsibility for day-to-day operational issues, to progressively make public transport accessible.

As queries relating to the accessibility of rail services, including advance notice requirements, are a matter for Irish Rail in the first instance. I have referred your question to the company for direct reply to you. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within ten working days.

question.p: 301. Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Transport whether a cross-departmental review has been considered to ensure transport accessibility policy aligns with broader national disability inclusion commitments. [19451/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport.

From a policy perspective, the Government launched the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People (NHRSDP) on 03 September 2025. The NHRSDP is the framework to bring about a transformative step-change in how all parts of Government approach their work when it comes to disability. The NHRSDP also reinforces the responsibility of all Government Departments and Agencies to perform their functions in ways that are aligned with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) and existing disability policies and strategies, for example the Autism Innovation Strategy.

Pillar 5 of the NHRSDP, 'Transport and Mobility', contains a number of priority transport actions which were developed with representatives of the disability community. In line with the agreed NHRSDP structures, these priority actions are the primary focus for all NHRSDP stakeholders this year. My Department will be monitoring this via formalised channels, under the auspices of the cross-Departmental/agency Pillar 5 Monitoring Group.

question.p: 304. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Transport to provide sufficient funding to Clare County Council to carry out essential works on the R460 road between Corofin and Lough Bunny which is in need of works; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19536/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million in our regional and local roads across the State. This will facilitate an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works.

In 2026, Clare County Council has been allocated a total of €31,788,700. Of this, €26,628,700 has been allocated for the protection and renewal of Clare's regional and local roads. This is an increase from the initial 2025 allocation of €25,779,500 for protection and renewal grants.
Clare County Council is responsible for deciding its annual programme for road maintenance and the Department has no role in that process.

Included in Clare County Council's grant allocation for regional and local roads this year is funding of €25,000 under the Safety Improvement Works Grant Programme for a scheme on the R460 at Lough Bunny Cross Tubber.

question.p: 305. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Transport the actions he is taking to reduce road deaths aside from the RSA Vision Zero Strategy; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19559/26]

351. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the actions he is taking to address road safety concerns for vulnerable roads users including pedestrians and cyclists as set out in a report (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19919/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 305 and 351 together.

The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030 and a great deal of work is currently underway to deliver on the targets set out in this Strategy.

I published the Phase 2 Road Safety Action Plan in July 2025. This phase of the Road Safety Strategy identifies 12 primary actions that are transformative in nature, and which are themed across the overarching, internationally recognised safe systems approach. These 12 actions are supported by a suite of a further 77 support actions which are also being implemented in partnership with road safety stakeholders.
Some of the key actions in the Phase 2 Action Plan include:
• Expanding network safety analysis of the road network to identify high-risk locations, guide investment decisions and prioritise safety interventions including for the local road network.
• Expanding the use of Safety Cameras
• Continued implementation of the 2023 Speed limit review.
• Reviewing and overhauling our learning to drive curriculum

We are progressing a significant legislative programme. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill is targeted for enactment by the summer and will, among other measures, restore direct collision data sharing with local authorities. The next Road Traffic Bill is also under development to advance Programme for Government commitments around graduated speeding penalties and the camera enforcement of mobile phone and seatbelt offences.

Safe Speeds are another important part of the Safe Systems approach. We have implemented in full Phase 1 of the Speed Limit Review reducing the default speed limit on rural local roads from 80km/h to 60km/h. Phase 2 in relation to reducing speed limits from 50km/h to 30km/h in urban/bult up areas is now underway. The introduction of 30km/h speed limits where appropriate will contribute to a safer urban environment for all road users.

A first National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed and I expect to publish it shortly. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future.

In the coming weeks, we will also be introducing regulations to fully ban scramblers from use in public places and enhance Garda powers of seizure. These regulations are being made in memory of Grace Lynch and the scrambler ban will be known as Grace’s Law.

Protecting vulnerable road users is a key priority for this government. Safe and Healthy Modes of Travel is one of the seven Safe Systems pillars that underpin the Strategy, and Primary Action 1 of the current Action Plan will see the National Transport Authority invest significantly in improved infrastructure for pedestrians and other active travellers in the coming years. Supporting this action, Budget 2026 has made €360m available for such investment over the next year.

This year we are investing over €1.5billion in our roads. In addition through schemes like the Low-Cost Safety Improvement Scheme and the Reactive Road Safety Programme my Department and TII are supporting local authorities to address identified road safety issues across the roads network.

There has been a significant increase in spending on public awareness, communications and education campaigns by the RSA. In 2026 the RSA has again ringfenced funding of €18 million for awareness, education and promotional campaigns. This will ensure a continued focus on campaigns that make our roads safer for all road users, including pedestrians and other vulnerable road users.

It is the policy of both the Government and the RSA to recommend the use of high-visibility vests and armbands by vulnerable road users. To support this, the RSA has been running the ‘Be Safe, Be Seen’ campaign for over a decade to support road safety for pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists.

As part of this campaign, the RSA each year distributes thousands of free high-visibility safety items including - high-vis jackets, high vis vests, high vis armbands, drawstring bags, rucksack covers and running bibs.

The Government continues to support this campaign and I would encourage all vulnerable road users to ensure that they are as safe as possible on our roads and to avail of these free high visibility safety materials.

question.p: 310. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport whether any obligation exists on local authorities to conduct a road design review following a fatal road traffic collision on a road under their management; if not, whether the Department has considered introducing such an obligation; whether he will consider a model (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19655/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: In accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, each local authority has statutory responsibility for the improvement and maintenance of their regional and local roads. Works on those roads are funded from local authorities' own resources and are supplemented by State grants.

Where a fatal road traffic collision occurs, the relevant local authority engineer and investigating member of An Garda Síochána meet at the site of the collision and jointly complete a collision report form named LA16. This is an action of the Road Safety Strategy 2021 - 2030.

The completed LA16 form, outlines the details of the collision, weather conditions and road conditions including signage, road markings, speed limit, roadside environment and classification of the road etc. These forms are submitted to the Roads Management Office who maintain the dataset.

My Department also funds a Network Safety Analysis of the Regional and Local Road Network across the entire country. Using available collision datasets high collision locations are identified and Locations of Interest (LoIs) reports are produced.

These LoI reports are then issued to the relevant local authority and form the basis for application for funding under the Safety Improvement Schemes Grant. In 2026 my Department allocated €14 million in Safety Improvement Schemes Grant to the sector which is funding over 330 safety schemes nationally which is an 8% increase over the 2025 allocation.

question.p: 311. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport whether Fingal County Council currently have access to collision location data for roads under its management; if not, when such access was last available; the interim arrangements that are in place to ensure these authorities can identify and address high-risk locations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19658/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Collision data are collected by members of An Garda Síochána at the scene of road traffic accidents. These data were previously shared with local authorities, via the Road Safety Authority, to enable them to identify locations of interest (accident blackspots) that would benefit from safety improvements. Due to the presence of personal information in the data, legal advice related to GDPR has meant that local authorities stopped receipt of collision data since November 2023. As well as sharing of the data, the local authorities have identified an issue with the legal basis to process the data, once received. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill 2025 will, once enacted, provide a legal basis for local authorities to receive and process the collision data.

As an interim measure, the Department of Transport has been undertaking detailed collision analysis on the regional and local road network to identify locations of interest. When locations of interest are identified, the Department notifies the affected local authority. In turn, local authorities can apply for funding of low-cost safety schemes for these locations of interest.

The General Scheme of the National Vehicle and Driver File Bill 2025 has been approved by Government and is with the Office of Parliamentary Counsel for drafting. The passage of this Bill is a Programme for Government commitment and will amend the Roads Act 1993 to provide a basis for the resumption of direct sharing of road traffic collision data with local authorities. The Bill will be published in the coming weeks with enactment targeted for the first half of 2026.

debateSection.heading: Taxi Regulations

question.p: 312. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Transport if his Department will investigate changes to commission fares by a company (details supplied); the specific oversight in regulating changes in commission taken by taxi operators; if his Department recognises the significant impact this has on the income of taxi drivers; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19682/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.

FreeNow commission rates are private consumer to business contract fees and are not governed by the Maximum Fare Order established by the NTA. SPSV operators are self-employed and may decide to sign-up, or not, with a licensed dispatch operator, such as FreeNow. They are not obliged by my Department or the NTA to be affiliated with any dispatch operator but where they choose to do so, they are free to contract with a dispatch operator of their choice. They also decide on their own hours of work within the SPSV regulatory framework.

It may be of interest to the Deputy that the NTA has published a Call for Inputs consultation on the dispatch operator licensing framework. A sustainable taxi sector is an important element of Ireland’s transport system, and I encourage all stakeholders to take the opportunity to feed into this important piece of work, as this input will inform the NTA's process and decision-making in revising the current dispatch operator framework. The closing date for the receipt of submissions is 17th April next. The public consultation can be viewed here: www.consult.nationaltransport.ie/en/content/call-inputs-dispatch-operators.

Given the NTA's responsibility in regulating dispatch operators, I have referred your question to the NTA for further information. Please advise my private office if you have not received a reply within 10 working days.

debateSection.summary: A referred reply was forwarded to the Deputy under Standing Orders

question.p: 313. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the frequency which the ministerial committee on road safety meets; and to provide a list of the dates of meetings in each of the years 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026. [19685/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030. The Ministerial Committee on Road Safety met five times in 2024, on 25 January, 27 March, 2 May, 12 June, and 11 September and once in 2025 on 16 April. The Phase 2 Action Plan 2025–2027 under the Strategy was published in July 2025.

The implementation of the Phase 2 Action Plan is overseen at Ministerial level by a new Road Safety Leadership Group. This Group is chaired by Minister Canney who is responsible for Road Safety and is attended by the Minister for Justice and Home Affairs. This Group also comprises senior officials from all key road safety partners including An Garda Síochána, the Road Safety Authority, Transport Infrastructure Ireland, National Transport Authority, the Courts Service, MBRS, HSA and the Local Authorities. This Group has held two meetings to date, on 5 November 2025 and 17 February 2026. The next meeting is scheduled to be held in April.

question.p: 317. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport to report on the work of his Department in the development of a transport demand management scheme for the greater Dublin area, in conjunction with the National Transport Authority; and to provide an indicative timeline for the completion of this scheme. [19778/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Within the Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022-2042, the National Transport Authority outlines how the transport system will be developed to meet the needs of a growing population while also halving emissions across the region - covering Dublin, Meath, Wicklow and Kildare - by 2030. As well as significant investment in active, shared and public transport infrastructure and services, the Strategy highlights that a key lever for reducing emissions as well as congestion will be a demand management scheme for the GDA. The new Moving Together strategy, which I published earlier this month, provides the impetus for bringing forward such a scheme.
I have referred the Deputy’s question to the NTA for a more detailed reply on the scheme and its timeline. If you do not receive a reply within 10 working days, please contact my private office.

question.p: 318. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport the way in which his Department measures the impact of active travel investment and infrastructure on modal shift. [19779/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to Active Travel. Funding is administered through the National Transport Authority (NTA), who, in partnership with local authorities, have responsibility for the selection and development of specific projects in each local authority area.

Investment in active travel has delivered approximately 1,100km of new walking and cycling infrastructure since 2020, as well as hundreds of junction upgrades and new pedestrian crossings. In 2025 alone, investment resulted in nearly 100km of new walking infrastructure, 70km of cycling infrastructure, 222 new pedestrian crossings, over 300 junction upgrades and 2 active travel bridges.

In terms of modal shift, there are several sources of data for the number of people cycling and walking rather than taking a car or public transport; however these data sources mainly measure transport mode share rather than changing transport habits which would demonstrate modal shift from car or public transport use to active travel modes and the impact that improvements in active travel investment are having on modal shift.

The primary source of national data available is through the National Household Travel Survey which was previously carried out by the NTA every four years, but moved to an annual basis since 2022. This Survey provides a comprehensive picture of daily travel habits of Irish residents. Latest figures from the 2024 NHTS shows that walking and cycling have a 20% mode share, compared to 74% for driving

Other data sources look at more specific areas, such as the Walking and Cycling Index (WACI). This is an independent survey based on local walking and cycling data and modelling and is the largest assessment of walking and cycling in Ireland's five cities. The WACI is produced every 2 years by the Walk Wheel Cycle Trust in partnership with the NTA. The first report was carried out in Dublin only in 2021, and was widened to include Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford in 2023. The 2025 reports were published by the NTA earlier this month and are available online. There is detailed information on active travel participation and perception contained within the reports; a key finding is that walking, wheeling and cycling removed up to 660,000 car trips from the roads each day across the five metropolitan areas.

Lastly, the NTA's annual Canal Cordon report is an annual study tracking how people commute into Dublin city centre. The following table outlines the results of this study for the years 2018-2023 inclusive by active travel, bus and car; other modes including taxi, goods vehicles, motorbike are not included below:

question.p: 319. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport the way in which his Department is working to encourage the delivery of commercial bus services. [19780/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.

The Department acknowledges the important role commercial operators play in responding to the demands of the sector and the vital service they deliver to their customers. The Department will continue to engage closely with commercial operators and representative groups, such as the Coach Tourism and Transport Council of Ireland (CTTC), to understand the ongoing and evolving needs of the sector.

The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally and for the scheduling and timetabling of these services in conjunction with the relevant transport operators, including the licensing of commercial bus services.

question.p: 320. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update regarding the roll-out of next generation ticketing. [19781/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has responsibility for the development of public transport infrastructure, including ticketing and technology projects.

The NTA's Next Generation Ticketing project will provide a transformative upgrade to the ticketing system for public transport passengers in Ireland. The project will facilitate a variety of payment methods on public transport services, involving a next-generation 'Account Based Ticketing' scheme incorporating both mobile and card-based payments for passengers.

Following a competitive procurement process, in April 2024 the NTA awarded an overall framework contract for the design, supply, installation and operation of a new multi-modal ticketing system to Spanish information technology company Indra Sistemas. Indra has designed, installed and operated similar systems internationally.

The Programme for Government commits to rolling out contactless fare payments on all public transport and to keeping fares low and affordable. Contactless fare payments, or Next Generation Ticketing, will be introduced initially as part of BusConnects Dublin, before being delivered nationwide, including on Bus Éireann services.

The initial focus of the project is on the Greater Dublin Area, rolled out across four phases. Phase 1 is due to launch in Summer 2027 which will test contactless payment on new validators or ticket machines.

I understand that Phase 2 will be ready in Summer 2028, allowing passengers on Dublin's bus and Luas services to use this new ticketing technology, including contactless payments on validators. Plans for later phases are under development.

Noting the NTA's responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question.p: 321. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport which railway stations have been selected for funding for retrofitting and accessibility improvements. [19782/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport.

Under the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 and the Public Transport Regulation Act 2009, the Oireachtas assigned statutory responsibility to the National Transport Authority (NTA) for promoting the development of an integrated, accessible public transport network and public transport infrastructure. The NTA in turn works with the relevant public transport operators, for example Irish Rail, who have responsibility for day-to-day operational issues, to progressively make public transport accessible.

As queries relating to the Accessibility at train stations are a matter for Irish Rail in the first instance. I have referred your question to the company for direct reply to you. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within ten working days.

summary.i: A referred reply was forwarded to the Deputy under Standing Orders.

question.p: 322. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the establishment of a transport security force. [19783/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I can assure you that my Department is actively progressing the legislative proposals required to deliver on the Government’s commitment to establish a Transport Security Force and is working closely with the National Transport Authority (NTA) in this regard.
The Programme for Government sets out a clear commitment: that a Transport Security Force will operate under the NTA with powers similar to those held by Airport Police and Customs Officers.

The ongoing work to establish it involves careful and informed consideration of the most appropriate model for the Force, with all key stakeholders fully engaged – the NTA, operators, trade unions, passenger groups, An Garda Síochána and the Department of Justice. Since assuming office, I have met with these stakeholders as a collective twice and continue to meet them bilaterally on this important matter. In addition the stakeholders also have ongoing engagement through their attendance at the Public Transport Safety Working Group, which is chaired by my Department, with the most recent meeting held on the 11th of February 2026.

My Department and the NTA are actively progressing the legislative proposals required to deliver on the Government’s commitment to establish a Transport Security Force, and the introduction of this Force will require the development of primary legislation, which can have a significant lead time, but it will be expedited, with a view to making progress on its foundations during 2026.

Antisocial behaviour on public transport remains a serious concern. It is those who use and work within the network who are most directly affected, and the establishment of the Transport Security Force will be key in addressing this issue, and this is a Government priority.

I fully support all the ongoing positive work to progress towards creating a safer public transport network for staff and passengers. In the meantime, we are committed to delivering a safe and secure public transport system, and we will maintain momentum on all fronts until the Transport Security Force is in place.

question.p: 323. Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Transport the steps being taken to ensure the cyber-resilience of Ireland’s public transport network systems from external threats. [19784/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The security of the systems that support Ireland's public transport network is a priority for my Department. Responsibilities for cyber security are clearly assigned and are delivered in conjunction with relevant national bodies and specialist security partners, ensuring alignment with recognised industry frameworks and Government guidance.

My officials engage regularly with the bodies responsible for delivering public transport services under the aegis of the Department to assure their continued alignment with these frameworks and obligations. These bodies will also fall within scope of forthcoming cybersecurity requirements arising from the transposition of the EU NIS2 Directive into Irish law.

question.p: 324. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport his views on the merits of creating a dedicated fund to provide EV charging infrastructure at all local authority buildings that will be usable by both the public and members of staff; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19807/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion and modernisation of the EV charging network over the coming years. Having an effective and reliable charging network is an essential part of enabling drivers to make the switch to electric vehicles.

While over 80% of charging is expected to happen at home, there is a vital need for a seamless public charging network that will provide for situations or instances where home charging is not possible.

The Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan, published in 2025, provides a pathway for the accelerated delivery of public destination and neighbourhood charging and will be led by Local Authorities who are developing local and regional EV charging network strategies and implementation plans.

This process will identify the number of charge points required in each area, including on-street chargers to serve residents without access to private off-street parking. While strategies are being finalised, ZEVI is funding pilot infrastructure projects in a number of Local Authorities, so as not to delay rollout and to provide charging infrastructure at locations that meet multiple user needs for Local Authority owned sites.

Local Authority Climate Action Charter ensures every local authority embeds decarbonisation, sustainable development and climate resilience into every aspect of the work they do. Local Authorities develop climate action roadmaps and report on progress to the Climate Action Regional Offices.
The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), includes requirements for EV recharging points at public buildings such as
1. New non-residential buildings with more than five car parking spaces and non-residential buildings undergoing major renovation, with more than five car parking spaces, Member States shall ensure:

(a) the installation of at least one recharging point for every five car parking spaces; (b) the installation of pre-cabling for at least 50 % of car parking spaces and ducting, namely conduits for electric cables, for the remaining car parking spaces, to enable the installation at a later stage of recharging points for electric vehicles, electrically power-assisted cycles and other L-category vehicle types
2. All non-residential buildings with more than 20 car parking spaces, Member States shall, by 1 January 2027, ensure:

(a) the installation of at least one recharging point for every 10 car parking spaces, or of ducting, namely conduits for electric cables, for at least 50 % of the car parking spaces to enable the installation at a later stage of recharging points for electric vehicles.
For buildings owned or occupied by public bodies, Member States shall ensure the installation of pre-cabling for at least 50 % of car parking spaces by 1 January 2033.
The transposition of this directive is led by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

question.p: 325. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the provision of EV charging infrastructure at public buildings; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19808/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion and modernisation of the publicly accessible EV charging network over the coming years. The infrastructure for EV charging in public spaces is crucial for the widespread adoption of electric vehicles.

While over 80% of charging is expected to happen at home, there is a vital need for a seamless public charging network that will provide for situations or instances where home charging is not possible.

The National EV Infrastructure Strategy sets out the Government's ambitions and plans for EV infrastructure delivery over the period 2026-2028 and is open for public consultation. Alongside the National Strategy, the Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan, published in 2025, provides a pathway for the accelerated delivery of public destination and neighbourhood charging and will be led by Local Authorities who are developing local and regional EV charging network strategies and implementation plans.

In addition to these plans which will provide publicly accessible charging in locations across the country, the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), Article 14, includes requirements for EV recharging points at public buildings, specifically.
For buildings owned or occupied by public bodies, Member States shall ensure the installation of pre-cabling for at least 50 % of car parking spaces by 1 January 2033.
It should be noted that responsibility for the transition of this Directive held by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

question.p: 329. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the most recent occasion whereby an accessibility report was carried out on Dublin Airport to ensure that it is as fully accessible as possible; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19816/26]

330. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the most recent occasion whereby an accessibility report was carried out on Shannon Airport to ensure that it is as fully accessible as possible; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19817/26]

331. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the most recent occasion whereby an accessibility report was carried out on Cork Airport to ensure that it is as fully accessible as possible; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19818/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 329, 330 and 331 together.

Regulation (EC) 1107 of 2006 protects the rights of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility when travelling by air. It ensures equal access to air travel for such persons and requires airports and air carriers to provide them with free assistance.

The Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) carries out annual inspections of the six commercial airports in Ireland, including Dublin, Cork and Shannon, as part of its remit as the National Enforcement Body for Regulation 1107 in Ireland.
The inspection reports are published on the IAA website and can be viewed at: www.iaa.ie/consumer-protection/persons-with-reduced-mobility/airport-accessibility-compliance-reports.
The most recently published reports cover inspections carried out in 2024, which were published in April 2025. The IAA are working to complete the 2025 reports, which will be published shortly.

question.p: 334. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Transport the reason persons changing an English driver licence to an Irish driver licence are having their licence for heavy goods vehicles (lorries, buses) removed from their licence; the reason these vehicles are not carrying over when the licence holder has gained them and holds them; if he will review this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19842/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I wish to advise that a person who is resident in Ireland must have an Irish or EU driving licence to drive here.

Driving licences issued by EU member states are mutually recognised and a holder of a member state-issued licence who moves to Ireland can drive on that licence until it expires. On expiry, the licence holder will then need to exchange their licence for an Irish licence where Ireland is their primary place of residence.

Until 2020, the UK was an EU member state and UK driving licences were recognised in Ireland as EU licences. Following the UK's withdrawal from the EU, Ireland and the UK entered into a licence exchange agreement and a UK driving licence can be exchanged for an equivalent category Irish licence and vice versa. However, if there is no equivalent category, that particular category will not be transferable.
In addition, a UK licence category will not be exchanged in Ireland where the licence category originated from a third country whose licences are not accepted for exchange in Ireland.
The following UK driving licence national codes do not have an equivalent in Ireland and are thus, not transferable to an Irish licence.

p.b: Category D1 and D1E Licence with Code 1 or Code 101 (not for hire or reward)

speech.p: The UK minibus (D1) and bus with trailer attached (D1E) categories with Code 1 or Code 101, indicating not for hire or reward, are not transferable when exchanged for an Irish licence, as these are national categories and are only valid for driving in the UK.
However, holders of UK category D1 and D1E driving licences without these codes may retain these categories when exchanging their UK licence.
The light articulated truck (EC1) category with Code 107 is granted in the UK and is not transferable as there is no equivalent category in Ireland.
The articulated truck (EC) category with Code 102 is granted in the UK and is not transferable as there is not equivalent category in Ireland.

question.p: 335. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport if any assessments have been carried out nationally of the condition of local roads; the proportion that are deemed in poor condition; the costs required to bring them up to standard; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19844/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million in our regional and local roads across the State. This will facilitate an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works.

As well as providing grant support to local authorities, my Department has supported the development of a Road Asset Management System for regional and local roads. The Road Management Office, which has been established as a shared service between 31 local authorities, together with my Department, has been working with local authorities to ensure that this road pavement management system includes a record of all pavement-related works and information on road surfaces and pavement condition.
The objective of the MapRoad pavement management system is to provide the data needed for evidence-based prioritisation and management of road work programmes by each road authority.

My Department has also produced a Pavement Survey Standard for regional and local roads for use in respect of road pavement management by local authorities. This standard requires local authorities to carry out a Pavement Survey Condition Index (PSCI) visual survey on regional, local primary and local secondary roads every two years and every five years for local tertiary roads.
The condition of the regional and local road network is recorded under the National Oversight and Audit Commission (NOAC) indicator R1 and is available to view on the NOAC website www.noac.ie.

question.p: 336. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport the reasons the Dublin to Rosslare rail line has the poorest quality of rail carriages; the reason no consideration is given to providing modern carriages on the route; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19845/26]

338. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport the plans in place to lengthen station platforms on the Dublin to Rosslare railway line given that this has been given as a reason by Irish Rail as to why they cannot put longer carriages on the route. [19847/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 336 and 338 together.

As Minister of Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding of public transport. The operation, maintenance and renewal of the rail network and stations on the network, including any proposed works at train stations and the carriages provided on the Dublin to Rosslare rail line, is a matter for Iarnród Éireann in the first instance.

In view of Iarnród Éireann's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the company for direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

Pending this more detailed response, I note that the DART+ Fleet project provides a ten-year procurement framework for new electric and battery-electric fleet. To date, three fleet orders have been placed comprising both battery-electric and electric carriages, bringing the total number of DART carriages ordered to 285, made up of 57 five-carriage trains.

It is intended that the first new battery-electric sets will initially be deployed on the Northern Commuter Line serving Dublin to/from Drogheda from 2027, while trains from the second order will allow commencement of DART services to Wicklow around 2029 and trains from the third order will replace the original DART fleet from 1984.

Across the wider rail network, deployment of the first and second orders will free up Intercity and Commuter trains for use on other train routes, providing a capacity boost. The location of where the redeployed fleet will be used will be determined by Iarnród Éireann in consultation with the NTA.

question.p: 344. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport the steps he will take to ensure the deployment of average speed cameras on high-risk routes as a matter of urgency; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19882/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras.
There are currently 5 average speed cameras in operation across the road network. These are located in the following locations -
• Dublin Port Tunnel
• N3 Cavan
• N5 Mayo
• N2 Meath

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

question.p: 345. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if he will support and fund a programme to redesign the 50 highest risk road sections with published timelines for implementation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19883/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the planning, design and construction of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals.

I understand from TII that TII does not rank roads against each other, but instead operates a dedicated Reactive Road Safety Programme for the national road network. Under this system—set out in TII standard GE-STY-01022 (“Network Safety Ranking and Prioritisation – Reactive Approach”) collision data is used to identify high-collision locations (1km sections) across the network.

Where such sites are detected, TII formally notifies the relevant Local Authority and requires the Local Authority to propose a scheme, as the road authority, to address the issues identified. TII subsequently provides funding for targeted safety improvement schemes to address the issues identified. This process is detailed in GE-STY-01036 (“Road Safety Improvement Schemes”). On average €26 million is allocated to this programme each year.

For more information on the Reactive Road Safety System please see this website: cdn.tii.ie/publications/GE-STY-01022-03.pdf and for more information on the Improvement Scheme process, please see this website: cdn.tii.ie/publications/GE-STY-01036-01.pdf

Separately, TII has recently published the Network-Wide Road Safety Assessment (NWA). This safety rating system evaluates approximately 2500km of the national primary road network by combining both historical collision data and data from current proactive infrastructure inspections. The website can be viewed here: tii-nwa-2024-map-national-primary-roads.pdf

In respect of the regional and local road network, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, each local authority has statutory responsibility for the improvement and maintenance of their regional and local roads. Works on those roads are funded from local authorities' own resources and are supplemented by State grants.

Where a fatal road traffic collision occurs, the relevant local authority engineer and investigating member of An Garda Síochána meet at the site of the collision and jointly complete a collision report form named LA16. This is an action of the Road Safety Strategy 2021 - 2030.

The completed LA16 form, outlines the details of the collision, weather conditions and road conditions including signage, road markings, speed limit, roadside environment and classification of the road etc. These forms are submitted to the Roads Management Office who maintain the dataset.

My Department also funds a Network Safety Analysis of the Regional and Local Road Network across the entire country. Using available collision datasets high collision locations are identified and Locations of Interest (LoIs) reports are produced.

These LoI reports are then issued to the relevant local authority and form the basis for application for funding under the Safety Improvement Schemes Grant. In 2026 my Department allocated €14 million in Safety Improvement Schemes Grant to the sector which is funding over 330 safety schemes nationally which is an 8% increase over the 2025 allocation.

question.p: 346. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport if, in the context of the All Island Strategic Rail Review or any other policy work, his Department has given consideration to the concept of the development of an inland express rail corridor linking Rosslare Europort and Wexford with Dublin via Waterford and Carlow; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19900/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Following the publication of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in July 2024, my Department, with the support of the European Investment Bank and in conjunction with the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland, oversaw the preparation of the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy. This Strategy was published in December 2025 and outlines the approach to sequencing and optimising the recommendations of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review in the coming years.

In the short-term to 2030, the Prioritisation Strategy specifies a number of 'Early Interventions' to be delivered in the coming years, including new track passing loops and platforms to boost the rail network’s resilience and capacity. These investments are funded to be fully delivered by 2030 under the NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for Transport, published in November 2025.

The Prioritisation Strategy also identifies 'Major Projects' with longer lead-in and development timelines. These projects are generally targeted to secure the necessary approvals within the next five years such that construction works could commence thereafter. Among these Major Projects, capacity and frequency enhancements, line speed improvements and electrification are planned on the Waterford line.

The Prioritisation Strategy has a 20-year time horizon, which does not cover the entire period to 2050 envisaged by the All-Island Strategic Rail Review. Projects not included in the Prioritisation Strategy, including the reinstatement of the line between Waterford and Wexford, are intended to be progressed in the longer-run.

It should be noted that individual programmes and projects referred to within the All-Island Strategic Rail Review and the Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy will be advanced subject to funding and relevant approvals, as required under the Infrastructure Guidelines.

question.p: 347. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the number of times and the dates the issue of capturing driver numbers in court for penalty point or disqualification offences has been on the agenda at the Ministerial Committee on Road Safety or meetings of the Road Safety Transformation Partnership Board over the past five years. [19910/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I wish to advise that my Department maintains the National Vehicle and Driver File (NVDF) database, which is the State’s record of all Irish licensed drivers. The Department’s role is to manage the database, including of penalty points and disqualifications on driver records based on information on offences provided from the Courts Service and An Garda Síochána.

A report published by the Department in December 2025 outlines the processes involved and provides detailed statistics for 2024. This report is available at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/publications/recording-of-penalty-points-and-disqualifications-on-driver-records/. A similar report will be shortly published, to provide the same statistics for 2025 once available.

The primary purpose of the Road Safety Leadership Group, and its predecessor the Ministerial Committee on Road Safety, is to review progress and drive delivery of the actions in the Government Road Safety Strategy. While capturing of driver numbers is an important road safety issue, it is an operational matter and it is for the most part addressed directly between the Department, Road Safety Authority, the Courts Services and An Garda Síochána.

question.p: 348. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport his views in relation to calls to declare a public health crisis in relation to the number of deaths on Irish roads (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19916/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: To reduce road deaths, in 1998 implementation began on the first national Road Safety Strategy. Over the course of that Strategy and its successors, we witnessed a significant improvement in safety on our roads. From 472 in 1997 that figure reduced to 133 by 2021. Unfortunately, more recent trends are less positive and I share the Deputy's concern and disappointment that the number of deaths on our roads has increased in recent years.

The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030 and a great deal of work is currently underway to deliver on the targets set out in this Strategy.

The Phase 2 Action Plan under the Road Safety Strategy which will run to December 2027 contains 12 primary and 77 supporting actions, with the potential to deliver real transformative change. These actions are grounded in the internationally recognised Safe Systems approach and will be delivered through partnership and collaborative working by road safety stakeholders. Some of the key actions include –
• investing significantly into new and improved active travel and public transport;
• expanding the use of safety cameras;
• expanding network safety analysis of the road network to identify high-risk locations, guide investment decisions and prioritise safety interventions including for the local road network;
• implementing in full all actions in the Phase 2 Action Plan based on the 2023 Speed limit review;
• reviewing and overhauling our learning to drive curriculum.

Delivery of the Phase 2 Action Plan is being co-ordinated by my Department and is being led by the Road Safety Leadership Group which brings together senior leaders from across road safety stakeholders including – AGS, DOJ, RSA, TII,NTA, HSA, MBRS and Local Authorities. This group is chaired at Ministerial level by Minister Canney and is attended by the Minister for Justice and Home Affairs.

Progress is being made. In February 2025, the first implementation phase of the speed limit review was introduced, which saw the default speed limit on rural and local roads reduced from 80km/h to 60km/h. Local authorities are now working on implement lower speed limits, where appropriate, of 30km/h in cities and towns and have been directed to conclude this process by 31 March 2027.

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras to encourage safer driving and the increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan. The first National Safety Camera Strategy is expected to be published shortly.

My Department provides funding to Local Authorities each year under the Low-Cost Safety Improvement Scheme to support small-scale engineering measures that address identified road safety issues. This year €14 million has been allocated, representing an increase of €1 million (approximately 8%) on 2025 allocations. In 2026, the Government has committed to provide over €1.5 billion in exchequer funding for national, regional and local roads. This represents a 13% increase in overall road funding when compared to 2025.

We are also progressing a significant legislative programme. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill is targeted for enactment by the summer and will, among other measures, restore direct collision data sharing with local authorities. The next Road Traffic Bill is also under development to advance Programme for Government commitments around graduated speeding penalties and the camera enforcement of mobile phone and seatbelt offences.

question.p: 349. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the action he is taking to address record number of deaths on Irish Roads in 2025 (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19917/26]

350. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding engagement he is having with the RSA that seeks to urgently address road safety concerns and record deaths on Irish Roads (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19918/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 349 and 350 together.

The current national framework for road safety is set out in the Government’s fifth Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030 and a great deal of work is currently underway to deliver on the targets set out in this Strategy.

I published the Phase 2 Road Safety Action Plan in July 2025. This phase of the Road Safety Strategy identifies 12 primary actions that are transformative in nature, and which are themed across the overarching, internationally recognised safe systems approach. These 12 actions are supported by a suite of a further 77 support actions which are also being implemented in partnership with road safety stakeholders.
Some of the key actions in the Phase 2 Action Plan include:
• Expanding network safety analysis of the road network to identify high-risk locations, guide investment decisions and prioritise safety interventions including for the local road network.
• Expanding the use of Safety Cameras
• Continued implementation of the 2023 Speed limit review.
• Reviewing and overhauling our learning to drive curriculum

We are progressing a significant legislative programme. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill is targeted for enactment by the summer and will, among other measures, restore direct collision data sharing with local authorities. The next Road Traffic Bill is also under development to advance Programme for Government commitments around graduated speeding penalties and the camera enforcement of mobile phone and seatbelt offences.

We have implemented in full Phase 1 of the Speed Limit Review reducing the default speed limit on rural local roads from 80km/h to 60km/h. Phase 2 in relation to reducing speed limits from 50km/h to 30km/h in urban/bult up areas is now underway. The introduction of 30km/h speed limits where appropriate will contribute to a safer urban environment for all road users.

The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan. A first National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed and I expect to publish it shortly. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future.

In the coming weeks, we will also be introducing regulations to fully ban scramblers from use in public places and enhance Garda powers of seizure. These regulations are being made in memory of Grace Lynch and the scrambler ban will be known as Grace’s Law.

Protecting vulnerable road users is a key priority. Safe and Healthy Modes of Travel is one of the seven Safe Systems pillars that underpin the Strategy, and Primary Action 1 of the current Action Plan will see the National Transport Authority invest significantly in improved infrastructure for pedestrians and other active travellers in the coming years. Supporting this action, Budget 2026 has made €360m available for such investment over the next year.

This year we are investing over €1.5billion in our roads. In addition through schemes like the Low-Cost Safety Improvement Scheme under which €14m in funding is available to local authorities for 2026 and the Reactive Road Safety Programme my Department and TII are supporting local authorities to address identified road safety issues across the roads network.

There has been a significant increase in spending on public awareness, communications and education campaigns by the RSA. In 2026 the RSA has again ringfenced funding of €18 million for awareness, education and promotional campaigns. This will ensure a continued focus on campaigns that make our roads safer for all road users, including and especially vulnerable road users.

In line with other public bodies the RSA is subject to the Code of Practice on the Governance of State Bodies. In that regard, an oversight agreement is in place between my Department and the RSA which sets out the roles and responsibilities of the RSA. As part of this oversight structure my Department holds four oversight meetings - one per quarter - annually with the RSA where the RSA reports on all areas of its work. These quarterly meetings are complemented by monthly operational updates for all of the RSA's services and significant projects, which my officials review and interrogate. In addition, my Department regularly engages with the RSA as members of the Road Safety Leadership Group as well as through the Road Safety Communications Steering Group which met 10 times in 2025.

summary.i: Question No. 350 answered with Question No. 349.
Question No. 351 answered with Question No. 305.

question.p: 352. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport his views on whether there are sufficient deterrents in place to reduce poor driving behaviour including the use of mobile phones while driving, speeding and driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19920/26]

353. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding engagement he is having with the RSA that seeks to reduce poor driving behaviour including the use of mobile phones while driving, speeding and driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19921/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 352 and 353 together.

The four main causes of deaths on our roads are speeding, distracted driving including use of a mobile phone, not wearing a seatbelt and intoxicated driving, all of which are offences under road traffic legislation. Failing to obey the speed limit may result in a driver being issued 3 penalty points and a Fixed Charge Notice (FCN) to the value of €160 by a member of An Garda Síochána. If this FCN is not paid within 28 days, it is then increased to €240. Similarly, using a mobile phone while driving may result in a driver being issued 3 penalty points and a FCN to the value of €120 by a member of An Garda Síochána. If this FCN is not paid within 28 days, it is then increased to €180. An initial FCN of €120 and three penalty points also applies to non wearing of a seatbelt. In addition, a person found guilty of driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs may be subject to a €5000 fine and or up to 6 months in prison as well as being disqualified from driving.

The Road Traffic Act 2024 also introduced mandatory drug testing at the scene of a serious collision, which came into effect in May 2024. This requires members of An Garda Síochána to conduct roadside drug tests at the scene of a crash. In addition under provisions in the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023, members of An Garda Síochána now have access to the Irish Motor Insurance Database, which provides insurance information at the roadside through automatic number plate recognition technology and allows for uninsured vehicles to be detected and seized.

My Department is also progressing a significant legislative programme. The National Vehicle and Driver File Bill is targeted for enactment by the summer and will, among other measures, provide legislative clarity on the application of penalty points in multiple-offence incidents, ensuring drivers committing more than one offence in a single incident receive multiple sets of penalty points. The next Road Traffic Bill is also under development to advance Programme for Government commitments around graduated speeding penalties and the camera enforcement of mobile phone and seatbelt offences.
Enforcement of road traffic legislation falls under the remit of An Garda Síochána. Tackling these behaviours also comes down to education and driver awareness.
A number of significant national campaigns were delivered by the RSA in 2025 targeting these dangerous behaviours. These included
• a speed awareness campaign for the reduction from 80km/h to 60km/h speed limits.
• a TV-led Drug driving campaign, highlighting the Gardaí’s ability to test for drugs at the roadside.
• a Drink Driving campaign designed to challenge the social acceptability of drink driving.

There has also been a significant increase in spending on public awareness, communications and education campaigns by the RSA. In 2026 the RSA has again ringfenced funding of €18 million for awareness, education and promotional campaigns, which matches the funding level from 2025. This will ensure a continued focus on campaigns that make our roads safer for all road users, including and especially vulnerable road users. The Road Safety Communications Steering Group established in 2024, and which brings together the RSA communication leads, my Department and other key stakeholders including the Department of Justice and AGS continues to work to ensure coordination across road safety campaigns.

The RSA is also focused on education initiatives. The Road Safety Matters transition year programme was piloted during the 2024-2025 academic year with the RSA successfully delivering training to teachers from almost 140 schools nationwide, representing over 12,700 students. The Programme entered phase 2 in 2025 and is continuing at pace. In 2026 the RSA aims to complete a national rollout to all 730 post-primary schools offering TY. Key units on this programme focus on alcohol, drugs, distracted driving and seatbelts.

summary.i: Question No. 353 answered with Question No. 352.
