question.p: 354. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport the number of NCT appeals lodged in each of the years since 2015; the cost of lodging an appeal; and whether his Department has reviewed whether the appeals mechanism is accessible and proportionate. [19949/26]
355. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport whether any independent external review mechanism exists for audit findings relating to NCT inspectors. [19950/26]

356. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport whether service credit penalties have ever been applied to a company (details supplied) under the NCTS contract; the value of such penalties; and the circumstances in which they were applied. [19951/26]
357. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department has assessed the impact of operational efficiency bonuses on inspection quality in the NCTS. [19952/26]
358. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Transport whether consideration is being given to introducing multiple providers in the next NCT contract after 2030. [19953/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 354 to 358, inclusive, together.

Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the operation, oversight, quality assurance and delivery of the National Car Testing service. As Minister, I have no function in respect of procurement or operational matters.

Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's questions to the Authority for direct reply. I would ask the Deputy to contact my office if a response has not been received within ten days.

question.p: 359. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport the average waiting time for a driving test applicant (details supplied) from January 2025 to date in 2026, broken down by month, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19994/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service. This includes all testing and scheduling matters. Therefore, the information requested by the Deputy is held by the Authority. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's questions to the RSA for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.

Pending this response, the latest information provided to me by the RSA indicates that as of 7 March, the waiting time for a driving test at the Mulhuddart and Mulhuddart Maple House test centres is 20 and 13 weeks respectively.

The wait time at both centres remain well above the Service Level Agreement target of an average 10-week national wait time and I expect the RSA to continue to work to bring the wait time in Mulhuddart down in line with the 10-week target as soon as possible. I am informed by the RSA that it is continuing to focus on addressing centres with higher demand and wait times.

The driving test estimator can be used to check the current average waiting time for an invitation to book a new driving test . Applicants can also change their preferred test centre through the online MyRoadSafety portal. As the average wait time at the Maple House centre is significantly shorter, candidates in the Mulhuddart area are encouraged to select this centre, where possible, when applying. I am also informed that the RSA has advised those awaiting a test in this area that the wait time in Mulhuddart Maple House centre is shorter than at the Mulhuddart centre.

Additionally, the Deputy may wish to note that the monthly statistics for waiting times at individual test centres are made available on the CSO website on a monthly basis and can be accessed via the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/ROA36

question.p: 360. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport further to a change in legislation from 31 March 2025, given that persons wishing to buy or renew their motor insurance must provide the driver number for all named drivers on their policy, the number of drivers that have been refused motor insurance for this reason (details supplied). [20011/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: I wish to advise that, since 31 March 2025, all motorists must provide their driver number when renewing or taking out motor insurance. Accordingly, insurance providers may only offer insurance to those who have provided their driver numbers and if someone does not provide their driver number, they will not be able to take out or renew their motor insurance.
The issuing of individual motor insurance policies is a commercial activity and my Department does not have access to the information requested.

question.p: 361. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Transport whether the Government has received any communication from the United States Government, the US Department of Transportation, Airlines for America, or the US Ambassador to Ireland regarding the Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Bill 2026 or the 32 million passenger cap at Dublin Airport; and if so, to provide details of those communications. [20019/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I wish to advise the Deputy that my officials and I have had ongoing engagement with the US Department of Transportation (USDoT), Airlines for America (A4A) and the US Ambassador Edward S. Walsh over the last year. This engagement has included in person meetings and written correspondence.

This engagement provided an opportunity for a discussion on the potential impacts of the passenger cap at Dublin Airport and also afforded me the opportunity to provide clarity in relation to the legislation that is currently being drafted in line with the Government decision to address the passenger cap as soon as possible.

In that regard, a General Scheme for the Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Bill 2026 was agreed by Government on 10 February 2026 and pre-legislative scrutiny of the Bill has commenced by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Transport. The Committee is currently meeting with interested parties and has indicated that it intends to complete its report by 24 April 2026. In the meantime, officials are progressing the formal drafting of the Bill with Office of the Parliamentary Counsel.

The proposed legislative approach will empower me to make an order to amend or revoke the 32 million passenger cap planning condition. The proposed legislation also precludes the imposition of future passenger caps as planning conditions.

In advance of making an order, I will engage with An Coimisiún Pleanála to carry out screening and if necessary, undertake full environmental assessments in line with EU law. I will take the outcome of those assessments into account and incorporate any measures necessary to mitigate the impact on the environment into an order.
Government has prioritised the drafting of the Bill and it is my intention to enact the Bill as soon as possible this year.

question.p: 362. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department is aware that a formal complaint (ID:91249) was filed with the European Commission on 2 March 2026 alleging that Ireland is in breach of six EU instruments at Dublin Airport, including Regulation 598/2014; and whether the Government intends to proceed with the Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Bill 2026 in advance of any response from the Commission to that complaint. [20020/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I can confirm that my Department is aware that a formal complaint was filed with the European Commission on 02 March 2026 alleging that Ireland is in breach of six EU instruments. It is my understanding that the EU Commission will process this complaint in line with its own complaints framework.

With regard to Regulation (EU) 598/2014, as the Deputy will be aware, on 08 of August 2025, An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) notified the EU Commission of the Dublin Airport operating restrictions set out in its July 2025 decision, as required under Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 598/2014, and the Commission subsequently undertook an assessment of the process followed by ACP in its decision.

On 10 February 2026, following completion of its assessment of ACP's July 2025 decision, the EU Commission issued a notification advising that the process used by ACP for the proposed introduction of operating restrictions did not fully follow the Balanced Approach process, as set out in Regulation (EU) 598/2014. In line with the provisions of the Regulation and the 2019 Aircraft Noise Act, as the independent competent authority for this matter, ACP will now be given time to examine this Decision, and to determine the most appropriate next steps.

Concerning the Dublin Airport passenger cap planning condition, the Government has been clear that it intends to address the passenger cap through legislation and approved the general scheme of the Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Bill 2026 to this end in February. The General Scheme is currently subject to pre-legislative scrutiny by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Transport. It is my intention to introduce the legislation into the Oireachtas as soon as possible taking account of any observations the Committee may have.

question.p: 363. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Transport whether the DAA has issued a formal instruction to a company (details supplied) to conduct a review of the North runway departure routes; and if so, to provide the date of the instruction; the terms of reference; the expected completion date; and if no instruction has been issued, to explain the reason, given that the DAA has been indicating since June 2023 that it was "working to fine tune" the routes and seeking to determine how such a process could be run. [20021/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for the question.

Following engagement with the daa on the matter of flightpaths at Dublin Airport, I have been advised that given the ongoing regulatory and planning processes in track regarding Dublin Airport it is not daa’s intention to embark on a flightpath review at this time.

Under EU legislation, the operator of an airport, daa in the case of Dublin Airport, is responsible for the design and maintenance of Instrument Flight Procedures (IFPs) which set flight paths into and out of an airport. Dublin airport, AirNav Ireland carries out the design and maintenance function on behalf of daa. The Irish Aviation Authority, as the civil aviation safety regulator in Ireland, has responsibility for ensuring that IFPs adhere to safety standards set out in national, EU and international regulations. Flight paths are also monitored for compliance with noise requirements by the Aircraft Noise Competent Authority, in line with EU Regulation 598/2014 and the Aircraft Noise Act 2019.

Separately, monitoring compliance with planning permission conditions is matter for the relevant planning authority that granted those permissions, and enforcement of planning conditions is a matter for those authorities.

question.p: 364. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Transport in view of his plans for a forum to reduce congestion, whether he is aware that the ESB has moved staff from its airport offices back to the city centre; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20064/26]

365. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Transport in view of his plans for a forum to reduce congestion in Dublin, his views that the Government funded Institute of Public Administrations plans to secure multi million euro prestigious offices in the city centre should be paused; his views that consideration should be given to decentralisation to an alternative site; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20066/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 364 and 365 together.

As the Deputy refers, I have convened a roundtable to consider the issue of congestion in the Greater Dublin Area in conjunction with key agencies, operators and local authorities, and options for alleviating immediate pressures on the system particularly the M50.

Early this month, my department published a strategic framework for improving the efficiency of the transport system over the medium to long-term. Moving Together: A Collaborative Approach to Systems Change in Transport 2026–2030 is a call for collective action across all levels of Government and the economy, and encourages employers and companies to find innovative ways for reducing transport demand related to their business activities, thus helping to optimise the use of the transport network for all.

While I look forward to that work progressing, as Minister for Transport I have no role in relation to decisions related to re-locating offices or buildings as described are operational and a matter for the relevant organisations or companies concerned - in this case ESB and the Institute of Public Administration.

summary.i: Question No. 365 answered with Question No. 364.
Question No. 366 answered with Question No. 187.

question.p: 367. Deputy Timmy Dooley asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the roll out of new automated speed cameras at road accident black spots across the country. [20100/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras.
There are currently 5 average speed cameras in operation across the road network. These are located in the following locations -
• Dublin Port Tunnel
• N3 Cavan
• N5 Mayo
• N2 Meath
In addition there are nine static safety cameras in operation. These are located at the following locations -
• N17 Mayo
• N59 Galway
• N13 Donegal
• N69 Limerick
• R772 Wexford
• N22 Cork
• N80 Carlow
• N25 Kilkenny
• Dolphin's Barn Dublin 12

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

question.p: 368. Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Transport for an update from the NTA on the promised pilot of a bus service from Annacotty-to-Annacotty Business Park; the expected start for the pilot; and update from the NTA on plans to increase the Castleconnell to Limerick City service. [20137/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: BusConnects is a transformative programme of investment in the bus system, providing better bus services across our cities, including Limerick. BusConnects is the largest investment in the bus system in the history of the State, and is managed by the National Transport Authority (NTA).
Noting the NTA's responsibility in the matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the NTA for a direct reply. Please contact my private office if you do not receive a reply with 10 days.

Pending this detailed response, I note that the new BusConnects Limerick network was published in draft form in March 2023 for public consultation, during which over 650 responses were received. This feedback was taken into account in the design of the final network plan.

During the public consultation process the NTA received feedback about the potential to extend services to Annacotty Business Park. The NTA has been working with Bus Éireann to identify how and when this need will be met.

question.p: 369. Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Transport if he will consider extending a route to include Kildare Town train station and Kildare village (details supplied). [20174/26]

question.p: 380. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has examined the way road signage could be redesigned to provide parity between Irish and English text; whether any review of current signage design standards is planned; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20304/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: Traffic signs must be clear, concise and consistent to ensure their messages are quickly and easily understood by road users. These fundamental principles directly impact road safety, as they help prevent collisions and facilitate smooth traffic flow.

‘Safe roads and roadsides’ are one of the specific areas of intervention in the Safe Systems approach set out in the Government’s Road Safety Strategy 2021 to 2030 ‘Our Journey Towards Vision Zero’. As road traffic sign installations have the potential to pose roadside hazards, minimising their size is critical to achieving safe and 'forgiving' roadsides.

Bilingual road traffic signs present unique challenges for both designers and road users across the globe. In Ireland, the design and provision of bilingual road traffic signs is governed by the Traffic Signs Manual which is published by the Department of Transport.
The current system of bilingual road signs in Ireland is long established and developed over many years and are considered safe and fit for purpose.
The key items which must be considered when looking at bilingual signage include:
• Clarity and Consistency: Road traffic signs must be clear, concise and consistent to ensure quick comprehension, which is crucial for road safety.

• Safe Roadsides: Minimising the size of road traffic sign installations is vital to reduce roadside hazards, aligning with the Safe Systems approach in the Government’s Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030.
• International Comparison: There is no universal standard for bilingual traffic signs. Ireland's approach is effective and compares favourably with other countries.

• Current Effectiveness: The existing method of displaying bilingual text on road traffic signs in Ireland has proven effective over five decades, striking a balance between language differentiation, cognitive load and space efficiency.
• Public Feedback: Ireland's road signs are well understood by the public and visitors with no record of clarity issues surrounding bilingual aspects.
• Risks from Changing: Altering the current approach could negatively impact legibility and road safety and introduce unintended consequences.
• Colour Complexity: Adding colours to differentiate languages could complicate signs, particularly for colourblind users, and dilute the current system's clarity and meaning.
• Official Languages Act : It was determined that Road Signs are exempt from the Official Languages Act due to their primary concern of clarity and road safety.
• It should be noted that the Irish text appears in italic letters at a 15% slant to distinguish the languages and ensures that the necessary message is clear.
• Irish place names are typically 40% longer, and if Irish is placed in capitals, it would result in much wider signs and may add significant additional safety concerns.

• It should be noted that the text of both languages has the same text height to ensure consistency of the message being imparted. The Irish text is positioned above, reflecting its priority in the Constitution.

• Cost and Implementation: Changing the current approach would be costly (estimated between €0.47b to €0.67b) and could disrupt the network over a long transition period, and in doing so present potential road safety risks and contravene circular economy policies.

question.p: 381. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding his plans to facilitate kerbside home electric charging points for residents who do not have a driveway; and the plans to allow householders channel a wire across the footpath. [20342/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The Government is fully committed to supporting a significant expansion and modernisation of the EV charging network over the coming years. Having an effective and reliable charging network is an essential part of enabling drivers to make the switch to electric vehicles.

Home charging is the primary charging method for most Irish EV owners as it’s convenient and cheaper for the consumer as well as assisting in the overall management of the national grid. Over 80% of charging is expected to happen at home.
There is also a need for a seamless public charging network that will provide for situations or instances where home charging is not possible.

In July 2025, the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE) adopted a Strategy Statement on Private Wires. Zero Emission Vehicles Ireland (ZEVI) in the Department of Transport fully supports this DCEE-led initiative. In December 2025, I secured government approval to commence drafting of the Private Wires Bill. The bill will amend the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 to enable private development of electricity wires in 4 specific circumstances.
• To permit a private wire linking a single user of electricity to a separate singular generation asset. This connection may also include storage technologies.
• To facilitate hybrid grid connections
• To allow on-street charging solutions for Electric Vehicles
• To allow a customer that self-supplies electricity to provide electricity to a separate customer in a contiguous premises

Department officials are working with officials in relevant Government Departments and local government to develop a framework under new legislation to enable people without access to off street parking to use a home charging solution for on street parking. We expect this to be finalised later this year.
In addition, the Regional and Local EV Charging Network Plan provides a pathway for the accelerated delivery of public destination and neighbourhood charging and will be led by Local Authorities.

Local authorities will be funded by ZEVI to develop local and regional EV charging network strategies and implementation plans. This process will identify the number of charge points required in each area, including chargers to serve residents without access to private off-street parking. While strategies are being finalised, ZEVI is funding pilot infrastructure projects in a number of Local Authorities, so as not to delay any initial rollout.

question.p: 383. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the National Safety Camera Strategy; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20557/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: Enforcement of road traffic offences, such as speeding, is the primary responsibility of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of speeding laws through the use of cameras. There are currently 5 average speed cameras in operation across the road network. In addition there are nine static safety cameras in operation.

The Programme for Government commits to further expansion of safety cameras across the road network to encourage safer driving. The increased deployment of safety cameras in the coming years is a key action to be delivered under Action 6 of the Phase 2 Action Plan, as part of the all-of-Government Road Safety Strategy.

To assist An Garda Síochána in meeting these objectives, a National Safety Camera Strategy has been developed. This Strategy will provide the framework for increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. The Strategy will focus on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future. I expect to publish this Strategy shortly and my Department is continuing to work closely with all road safety stakeholders including the NTA, TII, RSA and An Garda Síochána on how best to implement the Strategy.

It should also be noted that camera enforcement has been increasing. There are now 9,000 hours of GoSafe monitoring carried out on our roads each month and since late 2024, An Garda Síochána with the assistance of TII and local authorities installed three additional average speed camera zones and nine static camera locations.

question.p: 396. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Transport if he will consider reforming the motor tax online payment system to facilitate bulk purchases and renewals of motor tax by corporate fleet owners; if he has examined the system in operation in the UK, where multiple vehicle registrations can be uploaded at once during the payment process; the reason for not providing this facility to date in this jurisdiction; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20798/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Transport
speech.p: As Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, I wish to advise that the motor tax system is one of the business functions of the National Vehicle and Driver File (NVDF). The NVDF constitutes the national vehicle and driver registers and has a legal basis in Section 60 of the Finance Act 1993. The NVDF also supports driver services and is used to record penalty points.

The NVDF ecosystem requires ongoing maintenance and development to ensure a high-quality service for the public. The Department must therefore prioritise enhancements based on those that will deliver the greatest benefit to the widest range of users. For the medium term, priorities are guided by the Programme for Government, which includes progressing a digital alternative to the paper discs displayed on vehicle windscreens. In addition, system updates are needed to support the introduction of multi-offence incidents for penalty points. While a fleet-taxing facility would offer advantages for fleet operators, this functionality is not scheduled for development in the medium term.

question.p: 400. Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department has engaged with the NTA to ensure live service disruptions on public transport is communicated on other platforms besides a service (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20848/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally and for the scheduling and timetabling of these services in conjunction with the relevant transport operators.

In light of the NTA’s responsibility in this area, I have forwarded the Deputy's question to the NTA for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a response within ten working days.

question.p: 401. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 37 of 18 February 2026, if he will ensure that further consideration is given to the request of local authorities such as Cavan and Monaghan for additional funding for the non-national road network in 2026 taking into account the severe damage being caused to such roads with consistent heavy rainfall; and the submissions made by the local authorities for additional financial support; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20954/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads.

The 2026 regional and local road allocations were notified to local authorities on 17 February, and Cavan County Council has been allocated a total of €19,165,275. Of this, €18,755,275 has been allocated for the protection and renewal of Cavan's regional and local roads. This is an increase from the initial 2025 allocation of €18,218,150 for protection and renewal grants.

In 2026, Monaghan County Council has been allocated a total of €17,231,600. Of this, €16,486,600 has been allocated for the protection and renewal of Monaghan's regional and local roads. This is an increase from the initial 2025 allocation of €16,203,350 for protection and renewal grants.

Government is committed to assisting affected local authorities in the aftermath of Storm Chandra. My Department is liaising with affected counties, who are continuing to compile and assess damage on the ground to enable proper estimation of the total damage caused and the estimated cost of remediation.

It should be noted that Exchequer funding for regional and local roads is intended to supplement realistic contributions from local authorities’ own resources. Local authorities are also advised to set aside a contingency from Department allocations and own resources for severe weather events. As the statutory road authorities for their areas, it is also open to local authorities to prioritise investment on regional and local roads.

question.p: 402. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Transport if further consideration can be given to the implementation of safety measures on routes (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20955/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: The improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority, in accordance with the provisions of Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993. Works on those roads are funded from councils' own resources, which are supplemented by State grants for regional and local roads. The initial selection and prioritisation of works to be funded is a matter for the local authority.

On 17 February I announced an Exchequer investment of €718 million for regional and local roads across the State. This represents an increase in funding allocation of €26 million this year for road protection and renewal works.

My Department provides grant assistance to local authorities under the Regional and Local Road Grant Programme for a number of targeted programmes, including the Safety Improvement Programme. Each year, local authorities are invited to submit applications under this programme for consideration for funding in the subsequent year. In this context funding can be sought for traffic calming measures and other safety improvement works.
In 2026, Cavan County Council has been allocated a total of €19,165,275. Of this, €440,000 has been allocated for Safety Improvement Works on Cavan's regional and local roads.

Cavan County Council is responsible for deciding its annual programme for road maintenance and the Department has no role in that process. It is a matter for the Council to submit such an application for consideration for funding.

question.p: 403. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Transport the reason wheelchair-accessible bicycles are not routinely available on State-funded greenways; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21174/26]

speech.from: Minister for Transport
speech.p: As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to active travel and greenways. Under the Roads Act 1993, the planning, design, and construction of individual Greenways or active travel on national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.

Greenways are designed to be accessible to all, including those using wheelchairs and wheelchair-accessible bicycles. The development of active travel and greenway infrastructure is informed by a series of technical standards documentation including but not limited to the Cycle Design Manual and the Rural Cycleway Design manual. TII mandates compliance with specific guidelines for width, gradient, and surface quality to ensure a user-friendly and low-risk environment for all abilities.

The Government has long since recognised the strategic value of greenways as sustainable transport corridors, as well as catalysts for regional economic development, tourism, and community health and well-being. It is immensely positive that a number of local businesses have established themselves or expanded along greenway routes, including private bike shops that cater for greenway users.

Whilst not providing wheelchair-accessible bicycles on Greenways, the Department does provide support towards the provision of mobility bikes. The Department of Transport provides funding to Variety Ireland for its Recycle Mobility Scheme. Under this scheme, Variety Ireland has provided dozens of specially adapted trikes to children all around Ireland. These trikes are beneficial to children, who due to various disabilities, cannot cycle a regular bicycle. As each trike is specially adapted to an individual child’s needs, the cost for each trike can be very expensive. Without Government funding, they can be unobtainable for many families of children with special needs.

Given the bespoke nature of the trikes, they cannot be used by other children and would therefore be obsolete once the child outgrows it. Under the Recycle Mobility Scheme, once a child outgrows their trike, Variety Ireland take it back, upcycle it and then adapt it to another child’s particular needs. The Department of Transport provided €150,000 towards the Scheme in 2025 and funding levels for 2026 are yet to be determined. Funding is also contributed to the programme by the Department of Children, Disability, and Equality (DCDE).

Funding support was also provided to enable the recent opening of Ireland’s first Cycling Inclusion Centre of Excellence in Clondalkin in County Dublin, this facility creating a safe environment where people with and without disabilities can learn and cycle together.
The Department is committed to funding initiatives that ensure all members of society can access our walking and cycling infrastructure.

question.p: 404. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated cost of making the carer's allowance and carer's benefit tax-exempt; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20750/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I am advised by Revenue that the sharing of data on recipients of carer’s allowance and carer’s benefit by the Department of Social Protection only commenced on 1 January 2026. Therefore, it is not currently possible to estimate a cost associated with making these payments tax exempt as the cost depends on the recipients’ total income and their total tax credits and reliefs for the tax year, which will not be known until the year has concluded and taxpayers are given the opportunity to confirm their incomes, reliefs and credits by way of filing their income tax return. On this basis, it is not currently possible to estimate the cost associated with the change outlined by the Deputy.

It should be noted that not all carers who are in receipt of Carer’s income will have a tax liability, particularly if their income level is below the taxation threshold, or they have sufficient tax credits to reduce their liability to nil. A person’s tax liability will depend on their individual personal circumstances, income levels and personal credits available to them and their family.

question.p: 405. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there will be a review of the motorised transport grant scheme to allow for the inclusion of electric vehicles (EVs), given that EVs are currently exempt from VRT and that, under the existing scheme, VAT and VRT are excluded when purchasing a petrol/diesel car for persons with a disability; if such a review is planned, when it will take place, the expected timeline for the introduction of a revised scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20777/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The Deputy should note that my Department has no involvement in the Motorised Transport Grant which is under the remit of the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, but the Department of Finance does have oversight of the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS).
The Disabled Drivers & Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) provides relief from VRT and VAT on an adapted car, as well as an exemption from motor tax and an annual fuel grant.

Under DDS provisions, the reliefs from VRT and VAT are generous in nature amounting to up to €10,000, €16,000 or €22,000, depending on the level of adaption required for the vehicle. There is no differentiation between electric and other vehicles in terms of available VRT/VAT relief.

DDS Scheme recipients with a petrol or diesel vehicle may claim payment of a fuel grant. The fuel grant covers the excise tax elements of petrol, diesel and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). It is based on a per litre rate in respect of the mineral oil taxes applying to these products. An annual maximum of 2,730 litres applies in respect of a driver or passenger, and 4,100 litres in respect of an organisation.
As electricity supplied for household use is not subject to excise tax, there is no provision under the DDS to cover electricity used to recharge electric vehicles.

My Department and I acknowledge that the DDS is no longer fit-for-purpose. Work on improving this situation is already underway with a new grant-based scheme to be developed and led by the Department of Transport. This approach is consistent with that which is set out in the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030. I am advised that the Department of Transport has begun the development of this new Vehicle Adaption Scheme (VAS). The existing DDS remains with the Department of Finance and will continue to be reviewed in the context of new scheme developments by the Department of Transport.

When this government took office, it committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families. Budget 2026 is the first step in delivering on this ambition, providing some €3.83 billion to specialist disability services next year, an unprecedented increase of €618 million, or almost 20%. This funding will be vital in delivering the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People.

The commitment to develop a new scheme by the Department of Transport, and in this context review the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme, are strong commitments in this strategy to which the I am fully committed.

question.p: 406. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will make the carer's allowance and carer's benefit tax exempt similar to other social welfare supports in recognition of savings these carers offer the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18247/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Carers play a fundamental supporting role in society, and the Government are committed to supporting individuals and families with caring responsibilities. This is acknowledged by the broad range of commitments in the Programme for Government to improving supports for carers.

It is important to state that there has been no change in the Income Tax treatment of Carer’s Allowance and Carer’s Benefit. Carer’s Allowance and Carer’s Benefit are subject to Income Tax but are exempt from Universal Social Charge and Pay Related Social Insurance.

As the Deputy may be aware, there is a long-standing data sharing arrangement between both Revenue and the Department of Social Protection (DSP) which facilitates the operation of both the tax and welfare systems. DSP had been reporting information on a significant number of taxable DSP payments to Revenue, including Jobseekers Benefit, Maternity Benefit, One-Parent Family Payment, State Pension (Contributory or Non-Contributory) and Bereaved Partners Contributory Pension but information for Carer’s Allowance and Carer’s Benefit has not previously been shared

As data relating to Carer’s Allowance and Carer’s Benefit had not been shared between DSP and Revenue previously, it was the recipient’s responsibility to declare this income to Revenue. When a carer was granted the Allowance or Benefit, the DSP notice advised the carer that the Allowance or Benefit was taxable income. It was agreed by DSP and Revenue that from 1 January 2026, information on Carer's Allowance/Benefit payments will be included in the Taxable Payments Report shared directly with Revenue.

Where a person in receipt of payments from DSP also has an additional source of employment or occupational pension income, the mechanism used to collect tax due is by reducing the person’s annual tax credits and rate band, by the annual amount of their DSP income. This ensures that the DSP payment is paid gross to the recipient, while the salary or pension, as paid by their employer, will have any tax due on both the DSP income and the employment deducted from it. This aligns the taxation of Carer’s income with other taxable DSP payments and significantly reduces the risk of an end-of-year liability.

It should be noted that not all carers who are in receipt of Carer’s income will have a tax liability, particularly if their income level is below the taxation threshold, or they have sufficient tax credits to reduce their liability to nil. A person’s tax liability will depend on their individual personal circumstances, income levels and personal credits available to them and their family.

As the Deputy will appreciate decisions regarding taxation measures are made in the context of the annual Budget and Finance Bill processes, at the appropriate time, and having regard to available resources and the sound management of the public finances.

question.p: 407. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 452 of 17 February 2026, the position regarding the assessment and analysis that is carried out in relation to balancing taxation versus spending; if any further assessment of eliminating the USC has been carried out in this regard; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18494/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The Government published its Medium-Term Fiscal and Structural Plan (MTP) in December, setting out the fiscal strategy between now and the end of the decade.

The strategy set out in the Plan will support progress on implementing the key social and economic priorities of the Government while delivering on our commitment to sustainable public finances. This strategy is based on three core pillars: sustainability, resilience and readiness.

Firstly, the Government will continue to increase expenditure in public services in a sustainable way. Secondly, we are committing to large-scale infrastructure investment to boost the resilience of our economy. Thirdly, we will keep saving for the future by running budgetary surpluses and setting money aside in the Future Ireland Fund (FIF), as well as the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund (ICNF). To operationalise this, the Government has committed to fixed spending ceilings for the duration of the plan.

In relation to the Universal Social Charge (USC), as previously highlighted, research by the Department of Finance and the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) found that the USC represented a more stable form of revenue than income tax. Given the openness of the Irish economy and consequent susceptibility to economic shocks, the contribution that the USC makes to the stability of the State’s revenue sources is considerable.

In addition, the Department of Finance also carried out a review of the personal tax system in 2023. This review included analysis of the USC and was published as part of Budget 2024 documentation. Moreover, the annual Income Tax – Tax Strategy Group paper includes analysis in respect of income tax receipts, including USC.

The yield from USC in 2025 amounted to €5.6 billion. In 2026, it is projected to total approximately €5.8 billion. Given the level of revenue it raises, the USC has played a vital role in funding public services and increased capital expenditure over recent years. Accordingly, in order to stay within the parameters of the fiscal strategy, the abolition of USC would necessitate equivalent revenues to be raised elsewhere.

As the Deputy will be aware the Programme for Government (PfG) “Securing Ireland’s Future” contains a commitments to making progressive changes to personal income tax, including indexing credits and bands, if the economy remains strong.

question.p: 408. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the amount of each fuel tax that was taken by the Government on all fuels for each of the past five years. [18515/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I am advised by Revenue that the relevant excise duty rates on fuel are published on the Revenue website at www.revenue.ie/en/tax-professionals/tdm/excise/excise-duty-rates/energy-excise-duty-rates.pdf.

I am further advised by Revenue that a breakdown of excise receipts for 2024 and prior years is available on the Revenue website at www.revenue.ie/en/corporate/information-about-revenue/statistics/excise/receipts-volume-and-price/excise-receipts-commodity.aspx.

In relation to VAT, I am further advised by Revenue that traders are not required to identify the VAT yield generated from the supply of specific goods and services on their VAT returns. Therefore, it is not possible to provide the VAT yield on all fuel and energy related products and services using taxpayer information alone.

question.p: 409. Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will confirm whether the higher 15% corporation tax rate will be applied to all multinationals earning over €750 million in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18547/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Ireland’s Corporation Tax regime has been built on certainty and predictability, and the 12.5 per cent headline rate on trading income has been a cornerstone of that regime for over 20 years. This stability has enabled companies to plan long-term investments in Ireland, generating employment and increasing economic activity.

In October 2021 Ireland, along with almost 140 other countries in the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework, signed up to an historic agreement to reform the international tax framework as it applies to large corporate groups, to bring stability and reform to the global Corporation Tax framework.

Pillar Two of the agreement will see the adoption of a global minimum effective tax rate (ETR) of 15 per cent applying to multinational or large-scale domestic groups with global revenues in excess of €750m in at least two of the previous four years.

Ireland introduced Pillar Two compliant minimum tax rules in Finance (No.2) Act 2023 in accordance with the requirements of the EU Minimum Tax Directive, which provides for consistent implementation across the EU of the Pillar Two Model Rules. There are three discrete elements of the Model Rules, designed to ensure that a minimum effective tax rate of 15 per cent applies. These are the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), the Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR) and the optional Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax Rule (QDTT). In general, the IIR applies a top-up tax at the level of a parent entity where undertaxed profits arise in respect of its subsidiaries. The UTPR acts as a backstop rule, providing for collection of top-up tax via other group entities where collection does not occur via a parent entity under the IIR. A QDTT allows jurisdictions to collect any top-up tax due in respect of entities located in their jurisdiction, and applies in priority to an IIR or UTPR. Ireland has provided for a QDTT.

On 5 January 2026, a Side-by-Side Package in relation to Global Minimum Tax was approved and adopted by Members of the OECD / G20 Inclusive Framework on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS). The package delivers on the G7 ‘Statement on global minimum taxes’, and subsequent G20 Communiqué, which requested that the Inclusive Framework design a solution whereby the objectives of the Global Minimum Tax are preserved while developing a mechanism to allow for coexistence with the US tax system incorporating its pre-existing global minimum tax rules.

The US tax system only became a “Qualified Side-by-Side Regime” after rigorous assessment by all inclusive framework members to ensure that it meets defined eligibility criteria, including that there is no material risk of ETRs below 15 per cent.

Where an in-scope group is headquartered in a Qualified Side-by-Side jurisdiction, Pillar Two IIR or UTPR top-up taxes will not apply in respect of that group's subsidiaries in other jurisdictions. However QDTTs, where implemented, will continue to apply. Therefore companies that are members of an in-scope group (based on the turnover threshold) will continue to be subject to QDTT in Ireland, to achieve a 15% ETR on a jurisdictional level, including those that are members of US-parented groups. This will ensure that the minimum tax rules will continue to apply as intended and the original Pillar two objective continues to be achieved in 2026 and beyond.
It is my intention to bring forward legislation in this autumn's Finance Bill to provide for the Side-by-side Package, in line with this global agreement.

question.p: 413. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance his plans to amend the tax treatment of investments in Exchange Traded Funds, including Green ETFs, including the deemed disposal rule and exit tax; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18640/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: An Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) is an investment fund whose units are held in a recognised clearing system and are traded on a regulated stock exchange. There is no separate taxation regime for ETFs. As collective investment funds, they generally come within the regimes set out in the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 for such funds. The domicile of the ETF will generally determine the applicable fund regime, specifically whether the ETF falls within the domestic fund regime or the offshore fund regime. For most ETFs, investors are required to calculate, return and pay the income tax on the income and gains arising from their investment in the fund on a self-assessed basis.

Supporting and encouraging retail investment is a Government priority. Budget 2026 included a reduction in the taxation rate that applies to Irish and equivalent offshore funds, and Irish and certain foreign life assurance products, from 41% to 38%, which applies to investments in ETFs that are taxed under these regimes. This rate change took effect from 1 January 2026.

In addition, Budget 2026 included a commitment to publish a new approach to simplify and adapt the current taxation framework for retail investment while retaining necessary and important anti-avoidance protections in a proportionate manner. I expect to publish this in the coming months.

The work underway includes consideration of the Funds Sector 2030 Report, including the issue of deemed disposal and the taxation of ETFs, as well as the European Commission’s recommendation on Savings and Investment Accounts.

question.p: 416. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the current VAT rate for printed and digital maps will be removed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18912/26]

418. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the rationale for the current VAT treatment of printed maps at 13.5% and digital maps at 23%, while books, newspapers and magazines are zero rated; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18991/26]

419. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will review the current VAT treatment of printed maps at 13.5% and digital maps at 23%, with a view to applying a zero rate similar to that applied to books, newspapers and magazines; whether the impact of the current rates on small Irish publishers and sectors such as tourism and outdoor recreation has been assessed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18992/26]

420. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether EU VAT rules permit the application of a zero rate of VAT to printed and digital maps, similar to books, newspapers and magazines; if his Department has examined the possibility of applying such a rate in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18993/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 416, 418, 419 and 420 together.

As the Deputies will be aware, the EU VAT Directive, which Irish VAT law must comply, generally holds that all goods and services are liable for VAT at the standard rate. Where a good or service is included in a list under Annex III of the Directive, an exemption or reduced rate of VAT may be applied.

The supply of printed material not wholly dedicated to advertising is included under this list and extends to printed maps as the basis for the reduced rate being applied. As the Deputies may be aware, the temporary VAT rate of 9% introduced in July 2011 and again in November 2020 for the tourism and hospitality sectors included certain printed matter such as brochures, maps, and programmes. Consequently, when this VAT rate reverted to the 13.5% rate from 1 September 2023, it also changed the VAT rates on maps in printed form to this higher rate.
A 9% VAT rate has applied on a permanent basis to all electronic publications, including electronic maps, from 1 January 2019.

Examining a reduction in VAT rates applied to certain goods and services must be done in the context of the annual Budgetary process as tax reductions impose a cost on the Exchequer by narrowing the tax base. Officials in my Department are currently working on the Tax Strategy Group Papers which will be published in the summer and will form the basis of any decision to be made in the annual Budget later this year.

The Central Bank of Ireland publishes data on mortgage interest rate distributions. While it does not provide information on numbers of mortgage holders, the data (which is categorised into banks, lending non-banks and non-lending non-banks) may be useful to the Deputy.

question.p: 421. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to consider introducing a tax relief for PAYE individuals who engage the services of an accountant for the purposes of their tax return and incur fees (details supplied). [19019/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Under the tax code there are different rules to determine the deductibility of expenses depending on the nature of the income received. Accordingly, the rules for PAYE workers differ from those applicable to self-employed individuals.

The response to PQ 9357/26 dated 10 February 2026 concerned PAYE individuals engaging the services of an accountant for the purposes of their tax return and in that context addressed the applicable employment expense rules in section 114 Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (“TCA 1997”).
The rules around the deductibility of expenses for self-employed individuals and PAYE workers are further clarified below.

Section 81 TCA 1997 provides that expenses which are wholly and exclusively laid out or expended for the purposes of a trade or profession carried on by a self-employed individual are deductible in computing the profits of the trade or profession which are charged to income tax. Accountancy fees that relate to the preparation of business accounts or tax computations for the trade or profession are generally allowable under section 81 TCA 1997 on the basis that they are expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the trade or profession.

As previously outlined, Revenue have advised that to qualify for tax relief under section 114, the expenses must be wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the performance of the duties of the relevant employment. Accountancy fees incurred by individuals, whose only income is Schedule E income (including pension income), in obtaining assistance with the preparation of their personal tax returns are generally regarded as personal tax compliance costs and do not satisfy the rules outlined in section 114.

I am informed by Revenue that the rules in section 114 are strictly applied and there is a body of case law supporting the narrow application of the provisions of the section. For example, case law has determined that expenditure incurred by an employee which merely puts the employee in a position to exercise that employment or to meet obligations external to the performance of duties would not comply with section 114. The strict interpretation of the rule is outlined in Lomax v Newton, 34 TC 558, with the narrowness of the application of the legislation endorsed in the Irish cases of SP O’Broin v Giolla Meidhre, and SP O’Broin v Finbar Piggot ITR Vol II P366.

A person who takes a contrary view on the tax treatment of a matter may, if they are a chargeable persons within the self-assessment system, file an expression of doubt and if Revenue subsequently disallows the deduction, appeal the assessment to the independent Tax Appeals Commission (TAC) and the higher courts, if necessary. Similarly, a PAYE taxpayer who disagrees with Revenue’s determination may appeal that determination directly to the TAC.

question.p: 422. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the amount of money raised through deemed disposal taxes in the years 2020 to 2025 inclusive, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19093/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The deemed disposal rule is an anti-avoidance measure that applies to investments in Irish domiciled investment funds (including Irish domiciled Exchange Traded Funds or ‘ETFs’) and life assurance products, as well as equivalent offshore funds (including equivalent offshore ETFs) and certain foreign life assurance products.

Under the deemed disposal rule for investment funds, tax is levied eight years after an investment is made, and every subsequent eight years, regardless of whether or not a disposal has in fact occurred. The tax is levied on any gain in the value of the investment from the date of acquisition to the date of the deemed disposal. On the ultimate disposal of the units in the fund, any tax paid under the deemed disposal rule is allowed as a credit against the final tax liability. The purpose of the deemed disposal rule is to prevent the indefinite roll-up of income and gains and the associated loss of tax to the Exchequer.

I am informed by Revenue that data on the revenue raised because of the eight-year deemed disposal rule is not readily available. While it is possible to identify the amounts of tax paid by funds in respect of unit holders (being Investment Undertaking Tax (IUT)) and income tax accounted for by individuals in respect of their investments in Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds, it is not possible to provide a breakdown of the tax as between the amount relating to the eight-year deemed disposal and the amount relating to the other types of chargeable events.

The table below provides the estimated amount of overall income tax arising in 2020 to 2024 in respect of investments in investment funds, including IUT and income tax on Irish domiciled funds and certain offshore investment funds, which includes amounts in respect of ETFs. Data for 2025 is not yet available.

It is not possible to advise on the estimated individual number of investors affected by the eight-year deemed disposal each year. As already mentioned, the information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned by investors on account of deemed disposal rules from that which arises from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability.
* Total gross tax liability on income / gains from offshore funds per Form 11 return. Form 11 data for 2024 and 2025 is not yet available.

** IUT represents the gross amount of tax paid to Revenue. It is not possible to identify whether the figures for IUT represent amounts taxed at 25% in respect of corporate investors or 41% in respect of individual investors.

question.p: 423. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance when he expects to publish the roadmap on investment taxation reforms referenced in Budget 2026; whether that roadmap will examine the operation of the deemed disposal regime applied to Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19160/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The deemed disposal rule is an anti-avoidance measure that applies to investments in Irish domiciled investment funds (including Irish domiciled Exchange Traded Funds or ‘ETFs’) and life assurance products, as well as equivalent offshore funds (including equivalent offshore ETFs) and certain foreign life assurance products.

Supporting and encouraging retail investment is a Government priority. In addition to the reduction from 41% to 38 in the taxation rate that applies to Irish and equivalent offshore funds, and Irish and certain foreign life assurance products, Budget 2026 included a commitment to publish a new approach to simplify and adapt the current taxation framework for retail investment while retaining necessary and important anti-avoidance protections in a proportionate manner. I expect to publish this in the coming months.

The work underway on the new approach includes consideration of the Funds Sector 2030 Report, including the issue of deemed disposal and the taxation of ETFs, as well as the European Commission’s recommendation on Savings and Investment Accounts.

question.p: 424. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the current status of the proposed State-backed savings and investment scheme aimed at encouraging greater household participation in long-term investment; whether contribution limits and tax treatment have been determined; and the expected timeline for bringing forward proposals; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19161/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The Savings and Investments Union aims to create better financial opportunities across the EU, providing people with more opportunities to invest and provide for their current and future prosperity. In September 2025, the European Commission adopted a Recommendation on increasing the availability of Savings and Investment Accounts in Member States and this included an outline of their key characteristics.

Ireland is committed to support initiatives that enhance retail investor participation in capital markets. As such, I strongly welcome the publication of this Recommendation. While Ireland does not have a specific investment account for retail investors at present, the tax treatment of retail investments was considered as part of a broader review into the funds and asset management sector in Ireland, which culminated in the ‘Funds Sector 2030’ report that was published in October 2024.

In recognition of the importance of encouraging retail investment, Finance Bill 2025 provided for a reduction in the rate of taxation on returns from Irish and equivalent investment funds and Irish and certain foreign life assurance policies from 41% to 38%.

As part of Budget 2026, the government announced its intention to publish a roadmap in 2026, setting out the intended approach to simplify and adapt the tax framework to encourage retail investment in future Finance Bills. The roadmap will take into consideration developments at EU level in respect of the Savings and Investments Union, including the Recommendation on SIAs and draw upon best practice in other countries who operate successful savings accounts.
Officials in the Department of Finance are currently developing this roadmap and it will be published in the near future. Its findings will be used to identify next steps for this proposal.

question.p: 425. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 487 of 17 February 2026, if a further review is underway by his Department and Revenue to provide more clarity on the costs of abolition of the deemed disposal rule. [19209/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: As I outlined in Parliamentary Question No. 487 of 17 February 2026, I am informed by Revenue that data on the revenue raised because of the eight-year deemed disposal rule is not readily available. While it is possible to identify the amounts of tax paid by funds in respect of unit holders (being Investment Undertaking Tax (IUT)) and income tax accounted for by individuals in respect of their investments in Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds, it is not possible to provide a breakdown of the tax as between the amount relating to the eight-year deemed disposal and the amount relating to the other types of chargeable events.

I can confirm that my officials are examining whether other sources of data could assist in preparing an estimate of the proportion of IUT that relates to deemed disposal. This could assist when considering the cost of any changes to the taxation of retail investments.

question.p: 426. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the cost of further reductions in the taxation rate that applies to Irish and equivalent offshore funds, and Irish and certain foreign life assurance products, for each 1% of a reduction. [19210/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I am advised by the Revenue Commissioners that a ‘gross roll-up’ applies under the domestic funds and life assurance regimes such that there is no annual tax on income or gains arising to a domestic fund or life assurance policy. Instead, exit tax known as Investment Undertaking Tax (‘IUT) applies in respect of payments made to certain unit holders and Life Assurance Exit Tax (‘LAET’) applies in respect of payments made to certain policyholders. The fund and life assurance company are generally required to deduct the exit tax. However, for certain domestic investment funds, where the units are held on a recognised clearing system, such as the case with Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs), the fund is not required to deduct exit tax and the investor must self-assess the tax due.

In the case of a regulated offshore fund located in another EU or EEA state, or in an OECD Member State with which Ireland has a double taxation agreement (an ‘OECD/DTA country’), the tax treatment of an investment in such a fund is similar to that which applies in respect of an investment in an Irish domiciled regulated fund. However, not being Irish domiciled, these funds cannot apply Irish exit tax. Therefore, Irish investors in such funds are required to account for the tax through the self-assessment system. Similar treatment applies in respect of payments in respect of a foreign life policy with a life assurance company located in an EU or EEA state or in an OECD/DTA country.

Finance Act 2025 provided for a reduction in the rate of IUT, LAET and the rate of tax applicable to investments in the above-mentioned offshore funds and foreign life assurance policies, from 41% to 38%, to take effect from 1 January 2026. These changes form part of work underway to support and encourage retail investment.

I am informed by the Revenue Commissioners that, in relation to IUT, the cost of each 1% reduction in the rate is estimated at €1.4m. This cost does not take into account the tax which is paid in respect of domestic funds which are ETFs, as such tax is paid under the self-assessment system and is not separately identifiable from tax returns. In addition, the costings do not account for the fact that some IUT may be refundable. For example, IUT operated by the Courts Service may be refundable under section 189 Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 where the person is permanently incapacitated.
In relation to LAET, the cost of each 1% reduction in the rate is estimated at €4.2m.
In relation to investments in regulated offshore funds located in another EU or EEA state or in an OECD/DTA country, the cost of each 1% reduction in the rate is estimated at €0.8m.
In relation to offshore life policies with life companies located in another EU or EEA state or in an OECD/DTA country, the cost of each 1% reduction in the rate is estimated at €0.02m.
The above costings are based on the average of the tax payments received in the 8 most recent years, in order to account for fluctuations that can occur.

question.p: 427. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department tracks the total amount of tax revenue collected annually from electricity supplied to businesses in each of the past five years; the projected yield for the current year; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19211/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I am advised by Revenue that Electricity Tax is an excise duty charged on supplies of electricity to the final consumer. The liability arises at the point of supply, and the supplier is responsible for payment of the tax and for filing all returns. Supplies for domestic use are exempt from the tax. The total Electricity Tax collected in each of the last five years is set out in the table below.

I am further advised by Revenue that a detailed publication of aggregated Electricity Tax returns data for accounting periods from 2016 onwards is available on the Revenue website at: https://www.revenue.ie/en/corporate/information-about-revenue/statistics/excise/electricity-tax/index.aspx . The 2025 accounting year is due for publication in the coming weeks.

This publication contains details from the tax returns which help inform the aggregate information on total Electricity Tax collected. Analysis of the information available on the tax returns and published in aggregate form in the publication indicates that the vast majority (over 90 per cent) of Electricity Tax collected each year relates to business use.

question.p: 428. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the cost to the Exchequer of expanding the qualifying expenditures under the R&D credit in each of the years 2024 and 2025; the estimated cost for expansion of the R&D tax credit in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19212/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The Research and Development (R&D) tax credit regime recognises that research and development is a key driver of economic growth and plays an important role in the creation of high value employment. Research and development is critical to Ireland’s continuing competitiveness. The enhancements made to the R&D tax credit regime in recent Budgets reflect the Government’s commitment to enterprise supports for productive and innovative businesses in the State.

The R&D tax credit provides a 35 per cent credit on qualifying expenditure incurred on qualifying R&D activities in basic research, applied research or experimental development in a field of science or technology. In addition, the R&D activities must also seek to achieve a scientific or technological advancement and involve the resolution of scientific or technological uncertainty. For expenditure to qualify for the R&D tax credit it must be incurred by a company wholly and exclusively in the carrying on of research and development activities.

Recent Budgets have enhanced the R&D tax credit regime by increasing the rate of the R&D tax credit and increasing the first-year payment threshold (FYPT). Budget 2024 and Budget 2026 increased the rate of the R&D tax credit from 25 per cent to 30 per cent and subsequently from 30 per cent to 35 per cent respectively. The FYPT, which was introduced in Budget 2023, allowed for R&D tax credit claims up to €25,000 to be payable in full in the first year of claim. Subsequent Budgets increased this amount (to €50,000 and €75,000) and Budget 2026 provided for an additional increase in the FYPT to €87,500. These measures provided an increase in support to all R&D claimant companies but did not change or expand the definition of qualifying expenditure for the purposes of the R&D tax credit.

Budget 2026 also provided for a new measure to expand qualifying expenditure in respect of R&D employees, to allow 100 per cent of an R&D employee’s emoluments as qualifying costs where at least 95 per cent of their duties are spent on qualifying R&D activities. While this is an expansion to the definition of qualifying expenditure its primary purpose is to provide for some administrative simplification of the R&D tax credit regime for claimant companies and to reduce the potential for disputes on audits in respect of time apportionment. As such this individual measure is not expected to have a material Exchequer cost.

As the Deputy may be aware, the Research and Development Tax Credit and Innovation Compass was published in February. The Compass sets out a medium-term pathway for further work in relation to the R&D tax credit and potential tax supports for innovation. The Compass identified four broad directions for future policy work to be undertaken, one of which is in respect of qualifying expenditure for the purposes of the R&D tax credit. Officials in my Department are continuing to progress policy review work on the R&D tax credit, in line with the pathways laid out in the Compass.

question.p: 429. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the Government has examined the impact of VAT and other Exchequer-imposed charges on commercial electricity costs in the context of heightened energy price volatility since 2020; whether any temporary or permanent adjustments to such taxation measures are under consideration to support businesses in Budget 2027; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19213/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Officials in my Department are continuing to monitor international developments closely in relation to energy costs to assess their impact on the Irish economy. The Deputy will appreciate that movements in commodity prices in recent days have been extremely volatile.

It should be noted that VAT is a consumption tax which is payable on the supply or importation of goods and on the supply of services within the territory of the Member States of the European Union. The tax is ultimately payable by the final consumer of the good or service. VAT registered businesses can claim back the VAT on their inputs as part of their regular VAT return.

As the Deputy will be aware, following changes in the EU VAT Directive in April 2022, member states were given greater flexibility to apply reduced VAT rates to a range of goods and services, including electricity.
Ireland reduced VAT rate on electricity from 13.5% to 9%, from 1 May 2022. This 9% rate was extended on several occasions and in Budget 2026 it was extended until 31 December 2030.
