question.p: 434. Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the way in which the flat rate of tax for farmers is decided on an annual basis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19229/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The Flat-Rate Addition is reviewed each year in the run-up to the Budget in accordance with criteria set down in the EU VAT Directive. It is based on macro-economic data (i.e. agricultural inputs and production and the prevailing VAT rate structures) averaged over the preceding three years.

The methodology takes account of the final estimates of farming inputs, outputs and the VAT rate structures for the previous two years and a provisional forecast of agriculture inputs and outputs for the current year as provided by the CSO.
The review will take place in September in advance of the Budget 2027.

question.p: 435. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to clarify if local authorities are obliged to pay the residential zoned land tax; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19276/26]

436. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to clarify how much residential zoned land tax has been paid by local authorities in 2024 and 2025 respectively, by local authority and in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19277/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 435 and 436 together.

RZLT is an annual tax, calculated at a rate of 3% of the market value of the land within its scope, known as a relevant site. Relevant sites are identified by reference to maps published by local authorities, which are revised on an annual basis, and reflect land that the local authority has determined meets the relevant criteria for the tax, being that the land is zoned for residential or mixed-use (including residential) purposes and that it is serviced. Owners of such land, including local authorities, are required to register and pay the tax by 23 May each year.
I am advised by Revenue that the total receipts collected in 2025 are provisionally recorded as €49.2 million. As RZLT was first charged on 1 February 2025, there are no 2024 receipts.

Information in respect of the amount of residential zoned land tax collected to date, including registrations and returns by local authorities, is published on the Revenue website. Please see a link to the latest publication at: www.revenue.ie/en/corporate/documents/statistics/property-taxes/pt-stats-update-211025.pdf

summary.i: Question No. 436 answered with Question No. 435.

question.p: 437. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the revenue earned from VAT on large energy users in each of the years 2015 to date in 2026, in tabular form. [19391/26]

438. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide a breakdown of the revenue earned from VAT on electricity and gas from large energy users broken down by gas and electricity separately in each of the years 2015 to date in 2026, in tabular form. [19393/26]

481. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the revenue earned from VAT on energy broken down by gas and electricity charged to large energy users in each of the years 2015 to 2025 and to-date in 2026, in tabular form. [20568/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 437, 438 and 481 together.

I am informed by Revenue that traders are not required to separately identify the VAT from specific goods or services on their periodic VAT returns. Therefore, it is not possible to identify the VAT charged on the supply of electricity and gas, whether from large energy users or otherwise, using taxpayer information alone. While Revenue uses aggregate third-party data sources to tentatively estimate the VAT on electricity and gas supplied to households and VAT exempt sectors, this information is not sufficiently detailed to identify large energy users specifically.

It should also be noted that VAT-registered businesses, including large energy consumers, are generally entitled to reclaim as an input credit the VAT incurred on business related expenses such as electricity and gas, to the extent that those goods or services are used for the purposes of making taxable supplies in the furtherance of their business activity.

summary.i: Question No. 438 answered with Question No. 437.

question.p: 439. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the rationale for bringing in the deemed disposal rule as an anti avoidance measure in the Finance Act 2006; if there was any evidence of significant levels of tax avoidance regarding Irish funds, investments in life policies and investments in offshore funds prior to 2006; if there has been research carried out by his Department or by Revenue on the effectiveness of this measure regarding its stated purpose; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19419/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Finance Act 2000 introduced the gross roll-up taxation regime for investments in domestic funds and life policies. The general thrust of the regime is that there is no annual tax on income or gains arising within the investment. However, exit tax must be deducted on the occurrence of a “chargeable event”, which originally included –
- the making of relevant payments,
- the redemption of the investment, and
- the transfer by an investor of their investment.

Finance Act 2006 introduced the eight-year deemed disposal requirement for all investments that benefit from the gross roll-up regime. This was introduced as a new category of ‘chargeable event’. A deemed disposal occurs eight years following inception of a policy of life assurance or acquisition of a unit in a fund and then every eight years thereafter. Any gain on the investment which arises from the date of inception or the date of acquisition to the date of the deemed disposal is subject to tax. This ensures that income and gains aren’t being rolled up in life assurance policies or funds without being taxed indefinitely. On the ultimate disposal of the investment any tax paid which arose as a result of a deemed disposal is allowed as a credit against any final tax liability on disposal.

The rule was introduced to counter a specific avoidance scheme which had been identified by the Revenue Commissioners which involved the continual rolling over of certain life assurance policies without them becoming chargeable to tax. The scheme involved the indefinite deferral of tax beyond the intended fixed investment period of the specific life policy product. The introduction of the deemed disposal rule was thus to prevent the indefinite deferral of tax. The deemed disposal rule was also introduced in respect of investments in funds to ensure that such investment products did not have a comparable advantage in comparison to life products.

A further anti-avoidance measure was introduced in Finance Act 2007 in respect of Personal Portfolio Investment Undertakings (PPIUs). A PPIU is a fund, either domestic or offshore, where the selection of the property of the fund was, or can be, influenced by an individual who is the investor or by certain persons connected with the investor. To counteract the use of a PPIU to gain access to the gross roll-up regime, the higher rate of tax of 60 per cent applies to a gain arising on a chargeable event with respect to a PPIU. Similar provisions apply in respect of Personal Portfolio Life Policies.

Due to the mechanics of the eight-year deemed disposal and the data which is returned to Revenue, it is not possible to extract the exact tax yield of the eight-year deemed disposal provisions. However, as with all anti-avoidance rules, the eight-year deemed disposal rule and the anti-avoidance measure relating to PPIUs have a deterrent effect which it is not possible to put a value on.

question.p: 440. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 260 of 19 February 2026, to clarify if a payment break is registered as a missed payment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19455/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Payment breaks which are agreed between lenders and borrowers are not identified or registered as a missed payment (or a payment past due) on the borrower’s credit report recorded on the Consumer Credit Register.
However, payments which are due and are missed without agreement between a borrower and a lender will be identified as such on the borrower’s credit report.

question.p: 441. Deputy John Brady asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department or any body under its aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19496/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I am advised by Revenue that, in compliance with section 851A of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997, it is not permitted to disclose details relating to the tax affairs of any individual taxpayer or taxable entity, except in certain limited circumstances provided for in law, for example in the case of tax settlements meeting the criteria for publication under section 1086A of the TCA.
The List of Tax Defaulters is published within 3 months of the end of each quarter in Iris Oifigiúil and is also publicly available on the Revenue website www.revenue.ie.

question.p: 442. Deputy Natasha Newsome Drennan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if all NAMA files will be sent to the National Archives; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19539/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, as Minister for Finance, I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the National Asset Management Agency (NAMA).

However, I am advised by my officials that NAMA has a long-standing Records Management Policy, approved by the NAMA Board and informed by external legal advice, including Senior Counsel advice. While NAMA is not subject to the National Archives Act (the "Act"), I am advised that in framing its Records Management Policy, the NAMA Board was mindful that it may, at a future time, be subject to the Act.

Under this policy, specific categories of important NAMA records, such as NAMA Board and Committee papers, other governance-related records, NAMA policies and procedures, and records to support the integrity of NAMA financial information, have been identified to be retained and preserved following NAMA’s dissolution. These categories include records that have been identified as having potential historical significance.

Under NAMA’s Records Management Policy, other categories of records are retained for as long as is required under GDPR obligations, including personal information relating to debtors, data minimisation and storage limitation obligations.

question.p: 443. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance his views that the continued application and scheduled increases of the carbon tax on petrol and diesel, at a time when motorists are already facing significant increases in fuel prices due to global instability, is placing an unfair and disproportionate burden on working people, families and rural communities who rely on their cars; the additional VAT revenue being collected by the Exchequer as a result of these higher fuel prices; and whether he will immediately suspend or freeze the carbon tax on transport fuels in order to prevent the State from effectively profiting from rising fuel costs at the expense of Irish motorists. [19569/26]
490. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding tax on fuel (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20874/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 443 and 490 together.

The major disruption to global energy supply as a result of the situation in Iran and the Middle East is reflected in extremely volatile commodity prices over the past two weeks. Officials in my Department are continuing to closely monitor these developments to assess their impact on the Irish economy and society.

With regard to taxation, liquid fuels such as petrol, auto-diesel, heating kerosene and Marked Gas Oil (MGO)/green diesel are subject to excise duty in the form of Mineral Oil Tax (MOT) and must comply with minimum rates as set out in the EU Energy Tax Directive. MOT is applied on a volumetric basis, so revenue raised is determined by consumption levels rather than prices.

The Programme for Government committed to continue with the planned carbon tax increases, aligning with recommendations from the Climate Change Advisory Council and scientific experts, and to using the resulting revenues raised to support climate action measures and to ensure the most vulnerable are protected from unintended impacts of the tax increase. This includes funding for retrofitting and agri-environmental schemes, alongside targeted social welfare and other initiatives to prevent fuel poverty and ensure a just transition. These measures are designed to be progressive.

To give effect to the Programme for Government commitment to protect the vulnerable, a targeted package of social protection interventions has been developed, which is informed by ESRI research that was commissioned to address this issue specifically. As of Budget 2026, the Government has allocated over €4.2 billion in carbon tax revenue for the climate and just transition measures since 2020. ESRI analysis consistently shows the lower income deciles are better off as a result of the social protection measures funded by the increased carbon tax.

One of the social protection measures supported by carbon tax funds in Budget 2026 was the extension of the Fuel Allowance payment to Working Family Payment recipients. The measure means that 50,000 additional households will now receive the Fuel Allowance. As a result of this extension, over 470,000 households are now being supported by the Fuel Allowance.
The full use of carbon tax funds in Budget 2026 is set out in the document linked here: www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/2c8f3efb/The_Use_of_the_Carbon_Tax_Budget_2026.pdf

The carbon tax trajectory is an important part of Ireland’s overall policy package for tackling climate change. Finance Act 2020 is the legislation which underpins the carbon tax trajectory and the Government’s adherence to this legislation provides certainty to industry of Ireland’s commitment to decarbonisation. As such I do not intend to deviate from this policy direction which has been agreed and endorsed by the Programme for Government. The need for society and the economy to decouple from fossil fuel dependence is even more apparent now given the recent price shocks.

With regard to fuel prices and revenue it is important to note that the Mineral Oil Tax is a volumetric charge and therefore remains fixed regardless of price movement. However, VAT increases and decreases proportionally in line with price movement as it is calculated as a percentage of the total retail price.

The VAT rating of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within the categories of goods and services listed in Annex III of the EU VAT Directive, to which Member States are permitted to apply lower VAT rates subject to certain rules.

I am advised by Revenue that traders are not required to identify the VAT yield generated from the supply of specific goods and services on their VAT returns. Therefore, it is not possible to provide the VAT yield on all fuel and energy related products and services using taxpayer information alone.

Regarding the Deputy's reference to €36 million in additional tax revenue, I am advised by Revenue that to provide context, a uniform retail price increase of approximately 6.5 cent per litre across all fuel types would generate approximately €36 million in additional VAT revenue over a full calendar year. For shorter timeframes, significantly larger price increases would be required to generate this amount. For example, over a 30-day period, a uniform price increase of approximately 77 cent per litre across all fuel types would be required, while over 60 days, a uniform increase of 39 cent per litre across all fuel types would be required.

question.p: 444. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has engaged with the Central Bank of Ireland regarding the use by regulated financial service providers of facial image capture, facial recognition, or other facial biometric processing technologies for customer onboarding, authentication, fraud prevention, or identity verification purposes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19592/26]

445. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether the Central Bank of Ireland has issued, or is preparing to issue, supervisory guidance for regulated financial service providers regarding the use of facial biometric processing technologies, including requirements relating to lawful processing bases, consumer transparency, data minimisation, storage limitation, security safeguards, and the availability of non-biometric alternatives for customers; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19593/26]

446. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether regulated financial service providers operating in the State are required, as a matter of supervisory expectation or consumer protection regulation, to provide customers with a reasonable non-biometric alternative where facial image capture or facial biometric verification is used for onboarding, authentication, fraud prevention, or account access purposes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19594/26]

447. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department or the Central Bank of Ireland maintains information on the number of regulated financial service providers using facial image capture or facial biometric processing technologies for identity verification, customer onboarding, authentication, or fraud prevention; if so, the number of such firms and the general purposes for which such technologies are used; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19595/26]

448. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has considered whether the Consumer Protection Code or other financial regulatory frameworks should be updated to provide explicit standards governing the use of facial image capture and facial biometric technologies by regulated financial service providers, including standards concerning transparency to customers, consent mechanisms where applicable, retention periods, and alternative access methods for customers who do not wish to use biometric verification; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19596/26]

449. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department or the Central Bank of Ireland holds data on operational incidents, data protection incidents, or consumer complaints reported by regulated financial service providers relating to the use of facial image capture or facial biometric processing technologies since 1 January 2023; if so, the number of such incidents by year and general category; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19597/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 444 to 449, inclusive, together.

The Data Protection Commission (DPC) is the national independent authority in Ireland responsible for upholding the fundamental right of individuals in the European Union (EU) to have their personal data protected. As such, queries in relation to data protection should primarily be directed to the DPC through the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.

My department does or would not, hold any information in respect of operational incidents related to biometrics or wider data protection complaints. The Data Protection Commission (DPC) would be primarily responsible for complaints regarding data protection issues and in terms of reporting on such incidents.

The Central Bank of Ireland is not responsible for consumer complaints. Under the Central Bank’s Consumer Protection Code, all in-scope financial services firms must have a complaints handling procedure in place. This procedure should be available on the firm’s website. If consumers are not satisfied with the response from a financial services provider, they have the right to refer their complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO). The Central Bank of Ireland advises that it generally does not investigate individual consumer complaints about financial services firms.

The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) (among other provisions) provides a regulatory framework for biometric systems across all sectors of the economy, including financial services. The work to implement the EU AI Act in Ireland is being led by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and as such that Minister would be primary contact for policy questions relating to the EU AI Act. In January 2026, the Government approved a Memorandum brought forward by the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for the priority drafting of the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill, based on the General Scheme prepared by that department. The process of drafting this legislation is underway.

The General Scheme provides for the establishment of a new statutory independent body – AI Office of Ireland - under the remit of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, to act as the Single Point of Contact and central coordinating authority for the implementation and enforcement of the EU AI Act in the State. It also provides for the designation of Competent Authorities and rules on penalties for infringement of the Act.

In terms of the regulatory structure the Government has agreed that Ireland is adopting a distributed model of competent authorities for the AI Act, leveraging established sectoral regulatory authorities, with a designated central authority to provide coordination and several centralised functions. In this context, the Data Protection Commission (DPC) will hold regulatory responsibility for biometric systems.
The Government is firmly committed to the timely implementation of the EU Al Act which is a forward-looking framework that balances innovation with proportionate safeguards.

In summary, the EU AI Act defines biometric data in Article 3(34); Article 5(g) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of biometric systems that deduce or infer sensitive attributes such as race or political opinions. High risk biometric systems, as referenced in Article 6(2) and detailed in Annex III, Point 1 of the Regulation, are subject to stringent regulation rather than outright prohibition. These systems are considered high risk due to the potential for significant harm or influence on decision making outcomes. Remote biometric identification systems are considered high-risk AI systems under Annex III, Point 1 of the AI Act, with the exception of AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification, the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is who they claim to be.
It would be a matter for individual financial institutions if they wish to put in place reasonable alternative systems to the use of biometrics for accessing their financial services.

In terms of its regulatory and supervisory approach to the EU AI Act, the Central Bank is incorporating – and will continue to incorporate this implementation into its existing regulatory and supervisory procedures in respect of regulated financial services including where necessary subject to the processes under the Bank’s Administrative Sanctions Procedures. This is provided for under the published scheme of the Bill developed by the Department of Enterprise Tourism and Employment.

In that context, my department is engaged with this process along with the Central Bank, to the extent that the transposition impacts on the operation of regulated financial services – for which the Central Bank has regulatory responsibility under the EU AI Act and has been designated a Market Surveillance Authority pursuant to Article 74(6) of the EU AI Act.

The Central Bank continues to undertake market monitoring and supervisory risk assessment work relating to the use of AI across the Irish financial sector and internationally, as outlined in its recent publication of the 2026 Regulatory and Supervisory Outlook Report. In February 2026, the Central Bank issued a survey to the Banking and Payments sectors on current and future AI usage in order to gain an understanding of how regulated financial services firms are using AI and to obtain details of GenAI and non-GenAI use cases which will assist in the implementation of the EU AI Act and in development of the Central Bank’s approach to supervision of regulated firms’ use of AI more generally, including development of potential relevant supervisory guidance. The survey is due for completion by 31 March 2026.

The Central Bank has advised that it will be necessary to await the conclusion of the AI Act transposition to determine whether any additional changes are needed to existing guidance or indeed its Consumer Protection Code.

However, it is worth noting that the Consumer Protection Code is technology-neutral, meaning that regulated entities are obliged to meet the requirements of the Code irrespective of the delivery method used, and any underlying technology used in that delivery. Requirements applicable to the retention of records, and the use of digital platforms – including the need for appropriate testing, and to ensure that the technology produces consistent and objective outcomes for consumers, apply irrespective of the technology used. An overarching obligation on firms also requires that they secure their customers’ interests, and this would also apply to the use of technology in the provision of financial products and services.

The Central Bank’s General Guidance on the Consumer Protection Code also reminds firms that the requirements in the Code are without prejudice to their obligations under the General Data Protection Regulations. Certain types of sensitive personal data are subject to additional protection under the GDPR. These are listed under Article 9 of the GDPR as “special categories” of personal data. Genetic data and biometric data processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person is categorised as a special category. The Date Protection Commission[] (DPC) is the primary independent supervisory authority in Ireland, responsible for enforcing the GDPR, investigating breaches, and handling complaints. It oversees compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018 and the ePrivacy Regulations.

summary.i: Questions Nos. 445 to 449, inclusive, answered with Question No. 444.

question.p: 450. Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the reason the motor insurance transparency code is voluntary, despite this not being mentioned in the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025–2029; when the decision was made for the code to be voluntary; the rationale; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19632/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, one of the priority actions within the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025-2029 is enhancing transparency in insurance premiums, with particular reference to motor insurance, through working with the insurance industry to develop a transparency code.

The Motor Insurance Transparency Code was developed by a working group comprising insurers and intermediaries, with the support of the Department of Finance and the Central Bank of Ireland, to ensure strong alignment with regulatory requirements without mandating the disclosure of commercially sensitive information. The Code is designed to enhance trust, clarity, transparency, and understanding in how motor insurance premiums are communicated to consumers.

The Code is open to adoption by all insurers and intermediaries selling private motor insurance in the State, including cross-border entities. It sits under the legislative umbrella of the Central Bank of Ireland’s Consumer Protection Code (CPC), and aligns with relevant disclosure requirements and requirements to inform customers effectively. The revised CPC comes into effect on 24 March this year and will be legally binding on insurance companies and intermediaries. The Central Bank’s Administrative Sanctions Procedure (ASP) will be applicable in respect of non-compliance with the revised CPC.

Implementation of the Code will begin on a phased basis from March 2026, supported by staff training, updated documentation, and strengthened governance. The first review of the Code will take place within 18 months of implementation, and the Central Bank of Ireland will provide a report to the Minister for Finance in relation to its observations of insurers and intermediaries adherence to the Code and its impact.
The Department of Finance and Central Bank of Ireland will continue engagement with industry, via the working group, to monitor the implementation of the Code, in advance of the planned review.

Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to specify the interest rate on the €200,000,000 million loan from the EIB to the SBCI; to provide an exhaustive list of all of the lending partners of the SBCI; and if he will make a statement on the matter. question.p: 453. Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 105 of 4 of March 2026, the interest rate and/or annual return on investment for each commitment, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19635/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) has informed me that further to Parliamentary Question No. 105 of 4 of March 2026, as noted, the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) has committed over €2.5 billion to housing related investments since inception, targeting 25,000+ new homes by 2030.

These investments support Irish homebuilders through the provision of debt and equity financing solutions, typically delivered to the market through ISIF’s partner funds. ISIF evaluates each investment opportunity in accordance with its double bottom line mandate, requiring both a positive economic impact in Ireland, and a commercial return.

The Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) discloses its investments annually in the NTMA Annual Report. As ISIF is a commercial investor it cannot disclose any non-public or commercially sensitive information related to its investments.

question.p: 454. Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance further to Parliamentary Question No. 105 of 4 of March 2026, if each investment allows for forward purchase, or the purchase of new or second hand residential property, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19636/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) has informed me that further to Parliamentary Question No. 105 of 4 of March 2026, as noted, the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) has committed over €2.5 billion to housing related investments since inception, targeting 25,000+ new homes by 2030.

These investments support Irish homebuilders through the provision of debt and equity financing solutions, typically delivered to the market through ISIF’s partner funds. ISIF evaluates each investment opportunity in accordance with its double bottom line mandate, requiring both a positive economic impact in Ireland, and a commercial return.

The underlying investment strategies, including whether a fund is permitted to engage in forward purchase arrangements, or the purchase of new or second-hand residential property, are a matter for the individual ISIF partner funds based on their commercial and investment mandates. As these strategies are commercially sensitive, ISIF is not in a position to disclose investment level detail in relation to the specific structures (e.g., forward purchase, or the purchase of new or second-hand residential property) utilised by each fund.

question.p: 455. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will provide a schedule of the number of detections of domestic vehicles containing agricultural green diesel in each of the years from 2020 to date in 2026; the number of enforcements taken; the number of fines issued and totality of same; and the number of maximum fines issued over that time period. [19672/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: Revenue has responsibility for the collection of mineral oil tax and for tackling illicit trade in mineral oil products. It is an offence, under section 102 (as amended) of the Finance Act 1999, to use marked mineral oil as a propellant for a motor vehicle, or to keep it in the fuel tank of a vehicle. A person guilty of this offence is liable on summary conviction to a fine of €5,000. A trial judge may, in his or her discretion, mitigate this fine, provided that the amount so mitigated is not greater than 50 per cent of the amount of the fine.

I am advised by Revenue that, where marked mineral oil is detected in the fuel tank of a motor vehicle, the action that they take depends on the specific circumstances of the particular case. In the case of a first detection of marked mineral oil in the fuel tank of a private vehicle, or in certain other cases, they may offer the person concerned an opportunity to resolve the matter by way of payment of a compromise sum, in lieu of prosecution. In cases where marked mineral oil is found in the fuel tank of a commercial vehicle, the normal course would be to proceed by way of the institution of a prosecution under section 102 of the Finance Act 1999. In certain cases, the vehicle in which the marked mineral oil is detected is seized by Revenue.

Details of the numbers of detections of marked mineral oil made by Revenue in each of the years from 2020 to 2026 (end of February), are set out in the following table, along with the numbers of compromise sum payments in lieu of prosecution received in each of those time periods and the total amounts paid. The table indicates also the number and value of fines issued by the Courts as a result of a successful prosecution.

question.p: 456. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he is considering delaying the scheduled increase in carbon tax in light of the recent unprecedented increases in oil, diesel and gas prices linked to tensions and conflict in the Middle East; whether his Department has undertaken any assessment of the potential impact of further carbon tax increases on households and businesses during this period of heightened energy costs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19683/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The major disruption to global energy supply as a result of the situation in Iran and the Middle East is reflected in extremely volatile commodity prices over the past two weeks. Officials in my Department are continuing to closely monitor these developments to assess their impact on the Irish economy and society.

As the Deputy will be aware the Programme for Government committed to continue with the planned Carbon Tax increases, aligning with recommendations from the Climate Change Advisory Council and scientific experts, and to using the resulting revenues raised to support climate action measures and to ensure the most vulnerable are protected from unintended impacts of the tax increase. This includes funding for retrofitting and agri-environmental schemes, alongside targeted social welfare and other initiatives to prevent fuel poverty and ensure a just transition.

To ensure that the carbon tax policy is progressive, a targeted package of social protection interventions has been developed, which is informed by ESRI research that was commissioned to address this issue specifically. As at Budget 2026, the Government has allocated over €4.2 billion in carbon tax revenue for the climate and just transition measures since 2020. ESRI analysis shows the lower income deciles are better off as a result of the social protection measures funded by the increased carbon tax.

One of the social protection measures supported by carbon tax funds in Budget 2026 was the extension of the Fuel Allowance payment to Working Family Payment recipients. The measure means that 50,000 additional households will now receive the Fuel Allowance. As a result of this extension, over 470,000 households are now being supported by the Fuel Allowance.
The full use of carbon tax funds in Budget 2026 is set out in the document linked here: https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/2c8f3efb/The_Use_of_the_Carbon_Tax_Budget_2026.pdf

The carbon tax trajectory is an important part of Ireland’s overall policy package for tackling climate change. Finance Act 2020 is the legislation which underpins the carbon tax trajectory and the Government’s adherence to this legislation provides certainty to industry of Ireland’s commitment to decarbonisation. As such I do not intend to deviate from this policy direction which has been agreed and endorsed by the Programme for Government. The need for society and the economy to decouple from fossil fuel dependence is even more apparent now given the recent price shocks.

As regards the specific impact of carbon tax increases, the carbon tax increased from €63.50 euro per tonne of CO2 emitted to €71 per tonne of CO2 emitted on 8 October 2025 for all propellant fuels. The increase will apply to all other fuels from 1 May 2026.

summary.i: Question No. 457 answered with Question No. 459.
Question No. 458 answered with Question No. 459.

question.p: 459. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will address the anomaly whereby self employed workers are excluded from availing of tax free commuter supports under TaxSaver, despite representing a significant segment of the workforce. [19935/26]

457. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the annual number of beneficiaries of the TaxSaver scheme and the associated Exchequer cost for each of the years 2019 to 2025, in tabular form; the reasons for the decline in participation over that period; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19933/26]

458. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the annual number of TaxSaver scheme beneficiaries, by county, for each of the years 2019 to 2025; the analysis undertaken by his Department on regional disparities in uptake of the scheme, in tabular form. [19934/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 459, 457 and 458 together.
I thank the Deputy for her questions on the TaxSaver scheme.

As the Deputy may be aware, section 118(5A) of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (TCA) provides for an exemption from benefit-in-kind where an employer purchases a travel pass for one of their employees or directors.

Under section 118B TCA, an employer and employee may also enter into a salary sacrifice arrangement under which the employee agrees to sacrifice part of his or her salary, in exchange for a travel pass.
This is commonly known as the TaxSaver scheme.
Where a travel pass is purchased under the TaxSaver scheme or through a salary sacrifice arrangement certain conditions must be met, for example:
• the cost incurred must relate to a monthly or annual bus, railway or ferry travel pass;
• the travel pass must be issued by or on behalf of one or more approved transport providers; and
• the approved transport provider must be contracted or licensed to provide the transport services covered by the travel pass.

The TaxSaver scheme is an exemption from benefit-in-kind. Therefore, to avail of tax relief under the scheme, an employer must purchase a travel pass for an employee or director, or enter a salary sacrifice arrangement in exchange for a salary pass.
The scheme was implemented as tax-exempt benefit-in-kind in order to keep the implementation as simple as possible and reduce administrative burden for employers and employees.

With regard to the costs and beneficiaries of the scheme, the Deputy should note that there is no Revenue notification procedure for the employers, directors, employees, nor for the transport providers involved with the scheme.

Consequently, any estimate of the take-up and cost of the scheme is based on records provided by the National Transport Authority only on the number and value of TaxSaver tickets sold. Further, I am informed that a breakdown of beneficiaries by county is not currently provided to my Department.
The latest published estimates of the costs to the Exchequer and number of beneficiaries, as per the Department’s reporting on tax expenditures, are summarised in the table below.

I would ask the Deputy to note that estimates for the cost and beneficiaries of the scheme for 2025 will be published in coming months by my Department as part of the annual Tax Expenditures Report. I anticipate that this will be published in advance of Budget 2027.

While my Department has not analysed the decline in participation of the scheme in detail over recent years, it is likely due to changes in working and commuting patterns following the Covid-19 pandemic and the emergence of remote or blended working arrangements.
As with all tax expenditures, the TaxSaver scheme is kept under review by my Department officials.

question.p: 460. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding a pension tax relief matter (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19948/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: The Deputy will be aware that tax relief for individuals is granted at the marginal rate of income tax. The amount of pension contributions on which relief can be granted in a tax year is limited to an age-related percentage of the individual’s earnings, ranging from 15% for individuals aged under 30 years to 40% for individuals aged 60 years and over, and subject to an overall annual earnings’ cap of €115,000.

The annual earnings cap of €115,000 operates to limit the level of tax-relieved pension contributions made by an individual or on behalf of an employee in any one year. The annual earnings cap acts, in conjunction with age-related percentage limits of annual earnings, to put a ceiling on the annual amount of tax relief an individual taxpayer can obtain on pension contributions. Its primary purpose is to protect the Exchequer from large variations in contribution profiles over time, while also placing limits on the overall level of Exchequer support provided for supplementary pensions. The Deputy will appreciate that there could be significant cost in making any changes to the earnings cap and this must be balanced against other competing demands and considered as part of the annual Budget and Finance Bill process.

In relation to the Standard Fund Threshold (SFT), the Deputy will be aware that in 2023, the then Minister for Finance announced an independent examination of the SFT. Following consideration of this examination, the Government agreed to implement changes to the SFT in a phased manner. Finance Act 2024 provided for phased increases to the SFT beginning in 2026 with the SFT reaching €2.8 million by 2029. From 2030 future increases will take account of increases in average earnings.

It is important to emphasise that the SFT and the pensions earnings limit serve different policy purposes within the pension tax system. The SFT is the maximum allowable pension fund on retirement for tax purposes which was introduced in Budget and Finance Act 2006 to prevent over-funding of pensions through tax-relieved arrangements, whilst the earnings cap limits the amount of tax-relieved contributions that an individual or an employee can make towards pension savings in any one year.
As with all taxes, pensions taxation is kept under regular review by my Department.

question.p: 461. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the steps his Department is taking to tackle the financial burden facing households and homeowners seeking home insurance. [20015/26]

462. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department is aware of any reports which suggest that home insurance companies may be overpricing the future cost of a re-build so as to increase the cost of premiums; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20016/26]

463. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has any plans to introduce regulations around home insurance to ensure that in the event of a home being destroyed the whole amount for which the home is ensured will be paid out, even if it is below the market value or the full cost of rebuilding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20017/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 461, 462 and 463 together.

While neither I as Tánaiste and Minister for Finance, nor the Central Bank, can intervene directly in pricing under EU Solvency II rules, ensuring that consumers have access to affordable insurance cover remains a priority. The Government is firmly committed to addressing the cost and availability of insurance through implementing the reforms set out in the Programme for Government and the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025-2029, to deliver tangible improvements in cost, choice, and access for all consumers.

However, many factors influence the cost of home insurance, including rebuild costs, which in turn are impacted by costs such as building materials, energy, and labour. These costs have been subject to significant inflationary pressure since 2020. As construction and repair costs have generally increased, this can place upward pressure on home insurance premiums.

In 2022, the Central Bank of Ireland issued a Dear CEO letter highlighting growing concerns about the rising risk of under-insurance in the home insurance market. A review by the Central Bank has shown an increase in the number of home insurance claims where customers did not have sufficient cover.

This underscores the importance of regular engagement by consumers with their home insurance providers, to ensure they are sufficiently covered, especially given current inflationary pressures. Insurers also have a responsibility to ensure that they properly communicate the risks of under-insurance to their customers.

In addition, according to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), many insurance companies automatically increase the amount of buildings and contents cover when a policyholder renews their policy each year. This indexation helps protect the policyholder against under-insurance as it increases the value of their cover in line with inflation.

My officials engage regularly with Insurance Ireland, the representative body for the insurance industry, which has advised that consumers should review the rebuild cost of their property using the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland (SCSI) House Rebuild Calculator when taking out a new policy or renewing an existing policy. This calculator helps consumers determine an accurate estimate of what it would cost to rebuild their home, ensuring the sum insured on their policy is correctly aligned with the true rebuild cost and preventing both over-insurance and under-insurance.

To support consumer awareness, Insurance Ireland has published guidance to help educate consumers on over-insurance, under-insurance, and the average clause. This information is available on the Understanding Insurance website at: www.understandinginsurance.ie/our-blog/over-and-underinsurance.

Minister of State with special responsibility for Financial Services, Credit Unions and Insurance, Robert Troy, T.D. has met with Insurance Ireland and senior industry representatives regarding the progression of insurance-sector reforms. In these engagements, he has reiterated the Government’s expectation that the benefits arising from reforms, particularly those improving transparency and reducing claims costs must result in more affordable and accessible insurance products for consumers.

In addition, the Government is adopting a comprehensive and proactive approach to enhance competition in the Irish insurance sector, through the work of the Office for the Promotion of Competition in the Insurance Market (OPCIM). The OPCIM continues to play an important role in engaging with key stakeholders, including insurers, brokers, and representative bodies, and in facilitating discussions on issues related to the availability and affordability of insurance across the market.

The Government remains committed to addressing the cost and availability of insurance through implementing the reforms set out in the Programme for Government and the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025-2029. These reforms are designed to deliver a fairer, more sustainable and competitive insurance market which delivers tangible improvements in cost, choice, and access for all consumers.

summary.i: Question No. 462 answered with Question No. 461.
Question No. 463 answered with Question No. 461.

question.p: 464. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding any review ongoing of the pension tax relief earnings cap of €115,000; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20095/26]

465. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance his views on the merits of increasing the pension tax relief earnings cap of €115,000, which was set in 2011; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20096/26]

466. Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he has any plans to raise the pension tax relief earnings cap, which has remained fixed at €115,000 since 2011; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20165/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 464, 465 and 466 together.

As the Deputies will be aware, tax relief for individuals is granted at the marginal rate of income tax. The amount of pension contributions on which relief can be granted in a tax year is limited to an age-related percentage of the individual’s earnings, ranging from 15% for individuals aged under 30 years to 40% for individuals aged 60 years and over, and subject to an overall annual earnings’ cap of €115,000.

The annual earnings cap of €115,000 operates to limit the level of tax-relieved pension contributions made by an individual or on behalf of an employee in any one year. The annual earnings cap acts, in conjunction with age-related percentage limits of annual earnings, to put a ceiling on the annual amount of tax relief an individual taxpayer can obtain on pension contributions. Its primary purpose is to protect the Exchequer from large variations in contribution profiles over time, while also placing limits on the overall level of Exchequer support provided for supplementary pensions.

The Deputies will appreciate that there could be significant cost in making any changes to the earnings cap and this must be balanced against other competing demands and considered as part of the annual Budget and Finance Bill process.
As with all taxes, pensions taxation is kept under regular review by my Department.

summary.i: Question No. 465 answered with Question No. 464.
Question No. 466 answered with Question No. 464.

question.p: 467. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to respond to correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20234/26]

speech.from: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance
speech.p: As Minister for Finance, it would not be appropriate for me to comment on, or intervene in, individual cases.
In relation to the general points raised, it should be noted that creditors generally have the right to assign, or sell the benefits and rights, under a credit agreement to another creditor.

When a creditor's benefits under a credit agreement are sold to another entity, the debtor's obligations and rights do not change. The terms of the agreement at the time of the assignment remain in place.

The entity which acquires the legal rights of a creditor under a credit contract with a consumer, or which services such an agreement, is within the regulatory remit of the Central Bank of Ireland. Accordingly, the Central Bank's consumer protection codes, including the Code of Conduct on Mortgage Arrears, continue to apply in the same way.

If a consumer is not satisfied with the way a regulated firm is dealing with them, or if the firm is not complying with regulatory requirements, the consumer should make a formal complaint directly to the regulated firm.
If the consumer remains unsatisfied, they can then refer the complaint to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman.
