question.p: 533. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the expected completion date of the works on the Round Tower in Kells, County Meath; when the protective wrap will be removed (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20067/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation
speech.p: Kells Round Tower, Co. Meath is a National Monument, Number 158 in State care.

The Tower has experienced significant mortar loss and stone erosion over the centuries. Ministerial Consent for the conservation repairs was granted in September 2023 with works commencing following completion of the scaffolding erection in February 2024.

The conservation works, estimated at the time to be approximately two years in duration, are being undertaken by the skilled craft workers in the Trim National Monuments District and the OPW is keeping to this schedule in as far as possible.

It was necessary to pause works on site as a result of storm damage to the scaffolding which occurred during Storm Éowyn. While it was necessary to pause conservation works on site, the project continued with OPW stone masons working offsite, cutting and dressing the required stone for the tower.
At this point in time, all external works are complete with internal works still taking place. The target date for completion of the project is mid-quarter three, 2026.

question.p: 534. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if any consideration has been given by him for the publicly funded Institute of public administration plans to acquire new multi million euro offices to be paused in light of the continued housing crises or decentralised in light of the Dublin congestion crises; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20068/26]

speech.from: Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation (Deputy Jack Chambers)
speech.p: Within the current Programme for Government (PfG), prioritisation is focused on accelerating housing supply and investment in transport infrastructure (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/programme-for-government-securing-irelands-future.pdf).

This has been embodied in the updated National Development Plan (NDP) published July 2025 (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/press-releases/government-publishes-updated-national-development-plan/). The core ambition of the NDP Review is to deliver 300,000 additional homes by 2030 and to boost Ireland’s competitiveness. The updated review has set out Governmental capital commitment and investment of €275.4 billion over the period 2026 to 2035, including €10 billion to fund large strategic projects in transport, water and energy. The review sets out departmental ceilings to 2030 and overall expenditure ceilings to 2035 to provide the necessary long-term investment to:
• deliver transformative, critical and growth-enhancing infrastructure;
• scale up and strengthen our water, energy and transport systems;
• unlock housing supply;
• improve the living standards of the people of Ireland; and
• boost our international competitiveness

The Institute of Public Administration (IPA), a body under the aegis of this Department, has been tasked with an enhanced role in training and development for the Civil and Public Service. The expansion of the IPA’s remit, the vision of the IPA becoming a centre-of-excellence for public sector training and education, will see a substantial increase in the number of Civil and Public Servants supported by the Institute.
In this context, any proposals from the IPA to my Department to facilitate and support its expanded role in the Civil and Public Service will be considered in the appropriate manner by my Department.

question.p: 539. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the source of funding used by the State to discharge financial penalties imposed on Ireland by the European Union arising from infringement proceedings, including failure to transpose directives within the required timeframe; whether such penalties are paid directly from the Exchequer or another central fund; whether the costs are subsequently recouped from the Vote of the Department responsible for the failure to transpose or otherwise comply with EU law; the total amount paid by the State in such penalties in each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20485/26]

540. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether a formal mechanism exists within Government to hold Departments financially accountable where financial penalties are imposed on the State by the European Union arising from failure to transpose directives or otherwise comply with European Union law within the required timeframe; if such a mechanism exists, the details of the arrangements in place, including any requirement for costs to be recouped from the relevant Department's Vote; if no such mechanism exists, whether consideration is being given to introducing such arrangements; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20486/26]

speech.from: Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 539 and 540 together.

Over Ireland’s 50 years of EU membership, approximately 4,000 Directives have been transposed into Irish law. The vast majority are transposed on time, usually two years following publication. However, where this does not happen, the European Commission can open infringement proceedings against Ireland. Most infringements are resolved (once transposition is completed) at the initial stages of the infringement proceedings (Letter of Formal Notice or Reasoned Opinion). Where this does not occur, the European Commission can refer Ireland to the Court of Justice of the European Union for non/incomplete transposition. From 2020 to 2024, respectively, the Court of Justice of the European Union has found against Ireland in four infringement cases where financial penalties have been levied, reflected in the following table:

td.p: Department of Tourism, Culture Arts Gaeltacht Sport & Media
Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment

speech.p: Any penalties arising are paid from voted allocation of the Department. The Departmental Appropriation Accounts provide for the reporting of compensation and legal costs, and while there is no specific requirement to disclose EU Settlements or Fines separately to other such costs, Departments can report such settlements or fines there.

Currently, there is no additional mechanism which would impose further financial consequences on Departments where financial penalties are imposed on the State by the European Union arising from failure to transpose directives or otherwise comply with European Union law.

The Minister of State for European Affairs chairs the Interdepartmental Committee on EU Engagement, which monitors progress in the transposition of directives and oversees Ireland’s response to infringement proceedings. This co-ordination extends to engagement with the Office of the Attorney General, the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel and, where appropriate, national regulatory authorities and agencies. Taking this into account, my officials regularly engage with the Department of Foreign Affairs on EU matters and will seek information on effectiveness of the current oversight mechanism.
There are currently 46 infringement procedures initiated against Ireland. Details of current cases are available from the Department of Foreign Affairs at the following website:

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation
speech.p: The proposed development of a new Visitor Experience Centre at Trim Castle forms part of the Office of Public Works’ ongoing programme to enhance visitor facilities and interpretation at key heritage sites.

Planning approval for the project was granted by Meath County Council under the Part 8 planning process in February 2024 for the redevelopment of the historic Market House building located at the Trim Castle complex. Following this approval, a multidisciplinary design team was appointed to progress the detailed design, conservation strategy and tender documentation for the project.

The design team is currently advancing the detailed design phase, which includes a range of technical and conservation-related investigations associated with the adaptation of the historic structure, together with the preparation of statutory compliance documentation and specialist design inputs.
It is envisaged that tenders for the works will issue in Quarter 3 2026, with the contractor expected to start on site in Quarter 1 2027 for an estimated two-year construction period.

The new visitor centre at Trim Castle will provide state-of-the-art facilities including interactive exhibits, interpretation, educational resources and enhanced accessibility features to ensure that Trim Castle will be a major focal point for heritage and tourism in the region.

question.p: 555. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding significant increases in oil prices being charged, with an almost 50% increase since last order in some cases; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18561/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: I appreciate that this is an uncertain time for consumers. I recently advised members of the public to contact the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in relation to concerns related to home heating oil and fuel. The CCPC has assured me that all such complaints are being carefully and urgently assessed. The CCPC as an independent statutory body can avail of a range of powers to investigate, enforce and prosecute where clear breaches of the law are evident. I have also met with representatives of the fuel industry to discuss the energy market and pricing structures, along with the factors impacting costs in the current uncertain geopolitical environment.
Consumer protection law requires traders to provide key information in advance of a transaction, including the total price, taxes and charges included, so that consumers can make informed decisions.

The law recognises that there are situations where a trader may be unable to specify the final price in advance. When this happens, they must instead tell the consumer how the price will be calculated. In all cases, either the price itself, or the method used to calculate it, must be clearly communicated before any sale.

When prices rise suddenly, it can understandably cause frustration. Ireland operates an open market economy, which means businesses are permitted to set and change their own prices. If businesses are working in a way that could unfairly limit competition or push up prices, for example by agreeing prices with one another, the CCPC has strong powers to address this. Where it is suspected that competition or consumer law may have been breached, the CCPC will take the steps necessary to enforce the law. The powers available to the CCPC means breaches of competition law can result in severe penalties including criminal prosecution and administrative fines of up to 10% of turnover or €10 million, whichever is greater.

As part of the Programme for Government commitments, I have already initiated the process of further strengthening the powers of the CCPC in both its Consumer Protection and Competition functions. A public consultation opened on this intended legislative change before Christmas and closed on 27 February. I intend to seek Government approval to draft Heads of Bill in the coming months once the submissions to the consultation have been assessed.

question.p: 559. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment when he expects to publish the outcome of the public consultation on the proposal to extend the late working hours exemption for young persons to unlicensed premises under the Protection of Young Persons Act 1996; and whether he intends to introduce new regulations or revise the existing code of practice arising from this consultation. [18642/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: The Protection of Young Persons (Employment) Act 1996 safeguards the health of young workers and ensures that employment does not interfere with their education. It sets minimum age limits, maximum working hours, rest requirements, and prohibits late-night work for those under 18, while also requiring employers to keep specified records for young workers.

Under section 6 of the Act, 16- and 17-year-olds may work up to 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week, only between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m., except where regulations provide otherwise. The 2001 Regulations (S.I. No. 350 of 2001) allow those working on general duties in licensed premises to work until 11 p.m. during school holidays and on weekends with no school the next day.
My Department held a public consultation from the 10th of April to the 8th of May 2025 on
(i) whether a new regulation should allow work until 11 p.m. in certain unlicensed premises and
(ii) whether the Code of Practice for licensed premises should be amended.
The submissions received will be published on the Department’s website in due course.

Officials in my Department are currently examining and progressing work on whether a new regulation should permit young people to work until 11 p.m. in certain unlicensed premises, as well as whether the Code of Practice for licensed premises should be amended.

question.p: 562. Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the additional steps that Tourism Ireland will take to increase the number of US and UK tourists coming to Ireland during 2026. [18690/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: Tourism Ireland, the organisation responsible for marketing the island of Ireland overseas, continues to position Ireland as a leading global tourism destination. With an ambitious strategy for 2026 and beyond, Tourism Ireland aims to attract greater numbers of international visitors by strengthening Tourism Brand Ireland and showcasing the island’s iconic landscapes, vibrant culture, and rich heritage.

Aligned with the new Action Plan on Market Diversification, the funding allocated to Tourism Ireland in Budget 2026 will enable the organisation to pursue fresh growth opportunities. This includes expanding strategic source markets and focusing on attracting “value-adding visitors” whose spending supports the businesses and communities that rely on overseas tourism.

Diversification will remain a core theme, with efforts directed at driving demand through new and existing gateways in North America, strengthening the organisation’s presence in the United States and maintaining a strong performance in Great Britain.

Great Britain remains Ireland’s largest tourism market by volume, contributing €1.24 billion annually, or 21% of visitor spend. The British market also plays a vital role in supporting regional and seasonal tourism, with around 44% of British visitors travelling between October and March. Building on this strong foundation, Tourism Ireland continues to invest significantly in Great Britain, capitalising on opportunities to drive sustainable, year-round growth and encourage visitors to explore more regions across the island.

Tourism from the United States continues to be a major success story for the island of Ireland. As the largest market for overseas tourism revenue and the second-largest source of visitors and nights, the US has been a central focus of Tourism Ireland’s activity. In 2025, Ireland welcomed over 1.3 million US tourists, representing a +7% increase on 2024, reflecting the impact of sustained marketing, partnerships and long-term investment in the market.

Tourism Ireland has strengthened its presence across the US, including an expanded footprint on the West Coast, helping to deepen relationships with airlines, tour operators and media partners. These efforts, supported by extensive advertising, publicity, social and digital campaigns, have continued to drive demand and raise awareness for travel to Ireland.

Improved air access further underlines this positive momentum. For Winter 2025 through March 2026, there are 12% more airline seats available to the island of Ireland compared with the same period last year, including significant growth from key tourism markets such as the US (+17%) and Great Britain (+7%). This expanded connectivity reflects strong collaboration with airline partners and provides a solid platform for continued growth.

Tourism Ireland’s “Kickstart” campaign has also expanded to 19 US states, complemented by broader St Patrick’s Day promotions across additional gateway cities, further strengthening Ireland’s visibility and positioning the island strongly for the year ahead.

question.p: 563. Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether employment permit applicants in the manufacturing sector are covered by a sectoral employment order; whether applicants in the manufacturing sector are subjected to the same rates of pay and obligations as applicants in the construction sector; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18740/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: A Sectoral Employment Order (SEO) is a statutory wage-setting mechanism and may specify minimum rates of pay, as well as pension and sick pay entitlements for a defined economic sector, and they also include a dispute-resolution procedure.

Under this framework, the Labour Court undertakes an independent assessment of appropriate pay rates, taking into account the views of all interested parties, with the objective of supporting industrial harmony and sectoral competitiveness.
There is currently one SEO in effect, the Sectoral Employment Order (Construction Sector) 2024 (S.I. No. 620 of 2024). This Order amends the previous construction SEO made in 2023.
There is no SEO currently in place for the Manufacturing Sector.

Under Chapter 3 of the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act 2015, the Labour Court may initiate an examination of the terms and conditions relating to remuneration, and any associated sick pay or pension schemes, for a particular class or group of workers, following a request from a trade union and/or employers’ organisation.

From an employment permit system perspective, applicants in the manufacturing sector are processed under the same statutory framework that applies across all sectors. This framework provides for assessment of roles in line with the skills and labour market criteria set out in the Employment Permits Regulations.

Occupations may qualify for a Critical Skills Employment Permit where they are included on the Critical Skills Occupations List or alternatively may be eligible for a General Employment Permit where the role satisfies the relevant policy and regulatory requirements and is not listed on the Ineligible Occupations List.

Employers engaging permit holders are required to comply with all obligations attached to the specific permit type issued, including adherence to the regulatory conditions governing pay, working conditions, and the employment relationship.

question.p: 564. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding the most recent research that was carried out into best practice and workplace governance regarding driving for work; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18780/26]

565. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding any engagement he has had with the RSA to ensure that their handbook in relation to safe driving for work practices (details supplied) is consistently updated; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18781/26]

566. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the position regarding any additional work being done in his Department that seeks to improve safety measures in relation to driving for work practices; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18782/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 564, 565 and 566 together.

The ‘Driving for Work: Risk Management Guidance For Employers’ published in July 2025, has been jointly developed by the Road Safety Authority (RSA), the Health and Safety Authority (HSA) and An Garda Síochána(AGS), to help employers understand and manage the main risks that working drivers face and create when driving for work.
As with all other guidance documents, content will be updated to keep pace with any regulatory or work practice changes.

The HSA has had a lead role in delivering several actions in the current Government Road Safety Strategy Phase 2 Action Plan 2025 – 2027. The HSA’s main focus is around Safe Work-Related Road Use and Action 11 ‘Implement a multi-agency intervention programme on safe work-related road use, including education, evidence, engagement, and enforcement activities’. The HSA is implementing this in conjunction with An Garda Síochána and the RSA.
The key actions in enforcement and prevention activities in 2025 included:

• Driving for work Risk Management – Truck Fleet Conference held in November that involved international and national expert speakers. This was a cross-agency initiative attended by 314 people. The conference was streamed live and recorded for future use.
• The updated HSA BeSMART Driving for Work online risk assessment tool was launched in November 2025 in line with new Driving for work guidance.

• 218 inspections were carried out in 2025 by HSA with a specific focus on Driving for Work risk management compliance in Construction, Transport, Retail, Manufacturing, Quarrying and the public sector.
• Meetings with relevant stakeholders were held with the aim of determining what work-related collision data is available.

• HSA worked with RSA and European Transport Safety Council to establish an EU wide profile of work-related road collisions and data collection requirements from 2022-2024. The European Transport Safety Council’s ‘Tapping the potential for reducing work-related road deaths and injuries was published in December 2025 providing a profile of worker involvement in fatal road collisions in EU member states including Ireland from 2022-2024.
• In Quarter 1 of 2026, work is ongoing with RSA and AGS to determine the profile of worker involvement in road collisions nationally.
An Action plan for 2026 is in development including the following provisional list of initiatives.

• Carry out targeted enforcement, education, awareness raising and promotion activities to inform key employers and stakeholders on safe work-related road use hazard topics and enable improved compliance with relevant Occupational Safety and Health (OSH), Road Traffic and Road Safety regulatory requirements.
• Influence a sustained reduction in the number of road collision injuries and deaths in the course of work, including:
• Promotion of Driving for work Risk Management Guidance for Employers (A cross agency Initiative – HSA, RSA and AGS)
• Driving for work risk management seminar focusing on Van Fleet in May 2026
• Driving for work risk management seminar focusing on Grey Fleet in November 2026
• Carry out targeted workplace inspection program to assess compliance with regulatory requirements and report on compliance profile.

• In addition, the HSA is supporting other lead agencies in the advancement of other actions in the Road Safety Strategy including load securing legislation, HGV driver training, collision data analysis and reporting, Connected and Autonomous Vehicle Guidance and vehicle technical requirements. All these activities will influence the core Driving for Work program and improve driving for work practices for all working drivers over time.

The 2025 guidance provides the clearest current best-practice framework for employers, focusing on risk assessment, policies, driver competence, journey planning, and organisational accountability. This guidance was developed in line with international best practice and taking account of national and EU data on work related road collisions. The most recent data analysis was to establish an EU wide profile of work-related road collisions and data collection requirements from 2022-2024 ‘Tapping the potential for reducing work-related road deaths and injuries, published in December 2025. The European Transport Safety Council (ETSC) report relates to how accidents are defined and reported by the different bodies involved. The data in the ETSC report is collated and reported by the RSA for Ireland and includes data on all road deaths across 32 European countries.
The purpose of this data is for statistical analysis, to observe trends over time to inform road safety policy and awareness.

In Ireland, all fatal road collisions are investigated by the relevant authorities and primarily it is the role of the Gardaí. The RSA and the HSA also have statutory functions. The HSA has a role where the contributory factors for road collisions relate to the workplace, work requirements, or work-related actions/inactions. Not all road collisions involving a person in the course of work are reported to the HSA and this is something the HSA keeps under review. Under Occupational Safety and Health legislation, employers must report any accident to the HSA, that results in an employee missing more than three consecutive days at work, not including the day of the accident.

Where there is a serious road collision involving a person driving for work or working on or near the road they are generally reported to the HSA by the Gardaí. When this happens, the collision is triaged by the HSA to determine if it is work related i.e. related to an action or inaction of an employer, training, responsibilities or any other such work-related issue. If it is a serious incident involving occupational safety and health matters the HSA may investigate this further if appropriate.

question.p: 569. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if an update can be provided for a matter (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18814/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: A decision to grant the General Employment Permit (GEP) renewal application referenced by the Deputy was made on 12 March 2026, and the permit has since issued. The applicant has been formally notified of the outcome.

The delay in processing occurred because the Department required additional information from the employer, which had to be assessed before a final decision could be made. This matter was concluded on 10 March 2026, allowing the Employment Permits Section to proceed with approval.

To support applicants and employers, the Department has introduced a Self-Service Portal that provides real-time updates on application status. A dedicated mailbox for Oireachtas members is also available at tdepqueries@enterprise.gov.ie.[]

question.p: 570. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the total anticipated costs associated with his foreign travel for St Patrick's Day; the delegation size; and if a breakdown can be provided on these costs including on accommodation and flights. [18890/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: The Government’s St. Patrick’s Day programme for 2026 will highlight Ireland’s place in the world as a small, open trading economy. It will reflect our economic success, built on openness and strong partnerships, and Ireland’s long-standing commitment to multilateralism. A final breakdown of costs for my programme of engagement is not yet available, as costs have not yet been incurred. This information will be available in the coming weeks.

question.p: 571. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if in view of recent increases in oil prices (details supplied), he has had any engagement with the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission to request that they investigate price-gouging among suppliers; if not, whether he intends to; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18974/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: I appreciate that this is an uncertain time for consumers. I recently advised members of the public to contact the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in relation to concerns related to home heating oil and fuel. The CCPC has assured me that all such complaints are being carefully and urgently assessed. The CCPC as an independent statutory body can avail of a range of powers to investigate, enforce and prosecute where clear breaches of the law are evident. I have also met with representatives of the fuel industry to discuss the energy market and pricing structures, along with the factors impacting costs in the current uncertain geopolitical environment.
Consumer protection law requires traders to provide key information in advance of a transaction, including the total price, taxes and charges included, so that consumers can make informed decisions.

The law recognises that there are situations where a trader may be unable to specify the final price in advance. When this happens, they must instead tell the consumer how the price will be calculated. In all cases, either the price itself, or the method used to calculate it, must be clearly communicated before any sale.

When prices rise suddenly, it can understandably cause frustration. Ireland operates an open market economy, which means businesses are permitted to set and change their own prices. There is no legal definition of “price gouging” in Irish law. Any behaviour that breaches consumer protection or competition law falls that within the remit of the CCPC will be investigated and enforced accordingly. If businesses are working in a way that could unfairly limit competition or push up prices, for example by agreeing prices with one another, the CCPC has strong powers to address this. Where it is suspected that competition or consumer law may have been breached, the CCPC will take the steps necessary to enforce the law. The powers available to the CCPC means breaches of competition law can result in severe penalties including criminal prosecution and administrative fines of up to 10% of turnover or €10 million, whichever is greater.

As part of the Programme for Government commitments, I have already initiated the process of further strengthening the powers of the CCPC in both its Consumer Protection and Competition functions. A public consultation opened on this intended legislative change before Christmas and closed on 27 February. I intend to seek Government approval to draft Heads of Bill in the coming months once the submissions to the consultation have been assessed.

question.p: 572. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department has conducted any assessment on the viability of introducing a universal basic income model including the financial costs of same; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19030/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: In 2022 the Low Pay Commission published their report on piloting Universal Basic Income (UBI). The report was accompanied by a report, authored by ESRI under the terms of the Low Pay Commission / ESRI Research Partnership Agreement, titled ‘A universal basic income for Ireland: Lessons from the international literature’.

The ESRI report examined the universal basic income pilots that have taken place in other jurisdictions, what policy objectives a universal basic income pilot could address and its associated risks and financial implications.

In their report the Low Pay Commission noted that “the recommendations and guidelines in this report regarding how UBI might be piloted in Ireland should not be seen as an implicit endorsement of the concept of a UBI by the Low Pay Commission. The Low Pay Commission was not asked to evaluate the concept of a UBI. Nor was it asked to evaluate whether or not UBI should be piloted”.
The Commission’s report described five general principles that the Low Pay Commission recommended for the design of any UBI pilot for Ireland.
Both the Low Pay Commission and the ESRI reports provided an overview of gross costs of possible Universal Basic Income approaches.

I note that in 2022 the Commission on Taxation and Welfare reported that “The Commission does not support the development of a Universal Basic Income in Ireland” and that “Further, it is noted that resourcing such a pilot project may detract from the State’s ability to fund means-tested welfare schemes, or other targeted measures to address poverty.”

I also note that a three-year Basic Income for the Arts Pilot was conducted from September 2022 to August 2025. The evaluation of the pilot and the design of the successor scheme to the Basic Income for the Arts Pilot is a matter for the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport.

question.p: 573. Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his response to concerns (details supplied) in relation to short-term lets. [19089/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: As set out in the Government's new Policy Statement A New Era for Irish Tourism, which I published in December, the introduction of regulatory controls for the Short Term Letting (STL) Sector is to ensure that the tourism sector develops in a way that recognises and is complementary to the wider needs of local communities, both economically and socially.

In April of last year, I obtained Government approval for the General Scheme of the Short Term Letting and Tourism (STLT) Bill. Once enacted, the Bill will establish the statutory framework for the introduction of regulatory controls for the STL sector, including the creation of a national register.

Fáilte Ireland will be responsible for implementing and managing this register, ensuring compliance with the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation, which comes into effect on 20 May this year. The introduction of the new STL register has been welcomed by the tourism sector and will commence following the passage of the necessary legislation.

Under the new system, all STL accommodation providers will be required to register with Fáilte Ireland and display their registration number on any listing or advertisement for their property. As part of the registration process, providers must confirm that their property complies with planning requirements, meaning they either have the appropriate planning permission or are exempt from the requirement to obtain such permission.

The new Housing policy, proposed by the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage, James Browne T.D., and approved by Government on 15 April proposes to generally preclude new planning permissions for STL in cities and larger towns. Further to this, on 9 February last, the Cabinet Committee on Housing proposed to apply this to towns and cities with populations over 20,000 persons at the latest census. These policies are part of a broader Government strategy to tackle the housing shortage by ensuring that as many suitable properties as possible are available for long-term rental.

Following the introduction of the STL register, accommodation providers based in towns with a population of 20,000 or less at the last census, based on the census town boundaries (defined by CSO), will have two years to meet planning compliance requirements.

Accommodation providers based in towns with a population of more than 20,000 at the last census will need to confirm planning compliance on registration, with no further lead-in period, if they wish to register their STL property with Fáilte Ireland.

In line with existing established rights, where it can be proven that a residential property has been operated by an STL provider for at least 7 years and no enforcement action has been taken by the planning authority, planning permission for retention may be sought.

It will still be possible to offer a room based in your principal private residence (PPR) for STL on an ongoing basis or to sub-let an entire PPR on a short-term basis for a cumulative period of 90 days. Where the 90-day threshold is exceeded, planning permission for a change of use is required.

I understand that the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage is currently finalising a National Planning Statement (NPS) under section 25 of the Planning & Development Act 2024, for short-term letting activity, which will be subject to Government approval and will give effect to this decision. It will continue to be the case that change of use planning permission is necessary for STL, where not subject to exemptions first set out in 2019.

The NPS for short-term letting will ensure that there is a clear overall policy approach, both at national level and local authority level, to enable planning authorities to determine planning applications for short-term lets across the Country.

Fáilte Ireland estimates that, approximately 34,020 STL properties were advertised online in the State in October 2025, based on screen-scraped data from four major booking platforms. Up to 64% were listed as “entire” houses or apartments. This represents a 26% increase from an estimated 26,960 units in October 2022. In Donegal around 3,160 STL units were listed in October 2025, of which, 75% were advertised as entire properties. This represents a 14.5% increase from an estimated 2,760 listed in October 2022.

Tourism remains a vital part of the Irish economy, supporting 227,000 jobs and generating €6 billion in 2024. I fully recognise concerns about the impact on rural tourism and local economies of reducing STL availability. However, addressing Ireland’s housing needs is a priority, and Government must use every lever available, including returning some STL properties to the long-term rental market. The approach agreed on 9 February will balance greater housing supply with the need to protect rural and regional tourism and jobs.
My Department has, and continues to have, ongoing engagement with all stakeholders, including STL operators and platforms.

question.p: 574. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if, in relation to the Industrial Relations Provisions in Respect of Pension Entitlements of Retired Workers Bill 2021, he can clarify whether the Government will provide a money message should the Bills Office decide it needs one; if they can outline separately what measures the Government are taking to address the policy issues the Bill tries to address (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19245/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: A Money Message is a formal recommendation from Government and is typically required where a Private Members' Bill involves public expenditure which is incidental to the purpose of the Bill, in order for it to proceed to formal section by-section examination at Committee Stage. The decision on whether to provide a Money Message is a Cabinet decision and is therefore subject to Cabinet confidentiality. Requests for Money Messages are processed by the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform which liaises with the Department of the Taoiseach in respect of the Cabinet decision. Accordingly, it would not be appropriate for me to comment on such decisions.

The Bill, in its current format, cannot be supported by Government as the proposed changes would fundamentally undermine the very concept of industrial relations, a process essentially involving workers and their employers. The objective of this Bill is to create a formal route for retired workers (and their representative associations) to access industrial relations processes in respect of their pension entitlements. It is my view that the current legal framework provides adequate protections for retired workers. Retired workers have the ability to enforce their pension rights through various legal avenues, including the Pensions Act, the Pensions Authority, the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman, and the courts. In addition, there is a provision for pensioners to lodge a complaint with the Workplace Relations Commission within six months of retirement or from when the grievance was or should have been known, with a possible six-month extension for reasonable cause.

Furthermore, my Department’s position is that any amendment to the legislation governing the rights of retired persons is not an industrial relations issue but is a matter for the Department of Social Protection.

question.p: 575. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider establishing a national Exporter Recognition Symbol that Irish exporting firms could display at their premises, to highlight their contribution to the Irish economy and promote public awareness of Ireland’s export-led growth; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19248/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: My Department, through its agency Enterprise Ireland (EI), supports the development and growth of Irish enterprises in world markets. EI works in partnership with Irish businesses to help them start, grow, innovate, and win export sales in global markets. Enterprise Ireland’s 2025-2029 strategy, ‘Delivering for Ireland and Leading Globally,’ sets out ambitious targets to increase jobs in client companies to 275,000 and to increase exports to €50bn by 2029. The strategy aims to accelerate sustainable Irish business so that exporting Irish companies become the primary driver of the Irish economy by 2029.

Enterprise Ireland supports exporters with a range of grants and practical assistance. The “Get Exporting Programme” is an Enterprise Ireland initiative designed for companies with less than €10,000 in annual export sales to develop international strategies.

Enterprise Ireland also regularly sponsors awards designed to showcase exporting activity and the contribution Irish exporters make, working in partnership with representative bodies such as the Irish Exporters Association and the Small Firms Association in this regard. Enterprise Ireland is a consistent sponsor and partner of the Irish Exporters Association’s (IEA) Export Industry Awards and is particularly involved in the High Potential Start up category.

The Irish Exporters Association’s Export Industry Awards, now in its 24th year, is currently held as an annual event for recognising the achievements of Irish Exporters. The Irish Exporters Association (IEA) hosts these annual awards to recognize excellence across various sectors. With 13 categories, the Awards focus on innovation, AI, and sustainability. The overall Exporter of the Year 2026 is selected from the winners of the 13 individual categories.

InterTradeIreland sponsors the All-Island Trade Award at the Irish Exporters Association (IEA) Export Industry Awards, recognizing companies that demonstrate outstanding success in cross-border trade between Northern Ireland and Ireland.

question.p: 576. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider incorporating a public-facing Exporter Recognition Scheme into the implementation of Ireland’s Trade and Investment Strategy 2022–2026, to help promote Ireland’s trading reputation domestically as well as internationally; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19249/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: Exporter recognition schemes are government or industry-led initiatives designed to identify, reward, and facilitate high-performing exporters.

In Ireland, the Irish Exporters Association’s Export Industry Awards, now in its 24th year, is currently held as an annual event for recognising the achievements of Irish Exporters. The Irish Exporters Association (IEA) hosts these annual awards to recognize excellence across various sectors. Irish Exporters Association 2026 Awards features 13 categories and focuses on innovation, AI, and sustainability. The overall Exporter of the Year 2026 is selected from the winners of the 13 individual categories. InterTradeIreland sponsors the All-Island Trade Award at the Irish Exporters Association (IEA) Export Industry Awards, recognizing companies that demonstrate outstanding success in cross-border trade between Northern Ireland and Ireland.

InterTrade Ireland provide bespoke, one-on-one specialist support to help your business grow cross-border exports. The Trade Export Pathway assist with researching market opportunities and developing a robust sales plan, to help companies boost cross-border sales. Enterprise Ireland is a consistent sponsor and partner of the Irish Exporters Association’s (IEA) Export Industry Awards and is particularly involved in the High Potential Start up category.

Enterprise Ireland supports exporters with a range of grants and practical assistance. The “Get Exporting Programme” is an Enterprise Ireland initiative designed for companies with less than €10,000 in annual export sales to develop international strategies.

question.p: 577. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his Department or any body under it’s aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19495/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: The information requested is currently being collated by my Department and will be forwarded directly to the Deputy as soon as it is finalised.

question.p: 578. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will confirm whether the State has formally designated the Intellectual Property Office of Ireland as the national competent authority for the purposes of implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2411 on geographical indication protection for craft and industrial products; the measures that have been taken to inform and support producers in applying for GI status (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19520/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: My Department has responsibility for the implementation of EU Regulation 2023/2411 into Irish law and putting in place the legal framework for the new system for geographical indication protection for craft and industrial products.
I can confirm that the Intellectual Property Office of Ireland (IPOI) will be the designated national authority responsible for the national registration phase.

Work on the implementing regulations, to be set out in a Statutory Instrument, is ongoing in my Department. Owing to the complexity and extended nature of the drafting process, the department does not have the implementing legislation in place yet, however, it is my intention to have the legislation finalised and in force as soon as practicable.

In the interim, applications for craft and industrial GIs can be submitted to the IPOI through the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) GIportal from 1 December 2025 and the IPOI will commence the national registration phase only when the national implementing legislation enters into force. Until that date, applications submitted through the GIportal will be received in the IPOI but will not be examined or acknowledged.

To raise awareness of the new protection system, my Department, in conjunction with the Design and Craft Council of Ireland, the Intellectual Property Office of Ireland and the European Commission held a conference on Monday, 19th January in the RDS. More information about the conference and the recording of the event can be found on the European Commission website at www.single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/industry/strategy/intellectual-property/geographical-indications-craft-and-industrial-products/geographical-indications-capitals-tour_en .

The EUIPO will play a central role in the administration, promotion, and management of the new GI protection system. Detailed information about the new scheme and how to make an application is available on the EUIPO GI Hub website at www.euipo.europa.eu/en/gi-hub

speech.p: I appreciate that this is an uncertain time for consumers. In all cases, either the price itself, or the method used to calculate it, must be clearly communicated before any sale.

When prices rise suddenly, it can understandably cause frustration. Ireland operates an open market economy, which means businesses are permitted to set and change their own prices. There is no legal definition of “price gouging” in Irish law. Any behaviour that breaches consumer protection or competition law falls that within the remit of the CCPC will be investigated and enforced accordingly. question.p: 581. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the reason there is no single, national register of verified accessible tourism attractions and accommodation, despite Ireland’s obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; if he will commit to establishing such a register to support inclusive tourism and informed travel planning; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19649/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: Ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities by Ireland includes commitments to:
• Promote access to the physical environment, transportation, information, and services (Article 9).
• Support independent living and community inclusion (Article 19).
• Ensure equal participation in cultural life, recreation, leisure, and sport (Article 30).

Accessible and Inclusive Tourism falls across these obligations, particularly in ensuring that people with disabilities can plan travel with reliable, verified information which is vital, as travellers with disabilities frequently encounter inconsistent or inaccurate details.

An essential aspect of Ireland’s internationally renowned welcome is that it is experienced by all visitors, without restrictions. Accordingly, ensuring a ‘Welcome for All’ is a central tenet of the Government’s Tourism Policy, A New Era for Irish Tourism. In addition to it’s inherent heritage and reputational value, this traditional welcome has proven, and continues to be, invaluable for encouraging repeat visits and positive word-of mouth reviews. Everyone deserves the opportunity to explore, discover, and enjoy the world around them and for that reason all tourism businesses should aim to offer barrier-free tourism experiences. This means ensuring tourist destinations, products and services are universally accessible, regardless of a visitors physical limitations, disabilities, or age.

To meet this objective and indeed harness the growing, high value inclusive tourism market, the Government is working with the tourism agencies to establish and promote Ireland as an internationally recognised accessible and inclusive tourism destination. This will require improvements to tourism infrastructure, staff training and the use of innovative technology and the tourism agencies are working with industry and advocacy groups to identify and address barriers to access to tourist sites and services.

Regulation of tourism accommodation is an operational matter for Fáilte Ireland and the authority aims to position Ireland as a world leader in accessible and inclusive tourism by 2030 and is actively working toward achieving that goal. As visitor expectations continue to grow and more people seek accessible and inclusive experiences, it’s important that our approach is practical and informed by evidence. That means understanding what works on the ground for tourism businesses, learning from international best practice, and listening to the real experiences of visitors. By doing this, we can strengthen Ireland’s competitiveness, improve the visitor experience, and support sustainable growth across the tourism sector.

In 2024, Fáilte Ireland established a dedicated ‘inclusive tourism’ team to drive national efforts in making Ireland’s destinations, services, and tourism offerings accessible and inclusive. This work aims to embed universal access across the sector and raise awareness of accessible and inclusive tourism.

Fáilte Ireland is currently supporting tourism businesses to accurately describe their accessibility features and allow visitors to determine whether the experience on offer meets their individual needs. The Access for Success initiative, launched in 2025, supports tourism businesses in improving accessibility standards and providing accurate pre-travel information about their accessibility to visitors within a detailed section on their websites. It replaces self-declared ratings with a robust accessibility audit and industry training to improve the clarity and availability of accessibility information, boosting visitor confidence and booking conversion. In 2025, 69 hotels took part in the programme, and it has now expanded to include attractions and activity providers in 2026.
In addition to the Access for Success initiative, Fáilte Ireland is delivering

• an 'accessible and inclusive tourism' capability programme, to enhance skills and competencies for frontline staff and leadership teams in client businesses. This 'capability' is defined as the strategic creation and development of tourism experiences, environments, and services that are welcoming, safe, and usable by all individuals - regardless of ability, background, or personal circumstance.
• development of an access and inclusion events guide, available to all event organisers, to support the creation of more inclusive, accessible, and welcoming event experiences across the sector.

• investment, through Platforms for Growth 2, in 19 water activity sites featuring Changing Places Toilets (fully accessible toilet facilities designed for people with complex disabilities who need more space and specialised equipment than standard accessible toilets provide)' greatly expanding the provision of changing places facilities in Ireland beyond towns and cities, step changing opportunities for more people to experience Ireland’s beautiful rivers, lakes and beaches.

• work with the Centre of Excellence in Universal Design (National Disability Authority) in the review and design of a robust process for ensuring all Capital Investment schemes under their remit, to include access inclusion principles and practices.
• support to businesses in making their digital content fully accessible to WCAG 2.2 AA standards, through funding, expertise, and training.

• a partnership with VisitEngland, VisitScotland, VisitWales and Tourism Northern Ireland to develop a robust, standardised accessibility feature set, creating a common framework that tourism businesses can use to explain their accessibility features in a way that’s consistent, reliable and easy for visitors to understand.

This continuous drive for improvement to tourism infrastructure including accommodation, the use of innovative technology, and staff training, will better serve and harness the growing, high value inclusive Irish tourism market.

question.p: 582. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether accommodation supply is now recognised as core tourism infrastructure; how inclusive and sustainable tourism can be delivered without sufficient, affordable and accessible places for visitors to stay; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19651/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: This Government recognises the central importance of tourism to Ireland’s economy and to the vitality of communities across the country. A strong, sustainable and regionally balanced accommodation base is indeed fundamental to a sustainable and attractive tourism sector. Accommodation not only underpins the visitor experience and perceptions of value for money, but also strengthens the competitiveness of the wider tourism ecosystem and enables businesses of all sizes to grow and thrive.

Reliable, comprehensive data is essential to effective policy development and long-term planning. Fáilte Ireland maintains accommodation registers under the Tourist Traffic Acts and through the National Quality Assurance Framework (NQAF), providing an established evidence base for the sector. Currently, 225,782 tourism bedplaces are recorded across these registers, reflecting the scale of the industry and providing a solid platform for strategic development.

To further strengthen the data landscape, a statutory register for all Short-Term Letting (STL) accommodation will be introduced this summer. This measure will significantly enhance transparency and visibility across the full accommodation spectrum, ensuring a more complete and robust dataset to inform tourism policy and investment decisions.

In parallel, Fáilte Ireland has developed a Tourism Accommodation Capacity and Pipeline Monitor. This strategic tool tracks existing capacity and monitors developments as they progress through planning, construction and opening phases. It enables early identification of supply constraints, provides insights into regional and sectoral trends, and supports evidence-based decision making by policymakers and industry stakeholders.

Based on Q3 2025 data on projects under construction, the Fáilte Ireland pipeline monitor forecasts that nationally 12,750 new bedplaces, will be completed between now and the end of 2027. In addition, planning permission has been granted for a further 37,550 bedplaces nationally. The monitor will be refreshed with Q1 2026 data shortly.

The forthcoming Tourism Accommodation Strategy, a key commitment under A New Era for Irish Tourism, will establish a clear framework to strengthen, diversify and expand Ireland’s accommodation offering with the objective of realising an enhanced tourism accommodation offering, accessible to all visitors at a range of price points. Particular emphasis will be placed on unlocking development in areas with significant untapped tourism potential, supporting balanced regional growth and delivering sustainable, year-round economic benefits nationwide. A public consultation to support and inform preparation of the Strategy will be launched by my Department in the coming weeks and will be accessible to all interested parties.

Drawing on the response to the consultation, enhanced statutory data, the new STL register and the capacity and pipeline monitor, the Strategy will take an integrated, data-driven approach to long-term tourist accommodation planning.

This will ensure that Ireland’s tourism infrastructure evolves in line with changing consumer preferences and global travel trends, safeguarding the resilience and competitiveness of the sector into the future.

question.p: 583. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the engagement his Department has had with the European Commission regarding the implementation of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, including discussions on whether the list of prohibited practices under Article 5 of that Act may require further review in light of rapidly developing artificial intelligence technologies; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19674/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Niamh Smyth)
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) came into force on 02 August 2024, and the provisions of the AI Act will apply progressively, with a full roll-out by 2 August 2027.

My Department is leading on the implementation of the AI Act in Ireland, and my officials have been engaging with stakeholders across government to ascertain and put the necessary measures in place. Ireland is making very good progress on the implementation of the AI Act and has met its obligations that have come into effect up to this point in time.

Ireland has adopted a distributed model of regulation for the AI Act in Ireland, leveraging existing framework of regulatory bodies in Ireland. To date, thirteen public bodies have been designated as market surveillance authorities (MSA) and four as notifying authorities (NA), with some of those public bodies having a dual role as both an MSA and an NA.

In January 2026, Government approved the priority drafting of the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Bill, on the basis of the General Scheme prepared by my department. The General Scheme proposes to establish a new statutory independent body – AI Office of Ireland - under the remit of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, to act as the Single Point of Contact and central coordinating authority for the implementation and enforcement of the EU AI Act in the State. It also provides for the empowerment of designated Competent Authorities and rules on penalties for infringement of the Act.

At EU level, my Department regularly engages with the European Commission and other Member States through the EU AI Board and related expert and advisory structures on matters related to the implementation of the AI Act. These structures provide Ireland with a formal channel through which to work together with member states and provide advice and support to the Commission in relation to the implementation of the AI Act and AI policy more generally.

The AI Act takes a risk-based, tiered approach to AI governance. The prohibited practices under Article 5, which came into effect in August 2025, represent the Act's most stringent restrictions. The Commission published comprehensive non-binding Guidelines on Prohibited AI Practices in February 2025 to provide interpretive clarity for national authorities and operators. The AI Act already provides an in-built mechanism for the review of prohibited practices under Article 5. Under the Act, the European Commission is required to assess annually whether the list of prohibited practices requires amendment and to report its findings to the European Parliament and the Council. This ensures that the framework can respond to technological developments over time.

In parallel to this, the Digital Omnibus on AI was published by the European Commission on 19 November last year. This proposal is a targeted set of amendments to the AI Act, presented that seeks to facilitate the smooth and effective application of the rules for safe and trustworthy development and use of AI.

Ireland has welcomed the EU’s focus on simplification, having consistently advocated for targeted and proportionate regulation, ensuring the right balance between stimulating innovation, boosting competitiveness, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights, including democracy and the rule of law. As part of the EU legislative process for the Digital Omnibus on AI proposal, Ireland along with other Member States advocated for consideration whether targeted amendments to Article 5's list of prohibitions could help strengthen protections against the generation of illegal content.

On 13 March the Council of the EU agreed a position on the Digital Omnibus on AI proposal, which includes a proposal to amend the EU AI Act to add a prohibited AI practice related to the generation of illegal and harmful content. Ireland has worked with the Presidency of the Council (Cypress), the European Commission and member states in the process to reach agreement on this in the Council of the EU. The Parliament and Council are now expected to enter negotiations to reach an agreement on these proposals to amend the EU AI Act, with an aim to adopt an agreed proposal in advance of August this year.

I would like to assure the Deputy that the Government is committed to the timely implementation of the AI Act and my Department will continue to engage actively with the Commission and with counterparts across the EU to ensure regulatory framework keep pace with technological development.

question.p: 584. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the actions his Department is taking, in conjunction with relevant regulators and Departments, to address potential price gouging by energy providers in light of the recent unprecedented increases in oil, diesel and gas prices linked to tensions and conflict in the Middle East; whether any monitoring or regulatory measures are being considered to ensure fair pricing for consumers; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19684/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: I appreciate that this is an uncertain time for consumers. I recently advised members of the public to contact the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in relation to concerns related to home heating oil and fuel. The CCPC has assured me that all such complaints are being carefully and urgently assessed. The CCPC as an independent statutory body can avail of a range of powers to investigate, enforce and prosecute where clear breaches of the law are evident. I have also met with representatives of the fuel industry to discuss the energy market and pricing structures, along with the factors impacting costs in the current uncertain geopolitical environment.
Consumer protection law requires traders to provide key information in advance of a transaction, including the total price, taxes and charges included, so that consumers can make informed decisions.

The law recognises that there are situations where a trader may be unable to specify the final price in advance. When this happens, they must instead tell the consumer how the price will be calculated. In all cases, either the price itself, or the method used to calculate it, must be clearly communicated before any sale.

When prices rise suddenly, it can understandably cause frustration. Ireland operates an open market economy, which means businesses are permitted to set and change their own prices. If businesses are working in a way that could unfairly limit competition or push up prices, for example by agreeing prices with one another, the CCPC has strong powers to address this. Where it is suspected that competition or consumer law may have been breached, the CCPC will take the steps necessary to enforce the law. The powers available to the CCPC means breaches of competition law can result in severe penalties including criminal prosecution and administrative fines of up to 10% of turnover or €10 million, whichever is greater.

As part of the Programme for Government commitments, I have already initiated the process of further strengthening the powers of the CCPC in both its Consumer Protection and Competition functions. A public consultation opened on this intended legislative change before Christmas and closed on 27 February. I intend to seek Government approval to draft Heads of Bill in the coming months once the submissions to the consultation have been assessed.

question.p: 585. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his current plans to deal with price gouging occurring by certain fuel providers (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20161/26]

speech.p: I appreciate that this is an uncertain time for consumers. I recently advised members of the public to contact the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in relation to concerns related to home heating oil and fuel. The CCPC has assured me that all such complaints are being carefully and urgently assessed.

The CCPC as an independent statutory body can avail of a range of powers to investigate, enforce and prosecute where clear breaches of the law are evident. I have also met with representatives of the fuel industry to discuss the energy market and pricing structures, along with the factors impacting costs in the current uncertain geopolitical environment.
Consumer protection law requires traders to provide key information in advance of a transaction, including the total price, taxes and charges included, so that consumers can make informed decisions.

The law recognises that there are situations where a trader may be unable to specify the final price in advance. When this happens, they must instead tell the consumer how the price will be calculated. In all cases, either the price itself, or the method used to calculate it, must be clearly communicated before any sale.

When prices rise suddenly, it can understandably cause frustration. Ireland operates an open market economy, which means businesses are permitted to set and change their own prices. There is no legal definition of “price gouging” in Irish law. Any behaviour that breaches consumer protection or competition law falls within the remit of the CCPC and will be investigated and enforced accordingly. If businesses are working in a way that could unfairly limit competition or push up prices, for example by agreeing prices with one another, the CCPC has strong powers to address this. As part of the Programme for Government commitments, I have already initiated the process of further strengthening the powers of the CCPC in both its Consumer Protection and Competition functions. A public consultation opened on this intended legislative change before Christmas and closed on 27 February. I intend to seek Government approval to draft Heads of Bill in the coming months once the submissions to the consultation have been assessed.

question.p: 586. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the current status and expected timeline for the progression of the Protection of Employees (Employers' Insolvency) (Amendment) Bill 2025 (Bill No. 28 of 2025); the anticipated date for its completion of remaining Seanad Éireann stages; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20204/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
speech.p: The Protection of Employees (Employers' Insolvency) (Amendment) Bill 2025 completed Second Stage in the Seanad on 4 March 2026. The timeline for the enactment of the Bill is a matter for the Oireachtas. I expect the remaining stages in the Seanad to be scheduled after the Easter recess.
This Bill will amend the Protection of Employees (Employers’ Insolvency) Act 1984 to:
• expand access to the Insolvency Payments Scheme to protect employees of employers who cease trading without entering into liquidation, receivership or bankruptcy;
• align eligibility for the Insolvency Payments Scheme with broader Government policy on personal insolvency;
• ensure the salary ceiling applies uniformly to payments under the Insolvency Payments Scheme; and
• clarify how certain pension contributions are protected under the Insolvency Payments Scheme.

My officials and officials in the Department of Social Protection, which administers the Insolvency Payments Scheme on my behalf, are advancing the necessary preparations to ensure the Bill can be commenced smoothly after the Bill's enactment.

question.p: 587. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on issues raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20267/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Alan Dillon)
speech.p: The changes to the Minimum Annual Remuneration (MAR) thresholds for employment permits from the 1st of this month have been implemented in accordance with the statutory requirements set out in the Employment Permits Act 2024. Under this legislation, an annual review of the MAR must be undertaken, and where average weekly earnings have increased, the MAR must increase by at least a corresponding percentage. It is important to note that this is a legal obligation on my Department to conduct a review of the MAR under the Indexation provisions of the Employment Permits Act 2024.

The primary objective of the MAR framework is to ensure that employment permit holders have sufficient earnings to live in Ireland without reliance on State supports, and to prevent undercutting efforts to improve pay and conditions, or modernisation and productivity measures.

The review of the MAR which was finalised in December last, was underpinned by an extensive consultation process involving a wide range of sectors and stakeholders. Over 150 submissions were received during this process, and further engagement continued up to the implementation of the 2026 changes. In response to concerns raised by multiple sectors, all planned MAR increases for 2025 were deferred to allow for a comprehensive review of the approach to indexation and remuneration thresholds.

Following the conclusion of this review and the extended consultations, the previously deferred threshold increase was reduced from 15.8% to 7.66%. The outcome of this process was noted by Cabinet and published on 2nd December 2025.

For clarity, the Employment Permit system operates on the basis of an hourly rate calculated over a standard 39-hour week. Only basic pay, guaranteed premiums and health insurance elements of pay that form part of the contractual terms of the employment can be counted towards meeting the Minimum Annual Remuneration threshold for the permit. Any bonuses, subsistence payments, allowances, or other forms of non-guaranteed or variable income cannot be included when assessing compliance with MAR thresholds.

The Department acknowledges the concerns raised across sectors about the impact of MAR adjustments, and this was a core reason for deferring the original increases set out in 2023 and undertaking a multi-year approach to implementation. This process allowed for deeper engagement with employers, detailed financial and operational analysis, and a recalibration of the final rate of increase to reflect stakeholder input, resulting in significantly reduced increases to the thresholds.

My Department remains committed to ongoing, structured engagement with key sectors of the economy including transport and logistics sectors, including through enhanced cross-government collaboration developed with the Department of Transport.

question.p: 588. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the measures being undertaken by his Department to promote the take up of fibre to the home fibre broadband amongst Irish SMEs, considering data which suggests adoption remains low; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20270/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Niamh Smyth)
speech.p: The National Broadband Plan, led by the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport is the Irish Government’s central broadband initiative. It directly supports broadband availability for SMEs located in underserved areas by subsidising the rollout of fibre infrastructure through National Broadband Ireland.

While my Department does not have a role in broadband infrastructure, we are focused on ensuring that SMEs can make full use of the connectivity being delivered. In February, Government published the new National AI & Digital Strategy, Digital Ireland – Connecting our People, Securing our Future. This Strategy sets out a clear and ambitious roadmap for advancing Ireland’s digital and AI capabilities in the years ahead, underlying digital competitiveness as a foundation for economic resilience.
A wide range of enterprise supports are already in place to help SMEs accelerate their digital transformation:
• The Grow Digital Voucher offers up to €5,000 to small businesses (under 50 employees) to adopt digital tools like e-commerce, AI, cybersecurity, and website development.
• The Digital for Business consultancy scheme is a free service which connects businesses with expert advisors to assess their digital needs and develop tailored transformation plans.
• The Grow Digital Portal highlights real-world success stories from non-tech businesses that have successfully embraced digitalisation.

• Ireland’s four European Digital Innovation Hubs (Dublin, Cork, Mullingar, Sligo) support SMEs and public bodies in adopting advanced technologies such as AI, cybersecurity, and high-performance computing.

My Department recently announced a further €23 million in additional funding for these Hubs to help SMEs increase their use of AI and other cutting edge digital technologies. These Hubs are delivering practical supports that help SMEs understand, test and adopt advanced digital technologies with confidence.
The new Strategy also commits to reviewing both the Digital for Business consultancy scheme and Grow Digital Voucher to ensure they remain effective and continue to meet the needs of SMEs.

question.p: 591. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted due to St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026; and the amount paid. [20643/26]

speech.from: Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment

These rates are then applied to my Department’s recorded flight activity for the year concerned including all air travel taken by the Minister, Ministers of State and Department staff.
