question.p: 787. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the person or body that took the decision and the reason for excluding compulsory written research projects for Leaving Certificate subjects including history and geography from the answering through the Irish bonus marks scheme in each year since 2006; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19479/26]

788. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to the decision to exclude compulsory written research projects for Leaving Certificate subjects including history and geography from the answering through the Irish bonus marks scheme in each year since 2006 is contrary to the stated Mícheál Martin as Minister for Education’s position in 1999, which itself was a reiteration of Government policy from 1960s to that time; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19480/26]

789. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to the ‘decision’ to exclude compulsory written research projects for Leaving Certificate subjects including history and geography from the answering through Irish bonus marks scheme in each year since 2006 was not communicated to Irish-medium schools, their students or other students sitting their Leaving Certificate exams through Irish but in English medium schools; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19481/26]

790. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will publish all documents relating to when decisions annually were taken, by whom and the educational basis of those decisions to exclude compulsory written research projects for Leaving Certificate subjects including history and geography from the answering through the Irish bonus marks scheme in each year since 2006; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19482/26]

791. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm with regard to each of the following Leaving Certificate subjects (History; Geography; Economics; PE; Agricultural Science; Religion; Politics and Society; Computer Science; Religious Education), that answering through the Irish bonus marks scheme was applied by the State Examinations Commission on the entirety of each students written work submitted each and every year from the 1960s to 2005 inclusive, and it is intended that the State Examinations Commission will reinstate that position of awarding bonus marks on the entirety of each student’s assessed work, from this year’s 2026 student cohort; and if she will for each subject, detail the year a compulsory project or research component was introduced for Leaving Certification assessment, the weighted value of that project. [19483/26]

792. Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department officials of the State Examination Commission received correspondence regularly from 2008 on the matter of the failure to apply answering through Irish bonus marks to compulsory written research projects for Leaving Certificate subjects in each year since 2006; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19484/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 787 to 792, inclusive, together.

As the Deputy will be aware, the policy and practice of awarding additional marks to candidates sitting state examinations through the medium of Irish dates back to the 1920s. It was one of several initiatives taken in the early years of the State to strengthen the position of the Irish language in the education system, with the long-term objective of maintaining and reviving its use in everyday life.

The practice of awarding bonus marks for answering through Irish is implemented currently by the State Examinations Commission (SEC), according to the procedures described in Rule 29 of the Rules and Programme for Secondary Schools 2004/2005. That this applies to the written examinations only is set out in Rule 29, which states:
“... A candidate who answers in Irish at the written examination in the various subjects as set out below may be given bonus marks in addition to the marks gained in the subject.

Bonus marks at the rate of 10 per cent of the marks obtained will be given to a candidate who obtains less than 75 per cent of the total marks in the case of the following subjects: - Latin, Ancient Greek, Classical Studies, Hebrew Studies, History, Geography, Physics, Chemistry, Physics and Chemistry, Biology, Science, Business, Economics, Economic History, Agricultural Science, Agricultural Economics, Home Economics, Music, Business Studies, History and Appreciation of Art, Civic, Social and Political Education, Religious Education, Arabic, LCVP Link Modules-Written Component only. Bonus marks at the rate of 5 per cent will be given to a candidate who obtains less than 75 per cent of the total marks in the case of the following subjects: - French, German, Italian, Spanish, Mathematics, Applied Mathematics, Accounting, Engineering, Construction Studies, Materials Technology (Wood), Metalwork, Technology, Typewriting, Russian, Japanese. Bonus marks at the rate of 3 per cent will be given to a candidate who obtains less than 75% of the total marks in the case of the subject Art, Craft, Design (Junior Certificate). Above 75 per cent the bonus will be subjected to a uniform reduction until the candidate who scores 100 per cent gets no bonus.
No bonus will be given in the case of the following subjects: - Technical Graphics, Technical Drawing, Leaving Certificate Art (other than History and Appreciation of Art).
For the purpose of the award of bonus marks, Mathematics, Paper 1 and Paper 2, will be treated as separate subjects.
Candidates who answer partly in Irish and partly in English will receive no bonus marks”.
In addition to the subjects listed above, bonus marks are also awarded to candidates who take the formal written examinations through Irish in the Leaving Certificate Applied.
The decision to award either a 10% or 5% bonus is based on the projected volume of written production in Irish in each formal written examination. The rate of 3% no longer applies.
Documentation from the SEC to the Authorities of Post-Primary Schools regarding the bonus for answering through Irish states:
“Please note that in keeping with all other examinations that have components completed outside the formal written examination, bonus marks will not be awarded”.

New examinations were first held in Leaving Certificate History and Geography in 2006 which included written coursework. The coursework did not come within the ambit of Rule 29 and did not therefore attract the bonus marks. This was also the case in relation to the written coursework in LC Religious Education which was first examined the previous year in 2005.

Regarding the specific subjects listed below and the request for confirmation that answering through the Irish bonus marks scheme was applied by the SEC on the entirety of each students written work submitted each and every year from the 1960s to 2005 inclusive I am advised by the SEC as follows:
History:• examined by written examination only until 2006.
Geography:• examined by written examination only until 2006.
Economics:• examination by written examination only until 2021.
PE:• introduced as a new subject, and examined for the first time in 2020.
Computer Science:• introduced as a new subject, and examined for the first time in 2020.
Politics and Society: • introduced as new subject, and first examined in 2018.
Agricultural Science: • first examination in new specification in 2021.
Religious Education:• first examination in 2005. Since its introduction, the journal completed for the examination in Religious Education did not come within scope of the Irish Bonus marks.

As the Deputy will be aware. under the Senior Cycle Redevelopment programme, all new and revised Leaving Certificate Established subject specifications will incorporate Additional Assessment Components (AACs) that are not a traditional written examination, worth at least 40% of the total available mark, and externally assessed by the SEC.

Under circular 0002/2026 ‘Bonus for the completion of additional assessment components through Irish’, which supersedes Rule 29, the Irish bonus marks policy has now been extended for the first time to include those components of the State examinations which are coursework and completed through Irish, where appropriate. This extension of bonus marks to coursework arises primarily given the application of these revised assessment arrangements.

The SEC has also published circular S10/26 ‘Application of the Irish Bonus in State Examinations’, outlining the operational dimensions of the policy change including the applicable criteria and parameters relating to the awarding of the bonus marks.
Irish bonus marks will now apply to candidates who respond to both the written examination and the related AACs through the medium of Irish from the 2027 Leaving Certificate cohort onwards.

Given the application of these revised assessment arrangements, the bonus marks for Irish policy was reviewed ahead of the publication of the Senior Cycle Redevelopment Implementation Support Measures document published in May 2025 and an Information Note that was issued to schools in August 2025.

These extended arrangements will apply to all Leaving Certificate Established and Leaving Certificate Applied subjects in 2027 and in subsequent years, not just those that have been redeveloped within Tranche 1. This is to ensure students in that cohort and each subsequent cohort are not disadvantaged relative to each other by their respective subject choices.

My department has received a small amount of correspondence in relation to bonus marks over an extended number of years and I would draw the Deputy’s attention that such correspondence often relates to requests to remove the application of bonus marks entirely.

My department has a long-standing policy of encouraging the active use of the Irish language by all students and in all school communities. The extension of the Irish bonus marks builds on this objective, encouraging the use of the Irish language by all learners, in all schools.

question.p: 793. D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige cén dáta go sonrach a ghlac an tAire Oideachais agus Óige le cinneadh an Choimisiúin um Scrúduithe Stáit neamhaird a dhéanamh ar an bpolasaí, mar atá leagtha síos i Riail 29 de na Rules and Programmes for Secondary Schools a sheoltar chuile bhliain chuig gach iar-bhunscoil, marcanna bónais san Ardteistiméireacht a bhronnadh as freagairt go hiomlán trí Ghaeilge ar obair scrúduithe scríofa iarrthóirí ina hiomláine in 18 n-ábhar, ag ráta 10% den mharc aimsithe ag iarrthóir [19486/26]

794. D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige cén bunús atá leis an gcinneadh a ghlac an Coimisiún um Scrúduithe Stáit in 2006 gan cloí le Riail 29 de na Rules and Programmes for Secondary Schools maidir le marcanna bónais a bhronnadh ar an gcuid sin den Ardteistiméireacht ar obair thionscnaimh éigeantachta scríofa í [19487/26]

795. D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Oideachais agus Óige an ndearnadh aon mheasúnacht ar an tionchar ar thorthaí mac léinn Ardteistiméireachta le 20 bliain ó 2006 ón gcinneadh gan marcanna bónais a bhronnadh ar an gcuid sin den Ardteistiméireacht ar obair thionscnaimh éigeantachta scríofa í [19488/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 793, 794 and 795 together.
Molaim na ceisteanna réamhcheaptha 19486/26, 19487/26, agus 19488/26 a thógáil le chéile.

Mar is eol don Teachta, téann an polasaí agus an cleachtas maidir le marcanna breise a bhronnadh ar iarrthóirí a dhéanann scrúduithe poiblí trí mheán na Gaeilge siar go dtí na 1920idí agus cuireann an Coimisiún na Scrúduithe Stáit (CSS) é seo i bhfeidhm, de réir na nósanna imeachta a thuairiscítear i Rialachán 29 de na Rialacha agus Clár do Mheánscoileanna 2004/2005. Leagtar amach i Riail 29 go mbaineann sé seo leis na scrúduithe scríofa amháin, ina luaitear:
“...Féadfar marcanna bónais a thabhairt d’iarrthóir a fhreagraíonn i nGaeilge sa scrúdú scríofa sna hábhair éagsúla mar atá leagtha amach thíos sa bhreis ar na marcanna a ghnóthaítear san ábhar.

Tabharfar marcanna bónais ar ráta 10 faoin gcéad de na marcanna a fhaightear d’iarrthóir a fhaigheann níos lú ná 75 faoin gcéad de na marcanna iomlána i gcás na n-ábhar seo a leanas: - Laidin, Sean-Ghréigis, Léann Clasaiceach, Léann Eabhraise, Stair, Tíreolaíocht, Fisic, Ceimic, Fisic agus Ceimic, Bitheolaíocht, Eolaíocht, Gnó, Eacnamaíocht, Stair Eacnamaíoch, Eolaíocht Talmhaíochta, Eacnamaíocht Talmhaíochta, Eacnamaíocht Bhaile, Ceol, Staidéir Ghnó, Stair agus Meas ar an Ealaín, Oideachas Saoránach, Sóisialta agus Polaitiúil, Oideachas Reiligiúnach, Araibis, Modúil Nasctha GCAT - Comhpháirt Scríofa amháin. Tabharfar marcanna bónais ar ráta 5 faoin gcéad de na marcanna a fhaightear d’iarrthóir a fhaigheann níos lú ná 75 faoin gcéad de na marcanna iomlána i gcás na n-ábhar seo a leanas: - Fraincis, Gearmáinis, Iodáilis, Spáinnis, Matamaitic, Matamaitic Fheidhmeach, Cuntasaíocht, Innealtóireacht, Staidéir Foirgníochta, Teicneolaíocht Ábhar (Adhmad), Miotalóireacht, Teicneolaíocht, Clóscríobh, Rúisis, Seapáinis. Tabharfar marcanna bónais ar ráta 3 faoin gcéad d’iarrthóir a fhaigheann níos lú ná 75% de na marcanna iomlána i gcás an ábhair Ealaín, Ceardaíocht, Dearadh (Teastas Sóisearach). Os cionn 75 faoin gcéad, laghdófar an bónas go haonfhoirmeach go dtí nach bhfaighidh an t-iarrthóir a scórálann 100 faoin gcéad aon bhónas.
Ní thabharfar aon bhónas i gcás na n-ábhar seo a leanas: - Grafaicí Teicniúla, Líníocht Theicniúil, Ealaín na hArdteistiméireachta (seachas Stair agus Meas ar an Ealaín).
Chun críche bronnta marcanna bónais, déileálfar le Matamaitic, Páipéar 1 agus Páipéar 2, mar ábhair ar leithligh.
Ní bhfaighidh iarrthóirí a fhreagraíonn cuid acu i nGaeilge agus cuid acu i mBéarla aon mharcanna bónais”.
Chomh maith leis na hábhair atá liostaithe thuas, bronntar marcanna bónais ar iarrthóirí a dhéanann na scrúduithe foirmiúla scríofa trí Gaeilge san Ardteistiméireacht Fheidhmeach.
Braitheann an cinneadh bónas 10% nó 5% a bhronnadh ar an méid réamh-mheasta de tháirgeadh scríofa i nGaeilge i ngach scrúdú foirmiúil scríofa. Níl feidhm ag an ráta 3% a thuilleadh.
Deirtear sa doiciméadacht ón CSS chuig Údaráis na Scoileanna Iar-bhunscoile maidir leis an mbónas as freagra a thabhairt trí Gaeilge:
“Tabhair faoi deara, le do thoil, nach mbronnfar marcanna bónais, mar atá i gcás gach scrúduithe eile ina bhfuil comhpháirteanna a chomhlánaítear lasmuigh den scrúdú foirmiúil scríofa”.

Mar is eol don Teachta, faoin gclár Athfhorbartha don tSraith Shinsearach, cuimseoidh gach sonraíocht ábhair Bhunaithe Ardteistiméireachta nua agus athbhreithnithe Comhpháirteanna Measúnaithe Breise (CMBanna) nach scrúdú scríofa traidisiúnta iad, ar fiú 40% ar a laghad den mharc iomlán atá ar fáil, agus a mheasfaidh CSS go seachtrach.

Faoi chiorclán 0002/2026 ‘Bónas as comhpháirteanna breise measúnachta a chomhlánú trí Gaeilge’, a thagann in ionad Rialachán 29, tá an polasaí maidir le marcanna bónais Gaeilge sínte anois den chéad uair chun na comhpháirteanna sin de scrúduithe Stáit ar obair chúrsa iad agus a dhéantar trí Gaeilge a áireamh, i gcás inarb iomchuí.
Beidh marcanna bónais Gaeilge i bhfeidhm anois ar iarrthóirí a fhreagraíonn an scrúdú scríofa agus na CMBanna gaolmhara trí mheán na Gaeilge ó chohórt Ardteistiméireachta 2027 ar aghaidh.

question.p: 796. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department or any body under it’s aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19494/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: My Department has not made disclosures under Revenues opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment.

The information in respect of state bodies under the aegis of my department, within the scope of the Deputy’s question, is not held by my department. State bodies have been provided with the question and have been requested to respond directly to the Deputy.

question.p: 797. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to any issues within Education Training Boards providing employees with a contract of employment due to uncertainty of applying changes to current and new employee contracts following an agreement after industrial action taken some time ago; if she will outline the standard employment terms and conditions of employees in an ETB; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19511/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Each school Board of Management or ETB has sole responsibility for the appointment of its teachers. The ETB is a statutory body with its own corporate status established under the Education and Training Boards Act 2013.

Terms and conditions of employment for staff employed by ETBs are matters for the ETB concerned. While the recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for the individual school authority or in this case ETB it is subject to procedures agreed under Section 24(3) of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012).

question.p: 798. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question Nos. 339 and 341 of 5 March 2026, to provide a breakdown of the ‘Social Inclusion Miscellaneous’ for each year from 2020 to 2025 and to-date in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19541/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Further to Parliamentary Question Nos. 339 and 341 of 5 March 2026, please find attached a breakdown of the Social Inclusion Unit’s miscellaneous subhead as requested. Funding administered from Social Inclusion Unit’s miscellaneous subhead is mainly for payment of grants to seven alternative education provision settings. This provision is an alternative option, when all other supports, options and pathways have been tried and have not proved successful in maintaining the student’s engagement with mainstream education. These settings provide an important service for a small cohort of students who have become disengaged from mainstream school.
In addition, funding provided to two drugs task force projects is now administered from this subhead.

p.a: Miscellaneous Subhead - Breakdown of payments for the period 2020 – 2026.

question.p: 799. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department has been in contact with a national school (details supplied) following the recent announcement relating to its capital project; and if she will outline the next steps in the process. [19545/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The large-scale capital project referred to by the Deputy is at Architectural Planning Stage 3 – Tender Action and Award.
The brief for this school is to provide a replacement 8 classroom primary school and accommodation, including additional classrooms for children with special educational needs.
Planning permission for the project expired in 2024 and an extension of Planning Permission was required. The extension was granted by the Local Authority in late August 2025.

The department will continue to engage closely with patron bodies, management bodies and schools with respect to the timing of the progression of projects to tender and/or construction over the period 2026 to 2027. This will include continued engagement with St Joseph’s Special School, Carrabane with respect to the progression of its project to construction.

As you will be aware, I have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

Of the total €7.55 billion investment it is envisaged that circa. €5 billion will be used for project rollout to support the delivery and modernisation of school buildings across the Large Scale, Additional Accommodation, Modular, and Annual September Accommodation Needs programmes.

My department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of these projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, I have also published a list of the 105 school building projects in the first tranche to proceed to construction or tender over 2026 and 2027. This list includes the project referred to by the Deputy.

The 105 prioritised projects will progress to tender and/or construction on a rolling basis over the course of 2026 and 2027 and within the context of NDP funding parameters. The timing of project progression will reflect the need to carefully manage the rollout of these projects to construction on a controlled basis to ensure that projects are delivered efficiently, align with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework and remain within the parameters of NDP funding.

Department officials will continue to engage closely with patron bodies, management bodies and schools with respect to the timing of the progression of projects to tender and/or construction over the period 2026 to 2027. This will include continued engagement with the school referred to by the Deputy with respect to the progression of its project to tender and construction.

The current status of all projects continues to be set out under item number ten at the following link: www.gov.ie. This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender and construction.

question.p: 800. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the requirement for primary school teachers to complete Croke park hours; if this is set out as a requirement in their contracts; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19560/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The Croke Park Agreement hours are part of wider productivity measures introduced under the Public Service Agreements. In schools, the Croke Park Agreement hours are 33 additional hours a year at post primary (36 hours at primary) worked by teachers.

A central purpose of the Croke Park Agreement hours is to provide for certain essential activities such as staff meetings, parent-teacher meetings, school planning, subject planning and mandated Continuous Professional Development to take place without reducing tuition time. Utilisation of the additional hours for these purposes has practically eliminated school closures which were previously necessary for activities such as the ones mentioned above.

A review of the usage of Croke Park Hours is currently in progress under the auspices of the Teachers' Conciliation Council.. (TCC). As proceedings at the TCC are confidential, it would not be appropriate for me to make any further comment at this time.

question.p: 808. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of early intervention classes in special schools, by county, in each of the years 2017 to 2021, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19581/26]

809. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of early intervention classes in special schools, by county, in each of the years 2021 to 2026, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19582/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 808 and 809 together.

Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).

The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which advocates that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.
A breakdown of special classes including class type for the years requested is available on the NCSE website.

My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

summary.i: Question No. 809 answered with Question No. 808.

question.p: 810. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Education and Youth his views on issues that have been raised in relation to curriculum in a school (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19583/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The Education Act, 1998 sets out the key roles and functions that are discharged by patrons and boards of management in the running of schools. The Act provides that it is the duty of the board of management to manage the school on behalf of the patron, for the benefit of the students and their parents and to provide or cause to be provided an appropriate education for each student at the school.

The governance structure of schools is such that, in accordance with the Act, the patron of a school does not have a direct role in the day-to-day management of the school which is a matter for the board of management. However, section 19 of the Education Act provides for the patron, where they are of the opinion that the functions of a board are not being effectively discharged, following issuing a notice to the board members and consideration of any representations received, to authorise any person or persons as the patron may deem appropriate to report to the patron on any matter arising from or relating to the operation of that board. While the patron is required to inform the Minister where they propose to exercise functions under section 19, there is no requirement for the patron to provide the Minister with any further detail in relation to the matter.

Where a parent has an issue with the school that cannot be resolved informally the school should have a formal complaints procedure that can be followed. This should be available on the school’s website. If not, a parent can contact the school directly and request a copy of their complaint procedures. Complaints regarding the principal should be directed to management authority of the school. Where a parent is of the view that a school's board of management has failed to investigate or adequately investigate a complaint, it is open to them to raise the matter directly with the Chairperson of the Board of Management by correspondence marked “Private and Confidential”.
The Department does not have a role in investigating or responding to parental complaints as it is not directly involved in the day-to-day management of schools.

question.p: 811. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason provision is not being made for an extension to a new school building (details supplied), despite having been agreed last year. [19585/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: My department is delivering a large scale major project to provide the schools referred to by the Deputy with new permanent accommodation and this project is currently well advanced at construction with an expected completion date in the fourth quarter of 2026. The school authorities were advised that it was necessary to make provision for special education at the two school buildings due to the significantly increased demand for classes in their school planning area.

The department examined various options for how best to meet this need including the feasibility of expanding the current scale of the project. However, due to the availability of spare classrooms in the current overall school project and projected falling mainstream demographics at primary level, the department decided that the use of these spare mainstream classrooms for special education provision was consistent with the Education and Youth Sector Sectoral Capital Plan 2026 to 2030 which was published in January, 2026. This decision was outlined to the school authorities in detail at a meeting with my department officials in January.

While the NDP funding of €7.5 billion for school capital projects is substantial, the Department must manage the progression of a large pipeline of projects and meet the substantially increased need for special education provision within this funding. The Department prioritises projects to balance urgency, equity, and available resources, ensuring that investments are sustainable and provide maximum value for money. This includes the optimum use of existing accommodation particularly surplus accommodation. This allows my department to keep a strong focus on the provision of additional capacity to cater for demographics, new housing developments and the rollout of additional special classes for children with additional needs. This approach reflects my department's fundamental objective of ensuring the availability of a school place for every child.

My department will support the schools in the practical arrangements for implementing this decision and has organised a meeting between the school authorities and the project's design team in order to explore practical solutions to address issues raised by the schools.

question.p: 812. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of emergency works applications that have been submitted by a school (details supplied) in relation to current roof issues; when they were submitted; and the reasons for refusal. [19589/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.

An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.

The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.

The school in question have submitted three EWS applications pertaining to roof works. The most recent, in February 2026, was a resubmission of a December 2023 roof works application . This application is currently being reviewed by the Departments technical team. Once feedback has been received the EWS will engage further with the school as appropriate.
In January 2021 the school in question submitted an EWS for roof works. This application was refused as the works being sought did not meet the criteria set out in Circular Letter 0068/2020.

question.p: 813. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review a case (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19611/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Under the Teaching Council Acts 2001-2015 the Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State. As such my Department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.

The Teaching Council registers teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations, 2025. As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. The qualification requirements for each route are set down in the Schedule of the Regulations.

As a statutory body, the Teaching Council is mandated by law to properly determine and to authenticate the relevant standards and qualifications of all applicants for registration, including those who have qualified outside of Ireland.

It is the Council’s responsibility to ensure that all teachers entering the profession in Ireland have met the required standards. These standards have been established following extensive consultation with relevant stakeholders, research, and in accordance with Department of Education policies and priorities and developed over a number of years.

The Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs (EPSEN) Act 2004 provides that people with special educational needs are educated in an inclusive environment, as far as possible and have the same right to access and benefit from education as children who don’t have these needs. Central to the Department's policy is that all teachers teaching children with Special Educational Needs (SEN) should be qualified Primary or Post-primary teachers in the first instance.

Cognisant that teacher education policies vary among countries, Route 4 of the Registration Regulations provides for teachers who have qualified outside of the Republic of Ireland with an initial teacher education programme in teaching children with special educational needs in primary and post-primary settings. These teachers must be fully recognised by the competent authority/teacher licensing body in the country in which they qualified and have completed any post qualification requirements such as teacher induction. These applications are assessed by the Teaching Council to ensure that they meet the requirements for Special Educational Needs (SEN) teaching in Ireland and that they are of an equivalent standard to those required in the State.

The standards for Initial Teacher Education (ITE) in Ireland are set out in the Council's policy ‘Céim: Standards for Initial Teacher Education’. All teacher education programmes in Ireland must be aligned with Céim to gain professional accreditation with the Teaching Council. The standards set Inclusive Education as one of the seven core elements which must unpin all aspects of the programme of ITE. Once primary or post-primary qualified, teachers may apply for professional development in the area of SEN. All applications for registration of teachers who qualified out-of-state are assessed to ensure they are of a comparable standard to those achieved by graduates of accredited initial teacher education programmes in Ireland. All applications from teachers who qualified outside of the Republic of Ireland are processed in line with the EU Directive 2005/36/EU (recognition of professional qualifications) and are assessed under its general system in the same manner, regardless of whether the applicant qualified within or outside of the EU. All applications for are assessed on an individual, case by case basis. The assessments are holistic and include the individual combination of relevant qualifications, teaching experience, and lifelong learning. The relevant criteria are equally applied to all applicants.

The assessment of applications enables the Council to accommodate teachers who may have shortfalls identified in their qualifications by providing conditional registration for up to three years to enable those shortfalls to be addressed.

The person referred to by the Deputy has the Irish Language Requirement as a condition of registration, which can be addressed via an Aptitude test (Scrudú le hAghaidh Cáilíochta sa Ghaeilge) or via an Adaptation Period (Oiriúnú le hAghaidh Cáilíochta sa Ghaeilge).

Marino Institute of Education administer both the SCG and the OCG. Both the SCG and OCG programmes are designed to ensure that primary teachers qualified outside ROI can demonstrate they are sufficiently qualified and competent to teach the Irish language.
Information on the Irish language requirements, including the fee schedule, can be found on a dedicated website, ilrweb.ie.
If applicants have not addressed their registration condition(s) within the three-year period, they can apply for an extension of time to meet the condition.

Extensions are granted at the discretion of the Council. Further details on extension requests are available on the Teaching Council website. If the conditions are not met within the timeframe and if an extension request is not granted, a teacher’s registration will lapse.

I would encourage the person that the Deputy is referring to in this query to continue to engage with the Teaching Council. The Teaching Council is best placed to provide further information to teachers registered with conditions as to how best to meet any mandated conditions.

question.p: 814. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Education and Youth if plans have advanced for a new school building in Cork (details supplied); to provide clarification on the delays associated with the project; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19612/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The project to which the deputy refers is devolved for delivery to the National Development Finance Agency (NDFA) as part of a programme of school building projects. (Project Lee bundle).
The project brief provides for the development of a new 12 Classroom Primary School with a 2 class Special Education Needs (SEN) base.

The project is currently at Stage 2b of the architectural process (post planning permission), which allows for detailed design/planning, obtaining the necessary statutory permissions and the preparation of tender documents. A final grant of planning permission was received in October 2025.

The department have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project roll out.

Of the total €7.55 billion investment it is envisaged that circa. €5 billion will be used for project roll out to support the delivery and modernisation of school buildings across the Large Scale, Additional Accommodation, Modular, and Annual September Accommodation Needs programmes. Over the course of 2026 and 2027 there will be construction work at circa 10% of the school estate. These projects will, when completed, provide circa 57,000 additional and modernised school places with a strong SEN focus in all projects.

The department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued roll out of projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, a list of the 105 school building projects in the first tranche to proceed to construction or tender over 2026 and 2027 has also been published.

These projects are in addition to the €781.77 million in capital funding for County Cork schools since 2020. Over that period a total of 155 schools have been upgraded through the provision of a new school building, a large-scale extension or provision of modular accommodation. There are also currently 19 school projects in County Cork under construction. Another 12 school projects will go to tender or construction in 2026 and 2027 and this summer 35 schools are approved to undergo works as part of the Summer Works Scheme/Climate Action Scheme..

The first tranche of 105 school building projects includes 80 large scale and Additional School Accommodation scheme projects. These projects were prioritised with a strong focus on maximising existing capacity and prioritising project rollout to meet the most urgent needs particularly to support special education needs provision. Firstly, to facilitate the 45 projects that are currently already at tender stage (Stage 3) so that they can progress to construction as smoothly as possible over the course of 2026 and 2027.? Secondly, to facilitate 35 projects that currently have planning permission and are at pre-tender stage (Stage 2b) and have been prioritised to meet urgent requirements from a special needs perspective or to provide additional capacity to cater for demographics or to address very significant condition issues at the schools.

The department recognises that there are schools with important building projects that are not included in the first tranche of prioritised projects. As part of planning ahead for the next tranche of projects to progress to tender, the department-led prioritisation process will continue over the course of 2026 and 2027 to assess and evaluate the progression of individual projects through the design pipeline having regard to the continual need to maximise existing capacity and determine the prioritised needs going forward. This process will involve engagement with key stakeholders and individual schools and will ultimately inform the next tranches of programme rollout to tender. The department-led Energy and Condition Survey of the school estate, which will be finalised later in 2026, will provide an additional evidence base for assessing priorities.

Based on this ongoing prioritisation process some projects may be added to the list over the course of 2026 and 2027 having regard to their prioritisation and urgency of need and taking account also of the ongoing ability to progress them to tender and construction within the parameters of overall funding. Where appropriate, the department will also assess opportunities to undertake advance enabling works for the most urgent and complex projects to facilitate a smooth progression to construction in 2028 and beyond.

Any interim accommodation requirements will continue to be assessed and considered by the department on a case-by-case basis to determine the prioritised needs and approach for addressing same. The accommodation needs at Gaelscoil Chionn tSáile will be considered as part of the ongoing overall department-led prioritisation process, in consultation with the school’s patron and school authorities.
The NDFA will continue to engage directly with the respective school authorities to keep them fully informed of progress on this important project.

The current status of all projects continues to be set out under item number ten at the following link: [www.gov.ie]. This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender and construction.

question.p: 815. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will provide the outcome of a recent SNA review which was carried out at a school (details supplied); if the outcome is not yet available to provide an approximate timeframe for when this outcome will be available to the school; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19624/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: This government is fully committed to supporting children with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
Special education funding will exceed €3 billion in 2026 – up 58% since 2020 and the highest amount ever provided.

Special needs assistants (SNAs) play a key role in the successful inclusion of students with additional and significant care needs in schools to enable them to achieve their best outcomes and reach their full potential.

The number of SNAs allocated to schools nationally has increased by 45% between the 2020/21 school year and the present. By the end of the 2026/27 school year there will be close to 25,000 SNAs in our mainstream classes, special classes and special schools. It is important to note that there have been increases in SNAs in all counties and across all education settings since 2020, including mainstream, special classes and special schools.
I have listened carefully to all of the issues raised by parents and school communities.
It has now been agreed that there will be no reductions to special needs assistants for the next school year 2026/27.
All schools reviewed by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE) and allocated additional resources will receive them in the upcoming school year.
It was agreed that the SNA redeployment scheme, the SNA workforce development plan and changes to a 2014 circular outlining the role of a SNA will be advanced before any further decisions are taken.
The priority will be to ensure that the child-centred approach to the provision of special education is retained and enhanced in these policy developments.

After these key documents are agreed and published, the NCSE can commence reviews of supports provided to schools for the 2027/28 academic year which will uphold the integrity of the process, which allocates supports based on the needs of children.

The department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

question.p: 817. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to the emergency works application by a school (details supplied); the actions she will take to expedite this application to reflect the urgency in progressing these works; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19681/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.

An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property, or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.

The EWS operates on the basis of the minimal scope of works required to remedy an emergency situation. The EWS usually provides an interim solution until such time as a comprehensive solution can be provided under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS).
The application in question has already been approved and is with the school to progress.

question.p: 818. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the funding streams, emergency works schemes, or capital supports which are available to a school (details supplied) for the purposes of undertaking essential roof repairs and addressing severe mould issues within the school building. [19726/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I should explain that applications relating to the provision of funding for issues relating to an existing school building can fall under a number of different delivery mechanisms including, most frequently, the Summer Works Scheme and the Emergency Works Scheme.

The purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.

An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property, or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening. The EWS remains open on a year-round basis and it is open to the school in question to make an application for funding for any issues it believes may meet the criteria under the EWS.

The EWS operates on the basis of the minimal scope of works required to remedy an emergency situation. The EWS usually provides an interim solution until such time as a comprehensive solution can be provided under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS).

The purpose of the SWS is to enable individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis and, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school.

The Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (which was previously named the Summer Works Scheme) places a strong emphasis on sustainability. Schools can now undertake additional measures such as insulation upgrades, LED lighting installation, EV charger provision, bike rack facilities to support active travel and other climate-focused works alongside traditional maintenance.

In the case of the school in question my department can confirm an application was received from the school in question however the school was not on the list of approvals in the first tranche. Given that funding is limited in any particular year it is necessary to prioritise applications. Under the new climate action summer works scheme which operates on a multi annual basis, like previous summer works schemes, applications from schools that are not reached for funding or market prioritisation reasons in 2026 will qualify to be assessed for purposes of the funding available for climate action summer works in subsequent years.
It is anticipated that the next tranche of approvals will be in the latter half of 2026.

Full details of the of the announcement and the list of schools approved in the first tranche, the Circular (0029/2025) for the scheme and guidance documents for schools can be found at the below link;

question.p: 819. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Education and Youth reason two SEN classroom extensions requested by her Department are not now being provided alongside an ongoing project (details supplied); if reasoning is based on budgetary constraints; if so, the reason funding was not available for these important classroom additions; if the decision to omit the SEN classrooms will be reviewed and overturned given the need for increased special education capacity in the area; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19739/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: My department is delivering a large scale major project to provide the schools referred to by the Deputy with new permanent accommodation and this project is currently well advanced at construction with an expected completion date in the fourth quarter of 2026. The school authorities were advised that it was necessary to make provision for special education at the two school buildings due to the significantly increased demand for classes in their school planning area.

The department examined various options for how best to meet this need including the feasibility of expanding the current scale of the project. However, due to the availability of spare classrooms in the current overall school project and projected falling mainstream demographics at primary level, the department decided that the use of these spare mainstream classrooms for special education provision was consistent with the Education and Youth Sector Sectoral Capital Plan 2026 to 2030 which was published in January, 2026. This decision was outlined to the school authorities in detail at a meeting with my department officials in January.

While the NDP funding of €7.5 billion for school capital projects is substantial, the Department must manage the progression of a large pipeline of projects and meet the substantially increased need for special education provision within this funding. The Department prioritises projects to balance urgency, equity, and available resources, ensuring that investments are sustainable and provide maximum value for money. This includes the optimum use of existing accommodation particularly surplus accommodation. This allows my department to keep a strong focus on the provision of additional capacity to cater for demographics, new housing developments and the rollout of additional special classes for children with additional needs. This approach reflects my department's fundamental objective of ensuring the availability of a school place for every child.

My department will support the schools in the practical arrangements for implementing this decision and has organised a meeting between the school authorities and the project's design team in order to explore practical solutions to address issues raised by the schools.

question.p: 820. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Education and Youth to consider providing transport funding for schools who qualify for a championship (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19740/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.

Children are eligible for school transport where they satisfy the distance criterion and are attending their nearest national school or post primary education centre, having regard to ethos and language.

In accordance with the terms of my Department's School Transport Scheme, school transport services operate during the standard school year and facilitate a child's attendance in school. Transport to the event referred to by the Deputy does not come under the remit of the scheme.

question.p: 821. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Education and Youth the steps being taken to ensure that teachers are being supported to teach STEM; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19741/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: This Government is committed to ensuring that every child has a positive school experience, with access to qualified and engaged teachers who are dedicated to supporting their learning.

The Department of Education and Youth’s STEM Education Policy Statement 2017–2026 sets out the ambitious goals and actions required to achieve and improve the STEM education experience and outcomes for all learners from early learning and care to post-primary school.

The Redeveloped Primary School Curriculum is for all children attending primary and special schools and consists of the Primary Curriculum Framework (2023) and five curriculum specifications (published September 2025) which includes the STEM Education Specification (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics Education). Enactment of the curriculum is supported by professional learning and online resources.
In addition, a range of measures have been introduced to encourage more people to take up teaching STEM subjects.

Budget 2025 introduced a €2,000 annual bursary for student teachers in STEM fields (including maths, chemistry, physics, biology, computer science and engineering) during the final two years of their undergraduate teacher education, with a requirement to complete at least 2 years of post-qualification teaching in a recognised post-primary school. The aim of the scheme is to encourage more students to train as STEM teachers to help increase the number available to post-primary schools. The Department issued Circular 0019/2026 Concurrent Initial Teacher Education Bursary Scheme (STEM Bursary) in January 2026 setting out the eligibility criteria and application process.

Budgets 2024 and 2025 included the expansion of upskilling programmes including in STEM subjects, free to teachers, aimed at increasing the number of qualified teachers in high-demand subjects and reducing out-of-field teaching. New programmes including in computer science commenced in 2025 which complement existing programmes including Maths and Physics.

Those teachers who complete an upskilling programme will be able to apply to the Teaching Council for an additional subject to be added to their registration record. In the course of completing a programme each participant will be provided with content knowledge and empowered to become an effective and enthusiastic teacher of the particular subject. These flexible programmes boost teachers’ employment opportunities while addressing subject-specific teacher shortages.

The Department continues to promote the teaching profession through development of the Teaching Transforms campaign, which promotes the teaching profession and encourages students to follow a career in teaching. Promotion campaigns have been developed to coincide with the CAO closing date and change of mind deadline in recent years.

These measures reflect the commitment to ongoing investment in the education system and are designed to ensure a steady flow of qualified teachers, including in STEM subjects, into the profession. I am considering further measures to strengthen the teaching workforce and ensure schools have the support needed to provide an excellent education for every student.

question.p: 823. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide details of the €300 million to be used as a contingency fund for 2026 to 2030 period under the NDP Sectoral Plan; the way in which projects will be deemed eligible for funding under this stream; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19764/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, I have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

Over €2 billion will used to support the operation of the existing school estate through clarity and certainty on Minor Works and ICT grants, rollout of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme, delivery of climate initiatives, continued support for school maintenance through our emergency and summer works schemes and facilitating annual payments for existing schools built and operated under Public Private Partnerships.

The remaining €300 million, which represents just under 4% of the total allocation, will operate as contingency funding not as a separate funding stream for school projects. The contingency fund is allocated over a 5-year period to provide flexibility for a variety of potential issues including unforeseen site conditions, planning restrictions, or minor changes in project briefs. It also assists in safeguarding the programme against inflation and market fluctuations.
