The earlier sanctioning of new classes provides clarity for parents and allows schools more time for the planning and establishment of new special classes. The vast majority of new special classes being announced are being provided in available school accommodation which is being reconfigured as a special class. Each special class at primary level is allocated 1 teacher and 2 SNAs and at post-primary level, schools receive 1.5 teachers and 2 SNAs. Details of the new special classes are available on the NCSE website.

Of the 351 new special classes, 237 are being established in primary schools and 114 in post-primary schools. New special classes are being established in every county with 78 new special classes confirmed for Dublin so far. Further details on additional new special classes will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that sufficient special education placements remain available for students with special educational needs and will continue to review and monitor the situation as to where new specialist provision is required.

question.p: 849. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Education and Youth the definition of an "appropriate place" used by her Department; to consider ensuring that it include an equal opportunity for the child to attend their local school; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19976/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).

The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which promotes that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.

The Minister for Education and Youth has the function pursuant to s.7 of the Education Act 1998 (“the 1998 Act”), inter alia, having regard to the resources available, to ensure, subject to the provisions of that Act, that there is made available to each person resident in the State, including a person with a disability or who has other special educational needs, support services and a level and quality of education appropriate to meeting the needs and abilities of that person; to determine national educational policy; and to plan and coordinate the provision of education in recognised schools.

It is a matter for each parent/guardian to apply to a school of their choice for an educational placement for their child. It is a matter for each school to set and implement an admission policy, in accordance with the provisions of the 1998 Act.

If an application for enrolment is accepted by a school, the department makes the necessary supports available to that school to support the placement, in accordance with existing resources and general policy.

The department provides for a range of placement options and supports for schools and students with special educational needs in order to ensure that wherever a child is enrolled, they will have access to an appropriate education.

My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

question.p: 850. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Education and Youth her current plans to increase the amount of school places for special classes in mainstream schools; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19977/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.

My department and the NCSE continue to work closely with school patron bodies, school management bodies and schools to confirm new special classes for the next school year 2026/2027. The NCSE began sanctioning new special classes in January of this year, which is several months earlier than last year. 351 have been sanctioned to date and many more new special classes will be confirmed in the coming weeks. The earlier sanctioning of new classes provides clarity for parents and allows schools more time for the planning and establishment of new special classes. The vast majority of new special classes being announced are being provided in available school accommodation which is being reconfigured as a special class. Each special class at primary level is allocated 1 teacher and 2 SNAs and at post-primary level, schools receive 1.5 teachers and 2 SNAs. Details of the new special classes are available on the NCSE website.

Of the 351 new special classes, 237 are being established in primary schools and 114 in post-primary schools. New special classes are being established in every county. Further details on additional new special classes will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that sufficient special education placements remain available for students with special educational needs and will continue to review and monitor the situation as to where new specialist provision is required.

question.p: 851. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of schools in the Longford-Westmeath constituency that have received approval for a new school building but where construction has not yet commenced; and if she will provide a list of those schools; and the current status of each project.; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20022/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, I have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

The department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, I have also published a list of the 105 school building projects in the first tranche to proceed to construction or tender over 2026 and 2027. This list includes 1 project in the constituency of Longford and Westmeath. In addition, 6 schools are approved to undergo works as part of the Summer Works Scheme / Climate Action scheme this summer.

These projects are in addition to over €222 million in capital funding for schools in Longford and Westmeath since 2020. Over that period, a total of 47 schools have been upgraded either through provision of a new school building, a large-scale extension or provision of modular accommodation. There are also currently 11 school projects in Longford and Westmeath constituency under construction. Since 2020 a total of 87 special classes have been opened in Longford, of which 16 were sanctioned for September 2026.
I recognise that there are schools with important building projects that are not included in the first tranche of prioritised projects.

As part of planning ahead for the next tranche of projects to progress to tender, the department-led prioritisation process will continue over the course of 2026 and 2027 to assess and evaluate the progression of individual projects through the design pipeline having regard to the continual need to maximise existing capacity and determine the prioritised needs going forward. This process will involve engagement with key stakeholders and individual schools and will ultimately inform the next tranches of programme rollout to tender. The department-led Energy and Condition Survey of the school estate, which will be finalised later in 2026, will provide an additional evidence base for assessing priorities.

Based on this ongoing prioritisation process some projects may be added to the list over the course of 2026 and 2027 having regard to their prioritisation and urgency of need and taking account also of the ongoing ability to progress them to tender and construction within the parameters of overall funding. Where appropriate, the department will also assess opportunities to undertake advance enabling works for the most urgent and complex projects to facilitate a smooth progression to construction in 2028 and beyond.
Any interim accommodation requirements will continue to be assessed and considered by the department on a case-by-case basis to determine the prioritised needs and approach for addressing same.

The current status of all projects, including those in the Longford Westmeath constituency, is set out under item number ten at the following link (www.gov.ie). This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender and construction.

question.p: 852. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will address the serious concerns raised regarding the implementation of the new Senior Cycle Science Assessment and Accreditation of Learning Components (AACs), including the absence of sample AAC reports, the lack of marking schemes for sample written examination papers, insufficient clarity on project requirements, disparity of science and IT resources across schools, and the impact of these deficiencies on students and teachers (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20035/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, the Programme for Government commits to ‘continue the programme of reform of Senior Cycle to ensure that students benefit from up-to-date curricula, more diverse skills development and assessments, and reduced stress levels.’

As of September 2025, the revised Leaving Certificate science specifications and their associated Additional Assessment Components (AACs) are the established curriculum being followed by students. The live briefs for relevant Tranche 1 subjects were published by the SEC in January 2026. Students, teachers, and their schools are now actively working on their AACs in terms of planning and preparing for the various stages or phases involved in their completion.

AACs are designed to assess students’ skills and key competencies in a way that a terminal written examination cannot. Students will learn through exploring, analysing and investigating – not all of which involves laboratory work.

Through a combination of the Science Implementation Support Grant paid to schools in December 2024; the expanded science subject grant for the 2025/26 school year paid in December 2025; and the Climate Action Summer Works commitment announced in November 2025, approximately €45m in additional funding has been committed to the science subjects since the redeveloped science specifications were published. More generally, approximately 300 new or modernised science labs have been delivered since 2020.

In January, €35m in ICT grants funding issued to Primary and Post-Primary schools for the 2025/2026 school year. The €35 million in ICT grant funding represents the fourth tranche of ICT funding under the Digital Strategy and builds on the €135 million that has issued to date under the current strategy in addition to the €210 million issued under the previous strategy. Funding issues as a lump sum per school, plus a per capita amount, with an enhanced per capita rate for students enrolled in DEIS and Special schools and to pupils in mainstream special class primary settings. Using this model of funding, all schools are treated equally, fairly and transparently.
The introduction the revised science specifications is being supported by key publications and through a comprehensive programme of Teacher Professional Learning (TPL) provided by Oide.

The specifications published in August 2024 include a section on descriptors of quality for the AACs. In November 2024, the NCCA published Guidelines to support the Science in Practice Investigations which include setting out the steps involved over time and provide clarity on the role of the teacher.

SEC has provided a substantial body of material to support implementation, including sample written examination papers, sample and live AAC briefs, and supporting FAQ material for schools and teachers.

The published sample examination papers support familiarisation with the structure, format and level of demand of the papers and indicate the marks available for each question. In addition, the AAC briefs, both sample and live, set out how marks are allocated across the areas of content and provide clear guidance on how the AAC should be completed and presented.

The AAC briefs have been designed to facilitate a wide range of student approaches and to encourage student agency in how a brief is approached. Moreover, the AACs in LC sciences have been designed to support a process that is integrated longitudinally in teaching and learning, rather than merely the production of a report to be submitted for external assessment. The materials provided are intended to support that objective while giving students the flexibility to demonstrate their learning in a meaningful way. To publish sample AAC reports would be unhelpful in communicating the conceptualisation of science AACs as process rather than product.

The SEC has advised that examination papers and sample papers are not pretested. It is only when there is the added information of how candidates have actually engaged with and responded to questions in an examination setting that a suitable, effective and fair marking scheme can be produced. As a result, in line with established practice, and in the interest of absolute fairness, the SEC does not provide sample answers or marking schemes for sample papers.
More broadly, the SEC’s approach is guided by the need to ensure clarity, fairness and consistency for candidates, while also maintaining the integrity of the assessment process.

In relation to Generative Artificial Intelligence, the recently published SEC document Coursework Rules and Procedures 2025/2026 sets out the acceptable use and appropriate acknowledgement of AI tools in coursework.

A focus of all TPL provided explores how effective classroom learning and teaching develop students’ key competencies and support engagement with the AAC and the final examination. Teachers have engaged with full day Professional Learning Experiences (PLE) and a suite of collaborative events for each science subject.

A webinar specifically designed in collaboration with the SEC to support teacher engagement with the sample examination papers was provided immediately following the publication of the sample papers. 3,338 teachers across the three Science subjects attended.

This year, a full-day PLE was provided which focused explicitly on the AAC. This TPL involved detailed analysis of the AAC Guidelines, close examination of the learning outcomes assessed through the AAC, and practical exploration of how these learning outcomes can be embedded within classroom practice. Teachers engaged directly with the sample AAC brief and related materials to ensure a shared understanding of expectations.

Collectively, these measures demonstrate a coherent and sustained programme of professional learning support, ensuring that teachers are fully prepared to implement and support the AAC within the new science specifications.

My officials and I will continue to engage with all our education partners to ensure the redevelopment of senior cycle responds to the needs of our students, preparing them for their future lives in education and the workforce while upholding the high standards of fairness and equity for which the Leaving Certificate is known.

question.p: 853. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if the Special Transport Grant is available to young adult service users who are no longer in school (details supplied). [20036/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: The service referred to in this case is outside of the remit of the Department's School Transport Schemes. Responsibility for Day Services falls under the remit of the Department of Children, Equality and Disability/ HSE.

question.p: 854. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth to account for the historic development of the Irish-language exemption policy in the education system; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20037/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I can advise the Deputy that exemptions from the study of Irish have been in place since the foundation of the state when Irish became a core subject for all students.

Originally, exemptions catered for the needs for the children of diplomats and consular staff. Over time, the circumstance in which exemptions may be granted have broadened reflecting changes in our schools and society and from the 1990s have included special education needs in tandem with the integration of children with special education needs in mainstream education in line with the U.N. Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC 1989).

Following a comprehensive review of policy and practice in relation to exemptions from the study of Irish conducted by the department’s Inspectorate during 2014-2016, an extensive public consultation process was conducted in late 2018/early 2019, which informed the current circulars.
The key changes in the current circulars include:
• Application of the exemption policy to English-medium schools only
• Increase in the age at which an exemption can be granted to a student from abroad from 11 years of age to 12 years of age
• Explicit provision for students in special schools and special classes
• Inclusion of an appeals process

• Aligning the exemption system to the Special Education Teaching Allocation model that allows mainstream schools to provide additional teaching support for all students who require such support in their school based on their identified learning needs in school, as opposed to being based primarily upon a diagnosis of a particular disability.

• Aligning the exemption system to the Continuum of Support process which is focused on identifying and catering for the special educational needs of individual students in proportion to the impact of those needs on their learning and socialisation.

• Setting out department policy and expectation that all students should be encouraged to participate in Irish language and cultural activities, to the greatest extent possible and in a meaningful way, at a level appropriate to the students learning needs.

• Provision for students who experience a high level of multiple and persistent needs that are a significant barrier to the student’s participation and engagement in their learning and school life following two years of documented targeted intervention set out in a student support plan.
The number of exemptions granted by schools must be seen in the broader context:
• School enrolments at post-primary level have increased from 362,899 in 2018/19 to 425,411 in 2024/25, representing an increase of 17% at post-primary level.
• In 2024/25, there were 56,555 non-Irish nationals enrolled in post-primary schools.
• Over 17,000 students from Ukraine are currently enrolled in our schools, over 10,000 at primary level and over 7,000 at post-primary.

• The number of children with more complex special educational needs is increasing and this is evidenced by the almost 1,700 new special classes that have been provided in mainstream schools over the last five years and special school enrolments are increasing by 300 each year.

• There are almost 28,000 students with special educational needs enrolled in special classes and special schools in the 2024/2025 school year. This equates to almost 3% of our overall primary and post-primary student population.

The Department of Education and Youth is committed to the Irish language as a core element of the school curriculum. Irish is a vital part of our national identity and educational heritage, and its promotion remains a key priority.
The department is supporting the teaching, learning and assessment of Irish through a range of initiatives including:

“Is féidir liom, is féidir linn…”• The Action Plan for Irish in English-Medium Schools 2025 – 2027 was published in November 2025. It is a two year plan which aims to support schools and teachers to improve the teaching, learning and use of Irish, and to provide children and young people with more engaging and rewarding learning experiences. In particular, the Action Plan will support the development of pupils’/students’ oral language skills.
• The Policy on Gaeltacht Education
• The Policy for Irish-Medium Education outside of the Gaeltacht,

• Ongoing expansion of the Content and Learning Integrated Language (CLIL) project providing sustained support for teachers to adopt the CLIL approach to teaching another subject or element of a subject through Irish
• The PE through Irish project with resources now available for Junior Infants to 2nd Class and 3rd and 4th Class resources under development.
• Funding to Foras na Gaeilge for a range of projects including the
• Gaelbhratach programme
• Seideán Sí resource for primary level
• A lexicography project
• Increased resourcing of An Chomhairle um Oideachas Gaeltacht agus Gaelscolaíochta (COGG)

question.p: 855. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Education and Youth when the ongoing review of the special needs assistant contract will be completed; if this review will include consideration of updated qualification and skills requirements for the role; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20052/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: I would like to thank the Deputy for their question. My department recognises the value of the special needs assistant (SNA) role in the successful inclusion of students with additional and significant care needs in schools to enable them to achieve their best outcomes and reach their full potential.

You may be aware that my department is progressing the first Special Needs Assistants Workforce Development Plan (the plan) scheduled for delivery later this year. This plan provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and supporting the SNA role and will introduce a series of policy developments to strengthen clarity, direction and consistency within the workforce.
Proposals for the plan have been developed in consultation with SNAs, parents, children, , school management bodies, unions and other key stakeholders.
The plan comprises five main pillars:
1. Review and Development of the SNA role
2. Establishment of a Quality Framework
3. Establishment of an SNA Learning and Development Programme
4. Supporting SNA Recruitment, Retention and Diversity
5. Development of a Communications Strategy
The publication of the plan later in 2026 will be followed by an implementation period.

The work in progress under Pillar 4 Supporting SNA Recruitment, Retention and Diversity includes an extensive review of the SNA contract of employment currently set out in circulars 12/2005 and 15/2005 which will fulfil a commitment under the Building Momentum public service agreement.

The contract review, is at an advanced stage under Pillar 4 of the plan and involves a full reconsideration of all contract provisions and arrangements to comply with current employment legislation and to align with work on the SNA Workforce Development Plan.

Circular 0051/2019 – Recruitment and Appointment Procedures for Special Needs Assistants (SNAs) sets out the current minimum educational requirements for appointment to the post of SNA i.e. a level 3 qualification on the National Framework of Qualifications or a minimum of three grade Ds in the Junior Certificate, or equivalent. The working groups under pillar one, three and four of the plan are also considering the current minimum educational requirement for entry to the SNA role and determining what changes, if any, may be required.

In 2024, my department conducted a comprehensive national survey of SNAs which was completed by 7,410 SNAs, representing approximately 35% of the SNA workforce. Feedback from this survey indicates that 70% of the SNA Workforce hold an NFQ Level 6 or higher. This data has helped to develop a deeper knowledge and understanding of the role of the SNA in the different educational settings and to explore and enhance the role that SNAs play in facilitating inclusion. The Report on National Survey of Special Needs Assistants has been published on www.gov.ie. As part of these deliberations due consideration is to be given to the findings in reports from research conducted with the SNAs, teachers and school leaders. These reports are also available on the SNA Information Hub: SNA Publications.
Further updates, including information on the revised circular, will be published on the SNA Information Hub on www.gov.ie in due course as work progresses.

question.p: 856. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding an application of a school (details supplied) made under the climate action summer works scheme 2026 (category 7 climate action & windows); when the school will be notified of a decision; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20098/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The purpose of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) is to enable individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.

It is envisaged that approvals in any given year will involve a spread of categories rather than the traditional single category at a time. This is aimed at managing market capacity and maximising value for money opportunities for school authorities.

In November 2025, my colleague the former Minister of Education and Youth, Helen McEntee TD, announced the first tranche of approvals under the new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme. 297 projects were approved to proceed and involve primary, post primary and special schools, along with projects in all counties and across all categories of works.

My Department can confirm an application was received from the school in question however the school was not on the list of approvals in the first tranche. Given that funding is limited in any particular year it is necessary to prioritise applications. Under the new climate action summer works scheme which operates on a multi annual basis, like previous summer works schemes, applications from schools that are not reached for funding or market prioritisation reasons in 2026 will qualify to be assessed for purposes of the funding available for climate action summer works in subsequent years.
It is anticipated that the next tranche of approvals will be in the latter half of 2026.

Full details of the of the announcement and the list of schools approved in the first tranche, the Circular (0029/2025) for the scheme and guidance documents for schools can be found at the below link;

question.p: 857. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason students will be charged the full cost of leaving certificate fees in June 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20102/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Following the Government’s Budget 2026 announcement last October, examination entry fees will recommence for upcoming state examinations in 2026, at the same level as when they were last charged in 2019:
• €116 per entry for a Senior Cycle/Leaving Certificate candidate and
• €109 per entry for a Junior Cycle candidate.

In line with the arrangements which applied when fees were last charged, candidates who hold a full medical card, or who are covered for all services on a parent or guardian’s full medical card, are exempt from examination fees. It should be noted that the rate of examination entry fees has not been increased since 2012.

The State Examinations Commission advised schools in October 2025 that fees would be charged for the 2026 State examinations. A circular with further detail in relation to the SEC's Online Fee Service issued to schools this month. Full details of all fee rates are available here.

question.p: 858. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth if a child requires a medical card to be exempt from the leaving certificate fees; or is it sufficient that the parent has one; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20103/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Following the Government’s Budget 2026 announcement last October, examination entry fees will recommence for upcoming state examinations in 2026, at the same level as when they were last charged in 2019:
• €116 per entry for a Senior Cycle/Leaving Certificate candidate and
• €109 per entry for a Junior Cycle candidate.

In line with the arrangements which applied when fees were last charged, candidates who hold a full medical card, or who are covered for all services on a parent or guardian’s full medical card, are exempt from examination fees. It should be noted that the rate of examination entry fees has not been increased since 2012.
Full details of all fee rates are available here.

question.p: 859. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will consider including a school (details supplied) in County Meath in DEIS Band 1; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20104/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Addressing educational disadvantage is a priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth.

Currently, the DEIS programme supports almost 1,200 primary and post primary schools reaching approximately 260,000 students, with an annual investment of €180 million. Budget 2026 allocates an additional €16.5 million in 2026, rising to €48 million in 2027, to support the implementation of the new DEIS Strategy and introduce the DEIS Plus scheme.

The DEIS programme is targeted at schools with the highest concentrations of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage. Schools that were included in the most recent expansion of the programme in 2022 were those with the highest concentrations of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage as identified through the refined DEIS identification model. Those urban primary schools having the very highest concentrations of children and young people experiencing educational disadvantage were assigned Urban Band 1. Schools were not required to apply for inclusion in the DEIS programme, and the model was applied fairly and equally to all schools. A detailed paper on the refined DEIS identification model is available on gov.ie.
This government currently provides a range of supports that are available to all schools to help address disadvantage and create a more inclusive education system. These include:

• Inspectorate support helps improve education provision for all children and young people. They promote best practice and school improvement by advising teachers, principals and boards of management in schools.

• National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) provides educational psychological service to all primary and post-primary schools and special schools to support the well-being, academic, social and emotional development of all learners.

• The Special Education Teaching (SET) allocation provides a unified allocation for special education support teaching needs to each school based on each school’s educational profile and also encompasses an element of Language (EAL) support allocation. Under this SET model, schools are frontloaded with resources to provide support immediately to those pupils who need it without delay.

• Free schoolbooks are provided to all children and young people in the free education system. Through the Department of Social Protection, the School Meals Programme provides regular, nutritious food to children to support them in taking full advantage of the education provided to them.
• The Hot School Meals Programme is available to all primary schools, meaning that approximately 3,700 schools and organisations and 682,000 children are now eligible for the Schools Meals Programme.

My department is committed to addressing educational disadvantage in all schools to ensure all children can reach their potential. To this end, a new ten-year DEIS Strategy to 2035, will be published in the coming weeks. The new strategy will introduce innovative solutions to address educational disadvantage and continue to address the gap between DEIS and non-DEIS schools.

Over its lifetime, the new DEIS Strategy will focus on improving the opportunities and achievement levels of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage, developing more innovative approaches to tackling educational disadvantage, and working towards a more flexible system of supports to ensure that a school can receive the right support at the right time.
Any future changes to the identification model and overall allocation of resources will be considered within the context of the new ten-year DEIS Strategy.

question.p: 860. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 629 of 10 February 2026, if correspondence will be forwarded to the personnel in her Department who is dealing with this issue; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20105/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Further to Parliamentary Question No. 629 of 10 February 2026 in relation to the school referred to by the Deputy, my Department has been liaising with the Design Team in relation to the inflation agreement issue. My Department recently received additional information from the Design Team which is currently under review. The Design Team will be in contact with the Contractor once this review is complete.

question.p: 861. Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the funding avenues (grants, departmental supports, pilot schemes, discretionary or otherwise) that are available to a school (details supplied) for the provision of a small greenhouse and outdoor classroom on the school's grounds; if she will ask her Department to liaise with the school's management to investigate if funding such a project is possible; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20155/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I can advise the Deputy that under the 2nd National Strategy on Education for Sustainable Development – ESD to 2030, funding is available to schools for ESD projects.

In 2025, €860,000 was delivered to 390 primary and post primary schools across the country for a wide range of ESD projects including the development of school gardens and outdoor classrooms, forest schools, recycling systems, biodigesters and food waste management systems, composting systems, fast fashion projects, recycling initiatives, irrigation and rainwater collection systems, energy education initiatives, student led sustainability projects, teacher professional learning and a range of sustainability themed workshops.
7 primary schools and 3 post-primary schools in Co. Mayo received ESD to 2030 funding totalling €22,500.

Grants of up to €2,500 were available to schools in 2025 and the ESD projects funded were required to include an element of “local community action for sustainability”, a priority area in our ESD to 2030 strategy. Schools will report on their projects at the end of the 2025/26 school year and are also committed to publishing their schools Sustainability Policy Statement in accordance with the School Sector Climate Action Mandate. The department is mapping these Sustainability Policy Statements.

An ESD funding call will again issue to schools in September 2026 through the department's quarterly ESD Newsletter which issues to all schools and to which individuals can also subscribe. The ESD Newsletter contains lots of information on funding opportunities, resources, programmes, examples of best practice from primary and post primary schools around the country, teacher professional learning events, competitions etc., to support schools in their ESD related activities.

A further €466,000 in ESD to 2030 funding was provided to 21 organisations in 2025 to support a range of ESD programmes and supports for schools including the Nature Explorer Programme, the Picker Pals programme, the Heritage Keepers programme, the Farmer Time programme, the Wise Water programme, the Wool in School programme and the Grow it Yourself programme. Other projects include the Climate and Nature Summit, the Rubbish Film Festival and the student led Civil Engagement Roadshow. Many of the projects include workshops for students and engagement by students with local level and community action.

In addition to funding provided to schools, the department provided €498,246 in grant funding to ten national youth organisations and associated partner organisations under the Youth Climate Justice Fund in 2025. Grants were awarded to carry out youth-led projects related to climate justice at community, regional and national level.

A total of €10 million was allocated in December 2025 to primary and special schools in the free education system to support the purchase of physical resources aligned with the new Wellbeing Specification.

Funding may be used to purchase durable, reusable, low-maintenance and weather-resistant resources that support well-being activities including PE and outdoor learning. This can include items such as outdoor and adventure resources, playground materials, weatherproof picnic tables and benches, and long-term storage solutions for PE and well-being equipment, including indoor and weatherproof outdoor options.

ESD to 2030 aims to ensure that all learners acquire the skills needed to promote sustainable development in accordance with Sustainable Development Goal target 4.7. ESD incorporates the three interdependent and interlinked strands of sustainable development: Social Sustainability, Economic Sustainability and Environmental Sustainability.
ESD to 2030 contributes to delivery of the Climate Action Plan and the Sustainable Development Goals National Implementation Plan.

Further details on ESD to 2030 funding, the ESD to 2030 strategy, all issues of the ESD Newsletter, the Sustainability Toolkit for Schools and map of Schools Sustainability Policy Statements are all available on the ESD to 2030 webpage here: National Strategy on Education for Sustainable Development in Ireland
Further details on the Youth Climate Justice Funding is available here: Minister McEntee announces €498,000 for youth climate projects
Department officials have engaged directly with the Principal of the school on this matter as requested by the Deputy.

question.p: 862. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if provision can be made to allow a pupil (details supplied) to repeat sixth class as the pupil in question will only be aged 11 on enrolling at secondary school. [20157/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The primary school curriculum is designed as an eight-year course, including a two-year infant cycle followed by six years in standards from first to sixth, with children progressing to the next grade at the end of each school year.
My Department's policy in regard to the retention of pupils in primary schools is set out in Primary Circular 32/03 ‘Retention of Pupils in same Grade in Primary Schools’ (link available [here]).

Circular 32/03 recognises that in exceptional circumstances a school may conclude a pupil or student would benefit educationally by repeating a grade level having first consulted with the Special Educational Needs teacher, class teacher and parents. In such circumstances there should be a clear programme outlined for such a pupil that records precisely what new approach will be used for the pupil and what its expected benefit will be.

In summary decisions in relation to requests to repeat a year are only approved by the principal provided there is an educational basis for it, and it is clear that all parties agree that the pupil would benefit educationally by repeating a class.

question.p: 867. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Education and Youth to review an application from a school (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20220/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The purpose of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) is to enable individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.

It is envisaged that approvals in any given year will involve a spread of categories rather than the traditional single category at a time. This is aimed at managing market capacity and maximising value for money opportunities for school authorities.

In November 2025, my colleague the former Minister of Education and Youth, Helen McEntee TD, announced the first tranche of approvals under the new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme. 297 projects were approved to proceed and involve primary, post primary and special schools, along with projects in all counties and across all categories of works.

My Department can confirm an application was received from the school in question however the school was not on the list of approvals in the first tranche. Given that funding is limited in any particular year it is necessary to prioritise applications. Under the new climate action summer works scheme which operates on a multi annual basis, like previous summer works schemes, applications from schools that are not reached for funding or market prioritisation reasons in 2026 will qualify to be assessed for purposes of the funding available for climate action summer works in subsequent years.
It is anticipated that the next tranche of approvals will be in the latter half of 2026.

question.p: 871. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Education and Youth the procedures which apply where a student with a disability experiences significant distress or makes a mental health disclosure linked to difficulties accessing the curriculum; the way in which the responsibility is coordinated between schools, the National Council for Special Education and Tusla - Child and Family Agency in such circumstances; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20225/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth (Deputy Michael Moynihan)
speech.p: Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).

The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which advocates that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.

The department does not hold centralised comparative data on the level of individual student needs. Such data is maintained at individual school level and detailed within the individual student support file held by the school.
The Continuum of Support is the framework developed by NEPS for schools to identify, plan and provide support for children and young people who experience difficulties with their learning.

The National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) supports schools in implementing the Continuum of Support framework with each school taking responsibility for initial assessment, educational planning and supports for children and young people with special educational needs.
Under this model, a child or young person does not require a psychological assessment diagnosis in order to access additional support at school.

This Continuum of Support framework recognises that special educational needs occur along a continuum, ranging from mild to more significant, and from transient to enduring. It recognises that children require different levels of support depending on their identified educational needs, and that needs may change over time.
Using this framework helps to ensure flexible and timely allocation of supports, so that those children with the greatest level of need have access to the greatest level of support.

My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

question.p: 872. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will ensure additional funding is allocated to a school project (details supplied). [20226/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.

An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.

The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.
The application in question has been approved in line with the minimal scope of works on which the EWS operates and is currently with the school to progress.

question.p: 873. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if long term substitute SNAs have been given consideration and formally recognised within the SNA redeployment scheme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20233/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth (Deputy Michael Moynihan)
speech.p: I would like to thank the Deputy for his question.
I have listened carefully to all of the issues raised by parents and school communities.
It has now been agreed that there will be no reductions to special needs assistants for the next school year 2026/27.
All schools reviewed by the NCSE and allocated additional resources will receive them in the upcoming school year.
It was agreed that the SNA redeployment scheme, the SNA workforce development plan and changes to a 2014 circular outlining the role of a SNA will be advanced before any further decisions are taken.
The priority will be to ensure that the child-centred approach to the provision of special education is retained and enhanced in these policy developments.

After these key documents are agreed and published, the NCSE can commence reviews of supports provided to schools for the 2027/28 academic year which will uphold the integrity of the process, which allocates supports based on the needs of children.

My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

Updates and final details of the SNA Redeployment Scheme, including a comprehensive circular and guidelines, will be published on the NCSE website and the SNA Information Hub on www.gov.ie as work progresses.

question.p: 874. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding a school in Cork City to accommodate children with additional educational needs (details supplied). [20240/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.

My department and the NCSE continue to work closely with school patron bodies, school management bodies and schools to confirm new special classes for the next school year 2026/2027. The NCSE began sanctioning new special classes in January of this year, which is several months earlier than last year. 351 have been sanctioned to date and many more new special classes will be confirmed in the coming weeks. The earlier sanctioning of new classes provides clarity for parents and allows schools more time for the planning and establishment of new special classes. The vast majority of new special classes being announced are being provided in available school accommodation which is being reconfigured as a special class. Each special class at primary level is allocated 1 teacher and 2 SNAs and at post-primary level, schools receive 1.5 teachers and 2 SNAs. Details of the new special classes are available on the NCSE website.

Of the 351 new special classes, 237 are being established in primary schools and 114 in post-primary schools. New special classes are being established in every county with 38 confirmed for Cork so far. Further details on additional new special classes will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that sufficient special education placements remain available for students with special educational needs and will continue to review and monitor the situation as to where new specialist provision is required.

question.p: 875. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the additional accommodation application submitted by a school (details supplied). [20255/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter my Departments pipeline of school buildings for a project to provide eight general classrooms (one prefab replacement), one science laboratory with prep area, one design and communication graphics room, one music room, one special education tuition (SET) room, one textiles room, one construction room with prep area (prefab replacement), one GP Dining (prefab replacement) and a two classroom special education needs (SEN) base.
The project was devolved for delivery to Longford and Westmeath Education and Training Board (LWETB).

This project was approved to progress to Stage 2a (detailed design) by my Department in January 2024. My Department currently awaits the submission of the stage 2a report by LWETB. Once received the stage 2a report will be reviewed from both a technical and cost perspective. All projects, including this one, will undergo the necessary due diligence outlined in the Infrastructure Guidelines. Managing timing, scope, and cost is crucial to staying within budgetary limits for the overall program. Due to the detailed nature of the evaluation process, the need to ensure full cost compliance, and the requirement to align the project with the prioritisation framework under the National Development Plan.

As the Deputy will be aware, I have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

Of the total €7.55 billion investment it is envisaged that circa. €5 billion will be used for project rollout to support the delivery and modernisation of school buildings across the Large Scale, Additional Accommodation, Modular, and Annual September Accommodation Needs programmes. Over the course of 2026 and 2027 there will be construction work at circa. 10% of the school estate. These projects will, when completed, provide circa 57,000 additional and modernised school places with a strong SEN focus in all projects.

My department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, I have also published a list of the 105 school building projects in the first tranche to proceed to construction or tender over 2026 and 2027.

The first tranche of 105 school building projects includes 80 large scale and Additional School Accommodation scheme projects. These projects were prioritised with a strong focus on maximising existing capacity and prioritising project rollout to meet the most urgent needs particularly to support special education needs provision.

Firstly, to facilitate the 45 projects that are currently already at tender stage (Stage 3) so that they can progress to construction as smoothly as possible over the course of 2026 and 2027. Secondly, to facilitate 35 projects that currently have planning permission and are at pre-tender stage (Stage 2b) and have been prioritised to meet urgent requirements from a special needs perspective or to provide additional capacity to cater for demographics or to address very significant condition issues at the schools.
I recognise that there are schools with important building projects that are not included in the first tranche of prioritised projects.

As part of planning ahead for the next tranche of projects to progress to tender, the department-led prioritisation process will continue over the course of 2026 and 2027 to assess and evaluate the progression of individual projects through the design pipeline having regard to the continual need to maximise existing capacity and determine the prioritised needs going forward. This process will involve engagement with key stakeholders and individual schools and will ultimately inform the next tranches of programme rollout to tender. The department-led Energy and Condition Survey of the school estate, which will be finalised later in 2026, will provide an additional evidence base for assessing priorities.

Based on this ongoing prioritisation process some projects may be added to the list over the course of 2026 and 2027 having regard to their prioritisation and urgency of need and taking account also of the ongoing ability to progress them to tender and construction within the parameters of overall funding. Where appropriate, the department will also assess opportunities to undertake advance enabling works for the most urgent and complex projects to facilitate a smooth progression to construction in 2028 and beyond.
Any interim accommodation requirements will continue to be assessed and considered by the department on a case-by-case basis to determine the prioritised needs and approach for addressing same.
The accommodation needs at this school will be considered as part of the ongoing overall department-led prioritisation process, in consultation with the school’s patron and school authorities.

question.p: 879. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether the review of Circular 32/2017 will introduce national guidance requiring schools to provide reasonable accommodation within uniform policies for children with sensory processing difficulties or other additional needs; and the timeline for completion of that review. [20403/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Circular 32/2017 sets out the principles of cost-effective practice to be adopted by schools to reduce the cost of returning to school.

The Circular provides that schools should select school uniform items which are generic and can be purchased from a range of retailers. Only "iron on" or "sew on" crests should be used. Schools should provide parents with a list of all required items and indicate the likely costs of these required items at best value stores. Where an exclusive supply arrangement applies, it should be tendered for regularly. Schools should also consult with parents as to their views on how to reduce costs.

A working group, which includes the education partners, has been established to review the Circular. Matters such as affordability, comfort and sustainability of school uniforms will be considered as part of this work.
My department is also progressing the Charter Bill, which aims to strengthen engagement between schools, parents and students, including on issues such as school costs and uniform policies.

The overall aim of the Bill is to improve the level of engagement between the school community by inviting feedback, comment and observation from the school community and by further developing a listening culture in schools.

question.p: 880. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No’s 487, 489 and 490 of 3 March 2026, the number of early intervention preschool classes for autistic children in mainstream and special schools that have been redesignated to primary autism classes/other special classes for the 2026/2027 school year. [20437/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.

The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is, in the first instance, the primary body responsible for the matter the Deputy has raised. I will arrange for your query to be forwarded to the NCSE for their attention and direct reply. Deputies are also welcome to raise such queries with the NCSE directly through their dedicated Oireachtas email address.

The NCSE is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for children and young people with special educational needs. Where the NCSE identifies need for an early intervention class, the class is sanctioned and supports are provided by my department to ensure the school can accommodate the class. Generally, these classes are resourced at a 6:1 student/teacher ratio and two special needs assistants (SNAs) are allocated to each class.

Early intervention classes are available in mainstream and special school settings for children aged 3 -5 years old with a diagnosis of autism. There is also a small number dedicated to children who are deaf/hard of hearing. These classes are intended to provide early support to children before they start school and can aid their transition to junior infants. A list of special classes including class type is available on the NCSE website.

The NCSE in collaboration with the Department of Education and Youth may re-designate an early year’s class to a primary age class where there is verified demand for increased special class provision in the locality. Whilst all stakeholders are agreed on the value of early intervention, the NCSE must consider the legislative requirement for children over six to attend school.

The NCSE work closely with the department to ensure we explore all viable options in increasing such provision to meet the local need. In some areas, where students are leaving an early intervention class and have not secured suitable primary specialist provision, the NCSE may re-designate the class. This is done to ensure they can continue with their specialist educational placement at primary level.

Many of the early intervention classes sanctioned to date have been reclassified as the children enrolled reach primary level age. This allows the children to remain in the class at the school they attended for early intervention. However, this it is not always the case, and some classes continue to enrol a new cohort of children yearly.

My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

question.p: 881. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth the remedy that is open to parents, or her Department, to ensure that schools (details supplied) set out in their admission policies the school’s arrangements for students who attend the school without attending religious instruction in the school, as is required under the Education (Admissions to Schools) Act 2018; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20438/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Under the provisions of the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018, all schools have admissions policies, which have been approved by the patron and published on the school's website. The act requires where schools provide religious instruction that they set out in their admission policies the school’s arrangements for students, where the parent or in the case of a student who has reached the age of 18 years, the student, has requested that the student attend the school without attending religious instruction in the school.

Under the provisions of the Education Act, 1998 the Board of Management is the body charged with the direct governance of a school, therefore, the manner in which any school ensures that the right to attend school without attending religious instruction classes is upheld is a matter for the school concerned.

Each individual school must determine the particular arrangements which are most appropriate in its individual circumstances having regard to local issues such as available space, supervision requirements and how the school concerned organises classes etc. It is expected that this right will be upheld by schools on foot of a parental request.

Guidance for good practice is available to schools in the follow-up paper to the Report of the Forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Primary Sector which was published in 2014. The paper provides an overview of different types of arrangements that schools can put in place to facilitate parents who do not wish their children to attend religious instruction. The paper encourages school authorities to consider their policies and practices and to review whether they are taking the steps necessary to welcome all pupils and make them feel included.

As set out in the Education Plan 2025, the Department is committed to developing best practice guidance for primary schools in relation to arrangements to facilitate parental requests for children to attend school without attending religious instruction.

A review of current practices in schools is being undertaken that will develop a best practice guide. This guidance is intended to improve consistency across schools and to make expectations clearer for all stakeholders.

question.p: 884. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of home school community liaison co-ordinators (HSCL) that are employed, by county, in the years 2025 and 2026 to date; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20451/26]

885. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of hours schools receive from home school community liaisons, by DEIS schools; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20452/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 884 and 885 together.

Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) is under the remit of my department and has three strands - the statutory Educational Welfare Service (EWS), the Home School Community Liaison scheme (HSCL) and the School Completion Programme (SCP). The HSCL scheme is one of the key supports provided by my department as part of the overall Delivering Equality of Opportunity in School (DEIS) programme.

The HSCL scheme seeks to promote partnership between parents, teachers and community family support services, with a view to supporting improved attendance, participation and retention. All DEIS urban primary schools and all DEIS post-primary schools are included in the HSCL scheme, which currently serves 682 DEIS schools, catering for approximately 207,000 children and young people. The scheme is delivered in these schools by 528.5 full-time HSCL coordinators assigned to HSCL duties either in individual schools or in clusters of schools.

HSCL coordinators are released from teaching duties, for a maximum of five years, in order to work intensively with and support parents/guardians. The overarching goal of the HSCL coordinator is to improve educational outcomes for children through their work with the key adults in the child’s life.

In addition, a pilot project to support Traveller and Roma students, under the National Traveller and Roma Inclusion Strategy, is in operation in 4 locations with 1 HSCL coordinator assigned in each location. A further 10 HSCL coordinators support attendance, participation and retention of Traveller and Roma students across 14 non-DEIS post-primary schools.

As the Deputy will be aware, I have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

Of the total €7.55 billion investment it is envisaged that circa. €5 billion will be used for project rollout to support the delivery and modernisation of school buildings across the Large Scale, Additional Accommodation, Modular, and Annual September Accommodation Needs programmes. Over the course of 2026 and 2027 there will be construction work at circa. 10% of the school estate. These projects will, when completed, provide circa 57,000 additional and modernised school places with a strong SEN focus in all projects.

My department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, I have also published a list of the 105 school building projects in the first tranche to proceed to construction or tender over 2026 and 2027. This list includes one project in County Donegal.

In addition, there has been €223.54 million in capital funding for Donegal schools between 2020 and 2025. Over that period, a total of 68 schools has been upgraded either through provision of a new school building, a large-scale extension or provision of modular accommodation. There are also currently 11 school projects in Donegal under construction and this summer 26 schools?are approved to?undergo works as part of the Summer Works Scheme/Climate Action scheme. Since 2020 a total of 56 special classes has been opened in Donegal, 7 of which were sanctioned for September 2026.

The first tranche of 105 school building projects includes 80 large scale and Additional School Accommodation scheme projects. These projects were prioritised with a strong focus on maximising existing capacity and prioritising project rollout to meet the most urgent needs particularly to support special education needs provision.

Firstly, to facilitate the 45 projects that are currently already at tender stage (Stage 3) so that they can progress to construction as smoothly as possible over the course of 2026 and 2027. Secondly, to facilitate 35 projects that currently have planning permission and are at pre-tender stage (Stage 2b) and have been prioritised to meet urgent requirements from a special needs perspective or to provide additional capacity to cater for demographics or to address very significant condition issues at the schools.
I recognise that there are schools with important building projects that are not included in the first tranche of prioritised projects.

As part of planning ahead for the next tranche of projects to progress to tender, the department-led prioritisation process will continue over the course of 2026 and 2027 to assess and evaluate the progression of individual projects through the design pipeline having regard to the continual need to maximise existing capacity and determine the prioritised needs going forward. This process will involve engagement with key stakeholders and individual schools and will ultimately inform the next tranches of programme rollout to tender. The department-led Energy and Condition Survey of the school estate, which will be finalised later in 2026, will provide an additional evidence base for assessing priorities.

Based on this ongoing prioritisation process some projects may be added to the list over the course of 2026 and 2027 having regard to their prioritisation and urgency of need and taking account also of the ongoing ability to progress them to tender and construction within the parameters of overall funding. Where appropriate, the department will also assess opportunities to undertake advance enabling works for the most urgent and complex projects to facilitate a smooth progression to construction in 2028 and beyond.
Any interim accommodation requirements will continue to be assessed and considered by the department on a case-by-case basis to determine the prioritised needs and approach for addressing same.
The accommodation needs at this school will be considered as part of the ongoing overall department-led prioritisation process, in consultation with the school’s patron and school authorities.

question.p: 887. Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason urgent funding has not been provided from her Department to a school (details supplied) to replace two derelict prefab classrooms, in an already overcrowded school campus. [20455/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy may be aware, the purpose of the Emergency Works Scheme (EWS) is to provide funding specifically for unforeseen emergencies, or to provide funding to facilitate inclusion and access for pupils with special needs. It does so by ensuring the availability of funding for urgent works to those schools that are in need of resources as a result of an emergency situation.

An emergency is deemed to be a situation which poses an immediate risk to health, life, property or the environment, which is sudden, unforeseen and requires immediate action, and in the case of a school, if not corrected would prevent the school or part thereof from opening.

The EWS operates on the basis of a minimal scope works to address the emergency situation. The EWS is intended to remedy an emergency situation and usually provides only an interim measure until a permanent solution can be delivered under the Summer Works Scheme (SWS) which deals with upgrade works to the school.

The school in question made an application for funding for repair works to the prefab classroom, this application has been approved in line with the minimal scope of works on which the EWS operates and is currently with the school to progress. The school subsequently included additional works beyond the scope of works approved by the EWS when tendering. The school has been advised to remove these works from the tender package and resubmit a tender report in line with the approved scope of works in order to progress the project.

question.p: 888. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the filling of the post for the Education Welfare Officer in the Finglas area; her plans to expedite this appointment; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20474/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Tusla Education Support Service (TESS), which includes the statutory Educational Welfare Service (EWS), is under the remit of my department since 2021.

The primary role of the EWS is to ensure that every child either attends school regularly or otherwise receives a certain minimum education. Educational Welfare Officers (EWOs) are based throughout the country and work with children, young people and their families who are experiencing difficulty with school attendance. This is done through, home visits, educational welfare conferences and collaboratively working with different agencies. The main priority of the work is around the educational welfare of children and young people and to ensure that concerns around attendance are addressed before attendance becomes a crisis issue.

I can advise the Deputy that the EWO position in the Finglas area has been filled with a start date of 23rd March 2026. In the interim the wider EWO team are providing supports to this area, dealing with urgent cases and convening school attendance clinics.

question.p: 889. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 512 of 12 November 2025, to provide a further update on the matter, including an updated timeline; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20493/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The school has been granted capital funding for the provision of 2 Special Educational Needs (SEN) modular classrooms under the Department’s SEN Reconfiguration and Modular Accommodation programme.

This programme involves the use of Project Management supports which is designed to enable the accommodation to be provided as quickly as possible and help ease the administrative workload for school authorities in relation to the management and delivery of projects.
Rogerson Reddan (RR) has been appointed, from the Department’s Framework to design and tender the project and oversee all elements of construction.
The programme for delivery was recently delayed due to works required to divert an ESB cable which has now been completed.

question.p: 890. Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth if school capacity is set by each school or by her Department. [20532/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: In order to plan for school provision and analyse the relevant demographic data, my department divides the country into 314 school planning areas and uses a geographical information system, using data from a range of sources, including CSO census data, child benefit and school enrolment data, to identify where the pressure for school places across the country will arise and where additional school accommodation is needed at primary and post-primary level.

Major new residential developments have the potential to alter the demand for school places at a local level. In that regard, as part of the demographic demand analysis, my department monitors planning and construction activity in the residential sector. This involves the analysis of data sources from local authorities and the CSO along with the engagement with local authorities and the construction sector. In this way, up-to-date information on significant new residential developments is obtained and factored into the demographic analysis exercise. This is necessary to ensure that schools infrastructure planning is keeping pace with demographic changes, at a local level, where there is a constantly evolving picture with planned new residential development.

The annual enrolment process for new Junior Infants at primary and new First Years at post-primary is a very large-scale operation that is transacted at close to 4,000 schools across the country, involving some 140,000 pupils. My Department's main responsibility is to ensure that schools in an area can, between them, cater for all pupils seeking school places in the area. In relation to school admissions, it is the responsibility of the managerial authorities of all schools to implement an enrolment policy in accordance with the Education Act, 1998.

In accordance with the provisions of the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018, schools are required to clearly set out their selection criteria in their admission policies. The criteria to be applied by schools and the order of priority are a matter for the schools themselves. It is an important feature of the act that schools can only make a decision on an application for admission that is based on the school’s admission policy.

In school planning areas that are experiencing enrolment pressures, my department works with schools, patrons, and management bodies to ensure that there are sufficient school places available to meet the needs of children.
