question.p: 892. Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Education and Youth when an updated CID Circular is expected to be issued; if it will address issues where teachers provide service for years without access to permanent contracts; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20598/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: It was announced in April 2025 that teachers who will have taken up their first contract in a viable teaching post in September 2025 will become eligible for a permanent contract in September 2026.

The proposal to allow for permanent contracts after one year of service is an initiative to increase job security and to make teaching a more attractive, sustainable career. This measure will see teachers who started teaching in September 2025 gain a permanent contract a year earlier than they would have previously, by qualifying for the award of a contract of indefinite duration (CID), where they have been re-appointed following a competitive recruitment process and where there is a viable post in the school.
This will provide teachers with the certainty that they need, particularly for those who may be considering large financial commitments, such as those applying for mortgages.
This new measure applies to both newly qualified teachers, and to those teachers who have not yet managed to secure a permanent position, where those teachers satisfy the relevant criteria.
The circulars which give effect to this measure were published by the Department in February 2026.

question.p: 893. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Education and Youth the amount of carbon that will be emitted on all transport and related actions undertaken by her and all members of her staff during their St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026. [20605/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Due to a change in my commitments, I have not travelled, as originally planned, for St Patrick’s Day this year. It is estimated that the total amount of carbon due to be emitted from flights undertaken by the Minister of State at my department, Michael Moynihan T.D., and his staff during their St. Patrick’s Day trip in 2026 is 1.09 tonnes.

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth

question.p: 895. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted due to St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026; and the amount paid. [20642/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: In line with the provisions of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation circular 01/2020, all Government Departments, Offices and agencies are required, with effect from 1 January 2020, to record, monitor and value the greenhouse gas emissions associated with official air travel usage and, no later than 28 February each year to make a payment to the statutory Climate Action Fund related to these emissions for the preceding year.
In line with these provisions, the Department of Education and Youth will make payment in early 2027 to offset any of the carbon emitted associated with St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026.

question.p: 896. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Education and Youth the amount of carbon that has been emitted by transport used by her, the Junior Ministers in her Department, and their staff for each of the past five years; if she has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted because of transport; and the amount paid in each year. [20660/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: In line with the provisions of circular 01/2020, the Department of Education and Youth makes an annual contribution payment to the Climate Action Fund to offset carbon emissions from flights undertaken by Ministers and officials travelling on behalf of the Department. This payment is not broken down between travel undertaken by Ministers and travel undertaken by officials, but is based on the total amount of carbon emissions from flights, generated over the course of a given year. Payments are made in respect of emissions generated in the previous year.
A table showing payments made to offset these emissions is provided below:
In line with the circular's provisions, my Department will calculate and make a payment in early 2027 to offset any of the carbon emitted due to flights taken in 2026.

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy is aware, this school was approved under the Additional School Accommodation Scheme for a project consisting of one new mainstream classroom and the conversion of an existing mainstream classroom to provide a second SEN base, together with the associated ancillary accommodation. This remains the approved scope of works.

With regard to the school’s wider enrolment growth projections, any additional accommodation requirements beyond the approved scope would need to be considered through the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) application process, which is the standard mechanism for assessing and approving further needs arising from increased enrolments.

This would not result in the project being restarted. Should any additional accommodation be approved, it would be added to the existing project, and the current Design Team would be retained and instructed to incorporate the additional scope.

If a meeting or further engagement with the school is required to clarify matters or support progress, the Department will arrange this. The Department remains committed to working with the school to ensure that the appropriate accommodation is delivered.

question.p: 901. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm that consideration will be given to awarding a school (details supplied) three additional SNAs given the fact that the pupils of the school have a number of complex needs that require additional support; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20686/26]

919. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if a school's appeal (details supplied) for a second SNA can be given very strong consideration due to the urgent needs of pupils at the school for this support; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20910/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 901 and 919 together.

This government is fully committed to supporting children with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
Special education funding will exceed €3 billion in 2026 – up 58% since 2020 and the highest amount ever provided.

Special needs assistants (SNAs)play a key role in the successful inclusion of students with additional and significant care needs in schools to enable them to achieve their best outcomes and reach their full potential.

The number of SNAs allocated to schools nationally has increased by 45% between the 2020/21 school year and the present. By the end of the 2026/27 school year there will be close to 25,000 SNAs in our mainstream classes, special classes and special schools. It is important to note that there have been increases in SNAs in all counties and across all education settings since 2020, including mainstream, special classes and special schools.
It has now been agreed that there will be no reductions to special needs assistants for the next school year 2026/27.
All schools reviewed by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE) and allocated additional resources will receive them in the upcoming school year.
It was agreed that the SNA redeployment scheme, the SNA workforce development plan and changes to a 2014 circular outlining the role of a SNA will be advanced before any further decisions are taken.
The priority will be to ensure that the child-centred approach to the provision of special education is retained and enhanced in these policy developments.

After these key documents are agreed and published, the NCSE can commence reviews of supports provided to schools for the 2027/28 academic year which will uphold the integrity of the process, which allocates supports based on the needs of children.
Local special educational needs organisers (SENOs) remain available to assist and advise schools.

The department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to reach their full potential.

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The project referred to by the Deputy at Coláiste Cholmcille, Inverin is devolved for delivery to Galway and Roscommon Education and Training Board (GRETB). It provides for an extension and refurbishment of the existing building.

This project is currently at Stage 3 of the architectural design process (tender stage). A tender report was received and has been reviewed by the department from a technical and cost perspective in line with Public Infrastructure Guidelines. A Letter of Intent to the preferred contractor issued in February 2026.

The length of time a project takes to deliver depends on several factors, including scale and complexity and is subject to the time it takes to progress through the various design stages and the statutory approval process. GRETB will continue to liaise directly with the school authority to keep it updated on progress.

The department have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

Of the total €7.55 billion investment it is envisaged that circa. €5 billion will be used for project rollout to support the delivery and modernisation of school buildings across the Large Scale, Additional Accommodation, Modular, and Annual September Accommodation Needs programmes.

The department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of these projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. The 105 prioritised projects will progress to tender and/or construction on a rolling basis over the course of 2026 and 2027 and within the context of NDP funding parameters. The timing of project progression will reflect the need to carefully manage the rollout of these projects to construction on a controlled basis to ensure that projects are delivered efficiently, align with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines and Capital Works Management Framework and remain within the parameters of NDP funding.

This will include continued engagement with Colaiste Cholmcille, Inverin with respect to the progression of its project to construction.

The current status of all projects continues to be set out under item number ten at the following link: www.gov.ie. ?This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender and construction.?

The Stage 2b report for the project was received by my Department in December 2024. A comprehensive technical and cost review was undertaken by Department officials in line with the full due-diligence requirements set out in the Department’s Infrastructure Guidelines.
Following this assessment, approval to proceed to tender was granted in July 2025.

On 11 March 2026, the Department received the Tender Report from the school. This report is now undergoing a detailed evaluation from both a cost and technical perspective. Once this review has been completed, the Department will liaise with the school to advance the project to the next stage.

The Department will continue to progress this project in a timely and efficient manner. Subject to the completion of the tender evaluation, it is anticipated that the project will commence on site in Q2 2026, with completion expected by Q3 2027
With regard to the Deputy query on estimated cost ranges, the Department cannot release cost details at this stage, as such information is commercially sensitive at this time.
The Department remains committed to working closely with the school to ensure the delivery of this very important project.

question.p: 906. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline the eight school projects that are currently under construction in County Laois; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20748/26]

907. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide a list of the 29 schools in County Laois that have been upgraded to the provision of a new school building, a large extension, or provision of modular accommodation from 2020 to date in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20749/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 906 and 907 together.

As the Deputy will be aware, I have recently published the €7.55 billion NDP Sectoral Investment Plan for the Education and Youth Sectors for the period 2026 to 2030. This NDP Sectoral Plan involves a very strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity and prioritisation of school building projects to meet the most urgent needs. In this regard there will be a strong special education dimension to project rollout.

The department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, I have also published a list of the 105 school building projects in the first tranche to proceed to construction or tender over 2026 and 2027. This list includes 2 projects in County Laois. Additionally, 5 schools are approved to undergo works as part of the Summer Works Scheme / Climate Action scheme in Co Laois this summer.

These projects are in addition in the region of €147 million in capital funding for County Laois schools since 2020. Over that period, a total of 29 schools have been upgraded either through provision of a new school building, a large-scale extension or provision of modular accommodation. There are also currently 9 school projects in County Laois under construction. In addition, since 2020 a total of 64 special classes have been opened in County Laois, of which 7 were sanctioned for September 2026.

The current status of all projects, including those in County Laois, is set out under item number ten, at the following link (www.gov.ie). ?This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender, construction and project completions.?

summary.i: Question No. 907 answered with Question No. 906.

question.p: 908. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Education and Youth to respond to matters raised in correspondence regarding the planned opening of special classes in a school (details supplied); the associated construction works; the reasons for the delays; the steps being taken by her Department to ensure the project is completed within the timeline that was previously outlined to the school; the definitive timeline for the completion of the relevant construction works and the opening of the special classes; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20754/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The school to which the Deputy refers was granted capital funding for the provision of one Special Education Needs classroom (SEN) two Mainstream classrooms (MCR) and one Special Educational Tuition (SET) under my Department’s Devolved SEN Reconfiguration and Modular Accommodation programme in November 2024.

This programme involves the use of Project Management supports which is designed to enable the accommodation to be provided as quickly as possible and help ease the administrative workload for school authorities in relation to the management and delivery of projects. Kerrigan Sheanon Newman Project Management (KSN) has been appointed, from the Department’s Framework, to design and tender the project and oversee all elements of construction.

In relation to the modular project for Finglas Parochial National School, the application for planning permission was submitted and the local authority requested further information which was submitted to them in January 2026. The local authority has recently requested clarification on the further information submission, and this will be submitted to them this week. The project will be delivered as quickly as possible after receipt of planning permission and with the support of Project Managers.

Approximately 80% of all new special classes are being provided in schools with existing accommodation and the Department is supporting those schools with additional grant funding to facilitate any necessary re-purposing works.
Where schools require additional accommodation, usually in the form of modular accommodation, this is being fast-tracked by the Department to be delivered as quickly as possible.

In the meantime the school concerned, who have been sanctioned teachers, SNAs and have availed of the necessary training to support the opening of the classes, will be supported by the NCSE in any contingency arrangements which may be required pending the delivery of the accommodation.

In many cases these schools have spaces which can be used to support the contingency arrangements including general purpose rooms so it can be expected that they will be able to support children during this period.

question.p: 909. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Education and Youth to clarify her Department's current policy regarding the provision of modular accommodation for special classes; the reason schools that have exhausted existing internal capacity, but possess adequate external grounds, are being refused modular builds to open necessary ASD classes; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20755/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I wish to advise the Deputy that my department engages closely with the National Council for Special Education (NCSE) in relation to the forward planning of new special classes and additional special school places. This work involves a detailed review of statistical data in relation to forecasting demand for special class places, an analysis of available school accommodation, consideration of improved data sharing arrangements and a particular focus on the provision of special classes at post-primary level.

Any school, who opens a special class and is willing to open a further class is to be commended. For the academic year 26/27, it may not be possible or appropriate to open new special classes in every school who expresses an interest or who has expressed a prior interest in opening a new class. In addition, some classes may not be needed for the coming school year but can remain an option if need arises in later years.

In general, demographics are falling at primary level and this trend is due to continue. Therefore the Department of Education in conjunction with the NCSE considers it prudent to maximise the use of existing spare accommodation capacity in national schools within a general area in the first instance. This consideration is prior to the establishment of any additional special class that may require additional accommodation e.g. modular accommodation.

This approach can enable a special class to be established more quickly for the coming academic year as it is not bound by the provision of additional accommodation. This then means that the educational needs of children who require a specialist placement can be met at more easily. It may also allow for the earlier repurposing of existing accommodation to occur in a more streamlined and efficient manner.

This overall approach is consistent with the department’s commitment to supporting the educational needs of children who require specialist placements while at the same time meeting the requirements of the Government’s Infrastructure Guidelines.

The department is working very closely with the NCSE to ensure that the required analysis is thoroughly explored with a view to providing the most immediate and cost effective accommodation solutions for the establishment of new special classes for the 2026/27 school year. In some instances this analysis is complete and the appropriate accommodation solutions are being advanced. In the remaining cases, the outcome of the analysis is nearing completion and schools will be advised accordingly. Local SENOs will continue to engage with schools regarding the position and timing of the establishment of special classes.

Whilst the Department is committed to the provision of special class provision for all students as close to their home environment as possible, existing vacancies, available school accommodation and the swift provision of a new special class in a school with the capacity to do so, will necessitate classes opening not within a preferred National school – NCSE, through its SENO service is however committed to sourcing a local class placement for each student within the closest possible distance to that student’s address.

A number of factors are considered by my Department in determining the most appropriate construction method to meet a school’s accommodation requirements, including the timing and duration of that accommodation need, and other school-specific factors.

The Department will continue to build on the progress made over recent years with the continued rollout of projects on a prioritised basis to meet the most urgent needs in terms of provision of additional capacity and modernisation of existing facilities. In this regard, there will continue to be a strong emphasis on maximising existing capacity across the school estate and also ensuring that school admissions policies and processes are targeted at meeting local mainstream and special class requirements.

summary.i: Question No. 910 answered with Question No. 911.

question.p: 911. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way her Department justifies children and teenagers with additional needs being forced to travel outside their local communities for education when local schools are willing to accommodate them but are denied modular building approval; the way in which this aligns with the Government's commitments to inclusive education; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20757/26]

910. Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of primary and post-primary schools in County Wexford that have expressed a willingness to open a special class but have been unable to do so due to the Department's refusal or delay in sanctioning modular accommodation in the past 24 months; the steps being taken to urgently address this specific bottleneck; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20756/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 911 and 910 together.

Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government.?It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).

The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided.
This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which promotes that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.

My department and the NCSE continue to work closely with school patron bodies, school management bodies and schools to confirm new special classes for the next school year 2026/2027. The NCSE began sanctioning new special classes in January of this year, which is several months earlier than last year. 387 have been sanctioned to date and many more new special classes will be confirmed in the coming weeks. The earlier sanctioning of new classes provides clarity for parents and allows schools more time for the planning and establishment of new special classes. The vast majority of new special classes being announced are being provided in available school accommodation which is being reconfigured as a special class. Each special class at primary level is allocated 1 teacher and 2 SNAs and at post-primary level, schools receive 1.5 teachers and 2 SNAs. Details of the new special classes are available on the NCSE website.

Schools seeking to establish new special classes should continue to engage with the NCSE at local level. In sanctioning new special classes, the NCSE have due regard to the level of need in an area and the existing provision, including how many places are expected to be available through the normal movement of students from primary to post-primary or finishing school. Budget 2026 provides funding for over 400 new special classes.

Approximately 80% of all new special classes are being provided in schools with existing accommodation and the Department is supporting those schools with additional grant funding to facilitate any necessary re-purposing works.
Where schools require additional accommodation, usually in the form of modular accommodation, this is being fast tracked by the Department to be delivered as quickly as possible.

question.p: 912. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she has approved the NCCA draft specifications for Leaving Certificate English, which sets out a fundamental change in the English curriculum (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20817/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, through the Senior Cycle Redevelopment programme, the specifications for all Leaving Certificate Established curricular subjects are scheduled to be redeveloped by 2029, in annual groupings referred to as tranches.

Leaving Certificate English was included among the subjects constituting Tranche 2 scheduled for introduction in September 2026. These subjects include; Accounting, Construction Studies, Engineering, Geography, LCVP Link Modules, and Physical Education.
The specifications for all tranche 2 subjects, including English, have been approved by the Minister. The approved specification has been published and is available on curriculumonline.ie.

Timelines in respect of the introduction of the Tranche 2 subjects received careful consideration having regard to the planning, implementation and enactment aspects of each of the Tranche 2 specifications. Consequently in approving the specification, the then-Minister decided that enactment of the English specification will not proceed in school year 2026/27 as initially envisaged and, enactment will not be given effect before school year 2027/28.
In relation to the Deputy’s query on the inclusion of critical literacy in the revised Leaving Certificate English specification as published, my department has been advised by the NCCA as follows;

p.i: ‘Critical literacy is a way of teaching students to read any text ... from a position in which the reader questions the intentions of the author, explores the issue from multiple perspectives, considers sociocultural or political conditions, and takes action to interrupt and change current conditions.’ (Adams, 2023)

Critical literacy has its roots in pedagogical theory, where students are invited to engage in reflection, challenge their own assumptions and take action in the world around them. It moves away from an idea of students as passive recipients of knowledge to active, critical participants in their learning, preparing them to be engaged democratic citizens.

In the work of the development group, one of the key considerations was to empower students to critically engage with the world around them; to ask questions of the texts they were presented with in order to combat bias, misinformation and disinformation. This empowering of students to challenge status quo, to ask questions of the power structures at work behind the texts and be active participants in the work around them, is the central tenet of critical literacy.

The group were also clear that they wanted to ground the specification in sound educational theory and so referenced the works of four writers (among many others) whose ideas they supported; including Freire, Foucault, Shor, and Janks. The four references are outlined below:

Paulo Freire’s ‘Education for critical consciousness’ (1973) reflects on his work as an educator in Brazil, teaching the poor and oppressed how to read and outlines his support of dialogic pedagogy and the emancipatory power of education.

Paul Michel Foucault, was a French historian, philosopher and literary critic who campaigned extensively against homophobia and racial prejudice and reshaped research into critical theory. His ‘Power/knowledge’ (1980) is an influential text in the development of literary theory and the concept of literary works being not just aesthetic but also a result of the networks of power that surround them.

Ira Shore’s ‘What is critical literacy?’ (1999), outlines exactly what is meant by critical literacy in the questioning of power relations, discourses and identities, originating in a Deweyan constructivist education and associated with active theory, where students become active agents in their own education and in the world around them.

Hilary Janks ‘The importance of critical literacy’ (2012) outlines the increasing importance of critical literacy in the world today and provides a concrete approach to critical literacy in the classroom that would be very relevant and useful for teachers of the subject.

The inclusion of these four references (rather than a broad support for the writings of these theorists) gives the specification a grounding in philosophical and pedagogical theories and links with the work of the teacher in the classroom to help empower students to discuss, challenge, reflect and act. This supports the embedding of the key competencies of senior cycle education where students are asked to think and solve problems, to work with others and participate in society.

speech.p: The Deputy may also wish to note that the NCCA Subject Development Group which developed the specification, in line with established practice, included representatives of subject teachers in English and that the specifications underwent public consultation before their approval and publication.

question.p: 913. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware of the case of a school (details supplied); if her Department investigate the matter; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20829/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The school referred to was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline of school buildings under the Additional School Accommodation Scheme for a project providing 2 mainstream classrooms and 2 special education tuition rooms. This project is devolved to the school authority for delivery.
The Department is aware of the planning issue raised by the Planning Authority regarding the assessment of substantial works under Section 42 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended).

My Department has been actively engaging with both the school and the Design Team on this matter and has been advised that the local authority will permit the school to submit a retention application, which they expect to assess and progress over the coming weeks.
The contractor has been instructed to return to site next week, and the project remains on track for completion for the start of the new school year in September.
My Department will continue to work closely with the school to progress this much needed project.

summary.i: Question No. 914 answered with Question No. 915.

question.p: 915. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth if there are any plans to establish a new reading school for children with dyslexia; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20832/26]

914. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the percentile of children that receive a school place within the four reading schools in the State established to assist children with dyslexia; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20831/26]

916. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth if there are any plans to establish new reading classes for children with dyslexia; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20833/26]

917. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of places there are for placement in reading schools and reading classes for children with dyslexia; and the number of children that are on the waiting list; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20834/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Education and Youth
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 915, 914, 916 and 917 together.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.

At present, there are four special schools, and fourteen special classes attached to mainstream schools to support students with a specific learning disability such as severe dyslexia. I want to acknowledge the excellent work they do. It is important to note they were established at a time when there were much fewer additional supports in schools.

Each school prepares and publishes their own admissions policy and runs their own admissions process in line with the Admissions Act. Individual schools will determine the outcome of applications received by them in accordance with their own admissions policy and procedures.

In pursuit of a more inclusive education system it is important, as far as possible to support students to attend their local mainstream schools. This means that children and young people can be educated with their peers and are not required to travel long distances to attend special schools or classes.

15,000 special education teachers have been provided to enable schools to achieve this objective. In practical terms this means schools get a substantial additional teaching allocation to support students with special education needs who are in mainstream classes.
The additional resources are intended to support students with the greatest level of need, including those with a specific learning disability such as dyslexia, dyscalculia or dysgraphia.

Of course, I recognise the importance of building the capacity of teachers in mainstream schools to meet the needs of all students. To support this, 338 places are funded each year for teachers to attend post-graduate special education needs programmes. The NCSE offers dedicated professional learning opportunities for teachers supporting students with additional needs. The National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) also provides professional learning opportunities that are available to all primary and post-primary school teachers on supporting children and young people with special educational needs.

Funding is also made available to schools for the purchase of specialised equipment to assist students. Schools can apply to the NCSE, through their local special educational needs organiser (SENO) for such support.
The need for any additional provision or resources for schools to support students with dyslexia is subject to continual review by the NCSE.

My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that sufficient special education placements remain available for students with special educational needs and will continue to review and monitor the situation as to where new specialist provision is required.

summary.i: Question No. 916 answered with Question No. 915.
Question No. 917 answered with Question No. 915.

question.p: 918. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review an application by a school (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20859/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: The purpose of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) is to enable individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.

It is envisaged that approvals in any given year will involve a spread of categories rather than the traditional single category at a time. This is aimed at managing market capacity and maximising value for money opportunities for school authorities.

In November 2025, my colleague the former Minister of Education and Youth, Helen McEntee TD, announced the first tranche of approvals under the new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme. 297 projects were approved to proceed and involve primary, post primary and special schools, along with projects in all counties and across all categories of works.

My Department can confirm an application was received from the school in question however the school was not on the list of approvals in the first tranche. Given that funding is limited in any particular year it is necessary to prioritise applications. Under the new climate action summer works scheme which operates on a multi annual basis, like previous summer works schemes, applications from schools that are not reached for funding or market prioritisation reasons in 2026 will qualify to be assessed for purposes of the funding available for climate action summer works in subsequent years.
It is anticipated that the next tranche of approvals will be in the latter half of 2026.

Full details of the of the announcement and the list of schools approved in the first tranche, the Circular (0029/2025) for the scheme and guidance documents for schools can be found at the below link;

summary.i: Question No. 919 answered with Question No. 901.

question.p: 920. Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether or not fees (details supplied) will be waived and; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20922/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Following the Government’s Budget 2026 announcement last October, examination entry fees will recommence for upcoming state examinations in 2026, at the same level as when they were last charged in 2019:
• €116 per entry for a Senior Cycle/Leaving Certificate candidate; and
• €109 per entry for a Junior Cycle candidate.

In line with the arrangements which applied when fees were last charged, candidates who hold a full medical card, or who are covered for all services on a parent or guardian’s full medical card, are exempt from examination fees. It should be noted that the rate of examination entry fees has not been increased since 2012.

I can advise that the State Examinations Commission (SEC) initially notified schools that fees would be charged for the 2026 State examinations in October 2025. This was reiterated in other circulars which issued in November, January, and February. A further circular was issued to schools last week with details in relation to the SEC's Online Fee Service. Full details of all fee rates are available here.

question.p: 921. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth when it is proposed to include additional primary and second level schools in the DEIS Programme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20946/26]

speech.from: Minister for Education and Youth
speech.p: Addressing educational disadvantage is a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth. The DEIS programme is a key policy initiative for addressing educational disadvantage at school level. It provides a range of targeted support in addition to the universal supports available to all schools such as:

• Inspectorate support helps improve education provision for all children and young people. They promote best practice and school improvement by advising teachers, principals and boards of management in schools.

• National Educational Psychological Service (NEPS) provides educational psychological service to all primary and post-primary schools and special schools to support the well-being, academic, social and emotional development of all learners.

• The Special Education Teaching (SET) allocation provides a unified allocation for special education support teaching needs to each school based on each school’s educational profile and also encompasses an element of Language (EAL) support allocation. Under this SET model, schools are frontloaded with resources to provide support immediately to those pupils who need it without delay.
• Free schoolbooks are provided to all children and young people in the free education system.

• Through the Department of Social Protection, the School Meals Programme provides regular, nutritious food to children to support them in taking full advantage of the education provided to them. The Hot School Meals Programme is available to all primary schools, meaning that approximately 3,700 schools and organisations and 682,000 children are now eligible for the Schools Meals Programme.

Currently, the DEIS programme support almost 1,200 primary and post-primary schools reaching approximately 260,00 students, with an annual investment of over €180 million. Budget 2026 allocates an additional €16.5 million in 2026, rising to €48 million in 2027 to support the implementation of the new DEIS Strategy and the introduction of the DEIS Plus scheme which will commence in 2026.

The Minister is committed to addressing educational disadvantage in all schools to ensure all children can reach their full potential. To this end, a new ten-year DEIS Strategy to 2035 will be published in the coming weeks. The strategy will introduce innovative solutions to address educational disadvantage.

Over its lifetime. the new DEIS Strategy will focus on improving the opportunities and achievement levels of children and young people at risk of educational disadvantage and working towards a more flexible system of supports to ensure that a school can receive the right support at the right time.
Any future expansion of the DEIS programme and overall allocation of resources will be considered within the context of the new ten-year DEIS Strategy.

question.p: 922. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if his attention has been drawn to the campaign to create an Irish Academy of Fine Arts (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18345/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport (Deputy Patrick O'Donovan)
speech.p: My Department has been made aware of the campaign in question but has no role in this regard. While the future of the GPO is being considered by the Dublin City Taskforce with input from the Office of Public Works and a range of Government Departments and State bodies, the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science oversees policy, funding and governance for the higher and further education, research and innovation sectors.

question.p: 923. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport further to Parliamentary Question No. 599 of 24 February 2026, to list the artforms classified as ‘other’ in his response; to clarify his reference to one recipient being “blank”; whether this means that this recipient received the payment despite not clearly identifying the artform which they participated in; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18452/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: All BIA applicants provided extensive evidence about their artistic practice at time of application in the spring of 2022 in order to demonstrate eligibility. The survey data referred to in the Deputy's question was collected in October 2022 as part of the baselining survey and forms the basis of the research programme.

“Other” was chosen by those artists who didn’t feel represented by the available categories. “Other” also includes Architecture and Opera, which were grouped manually into "Other" because they are relatively small cohorts from a data evaluation perspective. In addition, artists often work on a multidisciplinary or interdisciplinary basis and therefore over the course of the BIA research may have moved between art forms.

In relation to the respondent who left a blank response, it should be noted that “Art form” is a mandatory field in the survey and my officials investigated the issue further. That respondent indicated in a later question in that survey that they were a singer and were paid the BIA.

question.p: 924. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide funding for a project (details supplied) from the Large Scale Infrastructure Fund; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18513/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) was established under the 2018 National Sports Policy to provide Exchequer support for larger sport facility projects, typically those requiring investment greater than the maximum available under the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF).

The first allocations under LSSIF 2018 were announced in January 2020 with €86.4 million awarded to 33 different projects. Additional funding of €37.6 million was allocated to 27 of these projects in December 2023, bringing the total awarded under LSSIF 2018 to €124 million.

In 2024, the second round of the LSSIF attracted unprecedented demand, with 96 applications seeking a combined total of €665 million in funding, including an application on behalf of the club referred to by the Deputy. In November 2024, grants amounting to €173 million were awarded to 35 projects. The club referred to by the Deputy did not receive an allocation.

The LSSIF is currently closed to applications and my current focus is on ensuring project delivery under the first two rounds of the LSSIF, 2018 and 2024. This process will inform any decisions regarding the timing of a future round but I am committed to ensuring sustained investment in sports facilities to meet our ambitious goals for sports participation nationwide.

question.p: 925. Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if the next round of Sports Capital Programme, which is due to open in late May, early June 2026, will link areas to the Pobal Deprivation Index; will the new programme continue to allocate funding dependent on a club's location (details supplied) and link this to the index or will all clubs in County Carlow be granted 95% of the total funding for any future project and clubs contribute 5%; the club in question would previously only have secured 70% funding, due to the area being considered for the overall project and would have to contribute 30% of the costs, which is a significant burden for smaller rural clubs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18576/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Over a quarter of a billion euro was allocated to 3,048 community sports clubs and facilities in 2024 under the most recent, 2023, round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF), representing the largest-ever investment in sports facilities in communities across Ireland. Out of a total of 3,046 successful applications allocations, 1,632 (54%) received at least 90% of the maximum valid grant applicable and only 6 applications received less than 50% of the maximum valid grant.

My Department is currently collating feedback from sporting clubs and organisations from this most recent round and this is very valuable input to our ongoing preparations for the next round. New guidelines will be published in advance of the next round and these will include the eligibility and likely assessment criteria for that next round.

In line with previous rounds of the Fund, a review of the current funding round has been undertaken and will be published shortly. I have asked my department to prepare for a 2026 round of the CSFF in the coming months. It is anticipated that the next CSFF round will particularly target areas and sports that have been under-invested in over the years. I am aiming to announce the opening of applications in the first half of this year.

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport

question.p: 928. Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the number of staff from his Department seconded from a firm in the private sector, per annum from 2022 to date in 2026; and the details of the company, in tabular form. [18624/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Since the establishment of the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport on 1st June 2025, no staff have been seconded into the Department from the private sector.

question.p: 930. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport further to Parliamentary Question No. 599 of 24 February 2026, to provide a breakdown of the 547 music recipients by their role or professional category within the music industry (details supplied); the number of recipients who were classified as full-time workers or part-time workers in the music industry; the number of applicants who declared a disability in their application; the number of those applicants who were subsequently awarded support; and to further provide any internal categorisation or statistical summaries used by his Department to classify applicants from the music sector within the scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18832/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport (Deputy Patrick O'Donovan)
speech.p: Music was the second-largest artform represented in the BIA recipients cohort with 547 reporting working in music. The BIA survey does not track the number of recipients who work full-time vs part-time. Rather, it tracks the number of hours spent each week on several activities, as this delivers more precise information.
Recipients who indicated “music” as their primary art form spent on average the following number of weekly hours on the below activities as of October 2022:

td.p: Weekly hours presenting and showing work
Weekly hours research and experimentation related to one’s practice
Weekly hours on management and administration related to one’s practice
Weekly hours training related to one’s practice
Weekly hours travelling for work including touring
Weekly hours volunteering in the arts
Weekly hours mentoring or coaching others

speech.p: 564 people reported a disability at the time of application. 157 BIA recipients reported a disability in October 2022.

Of the 547 BIA recipients who reported that music in their artform, the main category reported was musician at over 100 applicants. The remainder included a range of sub-categories including singer-songwriters, composers, producers, traditional musicians etc and a mixture of such categories and others. As the categories are self-reporting with a variety of terms and descriptions used, often overlapping, the Department did not produce a definite break-down of these categories for publication.

question.p: 931. [18887/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport (Deputy Patrick O'Donovan)
speech.p: Details of the costs associated with my foreign travel for St Patrick's Day will be published on the Department's website after the end of this Quarter. The Delegation consisted of myself, the Secretary General of the Department and my Private Secretary.
Personal expenses incurred by accompanying officials are claimed by the individual officers in accordance with applicable Civil Service procedures.

All flights relating to these trips were booked in accordance with Government Guidelines. My Department makes an annual payment to the Climate Action Fund scheme, administered by the Department of the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment to offset emissions for travel on commercial flights, in accordance with Circular 01/2020 (D/PER).

question.p: 933. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the engagement his Department has undertaken in relation to a sporting event (details supplied) taking place in Croke Park; if his Department is willing to commit resources as they have done with other recent major sporting events; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19028/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: A potential event such as the one referenced by the Deputy is fundamentally a commercial initiative and a matter for agreement between the event promoter and the venue operator in the first instance.

Should a specific request for support be received, my Department will assess that in line with the Government’s Major International Sports Events Policy and Strategy Framework, which sets out the criteria for evaluating such requests for public funding. This document is available on my Department's website at https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-culture-communications-and-sport/ogp-frameworks/major-international-sports-events-policy-and-strategy-framework/

A promoter has been in contact with my Department in recent weeks regarding the possibility of a major sporting event, which could encompass the specific event referred to, taking place in Dublin later in 2026. question.p: 934. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he can provide details on the youth forum which will take place in the lead-up to Ireland's Presidency and the online safety conference that will run during it; the position regarding the way in which young people will be engaged with on this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19143/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Ireland's Presidency of the EU in the second half of this year will be an important opportunity for Ireland to work with our partners across the EU to deliver on diverse and crucial policy priorities, while showcasing Ireland’s commitment to taking forward our shared interests across the EU.

Ireland's Presidency priorities and policy programme, including those of my Department, remain under development at present with the final overall Presidency programme expected to be published shortly before the start of Ireland's Presidency term.

However, as I have previously made clear, online safety for children is a key priority for me under Ireland's Presidency. In this regard, and as part of work on this priority, my Department is planning a targeted one-day youth forum in the lead up to the Presidency to engage with and obtain the perspectives of children and young people on aspects of their experience online including their views on how to make the internet safer. The outputs from the forum will also feed into a wider programme for a high level Presidency conference on online safety in September. More details on the youth forum and Presidency conference will be available in due course closer to the commencement of the Presidency.

question.p: 935. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he has met with representatives of a union (details supplied) who represent workers in RTÉ; if so, the dates; if he will provide a summary of the matters discussed in relation to the proposed workforce reduction and restructuring plan; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19197/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: I received an invitation to attend a meeting organised by the body which the Deputy has referred to. Due to prior commitments, I was unable to attend the meeting, and my Office conveyed my apologies.
It is also important to note that, given RTÉ's independence, as set out in the Broadcasting Act 2009, I have no role to play in its day-to-day operations, including human resource matters.

question.p: 936. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the mechanisms that will be in place to ensure that where production is outsourced to the commercial sector, there is full transparency and accountability regarding the expenditure of public funds, including safeguards to ensure that such arrangements do not result in reduced public oversight or diminished value for money; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19203/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The Revised General Scheme of the Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill, which was approved by Government in April 2025, provides that RTÉ shall pay an amount not less than 25% of its public funding into the independent programmes account for the purposes of commissioning sound and audiovisual programmes from producers who are independent of RTÉ and other broadcasters. The General Scheme also provides for additional transparency obligations on RTÉ in terms of its annual reporting on its commissioning activities.

The Joint Oireachtas Committee on Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport published its pre-legislative scrutiny report on the General Scheme on 17 September 2025 and recommended (Recommendation 66), inter alia, that 'the financial reporting requirements of RTÉ and independent producers regarding commissioned content be balanced against the impacts of disclosing commercially sensitive information on the competitiveness of the sector'.

I wrote to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on 13 February 2026 to inform them that I intended to address this recommendation in the published Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill by providing that the following information should be disclosed on an annual basis in respect of each programme commissioned by RTÉ:
• the total cost of the production within monetary bands (to be determined by Minister direction);
• the public contribution as a percentage of the total cost, which will be itemised individually, by reference to the type of public support, and cumulatively.

The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill will also provide for a wider range of measures to enhance the transparency, value-for-money and accountability in RTÉ and TG4. These include the assignment of the Comptroller and Auditor General as auditor of RTÉ and reforms to the system through which Coimisiún na Meán assesses the performance of, and recommends funding for, RTÉ and TG4.
The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill is scheduled for publication as part of the Spring 2026 Legislative Programme.

In addition to these additional transparency measures, Coimisiún na Meán has been undertaking a review of the guidance it provides to RTÉ and TG4 on the preparation by the public service media providers of Codes of Fair Trading Practice under section 112 of the Broadcasting Ac 2009. The Codes of Fair Trading Practice set out the principles that will be applied by the providers when agreeing terms for the commissioning of programming material from independent producers.

The current guidance published by Coimisiún na Meáns sets out that transparency should be one of the key principles underpinning a Codes of Fair Trading Practice. Under section 112(2) of the Broadcasting Act 2009, I, as Minister, am a statutory consultee on the preparation of new guidance by Coimisiún na Meán and I will be emphasising the importance of transparency as a key principle in commissioning decisions.

question.p: 937. Deputy Marian Harkin asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the position regarding the payment of the long awaited pension increase for An Post pensioners; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19216/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Under section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Services Act 1983, the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport with the concurrence of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, approves any superannuation schemes submitted by An Post. The operation of the schemes is a matter between the management of An Post, staff representatives and the trustees of the schemes.

In accordance with the Act and the relevant Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies, An Post must seek Ministerial approval from both Ministers to increase pensions and deferred pensions for members of the An Post superannuation scheme. Section 2.13 of the Code of Practice for Governance of State Bodies Superannuation and Remuneration annex sets out that NewERA advice should be sought in respect of pension amendment proposals, as is appropriate in their role as commercial and financial advisors to the Ministers.

On 23 October 2025, An Post wrote to my Department requesting consent for an increase to pensions in payment and deferred pensions, namely, to increase pensions in payment for members and deferred members of the An Post Superannuation Scheme by 6% per annum with effect from 1st January 2025 and 1% from 1st of June 2025, arising from its agreements with employee representative groups. In line with both the Code of Practice for State Bodies and the relevant legislation, Ministerial consent has been granted, and this was conveyed to An Post on 25 February 2026.

question.p: 938. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if disabled artists who are newly registered as self-employed will not be disadvantaged under the basic income for artists; and his plans to achieve that objective. [19224/26]

932. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport his plans to make permanent the basic income scheme beyond three-year pilots in order to provide certainty for artists; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18921/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 938 and 932 together.

I was delighted last month to announce that the Government had agreed on the broad parameters for a successor scheme to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot. Guidelines for the new scheme will be published in the coming weeks and applications will open for the new scheme following that, with 2,000 places available for artists to receive a weekly payment of €325.

This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision. The research clearly demonstrated both how precarious and difficult it is to be an artist and also the positive benefits for society as a whole if we invest in our artists.
The focus of the successor scheme is to support professional artists whose creative practice is based in Ireland. The broad parameters of the new scheme will be as follows:
- 2,000 artists will receive a payment of €325 per week
- the payments will last for 3 years
- participants of the pilot scheme can apply for the new scheme if they are eligible under the criteria of the new scheme.

With an allocation of €18.27 million for 2026, my Department is in a position to fund 2,000 artists. In relation to self-employment status, once selected for the scheme artists will have to register as self-employed if they have not previously been and the Department of Social Protection (DSP) will treat income from the scheme as income from self-employment for the purpose of its various means tests.

This is a ground-breaking support for the arts in Ireland and recognising the importance of supporting artistic practice and makes Ireland a world-leader in how we support our artists and culture and will help to sustain the careers of those artists who will receive it and retain their talent in the arts sector.

question.p: 939. Deputy Marian Harkin asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport when the next round of the Large Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) will open for applications; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19359/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) was established to provide support for larger sports facility projects and the cumulative investment since 2020 is €297 million across 68 projects.

While the LSSIF is closed to applications at present, my current focus is on ensuring project delivery under the first two rounds of the LSSIF. This process will inform any decisions regarding the timing of a future round, but I am committed to ensuring sustained investment in sports facilities to meet our ambitious goals for sports participation nationwide.

The LSSIF focuses on larger initiatives, particularly those related to high-performance sport, major spectator venues, and community-accessible facilities. The key aims of the LSSIF are to increase active participation in sport and the quality of that participation; increase the quantum and quality of social participation in sport; improve high performance in sport; increase active participation by those with a disability and provide similar access to facilities to all.

LSSIF is aimed primarily at National Governing Bodies (NGBs) and local authorities. Other bodies can also benefit, but applications have to be made and prioritised by a local authority and/or a NGB. The full marking scheme, guidelines and assessment process for LSSIF 2018 and 2024 are published on my Department’s website. I would encourage any prospective applicants to review these documents in preparation for a future LSSIF round, while noting that guidelines and conditions for a future round may differ from those previously published.

question.p: 940. Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the position regarding the delivery of recreational infrastructure such as swimming pools, football pitches and other amenities in North Kildare; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19381/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: My Department operates two capital funding programmes for sport, namely the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and the Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF). Sporting organisations can apply directly for CSFF funding while applications for LSSIF funding must be made through either a National Governing Body (NGB) of Sport or a Local Authority.

Over a quarter of a billion euro was allocated to 3,048 community sports clubs and facilities in 2024 from the 2023 round of the CSFF, representing the largest-ever investment in sports facilities in communities across Ireland. Almost €9 million was allocated to 103 sporting projects in Kildare from the 2023 round.

I have asked my department to prepare for the opening of a 2026 round of the CSFF in the coming months. It is anticipated that the next CSFF round will particularly target areas and sports that have been under-invested in over the years.

To date there has been two rounds of LSSIF with a cumulative investment of €297 million across 68 projects including €11,431,960 to projects in Kildare. My current focus is on ensuring project delivery under the first two rounds of the LSSIF, 2018 and 2024, and this process will inform any decisions regarding the timing of a future round. No decisions have yet been made regarding the next round of LSSIF.

question.p: 941. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will reinstate the Basic Income Scheme (BIA) and give some financial certainty and a sense of security to artists (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19392/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: I was delighted last month to announce that the Government had agreed on the broad parameters for a successor scheme to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot. Guidelines for the new scheme will be published in the coming weeks and applications will open for the new scheme following that, with 2,000 places available for artists to receive a weekly payment of €325.

This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision. The research clearly demonstrated both how precarious and difficult it is to be an artist and also the positive benefits for society as a whole if we invest in our artists.
The focus of the successor scheme is to support professional artists whose creative practice is based in Ireland. The broad parameters of the new scheme will be as follows:
- 2,000 artists will receive a payment of €325 per week
- the payments will last for 3 years
- participants of the pilot scheme can apply for the new scheme if they are eligible under the criteria of the new scheme.

With an allocation of €18.27 million for 2026, the Department is in a position to fund 2,000 artists. As I said at the launch of the scheme I intend to expand beyond 2000 artists, should more funding become available in future budget cycles. Given that I do not have sufficient funds to provide the BIA to all eligible artists I believe the fairest approach is to ensure that as many artists as possible benefit from the scheme over time, which is why I have proposed the 6 year rule. However, should it be possible to significantly increase the numbers funded, this matter can be revisited.

This is a ground-breaking support for the arts in Ireland and recognising the importance of supporting artistic practice and makes Ireland a world-leader in how we support our artists and culture and will help to sustain the careers of those artists who will receive it and retain their talent in the arts sector.

question.p: 942. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if his attention has been drawn to residents (details supplied) who have been using the dial-up method for internet access for almost eight years after their local internet line was damaged; if he will ensure that this damaged line is urgently repaired; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19431/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the government's initiative to deliver high-speed broadband services to all premises in Ireland.
The area in question is in the BLUE area on the broadband map which is available on my Department's website www.gov.ie/en/publication/5634d-national-broadband-plan-map/.

The BLUE area represents those areas where commercial providers are either currently delivering or have plans to deliver high-speed broadband services. The Department defines high-speed broadband as a connection with minimum speeds of 30Mbps download and 6Mbps upload.

The activities of commercial operators delivering high-speed broadband within BLUE areas are not planned or funded by the State and the Department has no statutory authority to intervene in that regard.

Per information available at https://bbchecker.comreg.ie/ the majority of the premises in the estate in question are currently capable of receiving High-Speed Broadband from multiple operators. There are 6 remaining premises in the estate that are capable of receiving speeds of up to 68 Mbps (part fibre) from Open eir’s local High Speed Broadband cabinet. These premises are included in open eir’s Full Fibre to the Home (FTTH) deployment programme per information available at www.openeir.ie/fibre/broadband-checker. The Department does not have sight of information that provides an estimated timeline of when Open eir will provide a full fibre connection to this premises.

In the event that a customer is receiving an inadequate broadband service, within the home, and they have not had a satisfactory resolution with their retail service provider regarding the damaged internet line the matter can be escalated to the Commission for Communications Regulation (ComReg).

ComReg is the independent body that issues licenses to telecommunication companies and can escalate complaints made by consumers to make sure that companies are delivering services in line with their license obligations.
ComReg can be contacted at:
Online - www.comreg.ie
Email - consumerline@comreg.ie

question.p: 943. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if his Department or any body under it’s aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19492/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: In compliance with section 851A of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997, it is not permitted to disclose details relating to the tax affairs of any individual taxpayer or taxable entity, except in certain limited circumstances provided for in law, for example in the case of tax settlements meeting the criteria for publication under section 1086A of the TCA.

In April 2024, the Department brought to the attention of its aegis bodies a letter from the Chairman of the Revenue Commissioners on the subject of corporate governance and tax compliance within Government Departments and bodies under their aegis. The letter, amongst other points of guidance, alerted public bodies to the “Karshan” ruling of the Supreme Court in October 2023 and provided guidance on the tax treatment of remuneration of persons engaged for short periods/specific contracts.
