question.p: 946. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the current timeline for agreed pension increases for EIR and An Post retirees; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19580/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Under section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Services Act 1983, the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, with the concurrence of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitilisation, approves any superannuation schemes submitted by An Post.

In accordance with the Act and section 2.13 of the Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies: Superannuation and Remuneration Annex, An Post must seek Ministerial approval from both Ministers to increase pensions and deferred pensions for members of the An Post superannuation scheme. Section 2.13 also requires the parent Department to seek NewERA advice in respect of pension amendment proposals, as is appropriate to NewERA's role as commercial and financial advisors to the Ministers.

On 23 October 2025, An Post wrote to my Department requesting consent for an increase in pensions in payment for members and deferred members of the An Post Superannuation Scheme by 6% per annum with effect from 1st January 2025 and 1% from 1 June 2025, arising from its agreements with employee representative groups. In line with both the Code of Practice and transfer of powers from Min/Finance to MPER, which are contained in the Postal and Telecommunications Act 1983, Ministerial consent was granted and was conveyed to An Post on 25 February 2026.

Further to section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Act 1983, as amended, and section 10 of the eircom superannuation scheme rules, my Department last August received a request for a pension increase of 2.1% for Eir pensioners, in respect of both pre and post vesting day service, with effect from 01 July 2025.

My officials sought the advice of NewERA on this pension increase proposal, who submitted their report on 06 February. Having considered the report, I approved the pension increase on 12 February, after which my officials sought the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure. The Minister for Public Expenditure gave his consent to the pension increase on 23 February, with the Minister for Finance giving his concurrence to the proposed increase on 03 March. Sanction for the pension increase was conveyed to Eir on 04 March.
Administration of the An Post and Eircom Superannuation Schemes, including payment of pension benefits and approved pension increases, are matters for the Trustees of those Schemes.

question.p: 947. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to consider implementing a policy to ensure that all sports clubs are required to have clear comprehensive adult safeguarding policies in place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19587/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Sport Ireland, which is funded by my Department, is the statutory body with responsibility for the development of sport, increasing participation at all levels and raising standards including athlete welfare.

Sport Ireland works with National Governing Bodies of Sport (NGBs) to ensure that appropriate policies are put in place to take a proactive approach to safeguarding by identifying and mitigating risks to athlete welfare. It also works with NGBs to ensure mechanisms are in place to appropriately react to and handle complaints or issues when they arise.
Ultimately, NGBs are independent autonomous organisations responsible for their own governance including safeguarding procedures and disciplinary and complaints processes.

I have referred the Deputy's questions to Sport Ireland for direct reply in relation to the matter raised by her and I would ask the Deputy to inform my office if a reply is not received within 10 days.

question.p: 948. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport his views on funding for local democracy reporters for the years 2025 and 2026; the criteria for papers to receive funding for local democracy reporters; if decisions to reduce allocations can be appealed and how; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19590/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Under the Local Democracy Reporting Scheme, a total of just over €6.8 million was awarded to the media sector with approximately €3.4 million being awarded in each of the years 2025 and 2026. This represents an important avenue of funding in support of predominantly local and regional media organisations in the provision of trustworthy public interest journalism while preserving and promoting media plurality and diversity. Full details of the most recent funding awarded can be found on Coimisiún na Meán's website here: www.cnam.ie/industry-and-professionals/media-development/support-funding/journalism-schemes/funding-offers-r1-nrs-r2-ldrs-crs/

The Scheme is operated by Coimisiún na Meán. Section 10 of the Broadcasting Act 2009, as amended by the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022, states that "the Commission shall be independent in the performance of its functions". As such, I have no statutory role in respect of the operation of funding schemes administered by Coimisiún na Meán.

Accordingly, questions around the application process including eligibility criteria and appeals are a matter for Coimisiún na Meán to address. Coimisiún na Meán have a dedicated email address to deal with queries from the Oireachtas and they can be emailed at oireachtasqueries@cnam.ie.

question.p: 949. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will provide an update on the Government's engagement with other EU Member States regarding proposals to introduce an EU wide digital age of majority for access to social media platforms, particularly in respect of users under 16 years of age; the timeline being considered for advancing such proposals at EU level; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19673/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: As set out in the National Digital and Artificial Intelligence Strategy, the Government is committed to working actively with like-minded EU Member States to explore options to introduce age restrictions on the use of social media - the so-called "digital age of majority - concentrating, in particular on those under 16.

In the European Union, there are differing views on whether there should be a digital age of majority, if so, what age it should be set at and if parental consent should be required. France is proposing to restrict access to social media for children under 15 years of age and I recently met my French counterpart and officials in my Department are continuing to engage with their French counterparts. Other EU Member States like Denmark, Spain, Greece and Italy have different proposals at various stages of implementation.

The National Digital Strategy also notes that any decision on the digital age of majority should take into account of European Commission expert panel on this matter. The panel met last week for the first time and is, I understand, due to report this summer.
The work of this expert panel will feed into deliberations during Ireland's Presidency on the potential to set a digital age of majority at European level in respect of social media.

question.p: 950. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the steps being taken under the Government's Digital and AI Strategy to develop and pilot age verification systems for social media use by persons under 16 years-of-age; the expected timeline for the pilot programme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19675/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Officials in my Department are working with the Government’s Chief Information Officer and his office on an age verification tool as part of Ireland's digital wallet which is being developed by the OGCIO under the framework of the EU eIDAS regulation (EU 2024/1183). This requires every EU member state to introduce a secure digital identity framework provided through a digital wallet but the wallet will be voluntary for citizens to use.

The aim of developing this tool is to support the application of Ireland’s online safety code being implemented by Coimisiún na Meán. Under Part B of the Code, designated video-sharing platform services are obliged to implement robust age assurance measures to ensure children do not normally see adult-only content, like pornography. The use of the digital wallet for age verification purposes is envisaged in guidelines produced by the European Commission under Article 28 of the Digital Services Act which deals with the protection of minors online. It is not intended that it will be the only option for platforms to meet their age verification requirements. Rather, it will provide a privacy preserving and secure option that respects users' rights and helps to safeguard children.

A pilot of this product is now envisaged, led by the OGCIO, over a period of some months and which will also be on a voluntary basis. The specifics of the pilot and exact timeline are yet to be finalised.

question.p: 954. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the public body which is responsible for ensuring the availability of broadband to a location (details supplied) which have been without fibre broadband since a line was damaged eight years ago but which appear to be shown as connected to fibre broadband on a national infrastructure database. [19796/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the government's initiative to deliver high-speed broadband services to all premises in Ireland.
The Eircode provided is in the BLUE area on the broadband map which is available on my Department's website www.gov.ie/en/publication/5634d-national-broadband-plan-map/.

The BLUE area represents those areas where commercial providers are either currently delivering or have plans to deliver high-speed broadband services. The Department defines high-speed broadband as a connection with minimum speeds of 30Mbps download and 6Mbps upload.

The activities of commercial operators delivering high-speed broadband within BLUE areas are not planned or funded by the State and the Department has no statutory authority to intervene in that regard.

Per information available at https://bbchecker.comreg.ie/ the premises in question and the surrounding premises are capable of receiving speeds of up to 68 Mbps (part fibre) from Open eir’s local High Speed Broadband cabinet. These premises are included in open eir’s Full Fibre to the Home (FTTH) deployment programme per information available at www.openeir.ie/fibre/broadband-checker. The Department does not have sight of information that provides an estimated timeline of when Open eir will provide a full fibre connection to this premises.

In the event that a customer is receiving an inadequate broadband service, within the home, and they have not had a satisfactory resolution with their retail service provider regarding the damaged internet line the matter can be escalated to the Commission for Communications Regulation (ComReg).

ComReg is the independent body that issues licenses to telecommunication companies and can escalate complaints made by consumers to make sure that companies are delivering services in line with their license obligations.
ComReg can be contacted at:
Online - www.comreg.ie
Email - consumerline@comreg.ie

question.p: 955. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will provide an explanation for the failure of National Broadband Ireland (NBI) and its contracted partners to deliver a confirmed broadband installation to a person (details supplied) in County Mayo on 20 February 2026, despite the person having received written confirmation from the chosen service provider that installation would occur on that date; and if he will outline what oversight exists to ensure that NBI and its partners meet their stated installation obligations. [19944/26]

956. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will address the continued service failures of NBI, including conflicting information given to customers by NBI, its installation partner (details supplied) and broadband service providers; and if he will confirm whether his Department plans to examine systemic issues in NBI's customer facing processes during the final phase of the State subsidised broadband rollout. [19945/26]

958. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the obligations placed on commercial broadband service providers who operate on the NBI network to ensure reliable communication, accurate installation scheduling, and minimum service standards; and the enforcement mechanisms which exist when providers repeatedly issue incorrect or misleading customer information. [19947/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 955, 956 and 958 together.

I propose to take Questions 19944/26, 19945/26 and 19947/26 together. The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government initiative to deliver high-speed broadband to all premises in Ireland. Having received clarification from Deputy Lawless, all three questions refer to a premises located in the AMBER area on the broadband map, which is available at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/5634d-national-broadband-plan-map/. The AMBER area is to be served by National Broadband Ireland (NBI), under the NBP contract.

NBI have advised that the premises in question, and neighbouring premises, are at the available to pre-order stage, with an anticipated Ready for Service timeframe of March-April 2026. No installation appointments take place during the pre-order stage as these are arranged by NBI's Connections Partners once the premises is marked as Ready for Service on the Network Map (nbi.ie/map/).

With regard to NBI’s service obligations, NBI is subject to quality-of-service standards set out in the NBP contract with the Minister. The NBP performance regime is built on a set of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) which track NBI's performance in connecting premises and operating the network service over the 25-year contract period. These KPIs cover the time required to connect customer premises, the number of consumer faults, network incident resolution times, system availability, and minimum upload and download speeds.

The NBP performance regime exists to ensure that orders received from Wholesale and Retail Service Providers (WSPs/RSPs) are addressed in a timely manner by NBI and that customers that are connected to the fibre to the home broadband service have a high standard in service availability, quality, and performance. Following on from the design and build phases of the network, NBI is required to adhere to agreed performance levels for both the connection of premises and operational performance of the network. The performance regime is in line with best regulatory practice; however, it is more granular for some KPIs.

NBI are required to provide the Department with quarterly performance monitoring reports for every KPI. If KPI targets are not maintained, the value of subsidy payments received by NBI is reduced, that is, NBI will be financially sanctioned.

With regard to the specific experience outlined by the Deputy, this relates primarily to the communication and scheduling processes of the RSP concerned. While NBI is the wholesale network operator, the customer's direct contractual relationship is with the RSP. It is the RSP’s responsibility to manage customer expectations, including the provision of accurate installation dates and timely communication.

Consumers or businesses who are dissatisfied with the service or information provided by their retail broadband provider may refer their complaint to the Commission for Communications Regulation (ComReg), the independent statutory body responsible for regulating the electronic communications sector. ComReg investigates complaints and ensures retail service providers deliver services in line with their licence obligations, including in relation to service quality and customer communications.
ComReg can be contacted at:
• Web: www.comreg.ie
• Email: consumerline@comreg.ie

summary.i: Question No. 956 answered with Question No. 955.

question.p: 957. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will provide a justification for the reason County Mayo has been among the last counties to receive National Broadband Ireland services, leaving some communities dependent on 3G mobile broadband for over eight years; and the measures his Department will take to prevent continued delays or miscommunications during the completion of the rollout. [19946/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government initiative to deliver high-speed broadband to all premises in Ireland. In addition, Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in December 2022, sets out a number of targets including that all Irish households and businesses will be covered by a Gigabit network no later than 2028.

The Programme for Government – Securing Ireland’s Future published in January 2025 sets a number of targets which include the completion of the installation of high-speed fibre broadband to 1.1 million people, including homes, farms, and businesses nationwide, by 2026.

National Broadband Ireland (NBI) have stated the route of the network rollout is not based on cost or an economic model. Instead, it is based on an engineering design that allows NBI to get to every premises as quickly as possible, working within the confines of how fibre networks are built and utilising existing infrastructure wherever possible.

In the Deputy's own county of Mayo a significant investment of €145 million is being made under the NBP. There are over 17,245 premises passed with a high-speed fibre broadband network and 20,812 are available to order/pre-order, with 5,096 premises now connected. A further circa 20,755 premises in Mayo will be passed by NBI’s high speed fibre broadband by the end of the network deployment.
Premises in the Knock Deployment Area are currently in the network build phase and have an anticipated connection date of between April and June 2026.

Premises located in the Belcare, Cloonfad, Kiltimagh Deployment Areas (DAs) are currently in the network build phase. These premises have an anticipated date for connection between July 2026 and September 2026.
Premises in the Claremorris, Dooleeg, Knockmore and Manulla DAs are also at network build phase and have an anticipated connection date of between October and December 2026.

Further details are available on specific areas within County Mayo and can be monitored via https://nbi.ie/reps/ . NBI has a dedicated email address, reps@nbi.ie, which can be used by Oireachtas members for specific queries. It should be noted that NBI provide this information for County Mayo based on NBI deployment areas rather than exact county boundaries.

summary.i: Question No. 958 answered with Question No. 955.

question.p: 959. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the current salary rate being paid to the chairperson and four commissioners of Coimisiún na Meán; the combined cost of these salaries since the commission was established, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20120/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Following the passage of the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act, Coimisiún na Meán was formally established on 15 March 2023. The Executive Chairperson and three Commissioners took up their duties on an administrative basis on 13 February 2023, and on a statutory basis with effect from 15 March 2023. A fourth Commissioner was subsequently appointed on 24 July 2023.

The Executive Chair was appointed on a salary rate equivalent to that of Secretary General (Level II), which currently stands at €264,378 per annum. The salaries for Commissioners were determined having regard to other similar regulators/regulatory bodies, and the current rate of salary is €198,711 per annum.

The combined cost of the salaries is as follows, noting that given the timing of establishment of An Coimisiún and appointment of Commissioners, the figures for 2023 and 2026 do not represent full year costs.

question.p: 960. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will commission an independent review of the compatibility of Coimisiún na Meán's regulatory framework with Article 40.6.1° of the Constitution and Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding freedom of expression; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20145/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: A free and independent media is a cornerstone of democracy and plays a vital role in informing people and holding institutions and interests to account. This is reflected in Article 40.6.1 of the Constitution and reinforced by equivalent provisions in the European Convention on Human Rights and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

Ireland has a robust legislative foundation and regulatory framework designed to protect media freedom and media plurality. The Online Safety and Media Regulation (OSMR) Act, which completed its passage through the Oireachtas and was signed into law by the President of Ireland on 10 December 2022, provided for the establishment of a new online safety and media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán. Importantly, the OSMR Act provides that An Coimisiún is independent in the exercise of its functions.

Notably, the legislative framework for media regulation is being updated through the Media (Regulation) Bill, which is due to commence its passage through the Oireachtas very shortly. The Bill will give effect to the main elements of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), an EU regulation which aims to strengthen the internal market for media services and protect media pluralism by harmonising different national rules and procedures.
On this basis, I do not believe it appropriate or necessary to commission an independent review as suggested by the Deputy.

question.p: 961. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he has examined Coimisiún na Meán's call for submissions on media literacy to counter disinformation, announced 10 March 2026; whether he is concerned that such initiatives risk positioning the regulator as an arbiter of truth and thereby controlling public discourse; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20147/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The National Counter Disinformation Strategy was published in April 2025. The strategy sets out 9 commitments and 36 actions, including at Commitment 4, adopting a lifelong approach to empowering all citizens with media literacy. The Strategy is also clear in stating that it is not the Government that decides what is or is not disinformation.

In fulfilment of the Programme for Government commitment to support implementation of the Strategy, I secured €1.1 million in Budget 2026 which is being allocated in support of media literacy initiatives, fact-checking and research.

In relation to media literacy, it was agreed with Coimisiún na Meán that it would distribute a portion of this funding in 2026 to support organisations delivering media literacy activities. This call, worth €200,000, is the first of two - the second call for submissions will seek to provide micro-grants for community-based media literacy activities.
Under this first call, eligible organisations will be able to apply for funding for projects that deliver at least one of the following objectives:

• Advancing empirical knowledge of effective media literacy strategies to counter disinformation as well as insights into the needs and capacities of different sectors delivering media literacy across the life course.
• Implementing Ireland’s national public library strategy for 2023-2027 ‘The Library is the Place’.

• Collaborating with key partners and established networks on developing educational content that empowers Irish people with the skills and knowledge to make informed choices about the media content and services that they consume, create and disseminate.
• Evaluating impact and capturing best practice for future delivery.

This is an important step in ensuring organisations across Ireland can develop projects that help people better understand and critically assess the information they encounter every day. By strengthening media literacy across our communities, we are helping to build a more resilient and informed society, as part of Coimisiún na Meán’s role in developing and regulating a thriving, diverse, creative, safe and trusted media landscape.

question.p: 962. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will direct Coimisiún na Meán to publish a full impact assessment on how its media services codes, fairness and impartiality rules, and media-pluralism policy are affecting viewpoint diversity and the viability of independent and smaller media outlets; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20151/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Section 46N of the Broadcasting Act 2009 allows for Coimisiún na Meán to make media service codes governing the standards and practices of broadcasters and providers of audiovisual on-demand media services. They regularly hold consultations with the public and various stakeholders when reviewing their codes and rules. They published a response to their consultation on the draft media codes and rules for broadcasting in July 2025 which can be found here (https://www.cnam.ie/app/uploads/2025/07/Response-to-Consultation_Stage-2_Broadcasting.pdf). They recently also held a public consultation on media plurality policy which can be found here (https://www.cnam.ie/app/uploads/2025/08/20250827_PConsult-Pluralism.pdf). Under Section 10 of the Act Coimisiún na Meán are independent in the performance of their functions and it would not be appropriate for me to direct them as proposed.

question.p: 963. Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if his Department will provide a timeline for a decision on the pension increase of 2.1% for Eir (formerly Eircom and Telecom Éireann) pensioners given by the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation and sent to his Department on 23 February 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20221/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Further to section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Act 1983, as amended, and section 10 of the Eircom Superannuation Scheme rules, my Department last August received a request for a pension increase of 2.1% for Eir pensioners, in respect of both pre and post vesting day service, with effect from 01 July 2025.

My officials sought the advice of NewERA on this pension increase proposal on 17 November, who submitted their report on 06 February. Having considered the report, I approved the pension increase on 12 February, after which my officials sought the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure. The Minister for Public Expenditure gave his consent to the pension increase on 23 February, with the Minister for Finance giving his concurrence to the proposed increase on 03 March. Sanction for the pension increase was conveyed to Eir on 04 March.
Administration of the Eircom Superannuation Scheme, including the payment of pension benefits and approved pension increases, is a matter for the Trustees of the Scheme.

question.p: 964. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he agrees with the findings of a recent report (details supplied) that take up of fibre to the home broadband continues to be below average amongst older people and amongst small businesses; if so, the policy measures his Department are pursuing to encourage the commencement of the process of copper switch-off which would have a significant impact in driving take up of fibre to the home amongst these groups; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20268/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: I am aware of the eir Digital Ireland Report published in February 2026, which draws on eir's internal network data, ComReg quarterly reports, Central Statistics Office research, and EU Digital Decade indicators to present a comprehensive picture of Ireland's digital connectivity landscape.

The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government initiative to deliver high-speed broadband to all premises in Ireland. In addition, Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in December 2022, sets out a number of targets including that all Irish households and businesses will be covered by a Gigabit network no later than 2028.

I am advised by National Broadband Ireland (NBI) that, over 456,567 premises are passed across 26 counties and available for immediate connection. 168,255 premises are already connected to the NBP high-speed broadband network. NBI are connecting circa 4,500 premises each month.

The Department recognises that infrastructure availability alone does not guarantee adoption, and that digital skills and participation remain lower among older people, those on lower incomes, and rural communities. The Government's Digital Inclusion Roadmap, "Digital for Good", sets out measures to address barriers including awareness, skills, affordability, and accessibility, which remain under active implementation.

Regarding copper switch-off, the Department supports the prioritisation of a managed transition from copper to fibre-based broadband, consistent with the Government's Digital Connectivity Strategy objective of gigabit network coverage for all Irish households and businesses by 2028. The main copper network is owned by eir, and the process for its retirement is governed by ComReg Decision D09/23, which establishes a structured framework consisting of an Enablement Phase, a Migration and Switch-off Phase, and a Decommission Phase. To date, no switch-off plan has been approved by ComReg.

As the timing of copper switch-off is largely a commercial matter for eir, subject to compliance with ComReg's regulatory framework, it would not be appropriate for the Department to direct the commencement of this process. However, the Department recognises that a well-managed copper switch-off could serve as a catalyst for increased fibre adoption among both older people and SMEs, and continues to engage with ComReg, through a bilateral working group on Copper Switch Off, and with eir, to monitor developments.

It is also worth noting that the European Commission published a Proposal for a Regulation for the Digital Networks Act on 21 January 2026, which envisages copper switch-off being triggered where at least 95% fibre coverage exists and affordable retail connectivity services are available, with a backstop date of 31 December 2035 after which Member States will be required to mandate switch-off in remaining areas, subject to limited exceptions.

question.p: 965. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the measures being undertaken by his Department to promote the take up of fibre to the home fibre broadband amongst Irish SMEs, considering data which suggests adoption remains low; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20269/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The policy objective of my Department, as set out in Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in 2022, is to ensure that all premises in Ireland including homes, farms, and businesses have access to high-speed gigabit broadband services by 2028. The Department will refresh this strategy in early 2026, maintaining the 2028 gigabit goal.

The majority of digital connectivity across the State will be delivered through commercial investment by the telecommunications industry, complemented by the roll-out of fibre, across mainly rural areas, under the National Broadband Plan (NBP) contract with National Broadband Ireland (NBI).

Significant progress has been made in deploying the infrastructure necessary to make this possible. As of the end of January 2026, NBI has completed 100% of design and survey work across the approximately 566,000 premises in the Intervention Area, with 85% of the network already built and the main infrastructure build on track to complete by end of 2026, in line with the Programme for Government commitment. According to the most recent ComReg data, gigabit-capable broadband is now available at 90% of all premises in Ireland, with fibre-to-the-premises (FTTP) available at 84%. ComReg data also shows that FTTP subscriptions increased by 21.11% year-on-year in Quarter 4 of 2025, to over 1 million connections by end of 2025 demonstrating that take-up of fibre connectivity for homes and businesses is increasing as services are deployed to areas where they had previously been unavailable.

It is important to note that my Department's role is focused on ensuring the availability of high-speed broadband infrastructure to all premises. The commercial broadband retailers operating in both the BLUE (commercial) and AMBER (State intervention) areas have their own programmes to encourage and support the adoption of high-speed broadband services within the business community. The decision to take up available services is ultimately a commercial matter for individual businesses and their chosen service providers.

Measures to encourage the digitalisation of enterprise, including the adoption by SMEs of available high-speed connectivity, fall primarily within the remit of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment who deliver a range of educational, awareness and enablement programmes to support small and medium-sized businesses in embracing digital technologies.

question.p: 966. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if his Department supports the prioritisation of the switching off of copper broadband technology; to set out the measures his Department have taken or supported to achieve this objective; if his Department has a national target date for when all copper broadband will be switched off within the State; if not, the reason there is no such policy objective; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20271/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The Government’s Digital Connectivity Strategy (DCS) aims to have all Irish households and businesses covered by a gigabit network by 2028. A fibre network is faster, consumes less energy and is more reliable than a copper network, and the transition away from legacy copper infrastructure to modern fibre is consistent with that objective. In this regard the Department supports the prioritisation of a managed transition from copper to fibre-based broadband.

The main copper network is owned by Eir (a private entity) and as such the ongoing operation and maintenance of this network is a matter for them. The process by which Eir can retire this network is laid out in ComReg Decision D09/23, “Framework for the Migration from Legacy Infrastructure to Modern Infrastructure.” The transition framework consists of three phases: an Enablement Phase; a Migration and Switch-off Phase; and a Decommission Phase. The starting point of the process is a formal Switch-off Proposal submitted by Eircom to ComReg. When ComReg is satisfied that the proposal fulfils the framework conditions set out in the Decision, it will approve it, at which point the proposal becomes Eircom’s Switch-off Plan. To date, no plan has been approved by ComReg.

In terms of measures to support the transition, the State’s primary contribution has been to ensure that high-quality fibre alternatives are available to all premises before any copper retirement takes place. The National Broadband Plan (NBP), delivered by National Broadband Ireland (NBI), is extending fibre coverage to approximately 566,000 premises in rural and harder-to-reach areas. As of end January 2026, 100% of design and survey work under the NBP is complete, 85% of the network is already built, and the main infrastructure build is on track to complete by end of 2026 in line with the Programme for Government commitment.

As the timing of the switch-off is largely a commercial matter for Eir, subject to it complying with the provisions of ComReg’s decision, it would not be appropriate for the Department to set a national target date for copper switch-off. However, the Department continues to engage with both ComReg, through a bilateral working group on Copper Switch Off, and Eir, to keep apprised of any developments in this area.

In addition, it is worth noting the European Commission published a "Proposal for a Regulation for the Digital Networks Act" on 21 January 2026 which states the following; "Until 31 December 2035, copper switch off is triggered when the following two conditions are cumulatively met (i) at least 95% fibre coverage; and (ii) availability of affordable retail connectivity services. After this date, the conditions will not play a role anymore and Member States will be required to mandate the switch-off in all the remaining copper switch-off areas with some exceptions."

question.p: 967. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if the relevant building and telecommunications regulations are now legally aligned with the terms of the Gigabit Infrastructure Act; the guidance available to developers to support their compliance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20272/26]

speech.from: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: The Gigabit Infrastructure Act (GIA) is a European regulation that came into force in May 2024, with the purpose of stimulating investment in Very High Capacity Networks, such as fibre and 5G network roll-out. The majority of the provisions in the GIA took effect in November 2025 with all provisions fully effective by May 2026. Although the Act takes direct legal effect under EU law, transposition of various elements of GIA into national law will be required in order to cater for certain aspects of GIA, such as designating competent bodies to carry out various tasks under the Act. The Act replaces the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive which the European Commission considered ineffective in achieving its aims.

Among the new provisions in the GIA is that public sector bodies must meet reasonable requests from operators to access physical infrastructure owned or controlled by those public sector bodies, such as public buildings. Another key feature of the GIA is that it seeks to enable stakeholders to exercise all of their rights and the compliance with all of their obligations under the Act via Single Information Points. This means, for example, if operators wish to assess opportunities to coordinate civil works with other entities, apply for permits or request access to public buildings, they should be able to do so via a single National Digital Entry Point to the digital tools and platforms associated with these activities.

In order to ensure effective implementation of the GIA, the Department has established a GIA Steering Group, comprised of a broad range of stakeholders, to facilitate coordination and collaboration on key issues. External expertise has also been on-boarded to assist on a range of matters related to the GIA.

With regard to the alignment of building and telecommunications regulations with the GIA, work is ongoing across the relevant Government Departments and agencies. The GIA introduces requirements in respect of physical infrastructure in new buildings and major renovation works to ensure that they are equipped with in-building physical infrastructure capable of supporting the deployment of gigabit-speed networks. The relevant building regulations in Ireland are a matter for the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. My Department continues to engage with that Department to ensure coherence between building regulations and the telecommunications provisions of the GIA.

The Department launched a public consultation in December 2025 on exclusions to Single Information Point transparency obligations. Member States have been allowed discretion to decide on which existing physical infrastructure should be made visible via the Single Information Point. This consultation includes the recommendations of an expert report specific to the Irish market. The Department is now analysing the submissions received. A further consultation on in-building physical infrastructure and fibre wiring specifications is expected to be launched shortly. These consultations will further inform the implementation of the GIA in Ireland.

question.p: 968. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether a county-level investment analysis from previous Community Sport Facilities Fund rounds has been completed to identify areas that have been historically under-invested; and if he will publish that analysis. [20405/26]

969. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the projected overall budget envelope for the 2026 round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund and whether this will exceed the €277.9 million allocated under the 2023 round. [20406/26]

971. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether the Department will publish draft guidelines for the next round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund at least four weeks in advance of the opening date in order to allow community clubs adequate preparation time. [20408/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 968, 969 and 971 together.

Over a quarter of a billion euro was allocated to 3,048 community sports clubs and facilities in 2024 under the most recent, 2023, round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF), representing the largest-ever investment in sports facilities in communities across Ireland. Details of all CSFF allocations are available on the Department's website at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-culture-communications-and-sport/collections/sports-capital-programme-allocations/.

New guidelines will be published in advance of the next round and these will include the eligibility and likely assessment criteria for that next round. In line with previous rounds of the Fund, a review of the current funding round has been undertaken and will be published shortly. I have asked my department to prepare for a 2026 round of the CSFF in the coming months. It is anticipated that the next CSFF round will particularly target areas and sports that have been under-invested in over the years. I expect to open this round in the coming months.

summary.i: Question No. 969 answered with Question No. 968.

question.p: 970. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport whether his Department has considered introducing a dedicated capital stream for large regional facilities in major urban areas such as Cork, where the scale of infrastructure required often exceeds the typical local grant thresholds. [20407/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: My Department operates two capital funding programmes for sport, namely the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and the Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF). Sporting organisations can apply directly for CSFF funding while applications for LSSIF funding must be made through either a National Governing Body (NGB) of Sport or a Local Authority.

Over a quarter of a billion euro was allocated to 3,048 community sports clubs and facilities in 2024 from the 2023 round of the CSFF, representing the largest-ever investment in sports facilities in communities across Ireland. Under the 2023 round of the CSFF, applicants could apply for up to €200,000 for local projects and up to €500,000 for regional projects.

In line with previous rounds of the Fund, a review of the current funding round has been undertaken and will be finalised shortly. I have asked my department to prepare for a further round of the CSFF in 2026 which I expect to open in the coming months. It is anticipated that the next CSFF round will particularly target areas and sports that have been under-invested in over the years.

To date there have been two rounds of LSSIF with a cumulative investment of €297 million across 68 projects. My current focus is on ensuring project delivery under the first two rounds of the LSSIF, 2018 and 2024, and this process will inform any decisions regarding the timing of a future round. No decisions have yet been made regarding the next round of LSSIF.

[20444/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: My Department operates two capital funding programmes for sport, namely the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and the Large-Scale Sport Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF). All CSFF grantees must sign a declaration that, from the date of the grant, they will not deny anybody access to any facility or part of a facility for which they received a grant on the grounds of gender, civil status, family status, age, disability, race, sexual orientation, religious belief, or membership of the Traveller or Roma community without just, reasonable and proper cause.

My Department routinely carries out compliance reviews and annual spot-checks of a proportion of grant-aided projects as allocations are drawn down, and participation and inclusion aspects are an important feature of those reviews.
In addition, the LSSIF requires that recipients of LSSIF funding must accommodate the needs of women and men, on a similar basis, with regard to accessing the facilities.
To date, there have been no instances of non-compliance with the gender-based access requirements of either capital funding programme.

question.p: 985. Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will provide the up to date position with regard to An Post pensions; to provide a clear timeline on when the 7% increase to An Post pensions will be implemented. [20775/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport
speech.p: Under section 46 of the Postal and Telecommunications Services Act 1983, the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport with the concurrence of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, approves any superannuation schemes submitted by An Post. The operation of the schemes is a matter between the management of An Post, staff representatives and the trustees of the schemes.

In accordance with the Act and the relevant Code of Practice for the Governance of State Bodies, An Post must seek Ministerial approval from both Ministers to increase pensions and deferred pensions for members of the An Post superannuation scheme. Section 2.13 of the Code of Practice for Governance of State Bodies Superannuation and Remuneration annex sets out that NewERA advice should be sought in respect of pension amendment proposals, as is appropriate in their role as commercial and financial advisors to the Ministers.

On 23 October 2025, An Post wrote to my Department requesting consent for an increase to pensions in payment and deferred pensions, namely, to increase pensions in payment for members and deferred members of the An Post Superannuation Scheme by 6% per annum with effect from 1st January 2025 and 1% from 1st of June 2025, arising from its agreements with employee representative groups. In line with both the Code of Practice for State Bodies and the relevant legislation, Ministerial consent has been granted, and this was conveyed to An Post on 25 February 2026.

question.p: 986. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the status of shark fin products and derivatives under Irish Law; the person or body responsible for enforcement; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20058/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Ireland is a party to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) which is implemented through the European Wildlife Trade Regulations and enforced through Section 53A of the Wildlife Act.

Many shark species were added to the CITES listings at CITES Convention of Parties (CoP) 19 and at the recent CITES CoP 20 further shark listing proposals were successful including deep water gulpher sharks.

Article I of The CITES Convention includes parts and derivatives as specimens for the purpose of the Convention. The Convention includes species threatened with extinction which are or may be affected by trade. Trade in specimens of these species must be subject to regulation.

While shark fins are seen in trade for consumption (primarily in east Asia) there is trade in shark fin powder (chondroitin sulphate) which is used by the pharmaceutical industry and shark liver extracts are used in shark-liver oil capsules and cosmetics.
Importers will need to apply to Ireland’s CITES Management Authority (which is in the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS)) for an import permit.
Enforcement of CITES trade imports is the responsibility of Revenue Customs at the borders (point of entry) with NPWS also authorised persons for any offences under the Wildlife Act.

question.p: 988. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if a bog (details supplied) is included in the Cessation of turf cutting compensation scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18242/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: My Department operates two schemes that support households and individuals to cease cutting turf and facilitate measures to restore the peatland habitat.

The Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme was established following engagement with stakeholders in 2011 for active domestic turf cutters arising from the restrictions on turf cutting on 53 raised bog special areas of conservation (SAC) and was extended in 2014 to include 36 raised bog natural heritage areas (NHA). This scheme has compensated those impacted by restrictions on turf-cutting on protected sites.

Additional bog plots not covered by the CTCCS may qualify for the Protected Raised Bog Restoration Incentive Scheme. This is a once off area based compensation scheme open to applications from property right holders who wish to have their lands included as part of the restoration scheme or where access is required for restoration works within a designated raised bog.
Whilst the exact location of the bog plot referred to is unknown, it is my understanding that there are no designated bogs in the townland name provided and hence these schemes may not apply.
The Deputy can contact my department directly, with regard to establishing if the lands mentioned are designated or not, if he so wishes.

question.p: 990. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding any review of the qualifying income thresholds for cost rental housing developments; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18281/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Under Delivering Homes, Building Communities, Ireland's housing plan to 2030, Cost Rental is a key element of the Government's strategy to improve affordability in the rental sector and to provide secure, long-term homes for moderate-income households. Cost Rental was introduced in 2021 as a new form of housing tenure in Ireland, where the tenant pays a rent which is set to cover the cost of delivering, managing and maintaining the home.

Eligibility and income parameters are a key tool in targeting State-supported Cost Rental homes at those who fall within the moderate income cohort. The primary condition for accessing Cost Rental housing is a net annual income under a certain limit, which is currently €66,000 per year for homes in Dublin and €59,000 elsewhere, set through secondary legislation. Net income is defined as gross income with income tax, USC, PRSI contributions and pension contributions deducted. The legislation does not set any minimum 'income threshold' for Cost Rental, but as with any letting of a home, the landlord must consider the issues of affordability and tenancy sustainability.
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to keep cost rental income limits under review, in order to ensure they remain fit for purpose. My Department is currently progressing this work.

question.p: 997. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 654 of 27 January 2026, the number of individual dwellings which were the subject of the remediation claims to date; the total number of estimated dwellings affected which are likely to apply under the scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18449/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the Use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 (the Act) commenced on 22 June 2023, and it underpins the current grant scheme and the related Regulations which were adopted on 29 June 2023.
The Scheme applies to the owners of dwellings located in Donegal, Mayo, Clare, Limerick and Sligo with further local authority areas to be designated under the scheme shortly.

As at the end of January 2026, 3,225 applications have been received under the current and previous scheme, of these 432 homes have been remediated with 1,136, homeowners notifying their relevant designated local authority of the date of commencement of their works to remediate their homes.
The total grant amount recouped to the five designated local authorities under the scheme from the period 2020 to date, amounts to approximately €272.7 million.

The original estimate following the expert group report was that approximately 7,500 homes may be impacted. This amount may change in the future depending on the number of homes impacted compared to the original estimate.

question.p: 998. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to Parliamentary Question No. 645 of 20 January 2026, the reasons why he has no plans to propose amendments to the provisions referred to; whether he has relied on any research or reports in forming this view; to outline any such research or reports; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18450/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: As set out in the reply to Question No. 645 of 20 January 2026, electoral law provides that a presiding officer may, at his or her own discretion, or if required by a personation agent present in the polling station, require any person attending to vote to produce one of the specified documents as evidence of identity. If he or she fails to produce the document or if the presiding officer is not satisfied that the person concerned is the person to whom the document produced relates, the person shall not be permitted to vote. The documents which may be accepted are prescribed in regulation 2(b) of the Electoral (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2024.
The Manual for Presiding Officers, prepared by my Department for each electoral event, advises presiding officers to seek evidence of identity:
• whenever requested by a personation agent present in the polling station;
• whenever the presiding officer suspects that a person is attempting to commit personation; and
• in the case of 25% of the persons attending to vote selected at random throughout the day.

The purpose of the requirement regarding evidence of identity is to strengthen the safeguards against the offence of personation, particularly against the possibility that the offence may be attempted on a widespread and organised basis. It is not intended that the provision would be so operated as to prevent qualified electors voting.

In 2023, the Government established An Coimisiún Toghcháin, the independent electoral commission. An Coimisiún's research, advisory and public information function sees the commission conduct research on electoral policy and procedure. An Coimisiún is also empowered to advise and make recommendations to the Government in relation to any proposals for legislative change, or any other policy matters concerning electoral policy or procedures. In addition, section 68 of the Electoral Reform Act 2022 provides for the preparation and publication of a post electoral event review (PEER) by An Coimisiún following any electoral event. To date, the PEERs published by An Coimisiún have not contained any recommendations in relation to the evidence of identity requirements set out in electoral law.

question.p: 999. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to elaborate on the January 2026 homelessness statistics by giving a breakdown of the lengths of time spent in emergency accommodation by the 17,112 people mentioned in the report; to state or estimate the average length of time that an adult person spends in emergency accommodation; and to state the earliest date on which any of the current 17,112 people first entered emergency accommodation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18455/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: My Department’s role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of local authorities in addressing homelessness at a local level.

Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of accommodation and related services for homeless persons rests with individual local authorities. Decisions on the assessment of households for homeless services, the most appropriate form of such support, and the allocation of that support are a matter for the local authority concerned.

My Department currently gathers and publishes data on a monthly basis on the number of homeless persons accommodated in emergency accommodation funded and overseen by local authorities. These reports are based on data provided by local authorities, produced through the Pathway Accommodation & Support System (PASS).

The monthly homelessness report includes details of individuals, families and the dependants of these families who accessed emergency accommodation during the relevant count week of the month in question. The most recently published data is in respect of January 2026. The reports are collated on a regional basis and are available on my Department's website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/homelessness-data, and are also published to the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation's open data portal: https://data.gov.ie/.

My Department also publishes quarterly progress reports which are based on quarterly performance reports submitted by the nine regional lead authorities responsible for the administration of homeless services at local level. The quarterly performance reports include regional information on the duration of stay data for single and family households. The duration of stay data is reported as six-monthly bands ranging from less than six months to more than 24 months. These bands refer to consecutive stays in emergency accommodation and are based on a point-in-time count, informed by emergency accommodation usage on the last night in the quarter.

The most recently published data is in respect of Q4 2025. Progress and performance reports are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/collections/homelessness-data/.

The Housing Plan, 'Delivering Homes, Building Communities', commits to further enhancing reporting in relation to the use of local authority homeless emergency accommodation to allow for an expansion of the information gathered and increased analysis of the reasons driving new homeless presentations and the progress being made to support households to exit emergency accommodation to a tenancy.

question.p: 1000. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to the recent opening of the state’s first purpose-built social housing with supports for older people (details supplied) if there are plans to roll-out further similar style facilities; if existing developments will be considered for adaptation for such purposes; if a single point of contact exists for stakeholders considering such developments; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18486/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (Deputy Kieran O'Donnell)
speech.p: The Government’s new housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030, includes measures which will increase delivery of housing for older people through increased delivery of social housing, increased delivery of more suitable homes in private housing and increased choice to support voluntary rightsizing. Government is committed to increasing housing available to older people to facilitate ageing in place with dignity and independence and to supporting rightsizing on a voluntary basis.

Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030, includes a Government commitment to work collaboratively through the establishment of a cooperation framework between the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage and the Department of Health on the integration of health and social care supports and housing for older people. This will include consideration of the learnings from the Richmond Place, Inchicore Pilot Model of supported housing for older people from both Departments' perspective, including the evaluations of this pilot project underway to inform policy in this area.

Under Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030, housing for older people is being continually delivered under the programmes managed by my Department, whereby Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) and local authorities can advance housing proposals for older people.

The design of the Inchicore pilot predates the publication by my Department of the Design Manual for Quality Housing (the Design Manual) which is available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/publication/b3e02-design-manual-for-quality-housing/. The Design Manual is intended to guide local authorities and AHBs, and their consultants, on the design of social housing including the internal layouts of individual social homes and its use is now mandatory for all new build social housing, following a Government decision in July 2025. The Design manual provides guidance and examples of a range of housing options including appropriate housing choices for smaller sized households, such as the increasing number of older people who want to remain in their community. The Design Manual includes specific Universal design (UD) internal layouts developed with the input of the Centre for Excellence in Universal Design.

question.p: 1001. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he is aware of growing delays in Tailte Eireann property registration times and the subsequent risks to the conveyancing process; if he or his officials have raised the matter with Tailte Eireann; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18516/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage (Deputy James Browne)
speech.p: Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency under the aegis of the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. Tailte Éireann provides a property registration system, property valuation service and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. Under section 8 of the Tailte Éireann Act 2022, Tailte Éireann is independent in the performance of its functions.

The continued increase in applications received for registration by Tailte Éireann year over year, and challenges in recruitment for some time, have resulted in longer processing times for certain application types, however these delays are alleviating, with significant progress achieved to date in reducing the age profile of applications on hand.

As part of Tailte Éireann's resourcing strategy, an accelerated recruitment programme was launched to address the high volume of vacancies and strengthen operational capacities in response to the increasing service demands. As a result, the Registration team within Tailte Éireann are now fully staffed with additional capacity to support ongoing improvements in the delivery of registration services and contribute to the timely processing of applications.

Outside of recruitment, every effort is being made by Tailte Éireann to further reduce application processing times, including implementation of revised procedures for more efficient handling of the large volume of applications that are lodged that do not meet the minimum requirements to proceed to registration and a targeted, organisation wide approach to reduce the age profile of applications pending registration.

Applications for registration which involve a transfer, charge or release of registered lands, where no change to the registry map is required account for approximately 60% of applications for registration. These applications are typically processed within 15 working days where the application is lodged in order.

Applications submitted electronically through eRegistration account for approximately 18% of all applications received and are processed within 10 working days. eDischarges are typically processed within 2 working days. Tailte Éireann continues to promote electronic registration services to its customers to improve processing times for all applicants.

Processing times for applications which do require a change to the map, and those requiring first registration of property, are improving due to the impact of resourcing and implemented procedural efficiencies outlined above.

It may be noted that the Registration of the legal effect of a conveyance comes at the end of the process, after the documents are executed and should, in the vast majority of cases, not lead to any delay in the conveyancing process as the purchaser is already in occupation of the property. In a recently published guide by the Law Society to avoid delays when selling property (www.lawsociety.ie/globalassets/documents/news/2024/speed-up-your-property-sale.pdf), the seller, or their solicitor, should have all of the required deeds and documents in order prior to putting the property on the market to avoid delays.

In cases where any delay in registration could have a potential impact, Tailte Éireann make every effort to expedite applications which are in order, where valid grounds exist, and where doing so does not impose a conflict in regard to priority given to any prior lodged dealing.

Lodging parties may contact Tailte Éireann in relation to a specific case by email at info@tailte.ie. Further information in relation to specific cases may be obtained by Oireachtas members by contacting the dedicated e-mail address in respect of Tailte Éireann at oireachtas@tailte.ie.

Tailte Éireann has advised me that improvements have been made to date in throughput times and I am confident that they have the resources and procedures in place to further reduce waiting times across all application types.

The information provided by Tailte Éireann below relates to all applications for registration on the National Land Register, including First Registration applications, as requested. Each application may contain a number of property transactions to be registered, for example a transfer of title, a mortgage/charge and a right of way in favour of the applicant may be lodged within one application. As shown in this table, the number of cases being processed by Tailte Éireann is increasing year on year. The number of applications being received is also increasing year on year, but processes that have been put in place are helping to manage this workload and decrease the backlog.

The number of applications processed in each year refers to all applications which have been brought to a final conclusion within the year and includes applications which have been completed, refused, rejected, withdrawn or abandoned as they could not be processed further.

Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency under the aegis of my Department.
