Question No. 1106 answered with Question No. 1024.
Question No. 1107 answered with Question No. 1024.

question.p: 1108. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding the criteria for awarding protected status to any animal; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20259/26]

1109. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding the protected status of seagulls; if it is under review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20260/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (Deputy Christopher O'Sullivan)
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1108 and 1109 together.
All naturally occurring wild birds, including all gulls, are protected under both EU and Irish law.
In EU legislation, all naturally occurring wild birds are protected under the Birds Directive (Directive 2009/147/EC on the conservation of wild birds).

Protected status for gulls in Ireland therefore derives in the first instance from its status as a species covered by Article 1 of the Directive and Ireland’s obligations as an EU Member. As such, the status of gulls as a protected species is not under review.
The Directive requires Member States to set down a general system of protection for birds and to prohibit, inter alia, (subject to certain exceptions):
- deliberate killing or capture by any method;
- deliberate destruction of, or damage to, their nests and eggs or removal of their nests;
- taking their eggs in the wild and keeping these eggs even if empty;
- deliberate disturbance of these birds particularly during the period of breeding and rearing, in so far as disturbance would be significant having regard to the objectives of this Directive;
- keeping birds of species the hunting and capture of which is prohibited.

The Birds Directive is implemented in Ireland under, inter alia, the Wildlife Acts 1976, the Wildlife (Amendment) Act 2000 and the European Communities (Birds and Natural Habitats) Regulations 2011 (SI 477/2011).
In relation to the protection of species other than birds, if species are listed on Annex II and/or Annex IV of the Habitats Directive then they also enjoy protected status.

Additionally most native mammals, and all native amphibians and reptiles are protected wild animals under the Wildlife Acts. For animal species not already covered by protected status, section 23 of the Wildlife Act 1976 allows the Minister to confer such status. Criteria that may be used to justify protected status include consideration of threats to the species, the conservation status of the species, whether the species is subject to hunting, or the importance of the Irish population of the species in an international context

summary.i: Question No. 1109 answered with Question No. 1108.

question.p: 1110. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he has assessed the impact of the new tenancy rules introduced on 1 March 2026 on the volume of notices of termination issued in the weeks preceding that date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20464/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) was established as a quasi-judicial independent statutory body under the Residential Tenancies Acts 2004-2026 to regulate the rental sector; provide information to tenants and landlords; maintain a national register of tenancies; facilitate the resolution of disputes between tenants and landlords; and conduct research and provide information to inform policy, including information to me on matters relating to the rented sector.

The RTB publishes reports on Notices of Termination received on a quarterly basis. This information is accessible to all members of the public and can be found on the RTB website at https://rtb.ie/data-insights/rtb-data-hub/notices-of-termination/
The next RTB data release is expected on 19 March 2026 and will include Notice of Termination data to Q4 2025. The data relating to Q1 2026 is expected to be published by the RTB on 14 May 2026.

My Department continually works with, and uses data provided by, the RTB to keep the operation of the RTB, the Residential Tenancies Acts and the residential rental sector under continuous review to ensure that an appropriately balanced policy and legislative framework is maintained.

question.p: 1111. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he has plans to reform the capital assistance scheme as it applies to approved housing bodies providing accommodation for persons with disabilities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20501/26]

1112. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will amend the capital assistance scheme to remove the current restriction on the acquisition of second-hand properties; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20502/26]

1114. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will permit the use of the capital assistance scheme for the acquisition of properties intended for use as respite centres; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20504/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1111, 1112 and 1114 together.

The Capital Assistance Scheme (CAS) provides up to 100% capital funding for the construction and acquisition of social homes by Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs), including purpose-built 'Group/Community Homes' for persons with a disability. Accordingly, a review of the scheme is not required in this respect.

There are currently no restrictions on the acquisition of second-hand properties through CAS. The acquisition of second-hand properties in 2026 is provided for through my Department's Social Housing Second Hand Acquisitions Programme. Some €373 million is available through the programme this year to support acquisitions for social housing qualified households. This budget includes €50 million specifically ring-fenced for use by AHBs via the CAS scheme for acquisitions to meet the urgent accommodation needs of persons with disabilities, older persons and care leavers.

The CAS scheme provides funding for long-term priority needs accommodation, allowing persons in the priority needs categories to live independently in their communities. As such, the provision of respite centres does not fall under the remit of CAS and is addressed by my colleagues in the Department of Health/HSE and the Department of Children, Disability and Equality.

summary.i: Question No. 1112 answered with Question No. 1111.

question.p: 1113. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will increase the funding thresholds for three- and four-bedroom houses to reflect prevailing market values; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20503/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: My Department provides Acquisition Cost Guidelines (ACGs) for the acquisition of second-hand properties by local authorities and Approved Housing Bodies for social housing qualified households . While guidelines are updated annually, with the most recent guidelines issuing in Q2 2025, my Department monitors price trends throughout the year and all incoming funding applications are considered with these trends in mind.

The ACGs reference lower and upper cost ranges, as well as an average benchmark cost, reflecting the prevailing range of prices across local authorities at the time of issue for 2 to 4 bed houses and 1 & 2 bed apartments. They are not applied as absolute ceilings or limits, but benchmarks for the acquisition of second-hand properties.

Accordingly, my Department considers all acquisition proposals, including where the cost of acquiring the property may exceed the guidelines provided, on a case-by-case basis having regard to appropriate value for money considerations and unmet need.

summary.i: Question No. 1114 answered with Question No. 1111.

question.p: 1115. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the current status of the retrospective defective concrete blocks scheme; the timeline for the final approval and full sign off of the scheme; the steps being taken to ensure that once approval is granted funding will be made available without delay; whether the relevant teams administering the scheme are fully resourced and prepared to process applications and payments immediately once approval is in place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20505/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the Use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 (the Act) commenced on 22 June 2023 which contains the current grant scheme and the related Regulations were adopted on 29 June 2023.

The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the Use of Defective Concrete Blocks (Amendment) Bill 2025 was initiated in Dáil Eireann on 2 December 2025, passed both Houses of the Oireachtas and was subsequently signed into law by the President, thereby becoming an Act, on the 23 December 2025.

The main provision of the 2025 Act provides that increases in the grant scheme cap and rates from October and November 2024 can retrospectively benefit homeowners that incurred qualifying costs under the grant scheme since 29 March 2024.

I have signed the Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the Use of Defective Concrete Blocks (Amendment) Act 2025 (Commencement) Order 2026 to give effect to these provisions which came into operation on 25 February 2026, with the related Regulations also adopted on 25 February 2026.

These will allow qualifying homeowners to apply to their designated local authority to have a new remediation option grant amount determined. It also doubles the time applicants have to complete works from 65 week to 130 weeks.

Funding is in place and a Departmental Circular issued from my Department on 27 February 2026 to the designated local authorities. This contained the documents providing detailed information on the process including a Ministerial Guidance Note and Your Questions Answered material along with a copy of the Commencement Order, 2025 Act and 2026 Regulations. This will allow the relevant local authorities to process applications for retrospective payments in a timely manner.
The detailed operation of the Scheme is a matter for the designated local authorities and the Housing Agency in the first instance. Their respective roles are set out clearly in the 2022 Act.

Under section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which he / she is responsible. As such, information on resources and staffing would be available directly from the respective local authority.

The allocation of staff across the Housing Agency is a matter for that organisation in the first instance. More information on their staffing can be sought from the Housing Agency via publicreps@housingagency.ie.

question.p: 1116. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he will review the provision within the defective concrete blocks scheme that limits eligibility in respect of rental properties where the dwelling has been rented for more than 20 years; whether he accepts that this provision may exclude homeowners whose properties were rented for periods but are still affected by defective blocks through no fault of their own; whether his Department is considering removing or amending this clause; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20506/26]

1117. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will review the rule within the defective concrete blocks scheme that restricts applicants to eligibility in respect of one rental property only; whether his Department has examined the impact of this restriction on families who may own more than one affected property due to inheritance or family circumstances; whether consideration is being given to removing this restriction to ensure equitable treatment of homeowners affected by defective blocks; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20507/26]

1118. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will review the damage threshold criteria within the defective concrete blocks scheme; whether consideration is being given to basing eligibility primarily on certified engineering testing and professional assessment rather than fixed damage thresholds; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20508/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1116, 1117 and 1118 together.
The Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme applies to the owners of dwellings located in designated local authority areas which are damaged due to the use of defective concrete blocks.
The relevant legislation does not contain a provision that limits eligibility in respect of rental properties where the dwelling has been rented for more than 20 years.
The dwelling must be:
• an individual's principal private residence, that is, a house which an individual owns (or co-owns) and occupies as his or her only main residence.

• a rented dwelling with a registered tenancy that was registered with the Residential Tenancies Boards (RTB) on or before 1 November 2021 subject to a maximum of one rental property per household and the introduction of a claw-back mechanism upon re-sale within a set time period depending on the remediation option used
and the 2022 Act defines a relevant owner as an individual who owns, whether jointly or not, a relevant dwelling and:
• became an owner of the dwelling prior to 31 January 2020, inherited the dwelling on or after 31 January 2020, or
• subject to Section 9(4) of the 2022 Act, purchased the dwelling on or after 31 January 2020.
• The charge against rental properties is to ensure the units are kept in the rental system.

The 'damage threshold' is the minimum level of damage which must be present in a home in order for that dwelling to be allowed access into the grant scheme. The damage itself must be linked to the suspected presence of defective concrete blocks in the home and will be considered as part of the Building Condition Assessment process by a competent building professional. The purpose of having a damage threshold is to ensure that the worst affected homes are prioritised first. In removing any damage threshold, this would have a significant negative impact on the capacity of the statutory process to address the worst affected houses first.
I currently have no plans to amend these conditions as set down by the Oireachtas.

It should be noted that where the Housing Agency determines that a dwelling which has been put forward has not met the damage threshold that determination can be appealed to the independent appeals panel which has been established to assess appeals made under the Remediation of Dwellings DCB grant scheme. The establishment of this Panel offers those affected by decisions made by the Housing Agency and Local Authorities an opportunity to have their cases assessed by an independent group of industry experts. The points of appeal that are available to a DCB applicant include the validation stage by the local authority, the damage threshold determination made by the Housing Agency, the remediation option, and the grant amount approved and where a local authority refuse to make a grant payment pursuant to grant approval. The Panel is statutorily independent and so independent in the performance of their functions.
A homeowner can also reapply to the grant scheme at a future date if the suspected presence of defective concrete blocks manifests to a point where the damage threshold is met.

summary.i: Question No. 1117 answered with Question No. 1116.
Question No. 1118 answered with Question No. 1116.

question.p: 1119. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to parliamentary questions submitted in 2025, for an update on the campaign to reinter the historical figures, commonly known as the Invincibles, with relatives who are buried at Kilmainham Gaol since 1883; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20509/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The question of whether any persons might be reburied in Glasnevin Cemetery is not one on which I can comment on as Glasnevin Cemetery is the responsibility of the Dublin Cemeteries Trust.

My responsibilities and indeed those of the Office of Public Works, in relation to Kilmainham Gaol, arise under the National Monuments Act 1930 as a national monument of which I am owner. These responsibilities relate to the maintenance and presentation of Kilmainham Gaol to the public and the consideration of any requests to me to grant consent under the Act of 1930 for works (including ground disturbance) to it.

question.p: 1120. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the current position in relation to a new project in County Laois (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20564/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The provision of a fire service in its functional area, including the establishment and maintenance of a fire brigade, the assessment of fire cover needs and the provision of fire station premises, is a statutory function of individual fire authorities under the Fire Services Acts, 1981 & 2003. My Department supports the fire authorities through setting general policy, providing a central training programme, issuing guidance on operational and other related matters and providing capital funding for equipment and priority infrastructural projects.

Project consideration stages from a Department perspective include submission of preliminary and detailed appraisals; submission of design brief; selection of a site; application for approval in principle; appointment of design consultants; submission of a preliminary design; planning application; submission of a preliminary cost plan, detailed design and cost plans; and tender process and construction stages - each step subject to approval from my Department.
In December 2024 Laois County Council submitted an updated preliminary appraisal for a proposed new fire station at Rathdowney, noting several issues with the existing station including,
- accessibility of the site for responding firefighters due to its central location on a narrow street within Rathdowney
- the stations limited size, poor layout; and
- limited welfare facilities, particularly in the context of the increased optimal crewing numbers of fire stations to 12 following the August 2023 WRC agreement with Retained firefighters.

Laois County Council have indicated a new fire station for Rathdowney to be their number one priority project for the Fire Services Capital Programme 2026 – 2030. The Council has secured a new site they regard as ideally situated with regard to the road network and traffic flow while retaining a central location close to the retained crews living and work environments.

Laois County Council have been given approval to progress the Rathdowney fire station project to full design and cost plan stage to advance the projects state of readiness for full approval. My Department will work closely with Laois County Council to progress their identified priority infrastructural projects, within the context of the totality of requests from fire authorities countrywide for capital funding.

question.p: 1121. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans to review the income eligibility thresholds for HAP in light of increasing rents; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20585/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The baseline income thresholds increased by €5,000 for all local authorities with effect from 1 January 2023. The thresholds thus increased to €40,000, €35,000 and €30,000 for Bands 1, 2 and 3 respectively. These thresholds are net income thresholds, i.e. gross household income less income tax, PRSI, Universal Social Charge and Additional Superannuation Contribution.

My Department has been examining the existing income limits in the context of current market and household income conditions, including the suitability or otherwise of the current framework having regard to the significantly changed landscape since the standardised income limits were introduced. This includes examining the findings of research commissioned by my Department and this work is ongoing.

I am not in a position at this point to indicate the outcome of these considerations but I envisage that the analysis will be concluded early in 2026 to facilitate a final determination on next steps, which I expect will include an increase in the income limits. I am also keen to put in place a more structured and frequent process for the review of these limits going forward.

The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) scheme continues to play a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q3 2025, more than 130,200 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 50,705 households actively in receipt of HAP support.

Under HAP, a tenant sources their own accommodation in the private rented market. This accommodation should be within the prescribed maximum HAP rent limits, which are based on household size and the rental market within the area concerned.

Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single person households. This additional measure recognises the challenges experienced by single person households, and the fact that both single and couple households have a one-bed need.

My Department has reviewed the use of these measures and their impact on the overall affordability of the HAP scheme for tenants. This review has highlighted that the affordability and sustainability of HAP tenancies continues to be impacted by pressures in the private rental market. My Department is now undertaking a review of existing HAP rent limits to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
It is intended that the review process will conclude before the end of Q2 this year.

question.p: 1126. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his attention has been drawn to the current industrial relations dispute within Tailte Éireann given the Government's failure to implement a pay agreement which was agreed between the trade union (details supplied), Tailte Éireann and Government Departments following the merging of Ordnance Survey Ireland into Tailte Éireann; the actions he is undertaking to ensure this pay agreement is implemented in full; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20700/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency under the aegis of my Department. Tailte Éireann provides a property registration system, property valuation service and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. Under Section 8 of the Tailte Éireann Act 2022, Tailte Éireann is independent in the performance of its functions.
I am aware of the issue raised in relation to the transfer of staff from Ordnance Survey Ireland (OSI) to Tailte Éireann.

By way of background, Tailte Éireann is the State agency formed on 1 March 2023 following the merger of Ordnance Survey Ireland, the Property Registration Authority and the Valuation Office. All the functions previously carried out by the Property Registration Authority, the Valuation Office, and Ordnance Survey Ireland are now being performed by Tailte Éireann.

As I understand it, public pay policy, which falls under the remit of my colleague, the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Services, Reform and Digitalisation, allows for public servants assimilating into a new organisation to transfer to the equivalent general service grade where doing so is equal to, or more beneficial than, their current terms. Grades of a higher value than the equivalent general service grade can be ring-fenced on a personal to holder basis. This ensures that no staff member is disadvantaged by the redeployment process.

My officials continue to engage with officials from the Department for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Services, Reform and Digitalisation with a view to exploring approaches to progress the matter in a manner that is consistent with established Government pay policy and the Public Service Agreement 2024-2026.

question.p: 1127. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason Lough Corrib was never added to the protected area register under the EU Water Framework Directive (WFD); the timeline for this oversight to be rectified; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20718/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage (Deputy James Browne)
speech.p: The Protected Area Register under the EU Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) (WFD) includes the River Corrib but not Lough Corrib. This was an administrative oversight in the transfer of the details of the S.I. into the Protected Area Register. This is currently being rectified, and I have been informed that this will be undertaken by the Environmental Protection Agency when the Protected Area Register is next updated, which will be by the end of 2026.

As previously referenced the River Corrib and Lough Corrib are both designated as salmonid waters under S.I. No 293 of 1988, and both covered by the Lough Corrib Special Area of Conservation (SAC). SACs are prime wildlife conservation areas in the country, considered to be important on a European as well as an Irish level. The legal basis on which SACs are selected and designated is the EU Habitats Directive, transposed into Irish law by the European Communities (Birds and Natural Habitats) Regulations 2011 (S.I. No. 477 of 2011), as amended. The Directive lists certain habitats and species that must be protected within SACs, including salmon, which is listed as a qualifying interest in the Corrib SAC:
https://www.npws.ie/sites/default/files/protected-sites/conservation_objectives/CO000297.pdf

In addition, the WFD requires all Member States to protect and improve water quality in all waters so that we achieve Good Ecological status by 2027. The waters of the River Corrib and Lough Corrib are both meeting their water quality targets of achieving at least Good Ecological Status, as required under the WFD.

question.p: 1128. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the measures his Department is implementing so that Lough Corrib and the Corrib River in County Galway can achieve a 'High Ecological Status' as referenced in the EU Water Framework Directive (WFD); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20719/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Lough Corrib and the Corrib River waterbodies are classified as Good Ecological Status Objective waterbodies under the EU Water Framework Directive (WFD). Both waterbodies are currently achieving their objective status and therefore meet their WFD environmental objectives.

On a national level a new revised and strengthened River Basin Management Plan, the Water Action Plan 2024, was launched by my Department in September 2024. The Water Action Plan is a strategic plan that outlines the national policies and high level goals that will protect and restore our natural waters up to 2027, and advances Ireland’s commitment to the implementation of the WFD. The Water Action Plan 2024 sets out a roadmap to restore Ireland’s water bodies to ‘Good Ecological Status’ or better and to protect water from any further deterioration. This plan fulfils a legal obligation under the EU Water Framework Directive. The aim of the plan is the identification and implementation of the “right measure in the right place”, and contains targeted measures to both restore and protect all water bodies. It is being supported by the integrated catchment approach through the development of Sectoral Action Work Plans and Catchment Management Work Plans by the Local Authority Waters Programme (LAWPRO).

LAWPRO, which is funded by my Department, coordinates efforts among Local Authorities to achieve our water quality objectives in our water bodies. LAWPRO has carried out and continues to undertake assessments within several Priority Areas for Action (PAAs) that flow into Lough Corrib including the Owenriff, Failmore, Cregg River and Headford Stream, and the Upper Clare and Sinking River PAAs.

Since 2024, a total of €127,210.59 has been allocated to projects across the Lough Corrib area through the Catchment Support Fund and Community Water Development Fund. Provided by my Department, this funding is administered by LAWPRO’s Communities team and has supported water quality improvement projects undertaken by groups such as Cáirde an Chlár, Corrib Beo, Annaghdown Anglers, Carra Mask Corrib Water Protection Group and the Headford and Corrib Anglers Association.

Funding is also provided by my Department towards the administration costs of the Farming for Water EIP, which is delivered by LAWPRO. The Farming for Water EIP funds a Community Animator through Corrib Beo to work directly with local farmers to encourage participation and implement practical and nature-based solutions to reduce nutrient loss and improve riverbank management in targeted areas for action in need of mitigation measures. The Farming for Water EIP project has received 21 applications to the value of €156,880 from farmers in the Corrib catchment to implement 162 measures that improve water quality and promote sustainable land management.

In addition, Local Authorities are also required to prepare a Local Authority Water Action Work Plan setting out the specific actions assigned to each authority for the protection and restoration of water quality under the Water Action Plan. LAWPRO is working with Local Authorities to develop a template for the work plans. I have been informed that a final version of the work plan template will be ready for use by local authorities in Q2 2026.

question.p: 1129. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will clarify a matter (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20744/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Section 34(8) of the Planning and Development Act 2000 remains the operative provision governing the planning authority’s initial decision period. In the ordinary case, that period is 8 weeks from receipt of the application, subject to the statutory variations provided for in section 34(8).

For RED III applications falling within section 34E, the new provisions do not replace section 34(8) with a 52-week decision period. Instead, section 34E introduces a maximum decision period of 52 weeks, measured from the date of the section 34D(a) completeness acknowledgement notice. While section 34(8) continues to govern the initial decision timetable, the planning authority must, in any event, issue its decision before the expiry of this 52-week long-stop.

Section 34(9) also continues to apply in these cases. Under that provision, a planning authority may seek an extension of the 8-week decision period with the applicant’s consent. However, any such extension cannot extend the decision period beyond the 52-week limit provided for in section 34E(2).

Guidance has issued to planning authorities on the implementation of RED III. This includes Departmental Circulars CEPP 1/2025, CEPP 2/2025 and CEPP 1/2026, the Department’s “Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) – Further Information” document, and guidance materials published by An Coimisiún Pleanála for planning authorities and prospective applicants

question.p: 1130. Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if all removals from a list (details supplied) or exceeding the income threshold for 2025/2026 could be postponed until the review is completed. [20752/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria in force at the time of assessment under section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended.

My Department has been examining the existing income limits in the context of current market and household income conditions, including the suitability or otherwise of the current framework having regard to the significantly changed landscape since the standardised income limits were introduced. This includes examining the findings of research commissioned by my Department and this work is ongoing.

I am not in a position at this point to indicate the outcome of these considerations but I envisage that the analysis will be concluded early in 2026 to facilitate a final determination on next steps.

question.p: 1131. Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if any assistance is available to a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20805/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: My Department, through the National Built Heritage Service (NBHS) and in conjunction with the local authorities, operates two annual schemes which aim to assist owners of historic structures in maintaining, preserving, and adapting these buildings to enable their protection.

The first of these schemes is the Built Heritage Investment Scheme (BHIS) which provides up to €50,000 for qualifying works. BHIS is aimed chiefly at smaller-scale repairs, upgrades, or other interventions, often being awarded to projects focused on individual homes, or to smaller or less complex structures or projects. Subject to funding, the next round of applications will open this summer for projects to be completed in 2027. Applications are made through the relevant Local Authority.

The second scheme is the Historic Structures Fund (HSF) which awards grants of up to €200,000. The HSF is targeted at large scale conservation works and applications must demonstrate a clear community or public benefit.
The HSF provides capital funding for works to qualifying structures which include the following:
• Protected Structures: Structures in the Record of Protected Structures (RPS) of each Local Authority;

• Structures eligible for or proposed for inclusion in the RPS but not yet formally approved for inclusion. Such structures must meet the criteria for inclusion in the RPS by the Local Authority, i.e. must be of special interest from an architectural, historical, archaeological, artistic, cultural, scientific, social or technical point of view;
• Structures or works within Architectural Conservation Areas (ACAs), or within the amenity of a National Monument, where exceptional circumstances apply.

An announcement of successful applications made under the 2026 scheme is expected to be made at the end of this month. Subject to funding, applications for the 2027 scheme will open later this year. Applications are made through the relevant Local Authority.

It is important to note that both BHIS and HSF operate on a match-funding basis whose awards are capped at 80% of costs, meaning any successful applicant will be required to invest a minimum 20% of project costs from their own funds. As both BHIS and HSF are extremely competitive funding programmes, it is also likely that awards will total less than 80% of costs in most cases, requiring a higher proportion of capital investment from the applicant themselves.

question.p: 1132. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the 2026 budget allocation for the tenant-in-situ scheme; and for housing acquisitions for each of the 31 local authorities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20837/26]

1133. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he can confirm that short- or long-term leases properties where the tenant qualifies for social housing, the property meets their housing need, and they have received a notice to quit are suitable for consideration by all local authorities for acquisition under the tenant-in-situ scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20838/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1132 and 1133 together.
Tenancy sustainment, or tenant-in-situ, is not a stand alone programme or scheme. It is a priority category of my Department's Social Housing Second Hand Acquisitions Programme.

The parameters of the 2026 Social Housing Second Hand Acquisitions Programme, including individual local authority priority category allocations were notified to local authorities via Department Circular in February.
€373 million is available for drawdown by local authorities and Approved Housing Bodies under the 2026 programme priorities as follows:
• Exits from Homelessness Acquisitions - €150 million
• AHB Priority Delivery Acquisitions, supporting older persons, persons with disabilities, care leavers - €50 million
• LA Priority Acquisitions including tenancy sustainment or tenant-in-situ acquisitions - €157 million.

A contingency fund of €16 million will also be retained. It will be available for local authorities that have drawndown most of their initial allocation but still have capacity to complete further acquisitions and drawdown funding from my Department this year.

The multi-annual approach introduced last year will continue in 2026. Local authorities may commit up to the value of 30% of their base 2026 allocations (total c.€85 million) for acquisitions that will complete or drawdown funding in 2027. This will allow priority acquisitions to progress in the closing months of 2026, with certainty on funding in 2027, if such purchases do not complete this year.

Further to this, Tenant in situ is an option for local authorities to support households in the most precarious housing situations. Such acquisitions are, and will continue to be, available to local authorities for use as a last resort when all other options have been exhausted.

However, they will never be the sole, or even the primary, option. The default first options should almost always be securing the sustainment of the tenancy with the landlord, securing alternative accommodation through the Tenancy Sustainment and Placefinder services, or allocating a local authority or Approved Housing Body tenancy via a new build home or re-let.

Where acquisitions are deemed necessary, Local authorities have delegated sanction to pursue individual priority acquisitions without recourse to my Department, where these acquisitions are in line with the broad parameters and criteria of the Second Hand Acquisitions Programme.
Those broad parameters include the following eligibility criteria:
• The property being acquired (not the tenant) must have been the subject of social housing support payments for a continuous period of at least two years.

• Tenancies must be registered with the Residential Tenancies Board and local authorities and AHBs must confirm they are responding to a valid ‘no fault’ NoT issued to the HAP or RAS tenant, and not landlord overtures.
• Tenancy Sustainment Acquisitions are not be permitted for households that have refused a reasonable offer of local authority or AHB social housing accommodation following receipt of a NoT

summary.i: Question No. 1133 answered with Question No. 1132.

question.p: 1134. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will work with community groups to restore native trees at a location used by the State (details supplied); and if not, the supports or funding he can provide in the context of restoration of biodiversity and nature. [20858/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: The National Parks and Wildlife Service of my Department offers funding for a number of initiatives to support efforts to restore biodiversity. The NPWS-operated Local Biodiversity Action Fund (LBAF) acknowledges the important role that targeted local action can play and provides targeted funding directly to local authorities to assist with the implementation of projects that support the objectives of the National Biodiversity Action Plan. Projects supported through this fund cover a range of biodiversity related activities, including tree planting, invasive alien species control, dune restoration, wetland surveys and hedgerow work. For further details, see www.npws.ie/legislation/national-biodiversity-action-plan/local-biodiversity-action-fund.

The Peatlands and Natura Community Engagement Scheme (PNCES) is a competitive grant program designed to support community-led initiatives that conserve and restore protected habitats. It encourages local groups to engage with their natural heritage, specifically targeting Natura 2000 sites (Special Areas of Conservation and Special Protection Areas) and all peatland areas. The target audience of the scheme is community-led and volunteer groups, heritage organisations, environmental groups, and educational institutions. Individuals are not permitted to apply to this scheme. See www.npws.ie/peatlands-and-turf-cutting/peatlands-and-natura-community-engagement-scheme-2026.

In addition to these focussed efforts, the NPWS also administers and supports a diverse range of broader nature restoration initiatives, including the NPWS Farm Plan Scheme and the Breeding Waders EIP.

question.p: 1135. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the progress of the drafting and publication of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Bill 2024, in light of the recent publication of the Joint Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage's report on pre-legislative scrutiny of the general scheme; his response to the recommendations contained in that report; and the expected timeline for the introduction of the Bill to the Oireachtas; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20890/26]

speech.from: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage
speech.p: Government approval was received on 18 September 2024 for the priority drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Bill. The purpose of this legislation is to place the defects remediation Scheme on a statutory footing, further to commitments contained in the Programme for Government and the national housing plan.

The Scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded under the Scheme.

The General Scheme of the Bill completed pre-legislative scrutiny in December 2025 and I have received the Joint Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage's report on pre-legislative scrutiny of the general scheme and it is being considered in the context of the drafting of the Bill. Many of the recommendations were already being progressed in some form by my Department prior to the PLS process and, as such, I expect that a good deal of it will be taken on board in the Scheme where possible.

The content of the final Bill will be a matter for the Government to agree in due course. The drafting of the Bill is being progressed at pace and I expect the legislation to be placed before the Oireachtas this year.

question.p: 1136. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of cases in which individuals with hearing impairments are being quoted over €5,000 for new hearing aids; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19284/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The primary responsibility for hearing loss care is with the Department of Health and the HSE. However, my Department provides a financial grant towards the cost of hearing aids under the Treatment Benefit scheme.

The Treatment Benefit scheme is funded by the Social Insurance Fund and administered by the Department of Social Protection. The scheme provides certain dental, optical, and medical appliance benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions. These treatments are also available to an insured person's dependent spouse or partner, if applicable.

The supports available under the scheme complement the services provided by the Department of Health and the HSE by ensuring insured contributors without medical cards have financial support to avail of treatments in an efficient and timely way

Under the medical appliance element of the Treatment Benefit scheme, my Department pays the full cost of a hearing aid up to a maximum of €500 (€1,000 for a pair) once every four years for eligible persons. It will also pay the full cost of repairs to aids, up to a maximum of €100, once every four years.

The number of hearing aid claims and the associated expenditure have increased significantly in recent years. In 2020 the number of claims for hearing aids was over 14,000 with expenditure of €11.5 million while in 2025 this had risen to over 34,000 claims and an expenditure of €30 million.
An important factor in the increase in claims and expenditure was an announcement in Budget 2021 where the payment changed to a flat rate grant of up to €500 per aid (€1,000 for a pair).

The current level of the grant provides for a person to receive a standard hearing aid free of charge. If a person requires or wishes to purchase more advanced hearing aids that are more expensive, the scheme provides a €1,000 contribution towards such aids.

My Department is represented on the National Hearing Care Plan Working Group which is jointly chaired by the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive. The Working Group has been tasked with developing recommendations for a holistic model of hearing care in Ireland. It is envisaged that the Working Group's Report will be finalised by the end of Quarter 2 of this year. Any recommendations in the Report relating to the Treatment Benefit scheme will be considered by my Department.
Any changes would need to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context, taking into account the sustainability challenges facing the Social Insurance Fund.

question.p: 1137. Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection to review the case of a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20595/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The person concerned reached pension age on 21 November 2023. An application for State pension (contributory) was received from the person concerned on 2 August 2023. A decision letter issued on 31 October 2023 to advise that they qualified for a reduced rate of pension based on their reckonable contribution record.

Public service employees employed prior to 6 April 1995 pay modified social insurance contributions. In cases where these employees have subsidiary employment for the same periods, they are liable for Class J PRSI which provides cover for occupational injuries only. Irrespective of the class of PRSI paid for the subsidiary employment, their modified social insurance from their primary employment takes precedence in the calculation of pensions, as in the case of the person concerned.

The records of my Department show that the claimant has 589 full-rate paid contributions, 45 full-rate credited contributions, 1961 modified-rate paid contributions and 14 modified-rate credited contributions. They have a yearly average of 13 full-rate contributions and credits, giving entitlement to 40% of the maximum rate of pension, currently €119.60 per week.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1138. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Social Protection the reasons a qualified adult allowance for a person (details supplied) has been reduced; the options that are available to the pensioner at this time; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18265/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Increase for Qualified Adult (IQA) allowance is a means-tested payment, payable to a claimant whose spouse, civil partner or cohabitant is being wholly or mainly maintained by them, and where that qualified adult’s personal means from any source does not exceed a means test income limit.

Where a qualified adult has weekly means of up to €100, the maximum rate of IQA is payable. Where their weekly means are over €100 and not more than €310, a tapering reduced rate of IQA is payable. If the qualified adult has means of more than €310 per week, this exceeds the means limit and there is no entitlement to an IQA payment. Where property or assets are held jointly, the qualified adult's means are assessed as half of the total amount. The family home is not included in the means assessment.

As part of my Department’s commitment to ensuring that claimants are receiving their full and correct entitlements, ongoing reviews of all means tested payments are carried out. In the case of an IQA allowance on State Pension (contributory), the primary claimant is contacted by my Department to notify them that their continuing entitlement to the means tested IQA payment is being examined. A questionnaire is required to be completed to include details of the means of their qualified adult.

A review questionnaire issued to the person concerned on 21 October 2025. Following the review, a letter issued on 12 January 2026 to advise that an increase in the IQA's means could impact on the rate of payment and offered an opportunity for the claimant to reply before the change came into effect. A further letter issued on 6 February 2026 to confirm that the allowance would reduce from €268.40 to €202.60 per week with effect from 13 February 2026 based on the new means test which found the qualified adult had weekly means of €162.00 based on savings. A copy of the means included in the review accompanied the letter.

If there has been a change in circumstances or the person concerned wishes to query any of the figures used in the mean assessment, they are welcome to write to the Department seeking a review, outlining the relevant details and including any supporting documents.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1139. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Social Protection whether he will recognise long-Covid as an occupational illness for healthcare workers; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18289/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection (Deputy Dara Calleary)
speech.p: In November 2023, my Department published a report on the inclusion of long COVID in the Occupational Injuries Benefit Regulations.

The report concluded that COVID-19 does not satisfy the statutory criteria for recognition as an occupational illness or accident at work. Specifically, it found that presumptions about workplace transmission would not be sustainable as it is not possible to establish with confidence that the disease has been contracted through a person’s occupation and not through community transmission. This is because data shows that community transmission was the primary means of transmission.

It is important to note that, even if Ireland did recognise COVID-19 as an occupational disease, this would not encompass long COVID and would only apply to new claims for new cases of COVID-19. As such, it would not benefit those who contracted COVID-19 during the pandemic.

However, my Department's range of income supports, including Illness Benefit and Invalidity Pension, at the same or higher rates of payment as Occupational Injuries Benefit, are available to people who cannot work due to the effects of long COVID.

It is important to note that entitlement to these supports is generally not dependent on the nature of the illness or disability but on the extent to which a particular illness or disability impairs or restricts a working age person’s capacity to work.

With regard to additional supports, my Department also provides an Additional Needs Payment under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme to help meet essential expenditure which a person could not reasonably be expected to meet out of their weekly income. This includes certain supplements to assist with ongoing or recurring costs that cannot be met from a person’s own resources and are deemed to be necessary.

With specific reference to workers in the health services, the Department's report found that the Temporary Scheme of Paid Leave for Public Health Service Employees was the appropriate channel through which a targeted sectoral support should be considered. This Temporary Scheme was a matter for the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, who extended it a number of times. The Scheme ended on 31 December 2025. Any employee of the public health sector remaining unwell after that date may utilise the full provisions of the Public Service Sick Leave Scheme which will provide further support.
I will arrange to meet with the Minister for Health shortly on this issue.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1140. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the case of a person (details supplied) whose application for a free vision test was refused; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18340/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: In general, medical or health related benefits fall within the remit of the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive (HSE). However, my Department administers the Treatment Benefit scheme which provides certain dental, optical, and medical appliances benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions.

Contributions made under PRSI classes A, E, P, H or S count towards eligibility for Treatment Benefit. The amount of social insurance contributions required depends on the person's age. In general, people must have;
• 260 PRSI contributions paid at any time, and
• 39 paid or credited contributions in the governing contribution year, or
• 26 paid contributions in each of the second and third last contribution years.
For claims made in 2026 the governing contribution year is 2024. The second last contribution year is 2024 and the third last contribution year is 2023.

The Treatment Benefit scheme is funded from the Social Insurance Fund. I am satisfied with the current scheme qualifying conditions as they are based on a qualifying person having made and continuing to make contributions to the Fund.

My Department does keep all schemes under constant review to ensure they meet their objectives. Any changes would need to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context, taking into account the sustainability challenges facing the Social Insurance Fund.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1141. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Social Protection the basis upon which the Office of the Registrar General requires the production of a third party’s birth certificate in order to recognise a foreign divorce for the purposes of a proposed marriage in the State; whether alternative forms of evidence of domicile at the time of divorce (including court pleadings, final judgments of divorce, and marriage licences issued by the relevant foreign jurisdiction) may be accepted where an ex-spouse refuses to engage; whether guidance will issue to the General Register Office to allow for greater flexibility in such cases; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18365/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Civil Registration Act 2004 provides that a registrar must be satisfied that a person who wished to marry is free to marry in the State. An impediment to marriage exists where either party to a proposed marriage is already married. Where one or both of the parties to an intended marriage was married previously, a registrar must establish whether an impediment continues to exist or whether the marriage has been dissolved, annulled or the former spouse is deceased. There can be serious legal consequences for parties who enter into a marriage based on a foreign divorce, where that divorce may not be recognised by an Irish court.

Where the divorce was granted outside of the EU recognition of the foreign divorce falls to be determined under the Domicile and Recognition of Foreign Divorces Act 1986 (The Act). The Act provides that a foreign divorce granted by the civil authority of a jurisdiction outside the EU is entitled to recognition under Irish law if at the time of the divorce proceedings at least one of the parties to the divorce was domiciled in the jurisdiction where the divorce was granted.

Under Irish law, domicile refers to a person’s firm intention to reside permanently in a place and where they have significant ties attached. A party to the divorce may have a domicile of origin in a jurisdiction if they can show that they were born there and continue to reside there at the time of initiating divorce proceedings in that jurisdiction. A person can also acquire a domicile of choice in the jurisdiction where the divorce was granted if they can demonstrate that at the time of the divorce proceedings they had abandoned their domicile of origin for that jurisdiction.

Either party to the divorce can have the requisite domicile for the purposes of recognising the legality of the divorce under Irish law. In circumstances where the recognition of a foreign divorce relies upon the domicile of the ex-spouse, documentary evidence in relation to them is required to be submitted. Evidence of their place of birth is strong evidence of the person’s domicile of origin, as is evidence of their residency in that jurisdiction following on from the granting of the divorce.

If the Deputy has details of a particular case the General Register Office (GRO) can provide assistance regarding the evidence or information that is necessary to support the recognition of a foreign divorce.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

speech.p: The number of recipients of Carer's Allowance in each year requested by the Deputy is provided in the table below.

question.p: 1144. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection the position in relation to reviews of carer’s allowance carried out in 2026; specifically if a carer is reviewed and is slightly over the current income limits but will be under the new income limits for carer’s allowance which take effect in July will their payment be impacted or will the Department apply some discretion in these cases; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18377/26]
1143. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of carer’s allowance reviews carried out in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18376/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1144 and 1143 together.

Carer's Allowance (CA) is a means-tested social assistance payment made to a person who is habitually resident in the State and who is providing full-time care and attention to a child or an adult who has such a disability that, as a result, they require that level of care.

From July 2026, the weekly income disregards for CA will increase from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for carers with a spouse / partner. These disregards are set down in legislation. If a recipient of CA is slightly over the current income limit, they will receive the appropriate reduced weekly rate of payment. When the new weekly income disregards take effect in July, anyone who is currently in receipt of a reduced weekly rate of CA due to their means will see an increase in their payment. Payments will be adjusted automatically to take account of the new income disregards, so customers do not need to contact the Department regarding these increases.
If there is a specific case that the Deputy would like examined, my Department would be glad to assist.
I hope this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

question.p: 1145. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Social Protection in relation to the recently-launched survey on the cost of disability, if his attention has been drawn to the fact that there is no large print version of the guidance document; if he is aware that the ‘easy read’ version is not suitable for those who need large print; that it is inaccessible to those with neurological issues; that the helpline is only open for two days a week, four hours a day; that the survey is not open for 12 weeks or more; whether these issues will be addressed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18401/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Government recognises the additional costs associated with having a disability and is committed to improving outcomes for disabled people. The Programme for Government includes a range of commitments to support disabled people including a commitment to introducing a permanent Annual Cost of Disability Support Payment.

On Friday 20 February, I launched a public consultation process on how a cost of disability payment can best be delivered. It is running for just over 6 weeks, closing on the 7th April. Members of the public can participate in the consultation by submitting written, video or phone call contributions. The consultation is open to everyone, with particular engagement encouraged from disabled people, their families and carers, Disabled Persons Organisations and representative groups.

To support participation, a range of accessible Plain English formats are available. These include Braille, shortform and longform ISL videos, an Easy to Read document designed with ACE Communication.

The Customer Communications Toolkit for the Public Service - A Universal Design Approach refers to large print as fonts using 14 point and above. The department published a screen-reader-friendly Word file of the guidance document in 16-point font. This version is fully unlocked, which allows readers to scale the text to any large print size they require. It was designed to support accessibility needs while giving users the flexibility to adjust formatting for maximum readability.

I want all voices to be included in this consultation. I encourage any interested parties to visit gov.ie/COD, where they will find guidance on how to engage with the consultation in whatever format best suits them.
I am pleased that we have already received over 400 submissions, in a variety of formats.
I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question.p: 1146. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason people in receipt of disability allowance, unlike people in receipt of invalidity pension, do not automatically transition to the State pension; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18412/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Disability Allowance is a weekly allowance paid to people with a disability who meet certain medical conditions and who pass a means test. Disability Allowance has been structured to support recipients to pursue employment opportunities, be that self-employment or insurable employment. People in receipt of Disability Allowance can take up employment or self-employment and continue to receive all or part of their social welfare payment, depending on their income.

Invalidity Pension is a pension paid to people who are “permanently incapable of work” because of illness or disability. It is based on a claimant's social insurance contributions and medical conditions and is not means tested.

It is this PRSI coverage that links the Invalidity Pension to the State Pension (Contributory) and allows for the transfer of those in receipt of the Invalidity Pension to the State Pension (Contributory) upon reaching State Pension Age. This is provided for under section 113A of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005.

A person who is in receipt of Disability Allowance may qualify in their own right for the State Pension (Contributory) based on their social insurance contributions. If they do not qualify, or qualify for a rate below the maximum, they may qualify for the means-tested State Pension (Non-Contributory).

For the purposes of the means-test for both Disability Allowance and State Pension (Non-Contributory), from application stage through the lifetime of a claim, an applicant must provide full and up to date details of any income(s), asset(s), savings and investment(s) held, including any changes that occur. As the means tests for Disability Allowance (DA) and the State Pension (Non-Contributory) use different rules there is a clause in Section 159 (ca) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005 that prevents the rate of payment for the State Pension (Non-Contributory) being lower than the rate the person is entitled to under the Disability Allowance scheme immediately before becoming entitled to State Pension (Non-Contributory).
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.
