Period(s) of Incapacity – There is no entitlement to Illness benefit for the first 6 days of a claim.

A person shall not be entitled to Illness for the first 6 days of any period of incapacity for work. The decision has been made in accordance with sections 940)2 and 40 (3)d of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005.
There is no entitlement to Illness Benefit when the customer is medically certified as capable of work.
The basis for this decision is the doctor’s certification that the customer is capable of work from 1st April 2017.
The decision was made in accordance with Section 40(3)(a) of the Social Welfare consolidation Act 2005.
All legislation and conditions of Illness Benefit quoted were in use at the time these overpayments occurred.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1148. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of people with a disability that had their free travel pass withdrawn after taking up employment in each of the past five years, by year , in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18456/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Everyone who is 66 or over and legally living permanently in the State is eligible for the Free Travel Scheme. Disabled persons under 66 may be entitled to use the Free Travel Scheme if in receipt of Invalidity Pension, Blind Pension or Disability Allowance, however this entitlement may be lost due to starting employment or earnings over the means threshold.
Data on the reasons why free travel was disallowed is not collated and is therefore not available. I therefore regret that it is not possible to answer the Deputy's question.

question.p: 1149. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the rules that lead to a person with a disability losing their free travel pass when they enter employment; whether he accepts that many people with disabilities face higher transport costs in order to access and remain in work; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18457/26]

1150. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department has examined if the potential loss of a free travel pass acts as a disincentive for people with disabilities who wish to take up employment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18458/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1149 and 1150 together.
Disability Allowance is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. The payment is subject to a medical assessment, a means test and a habitual residency requirement.

People on Disability Allowance can take up employment or self-employment and continue to receive all or part of their income support, depending on their earnings. People can earn up to €165 per week and keep their payment in full and can earn up to €527.60 per week and keep a portion of their payment and secondary benefits, such as Free Travel.

A person in receipt of a long-term disability payment, such as Disability Allowance, who moves off the payment to get a job, will retain their entitlement to Free Travel for a period of five years, providing all other qualifying conditions for the Free Travel Scheme are satisfied. Similarly, a person who transfers from Disability Allowance or Invalidity Pension to a Community Employment, Solas or Back to Work Scheme can retain their Free Travel for five years.

In July 2024, the Government extended the Free Travel Scheme to people aged over 17 and under age 66, who have never been medically fit to drive due to a disability or are medically certified as unfit to drive for a period of at least 12 months.

In the most recent Budget, people moving from Disability Allowance or Blind Pension to take up work will be able to retain their Fuel Allowance payment for up to five years. In addition, those with children who leave one of these payments to take up work will be eligible for the Back to Work Family Dividend.
These measures aim to smooth the transition from welfare to work while helping people address the cost of going to work.

The Government recognises the significant additional costs that disabled people can face in their daily lives and is committed to improving outcomes for disabled people by introducing permanent measures. That is why the Programme for Government includes a range of commitments to support disabled people which will be advanced over the lifetime of the Government, having regard to the overall policy and budgetary context. This includes a commitment to introduce an Annual Cost of Disability Payment.

In addition, under the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030, my Department is leading a Strategic Focus Network Summit on the Cost of Disability. This is a one-day event which will be held in May. It includes other Government departments as well as disabled people, their representatives and other stakeholders.

On February 20th, I launched a public consultation process on how a cost of disability payment can best be delivered and on the Summit. This will run until April 7th. People who have ideas about how we can make changes that will make a real difference to them are encouraged to visit gov.ie/COD, where they will find guidance on how to engage with the consultation process in whatever format best suits them.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

summary.i: Question No. 1150 answered with Question No. 1149.

question.p: 1151. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection the process that applies when a person with a disability who holds a free travel pass takes up employment, including the way in which their entitlement is reviewed; the criteria applied; the average time taken to reach a decision; the number of such reviews carried out in each of the past five years, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18459/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Free Travel Scheme is available to people over 66 years and to people in receipt of certain social welfare payments, or those medically certified as unfit to drive for a period of at least 12 months, who are over 17 and under 66 years. Free Travel recipients must be permanently resident in the State. The scheme permits travel for free on most CIÉ public transport services, Luas, Local Link and some 71 private operators.

Under the Make Work Pay initiative, a person under the age of 66 years is entitled to retain their entitlement to Free Travel for an extended period of 5 years after their entitlement to a disability related social protection scheme ceases due to taking up employment, providing all other qualifying conditions for the Free Travel Scheme are satisfied. As the person remains entitled to Free Travel due to taking up employment, there is no decision process or decision required for their Free Travel entitlement to continue.

In general, the entitlement to Free Travel is not reviewed during the 5 year extended period. However, where the customer returns to a social welfare payment, or is no longer resident in the State, their entitlement to Free Travel may be reviewed.
I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1152. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection the specific nutritional standards mandated by his Department under the School Meals Programme; the way in which compliance with those standards are monitored at supplier level; the auditing or oversight mechanisms currently in place; if there is a formal mechanism for parents and schools to raise concerns about the food provided to their children; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18475/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The objective of the School Meals Programme is to provide regular, nutritious food to children to support them in taking full advantage of the education provided to them. The programme is an important component of policies to encourage school attendance and extra educational achievement.

Clear nutritional standards have been in place for the School Meals Programme since its inception. A specific standard was set for School Meals under the Nutritional Standards for School Meals and Nutritional Standards for Hot School Meals. A technical Nutrition Subgroup comprised of Dietitians from the following organisations participated in developing these standards:
• The Irish Nutrition and Dietetic Institute of Ireland,
• The HSE
• Safefood
• The Food Safety Authority of Ireland.
These standards are available to all schools, organisations and suppliers and are publicly available on gov.ie www.gov.ie/en/department-of-social-protection/services/school-meals-scheme/website.

My Department provides the funding for the meals directly to the school. The primary relationship is between the school and supplier. It is the responsibility of each school board to select a supplier on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules. These rules clearly define the successful tenderer’s responsibilities and obligations, including in relation to compliance with Nutritional Standards for School Meals and Nutritional Standards for Hot School Meals. The Schools Procurement Unit, which is grant funded by the Department of Education and Youth, provides guidance to schools for all procurements including the School Meals Programme.

Nutritional standards are a priority for this Government. I have requested a review of the scheme’s nutrition standards to be undertaken. My Department has seconded a CORU-registered dietician for the School Meals Programme who is under the clinical supervision of the Department of Health. One of the main tasks is an in-depth review of school meal supplier menus and their compliance with the nutritional standards. The review by a CORU-registered Dietitian is underway. It is expected that the full report will be finalised in Q2 2026. The Dietician is also working on the creation and implementation of an audit tool for inspectors to use during inspections.

In the meantime, food that is high in saturated fat, sugar and salt, was removed from the school menus from September 2025. Up to now this food had been permitted, as an option once a week at most and only when selected by the child's parents.

All participating schools must submit to my Department a signed Service Level Agreement which clearly sets out the school’s responsibilities and obligations in terms of compliance with nutritional standards.

My Department has an oversight role in relation to the School Meals Programme and conducts regular inspections of schools which includes reviewing the menu. Under the existing audit process, 400 schools were inspected onsite in 2025 by Social Welfare Inspectors from this department. Approximately 150 desk assessments were conducted in 2025 by the School Meals Control team. For 2026, 400 schools will be inspected onsite by Social Welfare Inspectors and the desk assessments will be increased to reflect the expansion of the programme. Ongoing audits can increase or decrease based on risk assessments levels.

Any concerns with the quality of the food should be brought to the attention of the Principal and/or Board of Management who manage the contract with the Food Business organisation to ensure full compliance with the nutrition standards.

Under the Programme for Government my department will continue to improve the School Meals Scheme and ensure that suppliers adhere to robust guidelines on the nutritional value of meals, the dietary requirements of students, reduce food waste and utilise recyclable packaging.
I trust this clarifies the matter.

question.p: 1153. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 388 of 2 December 2025, if he will provide an update on the working group formed by his Department in relation to means derived from deprivation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18549/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The conditions to be satisfied for payment of means-tested payments are outlined in social welfare legislation and include an assessment of means which includes any income or assets which a person owns.

In addition, specific legislation within Part 3 of Rule 2(1) of the Third Schedule of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005 states that where a person has directly or indirectly deprived themselves of any income or property in order to qualify for a payment, or for a higher rate of payment than they would otherwise be entitled, that income or the value of the property shall be taken to be part of the means of that person.

The current legislation does not provide specifically for situations where the deprivation of income occurred a number of years ago, other than addressing it on a case by case basis, nor does it provide for a time frame for the means assessed under such deprivation to cease to apply or to change in value.

A working group has been established in my Department to examine how the matter could be addressed. The group comprises operational and policy representatives across the range of means-tested schemes in my Department and first met in late October 2025. The group continues to consider this complex and multifaceted issue.

question.p: 1154. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Social Protection to review the impact the Basic Income for Artists has on disability payments; and if he will make a statement on the way in which it can have the effect of making disabled artists ineligible for their disability payment and disabled people's consequent access to participation in the arts. [18570/26]

1155. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Social Protection to review the impact the Basic Income for Artists has on disability payments; and if he will make a statement on the way in which it can have the effect of making disabled artists ineligible for their disability payment and disabled people's consequent access to participation in the arts. [18571/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1154 and 1155 together.
The Department of Social Protection provides a suite of income supports for those who are unable to work due to illness or disability.

Disability Allowance is a means-tested social assistance payment for people with a disability who are aged between 16 and 66. In order to be eligible the disability must be expected to last for at least one year and the person must satisfy a habitual residency condition.

Social welfare legislation provides that for means-tested social assistance schemes, including Disability Allowance, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and his or her spouse or partner where applicable, are assessable for means-testing purposes. A person's home is not included in the means assessment. The purpose of the means test is to ensure that resources are directed to those with the greatest need.

My Department treats income from pilot Basic Income for the Arts Scheme as income from self-employment for the purpose of its various means tests, including Disability Allowance. We will treat income from the forthcoming new scheme in the same way. This means that where a scheme includes a disregard of a certain amount of income from self-employment, that disregard will be applied to income from the Basic Income for the Arts Scheme.

Over the last five budgets the Government has progressively improved payment rates and income disregards for disabled people. The weekly payment rates for Disability Allowance have increased by €51 in that time.

People on Disability Allowance and Blind Pension can take up employment or self-employment and continue to receive all or part of their payment, depending on their income. The earnings disregard has increased by almost 38% since Budget 2021 from €120 to €165 currently. This means that a person can earn up to €165 a week and keep their full rate payment. Earnings between €165 and €375 are assessed at 50%, and any earnings over €375 are fully assessed as means. As a result, people can earn up to €165 per week and keep their payment in full and can earn up to €527.60 per week and keep a portion of their payment.
If a person’s spouse, civil partner, or cohabitant works, their ‘net’ weekly earnings from work as an employee are assessed as follows:
• €20 per day, up to a maximum of €60, from work is deducted from their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant’s average net weekly earnings; and
• 60% of the balance is assessed as weekly means.

• In addition, Disability Allowance has one of the highest capital disregards operated by the Department of Social Protection. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. This is compared to €20,000 for most social welfare payments. A person’s family home is not assessed as means.
• I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question.p: 1159. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection whether a payment received under a State institutional redress scheme, including the mother and baby institutions payment scheme, is disregarded for the purposes of a means test when assessing eligibility for an exceptional needs payment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18653/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme, my Department may make Additional Needs Payments to help meet essential expenses that a person cannot pay from their weekly income or other personal and household resources.

Payments are made at the discretion of the officers administering the scheme, taking into account the requirements of the legislation, and all the relevant circumstances of the case in order to ensure that the payments target those most in need of assistance.

The decision process involves consideration of the need presented and the ability of the person and their household to meet that need. This entails an assessment, as opposed to a specific means test, of an applicant’s weekly household income, their savings and investments, their outgoings and the type of assistance needed. Other State supports that may already be available to the person are also considered.
This assessment does not apply to any payment received from a State redress scheme or where capital has accrued from such payments.

Any person who considers they may have an entitlement to an Additional Needs Payment is encouraged to contact their local community welfare service. There is a National Community Welfare Contact Centre in place - 0818-607080 - which will direct callers to the appropriate office. In addition, applications can be made online via www.mywelfare.ie.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1161. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Social Protection the way in which a person becomes an approved supplier/fitter of wigs under the wig grant scheme. [18704/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: In general, medical or health related benefits fall within the remit of the Department of Health and the HSE. However, the Department of Social Protection administers the Treatment Benefit Scheme which provides dental, optical, and medical appliance benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions. These treatments are also available to their dependent spouse or partner, if applicable.
The Hair Replacement Grant was introduced in May 2022 as an expansion of the range of grants provided under Treatment Benefit- Medical Appliances.

The payment assists people who have suffered hair loss, due to a disease or treatment of a disease such as cancer or certain types of alopecia, to purchase a hair replacement product. Suppliers may provide a non-surgical scalp hair replacement product once per calendar year if they have a contract with the department.

To be included in the Department's approved list of suppliers for hair replacement products, a provider must undertake to provide such products under the following terms and conditions of their contract with the department:
(a) Have and maintain professional indemnity insurance.
(b) Maintain tax compliance and provide proof of such as is required by the Minister from time to time.
(c) Operate a practice address which is open to the public during normal business hours and any advertisement should mention this address and its contact details.
(d) Provide a minimum of 12 months guarantee on any product provided.

Each provider must complete an application for a panel number and provide documentary evidence that the above terms and conditions have been satisfied. Once the contract has been signed and the panel number has been awarded the provider will have access to the online Welfare Partners portal through which they can check eligibility and make claims for the Hair Replacement Grant.

Currently there are nearly 170 providers contracted with the Department to operate the scheme covering all counties. In 2025 over 4,900 customers availed of the scheme to the value of over €2.4 million.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1163. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will address the situation whereby employees whose employer (details supplied) has entered a mandatory 30-day collective redundancy consultation period have been informed that they can not apply for the jobseekers pay related benefit (JPRB) during this period and will instead only qualify for an exceptional needs payment capped at €254 per week; the reason these workers are being left at a financial loss of approximately €800 compared with the JPRB rate of up to €450 per week; and the measures he plans to take to prevent this level of income loss for affected staff; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18790/26]

1164. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the correct procedure for employees of a company (details supplied) who obtain new employment during the statutory 30-day collective redundancy consultation period; the steps such employees are required to take in order to comply with his Departmental rules during this period; the reason departmental representatives were unable to provide accurate information to affected staff when queried on this matter; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18791/26]

1165. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the statutory process that applies where a company enters a creditors’ voluntary liquidation and triggers a thirty-day collective redundancy consultation period, during which employees are not dismissed, are not required to attend work, and receive no wages; the way in which his Department treats the employment status of workers during this period; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18797/26]

1166. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of the circumstances affecting employees of a company (details supplied), which ceased trading on 20 February 2026 and placed all staff on temporary unpaid lay-off pending a creditors’ voluntary liquidation expected to be completed approximately fourteen days after cessation, during which a statutory consultation period is running until 22 March 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18798/26]

1167. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he accepts that an anomaly arises whereby employees who are not working and receiving no wages during a statutory consultation period cannot access jobseeker’s benefit until the formal redundancy takes effect, even though their employment has effectively ended in practice; the policy in such cases; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18799/26]

1168. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason employees affected by the cessation of a company (details supplied) have received contradictory advice from Intreo offices, with some being instructed to apply for jobseeker’s payments and others told to cancel their claims; the action his Department will take to ensure consistent guidance for workers in similar circumstances; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18800/26]

1169. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the way in which PRSI contributions, continuity of insurance, and contribution records are treated for employees placed on temporary unpaid lay-off during a statutory consultation period prior to redundancy; whether gaps arise that could affect entitlements to future benefits; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18801/26]

1170. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the way in which employment status is recorded during a statutory consultation period where employees are still legally employed but are not working and are not being paid; the reason some employees of a company (details supplied) report that MyGov.ie lists them as ceased even though the company has not formally dismissed them; whether any administrative errors could affect redundancy entitlements or access to income supports; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18802/26]

1171. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the measures his Department plans to take to ensure that employees placed on temporary unpaid lay-off during a statutory redundancy consultation period are not left without any income support; if he will address the gap in the system in future cases; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18803/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1163 to 1171, inclusive, together.

My thoughts are with all those workers affected by this receivership. I know how concerning it is for each of them. I would like to assure the Deputy that my Department’s priority is to support all workers affected and to ensure that they receive their statutory entitlements and appropriate income supports in a timely manner.

When a company enters receivership, employees are typically placed in a statutory consultation period, usually lasting 30 days. During this period, they remain formally employed, even if they are not required to attend work or in receipt of wages. Employees continue to accrue entitlements, including arrears of wages and holiday pay during this time. Where a company is insolvent and is unable to meet its obligations to staff, employees will be entitled to outstanding employment related payments from the Social Insurance Fund under the Insolvency Payments Scheme, which is administered by my Department. This scheme, subject to statutory limits, covers arrears of wages, holiday pay and statutory minimum notice for up to 8 weeks, with a weekly pay cap of €600. Claims under the scheme are submitted on behalf of employees by the liquidator or other relevant employer representative once employment has ended. These wages will be paid through the payroll reporting system and statutory deductions, including PRSI charges, will be applied. This ensures the person’s PRSI record will be maintained.

Employees’ insurable employment records, available to employees on their MyGov.ie accounts, reflects information supplied by the employer through the normal payroll reporting system. Where an employer has incorrectly submitted a cessation date before the statutory process has concluded, this can usually be rectified by revised submissions and does not in itself impact future redundancy entitlements.

As explained above, where an employer is insolvent, employees continue to accrue entitlements, including arrears of wages and holiday pay during this time, which can be claimed via the Insolvency Payments Scheme. In order to protect these entitlements employees are advised not to apply for Jobseekers payments include Jobseekers Pay-Related Benefit, Jobseekers Benefit and Jobseekers Allowance during the consultation period. Applying prematurely for Jobseekers supports risks affecting their entitlements under the Insolvency Payments Schemes when it comes to calculating loss of earnings. Where an employee does make a claim for a Jobseekers payment my Department will contact the person to explain the possible impact and advise them of their options.

Workers who experience financial hardship during this consultation period can seek assistance from my Department’s Community Welfare Service. Applications for supports are dealt with as a matter of urgency and payment of such supports does not affect a person’s future statutory redundancy entitlements. Once the consultation period has been completed and employment has formally ceased, affected workers may then claim Jobseeker’s Pay-Related Benefit, Jobseeker’s Benefit or Jobseeker’s Allowance, subject to the usual qualifying conditions.

There is no statutory restriction on employees taking up alternative or additional employment during the consultation or receivership period, provided they do not formally resign from their current employment. Accepting other work does not affect an employee’s statutory redundancy entitlement so long as the employment contract with their original employer.

In the case referred to by the Deputy, my Department’s Employer Relations teams have engaged directly with the company’s representatives to provide information on entitlements and to support the timely submission of claims, including by attending meetings with affected staff. My officials have also clarified the position in relation to workers who obtain new employment during the consultation period.

Employees who have applied to the Department have been assessed for support based on their financial needs. Where appropriate, employees have been awarded a basic Supplementary Welfare Allowance payment that is in excess of €252.

I recognise that these are very difficult circumstances for the workers concerned. My Department will continue to work with the liquidator or other employer representatives and with affected employees to ensure that statutory income supports and pay-related entitlements are processed as quickly as possible, and that any administrative issues which arise in the recording of employment status are identified and addressed without disadvantage to the individuals involved.
If the Deputy or affected employees require further information or assistance, I would be more than happy to arrange for direct engagement with our support teams.

question.p: 1173. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on the funding of a training course for a person (details supplied) by her Department and Turas Nua. [18857/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: There is a mandatory requirement for a person in receipt of a jobseeker payment to engage with the Department's Intreo Employment Services, who provide a range of supports, guidance and employment programmes to assist the jobseeker find a pathway to employment.

A distinctive client journey has been embedded into the employment services process since 2022. All Jobseekers on the live register engage with Intreo in the first 12 months and are then referred firstly to the contracted Intreo Partner National Employment Service (NES) and after 24 months, to the Intreo Partner Local Area Employment Service (LAES), which is designed to engage with those with greater barriers to the labour market. Therefore, the jobseeker is referred to the most appropriate service at each point in time on their jobseeking journey.

Those closest to the labour market are provided with a clear overview of available services and are signposted to the most relevant supports, while individuals who require more assistance are offered a personalised support service from the outset.

When referred to one of the Department’s Intreo Partners, a person is assigned a personal advisor who assesses their skills, experience and work goals and agrees a personal progression plan, that may include relevant training and educational programmes to assist them in finding full-time sustained employment. Training requirements and any associated funding for training is determined by the relevant advisor which in this case was the Department’s Intreo partner, Turas Nua. I understand that the person concerned has been in touch with the Department about this matter and they are satisfied that the appropriate service is being provided to assist him find sustainable employment.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1174. Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on a disability allowance appeal for a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18869/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Disability Allowance (DA) is a weekly allowance paid to people with a specified disability who are aged 16 or over and under the age of 66. The allowance is subject to a medical assessment, a means test, and the habitual residency conditions.

The Department routinely reviews claims to ensure recipients continue to meet the qualifying conditions for DA. A medical review of the person concerned commenced on 11th June 2024 with the issuing of a medical self-review form. This was returned to the Department on 27th June 2024. Following a review further medical evidence was sought from their doctor in August 2024. This was subsequently received and their DA payment was maintained while the review process continued.

Having examined the medical evidence provided, the Department's Medical Assessor advised that the person concerned was not medically eligible for DA. The person was notified of the outcome of the review and afforded the opportunity to provide further medical evidence before the final decision. No response was received from the person concerned and on 28th May 2025 the claim was disallowed on medical grounds, with the right to seek a further review or an appeal outlined in the decision letter that issued.

Further evidence was later submitted in September, October and November 2025. Each submission was reviewed by a Medical Assessor who, on each occasion, provided a not eligible medical opinion to the Deciding Officer. The Deciding Officer subsequently confirmed the original decision and a review outcome letter issued.
At this time, no appeal has been received in relation to this case.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1175. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the total anticipated costs associated with his foreign travel for St Patricks Day; the delegation size; and if a breakdown can be provided on these costs including on accommodation and flights. [18899/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: As part of the Government’s St. Patrick’s Day programme for 2026, I travelled to Canada to promote Ireland, Irish values, and Ireland’s interests across the world. In terms of the delegation from Department of Social Protection, I travelled with my Private Secretary.
The full costs associated with this trip are yet to be determined and can be provided once the trip is completed and the Department of Foreign Affairs submit costs to my Department for processing.
However, the costs for the international flights for myself and my Private Secretary came to €1,775.93.
Due to my dual responsibilities, costs incurred for my St. Patrick’s Day trip to Canada will be shared with the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht.

question.p: 1176. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of family carers who have benefitted under the long term carers contribution scheme ensuring a full State pension for them, in each of the years since it was introduced, in tabular form. [19007/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: To address barriers faced by some long-term carers in accessing the State Pension Contributory (SPC), the Pensions Commission was asked to consider how people who have provided long-term care for incapacitated dependants can be accommodated within the State Pension system. The Commission recommended that long-term carers should be given access to the SPC and defined long-term caring as caring for more than 20 years. Setting the criteria of more than 20 years is in recognition of the existing access to SPC for carers who may have up to 20 years of caring periods.

Since January 2024, long-term carer's contributions can be awarded to a person who has cared for an incapacitated person for a period of 20 years or more. These contributions will be treated the same as paid contributions for SPC entitlement only and can be used to fill any gaps in a person's contribution record, including satisfying the minimum 520 contributions required for eligibility.

In general, to be entitled to the maximum personal rate of State Pension Contributory a person must have at least 40 years of reckonable contributions. Carers with at least 20 years of long-term carers contributions can use these contributions (along with other reckonable contributions) to meet this requirement.
The table below shows the number of carers that:
• were awarded at least 20 years of long-term carers contributions;
• and were in receipt of the maximum rate of State Pension Contributory at the specified reference date;
• and were not in receipt of the maximum rate of State Pension Contributory before the scheme was introduced.

td.p: Total unique carers across the three reference dates

speech.p: I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

The total number of people who received Maternity Benefit, Paternity Benefit, or Parent's Leave in each quarter of 2025 is shown in the table below. question.p: 1178. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Social Protection his plans to link maternity benefit, paternity benefit and parent’s leave and benefit to wages, as has been done with jobseeker’s benefit. [19009/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Programme for Government commits to introducing Pay-Related Parent's Benefit in a first instance and exploring other payments where a similar model could be applied.

A pay-related model was introduced on 31 March 2025 for Jobseeker’s Benefit. My Department will draw on the learnings and operational experience from it to inform options for Parent's Benefit and other family leave schemes.

To progress this commitment, I intend to issue a public consultation document on a pay-related approach to Parents' Benefit in the autumn, which will also help to inform decisions about other family and related benefits. This consultation will invite views from the public, employers and stakeholders to support the process and to assist in the development of any future proposals in this area.
I trust this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

question.p: 1179. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on the adequacy of the level of PRSI cover for hearing aids; if he will engage with the Minister for Finance in this regard in the context of future budgetary negotiations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19266/26]

1180. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on the adequacy of the level of PRSI cover for hearing aids; if he will engage with the Minister for Health in this regard in the context of future budgetary negotiations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19267/26]

1181. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on the adequacy of financial support available for people that require hearing aids but do not have a medical card; if this is under review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19268/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1179 to 1181, inclusive, together.

The primary responsibility for hearing loss care is with the Department of Health and the HSE. However, my Department provides a financial grant towards the cost of hearing aids under the Treatment Benefit scheme.

The Treatment Benefit scheme is funded by the Social Insurance Fund and administered by the Department of Social Protection. The scheme provides certain dental, optical, and medical appliance benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions. These treatments are also available to an insured person's dependent spouse or partner, if applicable.

The supports available under the scheme complement the services provided by the Department of Health and the HSE by ensuring insured contributors without medical cards have financial support to avail of treatments in an efficient and timely way.

Under the medical appliance element of the scheme, my Department pays the full cost of a hearing aid up to a maximum of €500 (€1,000 for a pair) once every four years for eligible persons. It will also pay the full cost of repairs to aids, up to a maximum of €100, once every four years.

The number of hearing aid claims and the associated expenditure have increased significantly in recent years. In 2020 the number of claims for hearing aids was over 14,000 with expenditure of €11.5 million, while in 2025 this had risen to over 34,000 claims and an expenditure of €30 million.

An important factor in the increase in claims and expenditure was an announcement in Budget 2021 where the payment changed to a flat rate grant of up to €500 per aid (€1,000 for a pair). This has enabled eligible persons to purchase standard hearing aids free of charge or, alternatively, receive a financial contribution towards purchasing more advanced hearing aid models.

My Department is represented on the National Hearing Care Plan Working Group which is jointly chaired by the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive. The Working Group has been tasked with developing recommendations for a holistic model of hearing care in Ireland. It is envisaged that the Working Group's Report will be finalised by the end of Quarter 2 of this year. Any recommendations in the Report relating to the Treatment Benefit scheme will be considered by my Department.
Any changes would need to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context, taking into account the sustainability challenges facing the Social Insurance Fund.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1183. Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of hot school meals that met each of the five basic nutritional values and none, that were assessed in the overall assessment of 400 school meals commissioned by his Department, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19299/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The objective of the School Meals Programme is to provide regular, nutritious food to children to support them in taking full advantage of the education provided to them. The programme is an important component of policies to encourage school attendance and extra educational achievement.

My Department has seconded a CORU-registered dietician for the School Meals Programme who is under the clinical supervision of the Department of Health. One of the main tasks is an in-depth review of school meal supplier menus and their compliance with the nutritional standards.

As of December 2025, 127 separate recipes from the main school meal suppliers had been analysed to determine their compliance with Nutrition Standards for Hot School Meals. The main findings of the interim report are as follows:
• 66% met at least three of the five standards.
• 80% contained adequate carbohydrate and did not include HFSS foods.
• Overall, meals were lacking in fruit and vegetables, with 30% including the required one serving of vegetables (40-80g).

This analysis will give an indication of the rate of compliance with Nutrition Standards. As this piece of work is ongoing, a detailed breakdown cannot be provided at this time. Final results, along with findings from in-school audits, will be included in a report due to be submitted to me at the end of June 2026.
I trust this clarifies the matter.

question.p: 1184. Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Social Protection his plans to provide increased funding to the Citizens Information Board to support the expansion of their citizen information services in Budget 2027; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19302/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Citizens Information Board (CIB) is the statutory body, under the aegis of my Department, that is responsible for supporting the provision of information, advice (including money and budgeting advice) and advocacy services on a wide range of public and social services.
CIB delivers on this remit through providing some services directly and through funding a number of companies, including eight regional companies of the Citizens Information Service (CIS).
Each CIS is an independent limited company overseen by a voluntary Board of Directors and each company makes decisions independently on the delivery of services in their own regions.

The Citizens Information Service delivery companies currently provide information, advice and advocacy services through 89 Citizens Information Centres, along with 20 outreach services which includes a virtual Citizens Information Centre in Wicklow library. In addition, there are 7 prison outreach services provided by the Citizens Information Services.

CIB has been allocated Exchequer funding of €69.432m in 2026 by my Department, which represents an increase of €2.88m from €66.543m in 2025. CIB have included a total of €18.3m to the eight CIS regional companies and €1.56m to the Citizens Information Phone Service (CIPS) for 2026.
I acknowledge and value the important work carried out by the Citizens Information Service (CIS) in providing people with independent information, advice and advocacy services.

CIB submit their annual funding requirements, including requests from the CIS, to the Department through the yearly annual estimates process. This submission forms part of the Department’s overall Budget 2027 request to the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation.

question.p: 1185. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide a county-by-county breakdown of the number of children availing of the Hot School Meals Programme this academic year, in tabular form. [19333/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The objective of the School Meals Programme is to provide regular, nutritious food to children to support them in taking full advantage of the education provided to them. The programme is an important component of policies to encourage school attendance and extra educational achievement.

All primary schools are eligible for the Hot School Meals Programme for the current 2025/2026 academic year. It is important to note that this academic school year started a few months ago and applications continue to be received and processed.
The school meals programme is not mandatory. The School Board of Management and Principal decide if they wish to offer the Hot School Meals or the cold lunch option.

As of 9th March 2026, there is a total of 2,709 primary/special schools in receipt of a school meal at lunch time. 2,486 schools have been awarded Hot School Meals in respect of 418,964 pupils, with a further 223 schools awarded the cold lunch option in respect of 33,117 pupils.

question.p: 1186. Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Social Protection for the status of a domiciliary care allowance appeal for a person (details supplied), in view of additional extensive care that the applicant requires; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19405/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA) is a monthly allowance payable to a parent/guardian in respect of a child aged under 16 who has a severe disability requiring continual or continuous care and attention substantially in excess of the care and attention normally required by a child of the same age and where the level of that disability is such that the child is likely to require this level of care and attention for at least 12 consecutive months. This level of care and attention must be required to allow the child to deal with the activities of daily living in areas such as mobility, personal care, feeding / diet, communication, speech / language, sleeping, behaviour, safety, sensory issues, including any other additional needs.

Eligibility for DCA is not based entirely on the type of disability or diagnosis but primarily on the impact of the child's disability, in terms of the associated overall level of care and attention required by the child compared to a child of a similar age who does not have such a disability. The decision process that applies in the consideration of whether a child meets the conditions for DCA includes the examination of all relevant factors identified as impacting on the child's additional care needs.

An application for DCA in respect of the child concerned was received by my Department on 30 October 2025. A Deciding Officer disallowed the claim as per decision dated 23 January 2026. Based on the information provided, the child was not considered to satisfy the conditions for DCA. This determination considered the supporting medical evidence that was provided by the applicant in their application. The Deciding Officer also had regard to the professional opinion of a departmental Medical Assessor in making their decision and a copy of this opinion was issued to the applicant for information along with the decision notification.

The person concerned requested a review of the above decision and provided further new information/evidence for consideration. Further to that review, following a re-examination of their application, including all the further new information/evidence that was provided by the applicant in support of their review request, a Deciding Officer decided not to revise the above original decision, as per review decision dated 10 March 2026 which issued directly to the person concerned.

We currently have not received a request for an appeal of the disallow decision. If the person concerned wishes to request an appeal, they can do so by contacting the Social Welfare Appeals Office directly.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1188. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department or any body under it’s aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19504/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I am advised by Revenue that, in compliance with section 851A of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997, it is not permitted to disclose details relating to the tax affairs of any individual taxpayer or taxable entity, except in certain limited circumstances provided for in law, for example in the case of tax settlements meeting the criteria for publication under section 1086A of the TCA.
The List of Tax Defaulters is published within 3 months of the end of each quarter in Iris Oifigiúil and is also publicly available on the Revenue website www.revenue.ie.

question.p: 1189. Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Social Protection the details of the support schemes for the purchase of hearing aids; the change in that scheme for each of the years 2019, 2022 and 2026, the number of people covered by the scheme in each of those years; and to set out the data that the Department collected on the cost charged by private providers of hearing aids. [19586/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: In general, medical or health related benefits fall within the remit of the Department of Health and the HSE. However, the Department of Social Protection administers the Treatment Benefit Scheme which provides dental, optical, and medical appliance benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions. These treatments are also available to their dependent spouse or partner, if applicable.

The Department’s Treatment Benefit Scheme- Medical Appliances provides a grant to assist in the purchase of hearing aids. The scheme provides for a €500 grant per hearing aid, per ear in a 4-year period. The scheme also provides for one repair per hearing aid in a 4-year period, up to a maximum of €100 per aid.

Prior to March 2021 the scheme provided for 50% of the purchase price up to a maximum of €500 per aid, once every four years. Legislation introduced in March 2021 removed the requirement for the customer to pay 50% of the cost, which effectively meant that a person was guaranteed to receive €500 per hearing aid rather than receiving up to €500 prior to that.
No changes have been made to the Treatment Benefit hearing aid grant since March 2021.

The Department does not hold figures on the number of people eligible for the scheme in any one year however, the number of claims made in respect of hearing aids under the Treatment Benefit Scheme- Medical Appliances in the years queried are as follows.

As part of the claims process, the provider is required to include the full price of the hearing aid as charged to the customer. In 2025 the Treatment Benefit Scheme hearing aid grant total expenditure was €28.9M in respect of over 31,800 claims, and data collected from suppliers suggests that the gross cost (including the Treatment Benefit element) to the customer was over €81.8M.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

summary.i: Question No. 1190 answered with Question No. 1191.

question.p: 1191. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Social Protection if consideration has been given to reclassifying maternity credits as paid contributions for the purposes of treatment benefit eligibility; if he will respond to matters raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19614/26]

1190. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Social Protection if consideration has been given to reclassifying maternity credits as paid contributions for the purposes of treatment benefit eligibility; if he will respond to matters raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19613/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1191 and 1190 together.

My Department administers the Treatment Benefit scheme which provides certain dental, optical and medical appliances benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions.
Under the dental element of the scheme, my Department pays the full cost of an oral examination once a calendar year. In addition, a payment is provided once a calendar year towards either:
• a scale and polish (€50 payment)
• a periodontal treatment (if clinically necessary) (€42 payment)

If the cost of either the scale and polish or the periodontal treatment is more than these payments, the customer must pay the remainder. This is capped at €15 for a scale and polish. There is no cap on the balance charged for periodontal treatment.

Contributions made under PRSI classes A, E, P, H or S count towards eligibility for Treatment Benefit. The amount of social insurance contributions required depends on the person's age. In general, people must have:
• 260 PRSI contributions paid at any time, and
• 39 paid or credited contributions in the governing contribution year, or
• 26 paid contributions in each of the second and third last contribution years.
For claims made in 2026 the governing contribution year is 2024. The second last contribution year is 2024 and the third last contribution year is 2023.

Credits that are received by persons who avail of Maternity Benefit or Maternity Leave do count towards meeting the requirement of having 39 paid or credited contributions in the governing contribution year. The alternative qualification route based on the second last and third last contribution years is based on the person having a certain number (26) of paid contributions in each of those years.

My Department does keep all schemes under constant review to ensure they meet their objectives. Any changes would need to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context, taking into account the sustainability challenges facing the Social Insurance Fund.
If the Deputy has additional detail on the case he refers to, my Department is happy to examine the matter to ensure the full position as to the person's entitlement is confirmed.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1192. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the case of a person (details supplied); if he will provide an update on the matter; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19638/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Carer's Support Grant (CSG) is an annual payment for carers who look after a person in need of full-time care and attention. The payment is made regardless of the carer's means but is subject to the certain conditions.
I can confirm that my Department received an application for the CSG in respect of the care of the person concerned on 24 February 2026.

In order to qualify for a CSG, a person must be providing full time care and attention. Full time care and attention is defined as not less than 35 hours in a period of 7 consecutive days, and care is provided on any 5 days, whether consecutive or not within a period of 7 consecutive days.
It is also a condition of eligibility for a CSG that the carer is not working, self-employed, or on a training or education course for more than 18.5 hours a week.

The application was disallowed as, based on the information provided in the application, the Deciding Officer decided that the applicant was not providing full time care as outlined above as the applicant declared working hours of 38 hours per week.

A letter issued to the applicant on 26 February 2026 informing them of the decision. They were also notified of their right to have this decision reviewed (where further information is available) or to appeal the decision to the Social Welfare Appeals Office.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1193. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the correspondence (details supplied) regarding the eligibility for carer's allowance; if his Department has any plans to review the current 18.5 hour weekly work limit for recipients of carer's allowance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19654/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: My Department provides a comprehensive package of income supports for full-time family carers, including Carer’s Allowance, Carer’s Benefit, Domiciliary Care Allowance and the Carer’s Support Grant. Combined expenditure on these schemes in 2026 is expected to exceed €2.2 billion.

Carer’s Allowance is a means-tested payment for people who are looking after someone who needs support because of age, physical or learning disability or illness, including mental illness. The primary objective of the Carer’s Allowance payment is to provide an income support to carers whose earning capacity is substantially reduced because of their full-time caring responsibilities.

A primary qualifying condition for the Carer’s Allowance payment is that the applicant must be providing full-time care and attention. The person being cared for must be so incapacitated as to require full-time care for at least 12 months. A person is regarded as providing full-time care where they provide at least 35 hours of care per week, over any five days in a seven-day period.

While carer income support payments are based on the provision of full-time care and attention, they also provide flexibility in terms of allowing carers to engage in work, training or education for up to 18.5 hours per week. In effect, a carer can participate in such activities for half of a full-time working week. During this time, adequate provision must be made for the care of the relevant person.

The 18.5-hour limit for Carer's Allowance reflects a careful balance between ensuring that the care recipient receives full-time care and enabling carers to maintain a connection to employment, training or education. Any proposal to amend this condition would need to preserve that balance and would have to be considered in the broader budgetary and policy context.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1194. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons that his officials have determined to date that must return pandemic unemployment payments (PUP); the totality of PUP that had been paid to persons; the total amount his Department is seeking to recover; the amount recovered to date; the number of enforcement actions his Department has engaged in to recover PUP from persons since the Department commenced requesting PUP back from persons; the number of persons that have filed appeals in respect of demands from the Department to return PUP; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19661/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Pandemic Unemployment Payment (PUP) was introduced on March 16th, 2020, as a social welfare payment for employees and self-employed people who lost their employment due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The level of income supports provided was unprecedented in terms of volume and speed of response. Almost 942,000 individuals applied for the Pandemic Unemployment Payment indicating the significant disruption which the Covid-19 pandemic caused to the labour market and society in general. The total scheme expenditure amounted to €9.1 billion over the period 2020 – 2022.

Up to the end of February, approximately 65,700 PUP overpayments have been raised totalling €139.5m, of which €50.4m has been recovered. To date, 5,355 Notice of Attachments have issued in relation to PUP overpayment cases. The project team assigned to PUP overpayments continue to work through cases and all outstanding debt will be pursued.
Appeals against overpayments is not recorded separately but since 2020, the total number of appeals submitted in relation to the PUP scheme is approximately 4,426.
I trust this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

question.p: 1195. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will clarify whether his Department uses debt collection agencies to recover social protection payments that were overpaid or paid in error; if he will provide a schedule of agencies or companies his Department has used in 2023, 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026 to recover payments; and the amount realised from this activity versus what was to be returned. [19662/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Department does not engage collection agencies or any outside bodies in recovering overpayments.

Overpayments of social welfare entitlements can occur where a person provides false or misleading information in their application or through error on the part of either the claimant or the Department. Persons who have been overpaid social welfare have a liability to refund the overpayment as they have been in receipt of a payment to which they were not entitled.

Where an overpayment occurs, the Department seeks to recover the full value by deducting instalments from on-going weekly payments or requires direct payments to be made where a social welfare payment is no longer in place. Where a person is no longer in receipt of a social welfare payment and the person does not engage in a repayment plan, the Department has powers of attachments to a person’s earnings or to funds held in financial institutions to recover an overpayment.
The Department does not engage collection agencies or any outside bodies in recovering overpayments.
I trust that this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1196. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Social Protection the payment entitlements for a person who is currently on disability allowance and will reach 65 years-of-age this year in view of the fact that the State Pension (Non Contributory) applies to people over 66 years of age; the payment which the person is entitled to in the intervening year; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19723/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Disability Allowance is my Department's primary social assistance payment. It is a means-tested social assistance payment for people living in Ireland with a disability aged between 16 and 66. The injury, disease or physical or mental disability must be expected to continue for at least a year and substantially restrict a person’s ability to undertake suitable work.
When a person reaches 66 years of age and no longer qualifies for Disability Allowance, they can then apply for the State Pension (Non Contributory).

Reaching age 65 does not cause a person to become ineligible for Disability Allowance as the payment is payable up to age 66. Therefore, there is no gap to cover until a person reaches state pension age.
I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question.p: 1197. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review correspondence (details supplied) regarding a carers allowance application; if he will provide an update on the application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19801/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Carer's Allowance (CA) is a means-tested social assistance payment made to a person who is habitually resident in the State and who is providing full-time care and attention to a child or an adult who has such a disability that as a result they require that level of care.
I can confirm that an application for CA was received from the person concerned on 20 January 2026.

It is a condition for receipt of CA that every claimant shall furnish such certificates, documents, information, and evidence as may be required for the purposes of deciding their claim. A request for further information issued to the person concerned on 28 January 2026.
To date, I can confirm this information has not been received.
Once the information requested is received, a decision will be made, and the person concerned will be notified directly of the outcome.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1198. Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of applications for disability allowance made by people with dementia aged up to 66 years-of-age for each of the years 2021-2025 and to-date in 2026; the number of applications that were accepted, rejected and under review; the main reasons why those applications were rejected; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19837/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The medical condition of qualifying recipients of Disability Allowance were submitted by their doctor as part of the application form. The application is then assessed by the Department’s medical assessors, who are experienced doctors with various sub-specialty qualifications and hold full registration with the Irish medical council.

In January 2026, there were 173,375 recipients of Disability Allowance. Of these, 114,927 (66%) have an ICD-10 code recorded. The main medical conditions of Disability Allowance recipients where a code is recorded are: Mental and Behavioural Disorders, which includes dementia, (49%), Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue (15%), Nervous System (7%), and Circulatory System (5%). A full breakdown is provided in Table 1 below.
The overall number of claims registered, awarded and rejected in each year from 2021 to 2025, and in January 2026, is presented in Table 2 below.
