question.p: 1199. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No.362 of 2 December 2025, if he will review the case of a person (details supplied); if he will provide an update on the matter; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19922/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Disability Allowance (DA) is a means-tested weekly payment for people aged 16 to 66 with a disability expected to last at least one year, subject to a medical assessment, a means test and the habitual residence condition.

The person concerned applied for DA in 2025 and has requested that her claim be backdated to 2019. Under social welfare legislation, while DA should be claimed within 7 days of the date of entitlement, a provision exists to backdate for up to 6 months where “good cause” for a late claim is shown, and in limited circumstances beyond 6 months (for example, proven incapacity preventing a DA claim)

In examining her request, the Department noted that the person concerned has been engaged with the social welfare system since 2019 and in receipt of other payments during that period, including Illness Benefit and other working-age supports, and therefore was not without income support in the period prior to her DA claim. The person concerned had been in employment for part of the period in question, so the statutory conditions for backdating beyond the normal limits were not satisfied
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1200. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Social Protection if the free travel pass can be extended to cover travel costs for persons who attend day care services provided by the HSE given that at present a daily charge exists; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19981/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Free Travel Scheme provides free travel on the main public and private transport services for those eligible under the scheme. These include road, rail and ferry services provided by companies such as Bus Átha Cliath, Bus Éireann and Iarnród Éireann, as well as Luas and services provided by over 70 private transport operators.

The objective of the Free Travel scheme is to ensure older people and people with disabilities remain active within their community. Therefore, access to a free travel pass for those aged under 66 is linked to a person being in receipt of certain primary Social Protection payments or people who are medically certified as unable to drive for a period of 12 months or more.

Any decision to expand the Free Travel Scheme to all persons who attend day care services provided by the HSE who are aged under 66 would require additional funding for the scheme and would have to be considered in the context of overall scheme policy and budgetary negotiations.
My Department does provide Additional Needs Payments as part of the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme for people who have an urgent need, which they cannot meet from their own resources.

These payments are available through our Community Welfare Officers and include help towards recurring travel costs that cannot be met from the person's own resources and are deemed to be necessary. Every decision is based on consideration of the circumstances of the case, taking account of the nature and extent of the need and of the resources of the person concerned.

Any person who considers they may have an entitlement to an Additional Needs Payment is encouraged to contact their local community welfare service. There is a National Community Welfare Contact Centre in place - 0818-607080 - which will direct callers to the appropriate office. In addition, applications can be made online via www.mywelfare.ie.
I trust that this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1201. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Social Protection the names of external cleaning companies that have a contract with his Department to provide cleaning services within the Department to-date in 2026, in tabular form. [20033/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: My Department holds two contracts for the provision of cleaning services within the Department of Social Protection.

question.p: 1202. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Social Protection if the qualifying criteria for the living alone allowance can be expanded so that a public sector pensioner (details supplied) who is ineligible for a qualifying payment may be considered eligible; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20038/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Primary weekly social welfare payments are intended to enable recipients to meet their basic day-to-day income needs. In addition to these primary payments, my Department also provides a range of other payments on a weekly, monthly, or less frequent basis. These payments are considered secondary in nature and cannot be made available to those who are not in receipt of a primary payment.

The Living Alone Increase (LAI) is one of those secondary payments. It is not a scheme or a stand-alone payment, but it is a supplement to a primary social protection payment of €22 per week made to people aged 66 years or over, who are in receipt of certain social welfare payments and who are living alone.

For those aged 66 or over, payments eligible for the LAI include State Pension (Contributory), State Pension (Non-contributory), Bereaved Partner’s (Contributory) Pension, Bereaved Partner's Pension under the Occupational Injuries Benefit Scheme, Incapacity Supplement under the Occupational Injuries Benefit Scheme and Deserted Wife's Benefit. LAI is also paid to people aged under 66 who live alone and are in receipt of Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, Incapacity Supplement or Blind Pension.

There are no circumstances where the LAI can be paid to people who are not in receipt of a primary qualifying payment from my Department or who do not meet the living alone eligibility criteria. Any change to the qualifying criteria for this payment would have to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context.
I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1203. Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Social Protection if there has been a change to the criteria recently in order for parents to be granted domiciliary care allowance for children who have specific needs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20061/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA) is a monthly allowance payable to a parent / guardian in respect of a child aged under 16 who has a severe disability requiring continual or continuous care and attention substantially in excess of the care and attention normally required by a child of the same age and where the level of the child's disability is such that the child is likely to require this level of care and attention for at least 12 consecutive months. This level of care and attention must be required to allow the child to deal with activities of daily living in areas such as mobility, personal care, feeding/diet, communication, speech/language, sleeping, behaviour, safety, sensory, issues, including any other additional needs.

Eligibility for DCA is not based entirely on the type of disability or diagnosis but primarily on the impact of the child's disability, in terms of the associated overall level of care and attention required by the child compared to a child of a similar age who does not have such a disability. The decision process that applies in the consideration of whether a child meets the conditions for DCA includes the examination of all relevant factors identified as impacting on the child's additional care needs.

There has been no recent change to the eligibility criteria for DCA. When reviewing an application for DCA, the claim is first referred to one of the Department’s Medical Assessors for their opinion. Medical Assessors are fully qualified and experienced practitioners who provide a second opinion to that of the person's own doctor for the guidance of the Department's Deciding Officers.

The assessment of the substantial extra and continual care needs of children with childhood development and behavioural disorders is more challenging compared to other childhood conditions given the wide spectrum of manifestation of conditions and bearing in mind the age attainment of developmental milestones. In all cases, determinations on eligibility for DCA are based on all of the medical and care needs information provided with the application and while specialist or assessment reports can be helpful in making quality and efficient decisions, they are not mandatory.

A parent / guardian should apply for DCA as soon as they believe their child meets the eligibility criteria. If an application is refused because sufficient medical evidence is not available, they can request a review of the decision once new medical information becomes available. Applying as soon as they believe the child meets the criteria helps ensure that the application is considered from the earliest possible date.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1204. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of State pension recipients to date that have sought a review of their pension rate based on the new long-term carers contribution scheme; the number of these reviews that led to a higher payment of pension; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20118/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Government acknowledges the important role that carers play and is fully committed to supporting them in that role. The enhanced state pension provision for people who have been caring for incapacitated dependents for 20 years or more was introduced from 1 January 2024. If a customer has over 20 years of caring for an incapacitated person, Long Term Carers Contributions (LTCCs) are included in their pension calculations. An online application for Long Term Carers Contributions is available on MyWelfare.
As we proactively review pension entitlement following the award of LTCCs we don't hold figures for the number of people who request these reviews.
Approximately 800 State pension (contributory) recipients qualified for a higher rate of pension following review.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1205. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of current State pension recipients benefitted from the long-term carers contribution scheme; and the additional total cost to the State for allowing these contributions. [20119/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: This Government acknowledges the important role that family carers play and is fully committed to supporting them in that role. Accordingly, carers are not excluded from access to the State Pension Contributory (SPC). Once a person has met the minimum requirement of 520 paid contributions, the State Pension system gives significant recognition to those whose work history includes extended periods outside of paid employment, often to raise families or in a full-time caring role including:
• PRSI credits (which include Credits for Carers Benefit and Carers Allowance).
• Homemaking Disregards and HomeCaring Periods to recognise caring periods of up to 20 years outside of paid employment in the calculation of a payment rate.

Despite these measures, some long-term carers of incapacitated dependants faced barriers in accessing the SPC. To address these barriers faced, long-term carers contributions (LTCC) were introduced. Since January 2024, long-term carers contributions can be awarded to a person who has cared for an incapacitated person for a period of 20 years or more. These contributions will be treated the same as paid contributions for SPC entitlement only and can be used to fill any gaps in a person's contribution record, including satisfying the minimum 520 contributions required for eligibility.
As of 28/02/2026, 1,816 carers were awarded the SPC and had at least 20 years of long-term carers contributions.
Before long-term carers contributions were introduced, carers over State Pension Age may have been on any of the following schemes:
• State Pension Non-Contributory
• Bereaved Partner's Contributory Pension
• State Pension Contributory (at a lower rate of payment)
• Qualified Adult on a spouse’s SPC claim
• Carers Allowance
However, some carers may not have been on any of these schemes and long-term carers contributions enabled them to receive a state pension for the first time.
The table below shows the estimated additional cost to the state arising from the introduction of long-term carers contributions, to the end of 2025.

The costing was made up of two elements. Firstly, costs were determined based on SPC payments for those who were awarded long-term carers contributions. Reductions to this initial estimate were then made to reflect payments in place prior to the award.

td.p: SPC recipients at the end of the year with at least 20 years of LTCC

speech.p: I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1206. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Social Protection if consideration has been given to increased support for individuals reliant on hearing aids under the treatment benefit scheme; in light of the high cost of equipment and the increasing cost of living; and the inability of many to meet such costs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20127/26]

1182. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection his plans to increase financial supports available for individuals in need of hearing aids; if he will consider increasing the level of support available under the treatment benefit scheme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19285/26]

1187. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Social Protection whether he will increase the supports for those in need of hearing aids in line with increased cost of those aids (details supplied). [19429/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1206, 1182 and 1187 together.

The primary responsibility for hearing loss care is with the Department of Health and the HSE. However, my Department provides a financial grant towards the cost of hearing aids under the Treatment Benefit scheme.

The Treatment Benefit scheme is funded by the Social Insurance Fund and administered by the Department of Social Protection. The scheme provides certain dental, optical, and medical appliance benefits to insured workers, the self-employed and retired people who have the required number of PRSI contributions. These treatments are also available to an insured person's dependent spouse or partner, if applicable.

The supports available under the scheme complement the services provided by the Department of Health and the HSE by ensuring insured contributors without medical cards have financial support to avail of treatments in an efficient and timely way.

Under the medical appliance element of the scheme, my Department pays the full cost of a hearing aid up to a maximum of €500 (€1,000 for a pair) once every four years for eligible persons. It will also pay the full cost of repairs to aids, up to a maximum of €100, once every four years.

The number of hearing aid claims and the associated expenditure have increased significantly in recent years. In 2020 the number of claims for hearing aids was over 14,000 with expenditure of €11.5 million while in 2025 this had risen to over 34,000 claims and an expenditure of €30 million.

An important factor in the increase in claims and expenditure was an announcement in Budget 2021 where the payment changed to a flat rate grant of up to €500 per aid (€1,000 for a pair). This has enabled eligible persons to purchase standard hearing aids free of charge or, alternatively, receive a financial contribution towards purchasing more advanced hearing aid models.

There are no plans to increase the hearing aid grant under the Treatment Benefit scheme at this time. However, my Department is represented on the National Hearing Care Plan Working Group which is jointly chaired by the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive. The Working Group has been tasked with developing recommendations for a holistic model of hearing care in Ireland. It is envisaged that the Working Group's Report will be finalised by the end of Quarter 2 of this year. Any recommendations in the Report relating to the Treatment Benefit scheme will be considered by my Department.
Any changes would need to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context, taking into account the sustainability challenges facing the Social Insurance Fund.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1207. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of deceased persons' estates from which his Department has sought repayment of social welfare payments, by payment type; the total value of repayments sought in each year for each of the past five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20166/26]

1208. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the criteria and procedures used by his Department when deciding whether to seek recovery of funds from the estate of a deceased person who was in receipt of a means tested payment; the way in which consistency and fairness are ensured in these decisions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20167/26]

1210. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection whether his Department collects or holds any data on whether the recovery of overpayments from estates disproportionately affects individuals who did not have children or who lived alone; and if not, whether the Department will conduct an assessment to ensure that recovery procedures operate equitably across all household types; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20169/26]

1211. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the maximum time period for which his Department may retrospectively seek repayment of social welfare overpayments from a deceased person's estate; whether his Department has considered introducing a statutory limitation period to ensure fairness and certainty for families; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20170/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1207, 1208, 1210 and 1211 together.

Overpayments of social welfare entitlements can occur through error on the part of either the claimant or the Department or where a person provides false or misleading information in the context of their claim.

All overpayment cases are treated in the same manner. Social welfare legislation provides that where any person received a social welfare payment or a portion of a payment they were not entitled to have received, the sum which was overpaid is recoverable from the person who received the payment. A Deciding Officer will determine the time period for which the overpayment is raised based on the facts and evidence of each case. Natural justice is provided to the customer or, in the case of a deceased customer the PR, to allow any further information to be provided, and the final decision can be reviewed or appealed to the Social Welfare Appeals Office. This ensures consistency and fairness in all overpayment decisions.

The legislation provides that the Personal Representative (PR) of a deceased person who, at any time, received a means-tested social assistance payment from the Department, is obliged to give notice to the Department of their intention to distribute the deceased's estate and to provide a schedule of the assets of the estate. The PR is requested not to distribute the estate, until they receive formal clearance from the Department.

Where there is an outstanding social welfare overpayment or where a new overpayment is raised based on the schedule of assets, my Department will pursue the overpayment from the estate of the customer. It is the policy of my Department to seek repayment of the full amount of all overpayments.

In Estates cases the Deciding Officer will compare the schedule of assets presented with the means disclosed over the lifetime of the claim. Where a discrepancy is determined, a revised decision will be required to retrospectively disallow or partially disallow the assistance paid to the deceased customer.

Recovery of any overpayment assessed and for which a revised decision is made is sought from the assets of the estate, allowing for reasonable funeral and legal expenses for which the estate is liable. Household composition has no bearing on the recovery of overpayments.
My Department is satisfied that the current procedures for raising overpayments and recovery are fair, consistent and equitable to all customers including deceased customers estate cases.

These overpayments are recovered from the financial institutions where possible.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

summary.i: Question No. 1208 answered with Question No. 1207.

question.p: 1209. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection the way in which the frequently of the entitlement to the State Pension Non Contributory is reviewed by his Department; whether annual reviews are carried out in all cases, particularly where an individual's income is affected by currency fluctuations arising from a United Kingdom pension; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20168/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: State pension non-contributory may be available to those who don’t qualify for State pension contributory based on their social insurance (PRSI) contribution record or if they only qualify for a reduced rate of State pension contributory.

State pension non-contributory is a means tested scheme. Items which count as means include cash income, including foreign pensions, the value of any property (excluding a person’s own home) and the value of any savings and investments which a person or their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant may have. In order to qualify for the State pension non-contributory a person must be habitually resident in the State.

As part of this Department’s commitment to ensuring that recipients receive their full and correct entitlements, the scheme area operates a cyclical review programme. Customers selected for review may be asked to complete and return a means questionnaire, together with any relevant supporting documentation. Once received, their entitlement is reviewed.

When conducting means reviews which include foreign currency payments, the Deciding Officer uses the European Central Bank exchange rate from the day prior to the means being calculated. If this results in a change in payment entitlement, the person is informed of the change. If the person is unhappy with the decision, the letter also explains their right of appeal to the Social Welfare Appeals Office and how to avail of this option.

While it is not currently feasible or practical to review all claims annually, both from a resourcing point of view and from the perspective of claimants, many of whom would have no change in their circumstances likely to impact on the rate of payment they receive, if a customer believes that a change in circumstances including a fluctuation in currency exchange rates may affect their means calculation, they may seek a review of their entitlement at any time.
I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

summary.i: Question No. 1210 answered with Question No. 1207.
Question No. 1211 answered with Question No. 1207.

question.p: 1212. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department is examining options to individualise disability allowance payment to ensure greater financial independence for persons with disabilities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20296/26]

1216. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review the means test for disability allowance in cases where the applicant is cohabiting or married, given that a partner's full time wages are fully assessed with no income disregard; if he will address the financial hardship this creates for couples where one partner has a disability and loses their payment as a result; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20528/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1212 and 1216 together.

Disability Allowance is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. The payment is subject to a medical assessment, a means test and a habitual residency requirement. The means test takes account of the income a person or couple has in terms of cash, property – other than the family home – and capital. The purpose of the means test is to ensure that limited resources are directed to those with the greatest need.

Disability Allowance has one of the highest capital disregards operated by the Department of Social Protection. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. This compares with €20,000 for most social welfare payments.

People in receipt of Disability Allowance and Blind Pension can take up employment or self-employment and continue to receive all or part of their payment, depending on their income. The earnings disregard has increased by almost 38% since Budget 2021 from €120 to €165 currently. This means that a person can earn up to €165 a week and keep their full rate payment. Earnings between €165 and €375 are assessed at 50%, and any earnings over €375 are fully assessed as means. As a result, people can earn up to €165 per week and keep their payment in full and can earn up to €527.60 per week and keep a portion of their payment, in addition to any secondary benefits they are receiving from my Department. Over the last five budgets the Government has progressively improved payment rates and income disregards for disabled people. The weekly payment rates for Disability Allowance have increased by €51 in that time.

The Programme for Government and the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030 include commitments to reform the Disability Allowance payment and remove anomalies in the current means test. In addition, my Department is currently reviewing means testing across all its social assistance schemes. The outcome of this review will be used to inform decisions regarding any further changes to means testing. Any changes to means testing arrangements can only be considered in the overall policy and budgetary context.

The Government is also committed to introducing a permanent Annual Cost of Disability Support Payment. My Department is leading a Strategic Focus Network Summit on the Cost of Disability. This is a one-day event which will be held in May. It includes other Government departments as well as disabled people, their representatives and other stakeholders.

On February 20th, I launched a public consultation process on how a cost of disability payment can best be delivered. This will run until April 7th. People who have ideas about how we can make changes that will make a real difference to them are encouraged to visit gov.ie/COD, where they will find guidance on how to engage with the consultation process in whatever format best suits them.

question.p: 1213. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department has examined barriers to financial inclusion faced by recipients of disability allowance, including where the payment is not recognised for mortgages, pensions or saving schemes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20297/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Department of Social Protection provides a suite of income supports for those who are unable to work due to illness or disability. However, the treatment of social welfare payments by financial institutions in terms of determining eligibility for mortgages or other services is outside of my Department's remit. Regulation of banking and financial services is a matter for the Minister for Finance.

Disability Allowance is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. The payment is subject to a medical assessment, a means test and a habitual residency requirement. The means test takes account of the income a person or couple has in terms of cash, property – other than the family home – and capital. The purpose of the means test is to ensure that limited resources are directed to those with the greatest need.

People in receipt of Disability Allowance can take up employment or self-employment and continue to receive all or part of their payment, depending on their income. The earnings disregard has increased by almost 38% since Budget 2021 from €120 to €165 currently. This means that a person can earn up to €165 a week and keep their full rate payment. Earnings between €165 and €375 are assessed at 50%, and any earnings over €375 are fully assessed as means. As a result, people can earn up to €165 per week and keep their payment in full and can earn up to €527.60 per week and keep a portion of their payment.

Disability Allowance has one of the highest capital disregards operated by the Department of Social Protection. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. This is compared to €20,000 for most social welfare payments. A person’s family home is not assessed as means.
The Government is committed to improving outcomes for people with a disability. As a result, a number of improvements were announced in Budget 2026. These include:

• A €10 increase in the weekly rates of payment, bringing the personal rates of payment to €254 per week from January 2026. As a result, there has been a €51 increase to weekly disability income support payments since Budget 2021.
• The highest ever increases in the Child Support Payment – an increase of €16 to €78 for children aged 12 or over, and of €8 to €58 for children under 12.
• A €20 increase in the rate of Domiciliary Care Allowance bringing the rate to €380 per month from January 2026.
• A €5 increase in the Fuel Allowance, bring it to €38 per week from January 2026. This will provide an additional €140 during the annual fuel season.

• People moving from Disability Allowance or Blind Pension to take up work will be able to retain their Fuel Allowance payment for five years. The Back to Work Family Dividend is also being extended to this group, where they have children.
• From January, we also extended the Wage Subsidy Scheme to people who acquire a disability while in employment and to those who transfer from Invalidity Pension to Partial Capacity Benefit.
• The number of bands in the Wage Subsidy Scheme is being reduced from six to three and the rates in all bands are being increased from April 2026.

• The Government allocated €3.8 billion to the Department of Children, Disability and Equality for disability services in 2026, including funding for Community Based Specialist Disability Services to ensure people with disabilities receive the right support, at the right time, in the right place. This represents a 20% increase year on year and represents an overall increase since 2020 of €1.8 billion.
• These measures build on the progress made over the last number of years.

question.p: 1214. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department has examined measures to protect entitlement to the free travel scheme for persons who lose eligibility for disability allowance due to changes in household means, including through marriage or cohabitation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20298/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The Free Travel Scheme provides free travel on the main public and private transport services for those eligible under the scheme. These include road, rail and ferry services provided by companies such as Bus Átha Cliath, Bus Éireann and Iarnród Éireann, as well as Luas and services provided by over 70 private transport operators.

The objective of the Free Travel scheme is to ensure older people and people with disabilities remain active within their community. Therefore, access to a free travel pass for those aged under 66 is linked to a person being in receipt of certain primary Social Protection payments or people who are medically certified as unable to drive for a period of 12 months or more.

While my Departments schemes are reviewed on an ongoing basis, any decision to expand the eligibility criteria for the free travel to allow persons who lose eligibility for disability allowance due to changes in household means to retain the pass can only be considered while taking account of the overall budgetary context and the availability of financial resources.

However, as part of the “Make Work Pay” initiative, persons who move directly from certain long term Social Protection schemes, such as Disability Allowance, to employment are entitled to retain their Free Travel entitlement for a further period of 5 years, where they previously had an entitlement.

As part of Budget 2024, the expansion of the Free Travel eligibility to people who are medically certified as unable to drive for a period of 12 months or longer was a significant measure. There is no requirement that a person must be in receipt of a Social Welfare payment or any means limits in order to qualify for a Free Travel Pass on these medical grounds, provided the other qualifying criteria are met.
I trust that this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1215. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will clarify whether a formal diagnosis is required for eligibility for domiciliary care allowance, in light of cases where applications have been refused on the basis of the absence of a diagnostic assessment, despite departmental guidance stating that DCA is awarded based on the level of care required rather than diagnosis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20519/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA) is a monthly allowance payable to a parent / guardian in respect of a child aged under 16 who has a severe disability requiring continual or continuous care and attention substantially in excess of the care and attention normally required by a child of the same age and where the level of the child's disability is such that the child is likely to require this level of care and attention for at least 12 consecutive months. This level of care and attention must be required to allow the child to deal with activities of daily living in areas such as mobility, personal care, feeding/diet, communication, speech/language, sleeping, behaviour, safety, sensory, issues, including any other additional needs.

Eligibility for DCA is not based entirely on the type of disability or diagnosis but primarily on the impact of the child's disability, in terms of the associated overall level of care and attention required by the child compared to a child of a similar age who does not have such a disability. The decision process that applies in the consideration of whether a child meets the conditions for DCA includes the examination of all relevant factors identified as impacting on the child's additional care needs.

When reviewing an application for Domiciliary Care Allowance, the claim is first referred to one of the Department’s Medical Assessors for their opinion. Medical Assessors are fully qualified and experienced practitioners who provide a second opinion to that of the person's own doctor for the guidance of the Department's Deciding Officers.

The assessment of the substantial extra and continual care needs of children with childhood development and behavioural disorders is more challenging compared to other childhood conditions given the wide spectrum of manifestation of conditions and bearing in mind the age attainment of developmental milestones. In all cases, determinations on eligibility for DCA are based on all of the medical and care needs information provided with the application and while specialist or assessment reports can be helpful in making quality and efficient decisions, they are not mandatory.
The average processing time for DCA applications is currently 6 weeks.

An online application was launched for Carers schemes and DCA in 2025, through my Department's MyWelfare service. This will assist with the management of application processing times, and will extend to Disability supports later in 2026.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

summary.i: Question No. 1216 answered with Question No. 1212.

question.p: 1217. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the amount of carbon that will be emitted on all transport and related actions undertaken by him and all members of his staff during their St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026. [20615/26]

1218. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the amount of carbon that will be emitted on all transport and related actions undertaken by all Junior Ministers in his Department and their members of staff during their St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026. [20633/26]
1219. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection if he has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted due to St Patrick’s Day trips in 2026; and the amount paid. [20652/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1219, 1217 and 1218 together.

In line with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation Circular 01/2020 (Procedures for Offsetting the Emissions Associated with Official Air Travel), my Department makes an annual payment to the statutory Climate Action Fund for the previous year's greenhouse gas emissions related to official air travel.

As part of the Government’s St. Patrick’s Day programme for 2026, I travelled to Canada to promote Ireland, Irish values, and Ireland’s interests across the world. In terms of the delegation from the Department of Social Protection, I travelled with my Private Secretary.

The associated carbon emissions were approximately 1,550 kg CO2e in total. This estimate covers the return flights to Canada, one domestic flight, and local ground transport. The 2027 payment under Circular 01/2020 will cover all air travel completed in 2026, including St. Patrick's Day trips.
There are no Junior Ministers currently assigned to my Department; accordingly, the question regarding Junior Ministers does not arise.

summary.i: Questions Nos. 1218 and 1219 answered with Question No. 1217.

question.p: 1220. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the amount of carbon that has been emitted by transport used by him, the Junior Ministers in his Department, and their staff for each of the past five years; if he has paid to offset any of the carbon emitted because of transport; and the amount paid in each year. [20670/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: In line with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation Circular 01/2020 (Procedures for Offsetting the Emissions Associated with Official Air Travel), my Department makes an annual payment to the statutory Climate Action Fund for the previous year's greenhouse gas emissions related to official air travel.

The table below sets out the carbon emissions and associated offset payments arising from official air travel undertaken by the Minister, Ministers of State, and their staff over the past five years. No ministerial air travel was undertaken in 2021 or 2024.

question.p: 1221. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection if he can outline the legislative basis that requires in-person attendance for the collection of jobseekers benefit; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20688/26]

1222. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection if his attention has been drawn to a situation (details supplied); if an exception can be made in relation to the requirement of in-person collection of jobseekers payments; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20689/26]

1223. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection the position regarding his Department's policy on the electronic transfer of social welfare payments; the way in which this can be accommodated in a case (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20690/26]

1224. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection the position regarding any review of his Department's policy in relation to the electronic transfer of social welfare payments in place of in person attendance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20691/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1221, 1222, 1223 and 1224 together.
My Department provides two main payment options for its customers: payment in cash at post offices or payment directly into customer accounts by Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT).

My Department may determine the payment method appropriate to a particular scheme or benefit. This is provided for under Article 192 of the Social Welfare (Consolidated Claims, Payment and Control) Regulations 2007 (S.I. 142 of 2007). For the Jobseekers Schemes the appropriate payment method is cash payable at a Post Office.

There are circumstances where a person, including a person that is able to work but has medical issues that makes attending in person difficult, is unable to attend the post office for payment. Each such case is looked at individually and alternative arrangements or accommodations will be put in place if required.

Similar to attendance at a post office, my Department is very aware there are circumstances where a person is unable to attend in person at an Intreo Centre. Again, each such case is looked at individually and alternative arrangements or accommodations will be put in place if required. At any point in time there will be a number of people who are “excused” from in person signing, and/or also availing of an alternative payment method. Such requests are not unusual and my Department deals with them with empathy.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

summary.i: Question No. 1222 answered with Question No. 1221.
Question No. 1223 answered with Question No. 1221.
Question No. 1224 answered with Question No. 1221.

question.p: 1225. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will review a decision on a carer's application in respect of a person (details supplied), in light of additional information that has been provided by the applicant's carer; if his Department will reconsider the application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20747/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: Carer's allowance (CA) is a means-tested social assistance payment made to a person who is habitually resident in the State and who is providing full-time care and attention to a child or an adult who has such a disability that as a result they require that level of care.
An application for CA was received from the person concerned 11 December 2025.

As part of the decision process, the application was referred for the professional opinion of a Department Medical Assessor. The claim was disallowed as the Deciding Officer, having regard to the opinion of the Medical Assessor, decided that the information supplied did not show that the care recipient required full time care. The claim was also disallowed as the Deciding Officer decided that the information supplied showed that the person concerned was in employment for more than the maximum hours of 18.5 hours per week.

The person concerned was notified of this decision via MyWelfare on 30 January 2026. They were also notified of their right to have the decision reviewed (where further information is available) or to appeal the decision to the Social Welfare Appeals Office (SWAO).

A review was initiated on foot of correspondence received on 12 March 2026. Following this review, the decision remained unchanged. The person concerned was notified of this decision on 12 March 2026.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question.p: 1226. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is satisfied by the adequacy of illness benefit in the context of the cost of living crisis; his views on reviewing its adequacy as income protection in high cost areas; and if he has corresponded with the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment about the adequacy of the five-day cap in place following a claim of statutory sick leave. [20774/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: The adequacy of core social protection payments is kept under ongoing review by my Department and is assessed through a structured, evidence-based process that informs Government decisions at Budget time.
In examining payment adequacy, my Department draws on a range of data sources and research, including:
• Consumer Price Index (CPI) data published by the Central Statistics Office;
• Analysis of income and poverty trends using the Survey on Income and Living Conditions (SILC);
• Distributional impact modelling undertaken as part of each Budget;
• International comparisons of minimum income supports through OECD and EU reporting mechanisms
Adequacy is therefore not determined by reference to a single benchmark figure, but by considering price trends, income distribution data, poverty indicators and fiscal sustainability.

The rate for Illness Benefit is determined annually as part of the Budget process and reflects broader considerations of adequacy, poverty reduction and fiscal capacity across the social protection system as a whole.

With regard to additional supports, my Department also provides an Additional Needs Payment under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme to help meet essential expenditure which a person could not reasonably be expected to meet out of their weekly income. This includes certain supplements to assist with ongoing or recurring costs that cannot be met from a person’s own resources and are deemed to be necessary.

Statutory sick leave is the responsibility of my colleague, the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. Workers have an entitlement to five statutory sick leave days in a year. Under the scheme, sick pay may be paid by an employer at 70% of a person’s normal pay, up to a maximum of €110 a day. Employers may operate sick leave schemes which are, on the whole, more favourable to the employee than what would be provided in terms of statutory sick leave. The specification of the number of statutory sick leave days is a matter for the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, following consultation with myself as Minister for Social Protection. I am satisfied with the number of such days (five) at this time.

My Department will continue to keep its range of supports under review to ensure that they meet their overall objectives. Any changes to the current system would need to be considered in an overall policy and budgetary context, taking account of the overall sustainability of the Social Insurance Fund.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1227. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Social Protection the current number of persons in receipt of the contributory and non-contributory pension; and the projected numbers for same in ten years' time, 20 years' time and 30 years' time; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20814/26]

speech.from: Minister for Social Protection
speech.p: In 2024, the European Commission published ‘2024 Ageing report- Economic & Budgetary projections for the EU Member States (2022-2070)’. The purpose of this report is to assess the long-term sustainability of public finances in the EU Member States. Long-term recipient projections for both State Pension Contributory and State Pension Non-Contributory were carried out by my Department’s Actuarial and Investment Analysis Unit for this report.

The table below shows the number of recipients of State Pension Contributory and State Pension Non-Contributory as of 28/02/2026. Additionally, the projected number of recipients (taken from the Ageing Report projections) are provided. These projections are rounded to the nearest 1,000 people.

State Pension Non-Contributory numbers are projected to fall over time as greater numbers qualify for the State Pension Contributory instead. In the future those reaching State Pension Age are projected to have stronger social insurance records, enabling a higher proportion of them to qualify for State Pension Contributory.

State Pension Contributory numbers are projected to significantly increase over time due to an ageing population. The Social Insurance Fund which helps to fund the State Pension Contributory through PRSI revenues, is likely to be in surplus in the short-term. However, given these changing demographics, the fund is likely to go into deficit at a future point. This will require a planned and gradual increase in social insurance rates over a long period of time.

In response to a report of the Pensions Commission, the then Government decided not to increase the State pension age. However, in order to address the future sustainability of the Social Insurance Fund, the Government instead decided to implement a series of gradual and incremental increases in PRSI rates across all three contributors to the Social Insurance Fund - employees, employers and the self-employed. These increases total 0.7% between 2024 and 2028, with increases after that point to be considered based on the most up-to-date data available from the next Actuarial Review of the Social Insurance Fund.

This Actuarial Review will continue to be undertaken every five years and will look at the sustainability of the Social Insurance Fund including projected future numbers of older people qualifying for State Pension Contributory and the required increases in PRSI rates to support this expenditure.
I hope this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question.p: 1228. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 228 of 3 March 2026, the actions he will take to address the specific staffing shortages in an embassy (details supplied) that is impacting on visa processing times; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18988/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: In the context of the staffing restrictions arising at the Embassy of Ireland in Moscow (more information is available on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade website: www.ireland.ie/en/dfa/overseas-travel/advice/russian-federation/ ), to ensure continuity of service, visa applications received by the Embassy of Ireland in Moscow are currently sent to the Dublin Visa Office for examination and processing. Every effort is being made to process applications as efficiently as possible and this is being kept under ongoing review.

summary.i: Question No. 1229 answered with Question No. 1344.

question.p: 1230. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has compared the costs of Go Safe speed cameras cost versus average speed cameras and static camera locations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20556/26]

1392. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the cost of rolling out the nine new static cameras and three new average speed cameras across the road network, by camera; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20560/26]

1393. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of the 19,901 safety camera zones nationwide that are located in Dublin; the average cost of implementing a safety camera zone; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20562/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1230, 1392 and 1393 together.

Speeding remains one of the greatest risk factors on our roads. Speed reduces the time people have to react and makes collisions much more likely. It also makes it more likely that when collisions happen, they will lead to death or very serious injuries.

Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, we need to use technology to work to reduce speeding on our roads. An Garda Síochána has contributed to making our roads safer through the use of mobile safety cameras, using service provider GoSafe to operate them on its behalf, enforcement cameras operated using a fleet of marked vehicles, and static speed cameras.

I am informed by the Garda authorities that the pilot project for the installation of nine static safety cameras and three average speed cameras was undertaken in conjunction with Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) and the relevant Local Authorities. The national provision of safety cameras forms part of an outsourced managed service contract with service provider GoSafe.

The individual cost of each camera cannot be disclosed as this information is commercially sensitive and forms part of the competitive tender process. However, the overall annual cost of the safety camera project is approximately €26 million.

390 new safety camera zones became operational from 1 January 2026, bringing the total number of safety camera zones nationwide to 1,901. The primary purpose of safety cameras is to reduce speed-related collisions, lessen injuries and save lives. The Deputy can find all zones and locations on the Garda Website using the following link: www.garda.ie/en/roads-policing/safety-cameras-save-lives/mobile-safety-camera-detection/[Mobile Safety Camera Detection - Garda].

An analysis of the cost and effectiveness of GoSafe cameras, average speed cameras and static camera locations is a matter for the Garda Commissioner, given his responsibility for operational policing matters, and the Minister for Transport who has responsibility for the Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030.

I am advised that road safety cameras operate in areas where there is a history of speed-related collisions, known as speed enforcement zones. The designation of specific sections of road as speed enforcement zones is based on an analysis of collision data. They are also there to be preventative, to be seen and to adjust driver behaviour.
Ongoing surveys are conducted to ascertain whether existing zones continue to represent locations where speeding is happening.

question.p: 1231. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of dedicated Garda roads policing personnel currently deployed in the Dublin Metropolitan Region; the way in which this compares with 2014 levels; the number of speeding detections in the Dublin region in each of the past five years; whether the Government has assessed the impact of the 43% national decline in speeding detections on road safety outcomes, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20592/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: An Garda Síochána play a vital role in enforcing road traffic law and in making our roads safer for all road users, including vulnerable road users. Road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. This includes a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies. In this regard it should be noted that around 65% of drug-driving and drink-driving checks are carried out by regular Gardaí.

The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Gardaí throughout the State and Garda policies.

I am fully committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs, with Budget 2026 providing unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment, training and staffing. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. As Garda recruitment continues and accelerates, additional Gardaí will become available to be deployed to priority areas.

An Garda Síochána publishes figures in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing by Garda Division, including the Dublin Metropolitan Region from 2014 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links:
www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html
www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html
The Deputy should select the most recent date and then select the file titled ‘Roads Policing by division 2014 to the most recent date" to access a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Division.

The Deputy may also be interested to note that An Garda Síochána publishes figures relating to Roads Policing Offences on a quarterly basis. This includes Fixed Charge Notices (FCNs) for offences relating to Speeding Overall as well as broken down into Intercept (Garda issued) and Non-Intercept (Speed Camera Van Operator). This can be found at the following link:
www.garda.ie/en/roads-policing/statistics/roads%20policing%20offences%20by%20region%20and%20division/
The Deputy can select the “Roads Policing” file for the time period required.

question.p: 1232. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department will restore road policing to 2014 levels.; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20990/26]

1287. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current number of Garda members assigned to Roads Policing Units; the way in which this compares with the number assigned in 2014; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18972/26]

1327. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current number of Gardaí assigned to dedicated roads policing units; the way this compares with the number assigned in 2014; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19656/26]

1331. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide details of current road policing levels compared with 2014; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19825/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1232, 1287, 1327 and 1331 together.

An Garda Síochána play a vital role in enforcing road traffic law and in making our roads safer for all road users, including vulnerable road users. Road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. This includes a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies. In this regard it should be noted that around 65% of drug-driving and drink-driving checks are carried out by regular Gardaí.

The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Gardaí throughout the State and Garda policies.

I am fully committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs, with Budget 2026 providing unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion to support recruitment, training and staffing. Recruitment into An Garda Síochána is now gathering real momentum and just under 800 trainees entered the Garda College in 2025, the highest number since 2018. As Garda recruitment continues and accelerates, additional Gardaí will become available to be deployed to priority areas.

An Garda Síochána publishes figures in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing by Garda Division from 2014 to the end of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links:
www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html
www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html
The Deputy should select the most recent date and then select the file titled ‘Roads Policing by division 2014 to the most recent date" to access a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Division.

The Deputy may also be interested to note that An Garda Síochána publishes figures relating to Roads Policing Offences on a quarterly basis. This includes Fixed Charge Notices (FCNs) for offences relating to Speeding Overall as well as broken down into Intercept (Garda issued) and Non-Intercept (Speed Camera Van Operator). This can be found at the following link:
www.garda.ie/en/roads-policing/statistics/roads%20policing%20offences%20by%20region%20and%20division/
The Deputy can select the “Roads Policing” file for the time period required.

question.p: 1233. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of new Garda community support vans that came into fleet in each of the years of 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026; the number of those Garda community support vans that were withdrawn from the fleet during same period, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18231/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational policing and responsibility for the allocation and deployment of resources and personnel available to him, including the Garda fleet.
I am informed by the Garda authorities that, as of 28 February 2026, there were 3,658 vehicles attached to the Garda fleet. This represents an increase of over 18% since the end of December 2020.

Garda authorities have provided the below table which shows the number of new Garda community support vans that came into fleet in each of the years of 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026 and the number of those Garda community support vans that were withdrawn from the fleet during same period.
The purchase and allocation of vehicles by An Garda Síochána is made on the basis of identified operational demands, the availability of resources and is reviewed on a continual basis.

question.p: 1234. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the operating hours and staffing levels of Cobh Garda station; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18241/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters and the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel, including opening hours of Garda Stations, throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions under Section 34 of the Act and, as Minister, I have no role in these independent functions.

An Garda Síochána publishes figures in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned to Cobh Garda station, County Cork as of January 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links:
www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/january-2026.html
The Deputy should select the current month and access the file titled “Garda Members by Division District Station” for a breakdown of total Garda numbers by Garda station.
Information in relation to the opening hours of individual Garda Stations is publicly available and can be found at the following link:
www.garda.ie/en/contact-us/station-directory/

I am advised that, in relation to Garda stations which are not open to the public on a 24/7 basis, telephone calls to a station during periods of closure are automatically routed to the nearest 24-hour station in the Community Engagement Area.
In cases of emergency, any person should call the 999 or 112.

question.p: 1235. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he has examined the adequacy of the current governance framework for public safety in Dublin City Centre; whether consideration is being given to legislative reform to provide for enhanced coordination between An Garda Síochána, local authorities and other relevant State agencies in the prevention of crime and anti-social behaviour; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18267/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Government is committed to the principle that everyone, wherever they live in Ireland, should feel safe and be safe. Building safe and secure communities across the country by investing in An Garda Síochána is a top priority for this Government. I want every part of the country to be a safe space for people to live and work in.
The Government is committed to tackling crime and anti-social behaviour and to building safer streets and stronger communities through a number of ongoing measures, including:
• Getting more Gardaí on our streets through increased recruitment;
• Continued expansion of youth justice and youth diversion measures;
• New laws which criminalise the grooming of children into a life of crime;
• The deployment of body-worn cameras, with nationwide roll-out to follow the current pilot project;
• Proposing solutions to public order and anti-social behaviour through the Local Leadership Programme which brings together local stakeholders in a structured manner;
• Over €4 million allocated to 42 projects through the Community Safety Fund, which re-invests the proceeds of crime into local safety projects.

A number of actions are also contained in the Programme for Government to reduce instances of anti-social behaviour. These include a commitment to enact legislation to combat anti-social behaviour through enhanced use of Anti-Social Behaviour Warnings and Anti-Social Behaviour Orders. Work to progress these commitments has commenced.

It is important to acknowledge that community safety is not just a matter for An Garda Síochána. The Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced in 2025, provides for the establishment of Local Community Safety Partnerships (LCSP) within each local authority area.

These Local Community Safety Partnerships are currently being established across the country to provide a more inclusive, community-led and multi-agency approach to local safety. They bring together a broad range of relevant stakeholders to address community safety issues in their area which will include residents, local councillors, community representatives, business and education representatives, and a range of public services including the HSE, Tusla, An Garda Síochána and the local authority. Each LCSP will focus on concerns identified and prioritised by local people and will develop and implement its own tailored community safety plan.

A total of 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships are being established. I have appointed members to 35 of these Safety Partnerships and 33 are fully operational having held inaugural meetings and elected their Chair and Vice Chair.

The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is providing support to local authorities and in particular to Local Community Safety Partnership teams, in the process of establishing and operating each Safety Partnership in their area.

question.p: 1236. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he has been briefed, in any capacity, on the operation or regulation of the exchange-of-duty system within the Irish Prison Service, including the review of that system referenced in organisational communications in November 2025. [18292/26]

1237. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department or the Irish Prison Service has conducted an internal audit, compliance assessment, or control review of exchange-of-duty practices involving unreciprocated exchanges or private financial arrangements between staff; and, if so, when such review commenced and whether its findings have been finalised. [18293/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1236 and 1237 together.

In relation to the Irish Prison Service (IPS) and rosters, the IPS is responsible for the day-to-day running and operations of the prisons. I am advised that the IPS HR Directorate have introduced a number of measures in recent years to both monitor and enhance attendance arrangements at a prison level. These include:
• Exchange of Duty compliance levels at each prison now form part of the annual deliverables for each Prison Governor;

• A review of Exchange of Duty policy, the most recent of which was in October 2024, focused on identifying measures to support improved compliance and accountability. Updates have also made to Exchange of Duty and working specific roster shifts;
• The introduction of HR Directorate annual compliance reviews of prisons with the Exchange of Duty system;

• Updating the current Time & Attendance System. The existing system is not user friendly and requires manual interventions to develop reports necessary to support prisons in monitoring levels of compliance; and

• The completion of a procurement process to install a system which will deliver enhanced monitoring and automatic restrictions for individual participation with the Exchange of Duty process, based on set parameters. This new system will be operational by the end of 2026.

My Department’s Internal Audit Unit has conducted audits across all of the prisons and they have examined attendance management in their work. A number of recommendations on attendance management practices, including the exchange of duty process, are being implemented.

summary.i: Question No. 1237 answered with Question No. 1236.

question.p: 1238. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the Department's policy regarding reviews of protected disclosure assessment decisions, including whether reviewers are required to be independent of the original decision-maker; whether reporting persons are informed of the reviewer's role or title; and the standard timeframe applied for issuing review outcomes. [18295/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: My Department’s policy, in relation to reviews of protected disclosures assessment decisions, complies with the protected disclosures Statutory Guidance for Public Bodies and Prescribed Persons. Reporting persons may request a review of an assessment decision to close a procedure or refer a matter to another procedure. My Department considers each request on a case-by-case basis.

A senior manager who was not involved in the initial assessment or a suitably qualified external person, as appropriate, conducts such reviews. The outcome of the review, including the reviewer’s role and title, is communicated to the reporting persons. While there is no statutory time limit for assessment decisions reviews, my Department endeavours to conclude such reviews within three months.

The Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitisation is the lead Department on protected disclosure legislation and provides guidance on all protected disclosure processes.

question.p: 1239. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total expenditure by his Department in settlement payments, compensation, damages or negotiated payments arising from the repudiation, cancellation or termination of international protection accommodation contracts, including payments already made, payments legally committed to, and any financial provisions recorded in the Department’s accounts, in aggregate , for each of the years 2021 to 2025, and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18305/26]

1240. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total expenditure by his Department, for 2025, and to date in 2026, in settlement payments, compensation, damages or negotiated payments arising from the repudiation, cancellation or termination of international protection accommodation contracts, including payments already made, payments legally committed to, and any financial provisions recorded in the Department’s accounts, in aggregate; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18306/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1239 and 1240 together.
The State is currently accommodating over 33,000 people in approximately 310 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country.

No expenditure as described by the Deputy has been incurred in relation to international protection accommodation from 2021 to the end of 2025. One payment has been incurred in 2026 as part of a confidential settlement agreement. A small number of similar matters are currently before the courts.

All expenditure on international protection accommodation, including any payments in this category, will be reflected in the Department's appropriation account for 2026 and will be subject to review by the Comptroller and Auditor general.

As we work towards a more stable and sustainable accommodation system in this sector, accommodation is being delivered through a range of channels, with a focus on developing more State-owned accommodation.

The Department continues to appraise the portfolio of existing accommodation with a view to consolidation where possible, along with better governance and compliance, and increased frequency of inspections of properties.

summary.i: Question No. 1240 answered with Question No. 1239.

question.p: 1241. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 748 of 4 February 2026, if he has received the relevant information from Garda Authorities to answer this question. [18312/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I refer to Parliamentary Question No.748 of 4 February where you sought "the number of competitions that were held in 2025 for sworn Gardai to apply to join divisional roads policing units; and the number of Gardai, by rank that applied for each competition, in tabular form."

The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes competitions for the Roads Policing Unit.
I am informed that no competitions were held in 2025 for Divisional Roads Policing Units, however, a regional competition for the Dublin Metropolitan Region (DMR) commenced in 2025.

It should be noted that the DMR has a Regional Roads Policing Unit that provides roads policing cover to all Garda Divisions within the DMR, and is based in Dublin Castle. All other Garda Divisions have Divisional Roads Policing Units.

An Garda Síochána play a vital role in enforcing road traffic law and in making our roads safer for all road users, including vulnerable road users. Road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. This includes a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies.

question.p: 1242. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 747 of 4 February 2026, if he has received the relevant information from Garda Authorities to answer this question. [18313/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I refer to Parliamentary Question No. 747 of 4 February 2026 where you sought: “the number of promotions from Sergeant to Inspector rank within An Garda Síochána which occurred in 2025, in tabular form.”
By law, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of Garda business.
I am advised by the Garda authorities, that during 2025, there were a total of 37 promotions from Sergeant to Inspector rank within An Garda Síochána.

question.p: 1243. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if an application for a person (details supplied) for a student visa will be expedited; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18314/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The person referred to by the Deputy applied to renew their immigration permission on 09 January 2026 and this application is currently in the queue for consideration.

The Registration Office within Immigration Service Delivery of my Department provide a live processing date, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing
They are currently processing applications submitted from 22 December 2025. In order to ensure a fair and equitable service, renewals are processed in order of date submitted.
If the application is approved, the person concerned can expect to receive their new Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card within the following 10-15 working days.

The person concerned can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s new Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/

As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question.p: 1244.
