Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of meetings which have taken place between him or officials in his Department and an organisation (details supplied) or bodies which are members of the organization in 2025; to provide a list of those meetings; the dates on which they took place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18354/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I can confirm that neither myself nor any officials from my Department have held meetings in 2025 with the organisation referenced, or with bodies which are members of the organisation referenced.

question.p: 1245. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a list of maintenance contracts using public funds that his Department or his agencies has where a company (details supplied) carry out works; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18357/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I can confirm that my Department and the agencies under its remit have no current maintenance contracts with the company referenced.

Day-to-day maintenance requests for my Department's buildings are managed through the Office of Public Works (OPW). In such routine operational scenarios, payments from my Department are made directly to the OPW as the contracting authority. This reflects the OPW’s role as the central contracting and management entity for State properties.

question.p: 1246. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if having a GP visit card would have a negative impact on residency or a future naturalisation application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18378/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: Last November I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States.

As part of this I intend to make a number of changes to the rules on the granting of Irish citizenship. One proposed change relates to the introduction of a new statutory naturalisation condition requiring applicants to be self-sufficient. Being self-sufficient will mean that the applicant should not be indebted to the State or be in receipt of certain social protection payments during a defined period prior to submitting an application. There will be certain payments that will not affect a person’s ability to apply and be granted citizenship.

The outlined conditions relating to self-sufficiency will require legislative change to the 1956 Act and consideration of the proposed changes will take place through the regular parliamentary process, and following consultation with other relevant Departments.

question.p: 1247. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration under which Vote was the deposit paid for the purchase of Citywest in August 2025 charged; whether it was allocated to Vote 13, Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration; under which capital subhead it was funded; whether prior sanction was issued by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation; did the expenditure remain within the subhead ceiling; the way in which the full €148 million reflected in Revised Estimates 2025, and where does the asset now sit on the State’s balance sheet; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18380/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The purchase of the Citywest property provided a unique opportunity to deliver a high-capacity State-owned asset, including an accommodation centre, in a strategic location. The facility is a key component in the State's implementation of the EU Migration Pact this year, acting as a screening centre and border procedure location as required under the Pact.

The full purchase price (including VAT) for the Citywest property was €148,253,530 and represents significant value for the State. The purchase will significantly reduce the current expenditure on State accommodation at this site over the coming years and increase the value for public money now and for the future. The payback period on the purchase price is approximately 4 years, due to the reduced running costs of a State-owned facility compared to the previous leasing model.

The full purchase of Citywest was funded from Vote 24 Justice, Home Affairs and Migration under the Subhead Programme C5 International Protection Seekers Accommodation, the capital allocation for which was increased from €40 million to €153.3 million in the Further Revised Estimate presented by the Minister to Dáil Éireann in September 2025 to allow for the full cost of the purchase of Citywest.

The purchase of the Citywest property was completed in compliance with Public Financial Procedures including Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation sanction procedures and Government Infrastructure Guidelines, which set out clear guidelines for the evaluation, planning, and management of public investment projects, including purchase or acquisitions of State assets of this kind.

Citywest is recorded as an asset in the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration fixed asset register and will be reported in the Appropriation Accounts 2025 for the Vote 24 Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.

question.p: 1248. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether a period of residence as an international protection applicant under the International Protection Act 2015 is or has been reckonable in an application for naturalisation. [18385/26]

1404. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if applications for citizenship submitted before December 2025 will be assessed on the criteria for naturalisation in place at the time of the application, namely after three years’ residence calculated from the date of arrival in the State/application for international protection; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20792/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1248 and 1404 together.
Time spent in the state as an applicant for International Protection is not reckonable residence towards becoming an Irish citizen.

Only once an individual has been granted an International Protection declaration and who have accrued the required period of reckonable residence in the State can they be considered for Irish citizenship.

Last November, I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States.
One such policy change related to the residency requirements of a person granted refugee status and who wishes to apply for Irish citizenship. This change came into effect on 8 December 2025.

Previously, individuals granted international protection status could apply for citizenship after a period of three years. Effective from 8 December 2025, refugees are generally required to have five years of reckonable residence in the State to meet the eligibility criteria for citizenship. Applications for citizenship submitted prior to 8 December 2025 will continue to be assessed in accordance with the previous residency requirement, while applications submitted on and after that date are assessed under the revised policy.
The recent policy change relates solely to the length of reckonable residence required following the grant of international protection.
The extension of the reckonable residence requirement reinforces the principle that Irish citizenship reflects a sustained and meaningful connection with the State, demonstrated over time.

All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually based on the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Applications are assessed in line with the policy and legislative framework in force at the time the application is made.

question.p: 1249. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether an organisation is a proscribed terrorist organisation in this State (details supplied); or if this organisation is free to recruit members and solicit funding here; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18398/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The organisation referred to by the Deputy is not the subject of a suppression order under section 19 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939.
I can assure the Deputy that the Government attaches the highest priority to countering security threats, including those related to terrorism.
There is a strong body of laws in place to counter terrorism and sustain our national security, most notably, the Offences Against the State Acts 1939 to 1998.
The Criminal Justice (Terrorist Offences) Acts 2005-2015 were enacted to give force to the State’s commitment to International Conventions on the suppression of terrorist related activities.

Section 5 provides that any organisation engaged in terrorist activity or terrorist-linked activity is an unlawful organisation within the meaning and for the purposes of the Offences Against the State Acts 1939 to 1998 and section 3 of the Criminal Law Act 1976. This is the case whether the organisation is inside or outside the State, or whether the terrorist activity occurs in or outside the State.

Thus it is not necessary for an organisation to be subject to a suppression order in accordance with section 19 of the 1939 Act, to allow for investigations or prosecutions to be carried out, where appropriate.
An Garda Síochána continues to put in place a robust framework of measures, both operational and intelligence based, to prevent and respond to security threats including those relating to terrorism.

The financing or recruiting for terrorism is a particular area of operational focus for An Garda Síochána. An Garda Síochána works closely with security and intelligence counterparts in other jurisdictions in that context.
It is a matter for An Garda Síochána in any particular circumstance to consider whether an offence may have occurred.

question.p: 1250. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide clarity on the legislative or regulatory frameworks that exist to address the use of online gaming platforms such as (details supplied) as vectors for child exploitation in Ireland; the oversight mechanisms which exist for such platforms operating in Ireland where children may be at risk; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18461/26]

1262. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will review correspondence (details supplied); if he will address the concerns raised therein; if he will respond to the specific questions outlined; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18552/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1250 and 1262 together.

My department is the lead department for EU negotiations on the proposed Regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, which will place further obligations on service providers to ensure that they take every measure to prevent the presence of child sexual abuse material and exploitation on their platforms.

The Irish Internet Hotline is the national reporting centre where members of the public can securely, anonymously, and confidentially report concerns in respect of illegal content online, including child sexual abuse material.
The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport, is the lead department for online safety and the associated regulation and oversight of online platforms.

The Online Safety and Media Regulation (OSMR) Act 2022 was commenced March 2023. It established a new online safety and media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, putting it at the heart of Ireland’s online safety framework, which consists of the Online Safety Code and the EU Digital Services Act (DSA) under which An Coimisiún is Ireland’s Digital Services Coordinator, and the Terrorist Content Online Regulation (TCOR) for which An Coimisiún is a competent authority. Under the framework, online platforms are required to put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security for minors, on their services. An Coimisiún is independent in the exercise of its functions.

Failure to adequately fulfil these obligations can lead to significant financial sanctions and continued non-compliance can lead to criminal sanctions for senior management under the OSMR. The Online Safety Code only applies to the designated Video Sharing Platforms Services, operating in Ireland and not online gaming platforms.

In respect of the platform referred to by the Deputy, I am advised that its European headquarters are in Amsterdam, and accordingly it is under the remit of the Dutch regulatory authorities. Therefore, any investigation or oversight is a matter for the Dutch regulator.

question.p: 1251. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the status of an application (details supplied) in view that it is over 24 months since the application was submitted which is beyond the standard processing timeframe for such application types; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18484/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department.

I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible.

It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service.
For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year.

Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve up the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times.

Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/

As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question.p: 1252. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of community service orders issued in each of the past ten years; and to provide a county-by-county breakdown of the actual works carries out pursuant to these orders, in tabular form. [18495/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: Community Service Orders are made in lieu of, and as an alternative to, a custodial sentence. I am advised by the Probation Service that community service is delivered locally as both group projects and individual placements for non-profit community groups or charitable organisations.

In group projects up to eight clients work under the instruction of a Community Service Supervisor, who is a direct employee of the Probation Service. The Community Service Supervisor will instruct, supervise and work alongside the participants. Individual placements are a partnership with a host organisation, which directly oversees the placement of a particular client, with support and direct link-in from a Probation Officer or Probation Assistant.

Community Service sites include community centres, sports clubs, HSE hospital grounds, schools, churches and graveyards, hostels, charities, horticultural sites. Projects undertaken by those issued with a Community Service Order can include gardening and grounds work, landscaping, Tidy Towns participation and litter collection, painting and decorating, graffiti removal and charity shop work.

I am advised by the Probation Service that it has various partnerships on a county basis with groups such as the Tidy Towns Ireland committees, Civic Trusts, local authorities, State bodies, and charity and sports organisations.

The Probation Service have advised that the below table shows the number of community service orders made from 2016 to 2024, the latest year for which annual figures have been published. They have further advised that the information sought by the Deputy , regarding a county-by-county breakdown of the actual works carried out pursuant to these orders, is not available in the format requested.
Community Service Orders 2016-2024

question.p: 1253. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a list of youth justice interventions funded by his Department. [18496/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: This Government has, in recent years, significantly increased the funding for youth justice initiatives. The budget allocation for Youth Justice measures has increased by 144% from 2020 to 2026. Following a significant increase of €7.3 million in additional core exchequer funding as part of Budget 2026, the total allocation for youth justice measures is now €43 million.

The Government’s focus on diversion and early interventions is a keystone in the Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027. The strategy emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It is aimed at promoting positive behavioural change and targeting this behaviour so that we can break the cycle of offending by young people.

Part 4 of the Children Act 2001 provides the statutory basis for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. The intention of this programme is to divert children, aged 12-17 years old, who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the Criminal Justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices.

Youth Diversion Projects are community-based, multi-agency youth crime prevention initiatives which primarily seek to divert young people who have been, or are at risk of becoming, involved in anti-social and/or criminal behaviour.

Young people who are deemed suitable by the Director of the Garda Youth Diversion Programme are referred to local Youth Diversion Projects, where, in collaboration with a Garda Juvenile Liaison Officer, these Projects provide supports to children to address their behaviour, engage in positive self-development, and connect with their communities.

There are currently 94 Youth Diversion Projects across the country that are funded by my Department. With these funds, these Projects employ dedicated Youth Justice workers who respond daily to the needs of young people across the country. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
The Department also fund specialised Youth Justice Projects catering to Harder-to-Reach, serious and prolific young offenders.

One of these is the Greentown Programme, established in 2020, which aims to disrupt the grooming of children into network-related criminal activity by adults and provides children with meaningful and practical routes out of these networks.

The Greentown Programme is made up of four strands – an intensive family programme to help with parenting and general family functioning, providing young people with pro-social opportunities, supporting communities to withstand gang and network influences, and targeting groomers and disrupting their networks.

The Greentown Programme has been in place in two trial sites and was extended for a further three years in 2023. Each trial site has an annual budget of over €600,000 and the intervention is managed by a qualified community based organisation with Department funding.

Support is provided from An Garda Síochána and expert youth justice services specialising in family support and engaging with hard-to-reach young people. Individuals who are considered Harder-to-Reach are engaged in prolific serious offending and may also be engaging in network-related criminal activity.

The extension of the programme has reduced the influence of criminal networks on children at risk of involvement in crime and improved the likelihood of pro-social outcomes for children who are already involved in criminal networks and learnings from this Programme will be disseminated across the YDP network in the future.

question.p: 1254. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to detail crime prevention measures identified in the 2026 revised estimates. [18497/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: As part of Budget 2026, €2.075 million was allocated for a range of crime prevention measures.

This funding supports the Community Alert Scheme, operated by Muintir na Tíre, Hotline.ie to tackle illegal online content, and initiatives in the areas of drug trafficking prevention, anti-corruption and penal policy.
Funding has also been provided to support a public awareness campaign relating to community safety.

question.p: 1255. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total euro value of grants provided from his Department for capital expenditure for installation and maintenance of community-based CCTV; if he can break down that number in terms of number of actual CCTV cameras; the figures by county, for each year from 2017 to-date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18499/26]

1410. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current and/or additional funding allocations being provided to local authorities, specifically Dublin City Council to expand the provision of CCTV within Dublin City Centre; the additional supports being provided by his Department to assist local authorities in improving safety, visibility and passive surveillance within the city centre; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [21175/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1255 and 1410 together.

Since 2017 my Department has administered a grant-aid scheme supporting communities and local authorities who wish to establish a community-based CCTV system in their area, which provides grants of up to €40,000 for capital expenditure and up to €5,000 for maintenance. To date, grants totalling over €968,000 have been approved for 36 Community CCTV schemes across the country.

Under the Community CCTV Grant Scheme, the balance of the capital funding and 100% of the minor maintenance grant will be issued once the systems are fully operational and supporting documentation is submitted.
Applications for Community CCTV must be authorised by the Garda Commissioner.

The Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023, which was signed into law in December 2023, provides for a new regime for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes. In order to introduce the new regime for CCTV, Part 5 of that Act must be commenced.

There is a new requirement under that Act for the Garda Commissioner to develop a Code of Practice for CCTV which will set out the procedures and standards to be followed, as well as the new rules around confidentiality, security, storage, access and retention of data and data subject rights.

I am advised by Garda authorities that work on the development of this Code of Practice is at an advanced stage and it is expected that implementation of a modernised CCTV platform for An Garda Síochána can commence in 2026.

The Government is committed to tackling crime and to building safer streets and stronger communities through a number of ongoing measures, including the introduction of Local Community Safety Partnerships around the country. These will develop tailored Community Safety Plans for every area and these in turn are expected to feed into local policing plans, where the response to crime and strategies for crime prevention are operational matters for the Garda Commissioner and his senior management team.

The attached table shows the amount of funding provided to CCTV schemes, by county and by year from 2017 to-date in 2026. Please note there were no payments in 2017, 2025 and 2026. The Department does not hold information related to the number of cameras installed by each scheme.

question.p: 1256. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 313 of 10 April 2025, if there are still 209 CCTV cameras in the Dublin metropolitan area that are authorised by the Garda Commissioner; if there has been an increase; if there has been an increase of CCTV cameras authorised by the Garda Commissioner; to identify the location and number of cameras; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18500/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the administration and management of An Garda Síochána. This includes all operational policing matter. As Minister, I have no role in such matters.
I am advised by the Garda authorities that there has been no change in the number of cameras authorised by the Commissioner in the Dublin Metropolitan Area since the 10 April 2025.

The table below provides a breakdown of the number of cameras across Dublin which are operated by An Garda Síochána. It should also be noted that An Garda Síochána have access to further cameras, including those operated by local authorities' as part of community CCTV schemes which are funded by my department and authorised by the Garda Commissioner.

question.p: 1257. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the date on which work began on the new CCTV Strategy by An Garda Síochána; whether his Department or any bodies other than An Garda Síochána are involved in the development of the new CCTV Strategy; if so, whether he will identify those bodies; if he will confirm when the CCTV strategy will be complete; if it will be published; whether changes to primary legislation or secondary legislation will be necessary for the implementation of the CCTV strategy; if legislative changes are necessary; if he can detail what those changes will be; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18501/26]

1258. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether any external consultants or otherwise were engaged with for the purposes of supporting the development of the new CCTV strategy being developed by An Garda Síochána; if he will identify the nature of that engagement; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18502/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1257 and 1258 together.

Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the administration and management of An Garda Síochána. This includes developing and delivering the policing policies and guidelines by which the service operate.
The current legal basis for public CCTV schemes is section 38 of the Garda Síochána Act 2005, as amended.

The Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023, which was signed into law in December 2023, will provide for a new regime for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes and repeal section 38 of the 2005 Act. In order to introduce the new regime for CCTV, Part 5 of that Act and section 6 and 7 must be commenced. Prior to commencement, an amendment is also required to the transitional arrangements in section 7 of the 2023 Act, for existing CCTV applications. That amendment has been included in the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Bill and is currently before the Houses of the Oireachtas.

There is also requirement under that Act for the Garda Commissioner to develop a Code of Practice for CCTV which will set out the procedures and standards to be followed, as well as the new rules around confidentiality, security, storage, access and retention of data and data subject rights.
An Garda Síochána launched a public consultation for a draft Code of Practice on Public Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) on the 27 January 2026.
Detailed information on the process is published and available on the Garda website at www.garda.ie/en/about-us/organisational-structure/garda-equipment/public-cctv/public-cctv.html
I understand that the responses are currently being assessed and considered by An Garda Síochána.

I also understand that An Garda Síochána are working on a new CCTV Strategy which will outline how CCTV infrastructure utilised by Gardaí can be modernised and integrated with other CCTV infrastructure throughout the State. I have requested an update from Garda authorities on the development of this modernised CCTV platform and I will write to the Deputy once the information is to hand.

summary.i: Question No. 1258 answered with Question No. 1257.

question.p: 1259. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide an update on the commencement of Part 5 of the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18503/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 provides for a new regime for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes. Part 5 of that Act, when commenced, will introduce these new arrangements.

There is a requirement under that Act for the Garda Commissioner to develop a Code of Practice for CCTV which will set out the procedures to be followed and I am advised that this work is at an advanced stage.

As part of developing this new Code of Practice, An Garda Síochána consulted with the bodies listed in Part 8 of the Act and conducted a public consultation to seek submissions for any views or observations on the draft Code of Practice for Part 5. This consultation period ended on 24 February 2026. The Garda Commissioner may, upon review of the submissions received, make any amendments he considers necessary to the draft Code.

Officials within my Department are in close contact with An Garda Síochána with a view to assisting them in progressing codes and other issues which need to be finalised for commencement to take place; however, it is a matter for the Garda Commissioner to finalise the Code of Practice.

Prior to commencement, an amendment is also required to the transitional arrangements in section 7 of the 2023 Act, for existing CCTV applications. That amendment has been included in the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Bill and is currently before the Houses of the Oireachtas.
I expect that the new CCTV provisions set out in Part 5 will be commenced this summer.

I am further advised by the Garda authorities that An Garda Síochána are currently working on a new CCTV Strategy which will outline how CCTV infrastructure utilised by Gardaí can be modernised and integrated with other CCTV infrastructure throughout the State.

question.p: 1260. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if there has been engagement between his officials and the European Commission in respect of the European Commission's recently published proposals for a new EU Cyber Security Act; if he will outline the extent of that engagement; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18504/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Proposal for a revised Cybersecurity Act, known as the Cybersecurity Act 2 (CSA2), was published on 20 January 2026. The Proposal is now under active discussion by the Council of the European Union through the work of the Horizontal Working Party on Cyber Issues. The European Commission is a participant in the meetings of the Working Party. Alongside this engagement, Department officials have also been engaging directly with the EU Commission on a range of issues including on relevant legislative files, as is appropriate, in advance of Ireland's Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2026.

It is expected that Ireland will make significant progress on the negotiation of the CSA2 with a view to bringing the file to general approach by the end of our Presidency in December. My Department is leading on supporting this work.

question.p: 1261. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fatal and serious road traffic collisions each year since 2010 where an unborn baby has died following the collision. [18531/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: Road safety is a shared responsibility, with the whole of Government response led by the Department of Transport. I can assure the Deputy that road safety is taken very seriously across Government.

The Road Safety Authority is the statutory body with responsibility for reporting on fatal, serious and minor injury collisions on public roads. They receive collision data from An Garda Síochána and produce official statistics to help develop evidence based road safety interventions. Road traffic collision data can be found at the following address:
www.rsa.ie/road-safety/statistics/road-traffic-collision-data
Road traffic policy and legislation falls under the remit of my colleague, the Minister for Transport, Darragh O'Brien.
An Garda Síochána plays a vital role in enforcing road traffic law and in making our roads safer for all road users, including vulnerable road users.

Road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. This includes a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies.

summary.i: Question No. 1262 answered with Question No. 1250.

question.p: 1268. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the percentage of the Garda roads policing motorcycle fleet that are 1250cc. [18664/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational policing matters, and responsibility for the allocation and deployment of resources and personnel available to him, including the Garda fleet.
I am informed by the Garda authorities that, as of 27 February 2026, there are 88 motorbikes in the Roads Policing fleet of which 30 are 1250cc. This represents 34.09% of the Roads Policing fleet.
The purchase and allocation of vehicles by An Garda Síochána is made on the basis of identified operational demands, the availability of resources and is reviewed on a continual basis.

An Garda Síochána publishes detailed information on the Garda fleet from 2008 to date, including a Divisional/District monthly breakdown. Monthly Fleet reports are currently available from 2020 to February 2026. This is publicly available on their website at the following link:
www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/finance-services/finance-fleet-management.html

question.p: 1269. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the Troubles Legacy Liaison Unit will provide family reports; and if so, if they will be subject to an applicable response period for families, those named, and the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18671/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Troubles Legacy Liaison Unit has been in place in An Garda Síochána since the start of the year. I was pleased to formally announce its establishment with the Garda Commissioner on 23 January.

As set out in the Joint Framework on addressing the legacy of the Troubles, the Unit has a dual purpose: firstly to act as a single point of contact in An Garda Síochána for cross-border cooperation on Troubles-related cases, and secondly to act as a central point of contact and co-ordination for victims and families in relation to Troubles-related investigations undertaken by An Garda Síochána. This approach recognises that investigations into Troubles-related incidents should be victim-centred.

The Unit is operating alongside the commitment of An Garda Síochána to investigate all unresolved Troubles-related incidents within its jurisdiction and ensure that any potential investigative opportunities are proactively pursued. The investigation of such cases continues to be undertaken by the relevant Garda Division in which the incident occurred with the support of national units as required.

As also set out in the Joint Framework, An Garda Síochána will endeavour to answer questions that a family may have in relation to the investigation of a Troubles-related incident and provide a report to the family. The provision of a family report may not prejudice an ongoing criminal investigation or prosecution.

The full operation of the Unit in line with what is envisaged in the Joint Framework will depend on the progress made by the UK Government in enacting the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill and the reformed Legacy Commission becoming fully operational.

Domestically, I intend to bring my legislative proposals to support the implementation of the Joint Framework before Government in May. The final processes and procedures under which the Unit will operate will be informed by the legislative framework.

To date, the Unit has recorded a small number of contacts from the public. I expect this to increase in the coming months and I would urge survivors and family members of victims to make contact if they have unanswered questions.

question.p: 1270. Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of protests which took place outside Leinster House that required additional Garda resources and physical barriers to be erected in the years of 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form. [18686/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The right to protest is enshrined in the Constitution and in law, and is a legitimate part of our democracy. It is, however, a right to peaceful protest and it comes with responsibility. It is the responsibility of everyone who wishes to engage in protest to do so in a peaceful manner and not in a way that infringes on the safety and rights of others.

While the Garda Commissioner is responsible by law for operational policing, I am assured that the Garda approach to policing protests is predicated on keeping people safe, preventing anti-social and criminal behaviour, and the management of traffic.

Protests create operational challenges for An Garda Síochána. Factors such as the number of persons protesting, the location of protests and actions at the protest, as well as the health safety and welfare of all, including Gardaí, require significant assessment. In response to these demands, Gardaí may deploy an increased presence or other measures, as deemed operationally necessary.

I am informed by Garda authorities that the below table provides information of the number of protests which took place outside Leinster House from 2024-2026. The data has been categorised as ‘protests that required 5, 10, 20+ additional members’ to assist in Policing Operations.

question.p: 1272. Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of cases involving the seizure of scrambler bikes or quad bikes that resulted in a prosecution file being prepared by gardaí in the years of 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form. [18688/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Garda Commissioner is responsible under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024 for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána. This includes enforcement of Road Traffic legislation.
I am advised by the Garda authorities that proceedings (charge, summons, caution) associated with any seizure of a scrambler or quad bike are not directly recorded on PULSE.

A separate crime incident may be created and a charge created in association with that; however, these are not linked directly with the seizure that is made under the section 41 of the Roads Traffic Act 2023. As a result it is not possible to reliably report a count of proceedings arising from detention incidents.
I am assured that Gardaí respond to all reports of anti-social behaviour and conduct operations on an ongoing basis to target the misuse of scramblers and quad bikes.

question.p: 1273. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of 999 calls made from 2020 to 2025 that resulted in a dispatch of a Garda resource within a day of the call, in tabular form. [18765/26]

1381. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of 999 calls from 2020 to 2025 which resulted in no Garda resource being dispatched, in tabular form. [20424/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1273 and 1381 together.

I am informed by Garda authorities that data from the GardaSAFE computer aided dispatch system is not yet supported by An Garda Síochána’s analysis service and therefore the information requested cannot be supplied at this time.

GardaSAFE was rolled out incrementally across the organisation in 2023. The initial focus has been on bedding in the new system and processes in the live operational environment in the Control Rooms to monitor call volumes etc.

Work is now commencing on use of GardaSAFE data for statistical purposes. Garda authorities expect initial reports on call volumes to be available in Q3 2026, with the incremental development of other reports to follow.

I am advised that an Garda Síochána operates a Regional Control Room strategy which ensures that Garda resources are available to respond to calls for service from the public, including situations where a local resource is not immediately available.

Calls for service, whether received through a local Garda station or the 999 ECAS system, are routed through the Regional Control Rooms and prioritised for response. Higher priority calls will always take priority over lower priority calls.

The Garda authorities inform me that An Garda Síochána aim is to answer 80% of 999 calls within 7 seconds and deploy resources immediately giving an estimated time of arrival. An Garda Síochána will take appropriate steps to deal with all incidents and ensure that emergency and life threatening calls receive priority. They will endeavour to get to callers within 15 minutes in urban locations and as soon as possible, given the distance to be travelled, in more rural areas.

question.p: 1274. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the plans to change or amend the Registration of Clubs (Ireland) Act 1904 with regard to the requirement to have a visitors' sign-in book; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18816/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The Registration of Clubs Acts 1904 to 2008 provide for the grant and renewal of a certification of registration by the courts for bona fide members' clubs. Those Acts permit the supply of intoxicating liquor to members of such a registered club on the club's premises and also to members of the public in limited, specified circumstances. In order to be eligible for the grant or renewal of a certificate of registration, a club's rules must comply with requirements set out in the Registration of Clubs Acts.
A register of clubs is kept by the Registrar of Clubs, i.e. the District Court clerk of the court district in which the club premises are situated.
I have no immediate plans to amend the Registration of Clubs Acts.

question.p: 1275. Development and implementation of road traffic legislation and policy falls within the remit of my colleague Darragh O'Brien TD, the Minister for Transport, and the vital role of enforcing road traffic laws is carried out by An Garda Síochána.

question.p: 1277. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 664 of 3 March 2026 regarding the designation of Britain as a safe third country, given that section 220 of the International Protection Bill 2026 requires the Minister to be satisfied that any proposed safe third country fully meets EU law standards, particularly in relation to non refoulement, access to a functioning asylum system and adequate protection guarantees, if he will outline what assessments have been carried out by his Department on the current prospects of Britain meeting these criteria; in the event that Britain does not meet the statutory and EU law requirements, the alternative arrangements or contingency measures he intends to put in place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18822/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: Section 220 of the International Protection Bill 2026, as passed by the Dáil, provides for the Minister to designate a country as a safe third country following an assessment of relevant information and subject to the criteria set out in the section regarding the protection of rights in the safe third country.
The Deputy will appreciate that the Bill is still before the Oireachtas, and I will not be able to perform the assessments required under section 220 until the Bill has been enacted.

The UK is currently designated as a safe third country under the provisions of the International Protection Act 2015 (as amended), following an assessment carried out according to similar criteria to those contained in the International Protection Bill 2026.

question.p: 1279. Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding an application (details supplied) for a join family visa application. [18914/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa application referred to was created on 07 November 2024. Supporting documentation was received in the Abu Dhabi Visa Office on 18 November 2024 where it awaits examination and processing.

My Department's business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification.

While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing, it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt.

While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available.
Processing times and decisions at the Overseas Visa Offices can be checked at the following link:
www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-offices/

I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides.

The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/

As an Oireachtas Member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question.p: 1280. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for the cost of each murder case to the State for the past ten years. [18920/26]
1281. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the cost of each murder case to the State for the past ten years, excluding the DPP's costs. [18924/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1280 and 1281 together.

Costs associated with the investigation, prosecution and trial of those accused of murder are borne across a number of State bodies and agencies, including An Garda Síochána, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Forensic Science Ireland, the Courts Service, the Office of the State Pathologist and, in cases where the defendant is remanded in custody, the Irish Prison Service. Costs associated with criminal legal aid and other administrative costs would also be applicable.

Given the unique and often complex circumstances that arise, as well as the range of stakeholders and the range of costs associated with such investigations, prosecutions and trials, the information sought by the Deputy is not available. Furthermore it should be noted that a significant element of the costs arising would relate to salary or pay. In this regard, the individuals concerned from the various State agencies and bodies involved, will, at any point in time, have responsibility for several areas of work and it is not possible to account for the specific hours that an individual may have been involved in a particular investigation, prosecution or trial.

Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason for the delay on processing naturalisation applications from persons who have applied who originated from Iran, Afghanistan, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan; the number of applications from persons from these countries; the length of time their applications are pending a decision; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18927/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants and I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible.

It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside the control of the Immigration Service.

My Department has taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These include introducing an online digital application, online payments, and eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times.

question.p: 1284. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for naturalisation received based on Irish descent and Irish associations (details supplied), in each of the years 2010 to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18928/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I can inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide statistics on the number of applications and decisions based on Section 16 'Irish Association' received each year, for the past sixteen years. This would require the manual examination of thousands of cases. Such an examination would require a disproportionate amount of time to compile.

Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/.

In response to the new guidelines, my Department provided an opportunity to in-progress applicants to provide submissions to take account of the new policy. I can confirm that my Department received over 1,500 submissions.

Following the introduction of the new Section 16 guidelines, arrangements to separately record such applications have now been put in place and will allow for the provision of better statistical data in the near future.
The number of decisions issued on the Irish Association applications since the introduction of the Guidelines in April 2025 is 340.

The guidelines provide clarity to both applicants and decision-makers on what factors may be considered when deciding whether to waive such naturalisation conditions under Section 16 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. These new guidelines have been developed in the interests of fair and transparent procedures and comprehensive decision making.
The new guidelines are available on my Department’s Immigration Service website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/

question.p: 1285. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications received, granted, refused, still pending a decision and in dispute for the immigrant investor programme; the value in euro of each application; the number of persons who have received a status or permission to reside in Ireland arising from the IIP for each year since its inception and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18929/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, the Government agreed to close the Immigrant Investor Programme (IIP) to further applications from 15 February 2023. In line with that Government decision, which provided inter alia for the orderly wind-down of the programme, my Department has continued to process applications for immigration permissions in respect of approved investments i.e. investments applied for prior to the closure of the programme and which have been approved by the IIP Evaluation Committee.

At present, there are 1192 investor applications undergoing, or awaiting, consideration. The IIP Unit is committed to ensuring that all applications will be examined on their merits and will endeavour to conclude all decisions in a timely manner.

The criteria applied when assessing applications under the IIP is set out in the guidance published on my Department's immigration website at: www.irishimmigration.ie/coming-to-live-in-ireland/i-want-to-invest-in-ireland/

Since the start of the programme in 2012 to end of 2025, 230 investor applications have been refused. Applications may be refused for a variety of reasons such as incomplete documentation, the application not meeting the eligibility criteria, the associated project not being in line with the IIP programme etc.
The IIP offers four investment options for potential investors.
• Enterprise Investment: A minimum of €1 million invested in an Irish enterprise for a period of at least three years;
• Investment Fund: A minimum of €1 million invested in an approved investment fund for a period of at least three years. Such funds must be approved and regulated by the Central Bank;
• Real Estate Investment Trusts: A minimum investment of €2 million in any Irish REIT that is listed on the Irish Stock Exchange, for a period of at least three years; and

• Endowment: A minimum €500,000 (or €400,000 where five or more applications are received) philanthropic donation to a project which is of public benefit to the arts, sports, health, culture or education in Ireland.

Statistics are not maintained in such a way as to provide the information on all IIP residence permissions granted. No residence permission has been given to any IIP applicant in the absence of the approved investment being made.
In relation to the number of cases "in dispute", I can advise the Deputy that 8 project owners have taken legal proceedings in relation to proposals that were unsuccessful.
I am not in a position to provide the value for each application nor can I comment on individual applications however the total value of investment from each year is provided in the table below.
The table below provides a breakdown of IIP applications received, approved and the value of investments since the inception of the programme to the end of 2025.

[19003/26]

[19984/26]

[19985/26]

[19986/26]

Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which her Department intends to monitor and evaluate the impact of the child maintenance calculator on child welfare, maintenance levels and financial outcomes for primary caregivers; and whether she will commit to refining the model based on real-world evidence. [19988/26]

1406. Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration how the child maintenance calculator will handle difficult issues that arise, such as putting a figure on lost income for parents who give up work to raise children; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20896/26]

1407. Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends the child maintenance calculator to be one-size-fits-all; if he has given consideration to how it will deal with self-employed people with variable incomes; how it will deal with edge cases - for example, those with lower liquid assists but with property or land, such as farmers; or those with non-salary income; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20897/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1288, 1335, 1339, 1340, 1341, 1342, 1343, 1406 and 1407 together.

The development of the Child Maintenance Guidelines was a key recommendation of the 2024 Review of the Enforcement of Child Maintenance Orders. An interdepartmental group (“The Child Maintenance Guidelines Committee”) was established in February 2024 to develop the child maintenance guidelines for use by all parties, on a voluntary basis, when putting child maintenance arrangements in place. The Committee was Chaired by my Department and its membership included representatives from the Department of Social Protection, Department of Children, Disability and Equality, Legal Aid Board, Courts Service and Tusla.

Development of the guidelines was informed by a comprehensive comparative review covering England and Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands. It was also critically important to listen to the views of parents who have been involved in making child maintenance arrangements. For this reason, in April 2025, the Committee conducted a survey-based consultation to get the public's views on important aspects of the guidelines. The published guidelines along with a comparative review of guidelines in other jurisdictions and a public consultation report can be accessed at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/child-maintenance-guidelines-for-ireland/

The Guidelines are compatible with Irish legislation on child maintenance and can be used by the courts. However, the courts are not obliged to consider the guidelines when making child maintenance orders. The objectives of the Guidelines include:
• To establish fair, consistent and predictable amounts of maintenance for children whose parents are not together.
• To increase transparency, consistency and predictability for those seeking and paying child maintenance.
• To reduce conflict and tension between parents by making the calculation of child maintenance more objective.
• To reduce the number of child maintenance applications made to the courts by giving parents guidance in setting the levels of child maintenance and by encouraging private maintenance agreements.
• To ensure consistent treatment of parents and children who are in similar circumstances.
• To promote a culture of payment of child maintenance.
• Once the Guidelines were finalised an accompanying online calculator was developed to make the guidelines more accessible.

The child maintenance calculator was launched on 26 February 2026, following publication of the Child Maintenance Guidelines on 19 January. The guidelines and accompanying calculator are a first for Ireland and a significant step forward to improving fairness, consistency and transparency when parents are making child maintenance arrangements.

The child maintenance calculator is intended as a voluntary support tool to help parents begin the process of working out an appropriate amount of child maintenance for their child or children. The estimate provided by the calculator is not legally binding or enforceable, nor will it change an existing court order. It is a guide only. Child maintenance is calculated by looking at: each parent’s gross annual income; share of parenting time; the age/number of the children; and the age/number of other dependent children each parent has.

Significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs are not included in the child maintenance estimate. The variation in costs of this nature due to individual circumstances mean that they are not suited to inclusion in guidelines and a calculator such as this. These types of expenses are typically handled outside the standard way of calculating maintenance. This is in line with best practises observed internationally, where these costs are typically adjudicated outside the guidance framework. Costs of these expenses are typically shared equally between parents. Furthermore, given that the guidelines and calculator are formula based and rely on aggregate data to estimate average costs of children, they will not be appropriate in all cases.
Particular circumstances where they may not be appropriate in estimating reasonable child maintenance payments include:
• either parent has significant financial or other assets including property;
• where non-parent carers, like grandparents, who may be involved in a child’s care are seeking maintenance;
• a parent is paying child maintenance for more than one child where the children are from different relationships;
• there are dependants with significant earnings, property or other financial resources; and
• there are significant costs related to disability, childcare, education or medical needs.
However, it may still help users to identify a potential rate of child maintenance or a starting point for discussion with the other parent.
In summary, the key principles in the guidelines and calculator include:
• Shared financial responsibility – Both parents are expected to contribute to the cost of raising their child based on their means;
• Income shares model – Maintenance is based on the combined income of both parents, with each parent contributing a proportion that reflects their share of that income;
• Recognition of parenting time – The amount of time a child spends with each parent is considered, as share of parenting time directly influences the costs each parent has;
• Continuity of expenditure – Children should, as far as possible, continue to benefit from the standard of living they would have enjoyed if their parents were living together; and
• Protection of basic personal needs – A self-support amount, set at the level of the ‘at risk-of-poverty’ threshold, is included to ensure parents retain sufficient income for basic personal needs.
Together, these principles aim to place the child at the centre of maintenance decisions.

The calculator’s key parameters will be regularly updated, to take account of annual movements in the Consumer Price Index and the Central Statistics Office’s annual Survey on Income and Living Conditions. Such updates will include the costs per child by gross household income decile; the minimum rates; household income deciles, and the self-support allowance. Regular updating and indexation of key parameters will help ensure the model and calculator remain grounded in real-world data and reflect evolving expenditure patterns. Information will also be updated on the website www.childmaintenancecalculator.ie to ensure the purpose, benefits and limitations of the online calculator are clearly outlined and available.

question.p: 1289. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the provision of a women's refuge in County Laois; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19014/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) and ensuring that victims and survivors receive the support and care they need are absolute priorities for me. This Government has taken unprecedented actions to tackle DSGBV, including by increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026 to support Cuan, the DSGBV Agency, as well as services working to implement the 'Zero Tolerance' Strategy. Cuan is committed to providing safe and accessible accommodation and support services for victims and survivors, wherever they are in Ireland.

Cuan is currently collaborating with Laois Domestic Abuse Services, Laois County Council, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, and the Housing Agency to deliver a capital project for an eight-unit refuge in Laois. I am advised that a site has been secured for this refuge.

Cuan is taking the lead on identifying an Approved Housing Body (AHB) through an expression of interest (EOI) process, with Laois Domestic Abuse Services reaffirming its role as the domestic violence service provider for this project. The EOI will seek eligible AHBs capable of accessing Capital Assistance Scheme funding and interested in partnering with Laois Domestic Abuse Services, who play a crucial role in delivering services locally.

summary.i: Question No. 1290 answered with Question No. 1297.
Question No. 1291 answered with Question No. 1297.

question.p: 1292. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the additional block extension at Midlands prison; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19017/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: On conclusion of the NDP Review in July 2025, I secured a total investment of €527 million from 2026 to 2030 for the IPS. €495 million is to be invested in infrastructural projects and, in line with the Programme for Government, includes an overall target of delivering over 1,500 spaces by 2031.

This will be the largest ever building programme in the prison estate and includes a large extension to the existing Cork Prison on the site of the old, decommissioned Cork Prison, a new block in Wheatfield, an additional block extension at Midlands prison, and additional spaces at Castlerea, Mountjoy, Cloverhill, Portlaoise, Limerick and the Dóchas centre.

Since 2024, 232 spaces have been constructed across the Prison Estate, with 126 constructed in 2024 and 106 constructed in 2025. The majority of these spaces are in use, with the remainder coming on stream very soon. There are plans to build another 65 spaces in 2026.
The block extension at Midlands prison has started the tender process for the technical design consultancy.

question.p: 1293. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the next recruitment campaign for prison officers will open; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19018/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The 2026 Recruit Prison Officer recruitment campaign is provisionally scheduled to open, in conjunction with Public Jobs, in September this year.

I am advised that the Irish Prison Service continually monitors the staffing requirements and vacancies that arise, coupled with routine reviews of the resource requirements across the estate based on the prisoner cohort and the overall prison population. In 2025, a total of 304 Recruit Prison Officers were recruited.

question.p: 1294. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the tendering process related to the operation of the contribution charging model for IPAS residents in employment or self-employment; the expected cost; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19044/26]

speech.from: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration
speech.p: The 2025 Programme for Government included a commitment to introducing a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation.

A proposal for working international protection applicants to contribute to the cost of their IPAS accommodation was considered by Government in November 2025 and is now being progressed by the Department.

IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all IP applicants are entitled to Material Reception Conditions. The Regulations further provide that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The contribution rates are set out in a Schedule to the Regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn.

The contribution to cost scheme will be implemented within a planned 12-month period, allowing for the development of systems and resources to assess eligibility, share data securely and collect and process payments.

The implementation process, which is underway, will include procurement of an appropriate third-party provider service, and this procurement process will involve further detailed analysis as the scheme comes into operation including determining the implementation cost.
The introduction of this contribution for international protection applicants who are working and earning and income is aligned with processes already in place in other EU member states.
The scheme will have a review and appeals process incorporated into the process as it is developed for implementation, expected by the end of 2026.
