speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1412, 1413, 1414 and 1415 together.

I was pleased to recently launch the Improved Liveweight Performance Action Plan, which outlines a number of actions to assist Irish farmers to enhance their productivity and profitability while contributing to our climate goals.

The Action Plan was developed collaboratively by Teagasc, Animal Health Ireland, the Irish Cattle and Breeding Federation, Bord Bia, and my Department, and sets out a comprehensive approach to improving liveweight performance.

The Action Plan comprises a number of areas including genetics, nutrition, infrastructure and animal health. Additionally, the Action Plan prioritises enhanced knowledge transfer through discussion groups, advisor training, and demonstration farms alongside better performance monitoring and bench-marking. Implementation is a collective responsibility. Each action identifies lead organisations and supporting partners, ensuring a coordinated effort. My Department will monitor progress and report annually to the Food Vision High Level Implementation Committee, which I chair.

A targeted consultation process with recognised farm representative bodies and industry stakeholders took place during January 2026. The consultation involved written submissions, and a meeting with representatives of the farm organisations and industry also took place during the consultation phase. Submissions received during the consultation were considered and reflected in the published plan, where appropriate.

question.p: 1416. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine his plans to review the slurry-spreading calendar given changing weather patterns, which can leave farmers not allowed spread slurry in decent weather with good soil conditions, and allow farmers to spread slurry when ground is saturated; this, compounded by the fact that many farmers do not have enough storage to hold slurry right through a very wet January, February and March, for example; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18316/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The Good Agricultural Practice for the Protection of Waters Regulations, or the GAP Regulations, (S.I. 588 of 2025) sets out the periods when the application of manures to land is prohibited. These are often termed, the closed period, with these regulations signed into law by my colleague the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

The GAP Regulations also set out the circumstances when soiled water, organic or chemical fertilisers must not be applied to land during the open spreading period. These include, when the land is waterlogged, flooded or likely to flood, or when Met Éireann forecasts heavy rain within 48 hours.
Underpinning the need for a closed period, there is clear research highlighting that the closed period aligns with periods of highest risk for nutrient loss from land.

There is now a significantly increased focus on water quality across the entire agri-food sector. Farmers have been making great strides in implementing actions at farm level to improve water quality and the Government is providing strong incentives to support this work which is underpinned by science.

Part of these efforts relate to improved timing of nutrient application to align with the crop's needs and maximising the value of the nutrients present in organic manures. As articulated by Teagasc, slurry should be spread when the potential for Nitrogen losses is low and the uptake of nutrients by a growing crop is high. These conditions typically occur in the Spring, and not the Autumn, where reducing sunshine hours increasingly limit growth and increase the risk of nutrient loss.

Ensuring application of fertiliser and organic manure at appropriate times and conditions is a key action under Teagasc's current 'Better Farming for Water – 8 Actions for Change’ campaign. This multi-actor advisory campaign commenced in 2024 at my Department's request to support farmers to make the right decisions in terms of applying nutrient, be it slurry or chemical fertiliser. thereby reducing nutrient losses to water.
The GAP regulations were recently reviewed and updated in December 2025 and there are no plans at this time to further review.

question.p: 1417. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider increasing funding to the horse racing and greyhound industry in Ireland in the upcoming budget, due to the significant economic impact these sectors have in rural Ireland in particular; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18427/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The horse and greyhound racing industries receive financial support from the State through the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund, under Section 12 of the Horse and Greyhound Racing Act, 2001. Payments are made from the Fund to Horse Racing Ireland (HRI) and to Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ).

The decision on the proposed amount to be allocated to the Fund in any year is made in the context of the annual budgetary estimates process. The Estimates for my Department, passed by both Houses as part of Budget 2026, include an allocation of €99.1 million for the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund. This will be distributed in accordance with Section 12(6) of the Horse and Greyhound Racing Act, 2001, with 80% or €79.3 million going to HRI, and 20%, equating to €19.8 million to RCÉ.

As required under the legislation, following approval by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Agriculture and Food and having been debated and passed by both Houses of the Oireachtas, this funding was secured for the two industries for 2026.
A similar process will be followed to secure funding for both industries in Budget 2027.

question.p: 1418. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason the sale of cattle on the open market will be restricted as part of the new TB action plan, particularly in relation to the sale of calves; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18440/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: In September 2025, I published the “Bovine TB Action Plan, Addressing Bovine TB in Ireland” which is based on scientific research and veterinary expertise. There are 5 measures which are underpinned by 30 actions:
Support herds free of bTB to remain free
Reduce the impact of wildlife on the spread of bTB
Detect and eliminate bTB infection as early as possible in herds with a bTB breakdown and avoid a future breakdown
Help farmers improve all areas of on-farm biosecurity
Reduce the impact of known high-risk animals in spreading bTB

My Department has introduced a number of measures to facilitate the sale of cattle from restricted herds to Controlled Finishing Units (CFU) to allow farmers to sell cattle have passed a bTB skin test whilst ensuring a competitive market place for the sale of these cattle. The online sales of cattle from bTB restricted herds to CFUs is where the cattle are recorded on farm and the sale is held online to CFUs; only authorised CFUs are allowed to bid at these online auctions and in the event of an agreed sale the animal moves directly from farm to CFU. My Department has a policy in place to facilitate these type of sales for farmers who are affected by a bTB restriction and all Regional Veterinary Offices have been advised of this policy.

In addition my Department has introduced a policy to allow the movement of calves from one restricted herd into another herd which is known as a Controlled Calf Rearing Unit (CCRU) with the option to trade on the open market after two clear tests. Farmers who wish to avail of this should contact their local Regional Veterinary Offices.
There are no restrictions on the sale of calves from herds that are not subject to a bTB restriction.

Further changes to the bTB programme as part of the implementation of the TB Action plan will be introduced over the next few weeks, and these will be communicated to farmers starting in week commencing 30 March.

My Department will continue to communicate with farmers to encourage the purchase of cattle of an equivalent or superior herd risk category through the Department’s website www.bovinetb.ie , social media and other communication channels as well as direct engagement with farmers.

question.p: 1420. speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: My Department regularly reviews its staffing assignments to ensure that our resources are being used to support our work in the most effective way possible. Secondment opportunities are utilised to achieve this objective while also providing staff members with opportunities to broaden their skills and continue their professional and personal development. Additionally, secondments provide an opportunity for the receiving organisation to fill a temporary position with a suitable candidate. Both the receiving and sending organisation benefit from shared learning, good practice, new ideas and experience.

My Department gives consideration to achieving a balance between filling seconded posts and the need to retain key expertise within the Department for ongoing responsibilities. The most significant number of secondments from my Department relate to officers seconded to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. My Department regularly reviews its overseas assignments, assessing vacancies in line with workforce planning, to ensure that our presence abroad supports the national interest, enhances market access and is delivering on the expected benefits. As the assignment to overseas roles often follow mid-year rotation cycles, officers on secondment do not correspond directly to the number of secondment posts.

question.p: 1424. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the implementation of the 31 recommendations outlined in the report of the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming, which was published in September 2025, the recommendations include: CAP supports; pensions, taxation, access to finance, access to land, collaborative arrangements, advisory services, education and training, gender balance, and the overall attractiveness of the sector; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18764/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The Programme for Government prioritises supporting inter-generational farm succession. Food Vision 2030, our shared strategy for the agri-food sector, states that generational renewal in farming is critically important to ensure the future viability and social sustainability of the Irish agri-food sector and of rural Ireland.

There are a number of supports for generational renewal currently available to farmers under Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan (CSP) 2023-2027. These supports are complemented by a suite of strong national taxation measures, access to finance supports, as well as advisory and education & training support. Despite these significant supports the average age of farmers continues to rise.

Farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions. The Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming was established to examine these issues and has produced a thorough analysis and made 31 recommendations across a wide range of areas.

I was pleased to launch their report last September. As noted by the Commission, this is an issue for all of the agri-food stakeholders to address; to support the environmental, social and economic sustainability of farming, and to enhance its image as a career.

An implementation group in my Department is currently considering the recommendations and will monitor implementation on an ongoing basis. The current CSP is fully programmed, and the budget has been committed. Therefore, recommendations in the report around CAP supports will need to be considered in the context of the new round post 2027, including the new CAP regulation and a new budget.

While some recommendations can only be progressed in the context of the next CAP, others can and will be implemented in a shorter time frame. I am pleased that some of the taxation recommendations have already been progressed in Budget 2026 and that work is ongoing in relation to many of the other recommendations.
The work of the Commission ensures we have a comprehensive, well-considered foundation for our ongoing work in encouraging generational renewal.

question.p: 1425. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of reports received of horse neglect, or cruelty due to the misuse of horses on public roads, by his Department from 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18830/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government. The welfare of equines is protected by legislation and there is a commitment in the Programme for Government to prioritise equine welfare and to build on existing inspectorate supports across the country, ensuring a consistent approach to dealing with horse welfare. It must be emphasised that primary responsibility for the health and welfare of equines lies with the owner or keeper.

It is important to note that the use of sulkies on public roads specifically, as with the use of all vehicles, including animal-drawn vehicles, is governed by the relevant provisions of the Roads and Road Traffic Acts. Matters in connection with this legislation are a matter for my colleague the Minister for Transport. In addition, the drivers of all vehicles used on public roads, including horse-drawn carriages, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána.

In December 2025, my Department provided funding of almost €6.5 million to 94 animal welfare charities throughout the country, under the Animal Welfare Grants programme. Of that figure, just over €4 million was awarded to charities involved in the care and welfare of horses.

My Department operates a confidential animal welfare helpline through which members of the public can report incidents of animal cruelty or neglect for investigation. The dedicated email address and helpline in place for reporting suspected cases of animal welfare are:
Helpline Phone No: 01 607 2379.
Email address - animalwelfare@agriculture.gov.ie

The number of reports received to my Department’s Animal Welfare helpline relating to horse neglect of cruelty due to the misuse of horses on public roads is available is the table below. Please note that my Department installed a new system for recording animal welfare complaints in 2022, which allowed more accurate reporting of data. The figures below for the years 2020 and 2021, are from the previous recording system and reflect the entire number of horse welfare complaints received and not just the number of complaints related to horse neglect or cruelty due to the misuse of horses on public roads, which are reflected in the years 2022 – 2026 year to date.

question.p: 1426. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to expedite aquaculture licence applications in respect of an applicant in County Kerry, (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18872/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: My Department considers applications for aquaculture and foreshore licences in accordance with the provisions of the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 1997, as amended, the Foreshore Act 1933 (as amended), and applicable national and EU legislation. The licensing process involves consultation with a wide range of scientific and technical advisers as well as various Statutory Consultees. The legislation also provides for a period of public consultation.

Decisions in respect of aquaculture licence applications are only taken following the fullest consideration of all consultations and public interest elements of each application, including environmental considerations.

All aquaculture licence applications, including the applications referred to by the Deputy, must be both technically assessed and screened for an Appropriate Assessment. My Department’s Marine Engineering Division reports on technical matters and the Marine Institute, as the scientific adviser to the Department, was requested to undertake a full Appropriate Assessment. The Final Appropriate Assessment Report in respect of applications for Valentia Harbour / Portmagee Channel SAC was received in May 2025.

Every effort is being made by my Department to expedite the determination of these applications having regard to the complexities involved and the need to fully comply with all relevant national and EU legislation.
As the applications referred to by the Deputy are currently under consideration it would not be appropriate for me to comment further on individual applications.

question.p: 1427. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the current guidelines for poultry farming in Ireland in light of the number of farmers directly and indirectly affected by avian influenza; and whether further measures or supports are being considered. [18877/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: Robust biosecurity is key to protecting poultry farms from incursions of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). To that end, I introduced S.I. No. 520 of 2025 (Avian Influenza (Biosecurity measures) Regulations 2025) and S.I. No. 532 of 2025 Avian Influenza (Precautionary Confinement of Birds and Restriction on Assembly of Live Birds) Regulations 2025 in November of last year.

All flock owners should ensure that they are implementing the appropriate biosecurity measures and remain vigilant for clinical signs of HPAI infection. They should also report any clinical signs of disease to their local Regional Veterinary Office without delay or to the Avian Influenza Hotline on 01 607 2512 (9am-6pm) or, outside of office hours, the National Disease Emergency Hotline on 01 492 8026.

The Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 provides that I, as Minister, may pay compensation to owners of animals if a cull of those animals is directed by my Department in the event of an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza.

The compensation may relate to the animal that is culled, or to an animal product, animal feed or similar item that is destroyed in relation to the outbreak. The compensation may not exceed the open market value of the animal or item. Compensation is payable only to the owner of the animals or items affected. Consequential losses are not eligible for compensation.
Further guidance on highly pathogenic avian influenza can be found on the Government website at: www.gov.ie/birdflu.

question.p: 1429. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the date bovine viral diarrhoea, BVD, sampling, which started as a three-year scheme in 2012, will cease; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18930/26]

1430. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of calves detected under the BVD sampling scheme per year; if a farm with no detections in the past five to ten years could opt out; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18931/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1429 and 1430 together.

The national BVD eradication programme has been instrumental in reducing the prevalence of BVD virus (BVDV) in the Irish cattle population. The incidence of BVD positive animals has decreased from 0.66% in 2013, the first year of the compulsory phase of the Eradication Programme, to 0.02% in 2025.

Herd-level prevalence, however, has slightly increased for the very first time in twelve years, in 2025 in comparison with 2024. This further emphasises the need for ongoing monitoring and enforcement of the eradication programme. The early detection of BVDV is crucial for the programme to allows the prompt action to prevent the spread of the virus within herds. For that reason, tissue tag testing remains compulsory for 2026.
The efforts of farmers in recent years in driving down the level of disease is acknowledged and appreciated.

My Department continue supporting the Action Plan 2026 of the BVD eradication programme operated by Animal Health Ireland, for taking a proactive and strengthened approach to tackling Bovine Viral Diarrhoea (BVD) in 2026 and beyond. The operation of the programme, including any decisions in relation to sampling and testing requirements, by AHI is guided by the recommendations of its BVD Technical Working Group.

It is widely recognised that the final stages of any eradication programme are very challenging, with a population that is increasingly susceptible to the disease. That is why we must ensure that the efforts of all those in combating a disease are not undermined as we move closer to eradication. As a result of the reduction in disease levels in recent years I have been able to amend the supports to farmers who have had a calf removed under the BVD programme in 2025 within the budgetary allocation for the BVD programme in 2026 to €200 for a dairy breed animal and €320 for a beef breed animal.
We know that disease outbreaks are a risk unless we maintain and improve our momentum. We cannot afford to slow our control measures if BVD free status is to be achieved.
The number of animals detected positive or inconclusive for BVD annually since 2013 is provided in the following table:

td.p: Number of initial BVDV positive animals per year

question.p: 1431. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine when a person (details supplied ) will receive BVD compensation for a number of animals culled in 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18932/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: My Department currently provides a variety of extensive supports to the Bovine Viral Diarrhoea (BVD) eradication programme. Among these are financial supports to herd owners who disclose BVD positive or inconclusive test results in their herd. Payments for animals born in 2025 and disclosed BVD positive to herdowners, including the named herdowner, will commence in April 2026.

Thanks to the efforts of all stakeholders in driving down disease levels I have been able to amend the support for a dairy breed animal under the programme from €160 and to €200 and for a beef breed animal from €220 to €320 respectively, to be paid to farmers who disclosed BVD virus positive or inconclusive animals during 2025 for the existing budgetary allocation to the BVD programme. Payments for 2025 born calves will be made in 2026.

question.p: 1434. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the 2024 and 2025 expenditure for forestry and bioenergy-related programmes under Vote 30; whether any underspends occurred in these areas compared with original allocations; to provide the value and reasons for any such underspends; the steps being taken to ensure the full drawdown and delivery of funding in future years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19022/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: In respect of forestry in 2024, the amount allocated was €115.3 million, and the outturn was €73.3 million. The variance in this amount relates to the fact that Afforestation is one of the many land use options available to landowners. Entry into the schemes contained within the Forestry Programme 2023-2027 is voluntary and the expenditure reflects this demand led nature accordingly. I am confident that the attractive rates and supports under the Forestry Programme, in conjunction with the Mid-Term Review, and our communications and engagement programme, will continue to grow the forestry sector, providing a sustainable land use option into the future.

As committed to under the Biomethane Strategy, my Department launched the first capital grant programme for the industry in August 2024. This programme is funded by the EU Recovery and Resilience Programme, REPowerEU. Building works under the scheme were required to completed by December 31st, 2025, with no funding issued to date.
The 2025 appropriation account, which includes expenditure for forestry and bioenergy-related programmes under Vote 30, is yet to be published.

question.p: 1435. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine further to Parliamentary Question No. 78 of 29 January 2026, to provide a cost for payment of TB compensation rates that fully reflect current market valuations to the farmers whose animal valuations (approximately 9% of TB reactors) are above the current compensation levels; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19023/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: Ireland’s TB Eradication Programme has a comprehensive compensation regime in place for herd-owners who are affected by bovine TB.
My Department provides a range of financial supports that focus on compensating farmers for both direct and indirect losses incurred as a result of a TB breakdown on the farm.

The On Farm Market Valuation Scheme (OFMV) is the principal compensation measure available to Herd-owners whose herds are affected by a bovine TB breakdown in their herd. The Scheme aims to compensate farmers up to the open market value of an animal as if they were not affected by disease, subject to ceilings.

In 2025 9% of animals under the OFMV scheme were valued above the scheme ceilings and the cost to compensate herdowners for valuation amounts above the scheme ceilings, at the time of valuation, would be approximately €1.2m.

In addition to the compensation package for eligible reactor animals that are removed during a TB breakdown, the Department operates three supplementary schemes that assist farmers with the indirect losses incurred as a result of a TB breakdown on their farm.

The Income Supplement Scheme is a targeted scheme which assists farmers who lose 9.5% or more of their herd to disease due to a single TB breakdown. Income supplement is only payable in cases where the 9.5% threshold is met in one continuous restriction period and where full Depopulation is not deemed an appropriate measure.

The Hardship Grant is a targeted scheme aimed at assisting eligible herd-owners who retain and feed animals during prolonged periods of restriction as a result of a TB breakdown and that have more animals than the same period in the previous year. The scheme runs each year for herds restricted between November 1st and April 30th.

Depopulation Grant is paid for each animal removed in the depopulation measure and for those herds that are partial or fully depopulated on foot of a veterinary decision made on analysis of the overall TB disease situation within a herd.

I welcome the increased budget allocation of €85 million for bTB in Budget 2026, providing a total budget of €157 million. This additional funding is vital in addressing this disease and I am confident it will help drive down the incidences of bovine TB levels for future years. This investment in the bTB programme will support additional targeted testing, additional resources for the wildlife programme and supporting on farm biosecurity through both direct support to farmers for improving biosecurity infrastructure on their farms and facilitating more engagement between farmers and their private veterinary practitioners through Targeted Advisory Service on Animal Health (TASAH) visits.

I am confident that this increased budget will allow the revamped bTB programme to focus on tackling disease levels through the implementation of the measures laid out in the new bTB Action Plan and will support and enable farm families who are currently dealing with the stress of a TB outbreak to navigate a way out of a TB restriction and protect those herds currently free from TB from the stress of a TB outbreak.

question.p: 1436. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the 2024 and 2025 expenditure for agri-environmental schemes under Vote 30; to detail whether any underspends occurred in these areas compared with the original allocations; to outline the specific schemes involved; the reasons for the underspend; the number of participants affected; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19024/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme (ACRES) is the Department’s flagship agri-environmental scheme under the CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027. It has an overall allocation of €1.5 billion.

ACRES builds on the previous agri-environment schemes such as GLAS, AEOS and REPS. It is innovative in that it includes a specific approach, the ACRES Co-operation approach, focusing on certain high priority geographical areas, and it is also implementing a results-based payment system on a national basis.

Over the lifetime of the scheme to date, €750 million has been paid to ACRES participants, with almost all eligible participants paid in respect of 2023 and 2024, and over 96% of all participants paid in respect of 2025. As outlined in the table below, there was no under spend on ACRES in either 2024 or 2025.

The details requested are contained in the table below. The year end allocation differs from the initial budget allocation due to a combination of additional funding being provided to my Department as part of a Supplementary Estimate and the allocation to ACRES of savings identified in other areas of my Department's Vote.
ACRES

My Department also administers is the Suckler Carbon Efficiency Programme (SCEP) under the CAP Strategic Plan. SCEP is a scheme which aims to provide support to beef farmers to improve the environmental sustainability of the national beef herd. The programme aims to build on the gains delivered in recent years through the Beef Data and Genomics Programme (BDGP) and the Beef Environmental Efficiency Programme (BEEP) by improving the genetic merit of the Irish suckler herd.

As highlighted in the table below, there were no savings under SCEP in either 2024 or 2025. Additional funds over the budget allocation (savings elsewhere in VOTE 30) were directed to this scheme to meet expenditure pressures in both years.
SCEP
The Eco Scheme under Pillar I of the CAP is another important agri-environmental scheme, but this is not administered through Vote expenditure as it is 100% EU financed.

question.p: 1437. Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the 2024 and 2025 expenditure for targeted agricultural modernisation scheme, TAMS, under Vote 30; to detail whether any underspends occurred; the number of eligible applicants who did not draw down funding in that period; the measures being taken to ensure the full utilisation of allocated TAMS funding in future years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19025/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme with a defined budgetary allocation. TAMS 3 has been hugely successful to date, with payments of over €142 million issuing to farmers since payments commenced in June 2024.

A budget of €72.27 million was allocated to TAMS in 2024 while expenditure amounted to €55.4 million, resulting in an under spend of €16.87 million. The need to put new administrative and IT structures in place, while simultaneously opening and rolling out the scheme for participants, meant that it took longer than expected to commence payments.

The TAMS payment system is now fully developed, which allowed my Department to fully utilise the TAMS budget of just over €86 million in 2025. A similar amount has been provided for TAMS this year and I expect my Department will again fully utilise this allocation.

It is not possible to outline the number of eligible applicants that did not draw down funding as payment claims are processed based on submission of receipts for completed investments. Approved applicants have a period of 12 months from approval to complete their investment and submit their payment claim.

question.p: 1438. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department holds statistics on the mortality rate in Europe from blue tongue among sheep, if he will furnish this Deputy with such statistics; and if he will outline the steps he is taking to protect sheep in Ireland from the disease. [19088/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: My Department does not collate mortality rate statistics pertaining to the rest of Europe. However, data of this type is publicly available via scientific journals. In some Member States, sheep have shown more obvious and severe clinical signs of bluetongue than cattle if they become infected, and mortality rates can reach 30 - 70%.

My Department has ongoing bluetongue surveillance in place, with the aim of identifying parts of the country where bluetongue serotype 3 (BTV3) is present, which can assist farmers in making informed decisions about vaccination. In December, I authorised the use of three BTV3 vaccines in Ireland under licence. Each of the three are approved for use with sheep. I urge sheep farmers to talk to their veterinary practitioner to decide whether vaccination is appropriate for them ahead of the higher risk summer months.
More information on bluetongue can be found on the Government website at: www.gov.ie/bluetongue

question.p: 1440. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason 84 consignments listed in his Department's most recently published import tables indicate a country of origin but contain neither CHED-P numbers nor gross tonnage; if this indicates incomplete documentation on TRACES NT; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19164/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: Irish import data is compiled using data from official trade statistics. The Central Statistics Office is responsible for official trade statistics in Ireland, while Eurostat has that responsibility at EU level.
TRACES NT is primarily a sanitary/phytosanitary control system, not the statistical trade dataset and is not the source of official trade statistics.
The absence of CHED-P numbers in the import tables does not indicate incomplete documentation on TRACES NT.
Further information on agri-food sector trade can be found in chapter six of:
www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/annual-review-and-outlook-for-agriculture-food-and-the-marine-2024/DAFM’s annual economic publication.

question.p: 1441. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the details of the specific sanitary and phytosanitary, SPS, controls recorded on TRACES NT for consignments of products of animal origin entering the State in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, including documentary checks, identity checks, physical checks, laboratory sampling and any follow-up actions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19165/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The following table supplies the details of the SPS controls conducted on Products of Animal Origin that were imported into Ireland from third countries in 2024, 2025 and 2026.

question.p: 1442. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of consignments in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026 for which sanitary and phytosanitary, SPS, checks were limited to documentary checks only, physical checks only, both documentary and physical checks, and laboratory sampling; the nature of the sampling performed; the number of consignments rejected or destroyed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19166/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: All consignments imported from third countries have an SPS documentary check, with a risk-based frequency of physical inspection and laboratory sample regime applied according to EU regulations. The laboratory samples are taken to analyse for a broad range of substances including: growth promoters, steroids, antibiotics, dyes, coccidiostats and other anti-parasitics, anti-inflammatory substances, insecticides, fungicides, heavy metals, microbiology, anti-microbial resistance, contaminants, multi residue pesticides, along with pests and diseases. Change in frequency is risk based and in line with EU requirements.

question.p: 1443. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department considers import controls to be effective where sanitary and phytosanitary, SPS, checks are not documented on TRACES NT; the measures in place to ensure completeness and reliability of control records; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19167/26]

1444. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the frequency of SPS checks recorded on TRACES NT at border control posts for high-risk third countries in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026; if the frequency applied accords with EU requirements; if any change in frequency has been implemented over this period; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19168/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1443 and 1444 together.

My Department carries out SPS checks on all consignments of live animals, products of animal origin, and plants, plant products and other objects imported into the EU through Irish Border Control Posts (BCPs) – Dublin and Rosslare Ports, and Dublin and Shannon Airports.

In relation to consignments of animals and products of animal origin, these may only be imported from third countries which are listed for entry into the EU, and must be accompanied by the relevant official health certificate signed by the competent authority of the exporting third country. My Department subjects each consignment to official controls at the relevant BCP, which consist of documentary checks and identity checks at a frequency rate of 100%. Animals are also subject to physical checks at a frequency of 100%, while products of animal origin are subject to physical checks at baseline frequencies rates laid down in Regulation (EU) 2019/2129. Those baseline rates are set for defined risk categories of goods, and range from 1% to 30%, with the possibility of increasing the higher rate to 50%. The required frequencies rates are recorded for each category of goods in TRACES NT, and my Department applies those rates to consignments of such goods presenting at our BCPs. The outcome of the official controls are recorded for each consignment in TRACES NT by Department staff at BCPs.

The baseline frequency rates are reviewed and updated in TRACES NT by the European Commission every four months, based on rejection rates across the EU for both categories of goods and countries of origin of those goods. My Department applies those altered frequency rates for physical checks on goods presented at our BCPs. In addition, my Department can apply a higher rate of physical checks where required under EU safeguard measures and special conditions, or where there is suspicion of non-compliance with EU entry requirements.

In terms of controls on consignments of plants and plant products and other objects, documentary checks are performed on all consignments, as well as identity and physical checks performed at an appropriate frequency dependent on the risk posed by each consignment.

Consignments of plants and plant products and other objects listed in Annex XI, Part A of implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 are subject to identity and physical checks at 100%, however plant health identity and physical checks can be carried out at a reduced frequency where this can be justified. In this context Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2389 establishes rules for the uniform application of frequency rates for identity checks and physical checks on consignments of plants, plant products and other objects, Annex I of this Regulation sets out the list of plants, plant products and other objects which are subject to identity checks and physical checks at specific frequency rates. For those plants and plant products and other objects listed under Annex XI Part B of implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 these are subject to identity and physical checks of 1%.

Certain animals and goods imported into the EU are, according to EU regulations, exempt from official controls at Border Control Posts (BCPs), and therefore the outcome of official controls is not required to be recorded in TRACES NT. Those exemptions from official controls at BCPs relate mainly to certain low-risk composite products, as well as specifically licensed commodities such as materials for research and diagnostic purposes. Exempted low-risk composite products must meet specific criteria laid down in EU regulations in order to be exempt from official controls at the BCP, and must be accompanied by appropriate documentation to the place of destination, the point of release for free circulation in the Union, or the premises of the operator responsible for the consignment. My Department systematically performs and records risk-based controls on these products to ensure they meet the eligibility criteria to be exempted from official controls at BCPs and the animal and public health requirements for entry into the EU.

summary.i: Question No. 1444 answered with Question No. 1443.

question.p: 1445. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number and type of follow-up actions taken under Part III of the CHED-P procedures for consignments entering the State in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026, particularly regarding detained consignments, consignments subject to RASFF notification, re dispatched goods, and shipments destroyed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19169/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The table below supplies the details on the number and type of follow up actions taken on Consignments of CHED-Ps in 2024, 2025 and 2026. A RASFF (Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed) is a network used by EU member states to notify and exchange information about risks to public health detected in food and feed. Intensified Official Controls are actions taken by the competent authorities at border control posts when a hazard has been already identified often through RASFF notifications or other risk assessments.

question.p: 1446. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason only two Irish establishments appear on the TRACES NT establishment directory for imports of products of animal origin; whether this reflects the actual number of approved importers; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19170/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: TRACES is the European Commission's online platform for animal and plant health certification, required for the importation of animals, animal products, food and feed of non-animal origin and plants into the European Union, and the intra-EU trade and EU exports of animals and certain animal products.
Food of animal origin, placed on the market in compliance with EU food law, does not require TRACES notification, in line with the principle of free movement of goods within the EU single market.

Establishments listed in this directory, on TRACES, can legally trade specified categories of certain products of animal origin within the EU. This includes the production, processing or handling of those products by operators, which are subject to approval by the relevant Competent Authority and is not an indication of operators who can import products of animal origin (POAO).
Any Irish operator can import POAO from a third country if they are registered on TRACES, with the appropriate activity.

question.p: 1447. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine , further to his reply of 5 February, in which he stated that all consignments were subject to sanitary and phytosanitary, SPS, checks, if he will clarify whether this is fully documented on TRACES NT; if not, why not; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19171/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: All consignments, including products of animal origin imported into Ireland from third countries are subject to SPS checks at Irish Border Control Posts and all information on the controls conducted on each consignment is recorded on TRACES NT.

question.p: 1448. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the quality assurance processes in place within his Department to validate statistical data on CHED-Ps and gross tonnage of imported products of animal origin prior to publication; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19172/26]

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The gross tonnage of consignments imported into Ireland from third countries is declared by the operator responsible for the consignments on the relevant CHED-P. This figure is automatically cross-referenced with the gross tonnage declared to Customs for the same consignment. The EU Single Window Environment for Customs (CERTEX) system performs this check. Where discrepancies arise between the tonnage declared on the CHED-P and that declared in the customs declaration, the consignment is held at the point of entry pending review by both Customs and my Department.

question.p: 1449. Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reasons for the significantly lower number of aquaculture licence determinations issued by his Department compared with forestry licence determinations, given that both involve environmental assessments, including appropriate assessment; the steps being taken to address the backlog of aquaculture licence applications awaiting determination; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19413/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: My Department considers all applications for aquaculture licences in accordance with the provisions of the 1997 Fisheries (Amendment) Act, the 1933 Foreshore Act and applicable national and EU legislation. The licensing process is complex and involves consultation with a wide range of scientific and technical advisers as well as various Statutory Consultees. The legislation also provides for a period of public consultation.

The time for processing an aquaculture licence varies depending on a number of factors including location, species, scale and intensity of production, statutory status of sites and potential visual impact. My Department also takes full account of all scientific and technical advice, in addition to all issues identified during the public and statutory consultation phases. Further factors that can impact the time taken to process an application can include: the requirement for an Appropriate Assessment and whether the application is required to be accompanied by an Environmental Impact Assessment Report; the need for additional underwater or archaeological assessments; and consideration of any submissions or observations raised during the public consultation period. Decisions in respect of aquaculture licence applications are only taken following the fullest consideration of all consultations and public interest elements of each application, including environmental considerations.

Every effort is being made by my Department to expedite the determination of all outstanding applications having regard to the complexities of each case and the need to fully comply with all relevant national and EU legislation.

question.p: 1450. Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of staff currently assigned to the aquaculture licensing division of his Department; whether additional resources or staffing are planned to address the backlog of aquaculture licence applications awaiting determination; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19414/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: My Department's Aquaculture & Foreshore Management Division (AFMD) is responsible for the licensing and regulation of Aquaculture in accordance with the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 1997, the Foreshore Act 1933, as amended, and applicable national and EU legislation. The Division is also responsible for management of foreshore through a system of leasing and licensing in respect of Fishery Harbour Centres and aquaculture/fishery related issues. At present the Division has a staffing contingent of 35 people, with a full-time equivalent of 33.9.

Factors that can impact the time taken to process an application can include the requirement for an Appropriate Assessment and whether the application is required to be accompanied by an Environmental Impact Assessment Report; the need for additional underwater or archaeological assessments; and consideration of any submissions or observations raised during the public consultation period. Decisions in respect of aquaculture licence applications are only taken following the fullest consideration of all consultations and public interest elements of each application, including environmental considerations.

Measures to increase the pace of environmental reporting have been taken by my Department, including agreement for fund two additional scientific advisers in the Marine Institute, as well as engaging external environmental contractors to assist in the interim.

question.p: 1452. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for a detailed up-to-date report on pair trawling (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19602/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: On 22nd July 2025, following a public consultation process held in 2024 on a review of trawling activity within the six nautical mile zone in which over 5,500 submission were received, Minister Heydon and I announced our decision to place certain restrictions on trawling activity by larger vessels, that is, vessels over 18 metres in length overall, in the inshore waters inside the six nautical mile zone and baselines. The decision was as follows:

From October 1st, 2026, trawling activity (the operating of trawl or seine nets) by fishing vessels over 18 metres in length overall inside the six nautical mile zone and the baselines will be prohibited.

In addition, a catch limit of 2,000 tonnes of sprat was permitted for vessels over 18 metres in length overall inside the six nautical mile zone and inside the baselines from October 11th, 2025 to September 30th, 2026 only.

On September 30th 2025, I signed Policy Directive 1 of 2025 giving legal effect to this decision. On this date, I also signed the Sea-Fisheries (Sprat Fishing) Regulations 2025 (S.I. No. 446 of 2025). These regulations provided for the monitoring of sprat caught by vessels over 18 metres in length overall (LOA) engaging in trawling activity within the six nautical mile zone in the period 11 October 2025 and 30th September 2026 inclusive.

On 23 October 2025, I signed a second statutory instrument - the Sea-Fisheries (Sprat Fishing Closure) Regulations 2025 (S.I. No. 501 of 2025) - revoking the Sea-Fisheries (Sprat Fishing) Regulations 2025 (S.I. No. 446 of 2025), and placing a prohibition on the fishing of sprat by means of the operation of trawl or seine nets by vessels over 18 metres LOA inside the six nautical mile zone and baselines with immediate effect. Regulations setting out sprat by-catch avoidance measures are also included in this statutory instrument. This prohibition was put in place further to a report from the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority that the 2,000 tonne catch limit for sprat, in place for vessels over 18 metres, had been taken.

On 9th February, an application for leave to commence Judicial Review proceedings on the matter was granted by the High Court. As this is now sub judice, it would be inappropriate for me to comment further at this time until the matter is resolved before the Courts.

speech.p: There are currently no plans to amend the Control of Dogs Regulations (S.I. 442 of 1998) by the addition of the Dogo Argentino breed to the list of restricted dog breeds.
The Control of Dogs Act 1986 places legal responsibilities on dog owners, including the requirement that their dogs are kept under effectual control at all times when in public places.

A high-level stakeholder group was established in 2024 to consider policy and legislative matters, specifically the Dog Control Acts and the Dog Breeding Establishments Act. I expect the report of the Stakeholder Group to be submitted to me very shortly and I will fully consider all of their recommendations, including any in relation to dog control legislation.

speech.from: Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: Trade data does not summarise the destination or end use of imported beef, including the proportion supplied to the catering sector. However, under Article 18 of Regulation (EC) no. 178/2002, food business operators are required to maintain traceability records on a ‘one step forward, one step back’ basis, including records of the businesses from which products were received and to which they were supplied.

The primary responsibility of maintaining records supporting traceability rests with the food business operator and these records must be made available on demand to authorised officers of the competent authorities who verify compliance. Labelling of meat products, as required by EU Regulation 2011/1169, EU Regulation 1760/2000 (beef traceability) also plays a central role in meat traceability.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland is the central competent authority maintaining responsibility for the food chain through service contracts with a number of government agencies and departments.

question.p: 1467. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline any assessments carried out on behalf of, or used by, his Department measuring the impact of Arctic ice melting on marine life, including fish stocks, in Irish waters; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20815/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
speech.p: The Marine Institute is the state agency responsible for marine research, technology development and innovation in Ireland. It provides scientific and technical advice to the Government to inform policy and support the sustainable development of Ireland's marine resources.

I am advised that the Marine Institute undertakes marine assessments – physical, biological and fish stock assessments – at bay and basin scales, to monitor environmental and ecological changes but does not undertake any specific assessments directly aiming to measure the impact of Arctic ice melt on marine life or fish stocks in Irish waters.

While not directly associated with measuring impact Arctic ice melt on marine life in Irish waters, in August 2024 the Marine Institute's R.V. Celtic Explorer was commissioned to undertake a survey off the west coast of Greenland as part of a collaborative project between the Universities of Texas, Oregon and Florida. The objective of this project was to examine rates of sediment build-up on terminal moraines of glaciers to improve predictions of ice sheet responses to climate impacts.

question.p: 1475. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will report on his meetings with survivor groups since his intervention at the 2025 Bessborough Commemoration; her plans to meet with other survivor groups; and if she has made representations to Cork City Council in respect of the Bessborough site, and public acquisition of the site, in particular. [20768/26]

1476. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if her attention has been brought to the proposed commercial development at the former Bessborough mother and baby home site in Cork; if she has engaged with the owners or Cork City Council regarding the future of the site; and if she will outline the steps the Government is taking to ensure the site is treated with appropriate sensitivity and consideration for survivors and relatives of those affected; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20865/26]

1477. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if consideration has been given to the preservation, memorialisation, or public commemoration of the Bessborough site, in consultation with survivors and advocacy groups; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20866/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1475, 1476 and 1477 together.

I am very conscious of the hurt felt by survivors and family members of people who died in Bessborough. One of the most tragic aspects of what happened is the uncertainty regarding the burial place of many children who were resident there.

The investigation of burial arrangements in Mother and Baby institutions including Bessborough was an important part of the work of the Commission of Investigation into Mother Homes Commission. Despite extensive efforts, the Commission was unable to find any evidence of burials of children who died there in the grounds. As no evidence of locations was found, the Commission did not consider it feasible to excavate the full available site, which amounts to 60 acres, or indeed the former 200 acre estate, significant parts of which have now been built on.
I am aware that there are differing views among survivor groups about how the site should now be treated.

The Government’s response to the legacy of Mother and Baby Institutions is set out in the Action Plan for Survivors and Former Residents of Mother and Baby and County Home Institutions. On foot of the Action Plan the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage wrote to local authorities including Cork City Council requesting that Development Plan processes give adequate consideration to incorporating appropriate measures to ensure the protection of unrecorded burial sites associated with an institution.

The Government's the Action Plan also contains clear commitments in relation to dignified local memorialisation of known or agreed burial sites. The Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage established a Working Group of Departmental and Local Authority officials to advance the commitment to local memorialisation. Officials in the relevant Departments will work together with a view to bringing forward proposals to support inclusive, survivor-led local memorialisation.

I am aware that planning permission has recently been granted to a development at the site. I note that Cork City Council has attached a number of conditions to the grant of planning, including requirements to have a Forensic Archaeological Monitoring Strategy and a forensic archaeologist in place to monitor excavation at the site. It is also specified that if human remains are located, all work on site should cease and relevant authorities be informed.

1511. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding indexing of Core Funding subsidies to reflect localised operational costs. [18646/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1480, 1510 and 1511 together.
I am aware that Tiernan’s Nursery has regrettably chosen to withdraw from Core Funding.

Under the Core Funding Partner Service Funding Agreement, Partner Services are required to comply with the rules of the Core Funding scheme, such as the associated fee management measures and minimum notice periods. In line with the Core Funding Partner Service Agreement, services considering withdrawing from the scheme during a programme year must give 3 months’ notice of their intention to withdraw to the scheme administrator, and 3 months’ written notice to parents/guardians.

Notification of the above service’s withdrawal was received by the scheme administrator, Pobal, on 24 February 2026. Accordingly, and in line with the Core Funding Agreement, the service provider is required to comply with the rules of the Core Funding scheme, including fee management measures, until 1 June 2026.

The Department, through the local Childcare Committees, has engaged directly with the provider in question to highlight the benefits of staying in Core Funding, not only for their services but also for the families who avail of them. The provider has not reversed that decision to date.
I hope that this service will decide to remain within the Core Funding scheme; so that it, and the families this service supports, can continue to avail of the benefits associated with Core Funding.
As Core Funding is an optional scheme, providers have the autonomy and business freedom to withdraw from or choose not to participate in Core Funding.

As per the table below, Tiernan’s Nursery’s projected full-year Core Funding allocation for the current programme year equates to €195,775.44. This represents an increase of almost 20% since the scheme was first introduced. The projected allocation for this programme year figure includes funding specifically ringfenced for improvements to staff pay; to support the Employment Regulation Order that came into effect on October 13, 2025.

speech.p: In the interest of clarity, transparency and consistent reporting, I have defined a service that left Core Funding below as any service that had a gap between contracts for Core Funding of 4 or more weeks. There are a number of reasons that a service might fall into this definition. For example, a service could have withdrawn from the scheme, been removed from the scheme for breach of rules, or experienced a delay in re-contracting following a change of circumstance application or between programme years. Many services have left and later re-joined the scheme. There may be a small number of services who left the scheme and subsequently closed at a later date and are not captured in the figures below.

The Department does not collate Core Funding service data based on postal codes. Withdrawal data is gathered at a local authority level. The table below provides a breakdown of the services in Dublin City, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown and South Dublin that left Core Funding in each programme year by county division as of 3 November 2025. Some services may have left and rejoined multiple times across the three years, and therefore the figures cannot be summed across programme years from the breakdown below.
The final 2025/2026 withdrawal figures will be confirmed categorically after the end of the programme year, which concludes in August 2026.

It should be noted that, as of 9 March 2026, there are 876 operating across these Local Authority Areas, 750 of whom are in receipt of Core Funding – representing an 85.62% take-up of Core Funding across those areas.

Core Funding is calculated based on a setting’s capacity (number/age of children, type/duration of service) and its associated staffing complement. Core Funding allocations are based on places, not on child registrations and attendance levels. Places do not have to be filled in order to be allocated Core Funding, but for capacity to be funded, there must be enough staff in place to satisfy the minimum staff to child ratios as set in the Regulations made under the Child Care Act 1991. This provides services a guaranteed minimum income, supporting stability where attendance may be fluctuating.

This was based on the recommendations of the Expert Group, who proposed that such a grant would support improved provider sustainability by focusing on the services to be delivered by the settings, rather than external factors.
When first introduced in 2022, Core Funding had an annual allocation of €259 million, of which, €210.8 million was entirely new funding to the sector.

That annual allocation has increased each year since and exceeds €390 million for the fourth and current year of Core Funding. This represents an increase of over 50% in Core Funding over three years. The additional funding is supporting further capacity growth, the maintenance of a fee management system to benefit families and significant improvements to pay and conditions in this valued sector.

The allocation for Core Funding for year 5 of the Scheme will increase again by 22% to over €480 million. This allows the Department to maintain fees at 2021 levels in Year 5, support further improvements in pay for staff, and support services in adhering to reduced maximum fee caps from September 2026 – ensuring sustainability and stability for the sector.

In addition to increased funding, the Department has also made changes to improve the sustainability of providers through, for example, targeted measures for small and sessional services, and a fee increase assessment and approval process for services with fees frozen at unsustainably low rates.

I do not want any provider to be faced with financial sustainability issues in their delivery of early learning and childcare services. To support services, there are wider financial supports available from the Department. Where a service is experiencing financial difficulty or has viability concerns, these can be accessed while remaining within Core Funding.

This support can take the form of assisting services with interpreting analysis of staff ratios and cash flow, financial support, as well as more specialised advice and support appropriate to individual circumstances.
These supports can be accessed by any Core Funding Partner Service by contacting their local County/City Childcare Committee.
I encourage all services to avail of these supports as an alternative to withdrawing from Core Funding and removing the benefit of Core Funding from children and their families.

Parents experiencing difficulty in relation to their early learning and childcare needs are encouraged to contact their local City/County Childcare Committee who can support and advise them on options in their area.
The Department has a list of all Core Funding Partner Services which is regularly updated on the Department’s website under How to Find a Partner Service.

question.p: 1481. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when pre-school fees will reduce in line with the Programme for Government; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18255/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Phase 1 report of Shaping the Future: the Early Years Action Plan was published on 17th December. The report sets out the next steps in the delivery of a number of Programme for Government commitments relating to Early Learning and Care (ELC) and School Age Childcare (SAC). A central objective of Shaping the Future is to reduce parental fees to an upper limit of €200 per month over the lifetime of the Government.

The Phase 1 report focuses on short-term actions to be undertaken in 2026 within the budgetary resources available for the year. In line with the Programme for Government commitment, a broad public consultation process is currently underway. Results of this consultation, as well as additional analysis, will inform Phase 2 of the Action Plan. Phase 2 actions will be published later in 2026 and will be undertaken from 2027 through to the end of 2029.

The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) provides subsidies – both universal and targeted - to reduce the costs to parents for children to participate in ELC and SAC. The NCS has been substantially expanded in recent years to further reduce the cost of ELC and SAC for families. This includes the extension of the universal subsidy to all children under 15 and two increases to the minimum hourly subsidy, which is now worth a minimum of €96.30 per week for 45 hours. In addition, from autumn 2026 we will reduce fees for lower-income families through the NCS, to ensure that families with incomes below the relative income poverty line receive the maximum subsidies.

The objective to reduce parental fees to an upper limit of €200 per month cannot be achieved through the NCS alone. The fee-freeze and maximum fee-caps required for Core Funding have been key to the progress in recent years in making ELC and SAC services more affordable. In September 2025, maximum fee caps were extended to all Partner Services in Core Funding. Budget 2026 enables Core Funding to continue to support fee-control measures. It will ensure fees remain at 2021 levels for a majority of providers. 2026 actions on affordability will include further reduction in some of the highest fees paid by parents by lowering the maximum fees that Core Funding Partner Services can charge.

It is important to stress that both Phase 1 and Phase 2 of Shaping the Future: the Early Years Action Plan are being informed by an extensive range of research, data-analysis, and public consultation processes that have been undertaken over recent years and that continue.

question.p: 1482. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason a family resource centre funding was not allocated to a centre (details supplied); the details of the criteria that the centre was judged on; and if they can provide a copy of the recommendations that was issued to the Minister in respect of her Departments shortlist and was the resource centre in question mentioned on this. [18259/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I wish to inform the Deputy that the commissioning of new Family Resource Centres is an operational matter for Tusla, which is responsible for the day-to-day administration of the Family Resource Centre Programme. Neither myself nor the Department have any involvement in the assessment process for new members of the Family Resource Centre Programme, or in shortlisting or selecting new Programme members.

The most recent expansion of the Family Resource Centre Programme followed a comprehensive national application and assessment process undertaken in 2025, which was led by Tusla and independently chaired by a representative of the University of Limerick. All applications were reviewed and scored against the clearly defined and published criteria, including population need, level of deprivation, child population data, existing service provision and existing service gaps. Decisions on the successful services were made by the assessment panel.

A total of forty-nine organisations applied for membership of the Family Resource Centre Programme, following an open call from Tusla for applications to join the Programme. This indicates the strong level of interest in communities around the country in having Family Resource Centres as part of their community infrastructure. I understand that Tusla was very impressed with the level of interest in joining the FRC Programme, and with the quality of the applications received. Regretfully, funding only allowed for fifteen new members to be selected, leaving thirty-four applications unsuccessful. I want to thank those organisations for their interest in joining the Programme, and for the important work they continue to do in their communities.

question.p: 1483. Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will confirm that all legal requirements necessary for the State's ratification of the UNCRC Optional Protocol on the Sale of Children are in place and have been fully met; and the timelines for completing the drafting of the remaining orders required to enable ratification. [18282/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Government is committed to ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and work is ongoing to ratify the Protocol as soon as possible.

In Irish treaty practice, the State must be in a position to meet all of the obligations it assumes under the terms of an international agreement from the moment it enters into force. Often it will not be possible for the State to meet these obligations without first taking steps required by domestic law, or otherwise, enabling it to do so. As work towards ratification of the protocol continues, the State is obliged to ensure that all legislative provisions are in place for it to meet these obligations.

The Department has recently received confirmation from the Attorney General’s Office that the suite of measures taken to ensure that Ireland is in a position to meet its obligations under the Protocol are sufficient to overcome barriers to ratification which had been previously identified.

The Department will now work with Departments of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and of Foreign Affairs and Trade to prepare the necessary measures required on ratification. Once this work is complete, Government approval will be sought to ratify the Protocol.

question.p: 1484. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of meetings she or her officials attended regarding the establishment of the Tusla training college; the extent to which the Department consulted on the curriculum and the type of qualifications students will receive; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18286/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Department officials were invited to and attended two meetings regarding the establishment of Tusla’s Training College. While the curriculum was designed by Tusla, the Department has been and remains available to provide support and input as required.

Tusla advise that trainees participating in the training college will be employed on a special purpose contract, which means they will be paid while they take part in six months of classroom-based learning, e-learning and supervised work-based practice. There will also be targeted training, peer support, reflective practice, supervision and wellbeing resources.

While there are currently no recognised qualifications associated with participation, Tusla is committed to exploring academic accreditation of this and related learning. The Training College acts as an in-depth onboarding programme to prepare diverse social care graduates for work in environments such as Special Care and Children's Residential Services.
