question.p: 1487. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the estimated number of childminders operating in Ireland from the childminder's home; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18298/26]

1488. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the estimated number of childminders operating in Ireland from the family's home; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18299/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1487 and 1488 together.

The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 distinguishes childminding which involves care in the childminder’s home from care that takes place in the child’s home, which may be carried out by a nanny, au pair or babysitter. This distinction is also reflected in the legal definition of a childminder set out in the primary legislation.

There is considerable lack of clarity about the number of children cared for by childminders, and the total number of childminders working in Ireland today. This reflects both the lack of administrative data on childminders not registered with Tusla, and the fact that the term ‘childminder’ in some surveys may be used either of someone working in the childminder’s home or of someone working in the child’s home (i.e. a nanny or au pair).

Census 2022 indicated that 15.9% (52,775) of children under 15 years who were in childcare were cared for by non-relative childminders working in the childminder’s home. A survey of Childminding Ireland members completed prior to the publication of the National Action Plan for Childminding indicated that on average childminders working in their own home care for 4 children, when both pre-school and school-age children are counted. On this basis, it is estimated that there are approximately 13,000 non-relative childminders caring for children in the childminder’s home.

The 2022 census data also indicated 6.1% (20,263) of children under 15 years who were in childcare were cared for by an au pair, nanny and/or childminder working in the child's home. The Department does not have data on the average number of children cared for by each au pair, nanny or childminder working in the child's home. As a result, the Department is not in a position to estimate the number of childminders operating in Ireland from the family's home.

In an IPSOS B&A survey of parents in 2025 commissioned by the Department, when asked about their main childcare arrangements, parents reported that 20% of non-school going children under 6 and 8% of school age children under 15 were cared for by a childminder in the childminder’s home. In the same survey, parents reported that 2% of non-school going children under 6 and 1% of school age children under 15 were cared for by an au pair or nanny in the child’s home. The survey does not indicate the number of children cared for by each childminder.

summary.i: Question No. 1488 answered with Question No. 1487.

question.p: 1489. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the sum of money ringfenced for the NCS for childminders for 2025/2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18300/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) provides financial support to help parents reduce the cost of early learning and childcare through a subsidy paid directly to the childcare provider.
Subsidies are available for children aged between 24 weeks and 15 years of age.

The minimum rate available to all families in Ireland is €2.14 per hour, which is available for up to 45 weekly hours. Depending on the child's age and the family's income, an income assessed subsidy may be available to provide additional support. This subsidy can be as much as €5.10 per hour, also for up to 45 weekly hours.
Childminders, as with other service providers, are eligible to offer the NCS once they are appropriately registered with Tusla.

The NCS yearly budget allocation is not ringfenced by type of service provider. Claims for each service provider type can and do vary year by year, and children move between service provider types within a given year and may even choose to claim in more than one service during the same week. The type of service provider chosen does not impact a family's NCS award, and families are welcome to attend the provider which best meets their family's needs.

question.p: 1490. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the average monthly fees paid for childminders operating in the childminder's home, by county, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18301/26]

1491. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the average monthly fees paid for childminders operating in the family's home, by county, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18302/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1490 and 1491 together.

The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 distinguishes childminding which involves care in the childminder’s home from care that takes place in the child’s home, which may be carried out by a nanny, au pair or babysitter. This distinction is also reflected in the legal definition of a childminder set out in the primary legislation.

The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 set out a pathway for the extension of regulation to childminders who work in the childminder’s home. Once registered with Tusla, childminders are able to take part in the National Childcare Scheme. The Childcare Support Act 2018, which provides a statutory basis for the National Childcare Scheme, specifies that only Tusla-registered childminders are eligible to participate in the Scheme. The limitation of public funding schemes to Tusla-registered providers helps to ensure that public funding is provided where there is assurance of the quality of provision.
We are now in a 3-year transition period (to September 2027) during which childminders are being encouraged and supported to register, but registration is not yet mandatory.
As of end-January 2026, 162 childminders were registered with Tusla.

Census 2022 indicated that 15.9% (52,775) of children under 15 years who were in childcare were cared for by non-relative childminders working in the childminder’s home. The 2022 census data also indicated 6.1% (20,263) of children under 15 years who were in childcare cared were cared for by an au pair, nanny and/or childminder working in the child's home.

Key contextual differences between childminders who work in the childminder’s home and someone who works in the child’s home have contributed to differences in the availability of data, but for both cohorts, the data relating to fees is limited. In relation to childminders working in the childminder’s home, there is no administrative data on childminders who are not yet registered with Tusla, which constitutes the large majority. In addition, data on those childminders who are already registered may not be representative of the cohort of childminders as a whole. In relation to nannies or au pairs, these are private arrangements between the childminders and the parents who are regarded as their employers, and the Department has no administrative data relating to these arrangements.
The Department commissioned an IPSOS B&A survey of parents in 2025. Data from this poll of more than 700 parents/guardians of children under 15 indicates that:

• The average cost per month per child for childminders in the childminder’s home was €589 for non-school going children and €389 for school-going children during term-time. Parents reported that the average hours per week of this care type was 25.2 hours for non-school going children.

• The average cost per month per child for an au pair/nanny in the child's home was €822 for non-school going children. Parents reported that the average hours per week of this care type was 28.9 hours for non-school going children.[]
This survey data cannot be broken down by county.

summary.i: Question No. 1491 answered with Question No. 1490.

question.p: 1492. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the annual average national cost of childcare; the average amount of financial relief provided through the NCS universal subsidy per annum to a family; the average amount of financial relief provided through the NCS income assessed subsidy per annum to a family (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18303/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Each year Pobal compiles data from early learning and childcare providers as part of the Annual Early Years Sector Profile (AEYSP). As part of the AEYSP survey, service providers are asked to indicate the fee charged for each care type per week before deductions for subsidies are applied. As the distribution of fees is skewed, with most data points having low values and a few very high values influencing the mean, the median value is reported below as it is considered more representative of the mid-point of the data.

The most recently published fee data for the 2024/25 programme year indicates that the average (median) weekly fee per child was €200.00 for full day care ELC. The average weekly fee for part time ELC was €114.50 and for sessional ELC the average stood at €75.00.

This data also indicates that the average (median) hourly fee for in term school age care was €5.00, while the weekly fee per child for out of term school age care was €175.00. The fee data are available at www.pobal.ie/childcare/fees.

This Department provides subsidies to offset childcare fees charged to parents, as well as two free years of preschool to all eligible children through the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Programme. The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) provides universal and income-assessed subsidies to help parents to meet the cost of early learning and childcare. All families can receive a universal subsidy but higher subsides are provided to families with the lowest levels of income through the income-assessed subsidy. Both subsidies are available for children aged between 24 weeks and 15 years of age. When considering the average value of claims for both awards, it is important to note that while a maximum of 45 weekly hours may be awarded, the number of hours claimed is a matter for each individual family’s needs and subject to what their chosen early learning and childcare provider is in a position to offer. This variability in family behaviour and claims should be borne in mind when considering the figures below.

The Universal subsidy is not means tested and provides €2.14 per hour for a maximum of 45 hours per week. For 2025, the average annual claim value for the Universal subsidy was €1,499.50. This relates to all Universal subsidy claims for the year 2025 with a ‘closed’ and ‘confirmed’ status.

Income-assessed subsidies are means tested and calculated based on a family’s individual circumstances. The subsidy is progressive and rates awarded depend on a number of factors including the level of family income, child’s age and educational stage and the number of children in a family. For this reason, a breakdown according to reckonable income bands is also provided, however, in general, this variability should be borne in mind. The average yearly claim value was €2,265.42 and the average subsidy rate of €3.47– for single child applications only, as specified by the Deputy. The data relates to all Income Assessed subsidy claims for the year 2025 with a ‘closed’ and ‘confirmed’ status.
Breakdown of average yearly claim value according to reckonable income:

Lastly, it should be noted that the average yearly claim value may be higher than the averages by band above. This is because some families move between income bands during the year, and the averages for each band only reflects the weeks they spent in that band, not the full year.

question.p: 1493. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the relief provided to families on the cost of childcare through the NCS income assessed subsidy and the NCS universal subsidy; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18304/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) provides financial support to help parents reduce the cost of early learning and childcare.
Subsidies are available for children aged between 24 weeks and 15 years of age.

The minimum rate available to all families in Ireland is €2.14 per hour, which is available for up to 45 weekly hours. Depending on the child's age and the family's income, an additional income assessed subsidy may be available to provide additional support. This subsidy can be as much as €5.10 per hour, also for up to 45 weekly hours.

In the case of children sponsored by approved bodies, the NCS also covers the full cost of childcare. The rate of this coverage increased in 2024 to reflect a €5.30 hourly rate for all children over 1 year old. Sponsored children under 1 year old continue to receive an hourly rate of €5.87.

question.p: 1495. D'fhiafraigh Deputy Brendan Smith den Aire Leanaí, Míchumais agus Comhionannais an gcuirfear bearta breise i bhfeidhm chun cabhrú le forbairt naíonraí lasmuigh de cheantair Ghaeltachta, an bhfuil bearta áirithe i bhfeidhm faoi láthair chun tacú le forbairtí den sórt sin; agus an ndéanfaidh sí ráiteas ina thaobh. [18364/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Cuirtear maoiniú ar fáil ón Roinn seo do sheirbhísí Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath-Óige agus Cúram Leanaí in Aois Scoile ar fáil ar an mbonn céanna do sheirbhísí trí mhéan na Gaeilge agus trí mheán an Bhéarla, bíodh siad laistigh agus lasmuigh de cheantair Ghaeltachta.

Tugann an Roinn Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail agus Gaeltachta tacaíocht sa bhreis do sheirbhisí Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath- Óige trí mhéan na Gaeilge sa Ghaeltachta tríd a gníomhaireachtaí agus a heagraíochtaí cosúil le Comhar Naíonraí na Gaeltachta.

I Meitheamh 2024, d'fhógair an Roinn Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail agus Gaeltachta maoiniú cúig bliana de €103k chun seirbhís chuimsitheach tacaíochta agus forbairtí do naíonraí taobh amuigh den Ghaeltacht, le riaradh ag Gaeloideachas. Ina theannta sin, tá an Roinn Leanaí, Míchumais agus Comhionannais tar éis maoiniú a chur ar fáil do Ghaeloideachas in 2025 agus 2026 chun tacaíocht a thabhairt do seirbhísí Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath-Óige trí mhéan na Gaeilge taobh amuigh den Ghaeltacht.

Soláthraíonn an Mol Foghlama um Scileanna a Choth, atá ar fáil go dátheangach i mBéarla agus i nGaeilge, rochtain éasca d’oideoir ar ábhair foghlama agus ar dheiseanna oiliúna i roinnt réimsí, cleachtas cuimsitheach, sláinte agus folláine, agus an Ghaeilge san áireamh.

Anuas ar sin, tá an Roinn faoi láthair ag obair le Ranna agus gníomhaireachtaí eile chun plean náisiúnta a ullmhú lena thuilleadh forbartha a dhéanamh ar sholáthar na Gaeilge sna n-earnáil Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath-Óige agus Cúram Leanaí in Aois Scoile.

Is gealltanas é forbairt an phlean seo faoi Phléann Gníomhaíochta cúig bliana don Ghaeilge. Meastar go dtacaíodh an pléann náisiúnta le cur chun feidhme dhá ghealltanas Na Chéad 5: Straitéis Uile-Rialtais do Naíonáin, Leanaí Óga agus a dTeaghlaigh: ‘‘Bearta a thabairt isteach leana chinntiú go mbeidh rochtain ag leanaí i gceantair Ghaeltachta i soláthar Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath-Óige lán- Ghaeilge’’ agus ‘‘Meicníochtaí a fhorbairt chun tacaíocht Gaeilge a chur ar fáil do sholáthar Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath-Óige in áiteanna a bhfuil céatadán ard leanaí ag foghlaim trí mheán na Gaeilge’’. Meastar freisin go dtacóidh an plean le seachadadh gealltanas sa Chlár Rialtais: ‘‘Tacú le Naíonraí agus le creis chun rochtain ar luathoideachas a chinntiú i bpobail Ghaeltachta agus níos faide’’ agus ‘‘Pleanáil a dhéanamh ar fhorbairt áiseanna faoi cheannas an Stáit i gcomhar le clár tógála na scoileanna, naíonraí lán- Ghaeilge san áireamh’’.

Chomh maith leis an bhfócas ar sheirbhisí Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath-Óige agus Cúram Leanaí in Aois Scoile trí mhéan an Ghaeilge, táthar ag súil go n-aireofar sa phlean náisiúnta nua freisin bearta chun tacú le seirbhísí Foghlaim agus Cúram na Luath- Óige trí mhéan an Bhéarla oibriú laistigh den chreat curaclaim luath-óige nuashonraithe Aistear.
Tá sé beartaithe an Plean a fhoilsiú sna míonna amach romhainn.

question.p: 1500. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her views on a matter (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18510/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for their question regarding the application of the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 in Day Service settings. Ensuring that families and carers are included in an adult’s circle of support is key to the proper implementation of the 2015 Act.

The 2015 Act is underpinned by a set of guiding principles that are the foundation for interpreting and administering the 2015 Act. The guiding principles, set out in Section 8 of the Act, are rooted in human rights and include giving effect to the person’s will and preferences, as well as considering and consulting the views of other people who are engaged in caring for the adult or have a bona fide interest in the welfare of the adult. It is designed to maximize a person's autonomy and places an emphasis on an intervener under the guiding principles to seek the views of other people including those involved in the care for the relevant person. This is to ensure that the will and preference of the individual is respected. This, in effect, recognises the importance of the role of family members and carers in supporting people with regards to decision-making.

Additionally, the HSE National Consent Policy highlights the importance of family in supporting decision-making and maximising decision-making capacity of those whose capacity may be in question. The policy notes that when interacting with a person whose capacity is in question, or may shortly be in question, healthcare workers must take all necessary and practicable steps to support the person in making the decision. A person must not be considered unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps have been taken to help him or her to do so. Such steps may include:
- Seeking the assistance of anyone the person asks to be consulted.
- Involving people who have a close, ongoing, personal relationship with the person, such as family or friends.

- Seeking the assistance of an independent advocate to support the person and to ensure that the person’s own voice is heard. This may be helpful particularly when healthcare workers and those close to the person disagree with the person’s will and preferences.

The policy goes on to note that support will usually be given by people who have a close, ongoing personal relationship with the person, such as family or friends, or by anybody chosen by the person. The support of these people may be helpful in eliciting the person’s values, beliefs and goals. If appropriate and practical to do so, the views of anyone the person requests to be consulted should be considered.

Additionally, it is important to note that parents are not excluded from becoming the decision supporter for an adult under the 2015 Act, if the Court determines that this is in line with the adult’s known will and preferences and if that person or persons are deemed suitable to act as such.

A review of the operation and effectiveness of the 2015 Act is provided for under the legislation and is also a commitment in the Programme for Government. This review will take place in consultation with a wide range of stakeholders and will be informed by feedback from those with lived experiences of the provisions of the Act.

question.p: 1501. Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality for an update in relation to the new Guardian ad litem national service and the recent stakeholder engagement she has had; if she will indicate when the start date for the new service will commence and come into force, with her approval; the transitional arrangements that are proposed for existing Guardians ad litem and their client children who are not part of the new Guardian ad litem national service when it comes into being; if she is confident that when the new Guardian ad litem national service is established there will be no waiting list for Guardians ad litem being appointed to children who are entitled to their support; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18514/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Guardian ad litem National Service is a nationally organised and managed service established to ensure that children’s voices are heard, and their best interests are independently presented, by an appointed Guardian ad litem, in child care proceedings. The target for commencement of Section 35 of the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2022 is the 23rd of June and the Department is continually working towards this launch date.

The Department has had a number of positive engagements with key stakeholders of the Guardian ad litem National Service in recent months including two very important policy consultations in Cork and Dublin in late February. These engagements have been extremely beneficial with the Executive Office now working to incorporate the feedback we have received into our policies and procedures.
I also personally met with the Association of Guardians ad litem Ireland (AGALI), in Leinster house, on the 24th of February.

Upon commencement, under Section 35Q of the 2022 Act, current Guardians ad litem whom are appointed under Section 26 Child Care Act 1991 are eligible to continue to be appointed to these children for a period of 12 months. This will allow for transitioning Guardians ad litem to close off their cases and provide the national service the opportunity to create a handover plan if necessary.

Children, and their best interests, are at the centre of the Guardian ad litem National Service. The Service is committed to working with all stakeholders to prevent disruption for children before, during, and after commencement. Procedures are being developed for timely appointment of Guardians ad litem to ensure that children will not experience a delay. In 2025, this Department developed a Project Implementation Plan to aid in the commencement of the new service and within this, there is a capacity plan included as well as resourcing measures to prevent waitlists.
I am confident that the Department will continue to engage meaningfully with stakeholders, including meeting with AGALI and other key stakeholders on a regular basis.

question.p: 1502. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to urgently provide additional capital funding to a vital project in County Kerry (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18544/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I wish to inform the Deputy that neither the Department nor Tusla currently have capital funding to support the building of new or refurbishment or extension of existing Family Resource Centres. Tusla does not have a dedicated budget for capital or building works for third party organisations such as Family Resource Centres.

The Family Resource Centre Programme is a community development programme that is financially supported by many State agencies in a partnership approach. Centres may draw on various sources of funding provided by other Government Departments, agencies and private sources.

I understand that as part of Kenmare Family Resource Centre’s engagement with Kerry County Council on an alternative premises, a premises purchased by Kerry County Council has now been located close to the current Kenmare FRC site, and at no cost to the Kenmare FRC. It is intended that the principal occupant of the building will be the Family Resource Centre.

Kenmare Family Resource Centre will have to finance work to adapt the accommodation it secures within the building to meet its needs. A meeting is scheduled for 23rd March with the Family Resource Centre Co-ordinator and the Council to discuss next steps.

I understand that on two occasions some years ago Tusla provided Kenmare Family Resource Centre with some one-off, end-of-year funding to assist in developing the FRC Programme in Kenmare by helping to secure a suitable building to provide services from. Due to circumstances beyond anyone’s control, including the Covid 19 pandemic and the lack of a suitable premises, this project had been delayed. Tusla has been engaging with the Family Resource Centre in the context of discharging this particular funding, which I understand is planned to go towards the costs of adapting the accommodation secured.

question.p: 1503. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the rationale behind Tusla's reported decision not to continue funding or supporting the specialist therapeutic fostering support service provided by a service (details supplied), as part of its ongoing regional reconfiguration; if an impact assessment has been carried out on the potential consequences of withdrawing this service for foster carers and children in care in South Tipperary and surrounding areas; the alternative therapeutic and professional supports that will be put in place for foster carers currently availing of these services; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18553/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Thank you for raising this issue which affects foster carers and their families.

Tusla has advised that at a recent meeting with foster carers affected by this situation, the Agency listened carefully to their opinions and concerns. Tusla advised that it was clear how strongly foster carers feel about the St. Bernard’s service and the importance of this support for them and the children in their care.

Tusla has advised that in retrospect, there was not appropriate consultation and engagement with foster carers and the Agency has written to the affected foster carers on the matter and apologised for the concern and worry this has caused them.

The Department has been advised that Tusla local management has taken the decision to maintain service provision with St. Bernard’s for 2026, with no disruption to current supports. Additionally, I understand that the Tusla local team will engage with Foster Carers throughout 2026 in the co-design of supports to be provided in 2027.

Tusla has communicated this to the affected foster carers and will meet with them in person in the coming weeks. Both Tusla and this Department are committed to supporting foster carers, and to providing them with the supports they need to look after the children and young people in their care.

question.p: 1507. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding the pilot and phased introduction of staffed local childminding networks, as committed to in the National Action Plan for Childminding; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18639/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 set out a pathway for the extension of regulation to childminders. As a result of the commencement of the relevant parts of the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Childminding Services Regulations, which came into effect on 30 September 2024, childminders are now able to apply to register with Tusla.

The regulation of childminding services is critical to the safeguarding of children. The route to registration under the new regulations requires childminders to undertake pre-registration training, as well as meeting certain regulatory requirements including Garda vetting, proof of insurance, first aid certification and child safeguarding training.

We are now in a 3-year transition period, to September 2027, during which childminders are being encouraged and supported to register, but registration is not yet mandatory. This phased approach aims to facilitate the largest possible number of childminders to enter the regulated sector, the sphere of quality assurance, and access to Government subsidies, while recognising the time and supports required for childminders to learn about and prepare for registration.

The National Action Plan has a number of specific objectives including the development of bespoke resources to support the quality of childminding provision, including through the development of staffed local childminding networks. The Action Plan is articulated in phases, with ambitions to achieve the different objectives at different phases. The introduction of the Childminding-specific Regulations marked the on-time completion of Phase 1 of the Plan and the commencement of Phase 2. The National Action Plan committed to pilot and introduce staffed local childminding networks during Phase 2, following preliminary research that was undertaken in Phase 1. Phase 3, which will begin by 2028, is expected to see progressive roll-out of staffed local childminding networks, if so determined by the findings of the pilot phase.

question.p: 1516. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether the access and inclusion model (AIM) will be extended to include children under three years of age from the commencement of the 2026/2027 programme year, including those who are not participating in the ECCE programme; the plans, funding allocations or timelines in this regard; whether consideration is being given to aligning AIM Level 7 support hours, currently capped at six additional hours per day, with the nine-hour maximum available under the National Childcare Scheme (NCS); whether this disparity will be addressed for the 2026/2027 programme year; when the rules and operational guidance for the 2026/2027 programme year will be published, to allow service providers to plan appropriately for September 2026 enrolments; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18774/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Access and Inclusion Model or AIM is a programme of supports designed to ensure that children with disabilities or additional needs can access the Early Childhood Care and Education or ECCE programme and early learning and care more broadly. The goal of AIM is to empower early learning and care providers to deliver an inclusive pre-school experience, ensuring that every eligible child can meaningfully participate in the ECCE programme and reap the benefits of quality early learning and care in any mainstream service participating in ECCE.
A core feature and strength of AIM is that it does not require a diagnosis. Instead, resources are allocated based on a child’s individual needs.

AIM was specifically designed to support children with additional needs to access and meaningfully participate in the ECCE programme and as such, AIM is directly linked to ECCE participation and currently applies only to children who meet the ECCE age eligibility criteria. However, ECCE-age children enrolled in a specialised (non-ECCE) pre-school or receiving specialised funding can access AIM Plus and AIM Non-Term supports outside of pre-school hours through the National Childcare Scheme (NCS).

Reflecting the Government’s strong commitment to affordable and accessible early learning and care, the AIM budget for 2026 is €85.05 million. This funding will support up to 9,000 children to access the ECCE programme this year through targeted AIM supports, as well as a 10% increase in the capitation rate for AIM Level 7, which was introduced from October 2025.

The ‘First 5’ whole-of-government strategy commits to the phased extension of AIM, a commitment that was reaffirmed by the findings of an independent end-of-year-three evaluation published in January 2024. Participants in the evaluation, including providers, educators, and parents, strongly supported the scaling up of AIM and expressed a desire to see AIM extended to hours outside of the ECCE entitlement.

Based on the evaluation’s findings, AIM is being extended on a phased basis as funding becomes available. The first phase was the expansion of hours and from September 2024, targeted AIM supports have been available to ECCE-eligible children outside of ECCE hours—both during term time and in holiday periods. Children can now access up to three additional hours per day during the ECCE term and up to six hours per day outside of term, through the National Childcare Scheme (NCS). There is at present no plan to further increase this additional hours provision.

The Programme for Government commits to ‘examine and expand the Access and Inclusion Model and make it available to younger children.’ Work is underway on a comprehensive policy development process during 2026 to extend AIM to children aged under three in early learning and care services, which will be underpinned by consultations with key stakeholders. It is critical that the new model will be strongly evidence-based and reflective of the developmental stages of children not yet in ECCE.

It is intended that over time, all children with additional needs registered in early learning and care services will have access to supports under AIM and consideration will be given therefore, at a later stage, to extending AIM to children attending school-age childcare.
Both of these policy responses are dependent on securing funding through the annual Budget process.
Rules for the 26/27 programme year are being updated at present and will be published online when completed.

question.p: 1517. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the actions taken to date on the back of the HIQA report into Tusla North Dublin on non-compliance with each standard; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18778/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Statutory and operational responsibility for the delivery of child protection and welfare services is a matter for Tusla, the Child and Family Agency. The Deputy is seeking information in relation to an operational matter for Tusla. Consequently, I have referred the matter to Tusla, and requested that a direct response be provided to the Deputy.

question.p: 1518. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of judgments as ‘Not Compliant’ made by HIQA into all Tusla run services as reported for inspections carried out in 2024 and 2025; and the number of these ‘Not Compliant’ judgments referred to staff in positions they were not fully qualified and/or trained for. [18783/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: HIQA is authorised by this Department under section 8(1)(c) of the Health Act 2007, to monitor the quality of service provided by Tusla, the Child and Family Agency to protect children and to promote the welfare of children. The Authority monitors the performance of the Tusla against the National Standards for the Protection and Welfare of Children and advises the Minister and Tusla, the Child and Family Agency.

Over the course of 2024 and 2025, HIQA published a total of 67 Inspection Reports relating to Children’s Services, with 31 Inspections conducted in 2024 and 36 in 2025. These Inspections covered the following Children’s Services:
• Special Care
• Children’s Residential Services
• Children’s Detention Schools
• Foster Care Services
• Child Protection and Welfare Services

While all 67 reports were reviewed by Tusla and the Department, neither organisation prepared indexes or centrally collated the number of instances of specific categories of non-compliance in the way that the Deputy requests. Each HIQA report was responded to individually to address the issues arising in that particular service. In reviewing these cases, the Department and Tusla both monitor emerging trends/themes arising in practice. Both emerging themes and specific cases of serious non-compliance are escalated within Tusla and the Department for remedial action.

Concerning the specific category of non-compliance in terms of training and qualifications, reflecting an ongoing changing environment and social work vacancies, Tusla has moved to a more multi-disciplinary way of working with children now allocated to social workers and other professional grades where necessary and appropriate to ensure they have the support of a key worker. All children continue to be overseen by social work management. It is important to note that while cases can be allocated to other professionals, these cases are still overseen by Social Work Management.

Typically, where a service is non-compliant concerning training or qualification of a staff member, this will be addressed in the resulting compliance plan that is submitted to HIQA to address the non-compliance. Key actions might include training and development (including mandatory and core training on Children First and business processes), additional specialist training and development on Signs of Safety, Cumulative Harm, Life Story Work, Working with Adolescents, Evidence-Based Family Interventions etc. Other remedial action on training and qualifications in a compliance plan might include coaching and mentoring, filling of vacancies, securing external support and ensuring allocation of professionally qualified social workers to high-risk cases.

question.p: 1520. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the priorities for her Department, specifically those relating to disability, ahead of Ireland holding the EU Presidency from July 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [18881/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2026 will be an important opportunity for Ireland to shape Europe’s policy direction, lead important aspects of the EU’s work, and showcase Ireland’s engagement, expertise and values at the heart of the European Union.

As the Member State holding the Presidency of the Council of the EU, Ireland will have the responsibility for progressing the EU agenda for the second half of 2026. The Department currently holds lead responsibility in Ireland for three active EU legislative proposals, which are currently being progressed by the Cyprus Presidency; where relevant, outstanding work on these will be progressed during the Irish Presidency. Those active files are:
2023/0169(COD) - EU legislative proposal on the protection of vulnerable adults: jurisdiction, applicable law, recognition and enforcement of measures and cooperation

2008/0140 (CNS) - Proposal for a Council Directive on implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation the equal treatment directive, and
2025/0550(COD) - The Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values Programme (CERV) aspects of the proposal for a regulation establishing the 'AgoraEU' programme for the period 2028-2034.
Securing agreement on these active files would make a tangible difference for disabled people in Ireland and across the EU.

In addition to progressing the EU agenda, the Presidency will also provide an opportunity to spotlight issues where we have special expertise and interest. In this regard, we plan to put particular emphasis on disabled people, marginalised groups and the participation of children and young people.

It is anticipated that the Department will host a variety of meetings, including a series of High Level Conferences, Senior Officials Meetings and associated Presidency events in the second half of 2026. During our Presidency, I intend to host a High-Level Conference specifically dedicated to Disability matters.

How we host our Presidency events is a practical way Ireland can demonstrate our values of inclusion and accessibility. To support this across the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU, the Department held a special event titled 'Hosting a Conference Accessible to All' in December 2025 for all Government Departments and Agencies. Contributors included officials from the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the National Disability Authority, the National Transport Authority and a representative from the Danish Secretariat of the European Presidency (2025).
Ireland's full policy programme and details on events to be held in Ireland will be published, as is usual practice, shortly before the start of our Presidency term, in June 2026.

[18990/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: This Government is committed to supporting people with disabilities to live meaningful and fulfilling lives, with a person-centred approach across all services provided.

As the Deputy may be aware, Budget 2026 provided funding of approximately €3.9 billion to Specialist Disability Services. Specialist Disability Residential services make up the largest part of the Disability funding disbursed by the HSE.

A key focus in 2026 will be on ensuring the budget meets the real cost of service, ensuring a stable base upon which to plan and expand services now and into the future. As of December 2025, approximately 90 service providers are delivering 8,911 residential places.

The current demand for residential placements is exceptionally high. In recent years, the delivery of residential services has come under growing and sustained pressure due to a range of contributing factors, including:
• Limited availability of appropriate housing options.
• Rising costs associated with establishing new residential placements.
• Significant recruitment and workforce challenges affecting all areas of disability services.
• Evolving and increasingly complex support needs among existing service users, leading to higher expenditure on necessary adaptations and enhanced supports.

In addition to funding ongoing residential placements for almost 9000 current residents, €65m has been allocated to Disability Residential Services in 2026 for new developments, which includes €40m of funding that will provide in the region of 199 residential placements.

This includes the creation of 72 new planned placements and 80 new unplanned, urgent placements, as referenced in the HSE’s National Service Plan for 2026. The plan outlines a shift towards a more planned and responsive service model, placing greater emphasis on long-term planning for residential placements. Strengthened operational processes will help the system manage the current high demand. The funding will also support new residents in existing placements that have become vacant and need enhancement. In limited cases, it may also support placements in nursing home settings.
The remaining €25m consists of:
• €6m to support 40 residential packages for children in care with complex needs, in coordination with Túsla.
• €6m to enhance 38 existing residential placements for individuals whose support needs have increased
• €3m for decongregation, to support the transition of 58 people from congregated settings to more appropriate homes in the community.
• €10m for U65s in Nursing Homes, which includes €8m to support 45 transitions to more appropriate settings, and €2m to enhance quality of life for those remaining in nursing homes.

Additionally, within the funding allocated for 2026, the HSE has begun work to establish Residential Placement Planning & Review Teams in each Regional Health Area. The aim of these teams will be to improve forward planning of residential placements, and to ensure that individuals are appropriately assessed in relation to support needs prior to placement in residential services and reviewed in a timely manner for duration of the placement in respect of quality of care and support needs.

question.p: 1525. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her views on the current situation under parent's leave and benefit (details supplied); if she will increase the leave for one parent families; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19004/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I acknowledge the significant challenges faced by one-parent families and reaffirm the commitment of Government to continue to address these. There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.

Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are entitled to nine weeks of paid parent's leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child, as required by the EU Work Life Balance Directive.

It is important to note that the entitlement under the 2019 Act is for each parent in their own right and is not an allocation per family. The Act was drafted to take account of the broad complexion of family life, including one parent families, and allows for an entitlement for the spouse, civil partner or cohabitant of the parent. Parents do not have to cohabit to be eligible for the entitlement. However, the leave is non-transferable to ensure that fathers as well as mothers are supported in their caring roles and to support women's equal labour market participation. The principle of non-transferability is also required by the EU Work-Life Balance Directive because of the importance of ensuring that the provision of family leave does not serve to disadvantage mothers participating in the labour market.

Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid parental leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis'.

It should be noted that the legislation only sets out the minimum entitlement to parental leave. Depending on an individual’s contract of employment, they may have more extensive rights to parental leave, as employers have the option to offer more than the entitlement set out in the legislation.

The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 complements existing family leaves and other entitlements already in place and provides additional flexibility to ensure that parents and carers can be supported to balance their working and family lives. Under this legislation, parents and carers have a right to request flexible working in line with Article 9 of the Directive EU 2019/1158. Five days leave per year for medical care purposes was also introduced under this Act.

Government is acutely aware of the additional challenges faced by one-parent families and their greater risk of poverty. Government will continue to address the challenges through taxation and welfare systems and the range of services provided. There is also a commitment in the Programme for Government 2025, ‘Securing Ireland’s Future’, to continue to prioritise and enhance supports for lone parents.

To the extent that the matter falls within the Department, I am committed to working with colleagues to support one-parent families through the development of enhanced and targeted supports for single parent families and am cognisant of the difficulties faced by lone parents and will examine where additional supports could be provided to them.
The One-parent family payment, which is a provision of the Department of Social Protection, is a payment for parents under 66 who are not cohabiting, and whose youngest child is under 7.

Family leave provisions are kept under review to ensure that they are effective and respond to the needs of families and also mindful of the impact of the leaves on workplaces. The Programme for Government sets out a commitment to examine the possible extension of parent's leave and benefit and additional flexibilities. The first Action Plan for the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 is currently in development and any changes to available supports for one-parent families will be considered in this context.

question.p: 1527. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the plans to finalise and enact the Equality (Miscellaneous Provision) Bill 2025 which would be a clear statement of Ireland’s commitment to gender equality; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19050/26]

1528. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if the Equality (Miscellaneous Provision) Bill 2025 will clearly prohibit intersectional discrimination so that older women, disabled women and Traveller and Roma women who have experienced this form of combined discrimination will be protected from discrimination; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19051/26]

1529. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if key areas such as social welfare, social housing, healthcare, and the functions of public bodies that impact on the lives of women (details supplied) will be explicitly covered by equality legislation; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19052/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1527, 1528 and 1529 together.

In November 2024, Government approved the publication of the General Scheme of the Equality (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill, which includes a number of legislative provisions arising from a review of Ireland’s equality legislation.

The Joint Oireachtas Committee on Children and Equality undertook pre-legislative scrutiny of the General Scheme and issued its report in October 2025. Officials in this Department are currently considering the recommendations of the report.

The General Scheme proposes to strengthen existing provisions on discrimination by allowing for intersectional claims. The recommendations of the Joint Oireachtas Committee regarding this proposal are being considered.

Notwithstanding certain exemptions provided for in the Acts, such as for actions required by law, the protections of the Employment Equality Acts and the Equal Status Acts apply to employees and service users of both public and private bodies. The General Scheme does not propose any changes to this and so the functions of public bodies will continue to be covered by this legislation.

question.p: 1530. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the number of enduring powers of attorney registered and activated under the decision support service since its commencement in April 2023 and provide a comparison with those registered and activated in 2022 under the previous system; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19112/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for their question regarding the Decision Support Service (DSS) and Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPAs). EPAs are a vital advance planning tool that enable adults to plan ahead for a time when they may have diminished decision-making capacity, ensuring that a person’s wishes are known and respected.

Under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, the DSS has a statutory role to process and register EPAs. The DSS publishes updated monthly figures[] regarding the number of registered EPAs on its website. As of the end of February 2026, the DSS had registered 5,743 EPAs. Additionally, the total number of EPAs notified to the DSS, as of the end of February, stands at 238.

It must be noted that registration of an EPA under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 has a different meaning from 'registration' under the Powers of Attorney Act 1996. Under the 2015 Act, the first stage is that an EPA is registered with the DSS when it is created by the donor. If the donor subsequently loses capacity, the attorney notifies the DSS and if the DSS accepts notification, the EPA is ‘activated’.

Under the 1996 Act, there was no requirement to register an EPA upon its creation. There was no review at that point in the process and no secure register. Given that when an EPA was created under the 1996 Act there was no requirement to submit it to the Courts, there are no figures on the number of EPAs created under that Act in 2022.

Under the 1996 Act, if the donor loses capacity, an application is made to the High Court to 'register' the EPA, which would be the equivalent of 'notifying' the EPA under the 2015 Act. According to the Court Service's Annual Report for 2022, the number of EPAs 'registered' that year was 1,245. This figure reflects the number of adults who have had their EPA take effect in 2022. It is important to note however, that this does not mean that these EPAs were created in that same year.

question.p: 1531. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the current average processing time for enduring powers of attorney applications submitted to the decision support service; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19113/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for their question regarding Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPA) applications. EPAs are a vital advance planning tool that enable adults to plan ahead for a time when they may have diminished decision-making capacity, ensuring that a person’s wishes are known and respected.

The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 ('the 2015 Act') provides a modern statutory framework to support decision-making by adults with capacity difficulties, including providing for a new EPA system which enables an individual to plan ahead by appointing someone they trust to act as their attorney and to make certain decisions on their behalf if they lose capacity in the future. The Decision Support Service (DSS) has statutory responsibility for the operation of many of the provisions of the 2015 Act, including processing and registering EPAs made under the Act.

The registration of an EPA is a statutory process governed by the 2015 Act and incorporates a number of safeguards. A correctly completed EPA will usually be reviewed for registration by the DSS within approximately 5 months, which includes a 5-week mandatory notice period. Usually, there is no expectation that the donor needs their attorney to step in as decision-maker during this period. However, if that situation changes pending completion of registration, the attorney can contact the DSS to ask for an expedited registration. This means that the EPA can move to the second stage of notification. The DSS has published procedures on expedited EPAs on its website at www.decisionsupportservice.ie/sites/default/files/2025-06/Procedure%20for%20urgent%20expedited%20EPAs%2026.06.25%20-%20FINAL.pdf .

The DSS keeps all of its timelines and processes under review. As of end February 2026, the DSS had registered 5,743 EPAs. The increasing number of registered EPAs indicates a high level of engagement with the new framework for EPAs as provided for in the 2015 Act, and a growing awareness by adults of the importance of planning for the future.

question.p: 1532. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the steps being taken to address the reported complexity and restrictive nature of the decision support service online portal, particularly for older people and those with limited digital access; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19114/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for their question regarding the online application process for Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPAs) under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act, 2015. EPAs are a vital advance planning tool that enable adults to plan ahead for a time when they may have diminished decision-making capacity, ensuring that a person’s wishes are known and respected.

The Decision Support Service (DSS) has statutory responsibility for the operation of many of the provisions of the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 including the registration of EPAs. Ensuring that the application system for decision support arrangements is as user-centric and as accessible as possible is a priority for my Department and is central to the work of the DSS.

On foot of stakeholder feedback the DSS has implemented a number of changes to improve the EPA application process, to reduce application processing times, and to address the accessibility needs of users of the service.

In that regard, since July 2024 the DSS introduced an accessibility policy which includes a dedicated EPA helpdesk service to ensure that individuals who require additional assistance in completing an online EPA application are supported in doing so. This helpdesk facility, together with helpful instructional videos and other guidance material provided on the DSS website, has seen the number of registered EPAs increase, and the timeframe for registration decrease.

While the DSS has a digital-first policy when it comes to EPA applications, it is important to note that there remains a facility for manual applications to be submitted by those who cannot, for a variety of reasons, utilise the online application system. The accessibility policy sets out that the DSS will ensure that individuals who are unable to utilize the online portal are facilitated in making an EPA application manually, and all applicants will be offered the support and advice required to ensure that they can complete their application to have their EPA registered.

Increasing awareness and accessibility remains a core priority for the DSS at all times. As part of this, in February 2026, the DSS launched a dedicated new website - www.myepa.ie - designed to guide individuals step by step through the process of creating an EPA in a clear and accessible way. The site brings together all relevant information and supports in one place and is intended to assist donors, attorneys and family members alike in understanding their options and responsibilities. It also provides guidance on beginning conversations about future planning and offers reassurance that support is available throughout the process.

Both my Department and the Decision Support Service, look forward to continued engagement with all stakeholders to ensure that those who face diminished decision-making capacity are enabled to retain as much autonomy over their lives as possible, and have their wishes documented and respected.

question.p: 1533. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the performance of the decision support service since its inception; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19115/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I thank the deputy for their question regarding the performance of the Decision Support Service under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act, 2015.

The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 ('the 2015 Act') provides a modern statutory framework to support decision-making by adults with capacity difficulties. The Decision Support Service (DSS), which was established under the Act, has statutory responsibility for the operation of many of the provisions of the 2015 Act, including processing and registering co-decision-making agreements (CDMAs), enduring powers of attorney (EPAs), the registration of decision-making representation orders (DMROs) as well as maintaining a panel of decision-making representatives.

In terms of the numbers of decision support arrangements, the DSS publishes updated monthly figures on its website. Since the commencement of the Act, these numbers have grown steadily each year. As of the end of February this year, 5,743 EPAs have been put in place alongside 2,105 DMROs and 194 CDMAs. 209 decision-making assistant agreements have been notified to the DSS. This shows that as people get to grips with these decision support arrangements, the new system is working to good effect.

In regard to the EPAs, the DSS have also recently launched a dedicated new website - www.myepa.ie - designed to guide individuals step by step through the process of creating an EPA in a clear and accessible way. The site brings together all relevant information and supports in one place and is intended to assist donors, attorneys and family members alike in understanding their options and responsibilities.

Furthermore, in regard to the Part 6 discharge process, the DSS has collaborated with colleagues in the Office of Wards of Court and the Office of the General Solicitor to provide information and assistance for the benefit of wards, their families and committees and for professionals. This has been to provide information about post-wardship supports and potential future engagement with the DSS following discharge from wardship. As part of its statutory functions to promote awareness and understanding about the 2015 Act generally, the DSS has also published information on its website at https://decisionsupportservice.ie/resources/wards-court with links to other useful resources.

Due to their critical role in the functioning of the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, the Act provided for a review of the statutory role of Director of the Decision Support Service, including on the effectiveness of the Director, on the adequacy of the functions assigned under this Act to the Director, and containing such recommendations that the Mental Health Commission considers would improve the effectiveness of the Director or the adequacy of the functions assigned to the Director under the 2015 Act.

This report was published on March 9th, and identifies that the Director has made good progress in establishing robust operational structures, systems and processes to implement a complex range of statutory functions under a complex and ambitious piece of legislation. This report can be found on the Department's website at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-children-disability-and-equality/publications/review-of-the-statutory-role-of-director-of-the-decision-support-service/.

These developments, among others, reflect the substantial progress achieved by the Decision Support Service. My Department will continue to engage with the Decision Support Service regarding its ongoing contribution to safeguarding and supporting adults with capacity difficulties and their families.

question.p: 1534. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to outline any planned reforms or legislative changes to the new enduring powers of attorney regime; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19116/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for their question regarding Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPAs). EPAs are a vital advance planning tool that enable adults to plan ahead for a time when they may have diminished decision-making capacity, ensuring that a person’s wishes are known and respected.

The new EPA registration process was established under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 (the 2015 Act). The 2015 Act is a hugely important piece of legislation which transforms how people are supported where they may not have capacity. The Act prioritises the specific needs and wishes of the individual and it represents an important milestone in bringing Ireland in closer compliance with the UNCRPD.

There are not any currently planned legislative changes to the EPA process. The recently announced Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) (Amendment) Bill 2026 marks a significant amendment to the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 to provide for legal certainty in individual wardship cases by enabling the wardship court to extend, in certain circumstances, the time period for making a capacity declaration under section 55(1) of the Act, in circumstances where the expiry of that time period is imminent and will not be met.

This will allow for an extension for such period as the wardship court considers necessary and proportionate in the circumstances where the court is satisfied that ‘good reason’ has been shown that the statutory deadline of 26 April 2026 will not be met, and where it is also in the interests of justice to grant the extension. The outer limit for any extension of time will be 18 months, or until 25 October 2027, whichever is the earlier.

While there are no currently planned legislative changes beyond those provided for in this Bill. The Programme for Government commits to a review of the 2015 Act within the lifetime of the Government, my Department intends to begin this review before the end of the year. The review will provide an opportunity for any and all persons with an interest in the Act to engage with the Department regarding the ongoing performance of the Act, including the new EPA regime. My Department will continue to work closely with the Decision Support Service, to ensure that EPAs, subject to the proper safeguards, are processed and registered in as prompt a manner as possible.

question.p: 1535. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if the Strategy Committee for the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 has been convened; the date of its first meeting; the membership of the Committee; the schedule of meetings for 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19128/26]

1536. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when the first Action Plan and detailed departmental actions, indicators and timelines under the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 will be published; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19129/26]

1538. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if the Gender Flagship Technical Support Instrument toolkit developed to support gender responsive policy and budget planning is being incorporated into the implementation of the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030; the extent to which it has been disseminated across Government Departments; the status of associated civil service training; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19131/26]

1539. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the dedicated budget allocation for the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 for the years 2025 to 2027; the staffing resources assigned to support implementation; the level of additional funding provided to other Departments; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19132/26]

1540. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way in which the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 is being coordinated with related national gender equality frameworks including EU supported gender mainstreaming measures; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19133/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1535, 1536, 1538, 1539 and 1540 together.

The new National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 was launched on the 18th November 2025. The Strategy has a single, simple vision: An Ireland where women and girls can thrive in a gender equal society.

Implementation of the Strategy will be guided by two Action Plans, the first of which will be adopted by Government in 2026 and will cover the period 2026-2028. Work on the first of these two Action Plans is at an advanced stage.

Implementation of the Strategy will be overseen by a Strategy Monitoring Committee. This Committee is currently in the process of being formed. It is expected that the Committee will be convened once its membership has been finalised.

Objective 1: Being Counted aims to progress gender mainstreaming and gender budgeting. This includes the introduction of mandatory training for public officials with a role in public policy making and budget allocation. As mentioned previously, the first Action Plan is currently in development and officials are developing actions to support gender responsive policy and budget planning.

The National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 is a Whole-of-Government Strategy and will coordinate efforts across Government to promote gender equality. Additionally, the Strategy will serve as the means through which Ireland meets its international obligations with regards to the promotion of gender equality. As outlined in the Strategy document, the Irish Government Economic and Evaluation Service will be requested to prepare a costing for the actions agreed in the Action Plans.

summary.i: Question No. 1536 answered with Question No. 1535.

question.p: 1537. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the status of the National Equality Data Strategy; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19130/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The National Equality Data Strategy 2026-2031 is available at: [www.gov.ie/en/department-of-children-disability-and-equality/publications/the-national-equality-data-strategy/].
This Strategy has been developed by the Central Statistics Office and the Department in partnership with a working group drawn from across Government and civil society.
Equality data is “any piece of information that is useful for the purposes of describing and analysing the state of equality”. This data is important for:
• the design and delivery of inclusive policies and services,
• enabling policymakers and the public to assess the scale and nature of discrimination suffered by vulnerable and marginalised groups, and
• analysing where needs are most acute and what impact interventions are having.

The Strategy requires all Government Departments to make a commitment to collect, use or disseminate equality data and to develop the organisational capacity to fulfil this commitment. It provides a general approach for identifying and filling current gaps in equality data, as well as developing standard practices in classification.

The Strategy will improve Ireland’s collection, disaggregation and use of equality data to enable policymakers to develop sound and inclusive evidence-informed policies that improve service delivery and outcomes across Ireland.
Work is now beginning on implementation, including the formation of a steering group to oversee, monitor and report on progress.
