question.p: 1589. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the planned level of investment in personal assistance services for 2026, particularly in light of recent calls for greater transparency on PA funding and the need to expand supports that enable independent living; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19996/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Personal Assistance (PA) is internationally recognised as a core mechanism for fulfilling the rights of disabled people to live independently and participate fully in the community as enshrined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The service is commonly characterised by its self-directed nature, enabling disabled people to exercise more choice and control over their supports. In Ireland, almost 3,000 people are currently in receipt of PA.

Budget 2026 provided €1.6m in funding to support the delivery of approximately 50,000 additional PA hours this year. This is in addition to the 95,000 additional hours funded by the Department last year. Provision of these funds will help increase service capacity, supporting people with disabilities to continue living in their own homes or with their families and enabling their independence.

Budget 2026 also provided approximately €15m to increase the rate payable for both PA and home support service delivery in the disability sector, bringing it from €25 per hour to €32.73. Provision of these funds will help sustain workforce capacity in the disability sector by ensuring rate parity with other sectors providing similar support services.

question.p: 1590. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the way her Department intends to oversee and ensure timely delivery of disability capital projects in Cork which are currently at early design stages; if she will list those capital projects; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19997/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Department is currently collating the information requested, and a reply will issue to the Deputy directly on this matter as soon as possible.

debateSection.summary: This Government intends to offer the very highest level of support to those statutory and voluntary organisations who provide specialist disability services across the country.

As such, this Department is providing €3.9 billion for HSE Specialist Disability Services in 2026, almost 20% (€628m) increase over 2025. It also follows significant year-on-year funding increases for the sector, from €2bn in 2020 to €3.9bn in 2026.

I announced €43 million in capital investment for much needed disability services in 2026 on 24 February. This represents a substantial increase of €16 million compared with 2025 and demonstrates the Government’s firm commitment to support and expand disability services. 2026 is the first of a five-year investment plan supported by €278 million in funding which I secured through the National Development Plan.

DCDE has built a close collaboration with the HSE and has created a performance management system which ensures continuous oversight of expenditure and project delivery. This system allows us to examine expenditure, consider the status of ongoing projects, identify variances and risks, and agree to any follow-up actions required.

It is important to note that while the strategy, policy direction and overall allocation for the disability sector is set at Ministerial level, funding allocations and management of individual capital projects is a matter for the HSE, as the funding and governance authority on behalf of the State.

The HSE adheres to strict National and EU public procurement procedures and the National Guidelines “Public Procurement Guidelines – Competitive Process’’ when undertaking any capital build works. In addition, the HSE complies with the Capital Works Management Framework (CWMF). The CWMF is an integrated set of contract forms, guidance and standards that are available for the delivery of capital build public works.
Following receipt of your question, the department has also sought an update from the HSE regarding the status of capital projects in Co. Cork. The HSE has advised of the
following projects currently considered
• 12006: St. Raphael’s Centre, Youghal.
Oakvale houses 28 residents across 5 bungalows. Planned work includes an extension of bedrooms to provide ensuites as well as interior works.
• 12166: Youghal
To facilitate planned works carried out in Oakvale, the purchase of an additional house to decant residents is also planned
• 12151: Shanakiel
HSE Contribution to a house extension for a service user in a Home Share arrangement
• 12156: Ballyhooley
To provide a Respite Centre at 16 Ard Abhainn, Ballyhooly, Co. Cork, P51 K162. Purchase of an existing residential house, refurbishment works are required to bring the property online.
• 12162: Carhoo, Kilcully
Acquisition of a 4-bedroom residential house by Disabilities Services to provide respite services in IHA North Cork.

I have also asked the HSE to examine a number of other disability projects which may be added to the Capital Plan which take into account the need for regional balance and ensure an appropriate blend across service areas.

question.p: 1594. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the waiting list for assessment of needs; the number of persons on the list; the length of time persons waiting for such an assessment to be carried out; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20047/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Government recognises that there are unacceptable delays in accessing Assessments of Need. The Department and the HSE are committed to addressing these delays.

Under the Disability Act, an Assessment of Need is an assessment process carried out by the HSE where a person is of the opinion that he/she may have a disability, for anyone born after 1st June 2002. It first establishes whether the person has a disability (as defined within the Act). It then identifies the health and education needs of the person with a disability and the services required to meet those needs.
It is important to note that children do not require an Assessment of Need to access health services, including Primary Care, Children’s Disability Network Teams or Mental Health Services.

Demand for Assessments of Need has increased significantly in recent years, reflecting both the increase in population and the number of families exploring all options to access services for their child. However, this demand is outpacing the capacity of the system to respond with the result that there were 20,209 applications overdue for completion nationwide at the end of 2025, according to the most recently available HSE data.

More positively, there has been continued improvement in the number of completed assessment of need reports with 5,939 reports completed nationally in 2025. This is a 43% increase compared to the number completed in 2024.

With regard to the length of time that a person is waiting for an assessment of need to be carried out, the HSE provides Assessment of Need data on a quarterly basis, the most recent of which is for Q4 2025. This data is provided in the table below at HSE Regional Health Area (RHA), broken down by applications overdue by under 3 months, between 1-3 months, and over three months.

p.b: Table 1. Assessment of Need reports overdue at end 2025

speech.p: In December 2025 Government announced a series of improvements to the Assessment of Need process which will make the process more effective and efficient for children and families. Over time, this should lead to a reduction in the waiting time to receive an assessment. This reform includes legislative reform and operational improvements to support the efficiency and effectiveness of the Assessment of Need process.

The proposed legislative changes will not remove any rights for parents to apply for an Assessment of Need for their child. They also will not alter the statutory six-month timeline set out in the Disability Act.

The General Scheme of the Disability (Amendment) Bill has been published on the Department’s website. An FAQ document has also been published, providing information on Assessment of Need and the proposed changes for parents and any other interested stakeholders.

It is important to recognise that legislation is only a part of the response. The Department is working with the HSE to identify further opportunities to enhance processes, improve training, and increase administrative supports for HSE Assessment Officers who are responsible for the production of assessment reports. This includes the establishment of working groups to address learning and development needs and to develop statutory guidelines.
The HSE is also implementing actions to address the wider issue of access to services and supports for children with disabilities including:

• Introduction of a Single Point of Access system by the HSE in 2026. This should make it easier for families to be referred to the right service, whether that is primary care, CDNT or mental health services. It aims to streamline referrals and reduce duplication, so children do not end up on multiple waiting lists.

• Implementation of the Autism Assessment and Intervention Pathways Protocol by the HSE in early 2026. The Protocol will provide a standardised assessment process across primary care, mental health and disability services. It will be the preferred assessment route for autism.
• The creation of eleven new HSE teams, initially, to support assessment processes, including AON, providing clinical guidance and administrative supports.
The provision of an effective and efficient Assessment of Need system continues to be a priority for the Government.

question.p: 1595. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the ranking applied to a group (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20069/26]

1596. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to review a matter in correspondence (details supplied) regarding ranking in a recent process; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20070/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1595 and 1596 together.

I wish to inform the Deputy that the commissioning of new Family Resource Centres is an operational matter for Tusla, which is responsible for the day-to-day administration of the Family Resource Centre Programme.

I can confirm that neither myself nor the Department have any involvement in the review or assessment process for new members of the Family Resource Centre Programme, or in shortlisting or selecting new Programme members. The press releases issued by the Department, welcoming new members to the Family Resource Centre Programme, were in response to information provided by Tusla after the assessment process was completed.

The most recent expansion of the Family Resource Centre Programme followed a comprehensive national application and assessment process undertaken in 2025, which was led by Tusla and independently chaired by a representative of the University of Limerick. All applications were reviewed and scored against the clearly defined and published criteria, including population need, level of deprivation, child population data, existing service provision and existing service gaps. Decisions on the successful services were made by the assessment panel.

As I mentioned earlier, a total of forty-nine organisations applied for membership of the Family Resource Centre Programme, following an open call from Tusla for applications to join the Programme. This indicates the strong level of interest in communities around the country in having Family Resource Centres as part of their community infrastructure. I understand that Tusla was very impressed with the level of interest in joining the FRC Programme, and with the quality of the applications received. Regretfully, funding only allowed for fifteen new members to be selected. The application for the group you have raised was not one of the 15 top ranked applications leaving this application and leaving thirty-three applications unsuccessful. I want to thank those organisations for their interest in joining the Programme, and for the important work they continue to do in their communities.

There is currently no additional funding available to further expand the Family Resource Centre Programme in 2026. I will continue to pursue the expansion of the FRC Programme through the budgetary process and in line with the Programme for Government commitment to work to increase funding and expand the capacity and network of Family Resource Centres. If successful in securing funds for future expansion of the FRC Programme, a new call for applications will be launched to ensure all existing and newly interested locations can apply. I understand that Tusla will, over the coming months, be in further contact with organisations whose applications were unsuccessful as part of this call, and that Tusla intends to engage with any parties interested in applying for any potential future open calls for applications.

summary.i: Question No. 1596 answered with Question No. 1595.

question.p: 1602. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if additional funding will be provided to Tusla in order that an organisation (details supplied) who offer support and guidance to families involved in fostering in Tipperary can operate going forward; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20162/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Thank you for raising this issue which affects foster carers and their families.

Tusla has advised that at a recent meeting with foster carers affected by this situation, the Agency listened carefully to their opinions and concerns. Tusla advised that it was clear how strongly foster carers feel about the St. Bernard’s service and the importance of this support for them and the children in their care.

Tusla has advised that in retrospect, there was not appropriate consultation and engagement with foster carers and the Agency has written to the affected foster carers on the matter and apologised for the concern and worry this has caused them.

The Department has been advised that Tusla local management has taken the decision to maintain service provision with St. Bernard’s for 2026, with no disruption to current supports. Additionally, I understand that the Tusla local team will engage with Foster Carers throughout 2026 in the co-design of supports to be provided in 2027.

Tusla has communicated this to the affected foster carers and will meet with them in person in the coming weeks. Both Tusla and this Department are committed to supporting foster carers, and to providing them with the supports they need to look after the children and young people in their care.

question.p: 1604. Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the steps being taking to alleviate parents in Kilcock who are struggling to locate childcare and afterschool services, given the acute shortages for these facilities in the area; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20203/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Improving access to quality and affordable Early Learning and Care and School Age Childcare is a key priority of Government.

Early learning and childcare capacity is increasing. Data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile 2024/25 shows that the estimated number of enrolments increased by approximately 25% from the 2021/22 programme year. However, it appears that demand for early learning and childcare remains higher than available supply in certain parts of the country, particularly for younger children.

The Department continues to support the ongoing development and resourcing of Core Funding which has given rise to a significant expansion of places since the scheme was first introduced. Core Funding, which is in its fourth programme year, funds services based on the number of places available.

This provides stability to services, and reduces the risk associated with opening a new service or expanding an already existing service. For the third programme year (2024/25), the allocation for Core Funding allowed for a 6% increase in capacity. Budget 2025 secured funding for the fourth programme year (2025/6) to facilitate a further 3.5% increase from September 2025. Budget 2026 has made provision for the fifth programme year (2026/7) for a further expansion in supply of 4.2%.

This increased investment will allow increases in the natural growth of the sector driven both by new services joining the sector and existing services offering more places and/or longer hours to families.
The total allocation for Core Funding in 2026/2027 programme year will increase to €436.54 million, an additional €43.90 million on the current full year allocation.

The Government is also supporting the expansion of capacity through capital funding. The Building Blocks Extension Grant Scheme is designed to increase capacity in the 1–3-year-old, pre–Early Childhood Care and Education, age range for full day care. Core Funding Partner Services could apply for capital funding to physically extend their premises or to construct or purchase new premises. The Scheme will deliver up to 1,500 full-day care places for 1- to 3-year-olds.

Following on from the success of the Building Blocks Extension Grant Scheme, a further Building Blocks scheme will open for applications in 2026. This round of capital funding will focus on funding extensions to existing premises to allow for increased numbers of children to be offered places on a full-time basis. Community and private providers who are currently Core Funding partner services will be eligible to apply for this scheme. I expect to announce details of the next Building Blocks scheme in the coming weeks.

Separately, I recently announced €135 million of capital investment over the coming five years for State-led services to provide high-quality, accessible early learning and childcare. The process will begin in 2026 with investment in buildings in what will be a ground-breaking initiative.
Up to eight buildings will be selected for investment this year. The State-led initiative will provide thousands of places up to 2030.

The Department also funds 30 City/County Childcare Committees, which provide support and assist families and early learning and childcare providers. The network of 30 City/County Childcare Committees across the country can assist in identifying vacant places in services for children and families who need them and engage proactively with services to explore possibilities for expansion among services, particularly where there is unmet need.

Parents experiencing difficulty in relation to their early learning and childcare needs should contact their local City/County Childcare Committee for assistance. The contact details for the Kildare County Childcare Committee may be found at www.kccc.ie

question.p: 1605. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the oversight mechanisms in place to ensure that assessment of need findings accurately reflect the functional impact of a child's disability; the review options available where parents believe an assessment of need does not reflect the documented impact on access to education; the way in which the coordination occurs between the Health Service Executive, the National Council for Special Education and schools where assessment of need findings appear inconsistent with medical, educational or functional assessments; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20227/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Under the Disability Act, an Assessment of Need is an assessment process carried out by the HSE where a person is of the opinion that he/she may have a disability, for anyone born after 1st June 2002. It first establishes whether the person has a disability (as defined within the Act). It then identifies the health and education needs of the person with a disability and the services required to meet those needs.

As part of the Assessment of Need process, the HSE Assessment Officer may request assistance from the National Council for Special Education (NCSE) to assess an applicant’s education needs. The NCSE can nominate a person with appropriate expertise to assist in carrying out this assessment of education needs. The Department of Education and Youth provides guidance on this process in the form of a circular. The most recent is Circular 0069/2025, which sets out the roles and responsibilities of schools and the NCSE in the Assessment of Need process.

While the Department of Children, Disability and Equality has policy responsibility for the Assessment of Need process, the Department of Education and Youth is responsible for policy in relation to special education supports in school settings and eligibility for special education supports. Officials in this Department have made enquiries regarding this matter with the Department of Education and Youth and the following outlines the position.

A formal report or diagnosis is not required to access early childhood care supports or mainstream education supports such as access to Special Needs Assistants or Special Education Teachers. At present a professional report, stating that a child has a special educational need and that this need is of such complexity that a special class placement could be considered, is currently required to access a special class or a special school. However, this report does not need to be obtained through the Assessment of Need process.
Any further queries with regard to access to education should be directed to the Department of Education and Youth.

The Disability Act 2005 provides for a complaints and appeals procedure for service users if they are unhappy with their Assessment of Need. Under the Act, an applicant or their parent/guardian can make a complaint in relation to one or more of the following grounds:
a determination by the assessment officer concerned that he or she does not have a disability;
the assessment under section 9 was not commenced within the time specified in section 9(5) or was not completed without undue delay;
the assessment under section 9 was not conducted in a manner that conforms to the standards determined by a body referred to in section 10;
the contents of the service statement provided;
the Executive or the education service provider, as the case may be, failed to provide or to fully provide a service specified in the service statement.

The HSE National Complaints Governance and Learning Team is responsible for the Assessment of Need complaints process. Information on the complaints process can be found on the Assessment of Need pages on the HSE website.

In addition, the Disability Appeals Officer is an independent officer appointed by the Minister for Disabilities (or Minister of State as delegated). They provide an appeals service for persons who wish to appeal:
• against a finding or recommendation of a Complaints Officer of the Health Service Executive made under Section 18(1) of the Disability Act 2005 (“the 2005 Act”), or
• against the failure of the HSE or an Educational Service Provider to implement a recommendation of a Complaints Officer of the HSE
Information on the appeals process can be found on Office of the Disability Appeals Officer page on the Department of Children, Disability and Equality gov.ie site.

question.p: 1606. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the current number of registered early learning and care places available in Galway City (details supplied), by age category, zero to one year, one to two years, and two to five years; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20246/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Data are not collated by the Department in the exact manner requested by the Deputy. The most closely aligning data available on capacity in County Galway is summarised below.
Each year, Pobal compiles data from Early Learning and Care (ELC) and School Age Childcare (SAC) providers as part of the Early Years Sector Profile.

Due to the small number of enrolments for those up to one year of age, it is not possible to reliably estimate national or county figures for this cohort. The most recently published capacity data for the 2024/25 programme year indicated that there were 913 estimated enrolments of one to two year olds and 7,220 estimated enrolments of two to five year olds in ELC services in County Galway.

Further information can be found on the Early Learning and Childcare data website. The Capacity Section of the website provides information on the number of children enrolled, services with vacant places, and services with a waiting list.

question.p: 1607. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether her Department holds data on the number of children currently on waiting lists for early learning and childcare services in Galway City (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20247/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: There is no centralised waiting list for Early Learning and Care (ELC) or School-Age Childcare (SAC) services. Each list is managed at service level.

Each year, Pobal compiles data from ELC and SAC providers as part of the Early Years Sector Profile. Providers are asked the number of children on a waiting list for a place for their service. While this data can be used to give an indication of demand, it should not be used as a measure of overall demand for ELC or SAC places as it is vulnerable to overestimating the actual number of children requiring a place. An individual child may be on multiple waiting lists in different services and may remain on one or multiple service lists after taking up a place.

The most recently published Annual Early Years Sector Profile capacity data for the 2024/25 programme year indicated that 45% of services in County Galway had at least one vacant place and 45% indicated that they had a waiting list.

question.p: 1609. Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether Galway City is being considered as a priority location for the development of the planned State led early learning and childcare services announced by her Department (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20249/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Improving access to quality and affordable Early Learning and Care and School Age Childcare is a key priority of Government.

I recently announced €135 million of capital investment over the coming five years for State-led services to provide high-quality, accessible early learning and childcare. The process will begin in 2026 with investment in buildings in what will be a ground-breaking initiative.

The Department is now assessing project options in order to identify which are best placed to deliver on the goals of the programme. Up to eight capital projects will be selected under the programme in 2026. No final decisions have yet been made on the specific projects but I look forward to sharing details of projects as they are agreed.

A forward planning model has been developed by officials in the Department of Children, Disability and Equality to better understand the nature of supply/demand misalignment and to inform decision making about capital investment. Analysis is ongoing of the data in this model in order to identify areas of greatest undersupply.

The forward planning model maps publicly-subsidised provision by service type and age group of children against the numbers of children in the corresponding age bracket in the local area and allows for granular and specific analysis to be undertaken.

Local City and County Childcare Committees will be supporting the development of projects in the State-led early learning and childcare programme so in the first instance, community early learning and childcare operators, local authorities, developers, or others who might have a suitable premises or project, including in Galway City, should contact their local City/County Childcare Committee, whose details can be found here www.gov.ie/en/department-of-children-disability-and-equality/publications/city-and-county-childcare-committees/

question.p: 1611. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will introduce mandatory autism and neurodiversity training requirements for Tusla social workers involved in child protection, family support and care proceedings. [20353/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: As this question relates to operational matters management by Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, this question has been referred to the Agency to reply directly to the Deputy.

I might add that, like other organisations, Tusla's learning and development plans will be informed by training needs assessments which will in turn take account of the knowledge and skills gaps of its staff.

question.p: 1612. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether the Department has conducted any review of the adequacy of training provided to Tusla staff in relation to autism, neurodiversity and disability awareness. [20354/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: Thank you Deputy, for your question relating to Tusla’s disability-informed assessment protocols, reasonable accommodation standards, or specialist procedural safeguards when child protection proceedings involve a diagnosed autism spectrum condition or intellectual disability.
Tusla is an agile and responsive organisation and is well placed to tailor its services to address the needs of those requiring its services, and the broader public.

Ensuring access to Tusla services is the responsibility of all Tusla staff. In the majority of cases the access needs of persons with disabilities or challenges are met by their frontline services on a day-to-day basis but sometimes additional support is required.

To help provide this support and to fulfil their responsibilities under Section 26 (2) of the Disability Act 2005, Tusla has identified 33 Disability Access Officers across their services throughout the country.

When required, their Disability Access Officers are there to help arrange and co-ordinate the provision of additional assistance and guidance to persons with disabilities or challenges in accessing their services. They can also act as a point of contact for people with disabilities or challenges wishing to access Tusla services.

A key part of this work is ensuring that it recruits and develops staff with the skills needed to perform roles based on the needs of its services. These service needs are a key input into the training needs assessments and the ensuing delivery of learning and development plans.
If anyone has additional needs in accessing Tusla services due to disability, they can contact one of the Disability Access Officers to discuss their needs and appropriate supports.

question.p: 1616. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when the review of the national personalised budgets will be completed by the NDA; when her Department will give further direction regarding the future development, scale, and implementation model of the programme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20473/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality (Deputy Emer Higgins)
speech.p: A personalised budget is an amount of funding allocated to an eligible person with a disability to enable them to make their own arrangements to meet specified support needs. A key strength of the personalised budget model is cited as the enhanced autonomy and flexibility it offers, enabling budget holders to purchase the supports or services that are most relevant and meaningful to them.
To test the delivery of the personalised budgets approach in the Irish context, the Personalised Budget Demonstrator Pilot was established in 2019, on a cost-neutral basis.

In May 2025, the Demonstrator Pilot commenced its evaluation phase which is expected to conclude shortly. Led by the National Disability Authority, the evaluation will provide insights into the barriers and facilitators to rolling out personalised budgets on a larger scale and will therefore inform next steps.

question.p: 1617. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will ensure provision is made for inflationary funding for section 39 disability residential services on an annual basis from Budget 2027 (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20497/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Government acknowledges the essential role of section 39 voluntary organisations who deliver residential services to many people across the country. My Department is committed to working with the HSE and the broader disability sector in order to ensure that valued service providers receive the funding they need to continue to deliver quality services and supports to disabled people in Ireland.

The Department provides funding to the HSE to deliver specialist disability services either directly or via Section 38 and Section 39 voluntary sector organisations. While this Department sets the strategy, policy direction and the overall allocation for the disability sector, funding allocations to individual service providers is an operational matter for the HSE as the funding authority.
Each year the Estimates process allows the HSE to request funding for the full cost of service provision, including cost increases experienced during the previous year.

In 2026 we are providing €3.9 billion for HSE Specialist Disability Services, an increase of €628m, or almost 20% over 2025. This is the largest ever increase in funding for Disability Services. It follows significant year on year increases resulting in an overall increase of €1.85bn or 91% since 2020.

Our key focus in 2026 is on ensuring the budget meets the real cost of services and ensuring a stable base upon which to plan and expand services now and into the future. The aim is to provide stability for a sector which has seen significant cost increases in recent years on top of a rising demand for services.
I trust this information is of use and I would like to thank the staff and volunteers in all Section 39 providers for the key work they do in improving peoples lives.

question.p: 1618. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if additional provision has been made in Budget 2026 for section 39 services currently carrying historical deficits; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20498/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Government acknowledges the essential role of section 39 voluntary organisations who deliver health and social care services to many people across the country. My Department is committed to working with the HSE and the broader disability sector in order to ensure that valued service providers receive the funding they need to continue to deliver quality services and supports to disabled people in Ireland.

The Department provides funding to the HSE to deliver specialist disability services either directly or via Section 38 and Section 39 voluntary sector organisations. While this Department sets the strategy, policy direction and the overall allocation for the disability sector, funding allocations to individual service providers is an operational matter for the HSE as the funding authority.

Operational deficits were identified as a systemic financial risk at the time of the transfer of services to the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth from the Department of Health. These risks are actively managed by the HSE through its oversight and monitoring of services, and where necessary, the provision of once-off supplementary funding and cash accelerations to organisations.

Most importantly, Government has also provided substantial additional funding to disability services since the transfer through the annual Estimates process to help meet the increasing cost of existing service while also incrementally expanding service provision to meet demand.

In 2026 we are providing €3.9 billion for HSE Specialist Disability Services, an increase of €628m, or almost 20% over 2025. This is the largest ever increase in funding for Disability Services. It follows significant year on year increases resulting in an overall increase of €1.85bn or 91% since 2020.

A key focus in 2026 will be on ensuring the budget meets the real cost of service, ensuring a stable base upon which to plan and expand services now and into the future. The HSE continues to work with its service partners to ensure the sustainability of quality service delivery.
I trust this information is of use and I would like to thank the staff and volunteers in all Section 39 providers for the key work they do in improving peoples lives.

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Government acknowledges the essential role of section 39 voluntary organisations who deliver residential services to many people across the country. My Department is committed to working with the HSE and the broader disability sector in order to ensure that valued service providers receive the funding they need to continue to deliver quality services and supports to disabled people in Ireland.

The Department provides funding to the HSE to deliver specialist disability services either directly or via Section 38 and Section 39 voluntary sector organisations. While this Department sets the strategy, policy direction and the overall allocation for the disability sector, funding allocations to individual service providers is an operational matter for the HSE as the funding authority.

In 2026 we are providing €3.9 billion for HSE Specialist Disability Services, an increase of €628m, or almost 20% over 2025. This is the largest ever increase in funding for Disability Services. It follows significant year on year increases resulting in an overall increase of €1.85bn or 91% since 2020.
The allocation of this funding is for the HSE to determine in line with funding requests received by Section 38 and Section 39 voluntary sector organisations.

question.p: 1620. Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will develop proposals to address the lack of funding for transport and replacement of vehicles for disability day services in section 39 organisations; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20500/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Specialist Disability Budget supports a range of services funded through the HSE and delivered by Section 38 and Section 39 organisations, as well as the HSE. This includes, among other services and supports, Day Services and Rehabilitative Training for people with specialist disability service requirements.

The provision of transport is not part of core services funded by the HSE. As a general rule, public transport is used in all circumstances where it is an option. This is in keeping with the principle of mainstreaming, with a clear focus on ensuring persons with a disability have access to the normal range of services and participate in community life as far as possible. In general, day service users are in receipt of disability allowance and are automatically entitled to the Free Travel Pass.

Under Pillar 5 of the Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030, the Department of Transport has lead responsibility for reducing and, where possible, eliminating transport barriers faced by disabled people. Under Pillar 5, there is a commitment to personal mobility, and supporting those who cannot use or easily access any public transport through the provision of enhanced personal mobility options.

It is recognised that viable public transport options are not always available throughout the country and that transport support needs vary between individuals. In the absence of transport options being made available by the National Transport Authority (NTA), some transport supports are provided by the HSE or funded agencies on a case-by-case basis, and a variety of transport solutions are pursued in different Health Regions. These include travel training to enable public transport to be used, where appropriate, local transport such as Local Link, private bus transport and some service providers provide transport where capacity exists.
As this question refers to service matters, I have asked the Health Service Executive (HSE) to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

1624. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on a matter (details supplied). [20551/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1621, 1622, 1623 and 1624 together.

The Department cannot comment on individual cases such as the one referred to the Deputy and is not in a position to comment on cases which may be under investigation by An Garda Síochána. Similarly, Tusla does not comment on individual cases. This is to protect the privacy of the children and families that Tusla work with and this is critically important in the subject matters with which Tusla are involved.
Information on Children Missing from Care, Child Trafficking and Child Sexual Exploitation is set out below.

The Department shares the wider public concern about the increased risk of child and human trafficking, particularly in the context of increased movement of people globally. Children in the care of the State are some of the most vulnerable individuals in our society. The Department and Tusla are committed to promoting safe and high-quality practice in all areas of alternative care, including in relation to protecting this vulnerable cohort from the risk of sexual exploitation and child trafficking.

Tusla and An Garda Síochána respond to all missing from care incidents under the Missing Children in Care Joint Protocol which is currently under review. Missing from care under the Joint Protocol is defined as “when the child's whereabouts are not known and the child's Absence Management Plan indicates concern for the child's safety”.

Most Children Missing from Care are aged 16/17 years of age. In general, it is more common for children from Tusla’s Separated Children Seeking International Protection (SCSIP) services to go missing. Children in mainstream Tusla services also go missing from care but more often is it on a temporary basis.

Children from both services can go missing from placement for short periods of time and on a frequent basis and responses to such episodes are managed in line with each child’s Absence Management Plan which clearly sets out the response from the services to these episodes. These episodes may include testing of boundaries such as breaking curfews or may be for more concerning reasons. When the episodes are of concern, staff respond in line with the Joint Protocol. Equally, children from both services can go missing for longer periods of time and equally in these instances staff respond to these episodes in line with the Joint Protocol.

The Garda are notified once a child is deemed missing – and once a child has been reported absent, the Gardaí have primary responsibility for investigating the child’s whereabouts. The Garda National Missing Person`s Unit has oversight over a Garda investigation on the ongoing attempts to locate the child, including liaison with Interpol, if there is a concern that the child has left the jurisdiction. This can include local police checks with relevant local authorities to assist the Garda investigation and liaison with Tusla.

The EU Migration Pact legislation was passed in 2024. It will, when implemented via the International Protection Bill, 2025 include children aged six and above to enhance protections for children and combat child trafficking and this will include biometric procedures and fingerprinting which will also assist in tracing Children Missing from Care.

The Child Sexual Exploitation Procedure was developed in 2021 to assist Tusla social workers, care workers in recognising indicators of child sexual exploitation, making appropriate referrals where such concerns exist and responding to cases where children may be at risk of sexual exploitation. This procedure is currently under review.

The procedure, Operation Cosnaím, sets out the pathways for reporting concerns of child sexual exploitation to An Garda Síochána, for children who are in the care of Tusla and for children who reside in a community setting, through the local Garda District. As part of “Operation Cosnaím” all concerns of suspected child trafficking and/or child sexual exploitation regarding a child who is in the care of Tusla, must be notified to a centralised point in the Garda National Protective Services Bureau.

Tusla continues to take the issue of potential Child Sexual Exploitation and Child Trafficking very seriously, including working with An Garda Síochána as required. All children are screened for indicators of trafficking; there is no mechanism currently to cross reference those with indicators of trafficking with those that go missing. Advances with Tusla’s electronic case management system may assist with this in the future. However, engagements are on-going with An Garda Síochána in relation to data collation and alignment, and to ensure Tusla are recording this data appropriately and through its Case Management System.

The Agency assessment relates to the ongoing safety and welfare of the child where trafficking may be one significant complicating factor in keeping a child safe from future harm. Tusla does not keep data on “trafficking risk assessments”. Where indicators of trafficking have been identified, the appropriate safety planning and Absence management plans are in place and An Garda Síochána notifications are made where appropriate.

Where no specific practice reviews were completed of trafficking, the Tusla Practice Assurance and Service Monitoring Team completed a ‘Review of the reporting and process management of concerns of child sexual exploitation and trafficking from Children’s Residential Centre’s in 2024. This examined the Agency’s Child Sexual Abuse Exploitation Procedure (August 2021).

Tusla currently provides extensive training to staff to support them on the identification of indicators of trafficking. This supports them in forming a suspicion of crime and notifying An Garda Síochána who are responsible for confirming if trafficking has occurred. Tusla has partnered with MECPATHS, a non - profit organisation which focuses specifically on the issue of child trafficking in Ireland. MECPATHS has been delivering ‘Hidden in Plain Sight (HIPS): Shining a light on Child Trafficking in Ireland’ training to Tusla, since late 2022. This collaboration is intended to raise awareness and provide frontline staff across Tusla services with training on Child Trafficking in Ireland, thus increasing the agency’s capacity to respond to this evolving area of need. Nearly 1,000 staff including those working in Residential Care, Fostering and Adoption, intake and duty, and the Unaccompanied Minors and Separated Children Seeking International Protection Team (SCSIP Service) participated in MECPATHS workshops. This training continues in 2026.
In respect of measures put in place to reduce number of children missing from care and child trafficking/exploitation, Tusla has confirmed the following:

• Regular engagement (sometimes daily) at operational level takes place with colleagues in Northern Ireland. Tusla also has an Operational Working Group with the Department of Health in Northern Ireland which meets 2-3 times per year. The purpose of the group is to formalise communication and joint working between Tusla, the relevant Northern Ireland Trusts, and the Strategic Planning and Performance Group of the Department of Health in Northern Ireland.

• Building on the already strong working relationship between Tusla and An Garda Siochána, an additional strategic focus was introduced through the establishment of an integrated management forum. This forum, developed specifically under the Tusla Separated Children Seeking International Protection Service, aims to enhance coordination in responses to missing children and those at risk of trafficking or exploitation, and facilitates the sharing of expertise, emerging trends, and learning with An Garda Siochána’s National Protective Services.
• A monthly internal Missing Children Forum is chaired by the Tusla Area Manager and includes representatives from Tusla’s Out of Hours Service and the Tusla National Garda Liaison Office.

• The Garda Tusla Joint Protocol is applied to any child who goes missing and regular strategy meetings take place. It is the role of An Garda Siochána to locate a missing person and Tusla share any relevant information to assist them in this role.
• The relevant case files for all missing children are allocated to a social worker to ensure regular communication is taking place with An Garda Siochána.

Tusla continues to work with Department of Justice, Migration and Home Affairs and others on preparing for the implementation of the Human Trafficking and Sexual Offences Act and the upcoming National Referral Mechanism which will see Tusla acquire new legal duties and responsibilities under its function as a Competent Authority. Other Competent Authorities will include the An Garda Síochána, Health Service Executive, Workplace Relations Commission, Department of Justice, and some others (to be confirmed).

Circular 01/2020 on Procedures for Offsetting the Emissions Associated with Official Air Travel requires the Department to record all official air travel, calculate the emissions associated with the air travel undertaken, and financially offset those emissions via the Climate Action Fund.

These calculations and payments are made annually and cover emissions from the preceding year. In that regard, travel undertaken in 2026, including all travel related to St. Patrick's Day, will be recorded on an ongoing basis and offset next year.

question.p: 1634. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality further to Parliamentary Question No's 731, 732 and 733 of 3 March 2026, if she is satisfied that cases will be allocated to non-social workers; who the professionals are she cites, as to who's cases will be allocated to; the level of oversight by social workers; the way in which that oversight will be conducted and the frequency given the very serious issues highlighted by the HIQA report into Tusla Dublin North City and the very impact of an absence of oversight; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20476/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The critical importance of children in care and children in need of child welfare and protection services being allocated a social worker is paramount, and the Department is working closely with Tusla on the recruitment and retention of social workers.

In 2025, Tusla received 106,444 referrals to its service, representing a 10% (9,778) increase since 2024, and 53% (36,732) increase since 2020. At the end of 2025, there were 5,879 children and young people in the care of Tusla. 86% are growing up and being cared for in foster homes across the country and 10% are living in a residential home. The other 4% are living in other settings (including disability centres, supported lodgings, special emergency arrangements etc). Of the 5,879 children in care above, 98% (5,777) have an allocated key worker. Social workers represented 89% (5,165) of the key workers allocated with the other 11% (612) being another qualified professional.

In 2025 there were also 23,612 children nationally that were open to child protection and welfare services, 77% (18,214) of these children had an allocated key worker. Social workers represent 82% (14,928) key workers allocated, with the other 18% (3,286) being another qualified professional. For the 5,398 children and young people who do not have a specific dedicated key worker allocated to them, available workers are assigned on a temporary basis and supports are provided to meet their immediate needs. Oversight of their case continues to be provided by social work management during this time. It is important to note that where a child is found to be at immediate risk, an immediate response is provided.

Tusla is committed to ensure that every child in care or open to its child protection services is allocated a key worker. The key worker works with the child and those in their life to collaboratively plan for that child and ensure that their needs are met in the long term including their health, education, social and family. They also complete any statutory responsibilities that protect and support the child. Where possible, the key workers will be social workers, but in line with Tusla’s move towards more integrated and multidisciplinary working, they may also be other qualified professionals such as social care leaders, social care workers, family support workers, therapists etc.

In respect of management of unallocated cases, all urgent cases receive an immediate social work service. Unallocated cases are new referrals but will also include cases where the social worker is no longer working on the case - due to illness, maternity leave or leaving the service. These cases are reviewed regularly to see if a case needs a more urgent response. Cases that are 'active on duty' may receive home visits, to complete assessments or to prepare care plans. Examples of actions being undertaken include telephone calls relating to concern, visits to see the child, completing initial assessments and where a child is in care, completing child in care reviews or care plans.

Reflecting an ongoing changing environment and social work vacancies, Tusla has moved to a more multi-disciplinary way of working with children now allocated to social workers and other professional grades where necessary and appropriate to ensure they have the support of a key worker. All children continue to be overseen by social work management. It is important to note that while cases can be allocated to other professionals, these cases are still overseen by Social Workers.
There are challenges around the current level of social work vacancies in Tusla and the challenges in recruiting sufficient numbers of social workers into Tusla.

Measures to reduce caseload pressure in Tusla have focused on recruitment of social work and social care staff at home and abroad and increased training places for social work and social care staff. With Tusla support, training places for social workers have almost doubled in the past 5 years and by the end of 2025, 340 placements in Tusla with further expansion planned. A social work apprenticeship scheme was introduced with 34 apprenticeships starting in 2024, 71 in 2025 and places expected to rise to 100 in 2026. A similar approach is planned for social care. Tusla’s continues to provide retention supports and management and teamwork training for workers so that caseloads are managed effectively and equitably. Tusla has also provided additional resources for more local supports including community and voluntary programmes to help assess and support cases more effectively.

The combined efforts on recruitment and retention have seen the Agency-wide social work and social care staffing numbers rise from 2,830.17 whole time equivalent (WTE) at the end of 2022 to 3.152.86 WTE at the end of 2025 representing an increase of 11% (322.15 WTE) over the 3 years. Across 2025 the increase was 4% (119.33 WTE).

Moving forward, Tusla’s reform programme will promote greater equity, capacity and quality across its regions and networks, with more consistent structures and spans of control, and an open and transparent approach to more equitable resource allocation. Both Tusla and the Department recognise that, as with any large-scale change, changes will take time to fully bed in, but Tusla teams will be working locally and nationally to monitor implementation closely and resolve issues quickly where they arise.

question.p: 1635. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her views on the need to ensure that adequate space is available for the second year of ECCE; if she has heard reports of parents finding that schools do not want to take children until they are five years of age but creches do not have the space for older children and do not feel that preschool is fit for children over five years; her views on the need for continuity of early years education and care for children; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20772/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme is a universal two-year pre-school programme available to all children within the eligible age range of 2 years and 8 months to 5 years and 6 months. A child must not reach 5 years and 6 months on or before June 30th of each programme year. The upper age limit of 5 years and 6 months for ECCE was set in consultation with the Department of Education and ensures that children transition into primary school with their peers.

The upper age-limit for the ECCE programme is consistent with the definition of a “pre-school child” in the primary legislation (the Child Care Act 1991), which is a “child who has not attained the age of six years, and who is not attending a recognised school”.

An independent review of the ECCE Programme was completed last year with the final report published October 2024. This review examined how the Programme is currently functioning and identified enhancements that could be made based on comprehensive stakeholder engagement with children, parents, ECCE providers and educators. Enhancements to the second year of ECCE were examined as part of this review.
Improving access to quality and affordable early learning and childcare is a key priority of Government.

Early learning and childcare capacity is increasing. Data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile 2024/25 shows that the estimated number of enrolments increased by approximately 25% from the 2021/22 programme year.

In some instances, it appears that demand for early learning and childcare remains higher than available supply in certain parts of the country, although analysis undertaken by the Department indicates that this primarily relates to full day provision for children of pre-ECCE age and that lack of supply of sessional pre-school places delivering the ECCE programme is not a widespread issue.

The Department funds 30 City/County Childcare Committees, which provide support and assist families and early learning and childcare providers. The network of 30 City/County Childcare Committees across the country can assist in identifying vacant places in services for children and families who need them and engage proactively with services to explore possibilities for expansion among services, particularly where there is unmet need.
Parents experiencing difficulty in relation to their early learning and childcare needs should contact their local City/County Childcare Committee for assistance.

question.p: 1636. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason for the refusal of an application to the mother and baby institutions payment scheme (details supplied); the reason incomplete or deficient historical records are being relied upon as grounds for exclusion despite acknowledged issues with the accuracy of such records; to set out the review or independent appeal mechanism that is available to applicants who cannot afford to pursue a High Court challenge in order to contest a refusal under the scheme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20788/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: While I try to be helpful at all times in the parliamentary process, the Deputy will be aware that I cannot be involved in individual cases and cannot comment on same.

The legislation underpinning the Payment Scheme - the Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme Act 2023 - provides for the explicit independence of the Chief Deciding Officer in administering the application process and making decisions on applications. Therefore, it would be inappropriate for me to engage in the process in relation to the status of individual applications. That said, I will try to be helpful in general terms.

In line with the Act, determinations are made based on evidence available to the Scheme including records held by state bodies, religious orders and other relevant archives. These records form the primary evidential basis for the examination of applications to the Scheme.

In the small number of instances where historical records may be incomplete or limited, the Scheme considers all available documentation in accordance with the framework set out in the Act. Thus, if an applicant has records or information that might be helpful in determining a residence in an institution in the Scheme, the Payment Scheme Office will be happy to consider it. Sometimes the Payment Scheme Office may call an applicant to clarify details and Section 23 provides that the Chief Deciding Officer may request that an applicant provide further information by way of affidavit, where he or she considers that the information available is incomplete or otherwise insufficient for the purpose of examining the application.
These measures are intended to ensure that applications can be considered as fully and fairly as possible.

Where an applicant is dissatisfied with a decision on their application, they can request a review. Requesting a review is a very straightforward process for the applicant but it rightly triggers a very comprehensive assessment of all aspects of the application within the Payment Scheme Office. After a review, if an applicant is dissatisfied with a review decision they may request an appeal. Appeals Officers operate independently outside of the Department. Further information on how to request a review of an application to the Scheme can be found on the Payment Scheme website here: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-children-disability-and-equality/publications/requesting-a-review-or-an-appeal/[]

All information on the Scheme, and the application process, can be found at the dedicated Payment Scheme website - gov.ie/paymentscheme. Resources include an information booklet, questions and answers, and short 'how to' videos on the straightforward application process. A Helpline is also available at +353 1 522 9992. Applicants will be supported throughout the application process with information and advice as and when they may need it.

Finally, I would like to advise you that public representatives can contact the Payment Scheme Office via a dedicated email address paymentschemereps@dcde.gov.ie if they are assisting constituents in relation to the Scheme.

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1640 and 1641 together.
Foster carers play a vital role in enabling our most vulnerable children to live in a safe, secure and stable home environment.

The foster care allowance was last increased at the end of 2024, meaning that foster carers now receive between €20,800 and €22,100 per year for each child in their care, depending on the age of the child.

The Programme for Government 2025 introduced a number of commitments relating to foster care. This included commitments to increase the foster care allowance, as well as examine and develop a pension solution for foster carers, in recognition of the enormous contribution they make to vulnerable children in our society.

In addition, work is underway within the Department on the development of a National Policy Framework for Alternative Care, which will deliver on a separate Programme for Government commitment to develop a national plan on alternative care. Officials in the Department are developing this Framework on the basis of evidence and robust consultation with stakeholders, including foster carers, care experienced individuals, and the public.

question.p: 1642. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if consideration will be given to releasing the records of the Mother and Baby Homes Commission of Investigation, with proper redactions of personal information; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20855/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: It is important to clarify that the records of the Mother and Baby Homes Commission of Investigation are already fully available to survivors seeking their own information.

The arrangements for preserving the records compiled by a Commission of Investigation in the course of its work are prescribed in Section 43(2) of the Commissions of Investigation Act 2004. This provides that, prior to its dissolution, a Commission must deposit all records with the prescribed Minister. On the expiry of a 30-year period thereafter, such records will be transferred to the National Archives and access is regulated in accordance with the National Archives Act, 1986.

Commission archives deposited with the Minister under the 2004 Act are subject to a general principle of confidentiality. Section 11(1) specifies that a Commission shall conduct its investigation in private unless certain conditions for hearing evidence in public are met. Section 11(3) of the 2004 Act prohibits any person (including the Minister) from disclosing or publishing any evidence given or the contents of any document produced by a witness while giving evidence in private, with very limited exceptions. The general principle of confidentiality that applies to a Commission’s archives has been upheld in the courts.

In 2020 the Commission of Investigation into Mother and Baby Homes informed the Department that it had created a database in relation to the mothers and children who passed through 15 of the 18 institutions under investigation. The Commission indicated it believed it would be a valuable resource to assist information and tracing services for mothers and children, but it also felt it was compelled by law to permanently redact much valuable information within.

To ensure that this database information could be preserved and be available to survivors directly, the Government brought forward legislation - the Commission of Investigation (Mother and Baby Homes and certain related Matters) Records, and another Matter, Act 2020. This Act provided for the deposit of the Commission's database with Tusla, in addition to transferring a copy of this database, together with the Commission's entire archive of records, to the Minister for Children.

Legislation enables the Department to process subject access requests from people who wish to seek access to personal information that may be contained within the database and the broader records of the Commission archives.

Following engagement with the Office of the Attorney General, the Data Protection Commissioner and independent experts in the area of GDPR, the Department published information for individuals including its privacy notice indicating what personal data the Department holds and how it processes it, and a guide on how to request access to personal information (Subject Access Request (SAR)). A dedicated phone line (01-2376001) provides information for callers on the SAR process, and information on this is also regularly communicated to survivors and former residents via quarterly updates pursuant to the Government Action Plan for Survivors. More information on how to access personal data which may be held in the records of the Mother and Baby Homes Commission of Investigation can be found here www.gov.ie/en/department-of-children-disability-and-equality/organisation-information/transfer-of-records-from-the-mother-and-baby-homes-commission-of-investigation/

For the avoidance of any doubt, it is important to clarify that the Commission was not in possession of original records and, therefore, no original records were impacted by the provisions in the 2004 legislation. State records remain in the possession of the relevant statutory body and appropriate access is regulated in accordance with relevant statute.

One of the seven major commitments in the aforementioned Government's Action Plan for Survivors and Former Residents of Mother and Baby and County Home Institutions was access to identity information. The Birth Information and Tracing Act 2022 provides a full and clear right of access to birth certificates and birth and early life information for all persons who were adopted, boarded out, nursed out or the subject of an illegal birth registration, or who otherwise have questions in relation to their origins. The 2022 Act enables Tusla to process the Commission database for the purpose of responding to requests from relevant persons for personal information. To date, under the Birth Information and Tracing Act, Tusla and the AAI have responded to over 17,500 requests for identity information.

question.p: 1643. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding the actions outlined for the childminding sector (details supplied), broken down per each action, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20869/26]

speech.from: Minister for Children, Disability and Equality
speech.p: The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 set out a pathway for the extension of regulation to childminders. As a result of the commencement of the relevant parts of the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Childminding Services Regulations, which came into effect on 30 September 2024, childminders are now able to apply to register with Tusla.

The introduction of the Childminding-specific Regulations marked the on-time completion of Phase 1 of the Plan and the commencement of Phase 2 (the transition phase). We are now in a 3-year transition period, to September 2027, during which childminders are being encouraged and supported to register, but registration is not yet mandatory. This phased approach aims to facilitate the largest possible number of childminders to enter the regulated sector, the sphere of quality assurance, and access to Government subsidies, while recognising the time and supports required for childminders to learn about and prepare for registration.
The table below sets out the progress to date in the phased implementation of the National Action Plan for Childminding.

td.p: Research and analyse numbers of childminders likely to come into the scope of regulation
Analyse likely increase in NCS costs
Establish Advisory group on regulation and inspection
Draft childminder specific regulations with consultation
Develop an appropriate and proportionate inspection system

question.p: 1645. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Health to confirm that funding is available for the implementation of options B and C outlined in the HIQA report into health services in the Mid-West region; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19621/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: In December 2025, I received Government support for proposals to adopt a blended approach to the progression of Options A, B and C from the HIQA review, to inform investment and to provide a short-, medium- and long-term view to how we plan for and deliver healthcare services for the people of the Mid West region.

Option A, as presented by HIQA, is being progressed at pace, with 128 additional beds having already been delivered in the Mid West since 2023. All avenues are being explored to deploy additional bed capacity as soon as possible. Current plans to increase capacity at University Hospital Limerick (UHL) will deliver up to 306 beds by the end of 2029. With additional beds planned for other Model 2 Hospitals in Ennis, Nenagh and St John’s, this would represent 420 additional beds in the region from 2024 to the end of the Acute Hospital Inpatient Bed Capacity Expansion Plan in 2031.
Investment in the hospitals in the Mid West region has increased from €370 million in 2019 to €689 million in 2024. The UHL budget has increased from €265 million to €507 million in the same period.

Staffing at the hospital has grown by 56% since December 2019. This includes 321 more WTE doctors (including consultants), 597 more nurses and midwives, as well as 190 more health and social care professionals.
The Capital Investment drawn down between 2020 and 2025 for the Mid West region was €369.2 million. Of that, €228.6 million was invested in UHL.

In addition, the HSE recently acquired a site at Raheen in Limerick for €14 million to further progress Option B of the HIQA review. Work is underway to appoint a project board to judiciously consider what services be retained on the Dooradoyle campus, which can be relocated to the new Raheen site, and which services can be relocated to Ennis, St John’s or Nenagh.

It would be premature to comment further on funding for the implementation of Options B and C, as I would not wish to pre-empt the finalisation of the strategic plan for the region for the near, medium and longer term. I will return to Government with a strategic plan for the services of the Mid West region later this year and how that aligns with funding allocated in this NDP cycle 2025-2030 or following NDP cycles.
Capital and current funding requirements will be determined as needed for individual, iterative and phased proposals as is the case for all capital and service developments.

question.p: 1646. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Health if there are any discussions or plans to move the HSE Environmental Health Inspectors under the remit of the Food Safety Authority; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20059/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Health
speech.p: The Health Service Executive’s National Environmental Health Service (NEHS) has a broad statutory remit which extends beyond food safety controls and includes public health functions such as tobacco and alcohol control, sunbeds, cosmetics and other environmental health activities.
There are no discussions or plans at present to transfer Environmental Health Officers from the HSE to the Food Safety Authority of Ireland.

question.p: 1647. Deputy Natasha Newsome Drennan asked the Minister for Health the work being carried out to improve labelling of origin on imported food products; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20461/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Health
speech.p: The labelling of food, including the indication of country of origin or place of provenance, is governed primarily by EU legislation, in particular Regulation (EU) No. 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers (FIC).

Under FIC Regulation (EU) No. 1169/2011, the declaration of the country of origin or place of provenance on food labels is not mandatory for all foods. However, where a food label includes any suggestion or indication of origin, the relevant country of origin rules must be complied with.
In addition, specific EU requirements apply to the mandatory declaration of origin for certain meats, including beef and fresh, chilled and frozen meat from sheep, pigs, poultry and goats.

Where country of origin or place of provenance rules apply, it is the responsibility of the food business operator to ensure that the information provided is accurate, clear and not misleading to the consumer. These requirements apply both to food prepacked for the final consumer and to food supplied as an ingredient to other food businesses, which includes imported foods.

In 2020, the European Commission put forward proposals to amend certain aspects of the FIC Regulation which included origin labelling. However, these proposals have not been progressed to-date by the Commission. Until such labelling revisions are agreed, the existing legal framework continues to apply.

In Ireland, the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) has statutory responsibility, under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, for the enforcement of food legislation, including food labelling requirements. Enforcement is carried out primarily through service contracts with official agencies acting on behalf of the FSAI, including the Health Service Executive, the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine and the Sea Fisheries Protection Authority.

Compliance with food labelling and origin requirements, including those applicable to imported foods, is monitored and verified through routine inspections and targeted official controls carried out by these official agencies.
