1945. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health if the laboratory verification and validation processes for SMA and SCID screening have been fully completed; and if not, when they will be finalised. [19688/26]

1946. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health whether all newly recruited staff for the expanded newborn screening programme have completed training; and when the finalised screening and treatment pathways for SMA and SCID will be published. [19689/26]

1947. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health to provide a breakdown of the way in which the €1.4 million allocated in Budget 2024 for SMA/SCID implementation has been spent to date; and whether any additional funding will be required to ensure timely commencement. [19690/26]

2027. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health when the expanded newborn bloodspot screening for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) will be fully operational nationwide; the steps being taken to ensure timely rollout across all maternity units; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20000/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1944 to 1947, inclusive, and 2027 together.

As Minister for Health, I am determined to support our screening programmes, which are a valuable part of our health service, enabling early treatment and care for many people, and improving the overall health of our population.

Currently, all babies (between 3 and 5 days old) are offered newborn bloodspot screening (generally known as the ‘heel prick’ test), which tests for nine rare but serious conditions that are treatable if detected early in life. The Programme for Government commits to continually reviewing the number of conditions babies are screened for.

Incremental progress continues to be made on the expansion of the National Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme (NNBSP). In 2023, two recommendations from the National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC) on the addition of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) and Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) to the NNBSP were approved.

In Budget 2024, an additional €1.4 million of new development funding was provided to support the SMA/SCID implementation process. This included the recruitment of additional staff, procurement of required machinery and purchase of test kits to enable testing to commence.

In terms of timelines, I am pleased to confirm that the implementation process is in its final stage, with screening for both SCID and SMA expected to be fully completed and offered to all babies born in Ireland in April 2026.

I am acutely aware of how difficult it is for parents, families and children who have received a diagnosis of a rare disease, and how challenging daily life can be for them. This is why I remain committed to the further expansion of screening in Ireland in accordance with internationally accepted criteria and best practice.

summary.i: Questions Nos. 1945 to 1947, inclusive, answered with Question No. 1944.

question.p: 1948. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the expected timelines and criteria for considering further conditions for inclusion in the National Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme, in line with the Programme for Government commitment to ongoing expansion. [19691/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: As Minister for Health, I am determined to support our screening programmes, which are a valuable part of our health service, enabling early treatment and care for many people, and improving the overall health of our population.

Currently, all newborn babies (between 3 and 5 days old) are offered newborn bloodspot screening (generally known as the ‘heel prick’), which tests for nine rare but serious conditions that are treatable, if detected early in life. The Programme for Government commits to continually reviewing the number of conditions babies are screened for.

I would highlight that any changes to Ireland’s screening programmes will be facilitated through established protocols. The National Screening Advisory Committee (NSAC) is the independent expert group that considers proposed changes to Ireland’s screening programmes. NSAC assesses the evidence in a robust and transparent manner, and against internationally accepted criteria, before making recommendations to myself as Minister for Health.

The rigorous processes utilised by NSAC are critical to ensure that our screening programmes are effective, quality assured and operating to safe standards, and that the benefits of screening outweigh the harms.

Incremental progress continues to be made on the expansion of the National Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme (NNBSP). In 2023, two recommendations from NSAC on the addition of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) and Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) to the NNBSP were approved.
In Budget 2024, an additional €1.4 million of new development funding was provided to support the SCID and SMA implementation process.
In terms of timelines, I am pleased to confirm that the implementation process is in its final stage, with screening for both SCID and SMA expected to be introduced in April 2026.
Once both conditions have been fully implemented, the number of conditions screened for in Ireland will increase to 11.
In terms of calls for the further expansion of the NNBSP, in 2024, NSAC established a Newborn Screening Subgroup to provide additional expertise to support the Committee’s decision-making processes.

In May 2025, the Newborn Screening Subgroup completed work on developing a framework for the prioritisation of proposals related to newborn screening. This framework was subsequently used to identify additional conditions, which have now been referred by NSAC to the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) to undergo a Health Technology Assessment (HTA), as resources allow.

HTAs facilitate the assessment of relevant evidence and knowledge on the effects and consequences of healthcare technologies in order to guide decisions regarding the appropriate use of technology and efficient allocation of resources. They involve a multi-disciplinary assessment of the clinical, economic, ethical, legal and societal perspectives that may be impacted by the introduction of a new technology. They are time-intensive and rigorous processes.

I am glad to note that the first of the aforementioned HTAs, to consider the addition of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia to the NNBSP, has now commenced and I look forward to receiving a recommendation from NSAC in this regard before the end of the year.

I am acutely aware of how difficult it is for parents, families and children who have received a diagnosis of a rare disease, and how challenging daily life can be for them. This is why I remain committed to the further expansion of screening in Ireland in accordance with internationally accepted criteria and best practice.

question.p: 1954. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health if she will establish a National Radiotherapy Equipment Replacement Programme to provide predictable, coordinated investment and ensure equitable access to modern radiotherapy regardless of location. [19702/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: Under the National Plan for Radiation Oncology (NPRO), an equipment replacement programme is currently in place across St Lukes Rathgar, St. James’s Hospital campus and Beaumont Hospital along with a phased expansion at Beaumont. The replacement programme is being progressed under the National Development Plan and is included in the Capital Plan 2026 and the Health Sectoral Plan 2026 -2030.

There are 23 Linear Accelerators (linacs) ranging in age from three to 18 years old, located across five public hospital locations: St Luke's Rathgar, Beaumont, St James, Galway University Hospital and Cork University Hospital.

State of the art radiation oncology centres opened in Cork and Galway in 2019 and 2023 respectively, representing €120 million capital investment. The linear accelerators at St Luke's Rathgar, Beaumont and St James’s Hospitals were installed between 2008 and 2016.

The HSE advises that the typical lifespan of a Linac is 10 - 15 years, although some can be used for longer. The lifespan of a machine depends on many factors, including the type of linac, how it is used, how it is maintained and the manufacturer support lifespan including software upgrades.

The Preliminary Design process for linac replacement within the St Luke’s Radiation Oncology Network in Dublin is ongoing. In addition, tenders for the main contract for the Beaumont Phase 2 expansion and replacement project are due to issue in the coming weeks.

question.p: 1955. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the immediate actions that are being taken to address the fact that 6,175 people breached the recommended 28-day wait time for an urgent colonoscopy between January and November 2025, given that these are symptomatic patients for whom delayed diagnosis increases the risk of later stage cancer. [19703/26]
1957. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the assessment her Department has made of the impact on cancer outcomes arising from delays in accessing urgent colonoscopy. [19705/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health (Deputy Jennifer Carroll MacNeill)
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1955 and 1957 together.

Colonoscopies play a key role in the diagnosis of colorectal (bowel) cancer. Under three successive national cancer strategies, the first being launched in 1996, there has been a marked improvement overall in survival rates for patients after receiving a colorectal cancer diagnosis, with 60% of all colorectal cancer patients living 10 years after diagnosis in 2014-2018, compared to 46% in 1994-1998.

The HSE recognises the importance of providing timely access to colonoscopy for patients and is working to significantly increase endoscopic activity. The 2026 HSE National Service Plan aims to increase attendances by 6,927 or 6.6% from the 2025 outturn to 111,894. HSE core activity will be augmented by the Waiting Time Action Plan, published in January this year, as part of this Government’s ongoing commitment to improving access to hospital care and sustainably reducing waiting times for patients. Under the Plan the National Treatment Purchase Fund has undertaken to provide some 20,000 endoscopy procedures in 2026.

The HSE are also implementing a range of additional measures to enhance capacity including the promotion of Faecal Immunochemical Testing (FIT) for triage, Capsule Endoscopy for colon capsule procedures and the development of an Advanced Nurse Practitioner led Transnasal Endoscopy (TNE) pilot at St Vincent’s University Hospital.

The Deputy might also note that in Pillar 2 of the Waiting Time Action Plan, Enabling Patient Care, there are two specific actions relating to endoscopy; the implementation of an eReferral system and a nationally procured Endoscopy Reporting System. These developments will enable and streamline the appropriate management of patients scheduled for colonoscopy services.

The HSE's National Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) has advised that based on current data, it will take several years before any impacts of the current capacity constraints might become apparent. The HSE will continue to implement mitigation measures and to ensure that patients referred for urgent review are seen as quickly as possible.

speech.p: It is acknowledged that many patients are still waiting too long for hospital appointments and treatments. I am conscious of the burden that this places on patients and their families.

I am focused on having a public healthcare service in which everyone has timely access to high-quality care including diagnostics, where and when they need it. This will require the health service to deliver more core activity through improved productivity and efficiencies, through ongoing reform and new enabling supports, and through targeted additional capacity.
In this regard, additional endoscopic activity is targeted in the 2026 HSE National Service Plan with attendances to increase by 6,927 or 6.6% from the 2025 outturn to 111,894.

HSE core activity will be augmented by the Waiting Time Action Plan, published in January this year, as part of this Government’s ongoing commitment to improving access to hospital care and sustainably reducing waiting times for patients. Under the Plan the National Treatment Purchase Fund has undertaken to provide some 20,000 endoscopy procedures in 2026.

The Deputy might also note that in Pillar 2 of the Waiting Time Action Plan, Enabling Patient Care, there are two specific actions relating to endoscopy; the implementation of an eReferral system and a nationally procured Endoscopy Reporting System. These developments will enable and streamline the appropriate management of patients scheduled for colonoscopy services.

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Health (Deputy Jennifer Murnane O'Connor)
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1959 to 1961, inclusive, and 2007 to 2010, inclusive, together.

I recently published the draft national drugs strategy. The draft strategy sets out an integrated, equitable and evidence-based response to drug use, reflecting the Government’s commitment to a health-led approach.

A Public Consultation (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/consultations/draft-national-drugs-strategy-public-consultation/) on the draft strategy is now open and the public and stakeholders are encouraged to have their say.

The Dept has mandated the HSE health regions to create regional structures to coordinate the planning, funding and delivery of drug services - HSE and community-based - in order to address disparities in the prevalence of treatment for problem drug or alcohol use and to support the implementation of the national drugs strategy. The health regions will have a critical role in ensuring the planning and delivery of services are aligned with population need and resource allocation.

To support the mandate of the health regions, the Dept has commissioned an audit of drug services which examines the relationship between the demand for treatment and area deprivation. This study will be published shortly.

The governance remit of the health regions should be supported by engagement with stakeholders, including community-based services and drug task forces. A process will be put in place to review existing structures, with a view to strengthen the input to the planning and delivery of drug services, enhance the integration of community-based services within primary care and involve people with lived and living experience.
I encourage all stakeholders to contribute to the public consultation on the draft strategy, so that it is an effective and comprehensive response to drug and harmful alcohol use.

question.p: 1962. Deputy Danny Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Health for an update on a matter regarding the National Ambulance Service (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19722/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The National Ambulance Service (NAS) is committed to continued expansion of its frontline workforce in 2026 through a series of planned new developments. As part of this, the HSE has confirmed that full time, permanent contracts are available for all Year Three graduates completing the Paramedic programme with NAS in 2026.

Graduates play a vital role in maintaining workforce capacity by filling vacancies arising from retirements and promotions, as well as supporting the creation of new posts linked to new service development under the National Service Plan. It is essential that NAS can prioritise the placement of these graduates to fill roles in areas with the greatest operational need.

To ensure a fair and transparent allocation of permanent posts, graduates have been asked to apply through a confined internal competition. This approach is consistent with recruitment processes used elsewhere in the health service. Graduates have been asked to select their three preferred locations within a region, and every effort will be made to accommodate first preferences. Where vacancies are oversubscribed, the process being implemented will ensure a fair and equitable allocation of roles.

While completing their BSc. (Hon) in Paramedic Studies, student paramedics hold a Specified Purpose Contract (SPC). As NAS works to fill the permanent positions, year-three graduates have been given a 16-week extension to their SPC to ensure continuity of service and employment for the graduates.

question.p: 1976. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Health to review correspondence (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19826/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The Minister recognises the importance of providing the best care possible to patients with this condition. Women’s Health has been and will continue to be a focus of the Department. The Government has made real progress in improving the healthcare available to women in Ireland.

Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices; therefore, I have asked the HSE for an update in this matter.

The HSE has advised that it follows statutory processes around the addition of medicines to the reimbursement list/schemes. Under those statutory processes, the HSE is legally required to consider a range of criteria which include unmet need, clinical evidence, economic evidence, budget impact and the resources available when making reimbursement decisions (i.e. add a medicine to the reimbursement list). The reimbursement decisions have to be in line with the relevant legislation, namely the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 (the legislation the HSE operates under for pricing and reimbursement of medicines).

In accordance with the legislation, a medicine must have a marketing authorisation (licence) to be included in the formal list of reimbursable items. A pharmaceutical company can apply to the HSE for reimbursement for a specific indication (use) of a specific licensed medicine. Medicines can have more than one licensed (market authorised) indication and each indication represents a separate application.

The European Medicines Agency (EMA) is a centralised agency of the European Union (EU) responsible for the scientific evaluation, supervision and safety monitoring of medicines in the EU. The EMA plays an integral role in the authorisation of medicines in the EU via the centralised procedure. The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the competent authority responsible for the regulation of human medicines in Ireland. A company can submit an application for a marketing authorisation directly to the HPRA if the product in question is not required to be approved through the centralised procedure.

Controls are in place within PCRS on claiming processes to ensure that only HSE approved indications are reimbursed across a range of medicines. Controls are currently in place for the GLP-1 agonists to restrict reimbursement support to the HSE approved indications.

Reimbursement approval is in place for semaglutide (Ozempic®) for the treatment of adults with insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance or contraindications and in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes under the General Medical Services and Long Term Illness Scheme from the 1st September 2018.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists licensed in Ireland including Ozempic® do not currently have an EU marketing authorisation for the treatment of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) or similar endocrine conditions. Off-label prescribing of GLP-1 agonists are not supported for reimbursement under Community Drug Schemes.
It is incumbent on a company to apply to the appropriate regulatory body for a marketing authorisation to extend the licence for a GLP-1 receptor agonist for the treatment of PCOS.
Once this is granted the HSE will process and assess any pricing and reimbursement application ,if received from a company, as efficiently as possible.

question.p: 1983. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Health for an update on the negotiations around the inclusion of the shingles vaccine in the national immunisation programme; when she will make a decision on whether to include the shingles vaccine in the national immunisation programme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19852/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The immunisation programme in Ireland is based on the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice.

The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.

The Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) has carried out a Health Technology Assessment (HTA) on the herpes zoster vaccine which protects against shingles. A HTA is a multidisciplinary research process that collects and summarises information about a health technology. HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.

HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

While the vaccine is considered safe and effective, its protective effect diminishes over time. HIQA also noted the substantial budget impact associated with vaccination. If made available to everyone aged 65 and older, vaccination would cost €218 million over five years.

Whilst the HTA found that the introduction of the shingles vaccine was not cost effective based on the cost of the vaccine, it found that it could be cost effective for vaccination of those at 75 years and 80 years if the cost of the vaccine was reduced by 80%.

Given that the healthcare budget is finite and decisions regarding increased spending relating to a change in one area could impact the provision of other health technologies and treatments within the healthcare system, the cost-effectiveness must be considered in any decision-making process.

My Department considered the findings of this HTA in 2024 and determined that the introduction of the vaccine could be reconsidered when the cost effectiveness of the vaccine is confirmed as being more favourable

I can confirm that the introduction of the shingles vaccine to the immunisation schedule in Ireland is again being actively considered for a cohort of immunocompromised individuals, in line with NIAC advice and cognisant of the cost effectiveness of market pricing and available funding.

question.p: 1985. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Health the number of whole time equivalent staff in sexual health service delivery in the HSE, by CHO, in each of the years 2021 to 2025, and to-date in 2026, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19854/26]

1984. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Health the action she proposes to take to address the fact that Ireland has the lowest penetration of long acting HIV treatment at 1%; the measures she proposes to take to address logistical issues around the increased resource constraints around the additional staffing requirements in sexual health services; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19853/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1985 and 1984 together.

Sexual health is a priority for this Government and for the Department of Health. The Programme for Government, Securing Ireland’s Future, 2025, commits to various actions to support better access to care for sexual health. These include developing an HIV Action Plan, increasing the availability of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and reduce waiting times for access to it, in addition to the publication of a new Sexual Health Strategy, a process completed in 2025.

The new National Sexual Health Strategy, 2025-2035 (NSHS) and National Sexual Health Action Plan, 2025-2038 (NSHAP), commit to developing Models of Care for sexual health and for HIV, to develop an HIV Action Plan, as per the Programme for Government commitment, and to expand community options for the delivery of PrEP, including widening access through primary care and exploring digital options.
The NSHS and NSHAP (included in one document) can be accessed at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/healthy-ireland/policy-information/national-sexual-health-strategy-2025-2035/.

Work is commencing on the HIV Action Plan; a subgroup of the NSHS Implementation Group focussing on sexual health services has been convened and will oversee and co-ordinate drafting. A stakeholder consultation request has been shared with clinical, sexual health and public health experts, other relevant divisions of the HSE, community and research partners and representative organisations working with people at risk of and living with HIV.

HSE resources with regard to HIV care are available here: https://www2.hse.ie/conditions/hiv/ . In Ireland, in accordance with the Infectious Diseases Regulations, there is no charge to an individual for the treatment of HIV.

With respect to staffing in our national network of 23 STI clinics, additional staff to deliver HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) were allocated in 2019-2020 on the commencement of our national PrEP programme.

The CSO’s population estimates indicate that the population has grown from 4,958,500 people in April, 2019, the year that the PrEP programme commenced, to 5,458,600 people approximately in April 2025 (the most recent figures available). This indicates an increase of over 500,000 people from 2019 to the present.

In addition to demographic increase, the 2019-2026 time interval has also seen significant increases in STI and HIV diagnoses in 2022 and 2023, although rates have declined slightly in 2024 and 2025, largely as a result of significant decreases in gonorrhoea and chlamydia rates.

Clinical criteria for PrEP eligibility have also been widened, increasing the number of people eligible. The number of individuals re-imbursed for PrEP at least once expanding from 1763 in 2020 to 7,037 users by the end of 2025, a year in which an additional 2,196 new PrEP users were added.

The National Sexual Health Strategy acknowledges pressure on services. In order to expand PrEP services and provide additional supports to our rapidly growing population, a number of measures were taken.

There are currently 13 approved public PrEP services, located in public STI clinics, and 42 approved private or general practitioner (GP) PrEP providers. Appointments at the 13 public PrEP services are free of charge, however, the private providers charge for consultations. Free PrEP medication is available to all individuals who meet clinical eligibility criteria, attending HSE approved PrEP services.

Additional funding of €550,000, through Budget 2025, and an additional €100,000 in 2026, were allocated to further support delivery of the PrEP scheme. The total allocation for PrEP has therefore been increased to €6.55m in 2026. The 2025 allocation included funding for 7WTE to increase capacity for in-person appointments within the STI clinics delivering PrEP, with all staff in place, and increasing capacity for PrEP appointments, by October, 2025. .Additional staff to support the PrEP programme have also been of assistance in terms of the overall workload and mission of the clinics.

In order to further increase the number of providers, a PrEP competency framework and eLearning platform were developed; these can be accessed by GPs and other private providers with an interest in providing PrEP. Following the introduction of training, provider numbers have increased substantially in 2025, with 42 private services now delivering PrEP in early 2026, as compared with 17 in 2023. Additional services are undertaking the training currently.

Further review of HIV treatment, eligibility and access to PrEP and PEP are being considered as part of the development of the Models of Care for HIV and for sexual health and as part of the development process for the HIV Action Plan, as laid out in the NSHS and NSHAP.

With respect to HIV medications, the HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines, in accordance with the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013. The Minister for Health has no role in decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines.

For a medicine to be considered for inclusion on the reimbursement list, it is necessary for marketing authorisation holders of medicines to go through the formal pricing and reimbursement application processes with the HSE. The State encourages all pharmaceutical companies to submit timely applications for pricing and reimbursement of their drugs when they receive marketing authorisation from the European Commission.
The HSE maintains a tracker with information on the status of medicines pricing and reimbursement applications: www.sspcrs.ie/portal/rdt/pub/application/home.

As the details of HIV treatment regimens and staffing within public clinics providing sexual health related care, including the national network of STI clinics, HIV treatment centres and SATUs are clinical and service matters, I have also asked the HSE to provide additional information to the Deputy as soon as possible.

question.p: 1993. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health whether her Department or the Health Service Executive has undertaken any national or regional analysis examining the relationship between funded staff vacancy levels and agency staffing expenditure in the public health service; if such analysis has been undertaken, to provide the dates, methodology and key findings of that analysis; and if no such analysis has been undertaken, the reason the Department has not conducted such analysis given the scale of agency staffing expenditure within the publicly funded health system. [19885/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The Department of Health and the HSE actively examine, on an ongoing basis, the relationship between funded staffing levels, vacancies and agency expenditure as part of the health service’s workforce planning, financial oversight and agency expenditure cost reduction arrangements.

This work is being progressed through the Productivity and Savings Taskforce in 2026. As part of this process, all Health Regions and National Services have submitted agency expenditure reduction plans, setting out how agency usage will be reduced in the context of funded workforce levels, recruitment activity, staff absence and service demand. These plans have undergone a formal central assessment and approval by HSE National HR and National Finance.

In developing and assessing these plans, detailed national and regional analysis has been undertaken, including examination of agency spend drivers; agency spend as a proportion of overall pay; staff category profiles; on-framework versus off-framework agency usage; staff absence rates; net WTE changes and variances against WTE limits; and trend and pattern analysis linking vacancies, absence and agency expenditure. Priority issues identified through this analysis have been fed back to regions and are being addressed through targeted actions.

The implementation of these plans is now moving into a structured monitoring phase. For 2026, a maximum agency expenditure limit has been set across relevant HSE services, with specific limits by Health Region. Adherence to these limits is a core performance metric, supported by a developing suite of complementary indicators including vacancy and WTE metrics, agency conversion targets, absence rates and agency spend as a percentage of total pay. These measures are being monitored on a monthly basis and used to track progress against regional plans and to inform corrective action where required.

In parallel, the HSE’s National HR function routinely analyses vacancy levels, recruitment pipelines, workforce supply constraints and absence trends at both national and regional level, and this work directly informs regional workforce planning and agency reduction measures. Regional management teams also review vacancy and agency usage locally, recognising that while the underlying drivers are common across the health service, their scale and operational impact vary by region and service area.

This integrated approach reflects the move towards greater regional autonomy and accountability set out in the HSE’s 2026 National Service Plan. It ensures that the interaction between vacancies, recruitment and agency usage is continuously assessed through existing governance and performance management arrangements, with a clear focus on delivering sustained reductions in agency expenditure.

question.p: 1995. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the measures introduced since 2024 to reduce reliance on agency staffing within the public health service; the targets set by her Department or the Health Service Executive for reducing agency expenditure; the progress made against those targets to date; and the number of agency workers who have transitioned to direct employment contracts with the Health Service Executive under agency conversion initiatives. [19887/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health (Deputy Jennifer Carroll MacNeill)
speech.p: The HSE's 2024 National Service Plan (NSP) set a full year target for the reduction of pay costs for agency staff working in Department of Health funded services of €250m. In order to meet this target controls on the use of agency staff were introduced by the HSE in July 2025. These included:
• Restricting the authority to approve the use of agency staff to senior operational managers.
• A ban on the use of agency staff from providers not included on procurement frameworks.
• A ban on the use of agency staff in management and administrative functions.

By the end of 2024, pay costs for agency staff working in Department of Health funded HSE services had risen to €682m an increase of €52m on the 2023 figure. In 2025 pay costs for agency staff working in Department of Health funded HSE services had risen by a further €82m to €816m.

The HSE's 2026 NSP set an upper limit on agency costs of €720m. As part of the work of the Department of Health and the HSE's Productivity and Savings Taskforce the Regional Executive Officers responsible for the management of the HSE's Regional Health Authorities have been required to submit plans to reach this limit. These plans have been reviewed and approved by the HSE National HR and National Finance and a set of performance indicators are being developed to support a structured oversight process.

The performance indicators will measure performance in metrics that support the ultimate goal of agency cost control. These metrics, which include vacancy and WTE metrics, agency conversion targets and absence rates will be monitored monthly to review progress against the regional plans and to inform any corrective action that may be required.

As part of HSE's 2024 Pay and Numbers Strategy there was a commitment to convert 960 Whole Time Equivalent (WTE) agency staff working in HSE services funded by the Department of Health into HSE employees. As of January 2026, 869 WTE had completed the conversion process and were onboarded as HSE staff.

question.p: 1996. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Health the reason 50 beds and associated supports at the new Central Mental Hospital (CMH) have not opened, given the urgent need and concerns raised in a recent programme (details supplied) for appropriate mental health facilities; if she will give a commitment to ensure these 50 beds are made available immediately; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19888/26]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Health
speech.p: Both I, and the Department of Health in conjunction with the HSE, recognise the need for more person-centred and accessible mental health services. Significant progress has been made towards this objective over recent times under implementation of our national mental health policy Sharing the Vision 2020-2030. Sharing the Vision builds on well-established cross-sectoral links to develop a range of mental health supports to ensure timely and appropriate care in an appropriate setting. This includes improving interlinkages between the specialist HSE National Forensic Mental Health Service (NFMHS) and the judicial system.

It is acknowledged that demand for forensic mental health services has grown in recent years, particularly in the last five years. This includes demand for inpatient beds at the Central Mental Hospital (CMH) at Portrane. The HSE actively manages the CMH waiting list for admission and works closely with the Irish Prison Service to prioritise access for those with the greatest clinical need.

The new National Forensic Mental Health Service (NFMHS) 170-bed complex at Portrane includes a new 130-bed CMH, a 30-bed Intensive Care Rehabilitation Unit (ICRU) and a 10-bed forensic Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service Unit. The CMH relocated to its new state-of-the-art purpose-built health facility in November 2022, transferring 93 patients to the new NFMHS campus. It was always intended that the new facility at Portrane would become operational on a phased basis.

At present, there are 114 operational beds in the CMH, which represents a 20% increase in bed capacity compared to the old hospital in Dundrum. When the 130 CMH beds are fully opened, which is expected by the end of April 2026, this will result in a 37% increase in bed capacity since November 2022.

I secured €2.1 million under Budget 2025 to recruit the staff necessary to open the remaining beds in the CMH, thus ensuring continuity of care for patients there. In addition, I allocated €2.8m in new funding under Budget 2026 for an additional 30 Whole Time Equivalent (WTE) posts to open the first phase of 10 beds in the new ICRU. Opening these beds, will allow patients to be moved more efficiently through the various levels of high-quality supports offered at Portrane, which will in turn allow for further admissions across the wider NFMHS.

When these 10 ICRU beds come on stream towards the end of this year, they will bring the total number of operational beds on the NFMHS campus to 140. This represents an increase of 45 beds or 47% when compared to Dundrum. The new funding provided this year will bring the total NFMHS staff complement to approximately 580 WTEs.

While the Department of Health and the HSE fully appreciates the increasing demands on the prison service, it is important to stress that the NFMHS campus in Portrane is a specialist tertiary healthcare facility. This facility is approved for the purposes of the Mental Health Act 2001 and the Criminal Law (Insanity) Act 2006. Every effort will continue to be made by the health sector to help address acknowledged waiting list pressures to access the NFMHS overall, including on-going recruitment of specialist health professionals.

I will continue to work closely with the HSE to ensure that all aspects of our mental health care programme are improved over this year and beyond to develop capacity in the system to meet future demand. This includes consideration under Estimates 2027 to open the remaining beds at Portrane.

question.p: 1997. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Health the legal measures or other options that are in place in a situation where a family member believes another family member is exercising coercive control over a parent, where that family member has moved in with that parent; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19899/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: Safeguarding adults who may be at risk of abuse is a key objective of my Department, every statutory body under its aegis and every relevant service that interacts with such adults. Currently, there are various structures and processes in place within the health and social care sector, to protect against abuse and ensure prompt action.

There are Safeguarding and Protection Teams in place in each Health Region. Details of these Teams can be found here - www.hse.ie/eng/about/who/socialcare/safeguardingvulnerableadults/safeguarprotectteams.html.

Anyone who has a concern about the safeguarding of adults at risk is strongly encouraged to make contact with the local HSE Safeguarding and Protection Team for that area. Concerns can also be raised with the HSE Safeguarding and Protection Teams via the HSE’s online portal which can be found here -https://adultsafeguardingportal.hse.ie/web/portal/pages/sapublic.
If it is believed that someone is in immediate danger or that criminal activity has occurred, contact should also be made with An Garda Síochána.

In order to expand and strengthen the existing supports and protections for adults at risk of abuse in the health and social care sector, on 9 December 2025 Cabinet approved Ireland’s first ever National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care sector. Publication of the policy is a commitment in the Programme for Government and also in the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030. The policy framework will extend across all public, private and voluntary health and social care services.

Included are a range of both legislative and non-legislative measures that will significantly expand and strengthen existing supports and protections for adults at risk of harm across the health and social care sector (including disability services). The Government has also approved the development of legislation to underpin these commitments.

The HSE Chief Social Worker is preparing an implementation plan for the new policy framework and the Department of Health has commenced the drafting of the General Scheme of a Safeguarding Bill to support implementation of the policy.

question.p: 1998. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Health to consider including stiff person syndrome on the long term illness scheme; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19903/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The Long-Term Illness (LTI) Scheme was established under Section 59(3) of the Health Act 1970 (as amended). Regulations were made in 1971, 1973 and 1975, prescribing 16 conditions to be covered by the Scheme. Further information, including the list of conditions, can be found at:
/www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/lti/about/.

Under the LTI Scheme, patients receive drugs, medicines, and medical and surgical appliances directly related to the treatment of their illness, free of charge. While there are currently no plans to extend the list of conditions, it is important to remember that the LTI Scheme exists within a wider eligibility framework.

People who cannot, without undue hardship, arrange for the provision of medical services for themselves and their dependants may be eligible for a medical card under the General Medical Services (GMS) Scheme. In accordance with the provisions of the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE.

In certain circumstances the HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card, even though an applicant exceeds the income guidelines, where he or she faces difficult financial circumstances, such as extra costs arising from illness. The HSE afford applicants the opportunity to furnish supporting documentation to determine whether undue hardship exists and to fully take account of all relevant circumstances that may benefit them in assessment.
In circumstances where an applicant is still over the income limit for a medical card, they are then assessed for a GP visit card, which entitles the applicant to GP visits without charge.

The issue of granting medical card eligibility based on having a particular disability or illness was previously examined in 2014 by the HSE Expert Panel on Medical Need and Medical Card Eligibility. The Group concluded that it was not feasible, desirable, nor ethically justifiable to list medical conditions in priority order for medical card eligibility. In following the Expert Group’s advice, a person’s means remains the main qualifier for a medical card.

Under the Drugs Payment Scheme (DPS), no individual or family pays more than €80 a month towards the cost of approved prescribed medicines. The DPS is not means tested and is available to anyone ordinarily resident in Ireland. The DPS significantly reduces the cost burden for families and individuals with ongoing expenditure on medicines.

There has been a significant focus on improving access to and the affordability of healthcare services over the last few years. This includes reductions in the DPS threshold, expansion of access to free GP care, and the abolition of all public in-patient hospital charges for children and adults. These measures continue to create a health and social care service that offers affordable access to quality healthcare.

Individuals may also be entitled to claim tax relief on the cost of their medical expenses, including medicines prescribed by a doctor, dentist, or consultant. Relief is at the standard tax rate of 20%.

question.p: 2000. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Health her plans to raise awareness of the new organ donation consent legislation as awareness levels are very low; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19909/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: Part 2 of the Human Tissue (Transplantation, Post-Mortem, Anatomical Examination and Public Display) Act 2024, which commenced on 17 June 2025, provides for the first time a national legislative framework for organ donation and transplant services in Ireland.

Conscious of the need for the public to be informed of the changes to the organ donation system, the Department of Health ran a heralding campaign from 26 May to 16 June 2025. The public awareness campaign communicated the Act’s implications for the public, supported understanding of what deemed consent means, and provided reassurance that peoples' wishes will be respected. The campaign was delivered through a wide variety of channels, including television, radio, outdoor advertising, social media, and online platforms.

This was followed by a further campaign by the HSE to provide additional detail on the changes. These campaigns were supplemented by information available at gov.ie/organdonation and hse.ie/organdonation.
The majority of people in Ireland are in favour of organ donation, and the new system changes the default assumption to one that matches the prevailing public attitudes regarding organ donation.

Consent is the cornerstone of this legislation. Under this new legislation, all adults in Ireland are considered to have agreed to be an organ donor when they die unless they have recorded a decision not to donate on the Relevant Organ Donation Opt-Out Register or are in one of the excluded groups. It is important to reassure people that family members will always be consulted before any action is taken. This is commonly referred to as a soft opt-out system of organ donation.

The obligation to ensure that the public are informed and have access to information about organ donation is not confined to commencement itself. The HSE continue to have responsibility for awareness campaigns on organ donation and has extensive experience in this area.
As the responsibility for awareness campaigns on organ donation lies with the HSE, I have referred the aspect concerning plans for such to the HSE for direct reply.

question.p: 2003. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Health the criteria for referring patients under the National Treatment Purchase Fund from the public waiting list at Beaumont Hospital for treatment in another hospital given patients are waiting 2 years for treatment currently (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19923/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The National Treatment Purchase Fund arranges hospital treatment for patients on a public hospital waiting list by sourcing capacity in the public and private healthcare systems. The NTPF may consider a patient eligible for treatment in a private hospital if they are on a waiting list; are ready, fit and available to proceed with treatment; are deemed clinically suitable for treatment elsewhere by their public hospital; and they are waiting for a treatment that the NTPF has been able to source.

Under the Health Act 2004, the Health Service Executive (HSE) is required to manage and deliver, or arrange to be delivered on its behalf, health and personal social services. The Minister for Health is prohibited from directing the HSE to provide a treatment or a personal service to any individual or to confer eligibility on any individual.
In relation to the particular patient query raised, as this is a service matter, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

[19961/26]

[19962/26]

2013. 2014. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health whether her Department maintains national data on discretionary medical card decisions affecting persons aged over 70 years-of-age; the number of discretionary applications considered for that cohort in each of the years from 2020 to 2025; the number approved; the number refused; and whether any policy review has been undertaken in relation to eligibility thresholds for older persons. [19964/26]

2015. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the number of applications for discretionary medical cards under the general medical services scheme that were refused but where applicants were subsequently granted a GP visit card in each of the years from 2020 to 2025; and whether the Department monitors such outcomes as part of its policy oversight of medical card eligibility decisions. [19965/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 2011 to 2015, inclusive, together.

Under the Health Act 1970, eligibility for a medical card is based primarily on means. The Act obliges the HSE to assess whether a person is unable, without undue hardship, to arrange general practitioner medical and surgical services for himself or herself and his or her family, having regard to his or her overall financial position and reasonable expenditure. In doing this, the HSE assesses each medical card application on a qualifying financial threshold. However, every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card and, in particular, to take full account of the difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. The HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card, even though an applicant exceeds the income threshold where they face difficult financial circumstances, such as extra costs arising from an illness. Social and medical issues are also considered when determining whether undue hardship exists for an individual accessing general practitioner or other medical services.
Where a person's sole household income is derived from Social Protection payment, he/she will be awarded a medical card.
It is important to note that the processing of medical card applications is centralised within the HSE National Medical Card Unit in Dublin.
As part of the question is a service matter, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question.p: 2016. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the recent changes to the practice of issuing permanent contracts to newly qualified paramedics in the National Ambulance Service; the reason for this change; when the change was brought to the attention of her Department; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [19970/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: On behalf of the Minister for Health, Jennifer Carroll MacNeill TD, I would like to thank you for your email.

The National Ambulance Service (NAS) is committed to continued expansion of its frontline workforce in 2026 through a series of planned new developments. As part of this, the HSE has confirmed that full time, permanent contracts are available for all Year Three graduates completing the Paramedic programme with NAS in 2026.

Graduates play a vital role in maintaining workforce capacity by filling vacancies arising from retirements and promotions, as well as supporting the creation of new posts linked to new service development under the National Service Plan. It is essential that NAS can prioritise the placement of these graduates to fill roles in areas with the greatest operational need.

To ensure a fair and transparent allocation of permanent posts, graduates have been asked to apply through a confined internal competition. This approach is consistent with recruitment processes used elsewhere in the health service. Graduates have been asked to select their three preferred locations within a region, and every effort will be made to accommodate first preferences. Where vacancies are oversubscribed, the process being implemented will ensure a fair and equitable allocation of roles.

While completing their BSc. (Hon) in Paramedic Studies, student paramedics hold a Specified Purpose Contract (SPC). As NAS works to fill the permanent positions, year-three graduates have been given a 16-week extension to their SPC to ensure continuity of service and employment for the graduates.

question.p: 2017. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the number of newly qualified paramedics that have recently completed training with the National Ambulance Service but have not been issued permanent contracts. [19971/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The National Ambulance Service (NAS) is committed to continued expansion of its frontline workforce in 2026 through a series of planned new developments. As part of this, the HSE has confirmed that full time, permanent contracts are available for all Year Three graduates completing the Paramedic programme with NAS in 2026.

Graduates play a vital role in maintaining workforce capacity by filling vacancies arising from retirements and promotions, as well as supporting the creation of new posts linked to new service development under the National Service Plan. It is essential that NAS can prioritise the placement of these graduates to fill roles in areas with the greatest operational need.

Following constructive engagement with SIPTU and Unite on 10 March 2026, agreement has been reached on revised arrangements for assigning graduate paramedics to permanent posts. Graduate paramedics will be offered permanent appointment by assignment to funded and approved vacancies as close to their home address as possible, while also taking account of service priorities. Where locations are oversubscribed, offers will be made using the original recruitment panel order, and there are more than enough vacant or new funded posts to accommodate all 69 graduates.

While completing their BSc. (Hon) in Paramedic Studies, student paramedics hold a Specified Purpose Contract (SPC). As NAS works to complete the staff transfer process for existing permanent staff and assign graduates to permanent positions, year three graduates have been given a 16 week extension to their SPC to ensure continuity of service and employment.

Plans for 2026 include a further major investment in the National Ambulance Service: an additional 263 whole time equivalents and €20 million in new funding. This will deliver 21 extra crewed ambulances operating at peak demand, four additional Intermediate Care Vehicles, and continued development of the clinical hub and alternative pathways.

This will deliver 21 extra crewed ambulances operating at peak demand, four additional Intermediate Care Vehicles, and continued development of the clinical hub and alternative pathways.

question.p: 2028. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the position regarding the work of the Implementation Oversight Group established under the National Rare Disease Strategy 2025-2030, including its current priorities and expected timelines for publishing the full implementation plan; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20001/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for the question, The Implementation Oversight Group held its first meeting in February 2026 and meetings are expected to be quarterly. Two people with lived experience of rare diseases are included in its membership and additional patient partners will be invited in due course to support the strategy’s wider implementation.
An implementation plan is in development and will be published in 2026, with regular updates shared with the rare diseases community.

question.p: 2029. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to reduce diagnostic delays for people with rare diseases, given evidence that the average time to diagnosis in Ireland exceeds six years, and that many patients experience initial misdiagnosis; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20002/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The National Rare Disease Strategy 2025 - 2030 recommends the expansion of screening, diagnostics and genetic counselling services in line with best practice to reduce diagnosis times. This is being addressed through expediting prioritisation, review and evaluation process for potential additions to the National Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme (NNBSP), supported by the review team within HIQA. Supporting and enhancing the Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme (NNBSP) will enable further expansion as per the National Screening Advisory Group (NSAC) recommendations. In conjunction with the HSE, the development and implementation of diagnostic pathways will reduce diagnosis times for all people living with a rare disease.

The EURODIS Rare Barometer Survey finds a 5 year average wait time across the EU from the time first symptoms appear to time of diagnosis. This underscores that while Ireland has work to do, this challenge is not unique to Ireland. It further highlights the essential need for international collaboration with our EU counterparts to share expertise.

Having access to efficient genetic and genomic testing services can assist clinicians in reaching a diagnosis, and the rapidly-developing technologies in this field offer the potential to significantly accelerate this process. Testing, diagnostics, analysis, and clinical interpretation are key in terms making an informed decision on the most appropriate treatment path for the patient. The 2025 Programme for Government includes a commitment to support the National Strategy for Accelerating Genetic and Genomic Medicine in Ireland, which will put in place the resources, processes, and infrastructure to take the next steps in delivering future-proof and equitable genetic and genomic services in Ireland.

A number of key strategic measures are being implemented to address challenges relating to testing delays that arise due to the increasing numbers of tests requested by clinical genetic and genomic services. The National Genomic Test Directory for Rare Diseases was launched at the end of 2024 to limit unnecessary test requests and to ensure that only the specific and required genetic and genomic tests for a particular patient are ordered, ultimately helping speed up the diagnosis of rare disease patients.

The above, in combination with work currently being undertaken by the HSE to expand the clinical genetics workforce through strategic hiring of clinical geneticists, bioinformaticians, and other key staff, will serve to increase quality of care and improve the rate at which diagnoses can be returned to all patients including those living with rare diseases. The Department of Health is continuing to work closely with the HSE's National Genetics and Genomics Office in implementing the National Strategy for Accelerating Genetic and Genomic Medicine in Ireland.

question.p: 2030. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the way in which her Department plans to expand Ireland's participation in rare disease research and clinical trials, particularly through the Rare Disease Research Catalyst Consortium and the Rare Disease Clinical Trial Network; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20003/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: The National Rare Disease Strategy 2025-2030 supports a coordinated and structured approach to ensure high-quality rare disease research and innovation in Ireland, by building capability for clinical research (including clinical trials) within the health service. This requires collaboration both nationally and internationally with the pharmaceutical industry, government, people living with a rare disease, patient organisations, healthcare professionals and academic partners. The aim is to increase the opportunities for people living with rare diseases to participate in healthcare research and clinical trials and support healthcare professionals to engage in rare disease research.

The Rare Diseases Clinical Trials Network (RDCTN) (2022-2027) is funded through the Health Research Board (HRB). It aims to increase activity in rare disease clinical trials in Ireland in collaboration with patients, researchers, industry partners and the European Reference Networks (ERNs). The objective is to support how trials are conducted in Ireland, and to improve access for Irish patients to high-quality clinical trials.

The Rare Disease Research and Innovation Catalyst Award (RDCat) is a 3-year HRB-funded project (from December 2023) that aims to boost rare disease research capacity in Ireland. The award brings together key stakeholders by creating a consortium of Irish healthcare professionals, patient representatives and researchers. The goal of the project is to increase the influence of rare diseases patients in research and policy; enhance Irish engagement with national and international networks including RDCTN, ERDERA and ERNs; to increase rare diseases research activity in Ireland.

Ireland has participated in the European Rare Diseases Alliance (ERDERA) since January 2024. ERDERA aims to increase patient need-led research with a focus on new diagnostic methods and pathways, digital solutions, and patient data.

question.p: 2031. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the steps being taken to increase rare disease education and training for healthcare professionals, including the integration of new HSE rare disease training programmes and collaboration with the National Rare Diseases Office; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20004/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for raising this important issue.

As you will be aware, education and training was identified as under the eleven priorities that made up the recommendations published in the National Rare Disease Strategy. Findings from the Patient Forum and Public Consultation highlighted the importance of healthcare professionals being informed about rare diseases. If a healthcare professional is aware of a rare disease, it can reduce the waiting times for diagnosis and allow them to direct the patient and family towards additional supports.
The National Rare Disease Strategy recognises that strengthening education and training is essential to improving diagnosis, care, treatment and support for people living with a rare disease.

Development of rare disease education modules and learning activities is already underway, including the Rare Disease Education Programme for healthcare professionals that was developed by the National Rare Diseases Office.

A key next step is the further integration of rare disease education and training into professional curricula and training programmes. Delivering this will require a collaborative approach involving the National Rare Diseases Office, healthcare professional and health and social care professional training institutions, professional training bodies, and the European Reference Networks.

question.p: 2033. Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 244 of 25 February 2026, when an assessment will be conducted to justify or amend the current application of the non-clinical requirement "from the outset" in the reimbursement of continuous glucose monitoring sensors; if she will authorise funding for the extension of reimbursement to all people who need these sensors in line with clinical best practice as sought by the clinicians who are prescribing these products for seriously ill patients; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20012/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and devices ,therefore, I have asked the HSE for an update in this matter.

The HSE has advised that the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) Rapid Health Technology Assessment (HTA) of Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus was published on 29th September 2023. The published document can be found at: Rapid Health Technology Assessment of Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus | HIQA (www.hiqa.ie/reports-and-publications/health-technology-assessment/rapid-health-technology-assessment-continuous)

The HTA recommended the establishment of a single managed access programme for all CGM systems for all individuals with type 1 diabetes mellitus regardless of age, noting that such a system would need clearly defined criteria for access. Following on from the recommendations in this HTA, the HSE-MMP, in conjunction with the HSE-PCRS, and with the support of the HSE Chief Clinical Officer, introduced an online reimbursement application system for all CGM sensors on 1st December 2023.
Reimbursement support for CGM sensors at this point in time is based on the HIQA HTA and is for patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus regardless of age, who have required insulin from the outset.

To date, a HTA of CGM sensors for people with type 2 diabetes mellitus, type 3c diabetes, or other types of diabetes excluded from the HTA referenced above, such as latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA), monogenic forms of diabetes etc. has not been undertaken. Therefore, there is limited information to support the extension of reimbursement to this cohort, including cost-effectiveness assessment and budget impact of same.

The HSE-MMP and National Clinical Programme for Diabetes, with the support of the HSE Chief Clinical Officer, submitted a joint proposal requesting HIQA to consider including a HTA of CGM for patients with insulin-dependent diabetes in their 2026 workplan. A HTA could identify if CGM technology is clinically and cost-effective in patients with insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes, which populations of patients will likely derive greatest benefit from the availability of CGM, and could support decision making regarding long-term funding and availability of this technology.

question.p: 2034. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Health the steps she will take to ensure that givinostat is available at the earliest opportunity to sufferers of Duchenne muscular dystrophy; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20013/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices; therefore, the matter has been referred to the HSE for attention and direct reply to the Deputy.

question.p: 2035. Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Health if she will implement a plan to support individuals with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, including the development of specialist multidisciplinary teams, and ensuring enhanced and immediate access to givinostat (Duvyzat) and similar treatments. [20014/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: It is estimated that there are approx. 110 people in Ireland living with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and the majority are under 18 years of age. Children diagnosed with muscular dystrophy are under the care of a paediatric neurologist who specialises in neuromuscular conditions. There are specialist clinics based in Children’s Health Ireland, the CRC and at Enable Ireland Cork and Cork University Hospital who provide specialised and expert multidisciplinary care.

The Neuromuscular service (NM) in Beaumont hospital provides outpatient and inpatient service for adults with acquired and hereditary neuromuscular disorders (muscle, peripheral nerve and neuromuscular junction disorders), accepting referrals from all over Ireland.
Givinostat, sold under the brand name Duvyzat®, is a medication used to treat DMD in patients aged 6 years and older. The marketing authorisation holder for this medicine is Italfarmaco S.p.A.
On the 6th June 2025, Givinostat (Duvyzat®) was granted conditional marketing authorisation by the European Commission for ambulant patients (patients who retain the ability to walk).

p.b: Pricing and reimbursement status of Givinostat (Duvyzat®)

speech.p: In terms of pricing and reimbursement, under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 pharmaceutical companies are required to submit formal applications to the HSE if they wish for their medicines to be added to the list of reimbursable items / funded via hospitals once granted marketing authorisation in the EU.

Once a pharmaceutical company submits a pricing and reimbursement application for a new drug to the Corporate Pharmaceutical Unit (CPU) in the HSE, it is generally referred to the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE) if the drug is expected to have a significant budget impact due to its high cost, addresses an unmet clinical need or offers substantial therapeutic benefits over existing treatments, requiring a complex pharmacoeconomic evaluation.

On the 6th August 2025 a pricing and reimbursement application from the Marketing Authorisation Holder for Givinostat (Duvyzat®) was made to the HSE. A full Health Technology Assessment (HTA) was commissioned by the HSE on the 26th August 2025. A full HTA was received from the applicant on the 15th January 2026.

The NCPE assessment concluded on the 3rd March 2026 with a recommendation submitted to the HSE. The HSE Corporate Pharmaceutical Unit (CPU) is the interface between the HSE and the Pharmaceutical Industry in relation to medicine pricing and reimbursement applications.

A technical summary and plain English summary of the report is available on the NCPE website at: [Givinostat (Duvyzat®). HTA ID: 25048 | National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics] (www.ncpe.ie/givinostat-duvyzat-hta-id-25048-2/)
The next step in the process is for the HSE CPU to commence commercial negotiations with the pharmaceutical company with a view to achieving the best possible commercial offer on behalf of the State.
Once negotiations conclude the HSE Drugs Group reviews and considers the pricing application (including the final price offered) and makes a recommendation to the HSE Senior Leadership Team (SLT).
The HSE SLT has final decision making authority on whether to reimburse a medicine.

As the plan to support individuals with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy includes the development of specialist multidisciplinary teams is a service matter, I have the asked the HSE to reply directly to the Deputy on this matter.

question.p: 2036. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Health for an update on the outcome of discussions and engagement between the DOH, HSE and IPU, on the changes to monitored dosing which have been paused which were due to come into effect on 1 January 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20018/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: Firstly, I would like to reiterate that the State has never funded monitored dosage systems (“blister packs”) for any cohort of patient, nor for any of the community drug schemes. There has been no change to that service by the State. It has always been a privately funded service. It is imperative to recognise that the State has not imposed a new charge on the use of “blister packs”.
The changes to phased dispensing, which is different to blister-packing, were agreed under the Community Pharmacy Agreement 2025. These phased dispensing changes are now paused until 31st March 2026.

There is ongoing engagement between my Department officials, the Health Service Executive and the Irish Pharmacy Union. No details on the potential outcome of such engagement are available at this time. I will be in a position to provide an update on these matters at a later date.

speech.from: Minister for Health
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, the HSE operates the EU Treatment Abroad Scheme (TAS), for persons entitled under EU Regulation 883/04. The TAS is a consultant led scheme and allows for an Ireland-based public consultant to refer a public patient who is normally resident in Ireland for treatment in the public healthcare system of another EU member state, the UK or Switzerland. Subject to the EU Regulations and Guidelines, the TAS provides for the cost of approved public treatments in another EU/EEA member state, the UK or Switzerland through the issue of form S2 (IE) where the treatment is:
• among the benefits provided for by Irish legislation;
• not available in Ireland;
• not available within the time normally necessary for obtaining it in Ireland, taking account of the patient's current state of health and the probable course of the disease;
• medically necessary and will meet the patient’s needs;
• a proven form of medical treatment and not experimental or test treatment;
• provided in a recognised public hospital or other institution that will accept EU/EEA form S2 (IE) and;
• is under the control of a registered medical practitioner.
The HSE provides further information for patients on the HSE TAS website: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/treatment-abroad-scheme/.

Patients are advised to contact the HSE TAS office directly, for advice on making an application for treatment abroad, in advance of traveling abroad. Contact details are available on the TAS Website.
As this is a service matter, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly, as soon as possible.

question.p: 2065. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Health the options for funding available to assist adults who do not possess a medical card and who are employed fulltime, to meet the high cost of hearing aids; the pathway to access funding; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [20126/26]

speech.from: Minister for Health (Deputy Jennifer Carroll MacNeill)
speech.p: The Health Service Executive (HSE) provides a range of hearing services free of charge to children under the age of 18. This includes screening, assessment, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and devices, as needed, including hearing aids and cochlear implants. These services are provided to children referred from child health service and school health service examinations who are discovered to have hearing problems.
The HSE also offers assessment and rehabilitation for adult medical card holders, free of charge. This includes the provision, fitting and repair of appropriate hearing aids.

In accordance with the provisions of the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, primarily based on an assessment of means. The HSE may exercise discretion and grant a medical card, even though an applicant exceeds the income guidelines, where he or she faces difficult financial circumstances. The HSE afford applicants the opportunity to furnish supporting documentation to determine whether undue hardship exists and to fully take account of all relevant circumstances that may benefit them in assessment.

The Treatment Benefit Scheme is funded by the Social Insurance Fund and administered by the Department of Social Protection. The scheme provides certain dental, optical, and medical appliance benefits to qualified people who have the required number of PRSI contributions. This includes up to €1,000 for a pair of hearing aids, and up to €100 toward repairs, within a 4-year calendar period. Changes to the Treatment Benefit Scheme, including the level of the grant etc, would be a matter for the Minister for Social Protection.

The National Hearing Care Plan Working Group is jointly chaired by the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive (HSE). Membership of the Working Group is drawn from relevant stakeholders, including clinicians, the Irish Society of Hearing Aid Audiologists (ISHAA), the Irish Academy of Audiology (IAA), and the Department of Social Protection. The Working Group has been tasked with developing recommendations for a holistic model of hearing care in Ireland. A public consultation process is due to commence this month, with the National Hearing Care Plan to be finalised in Q2 2026.
