question.p: 2245. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science when funding will be released for on-site student accommodation for a university (detail supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18909/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: The forthcoming National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026-2035 aims to increase the supply of student accommodation beds for full-time students attending publicly funded Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). A key initiative under the strategy is the Technological Sector Student Accommodation Programme. The institution referred to by the Deputy has submitted a number of proposals which are being evaluated as part of this process. Preliminary Business Cases for developments in relation to this Programme are expected to be provided on a rolling basis throughout 2026.

question.p: 2246. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department has received any communication from organisations (details supplied) regarding the specific building conditions reported on 25 February 2026; his views on reports that students and staff at the Waterford campuses are working in environments with black mould, bracket fungus, and a recorded workspace temperature of 5 degrees Celsius; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18910/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I can confirm to the Deputy that my Department has not received communications from either South East Technological University (SETU), nor the Teachers' Union of Ireland (TUI), on the issues set out in the Deputy's query. As the Deputy will be aware, higher education institutions are autonomous bodies, as set out in legislation with their own management structures and, as such, are responsible for decisions in relation to existing facilities. My Department has disbursed almost €13.59m between 2022 and 2024 to SETU under the Devolved Capital Grant. A further €3.35m was disbursed to SETU last November for the 2026/27 period. The purpose of the Devolved Capital Grant is to provide flexible capital funding to eligible higher education institutions to support small-scale building works. It is a matter for each institution to prioritise the works undertaken within the terms and conditions of the grant. In addition to the Devolved Capital Grant, my Department is currently supporting a number of major capital projects at SETU including:
• Contracts were signed for the five buildings in Higher Education PPP Bundle 2, including Waterford and Carlow, on the 26th June 2025 with construction commencing immediately thereafter.

• The construction period for the Waterford building is 36 months and is expected to be complete in Q2 2028 while the construction period for the Carlow building is 27 months and so is expected to be complete in Q3 2027.
• SETU have received approval for the introduction of a new pharmacy programme and the establishment of a new veterinary school.
• SETU delivered 15 apprenticeship craft training blocks in 2024 under the Apprenticeship Expansion Programme.

question.p: 2247. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether students enrolled in full-time programmes delivered by Teagasc are eligible to access supports under the fund for students with disabilities; whether Teagasc may apply for FSD funding on behalf of it’s students; if so , the mechanism by which such applications should be made; if not, the measures he will take to ensure that students of Teagasc are not disadvantaged in accessing disability supports compared to students in other publicly funded Further and Higher Education institutions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18913/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: The purpose of the Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD) is to assist higher education institutions in ensuring students with disabilities have the necessary assistance and equipment to enable them access, fully participate in and successfully complete their chosen course of study. The FSD is one of the main funding sources supporting participation by students with disabilities in approved higher education courses in Ireland. The FSD for higher education institutions is managed by the Higher Education Authority (HEA) on behalf of the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (DFHERIS). Agricultural colleges are not funded by my Department or through the HEA and are therefore not eligible for FSD Funding.

summary.i: Question No. 2248 answered with Question No. 2271.

question.p: 2249. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department has made changes to funding to the Galway-Roscommon ETB for Adult English language classes; if he is aware of cuts to the number of Adult Education Teachers working in the Galway-Roscommon ETB network and how many teaching roles have been cut; if he is aware of cuts to classes available within the Galway-Roscommon ETB network; whether these cuts were a result of funding cuts; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19283/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: By way of background, the 16 Education and Training Boards (ETBs) provide free English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) classes for those who needs support in developing English language proficiency. Courses range from beginner to intermediate levels, as well as advanced or professional ESOL. In some ETBs, ESOL courses are also linked to career areas such as healthcare, hospitality, and childcare.

Following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine in 2022, significant temporary funding was allocated to support ESOL provision for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection. These temporary allocations enabled ETBs to meet urgent and exceptional levels of demand during the emergency phase of assisting displaced Ukrainians in Ireland.

In 2023, a temporary allocation of €25 million was provided for ESOL. In 2024, the allocation was €15 million, with a further €10 million allocated through the Supplementary Estimates. In 2025, €20 million was again provided on a temporary basis. However, in line with the fiscal parameters for Budget 2026 and the ending of temporary funding, ESOL funding has now reverted to its pre-2022 core allocation of €4.2 million.

While this temporary funding facilitated a rapid expansion of ESOL classes across the country, it was always intended to be time-bound. I wish to acknowledge the fact that ETBs and their staff showed significant commitment, flexibility and creativity in responding to this unprecedented demand, and their efforts supported thousands of newly arrived individuals in integrating into Irish communities.

However, It is important to note that ESOL provision has not ceased. ESOL programmes continue to be delivered across all ETBs within their core allocations. Galway and Roscommon ETB, for example, forecasts that approximately 3,100 beneficiaries will access ESOL provision in 2026, according to its draft Annual Service Plan.

Turning to the delivery of ESOL programmes, it is typically delivered by ETB staff employed under existing grades and terms. This includes tutor roles and the newly established Adult Educator grade. Many delivery staff in the FET sector, including some ESOL tutors and adult educators, are employed on fixed-term contracts. This supports an agile FET system that can respond to changing local education and training needs. These contracts are managed in line with employment law, including the Fixed-Term Work Act 2003.

Under Section 9 of the Act, an employer may not keep an employee on a fixed term contract for more than four years. Employment beyond this requires a Contract of Indefinite Duration, or CID. This applies to all ETB staff except those on teacher contracts.

Many ETB staff who were hired to meet the increased demand after the war in Ukraine have not yet reached the four-year threshold for eligibility for a CID under employment law. ETBs, as employers, are responsible for the management of staffing matters, including the issuance of CIDs, subject to Ministerial consents and approvals as may apply. My Department does not collect contract-level staffing data and does not hold information on the number of fixed-term or non-permanent staff per county.

SOLAS and Education and Training Boards Ireland have been engaging with ETBs in recent months to assess the impact of the cessation of temporary ESOL funding. SOLAS has advised my officials that ETBs are assessing how best to adapt provision within their core allocation.

SOLAS has advised my officials that it is establishing a working group to examine the impacts of the transition away from temporary funding and to explore approaches to maximise ESOL provision within the annual allocation of €4.2 million. Provision for ESOL is relevant across several government departments, and several departments also fund community based ESOL programmes nationally. My officials have also been engaging with these departments since ESOL funding has reverted to the core annual allocation. Should a more coordinated cross-departmental approach to ESOL provision emerge, my Department will work to support that process.

question.p: 2250. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to enhance the supports that are provided to learners with special educational needs in further education, specifically within Youthreach; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19350/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless)
speech.p: The Youthreach programme provides two-years of education and training to young people who leave school with limited qualifications. Learners receive allowances of €45 per week if under 18 years old or €254 per week if over 18 years old. Learners generally achieve certification at National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) Levels 3 and 4. Youthreach offers a distinct alternative to post-primary education which can prove particularly effective for learners with special educational needs. Its structure, staffing, curriculum, and teaching approaches are intentionally designed to respond to learners’ social, emotional, mental-health, and educational challenges. Research shows strong outcomes in social and personal development and in achieving certification. Central to the programme is a learner-centred ethos, ensuring that each participant’s individual learning profile and personal needs are recognised and supported which is an approach especially valuable for those with special educational needs. Additionally, the Special Educational Needs Initiative (SENI) was introduced in 2007 across 20 Youthreach centres identified as having a particularly high prevalence of learners with special educational needs. Under this programme, these centres receive an additional €38,500 annually for every 25 learners to provide enhanced supports. This funding is used for additional staffing, staff development and training to strengthen capacity within centres. The allocation supports mentoring, needs assessment, targeted teaching and learning interventions, and, where appropriate, inter-agency collaboration with relevant local services. I will continue to work to ensure that learners with special educational needs can access the programmes and supports they need to reach their full potential.

p.i: The following revised reply was received on 14 May 2026.

speech.p: The Youthreach programme provides two-years of education and training to young people who leave school with limited qualifications. Learners receive allowances of €45 per week if under 18 years old or €254 per week if over 18 years old. Learners generally achieve certification at National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) Levels 3 and 4. Youthreach offers a distinct alternative to post-primary education which can prove particularly effective for learners with special educational needs. Its structure, staffing, curriculum, and teaching approaches are intentionally designed to respond to learners’ social, emotional, mental-health, and educational challenges. Research shows strong outcomes in social and personal development and in achieving certification. Central to the programme is a learner-centred ethos, ensuring that each participant’s individual learning profile and personal needs are recognised and supported which is an approach especially valuable for those with special educational needs. Additionally, the Special Educational Needs Initiative (SENI) was introduced in 2007 in Youthreach centres identified as having a particularly high prevalence of learners with special educational needs. Under this programme, nineteen centres receive an additional €52,000 annually to provide enhanced supports. This funding is used for additional staffing, staff development and training to strengthen capacity within centres. The allocation supports mentoring, needs assessment, targeted teaching and learning interventions, and, where appropriate, inter-agency collaboration with relevant local services. I will continue to work to ensure that learners with special educational needs can access the programmes and supports they need to reach their full potential.

question.p: 2251. Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the plans to redevelop the old swimming pool on the South Campus of Maynooth University as a critical piece of local infrastructure; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19382/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless)
speech.p: I am aware of ongoing plans under consideration for the strategic future of both the St Patrick's Pontifical and Maynooth University campuses. There is currently an agreement between both autonomous institutes for shared use of the campus facilities. I recently met separately with both executive teams from both St Patrick's and Maynooth University in which we discussed their respective strategic ambitions.

I am aware that engagement is also ongoing with the local authority and other community groups to develop shared facilities, including a swimming pool, and I am fully supportive and encouraging of this and have made this known in my correspondence and engagements with all concerned parties.

More widely, I am supportive of the plans and vision the university has articulated and the benefit of campus facilities for both students and the wider Maynooth community. I recommend that the University continue to engage closely with the HEA as it develops its proposals ensuring alignment and adherence to the relevant requirements on public sector bodies and as it continues to refine its strategic objectives and development. The university's continued growth provides benefits both nationally and locally.

question.p: 2252. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of ETB teachers that have been laid off; the number of others that will follow due to changes in tendering processes; to outline the anomalies and inconsistencies uncovered by the EPS which led to the decision to change the processes; the number of ETB classes that will be cancelled as a result; the reason ETBs locally are being to carry out this tendering process without the resources to do so; the length of time this process will take; the expected impact on the framework; the emergency interventions the minister will take; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19388/26]

2258. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the effects the pause on the use of the Education Procurement Service (EPS) will have on the provision of ETB courses; whether any scheduled classes / education programmes that were meant to be provided through this procurement service have been cancelled; the measures that have been implemented to ensure continuity of classes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20053/26]

2259. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the effects the pause on the use of the Education Procurement Service (EPS) will have on the education system; whether any scheduled classes / education programmes that were meant to be provided through this procurement service have been cancelled; the measures that have been implemented to ensure continuity of classes; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20054/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 2252, 2258 and 2259 together.

Deputies, thank you for your questions. I am pleased to take this opportunity to provide assurances to you both that the cessation of this tender process will not result in any ETB staff being laid off. Moreover, no disruption to learners or to the delivery of services is anticipated It may be helpful to provide some background on the role of Contracted Training. It is a long-established component of Further Education and Training (FET) provision where ETBs engage external training providers where specialist expertise is required or where flexible responsive training is needed to meet local learner or employer demand. These providers are responsible for delivering the programmes using their own staff, and ETB staff do not participate in the delivery of these procured services. Multi-supplier frameworks are a recognised and widely used procurement mechanism across the public service. They support compliance with national and EU procurement regulations, provide access to pre-qualified suppliers, and allow for efficient and cost-effective delivery of specialist services. It is at the discretion of each ETB as to whether to utilise any framework in place or procure contracted training services through their standard local procurement procedures in accordance with public procurement legislation. Turning to the tender in question, it sought to establish the fourth iteration of such a framework for Contracted Training. Education Procurement Services (EPS) issued a Request for Tender (RFT) in September 2025 with a closing date of November 2025. Following the evaluation of submissions, EPS discontinued the process on 19 February 2026 after identifying issues which, in its assessment and following legal advice, required cancellation in the interests of fairness, transparency, and adherence to procurement requirements. As the tender remains within the statutory standstill and post-decision correspondence period, EPS has advised my officials that it is not appropriate to provide further detail at this time. Arrangements are in place to facilitate contracting of training in the period until a new framework is in place. ETBs have used the outgoing framework before its expiry to contract training which will be delivered over the remainder of the academic year. For additional training demands that arise, ETBs will procure contracted training services through their standard local procurement procedures in accordance with public procurement legislation. ETBI has issued draft guidance to ETBs on managing any interim procurement requirements should they arise and has advised that final guidelines will issue during the week commencing 16 March. ETBI is engaging directly with Directors of FET and ETB Chief Executives to coordinate a consistent sectoral approach. Work is also underway between EPS and ETBI on preparations for a new procurement process. A Prior Information Notice is expected to issue shortly to formally signal the forthcoming competition. The objective remains to establish a national panel of suitably qualified providers capable of delivering high-quality, flexible training provision across the ETB network. My Department will continue to work with SOLAS to ensure that learners, training provision, and staff are supported and that continuity of service is maintained throughout the transition to a new framework.

question.p: 2253. Deputy Natasha Newsome Drennan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department will carry out a review of travel subsistence allowance provided by Education Training Boards; into the need for a supplementary allowance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19463/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: My Department is committed to breaking down cost barriers, making Further Education and Training (FET) more accessible than ever before. In FET, courses are free or heavily subsidised. Direct financial supports are also provided to eligible learners. Learners in receipt of certain social welfare payments can transfer to a learner allowance when participating in certain courses. The rate depends on an individual’s social welfare payment. For example, a learner over 18 years old in receipt of Jobseekers' or Supplementary Welfare Allowances will transfer to a learner allowance of at least €254/week with additional payments for qualifying dependants. Those under 18, with no social welfare entitlement, may receive up to €45/week. Learners with underlying social welfare entitlements may keep secondary benefits such as medical cards. Supplementary allowances for food, travel or accommodation are also available to eligible learners. From January 2026, my Department increased learner allowances in line with increases to social welfare increases. Each year, as part of the annual estimates process, my Department reviews the financial supports available to adult learners across the tertiary education sector and adjusts these supports as needed, taking account of the available budget and the measures most likely to deliver the greatest benefit for learners. As part of this work, my Department engages with learners from across the tertiary system through the annual “Cost of Education” event.

question.p: 2254. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department or any body under it’s aegis made a disclosure under Revenue's recent disclosure opportunity to regularise misclassification of self-employment; if so, to provide details of the numbers of workers affected and the amount paid to Revenue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science

Accordingly, this is a Nil Return. My Department does not hold records of any disclosures made to the Revenue Commission by our aegis bodies. question.p: 2255. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to consider the creation of an academy for the fine arts; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19588/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: As the Minister with oversight of the State’s higher education provision, my remit extends to institutions that are overseen by the Higher Education Authority (HEA) and receive public funding in line with national policy. In accordance with the Higher Education Authority Act 2022, all publicly funded institutes are required to adhere to parameters relating to quality assurance and strategic development in accordance with national priorities.
My department supports a number of specialist institutions in the arts and creative disciplines and a number of schools and faculties of art across a the University and TU sectors.

Outside the publicly funded framework, there also exists within the Irish landscape a range of private educational establishments offering programmes across various disciplines, including in specialist areas. While recognising the important contribution made by private colleges and academies, it is important to note that, as autonomous entities, their establishment was not at the direction of the State but arose from the initiative of their respective founders.

There is no legal impediment to the creation of an academy of fine arts under private ownership in the State. However, in order to offer awards on the National Framework of Qualifications, such bodies would need to meet the required quality standards laid down in the Qualifications and Quality Assurance Act, amended in 2019 and upheld under statute by Quality and Qualifications Ireland.

With regard to the potential for an academy to be created within the public system as it stands, while the Department recognises the vital contribution of the fine arts to Irish education, culture, society and the wider economy, in terms of the institutional structures of higher education, our current focus is on strengthening and supporting the existing framework in line with national policy.

I recognise the significant economic and social potential of the creative and cultural sectors, and the opportunities that can be realised through sustained policy and investment support. I would like to outline some of the initiatives that are currently under way in this regard. Under the Creative Youth Plan 2023–2027, officials in my department are progressing work to define the “creative campus” concept. This work includes engagement with the sector to identify best practice and to develop a model which will serve as a resource for institutions wishing to further develop and embed creativity in their practices. In parallel, under the Digital Creative Industries Roadmap 2024–2026, my officials are developing a proposal for Shared Island funding to support research, innovation, and skills development on an all-island basis, aligned with the needs of the digital creative industries. There is also increased collaboration between Ireland and the UK, with the AHRC and Research Ireland jointly supporting a new programme to strengthen the impact of creative economy research and to foster networks between researchers and wider stakeholders.

question.p: 2256. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his Department will review the residency criteria for the Free Fees Initiative and EU fee status as it applies to the children of Irish citizens who were forced to emigrate for economic reasons (details supplied); if he is aware of the significant financial barrier the 'three of the last five years' residency rule places on young Irish citizens who wish to return to Ireland for university; if he will consider an exemption or alternative path for students who can demonstrate a strong link to the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19843/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: Under the Free Fees Initiative, the State pays tuition fees, exclusive of the student contribution, on behalf of eligible students attending approved full-time undergraduate courses. To qualify for funding under the Department's Free Fees Initiative, students must meet the criteria of the scheme including residency, nationality and progression requirements. In order to meet the residency criteria a student must have been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK state for at least three of the five years preceding their entry to an approved third level course. The three out of five-year rule takes cognisance of students who wish to take time out to travel or work abroad. Such students can still meet the residency requirement if they have not been outside the countries referenced above for more than two of the previous five years. Similar, and in some cases more restrictive residency criteria apply in other countries. For example, in the UK, a student must be resident for the three years immediately preceding his/her commencement in college. All students are required to meet the residency criteria of the scheme preceding their entry to an approved third level course. Under EU law, nationals of other EU jurisdictions are entitled to access education on the same basis as Irish citizens. Therefore, it would not be feasible to provide an exemption for persons of Irish nationality only. The Deputy may wish to note that the Government has previously requested the higher education institutions to charge the more moderate EU fee rate for full-time new entrant undergraduate students that hold EU/EEA/Swiss nationality but do not meet the residency clause of the Free Fees Initiative, and who have completed at least five academic years of study (at either primary or post-primary level) in an EU/EEA/Swiss state. Where students do not qualify for free fees funding, for instance where they have already obtained an undergraduate qualification, they must pay the appropriate fee as determined by each higher education institution. These institutions are autonomous bodies and the level of fee payable by students who do not meet the requirements of the Free Fees Initiative is a matter for the relevant institution to determine. Where a student requires guidance on the determination of such fees, it is necessary that they engage with the fees office of the institution they wish to attend. The individual in question may wish to consider options under the SpringBoard+ programme. However, the applicant must be resident in the Republic of Ireland to qualify. Details of the courses under Springboard+ are available at: https://hea.ie/springboard/

question.p: 2257. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to confirm that there are NCI courses which are not eligible for the free fees initiative; to confirm the number of these; the reason they are not covered; if he will reassess the courses so they are covered; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19871/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, the National College of Ireland (NCI) is a private higher education institution. It receives some public funding from the HEA by way of an annual grant and a grant in lieu of tuition fees for approved courses under the Free Fees Initiative. The NCI offers a wide range of full-time and part-time courses at different levels from foundation through to certificate, diploma, degree and postgraduate level. Approved courses under the Free Fees Initiative (FFI) are restricted to full-time undergraduate courses in the public higher education system and a limited number of designated courses in private institutions. My Department does not keep a list of all courses that might be available in higher education institutions at any one time or a list of courses that are ineligible for State funding. However, details of the courses offered by the NCI are available on its website at: https://www.ncirl.ie/Study/All-Courses. It is open to private institutions, like the NCI, to develop and operate courses outside of those approved for State funding, without an expectation of public funding. The extension of free fees funding to additional courses in private institutions only applies where a specific teaching and learning need has been identified by my Department, another Department or the Higher Education Authority (HEA). It remains open to NCI to apply for funding through competitive call processes, such as Springboard+, to provide courses in response to national skill needs.

[20278/26]

[20279/26]

[20280/26]

Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the oversight or intervention that was undertaken by SOLAS and the Dublin and Dún Laoghaire Education and Training Board when it became apparent that the Youthreach centre at a location (details supplied) was experiencing repeated closures and restricted provision; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20281/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 2266, 2260, 2261, 2262, 2263, 2264 and 2265 together.

My officials have been in communication with Dublin and Dun Laoghaire ETB (DDLETB) regarding the closures of Youthreach Balbriggan during the current academic year. DDLETB have confirmed that there were 14 days when the Centre closed at 1pm during the first term due to staffing shortages. DDLETB’s human resources team worked closely with the Centre to resolve this matter, and the staffing issue has now been fully resolved. Temporary closures occurred on 11 days between 10th November and 23rd February because of roof damage caused by severe weather conditions. Due to the associated health and safety concerns, Youthreach Balbriggan decided to temporarily close the Centre to learners until repairs were completed. During this period some learners also maintained a reduced onsite timetable and engaged in blended learning due to reduced classroom space caused by the weather damage. Staff remained fully available, maintaining an onsite presence, to ensure students had access to support and continued their studies and submitted coursework under supervision. DDLETB and Youthreach Balbriggan worked proactively with the landlord to ensure that the repairs were carried out as quickly as possible. The roof has now been fully repaired, and, as of 11 March, all learners have returned onsite to full-time hours on their programme. There are currently 20 students enrolled in Youthreach Balbriggan for the academic year 2025/26. DDLETB are working closely with Youthreach Balbriggan to ensure that additional supports are provided to these learners. Both DDLETB and Youthreach Balbriggan remain committed to ensuring that students receive their full year’s allocation of tuition hours, as well as any additional support necessary to ensure they complete their programmes of education and training on time, to a high standard, and receive their certification.

question.p: 2267. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the expected date on which the performance and evaluation framework for the National Demonstration Park for Modern Methods of Construction will be formally approved; whether the framework will be published; and whether it will include measurable targets relating to housing output, training capacity, and construction efficiency. [20399/26]

2269. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether a written risk assessment or project assurance review was undertaken prior to the decision to commence capital works on the National Demonstration Park for Modern Methods of Construction before the performance and evaluation framework had been finalised; and if so, whether he will publish or summarise that assessment. [20401/26]

2270. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the total capital allocation approved to date for the National Demonstration Park for Modern Methods of Construction; the expenditure incurred to date; and the projected total cost of completion. [20402/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 2267, 2269 and 2270 together.
Greater adoption of Modern Methods of Construction (MMC) is key to the Government’s approach to increasing innovation and achieving productivity gains in the delivery of housing.

In order to help the adoption of innovative solutions in housing delivery, Housing for All and the Roadmap for Increased Adoption of MMC in Public Housing Delivery detailed a National Demonstration Park for MMC as a deliverable.

Currently under construction at the National Construction Training Campus in Mount Lucas, the objectives of the National Demonstration Park for MMC include to provide an accessible ‘flagship’ location for MMC demonstration in Ireland, and in so doing to facilitate the showcasing of innovative MMC products and systems particularly for the housing sector.

The project is being led by the Laois–Offaly Education and Training Board (LOETB), which manages the National Construction Training Campus. The Park is situated on the 33-acre Mount Lucas training site, of which 16 acres are actively used for training and testing. LOETB, through the National Construction Training Campus, offer a wide array of construction programmes, including retrofitting, NZEB, MMC, skilled utilities, and scaffolding.

The development of the Park is supported by a Project Advisory Group consisting of the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (DFHERIS); Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (DETE); Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH); SOLAS; and LOETB.
The total capital allocation approved to date for the National Demonstration Park for Modern Methods of Construction is €9,500,00 for Phase 1. The expenditure incurred to date is €2,425,405.
A number of assessments of the project have been undertaken, including a Stage 1 Civil & Structural Engineering Report, a Site Investigation Report, and a Foundation Solution Report.

A decision was made by the Project Advisory Group to commence capital works in parallel with development of evaluation metrics to ensure delivery of the physical infrastructure in alignment with the expected timing of agreement on the operational framework. In the first instance, these metrics are related to the enabling groundworks and confirming the housing units to be delivered. These details are outlined in Memoranda of Understanding between the relevant parties. Such documents, which reflect internal working agreements between parties, are not typically published.

question.p: 2268. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the membership of the Project Advisory Group overseeing the National Demonstration Park for Modern Methods of Construction; the entities that have entered into Memoranda of Understanding governing the development of the Park; and whether those agreements will be published. [20400/26]

speech.p: Greater adoption of Modern Methods of Construction (MMC) is key to the Government’s approach to increasing innovation and achieving productivity gains in the delivery of housing. question.p: 2271. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the rationale for removing the ringfenced allocation of €20 million for the provision of English language classes (ESOL) across the ETB network; whether he is aware of the cuts to class provision and the cuts to adult education teaching positions as a result of this removal of funding; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20563/26]

2248. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to cuts to the number of adult education teachers working in the Galway-Roscommon ETB network particularly those who have not received a contract of indefinite duration (details supplied); if his attention has been drawn to cuts to classes available within the Galway-Roscommon ETB network; whether these cuts were a result of funding cuts; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [19041/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 2271 and 2248 together.

By way of background, the 16 Education and Training Boards (ETBs) provide free English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) classes for those who needs support in developing English language proficiency. Courses range from beginner to intermediate levels, as well as advanced or professional ESOL. In some ETBs, ESOL courses are also linked to career areas such as healthcare, hospitality, and childcare.

Following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine in 2022, significant temporary funding was allocated to support ESOL provision for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection. These temporary allocations enabled ETBs to meet urgent and exceptional levels of demand during the emergency phase of assisting displaced Ukrainians in Ireland.

In 2023, a temporary allocation of €25 million was provided for ESOL. In 2024, the allocation was €15 million, with a further €10 million allocated through the Supplementary Estimates. In 2025, €20 million was again provided on a temporary basis. However, in line with the fiscal parameters for Budget 2026 and the ending of temporary funding, ESOL funding has now reverted to its pre-2022 core allocation of €4.2 million.

While this temporary funding facilitated a rapid expansion of ESOL classes across the country, it was always intended to be time-bound. I wish to acknowledge the fact that ETBs and their staff showed significant commitment, flexibility and creativity in responding to this unprecedented demand, and their efforts supported thousands of newly arrived individuals in integrating into Irish communities.

However, It is important to note that ESOL provision has not ceased. ESOL programmes continue to be delivered across all ETBs within their core allocations. Galway and Roscommon ETB, for example, forecasts that approximately 3,100 beneficiaries will access ESOL provision in 2026, according to its draft Annual Service Plan.

Turning to the delivery of ESOL programmes, it is typically delivered by ETB staff employed under existing grades and terms. This includes tutor roles and the newly established Adult Educator grade. Many delivery staff in the FET sector, including some ESOL tutors and adult educators, are employed on fixed-term contracts. This supports an agile FET system that can respond to changing local education and training needs. These contracts are managed in line with employment law, including the Fixed-Term Work Act 2003.

Under Section 9 of the Act, an employer may not keep an employee on a fixed term contract for more than four years. Employment beyond this requires a Contract of Indefinite Duration, or CID. This applies to all ETB staff except those on teacher contracts.

Many ETB staff who were hired to meet the increased demand after the war in Ukraine have not yet reached the four-year threshold for eligibility for a CID under employment law. ETBs, as employers, are responsible for the management of staffing matters, including the issuance of CIDs, subject to Ministerial consents and approvals as may apply. My Department does not collect contract-level staffing data and does not hold information on the number of fixed-term or non-permanent staff per county.

SOLAS and Education and Training Boards Ireland have been engaging with ETBs in recent months to assess the impact of the cessation of temporary ESOL funding. SOLAS has advised my officials that ETBs are assessing how best to adapt provision within their core allocation.

SOLAS has advised my officials that it is establishing a working group to examine the impacts of the transition away from temporary funding and to explore approaches to maximise ESOL provision within the annual allocation of €4.2 million. Provision for ESOL is relevant across several government departments, and several departments also fund community based ESOL programmes nationally. My officials have also been engaging with these departments since ESOL funding has reverted to the core annual allocation. Should a more coordinated cross-departmental approach to ESOL provision emerge, my Department will work to support that process.

question.p: 2272. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to concerns related to the lack of provision of online versions of course material in some college courses that are supported under SUSI, for prospective students with medical conditions that prevent them from attending in person classes; if this is under review; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20574/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: While I am not in a position to comment on an individual case, any student who experiences difficulties accessing course materials, including those arising from medical conditions, is generally advised to engage in the first instance with the relevant supports within their further or higher education institution, such as the access or disability support offices. These services are responsible for working with students and academic staff to respond to extenuating circumstances and provide reasonable accommodations and appropriate supports. Ensuring that third level education is accessible and inclusive for students with additional needs is a priority for me and for my department. Institutions are expected to make appropriate supports available to students who declare disabilities or medical conditions, and significant State investment is provided to support access and inclusion across the higher education system. The main form of financial assistance available to further and higher education students is the Student Grant Scheme administered by SUSI. Under the current legislation, fully online and distance learning courses do not qualify for grant assistance under the Student Grant Scheme. My department does, however, recognise that many learners, particularly those with health challenges or caring responsibilities require more flexible forms of learning. In the 2024/25 academic year, a new Part-Time Fee Scheme for Specified Undergraduate Courses was introduced to provide fee support to eligible part-time students attending specified publicly funded undergraduate courses leading to a major award. This includes specified in-person and blended/hybrid courses. Its aim is to provide additional flexibility in respect of course provision to students who are socio-economically disadvantaged. The new scheme does not extend to fully online courses. Higher education institutions are autonomous bodies with responsibility for their own academic programmes and teaching and learning arrangements. As such, decisions relating to the delivery of course materials, including whether materials are provided online, fall within the remit of the individual institution.

question.p: 2273. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to the case of a person (details supplied) with a medical condition that has been prevented them from pursuing a college course due to the lack of online options in the SUSI sponsored course; the actions he will take to address this issue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20575/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: As the Deputy is aware, the decision on eligibility for a student grant is a matter, in the first instance, for the awarding authority, SUSI to determine. The main form of financial assistance available to higher education students is the Student Grant Scheme administered by SUSI. Under the current legislation, fully online and distance learning courses do not qualify for grant assistance under the Student Grant Scheme, and this includes the online programme referenced. My Department does, however, recognise that many learners, particularly those with health challenges or caring responsibilities require more flexible forms of learning. In the 2024/25 academic year, a new Part-Time Fee Scheme for Specified Undergraduate Courses was introduced to provide fee support to eligible part-time students attending specified publicly funded undergraduate courses leading to a major award. This includes specified in-person and blended/hybrid courses. The new scheme does not extend to fully online courses. My Department is committed to supporting flexible forms of learning and will keep the policies surrounding support for part-time students under review. Any future expansion of the parameters of the scheme can only be considered in the context of the budgetary allocation, having regard to overall resource constraints and other competing demands in the further and higher education sector.

question.p: 2280. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline the extent of further and higher education and research links between Ireland and India; how those links can be further enhanced; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20808/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: In 2024, I visited India, where I saw examples of collaboration between Irish and Indian higher education institutions (HEIs). Ireland’s higher education presence in India has expanded rapidly over the last decade.

Indian students now represent the second largest group of international students coming to Ireland from abroad, with approximately 11,000 in Irish institutions in 2024. Indian students make up over 20% of all international students in Ireland, driving skills availability in critical growth sectors. Most Indian students (roughly 90%) choose Ireland to pursue a master’s programme- majorly IT, computing, engineering, science, and business.

Indian universities are rapidly increasing their international linkages, supported by India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which encourages, inter alia, joint degrees and collaborative research, as well international campus set up in India. Irish HEIs have over 30 collaborations with Indian universities, including with: IIT Delhi, IIT Madras, Delhi University, OP Jindal Global University, VIT, Manipal, Symbiosis, Krea University amongst others.

There are also important but relatively low levels of research and innovation links between Ireland and India both at bilateral level and under the EU Framework Programme, Horizon Europe. There are 17 collaborative links across 14 projects under Horizon Europe to date involving Irish and Indian research and innovation partners. Horizon Europe projects also include participants from other countries.

Research Ireland supports about 90 collaborative links between the Irish and Indian research and innovation communities. This includes engagement with the Research Ireland Research Centres such as CURAM (medical devices), CONNECT (future networks and communications) and iForm (advanced manufacturing).

The most effective way for Irish researchers and businesses to engage with counterparts in other countries is through the EU programmes. One of the new features of the current Horizon Europe programme is that countries with advanced research and innovations systems that are not geographically close to Europe can associate to the programme.

In February 2026, the European Commission announced that it is in exploratory talks with India about its possible association to Horizon Europe. India’s association to Horizon Europe would provide new opportunities to enhance collaboration between our countries.

question.p: 2281. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to outline his Department's policy approach to the use of generative AI by students and researchers across the further and higher education system; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [20809/26]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: My Department is adopting a coordinated approach in supporting higher education institutions in their use of generative AI. The Department takes very seriously the potential threat that artificial intelligence (AI) may pose to academic integrity. Academic integrity is, in the first instance, a matter for individual higher education institutions, supported by Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI). QQI established the National Academic Integrity Network (NAIN) in 2019, a peer-led network that helps institutions address academic misconduct, including issues arising from the use of AI tools. NAIN has developed Academic Integrity Guidelines and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Guidelines for Educators to support institutions, learners, and staff. These Guidelines are designed to foster an ethical approach to the use of AI, help students build informed awareness of its capabilities and limitations, and mitigate risks to academic integrity. The Higher Education Authority leads on policy development on the use of Generative AI with regards to teaching and learning in higher education settings. In December 2025, the HEA published Generative AI in Higher Education Teaching & Learning: Policy Framework, a new national framework to guide the responsible, values-based adoption of generative artificial intelligence in Irish higher education. The framework provides a shared reference point for higher education institutions as they navigate the opportunities and challenges presented by generative AI tools in teaching, learning and assessment. It is accompanied by a suite of supporting instruments, principles and guidance designed to help institutions translate policy intent into practice while respecting academic freedom and institutional autonomy.

question.p: 2282. D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta an bhfuil aon dul chun cinn déanta chun cúrsa oiliúna lán-Ghaeilge luathbhlianta a bhunú; agus an ndéanfaidh sé ráiteas ina thaobh. [19812/26]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: Cheadaigh mo Roinn plean oibre don tréimhse ó Mheán Fómhair 2023 go dtí Lúnasa 2026 ar fiú €3,734,500 é don eagraíocht Comhar Naíonraí na Gaeltachta (CNNG) chun seirbhísí a chur ar fáil san earnáil luathbhlianta sa Ghaeltacht.

Anuas air sin, tacaíonn Údarás na Gaeltachta leis an earnáil luathbhlianta sa Ghaeltacht trí dheontas reáchtála a sholáthar do CNNG a chuireann ar a gcumas tacú le bunú, forbairt agus reáchtáil seirbhísí luathoideachais trí Ghaeilge sa Ghaeltacht. Tá breis agus 135 seirbhís luathbhlianta á gcur ar fáil ag CNNG fud fad na Gaeltachta. Sa mbreis air sin, cuireann an tÚdarás tacaíocht ar fáil do Mhuintearas CTR atá ag reáchtáil dhá sheirbhís luathbhlianta - naíolann na nOileán agus naíolann Ghaoth Dobhair. Tuigtear dom go bhfuil Scéim Oiliúna Ghaeltachta á fheidhmiú ag CNNG agus éileamh ard uirthi. Faoin socrú seo, tá páirtnéireacht déanta le Coláiste Chamuis i gConamara agus tá cúrsa deartha go speisialta acu do mhúinteoirí naíonra. Beidh deis, dá bharr, ag múinteoirí naíonra freastal ar chúrsa Gaeilge le Coláiste Chamuis thar deireadh seachtaine i mí an Mhárta. Tá scéim nua comhairleoireachta fógartha le déanaí chomh maith faoina dtabharfaidh comhairleoir luathbhlianta cuairteanna ar naíonraí timpeall na tíre ar mhaithe le tacú le forbairt an tumoideachais sna seirbhísí. Ina theannta seo, tacaíonn obair fho-chuideachta de chuid an Údaráis, Muintearas CTR, le hoiliúint agus tacaíochtaí a chur ar fáil d’earnálacha éagsúla, earnáil na luathbhlianta san áireamh. Tá Muintearas CTR ag súil le tús a chur le forbairt chúrsaí oiliúna ábhartha trí Ghaeilge don earnáil luathbhlianta i mbliana. Cuireadh síneadh bliana ar chostas €1m leis an chomhaontú reatha atá ag mo Roinn le hAcadamh na hOllscolaíochta Gaeilge don bhliain acadúil 2025/26. Bhí beart mar chuid den chomhaontú deontais maidir le cúrsaí céime trí Ghaeilge a fhorbairt don réimse luathoideachais / luathbhlianta ach níor éirigh leis an eagraíocht ceapachán a dhéanamh chuige sin go fóill. Beifear ag amharc ar an mhír seo arís in aon chomhaontú nua a aontófar leis an Acadamh amach anseo. Idir an dá linn, eagraíonn Acadamh na hOllscolaíochta Gaeilge i gcomhair le CNNG sraith ceardlanna d’oibrithe luathbhlianta na Gaeltachta. I 2024 d’fhógair mo Roinn maoiniú de €667,728 thar cúig bliana don eagraíocht, Gaeloideachas Teo., do scéim nua a fhéachfaidh le seirbhís tacaíochta agus forbartha a chuir fáil do naíonraí lasmuigh den Ghaeltacht. Tá an tÚdarás tiomanta i dtreo fhorbairt earnáil na luathbhlianta le fada agus tá aitheanta ag an eagraíocht, agus ag mo Roinn fhéin, an ról fíor-thábhachtach atá ag soláthar seirbhísí luathbhlianta sa nGaeltacht i dtodhchaí na Gaeilge agus na Gaeltachta. Chuige sin, tá oifigigh mo Roinne agus an Údaráis ag obair leis an Roinn Leanaí, Míchumais agus Comhionannais chun plean náisiúnta a fhorbairt don soláthar trí Ghaeilge san earnáil luathbhlianta. Táthar ag súil go mbeidh tacaíochtaí dírithe ar fhorbairt ghné na hoiliúna/traenála trí mheán na Gaeilge cuimsithe faoin bplean seo agus tuigtear go bhfoilseofar é sna míonna amach romhainn.

question.p: 2287. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the percentage of LEADER funding allocated to projects in the respective LAG areas; the amount drawn down; the amount of funding remaining to the allocated (in tabular form); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [18978/26]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: My Department is responsible for the LEADER programme, which is part of Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan covering 2023 to 2027, and which is co-funded by the EU and the Exchequer. At the outset of the 2023-2027 LEADER Programme, Local Action Groups (LAGs) were selected to deliver LEADER following submission of a Local Development Strategy (LDS) setting out how they would implement the programme and utilise the available budget. Funding was then allocated to each area at the beginning of the programme to provide each LAG with greater flexibility in selecting and approving projects which will have a meaningful impact in their areas. Each LAG is expected to manage its budget efficiently across the entire multi annual programming period. The information in the below table shows the total project budget, the amount and percentage approved by each LAG for projects, the amount remaining to the allocated by each LAG, and the project budget claimed, as of 13 March 2026. It should be noted that there are many variables within the data presented, including each LAG implementing their own specific LDS, the budget allocated to each LAG, the diverse range of funding amounts a beneficiary can apply for, possible project underspends, and the effort required to engage with hard-to-reach communities. I fully expect each LAG to utilise its budget over the lifetime of the programme and I look forward to seeing the outcomes of the current programme emerge over the coming months and years, as these projects are delivered.

question.p: 2288. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if, through the Pobal , Clár CSP and Dormant Accounts he can provide a list of all non-statutory organisations in County Mayo funded to provide the following services for older people and the amount of funding provided to each organisation for each service: kitchen and food providing facilities; community cars/ transport for patients undergoing treatments, day centre services, laundry services, home help and home living supports, repairs and maintenance, housing scheme supports, in tabular form. [19175/26]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: My Department delivers a range of funding programmes which seek to improve the lives of all members of our communities, including older people across the country. Details of the thousands of allocations provided by my Department to organisations in communities across the country can be found at gov.ie/drcdg - Funding allocated by the department.

Pobal, an agency under the remit of my Department is responsible for the administration of the Community Services Programme (CSP). CSP currently supports 426 community-based social enterprise organisations nationwide, to provide local services through a co-funding model. Eleven organisations in County Mayo are categorised as primarily providing ‘Services for Older People’; however they also provide services for the wider disadvantaged community. Further details on the eleven organisations are provided in the attached table. I would note that details on all CSP allocations are available on my Department’s website at: gov.ie/drcdg - Community Services Programme - Funding Allocations

The CLÁR programme provides capital funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in designated rural areas which have experienced disadvantage and significant levels of depopulation over a defined period. These supports provide a range of enhancements to facilities and services including transport for the elderly and those who are vulnerable in our communities. Details on relevant CLÁR allocations in County Mayo is provided in the attached table. I would note that details all funding allocated under CLÁR can be found on my Department’s website at gov.ie/drcdg - CLÁR
I was pleased to recently announce the expansion of eligible areas under the CLÁR programme. The scheme is currently open for applications and details can be found on the Department's website.

With regard to the Dormant Accounts Fund, funding is provided via several Government Departments. Legislation in relation to Dormant Accounts sets out that money in the Dormant Accounts Fund to be used by Government to fund programmes or projects which would assist:
the personal and social development of persons who are economically or socially disadvantaged;
the educational development of persons who are educationally disadvantaged; or
persons with a disability
Details on the 2026 Dormant Accounts Fund Action Plan can be found at gov.ie/drcdg - Dormant Accounts Fund

Finally, I would note that some of the services referred to by the Deputy fall under the remit of other Departments and agencies across Government and it would be a matter for them to report on such service provision.
Additional information in the following table: data.oireachtas.ie/ie/oireachtas/caighdeanOifigiul/2026/2026-03-20_pq-2288-18-03-2026_en.docx

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: My Department is responsible for the Seniors Alert Scheme which encourages community support for older people in our communities through the provision of personal monitored alarms to enable them to live securely in their homes with confidence, independence and peace of mind. Funding is available under the scheme towards the purchase by a registered community-based organisation of a personal alarm or pendant and one year of monitoring. The table below shows the number of participants approved for the scheme in the years 2023 to 2025:

The scheme has a budget allocation of €3.2million in 2026, with additional support from the 2026 Dormant Accounts Fund. question.p: 2290. Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when consideration of the review of CLÁR areas nationally, undertaken in 2021 using the 2016 Census of Population data, will be concluded and additional areas added; and if additional areas across County Donegal are being considered. [19400/26]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: The CLAR programme provides funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in designated rural areas. Last year I approved over €14m million for 238 projects under the programme, with funding being provided for community facilities and amenities, community vehicles and specific support for island communities. I was delighted to launch the 2026 CLÁR programme last week with an increased allocation of €12 million. The Programme for Government makes a commitment to carry out a comprehensive review of the eligible CLÁR areas. The statistical analysis for this review based on Census 2022 data has now been completed and I have published the resulting report on my Department's website. Following on from the report, I have added a further 110 Electoral Divisions (ED's) nationwide including 24 additional ED's for Co Donegal. This brings the population covered by the CLÁR programme to over 1 million people for the first time since it was introduced. Full details of all the new and existing EDs are available on my Department's website.

question.p: 2291. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the total amount of funding allocated to respective local authorities in 2025 for all rural schemes provided by his Department (details supplied), including the town and village renewal scheme, CLÁR, LEADER, LIS, outdoor recreation and rural regeneration, by county, in tabular form. [19460/26]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: The details requested by the Deputy regarding funding allocated by my Department to local authorities under rural schemes in 2025 are outlined in the attached table.
The table sets out a breakdown of funding allocated to respective local authorities in 2025 in respect of the following rural schemes:
Town & Village Renewal Scheme (TVRS)
Rural Regeneration and Development Fund (RRDF)
Local Improvement Scheme (LIS)
CLÁR
Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS)
LEADER

Information has been provided in respect of LEADER, but it is important to clarify that LEADER funding is allocated to Local Action Groups on a programme basis and not to local authorities. In addition, it is allocated on a multi-annual basis for the entirety of the 2023-2027 programme, and therefore the 2025 figures provided relate to approval of projects at local level by Local Action Groups, rather than allocations made by the Department. The level of such approvals will naturally vary between areas and years given the structure of the LEADER programme. Funding is drawn down by LAGs as these approved projects progress to completion across the programming period.

The details of a funding allocation of €50m to local authorities in 2024 under the second iteration of the Community Recognition Fund is detailed in the response the Deputy’s previous question (reference Dáil Question Number 611 of 5th March). This funding allocation was based on the number of new arrivals hosted in each local authority area. Some €32m of projects were announced in 2025 which were funded from this €50m allocation. There was no new allocation of funding under CRF in 2025. Given the structure and timing of the schemes in question, allocations made in 2025 and reported in the table may not include all the allocations from a single iteration of a scheme. Further detail in this regard is set out in the following explanatory notes to the attached table. Details in relation to projects allocated funding across schemes are available on my Department’s website. TVRS - Funding of €32.94 million allocated to local authorities in 2025 relates to projects approved for funding under the 2025 Town and Village Renewal Scheme (Main scheme, Project Development Measure and Building or Land Acquisition Measure). RRDF - Funding of €18.9 million was allocated to local authorities in 2025 under an RRDF Category 2 Call for Proposals. Category 2 provides funding to allow Project Leads undertake and complete the initial planning, design and technical works required to of any large-scale project. This sees potential, large scale RRDF projects developed to a stage allowing for greater certainty regarding scope, cost and delivery timelines to apply for further funding under a ‘Category 1’ RRDF application. CLÁR - Funding of €11.94 million to local authorities in 2025 under the CLÁR Programme related to allocations under Measure 1 of the 2025 Programme. ORIS - Funding of €20.66 million was provided to local authorities in 2025 under measures 1, 2 and 3 and the Project Development Measure (PDM) of the 2024/25 Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme. LEADER - It is important to clarify that LEADER funding is not allocated to the local authorities, and is not allocated on an annual basis. For the 2023-2027 LEADER programme, funding was allocated in advance to the Local Action Group (LAG) in each sub-regional areas across the country, and each LAG is then responsible for selecting and awarding LEADER funding to projects within their geographical area. In general, these sub-regional areas are aligned to the administrative county boundaries, except in the case of Dublin and Cork. When viewing these figures, it should be noted that the timing of when LAGs approve projects from within their overall 2023-2027 allocation can vary significantly depending on factors such as the timing of when LAGs were set up, the timing of their engagement with potential applicants to develop applications, etc.
Additional information in the following table: data.oireachtas.ie/ie/oireachtas/caighdeanOifigiul/2026/2026-03-20_pq-2291-18-03-2026_en.pdf
